title: How to improve UiPath OCR with Google Cloud Vision
description: Compare UiPath OCR and Google Cloud Vision and get practical tips to boost OCR accuracy and integration in UiPath workflows.
heading: How to improve UiPath OCR with Google Cloud Vision
body:
If you are tired of UiPath OCR missing text like it is playing psychic hide and seek then Google Cloud Vision might be the adult supervision your automation needs. UiPath ships with built in engines that are fast and cheap for predictable screens. Google Cloud Vision gives you high end models that handle noisy images messy layouts handwriting and many languages at once.

Why pair UiPath with Google Cloud Vision

Use Google Cloud Vision when your documents look like they survived a minor apocalypse. It excels on scans with noise, skewed pages, mixed fonts and non Latin scripts. The tradeoffs are real though. You will pay per request, face a bit more latency, and manage API credentials. Still the OCR accuracy gains for complex inputs can justify everything else.

When UiPath native OCR is enough

  • Consistent, single font screens where speed matters
  • Low volume runs that must avoid cloud costs
  • Offline robots with no internet access

Preprocessing that actually matters

Do preprocessing in UiPath before shipping images out. Most accuracy wins come from cleaning the image not from tweaking the API. Try these steps in your workflow.

  • Convert to grayscale and apply thresholding to boost contrast
  • Deskew and crop to remove borders and UI chrome
  • Increase DPI for tiny print and resample intelligently
  • Remove repeated noise with a median blur when appropriate

How to call the Vision API from UiPath

Create a Google Cloud project and enable the Vision API. Make a service account and download the JSON key for secure machine to machine auth. From UiPath you can either use a community activity that wraps the API or send a plain HTTP request. Send images as base64 in the request body and choose the detection mode that fits your content, such as TEXT_DETECTION or DOCUMENT_TEXT_DETECTION.

The API response includes detected text blocks, bounding polygons confidence scores and language hints. Parse the JSON into structured fields, use confidence thresholds to accept or reject text and apply regex cleanup to normalize results for downstream automation.

Operational tradeoffs and production tips

  • Plan for retries and exponential backoff on transient network errors
  • Monitor cost and set budgets if you process high volume
  • Batch small images to reduce per request overhead where possible
  • Keep a fallback to UiPath native OCR for quick low accuracy needs
  • Log confidence distributions to catch drifting input quality

Bottom line, Google Cloud Vision will rescue many messy OCR cases and boost overall accuracy for RPA text extraction. UiPath native engines still win for speed and cost in simple scenarios. Use both tools where they fit and automate with a tiny bit of humility and a lot of preprocessing.
seo_title: Get better OCR in UiPath with Google Cloud Vision today
seo_heading: Practical UiPath and Google Cloud Vision tips for tougher OCR jobs

title: Send Gmail Emails with UiPath Example
description: Compact guide to send Gmail from UiPath with authentication activity setup and testing for reliable email automation
heading: Send Gmail Emails with UiPath Example Guide
body:
Quick summary for the brave

If you want UiPath to send Gmail messages on your behalf and avoid doing it by hand while wearing pajamas, this guide will get you there. You will learn which package to install, how to authenticate safely, which activity to use for SMTP or Google API, and how to make the whole thing robust enough to survive flaky networks and morning coffee spills.

Install the right package and pick the activity

Open Manage Packages and install either UiPath.GSuite or UiPath.Mail.Activities from the official feed. Yes that sounds basic. Yes people still pick the wrong package and then curse at runtime errors. Pick the correct package and you will save debugging time and dignity.

  • UiPath.Mail.Activities works with SMTP and the Send SMTP Mail Message activity
  • UiPath.GSuite uses the Google API and the GSuite Send Mail activity

Authentication choices that do not make you cry

Pick authentication based on your environment. For quick tests or personal accounts use an app password when two factor authentication is enabled. For production use OAuth with a service account and proper API scopes for sending mail. Follow the Google console steps to create credentials and grant the send mail scope.

Store secrets securely in Secure Credentials or Orchestrator assets. Do not hard code usernames or passwords in workflows unless you enjoy firefighting incidents at 3 AM.

Build the workflow and wire up inputs

Create a focused Sequence or Workflow so your email logic is in one place. That makes debugging less miserable and lets you reuse the sequence for different data sources.

  • Add either Send SMTP Mail Message or GSuite Send Mail activity depending on auth method
  • Populate From, To, Subject, Body, and Attachments using variables and arguments
  • Use arguments so other workflows can call this email sequence with different values

Email formatting and attachments

Use the IsBodyHtml property when sending rich HTML content. Put files into the Attachments collection for multiple files. Send to multiple recipients by separating addresses as required by the activity. Validate email addresses before sending to reduce bounced messages and avoid awkward follow ups.

Test like a human who likes order

Test with a sandbox account first. Wrap the send action in a Try Catch and log failures with useful messages. Add retry logic for transient network errors and consider backoff for repeated failures. Good logging and retries turn flaky automation into reliable automation rather than a drama series.

Checklist before you press run

  • Correct package installed
  • Authentication method chosen and credentials stored securely
  • Sequence or workflow separated from data processing
  • Send activity configured with From, To, Subject, Body and Attachments
  • IsBodyHtml set for HTML content and Attachments collection populated
  • Try Catch plus logging and retry logic in place

If you follow these steps you will have a maintainable UiPath email workflow that supports Gmail via SMTP or the Google API. Do the setup once, then enjoy less inbox drama and more automation that actually behaves.
seo_title: Automate Gmail sends from UiPath without crying over OAuth
seo_heading: Step by step Gmail automation in UiPath with SMTP and GSuite tips

title: Send Email Attachments from Gmail with UiPath Tutorial
description: Quick guide to sending Gmail attachments with UiPath covering authentication packages activities and error handling for reliable automation
heading: Send Email Attachments from Gmail with UiPath Tutorial
body:
Quick summary

Want to send attachments from Gmail with UiPath and not have your robot panic at runtime? This guide walks through Gmail authentication, the right UiPath mail activities, creating a reliable attachments list, configuring the Send SMTP Mail Message activity, and adding the defensive coding that stops your process from melting down. It is short enough to read between meetings and thorough enough to actually work.

What you will need

  • A Gmail account with either OAuth credentials or an App Password for accounts with two factor authentication
  • UiPath Studio and the official Mail activities or the GSuite package installed from Manage Packages
  • Attachments stored with absolute paths and a workflow variable for a List(of String) of file paths
  • Secure asset store for credentials when not using OAuth

Prepare Gmail authentication

Do not enable less secure app access if you can avoid it. Instead create OAuth credentials for the GSuite package or generate an App Password if your account has two factor authentication turned on. App Passwords are simple and fast when you are testing, and OAuth is the long term option when IT insists on proper scopes and token refresh.

Install the right UiPath package

Open Manage Packages and install either the official UiPath.Mail.Activities package or the UiPath GSuite package depending on your chosen auth path. The Mail activities include Send SMTP Mail Message and helper activities for attachments and SSL. The GSuite package gives you OAuth flows and less credential juggling when you scale across many accounts.

Build a robust attachment list

Use absolute file paths. Create a List(of String) variable and populate it with the paths of files you want to attach. Always check file existence before you attempt to attach anything to prevent runs that fail on missing files. A little preflight checking saves a lot of angry emails and status updates.

Configure the Send SMTP Mail Message activity

Set the Host to smtp.gmail.com and use port 587. Enable SSL when using SMTP and supply credentials via a secure asset or let the GSuite package handle OAuth tokens. Fill the To subject body and Attachments properties with variables from your workflow. If you attach multiple files pass the List(of String) to the Attachments property. Keep credentials out of plain text and in assets or secure stores.

Run tests and add error handling

Run in Debug mode and watch the Output panel for exceptions. Wrap the mail send activity in a Try Catch to trap authentication failures missing files and network hiccups. In the Catch log clear messages so future you knows whether to blame credentials the file system or Google. Add retries for transient network errors and fail gracefully when the problem is persistent.

Troubleshooting tips and quick wins

  • If you see authentication errors check that the App Password or OAuth scope matches the package you installed
  • If attachments do not arrive verify file paths and confirm files exist before sending
  • For intermittent failures add a retry and exponential backoff rather than screaming into logs
  • Use secure assets for usernames and passwords instead of embedding them in workflows

Wrap up

This guide covered setting up Gmail authentication installing the right UiPath package building a solid attachment list configuring Send SMTP Mail Message and testing with Try Catch and logging for resilience. Follow these steps and your RPA process will deliver attachments reliably and with less drama than a last minute human.

Tip Keep a small test mailbox for automation testing. It is cheaper than explaining to your boss why 300 test emails landed in Production.
seo_title: Automate Gmail attachments with UiPath for predictable delivery
seo_heading: Step by step UiPath Studio guide for sending Gmail attachments securely

title: How to Send Outlook Emails in UiPath Tutorial
description: Quick guide to sending Outlook emails with UiPath using Send Outlook Mail Message activity with attachments and error handling
heading: How to Send Outlook Emails in UiPath Tutorial
body:
Why use UiPath to send Outlook mail

Yes robots can send email and no they will not stage a mutiny. Using UiPath with Outlook gets you desktop profile access and a sane way to deliver reports alerts and confirmations without finger tapping. This guide walks through the Send Outlook Mail Message activity and practical error handling so your automations do not blow up in production.

Set up the Outlook Application Scope

Drop in the Outlook Application Scope and pick the correct account profile. The scope lets UiPath reuse your desktop Outlook profile for sending and reading folders. If the machine does not have a profile the send activity will behave like a diva and fail.

Quick checklist

  • Confirm the target machine has an Outlook profile
  • Pick the right account if multiple profiles exist
  • Use separate robot accounts for unattended runs when possible

Configure the Send Outlook Mail Message activity

Drag Send Outlook Mail Message into the workflow and populate the usual fields. Use variables for dynamic content and set IsBodyHtml to true if you want fancy formatting or a corporate signature in full color.

  • To use a string or an array for multiple recipients
  • Subject keep it short unless you enjoy confusing recipients
  • Body use a variable when building HTML or dynamic content
  • CC and BCC use them wisely and do not spam

MailMessage variable tip

For complex messages construct a MailMessage variable and assign it to the activity. This makes adding alternate views inline attachments and advanced headers easier and cleaner than wrestling string concatenation.

Attachments and file handling

You can pass a list of file paths into the Attachments property or use Attach Files when working with a single file. Do not assume file paths exist. Verify them first or your robot will dutifully send an empty promise.

  • Check File Exists before adding to attachments
  • Consider zipping large folders when mail servers have limits
  • Use absolute paths and avoid transient temp files when possible

Run in debug mode and handle errors

Always run the workflow in debug mode first. That gives you a chance to catch profile issues authentication popups and permission quirks before someone notices an important report never arrived.

Wrap the send activity in a Try Catch block and log exceptions. For unattended robots log the error and either retry or escalate based on your SLA. Useful logs make accidents easier to fix than a cold stare from a manager.

Common problems and fixes

  • Authentication prompts show up during unattended runs make sure a profile is configured or switch to SMTP with credentials for headless scenarios
  • Attachments not delivered verify file sizes and server limits and try zipping when necessary
  • HTML looks wrong set IsBodyHtml to true and test the output in a real client

Final checklist before you go live

  • Outlook profile exists and is correct on the robot machine
  • Send Outlook Mail Message fields are populated using variables where needed
  • Attachments are validated and zipped if large
  • Try Catch and logging are in place for graceful failure
  • Consider SMTP with credentials for unattended environments without a desktop profile

There you go a solid pragmatic flow for Outlook email automation with UiPath that survives real world quirks. Now go automate those reports and let the robot take the boring tasks while you pretend to be indispensable.
seo_title: Automate Outlook emails with UiPath for reliable reports
seo_heading: Send Outlook messages from UiPath with attachments and error handling

title: Send Outlook Attachments in UiPath Automation Example
description: Learn how to send Outlook attachments using UiPath activities with a short tutorial and practical tips for reliable email automation
heading: Send Outlook Attachments with UiPath Automation Example
body:
Quick warning and promise

This is a short, practical guide for sending Outlook attachments with UiPath that spares you the ritual of guesswork. You will build a tidy Sequence in UiPath Studio use the Send Outlook Mail Message activity and hand it a list of file paths. If that sounds boring keep in mind automation makes you look like a wizard at work while your coffee cools.

What you need before you start

  • UiPath Studio with the Mail Activities package installed and updated
  • Microsoft Outlook installed and a profile logged in so UiPath can talk to the mailbox
  • Files to attach stored in an accessible folder or created by your workflow

Build the workflow

Here is a simple flow that actually works in real life. No voodoo required.

  1. Create a new Process in UiPath Studio and add a Sequence for clarity and fewer mysterious errors later.
  2. Drag the Send Outlook Mail Message activity from Outlook Activities into the Sequence.
  3. Populate the To field with recipient addresses set a clear Subject and Body and give the activity a friendly name.
  4. Provide attachments as a List of String or a String array and assign that to the Attachments argument.

Example attachment variable

attachments = New List(Of String) From { "invoice.pdf", "report.xlsx" }

Assign that variable to the Attachments property of the Send Outlook Mail Message activity. UiPath will pass those file paths to Outlook to compose the outgoing message.

Collect attachments from a folder

Want to avoid hand typing file names like a caveman? Use Directory.GetFiles to gather files programmatically then filter by extension. That scales nicely when the job grows.

folderPath = "C\\Path\\To\\Attachments"  ' set this in a variable
attachments = Directory.GetFiles(folderPath, "*.pdf").ToList()

If you need multiple extensions build a small filter and combine results or use LINQ to filter the array before converting to a List.

Run and debug like a human

Run the workflow and watch the Output panel for exceptions. If messages fail to send confirm Outlook is running and the mailbox is accessible. Sometimes Outlook will pop up a security prompt which will happily ruin your unattended run. Test interactively first.

Wrap it with Try Catch

Errors you should expect include missing files and messaging exceptions. Wrap the Send Outlook Mail Message activity in a Try Catch and log enough context to fix the problem without a séance.

Try
  Send Outlook Mail Message with attachments argument set to attachments
Catch ex As System.IO.FileNotFoundException
  Log Message "Missing attachment" and the file path
Catch ex As System.Exception
  Log Message "Email failed to send" and ex.Message
End Try

Scaling tips that do actual work

  • Loop over a list of recipients and reuse the same attachments variable if appropriate
  • Generate attachments dynamically from reports or templates then add paths to the list before sending
  • Filter Directory.GetFiles by extension to avoid accidentally attaching 10 megabytes of ancient logs

Parting wisdom

Sending Outlook attachments in UiPath is boring and reliable when built correctly. Keep your workflow tidy collect files programmatically handle exceptions and test with Outlook running. Then sit back while the robot does the tedious part and you get the glory.
seo_title: UiPath guide to sending Outlook attachments fast and reliable
seo_heading: Step by step UiPath workflow to attach files and send Outlook mail

title: UiPath Web Scraping Tutorial
description: Step by step UiPath web scraping tutorial covering Data Scraping wizard selectors pagination cleaning and export to Excel for reliable automation
heading: UiPath Web Scraping Tutorial for Practical Data Extraction
body:
Quick overview

If you want tidy spreadsheets and fewer late night debugging sprints, this guide walks through web scraping with UiPath like an adult. You will learn how to set up a project in UiPath Studio use the Data Scraping wizard inspect selectors handle pagination clean results and export to Excel or CSV. Yes this is automation. Yes this will save you time. No you will not miss clicking things forever.

Get started with the project

Start a blank project in UiPath Studio and add the UiPath UIAutomation package. Name your workflows clearly so future you does not curse past you. Launch the Data Scraping wizard from the Design ribbon and pick a sample element. The wizard looks for repeated patterns so pick a row or a card that repeats across the page.

Choose the right scraping mode

  • Data Scraping is your friend for HTML tables and tidy lists.
  • Screen Scraping helps when the page renders with heavy client side magic or when elements are not in the DOM yet.
  • Anchor based selectors matter when elements move around or when content is unstable.

Selectors and Ui Explorer

Review the generated selectors and test extraction in the wizard preview. For fragile targets open Ui Explorer and hunt for stable attributes like id data attributes or text that rarely changes. Wildcards can save you from brittle selectors but use them sparingly. Logging selector values during development helps when things break and you need to prove to someone that the internet is trying to sabotage you.

Handle pagination the practical way

Either capture the Next control in the Data Scraping wizard or build a loop that clicks a Next button checks for a termination condition and waits for the page to finish loading. Use WaitForReady and small delays to avoid race conditions. For infinite scroll you will need a loop that scrolls and waits until no new items appear.

Clean the data and transform it

Use DataTable activities Filter Data Table Assign and Regex to tidy up extracted text. Trim whitespace convert types and normalize dates before export so Excel does not helpfully turn your ID numbers into scientific notation. A few Assign activities go a long way for converting strings to numbers and for handling empty values.

Export and error handling

Write Range writes your final DataTable into an Excel workbook and Write CSV is a simpler option for quick exports. Wrap fragile extraction flows in Try Catch blocks and add logging so errors are visible and actionable instead of mysterious. Test extraction on multiple pages and add replay friendly delays to reduce flakiness.

Final tips and checklist

  • Prefer stable attributes like id or data values over visual position.
  • Use Ui Explorer for complex or dynamic controls.
  • Test on several pages before you celebrate.
  • Add logging and Try Catch so failures are diagnosable and not dramatic.
  • Keep wildcards to a minimum and document any brittle selectors.

Follow these steps and you will have a repeatable UiPath web scraping flow that handles pagination cleans data and produces reliable Excel exports. Automation does the boring work so you can take the credit and enjoy slightly fewer headaches.
seo_title: UiPath web scraping for smart data extraction and Excel export
seo_heading: Complete UiPath Studio guide to selectors pagination cleaning and export

title: Data Scrape Web Text to Excel with UiPath Example
description: Step by step guide to extract web text and export to Excel using UiPath data scraping and Write Range for reliable Excel output.
heading: Data Scrape Web Text to Excel with UiPath Example Guide
body:
Quick overview that does not waste your time

If you want to grab text from a web page and shove it into Excel without turning your morning coffee into tears then this guide is for you. You will use UiPath Studio and the Data Scraping wizard to capture repeating content, tidy it up in a DataTable and write it out with the Write Range activity. Follow the steps and avoid selector drama.

What you need before you start

  • UiPath Studio installed and a working project
  • A target web page with a table or repeating list to scrape
  • Excel installed or the UiPath Excel activities package ready
  • Basic familiarity with selectors and DataTable objects

Step by step workflow

  1. Step 1 - Prepare the page and open UiPath Studio

    Navigate to the page that contains the table or list you want to scrape. Clean the page if you can. Popups, lazy loaded content and rogue adverts will make scraping feel like a puzzle game where the prize is frustration.

  2. Step 2 - Use the Data Scraping wizard

    From the Design tab run Data Scraping and click one example of the repeating element. The wizard tries to detect the pattern and will propose column definitions based on visible structure. Accept the good bits and tweak the rest.

  3. Step 3 - Fine tune selectors and handle pagination

    Preview the extraction in the wizard. Replace fragile absolute selectors with stable attributes or relative anchors. If the table spans multiple pages add a loop that clicks next page or use the wizard options for multiple pages. Remember that a little extra resilience now saves emergency debugging later.

  4. Step 4 - Store results in a DataTable and clean data

    The scraping activity outputs a DataTable. Add simple hygiene steps such as trimming strings, replacing empty values, and normalizing dates or numbers. Log a sample row with Log Message or Write Line to validate extraction without rowing back through the browser.

  5. Step 5 - Export to Excel with Write Range

    Use the Excel activities package and the Write Range activity to push your DataTable into a worksheet. Choose Append when adding to existing files and set AutoFilter if you want a quick tidy up in the sheet. Verify that headers in Excel match the DataTable columns and then save the workbook.

Tips for selector misery prevention

  • Favor relative anchors and attribute based selectors over long absolute XPaths or CSS paths
  • Use Element Exists or Try Catch to handle missing elements gracefully
  • When pages change slightly update your selector logic instead of rewriting the whole workflow

Basic error handling and resilience

Wrap fragile steps in Try Catch and provide fallback actions like retries, waits for elements, or alternate selectors. For pagination failures log a warning and save what you have. For unexpected structure changes add a quick validation step that checks column counts or sample cell values before writing to Excel.

Recap and why this matters

In short you will identify the target page, use Data Scraping to capture the repeating pattern, refine selectors for robustness, clean the DataTable and then export with Write Range. This keeps your RPA workflow predictable and reduces surprise breakage on the next site tweak.

Go forth and automate responsibly. If something breaks remember that relative selectors are your friend and logging is a tiny insurance policy that costs almost nothing and saves reputations.
seo_title: Export web tables to Excel with UiPath and reliable RPA today
seo_heading: UiPath data scraping guide for web text to Excel with robust selectors

title: Web Scrape and Follow URL Links in UiPath Example Tutorial
description: Quick UiPath guide to scrape web pages follow links extract href values and save results to a DataTable for automation projects
heading: Web Scrape and Follow URL Links in UiPath Example Tutorial
body:
This tutorial covers web scraping and following link URLs in UiPath using Data Scraping Get Attribute and browser navigation.

  1. Create a new UiPath project and open the target web page
  2. Capture links using Data Scraping or Find Children plus Get Attribute
  3. Iterate links with For Each and navigate to each URL
  4. Scrape page details and append records to a DataTable
  5. Export results and add error handling

Create a new UiPath process and launch the target web page with Open Browser. Pick a browser that behaves well with selectors and enable a clear timeout setting to avoid flaky runs.

Capture link elements by using Data Scraping for table style lists or use Find Children when the layout is custom. Use Get Attribute to read href from each anchor element and store addresses in a list variable.

Use a For Each activity to loop through the list of addresses. Assign the current address to a string variable and then use Navigate To or Click on the anchor when the element is still present. Navigating by URL often avoids click timing problems.

After navigation scrape required fields with Data Scraping or targeted selectors. Use Add Data Row to append each result to a DataTable so records accumulate in a structured way that supports further processing.

When processing ends write the DataTable to a CSV file with Write CSV. Add Try Catch blocks and small delays to handle intermittent failures slow responses and dynamic content. Consider logging the current URL and row index for faster debugging.

This workflow results in a reliable list of scraped records with visited links and a CSV output that can feed downstream automation or analysis. The pattern scales from small lists to paginated sites with a few adjustments to selector logic and navigation pacing.

Tip

Prefer reading href values and using Navigate To when possible. That approach reduces selector fragility and speeds up runs. Add a visible log of current URL so failures point directly to the problematic page.

title: Fix UiPath Activity Missing and Not Loaded Error
description: Quick fixes for UiPath activities missing or not loading Learn steps to restore packages clear cache and repair Designer activity errors
heading: Fix UiPath Activity Missing and Not Loaded Error
body:
Quick checklist to find lost UiPath activities

So your UiPath activities went on vacation and the Designer is sulking with a not loaded error. Before you start blaming your project or whispering ancient dependency spells try this tidy troubleshooting run book. It covers Manage Packages and project dependencies, reinstalling packages, clearing the package cache, and matching versions so your RPA project stops playing hide and seek.

What usually broke and why you care

UiPath Studio depends on activity packages such as UiPath.UIAutomation.Activities and other third party packages. If a package is missing or the wrong version is referenced the Designer will show missing activities or not loaded errors and the toolbox will look embarrassingly empty. This is a dependency problem, not a personality disorder.

Step 1 - Check Manage Packages and project dependencies

Open Manage Packages in UiPath Studio and look for UiPath.UIAutomation.Activities and any other activity packages your project needs. If a package is absent install the correct version that matches the project target framework and the Studio version. If it is present but flagged as incompatible consider choosing a different version.

Step 2 - Reinstall the problematic activity package

Uninstall the offending package via Manage Packages and then install it again. This forces Studio to fetch a fresh copy and often fixes issues caused by partial downloads or corrupted local copies. Try to pick a major version that matches the rest of your solution to avoid compatibility drama.

Step 3 - Clear the local package cache

Sometimes the cache contains stale files that fool Studio into using garbage. Close UiPath Studio and delete the cached packages saved under your user profile at AppData/Local/UiPath/Packages. If you use custom feeds remove any stale cached feeds too. When Studio restarts it will redownload what it needs.

Step 4 - Restart Studio and reload the project

Yes restarting is boring but effective. Reload the project after the cache clear so dependency resolution can run again. The Designer will rebuild the activity tree and the missing toolbox entries often reappear like nothing dramatic ever happened.

Step 5 - Repair Studio or match versions when problems persist

If the above steps do not help verify that your Studio version is compatible with the activity package versions you are using. Check the package release notes for supported Studio versions and confirm the project target framework. Use the official installer repair option or reinstall Studio if you suspect corruption.

Extra tips that save sweat and late night debugging

  • Pin package versions in project.json when moving projects across machines to avoid version drift and surprise behavior.
  • Prefer stable package feeds for production projects to reduce flaky downloads and unexpected breaking changes.
  • Keep UiPath Studio and important activity packages on supported and tested versions to avoid compatibility issues.
  • If you use custom activity feeds make sure the feed URL and credentials are correct so Manage Packages can actually see the packages.

Recap and last sarcastic thought

Check Manage Packages, reinstall the problematic activity, clear the package cache at AppData/Local/UiPath/Packages, restart Studio, and repair or align versions if needed. These steps fix most activity missing and not loaded errors without invoking rituals or sacrificing your weekend. If the problem still refuses to die open a support ticket and offer your favorite coffee as a peace offering.
seo_title: When UiPath Activities Vanish Fix the Not Loaded Error Fast
seo_heading: Recover missing UiPath activities and stop the not loaded error mess

title: Switch UiPath Orchestrator language back to English
description: Fast steps to change UiPath Orchestrator language back to English and make menus readable again
heading: Switch UiPath Orchestrator language back to English
body:
If UiPath Orchestrator suddenly decided to speak a language you do not know you can make it stop and go back to English without sacrificing your will to live. This guide walks you through the few clicks that fix the user interface language and shows a couple of tricks for stubborn browsers and tenant defaults.

Quick steps to switch to English

  1. Log into UiPath Orchestrator using your normal browser and credentials.
  2. Open your user profile by clicking the avatar or username in the top bar.
  3. Find the language dropdown and choose English from the list.
  4. Save your changes and refresh the page. If nothing changes try a hard reload using Ctrl F5 or open a private browser window.

Details you actually need

Log in and access account settings

Use whatever Orchestrator URL your team uses and sign in. Once you land on the dashboard look for the user avatar or your name usually in the top right. Click that to open account or profile settings.

Change the language setting

Inside your profile look for a language dropdown. Select English and hit the save or update button. Some versions of Orchestrator place language under personal settings or preferences if you do not see it right away.

Reload and verify

After saving refresh the browser. If the interface still looks like a riddle try Ctrl F5 to force a cache bypass. You can also check in a private window to confirm the change without dealing with cookies and cached files.

Troubleshooting when English will not stick

  • Browser cache and cookies may override the new UI language. Clear them and try again.
  • If multiple users report the problem the tenant default language could be set to something else. Ask an Orchestrator administrator to update the tenant settings.
  • Logging out and back in sometimes helps when session data is stale.
  • Try a different browser or a private window to rule out local profile issues.

When the tenant default needs fixing

Tenant level settings can enforce a default language for accounts. If you are not an admin ask your Orchestrator administrator to change the tenant default language. Admins can update tenant or global preferences so new and existing users inherit English as the interface language.

Quick checklist

  • Log in to Orchestrator
  • Open profile and pick English
  • Save and refresh with Ctrl F5
  • Clear cache or use a private window if needed
  • Contact your Orchestrator admin for tenant defaults

There you go. Menus readable again, mystery messages returned to plain English, and you can get back to automating rather than translating. If the problem persists it is probably a cache or tenant policy issue and not a hostile user interface conspiracy.
seo_title: Quick fix to make UiPath Orchestrator use English UI in minutes
seo_heading: Reset your Orchestrator language setting so menus show English

title: How to register for UiPath Orchestrator online
description: Fast step by step guide to register for UiPath Orchestrator online and get a tenant running on Automation Cloud
heading: How to register for UiPath Orchestrator online step by step
body:
Step by step setup for a UiPath tenant with robots and Studio links

Welcome to the glamorous world of RPA onboarding where you will register for UiPath Orchestrator and try not to break anything important. This short tutorial walks you from account signup to a working Orchestrator tenant on Automation Cloud with all the boring but vital bits in place. Expect a little waiting, a little clicking, and a lot of satisfaction when robots start doing the boring work.

Open the Automation Cloud portal

Fire up your browser and go to the Automation Cloud portal. This is the control room for Orchestrator where tenants live and where you will manage robots and deployments. No special hardware required, just an internet connection and the will to automate.

Create or sign in to a UiPath account

Use a business email for production work. Personal emails may let you trial things but a company address saves grief later when teammates get invited. If you already have an account just sign in and skip ahead. If not follow the prompts to create one.

Verify your email and activate the account

Expect a verification email with an activation link. Yes the verification dance is still a thing. Click the link to unlock organization setup options and proceed to tenant provisioning.

Create an Organization and provision an Orchestrator tenant

title: How to Deploy to UiPath Orchestrator Example
description: Step by step guide to publish package deploy processes map robots and run jobs in UiPath Orchestrator with best practices for versioning and monitoring
heading: How to Deploy to UiPath Orchestrator Example Guide
body:
Quick overview

Want to move a UiPath process from Studio into Orchestrator and make it actually behave in production? Good. This guide walks through packaging, publishing to an Orchestrator feed, creating a process, mapping robots and environments, launching jobs, and checking logs. You will learn the versioning and naming habits that keep your automation from turning into a mystery meat sandwich.

Prepare the UiPath project

Before you click publish stop and check the boring but crucial stuff. Set the main workflow, confirm all dependencies, and give the project a clear version in project.json. Treat the version number like a pizza box label. If there is no label then everyone fights over who took the best slice.

  • Validate the main workflow path so Orchestrator knows where to start.
  • Lock down package dependencies so you do not end up with surprise library versions at runtime.
  • Use semantic versioning, for example 1.2.0, and bump it for meaningful changes.

Publish the package to an Orchestrator feed

From UiPath Studio choose the Orchestrator feed or a custom NuGet feed and publish. This pushes a NuGet package to Orchestrator so the platform can keep the deployment history and serve specific package versions to your robots. No magic is invented here just the standard publish flow.

Naming and versioning best practices

Name your package and processes with predictable patterns. That saves searches and your reputation. Include environment hints, module names, or sprint numbers as needed, and never rely on pure memory to find the right build.

Create the process in Orchestrator and select a package version

In Orchestrator create a process by selecting the published package and picking the required package version. Choose a descriptive process name that will still make sense to humans in six months when someone asks why the job failed at 3 AM.

Map robots to environments and assign execution targets

Create an environment in Orchestrator and add the robots that belong there. Then map the process to that environment and assign an execution target. This step avoids the classic issue where your production job runs on a developer laptop because of poor mapping and questionable life choices.

  1. Create an environment and add available robots to it.
  2. Map the process to the environment so Orchestrator knows where to run the package.
  3. Set the execution target to a specific robot or to the environment as a whole for flexible routing.

Start a job or schedule a trigger

Kick off a job manually from the Processes area or configure a trigger for scheduled runs. Use unattended robots for automated production runs without human babysitting. Use attended robots when you need a human in the loop to click things, hold coffee, or provide credentials.

Monitor jobs and review logs

Head to the Jobs page to watch status codes and execution history. Use the Logs page to dive into step level output and to download files if needed. Log filtering will help you find the real error faster than blaming the network.

  • Check status codes to determine success or failure.
  • Filter logs by level or keyword to zero in on exceptions.
  • Download output or assets from the job if the process writes files back to Orchestrator.

Troubleshooting and common pitfalls

Version drift is the usual villain. If a robot is running the wrong package version verify the process package mapping and robot targeting. If jobs fail on one machine but not another check machine level dependencies and package cache. And yes turning it off and on again still works sometimes.

Final checklist and best practices

Follow these rules and you will sleep easier in production. Test every deployment in a development environment first. Keep semantic versioning for clarity. Use predictable names to help on call responders find the right process. And document runbook steps so the next person does not have to guess which button to press under pressure.

Follow the flow in this guide and you will be deploying packages, mapping environments, and monitoring jobs in UiPath Orchestrator with fewer surprises and more control. Predictability will save your career and maybe your weekend plans.

title: Configure UiPath Assistant Machine Key and Orchestrator URL
description: Step by step guide to configure UiPath Assistant with a machine key and Orchestrator URL for reliable robot connection and management
heading: Configure UiPath Assistant Machine Key and Orchestrator URL
body:
Register robots with Orchestrator using machine key and tenant URL

So you want your workstation to stop being a lonely island and become a full fledged UiPath robot. Good choice. This guide walks you through registering a machine in Orchestrator and linking UiPath Assistant with the tenant URL and machine key so your robots can be managed like responsible little automatons.

What you need before you begin

  • Access to UiPath Orchestrator with permission to view or create machines
  • UiPath Assistant installed on the workstation that will run processes
  • The machine entry already created in Orchestrator or ready to be created
  • Network access to the Orchestrator tenant URL and any required firewall rules

Step 1 Get the machine key from Orchestrator

Log into Orchestrator and go to the Machines area. Find the machine record you want to register and copy the machine key shown for that entry. Treat this key like a password because that is essentially what it is. Do not paste it into an open chat window and then blame autocorrect for your troubles.

Step 2 Open UiPath Assistant and find the Orchestrator settings

Launch UiPath Assistant on the workstation. Open the settings menu and choose Orchestrator or Orchestrator settings. This is where you will paste the tenant URL and the machine key to register the robot with Orchestrator.

Step 3 Enter the tenant URL and paste the machine key

In the Assistant settings paste the exact tenant URL you copied from Orchestrator and paste the machine key into the machine key field. Use the exact values shown in Orchestrator to avoid connection errors. Extra spaces or a missing slash are the digital equivalent of tripping over nothing.

Step 4 Match the machine name and set folder mapping

When Assistant asks for the machine name use the same name that appears in Orchestrator. Then select the correct folder or environment for process permissions. Matching names keeps DNS level confusion and human drama to a minimum.

Step 5 Connect and verify the robot status

Click connect and watch the Assistant report a connected status. Then switch back to Orchestrator and confirm the robot shows as online and licensed. If it stays pending recheck the tenant URL and the machine key copy for stray spaces or characters.

Troubleshooting checklist

  • Verify the tenant URL exactly matches the tenant page in Orchestrator
  • Confirm the machine key was copied fully and pasted without extra whitespace
  • Check network connectivity and DNS resolution to Orchestrator
  • Ensure the machine record in Orchestrator is not already bound to another workstation
  • Restart UiPath services on the workstation if registration seems stuck

Tips and final notes

When copying the machine key use a clipboard manager with timestamps so you can recover the original if a paste goes sideways. Also double check that the correct folder mapping is applied so your robot actually has permission to run the intended processes. Follow the steps in order and you will spare yourself a lot of mysterious failures and awkward support tickets.

body:
How to make UiPath Orchestrator run things while you drink coffee

If you want robots that actually behave like robots and run when they are supposed to then triggers are your new best friend. This guide walks you through creating triggers in UiPath Orchestrator for both scheduled runs and queue driven automation. We keep the steps practical and the commentary mildly judgmental.

Prepare the package and release

Start in UiPath Studio and publish the project you want to run. Once it lands in the Orchestrator library it becomes a package that a release can point to. Think of the package as the executable brain and the release as the name tag the Orchestrator uses to find the brain.

Open the Triggers area and add a trigger

In Orchestrator navigate to the Triggers section for the folder or tenant that holds your release. You will see existing triggers and an option to add a new one. Click add and choose whether this trigger should run on a schedule or fire when queue events occur.

Scheduled triggers

Schedule triggers run at defined times. Choose the target release and pick a recurrence. Options include daily weekly or you can use a cron expression for complicated schedules. Set the start time and any recurrence rules. If you like living dangerously test the schedule with a short interval first to confirm everything starts properly.

Queue triggers

Queue triggers respond to queue activity. Select the queue name and add filters or thresholds that control when jobs are created. You can react to new items or to status changes depending on your business logic. This is perfect for event driven automation where humans feed work into a queue and robots eat it for breakfast.

Configure target environment and robots

Make sure the release points to the correct environment and that there are available robots. If your robots are offline they will not show up for jobs and everything will look very unhappy but predictable. Use the Machines and Environments views to verify connectivity and licensing.

Save the trigger and verify runs

Save the trigger and monitor the Jobs or Transactions page to see jobs start. Expect a small thrill when the first job runs on schedule. Use the audit logs and job details to investigate failures or permission problems.

Troubleshooting checklist

  • Confirm the package is published and the release exists
  • Verify the release targets the right environment and robots are available
  • Check permissions for the service account that creates jobs
  • Review audit logs and job details for errors and stack traces
  • Test cron expressions with a short interval to avoid surprises

Best practices and final tips

Prefer cron expressions for complex recurrence patterns because they are flexible and unforgiving. Always test with a fast interval before committing to a production cadence. For queue triggers keep filters tight to avoid flooding the system with tiny jobs. And yes you should monitor jobs and set alerts so you do not find out about failures from an angry user at 8 a m.

Follow these steps and you will have a repeatable pattern for automating recurring and event driven workflows in UiPath Orchestrator. The robots will do the work and you will get the rare joy of predictable automation. Try not to gloat too much when everything works.

This tutorial shows how to create and use UiPath Queues in Orchestrator and build a workflow that adds processes to a queue processes transactions and handles retries.

Create a Queue in Orchestrator

Open Orchestrator navigate to Queues and create a new queue. Set unique name and optional Auto Retry count. Configure Max Retry and queue specific settings so that queue behavior matches the workload.

Add items from Studio

Use the Add Queue Item activity for single items or Add Queue Items for batches. Populate Reference and SpecificContent keys to store structured data. Reference helps trace each transaction across logs and dashboards.

Fetch transactions and process

Monitor and tune

Watch queue metrics in Orchestrator use Filters for failed items and add alerts for sudden spikes. Tune Auto Retry and Max Retry to balance throughput and duplicate processing risk.

This tutorial covered creating a queue in Orchestrator adding items from Studio implementing the transaction pattern handling status updates and monitoring queue health for robust RPA operations.

Tip

Use SpecificContent for structured fields and a unique Reference to avoid duplicates. Enable Auto Retry only when the workflow is idempotent and logs provide enough context to safely retry failed transactions.

Step 5 After processing set the status using Set Transaction Status or use Add Queue Item with annotations when requeueing is needed. Proper status updates keep dashboards honest and audits painless.

Summary of the tutorial The guide covered queue creation retrieval of a queue item reading SpecificContent fields handling errors and marking transaction status. Following these steps yields predictable data extraction from UiPath queues with fewer surprises and fewer scream worthy moments.

title: How to set and increase a UiPath robot's screen resolution
description: Quick guide to set and raise UiPath robot screen resolution for reliable UI automation on headless or remote machines.
heading: How to set and increase a UiPath robot's screen resolution
body:
If your UiPath robot keeps clicking the wallpaper instead of the button you asked for you probably have a flaky display environment. This guide walks through setting a steady screen resolution for remote and headless Windows machines so your RPA workflows stop playing pin the tail on the UI.

Why screen resolution matters for UiPath robots

UI automation is picky. Coordinates and element positions depend on the desktop resolution and DPI scale. If the robot sees a different desktop size than the one you tested the result is misplaced clicks and failing selectors. Consistent resolution and scale across development and unattended hosts reduces flaky runs and endless debugging.

Quick checklist

  • Start a remote display session at the desired resolution such as 1920x1080
  • Set Windows display resolution and DPI scale to match
  • Make the display persistent on headless or VM hosts with a dummy plug or VM display setting
  • Run tests in an interactive session and avoid running the robot as a service

Step 1 Connect with a remote display session

Use RDP or your remote client and choose a display size before connecting. Picking 1920x1080 is a good default because many apps assume a full HD canvas. For interactive debugging force a full screen session so the OS creates a desktop with the expected framebuffer and DPI values.

Step 2 Set Windows display resolution and scale

Open Settings > System > Display and set the Display resolution to the same value you used in the remote client. Match the Scale and layout value so UI elements keep their size. If controls look blurry increase or decrease scale and retest until clicks and typing land on the right controls.

Step 3 Keep a display when nobody is logged on

Unattended machines are the usual culprits. Headless servers often drop the framebuffer when no one is logged on which makes UI automation collapse like a souffle.

  • Cheap fix Plug in a dummy HDMI or VGA display adapter to fake a monitor. The OS thinks a screen is attached and keeps the desktop active.
  • Virtual machines Use the hypervisor display option. Most hypervisors let you lock a virtual display resolution or expose a virtual display adapter so the framebuffer stays alive even when no user is connected.
  • Alternative Use a persistent remote display or a virtual display driver if your environment supports it. The goal is a stable desktop buffer so UiPath can find elements by coordinates and selectors.

Step 4 Test in an interactive session and save settings

Log into the machine interactively and run a full test process that clicks, types, and moves the mouse. If actions land in the wrong places raise the resolution or adjust scale then retest. Once everything lines up save the display settings and reboot to confirm they persist.

If you run robots as Windows services switch them to run under a logged in user account or as a scheduled task configured to run only when the user is logged on. Services do not provide a true interactive desktop and will break UI automation.

Troubleshooting tips

  • Blurry UI If text and controls are blurry check DPI scale mismatches between the client and the remote host.
  • Shifted clicks Verify the remote client resolution matches the OS resolution on the target machine.
  • VM driver issues Ensure the guest additions or VM tools are installed so the virtual display supports the resolution you want.
  • Keep environments consistent Use the same resolution and scale in dev, test, and production to avoid surprises.

Follow these steps and your UiPath robot will stop auditioning for a magic show and start doing useful work. If it still misbehaves double check the display adapter and the account the robot runs under. Consistent display settings are the least glamorous but most effective way to stop flaky automation.
