title: UiPath Invalid Machine Key Error Fix
description: Fix UiPath Invalid Machine Key error with clear steps to copy and register the machine key in Orchestrator and troubleshoot common causes
heading: UiPath Invalid Machine Key Error Fix Guide
body:
So your UiPath Robot showed up to register and Orchestrator told it the machine key was invalid. That is not a personality critique, it is a configuration problem that we can fix without summoning IT exorcists. This guide walks you through the practical steps to diagnose and resolve the Invalid Machine Key error so your automation can get back to doing boring repetitive things for you.

Where to get the machine key

Navigate to the Orchestrator Machines page and open the specific machine entry. Copy the value labeled machine key. That alphanumeric secret string is what lets a Robot register with Orchestrator. If you copy it wrong you will get an invalid key error and then we all suffer together.

Common reasons the key is rejected

  • Wrong key pasted into UiPath Assistant or Robot settings
  • Targeting the wrong machine record in Orchestrator
  • Duplicate machine names in the tenant causing registration conflicts
  • Network or TLS handshake problems blocking registration
  • Robot service needs a restart to pick up new settings

Step by step fix

  1. Copy a fresh machine key. Open the machine entry in Orchestrator and generate or copy the current machine key. Do not try to memorize it, that will not help.
  2. Paste into UiPath Assistant or Robot Tray. Open Orchestrator settings in UiPath Assistant or the legacy Robot Tray and paste the machine key into the Machine Key field then press connect. If you still see invalid key it usually means the wrong machine record was targeted or the copy failed.
  3. Verify the machine name. Compare the local host name on the robot machine with the Orchestrator machine name. On Windows use the hostname command or System Properties. If names do not match Orchestrator will try to attach the key to the wrong machine record.
  4. Remove duplicate machine entries. If a rogue registration exists remove the extra machine records from the tenant. Duplicate names are a classic cause of this error because Orchestrator gets confused and so do we.
  5. Restart the Robot service. Restart the UiPath Agent or Robot service on the workstation and then try registration again. Sometimes the Robot is just being dramatic and needs a reboot.
  6. Check network and TLS. Ensure outbound traffic to Orchestrator is allowed on port 443 and that TLS 1.2 is enabled between the Robot and Orchestrator. Modern Orchestrator will refuse older TLS versions. Firewalls and corporate proxies are common villains here.
  7. Recreate the machine record if needed. If registration still fails delete the existing machine entry in Orchestrator and create a new machine or use a machine template. Generate a fresh machine key and attempt registration again.
  8. Assign environment and license. After successful registration add the Robot to the correct environment and confirm a license is available in the tenant. A missing environment assignment can look exactly like a registration failure when the problem is really placement.

Quick checks to run first

  • Confirm you copied the entire key without trailing spaces
  • Check UiPath Assistant or Robot Tray for the exact error message
  • Look at Robot logs and Windows Event Viewer for TLS or network errors
  • Ask a coworker if they touched Orchestrator settings and then glare politely

When to escalate

If you followed the steps above and the Robot still cannot register gather the Robot logs and a screenshot of the Orchestrator machine entry then open a ticket with your Orchestrator admin or UiPath support. Provide the time of the attempt and any network error messages. That will save everyone time and reduce the number of passive aggressive chat messages.

Follow these steps and most Invalid Machine Key headaches go away. If not you have a clearer error story to hand to support and you will look suspiciously competent while doing it.
seo_title: How to fix UiPath Robot registration when machine key fails
seo_heading: Step by step troubleshooting for UiPath invalid machine key and registration

title: Simple Apache Struts 2.5 Example
description: Short tutorial to set up a minimal Apache Struts 2.5 app with action mapping configuration and a JSP view
heading: Simple Apache Struts 2.5 Example Tutorial
body:
This tutorial shows how to build a minimal Apache Struts 2.5 application from project setup to a working action and JSP view

  1. Create a new web project
  2. Add Struts 2 dependencies
  3. Configure web.xml and struts.xml
  4. Create an Action class
  5. Create a JSP view and run the app

Create a new web project Start with a Maven or Gradle web project. Use group and artifact names that avoid embarrassing package choices. Choose packaging war if deployment to Tomcat is planned.

Add Struts 2 dependencies Add the Struts core jar and required plugins to the build file. Include a logging library for sane stack traces. The build tool will handle transitive jars, so manual jar juggling is optional unless nostalgia is a hobby.

Configure web.xml and struts.xml Register the Struts filter in web.xml and add a simple struts.xml value stack mapping. A minimal action mapping looks like this inside struts.xml

< action name="hello" class="com.example.HelloAction"> < result> hello.jsp< /result> < /action>

Create an Action class Write a plain Java class that extends ActionSupport or implements Action. Keep logic tiny for a demo. Example

public class HelloAction extends ActionSupport { public String execute() { return SUCCESS } }

Create a JSP view and run the app Add a simple JSP named hello.jsp that reads request attributes or uses OGNL for form data. Deploy to a servlet container and visit the mapped URL to see the action in glorious functioning form.

This walk through covered creating a project adding dependencies configuring Struts mapping writing a basic action and producing a JSP view so the framework can do its job and respond to a request

Tip

Enable the Struts dev mode during development by setting the constant struts.devMode to true. That provides clearer error messages and saves hours of guesswork when the configuration file has betrayed the developer.

title: Apache Struts with Eclipse and Tomcat Example
description: Step by step guide to build and run an Apache Struts app using Eclipse and Tomcat with configuration tips and deployment hints
heading: Apache Struts with Eclipse and Tomcat Example
body:
This tutorial shows how to build a simple Apache Struts web application using Eclipse and Tomcat and then deploy and test the application.

  1. Install Java and prepare the IDE
  2. Configure Tomcat in Eclipse
  3. Create a Dynamic Web Project
  4. Add Struts libraries and configuration files
  5. Create Action classes and JSP views
  6. Configure web descriptor and Struts config
  7. Deploy and test on Tomcat

Install Java and prepare the IDE

Install a recent Java JDK and point Eclipse to the Java home. Use the Eclipse package for Enterprise Java Developers to avoid missing tools. This step is boring but mandatory.

Configure Tomcat in Eclipse

Add a Tomcat runtime in Eclipse preferences and create a server in the Servers view. The server will host the web application during development and testing.

Create a Dynamic Web Project

Create a new Dynamic Web Project in Eclipse and choose a web module version that works with the chosen Struts release. This project becomes the workspace for controllers views and config files.

Add Struts libraries and configuration files

Add necessary Struts jars to the WEB INF lib folder or use Maven to manage dependencies. Add the main Struts configuration file named struts-config.xml and place mapping details there.

Create Action classes and JSP views

Implement Action classes to handle form data and business logic. Create JSP pages for form input and result rendering. Use tag libraries supplied by the framework for cleaner pages.

Configure web descriptor and Struts config

Edit web.xml to register the Struts filter or servlet and map URL patterns. Confirm that struts-config.xml references actions and forwards correctly.

Deploy and test on Tomcat

Start the Tomcat server from Eclipse and publish the project. Use a browser to hit the mapped URL and verify the action dispatch and page rendering work as expected.

This guide covered setup of Java Eclipse and Tomcat creation of a web project adding Struts dependencies creation of Action classes and JSP views and deployment to the application server. The sequence will get a basic Struts app running and ready for enhancement.

Tip

Use Maven to manage Struts dependencies to avoid jar version conflicts. Keep configuration files small and add logging early to simplify debugging.

title: Struts Hello World Example v. 2.5
description: Step by step guide to build a Hello World app with Apache Struts 2.5 using Maven action class and JSP view
heading: Struts Hello World Example v. 2.5 Tutorial
body:
This tutorial shows how to build a minimal Hello World application using Apache Struts 2.5 and run the example on a servlet container.

  1. Set up the Maven web project and add Struts dependency
  2. Configure web filter and Struts XML
  3. Create an Action class to handle the request
  4. Build a JSP view and map the result
  5. Deploy to Tomcat and test the action

Set up the Maven web project with packaging war and add dependency for struts2-core and any logging bridge. Use a standard directory layout so future developers do not cry.

Configure the web layer by registering StrutsPrepareAndExecuteFilter in web.xml and create struts.xml to map action names to result pages. Yes XML makes a cameo in this show.

Create an Action class that returns SUCCESS and exposes a getter for a message property. Keep the class simple and testable. No framework magic required beyond a standard POJO.

Build a JSP view that prints the message using expression language or OGNL tag from the Struts taglib. Map the JSP path as the result for the Action class in struts.xml.

Package the project as a WAR and deploy to Tomcat or any servlet container. Open the browser and call the mapped action URL to see Hello World delivered by the framework.

The tutorial covered a working flow from Maven setup to a running action and JSP view. Following the steps results in a minimal Struts 2.5 Hello World app that demonstrates the core request flow and configuration pieces while keeping surprises to a minimum.

Tip

Enable development mode in Struts properties while building to see helpful errors and stack traces and disable that mode for production deployments.

title: Struts Tags and the Struts 2 Taglib library for HTML in JSPs
description: Practical guide to using Struts 2 taglib to produce HTML in JSPs with form binding and best practices
heading: Struts Tags and the Struts 2 Taglib library for HTML in JSPs
body:
This tutorial shows how to use the Struts 2 taglib to generate HTML in JSP pages and bind form fields to Action properties.

  1. Register the tag library in the JSP
  2. Create forms and UI using Struts tags
  3. Bind tags to Action properties
  4. Customize attributes and themes
  5. Render pages and test behavior

Registering the tag library requires adding the correct taglib directive and ensuring the web application has the Struts 2 libraries on the classpath. This gives JSP access to the tag set that replaces raw HTML for common UI concerns.

Using forms and UI tags reduces repetitive markup. Use the form related tag to wrap fields and the field related tags to render labels inputs and selects. The tag library helps with parameter encoding validation messages and URL generation without manual string assembly.

Binding tags to Action properties allows automatic data flow between the page and the server side. Name attributes on tags map to getters and setters on the Action class. Validation and type conversion occur before the Action sees the values which keeps controllers pleasantly uncluttered.

Customizing attributes and themes gives control over rendered HTML and CSS hooks. Set CSS classes id attributes and theme values to match the front end design system. If the default templates are too opinionated override templates or supply custom templates in the classpath.

Rendering and testing means deploying the JSP and exercising forms while watching for form parameter names and validation messages. Browser developer tools reveal generated markup which helps when a style rule refuses to cooperate.

Quick recap The tutorial covered registering the tag library using the JSP directive using Struts tags for forms and fields binding those tags to Action properties customizing presentation and testing the rendered HTML. The Struts 2 taglib trades manual markup for declarative binding and consistent behavior which most developers find worth the small learning curve.

Tip

Tip Use meaningful name attributes that match Action property names and prefer the framework conversion over manual parsing. When debugging turn on the framework dev logging to see how values travel from form to Action so the mystery of missing form values disappears faster than one might expect.

title: Struts Form Handling and Annotation Action Mappings Tutorial
description: Learn Struts form binding validation and annotation based action mappings for Java web apps with clear steps and practical tips
heading: Struts Form Handling and Annotation Action Mappings Tutorial
body:
This tutorial teaches form binding validation and annotation based action mappings in Struts for Java web applications

  1. Prepare project and dependencies
  2. Create form bean and action class
  3. Add annotation based action mappings
  4. Handle submission and validation
  5. Define result views
  6. Test flow and fix issues

Prepare project and dependencies Use a standard Maven or Gradle setup and include Struts core and commons dependencies. The chosen build tool manages library versions and keeps the classpath tidy.

Create form bean and action class Define a plain Java bean for form fields with getters and setters. Create an action class that exposes properties that match form field names. The framework performs automatic data population when the form posts.

Add annotation based action mappings Use annotations on the action class to declare mappings instead of XML. Example annotations look like @Action("save") and @Result(name="success", location="/success.jsp"). Annotation mappings keep configuration close to handler logic which reduces context switching.

Handle submission and validation Implement validation either with validation framework annotations or with validate methods on the action. Return logical result names such as success or input to control flow. Validation feedback binds back to form fields and helps users correct mistakes without guessing.

Define result views Map logical result names to JSP or other view resources using the annotation results. Keep view paths consistent and avoid hard coded references scattered across multiple classes.

Test flow and fix issues Run through form submission scenarios for happy path and validation errors. Check parameter names, action mapping values and result locations when unexpected pages appear. Logging helps trace the dispatch sequence when behavior seems mysterious.

The tutorial covered how to wire Struts form objects to action classes configure annotation based action mappings perform validation and map results to views. Following the step list allows a clean form handling flow with minimal XML and clearer action organization

Tip

Prefer small focused actions and annotate with clear value names. Naming consistency makes debugging less soul crushing and keeps the project readable for future developers

title: Form Validation Example Apache Struts Tutorial
description: Learn Apache Struts form validation with ActionForm rules JSP integration and client side checks for robust web forms
heading: Form Validation Example Apache Struts Tutorial Guide
body:
This tutorial shows how to implement server side and client side form validation in Apache Struts using ActionForm and the Struts validation framework.

  1. Prepare project and Struts configuration
  2. Create ActionForm and validation rules
  3. Build JSP form with error display
  4. Implement Action class and wiring
  5. Test and refine with client side checks

Step 1 Prepare project and Struts configuration. Add Struts libraries to the web application and register the Struts servlet in web xml. Create or update struts config xml to declare form beans and action mappings. This gives a routing map for form processing so nothing wanders off into exception land.

Step 2 Create ActionForm and validation rules. Define a Java form bean with getters and setters for each field. Add validation rules in validation xml or use annotations depending on Struts version. Keep rules simple and use required and type checks first because basic mistakes cause the most drama.

Step 3 Build JSP form with error display. Use Struts tag library or standard JSP markup to bind form fields to the ActionForm. Add error placeholders so users see friendly messages next to the offending fields rather than a stack trace that scares everyone.

Step 4 Implement Action class and wiring. In the Action class validate business logic beyond the basic field rules and forward to success or input pages based on validation results. Populate form and request attributes for redisplay so users do not lose typed values after a validation failure.

Step 5 Test and refine with client side checks. Enable Struts client side validation or add custom JavaScript for immediate feedback. Client side checks reduce round trips while server side rules remain authoritative and secure.

The example demonstrates how to combine ActionForm beans validation xml action mappings and JSP error handling to create reliable form flows. Following these steps produces predictable validation behavior and cleaner user experience without magical surprises.

Tip

Tip Keep validation rules DRY. Centralize common checks in validation xml or reusable methods so maintaining rules across forms does not become a craft of heroic debugging.

title: Annotations Struts 2 Actions and Properties Files
description: Learn how to use annotations with Struts 2 actions and properties files as message bundles for localization and cleaner action code
heading: Annotations Struts 2 Actions and Properties Files
body:
Welcome to the thrilling world of Struts 2 localization where annotations make your code less sad and message bundles do the heavy lifting for i18n. This guide is short on ceremony and long on practical steps you can follow without crying into your IDE.

Why use annotations with Struts 2 and message bundles

XML configuration is fine if you enjoy scrolling through verbose files. Annotations keep routing and view mapping next to the action logic so refactors do not feel like spelunking. Message bundles move user facing strings out of code so translators do not hunt for them inside Java methods.

Get your build ready

Add the Struts 2 web framework jars and enable annotation scanning in your Maven or Gradle build so the container can find @Action and @Result annotations at deployment. If you want more magic add the Convention plugin to reduce explicit mappings.

Checklist

  • Include Struts 2 core and any plugins you need in dependencies
  • Enable annotation support so scanning runs during deployment
  • Add the Convention plugin when you prefer inference over typing

Create annotated action classes

Put @Action and @Result annotations on your class or methods to avoid bulky XML. This keeps the handler logic close to the routing rules and makes the project easier to refactor.

@Action("hello")
@Result(name = "success", location = "/hello.jsp")
public class HelloAction extends ActionSupport {
  public String execute() {
    // call getText("welcome.message") to fetch localized output
  }
}

Extending ActionSupport gives you getText for free. If you prefer testing or inversion you can implement TextProvider instead and wire things more explicitly.

Message bundles and properties files

Create message files such as messages.properties and messages_en.properties and place them on the classpath under resources. Use simple keys like welcome.message and error.required so translators can read them without a map.

File placement

  • src/main/resources/messages.properties for default messages
  • src/main/resources/messages_en.properties for English
  • Use locale suffixes for other languages

Fetch messages from actions and views

Call getText("welcome.message") inside action methods or JSP tags. This centralizes user facing strings and gives you locale aware rendering without manual string assembly. JSPs and FreeMarker templates can call the same API so you do not duplicate logic.

Map results with annotations and the Convention plugin

Use @Result to point to JSPs or FreeMarker templates. Annotation based result mapping removes the need to open global config just to change a view path. The Convention plugin can even infer view locations so you type less and sleep more.

Test localization and fallback behavior

Switch the Accept Language header in your browser or set the locale programmatically in a session to test i18n. Remove a translation key from a locale file to verify fallback to messages.properties. If the key is missing entirely Struts will return the key name which is better than silent failure.

Quick test ideas

  • Change the browser Accept Language header and reload a page
  • Programmatically set the locale for an authenticated session and confirm UI text changes
  • Delete a key in messages_fr.properties and confirm fallback to default messages.properties

Summary and best practices

In short add the Struts 2 dependencies and enable annotation scanning. Create action classes with @Action and @Result so your routing stays readable. Move strings into properties files named by locale and call getText to retrieve them. Use the Convention plugin for less configuration fuss and always test locale fallback so users and translators are both happy.

If you want one liner goals here you go

  • Add dependencies and enable annotations
  • Create annotated actions and message bundles
  • Fetch messages through the Struts API and test localization

Now go refactor that XML and enjoy the smaller file count. Your future self will thank you or at least file fewer bug reports.
seo_title: Get Struts 2 Actions to Play Nice with Message Bundles
seo_heading: Annotate Struts 2 actions and use properties files for i18n

title: Struts 2 i18n ApplicationResources as MessageResources
description: Configure Struts 2 to use an ApplicationResources properties file as the message bundle and enable localization with getText and the i18n interceptor
heading: Struts 2 i18n ApplicationResources as MessageResources
body:
If you want Struts2 to stop guessing at your text and actually use a neat ApplicationResources bundle for localization then this short guide will get you there with minimal ritual chanting and no dead sacrifices. You will learn how to add properties files to the classpath how to point Struts at them and how to make getText and the s text tag read the right language.

Prepare the properties files for localization

Put a file named ApplicationResources.properties on the classpath for default messages. Add language variants with the usual suffixes for locale fallback like ApplicationResources_fr.properties or ApplicationResources_es.properties. Save files in UTF 8 so accented characters do not turn into embarrassing mojibake.

File naming and encoding

  • Use consistent keys across all language files to avoid missing text surprises
  • Prefer UTF 8 encoding unless your build pipeline already converts things reliably
  • Keep the files on the classpath so the resource bundle loader can find them

Configure Struts 2 to use the bundle

Tell Struts which resource bundle to use by adding a constant in struts.xml or by setting it in struts.properties. That points the framework at ApplicationResources without drama.

<constant name="struts.custom.i18n.resources" value="ApplicationResources" />

Or in struts.properties use a single line like this

struts.custom.i18n.resources=ApplicationResources

Use messages in actions and views

Actions that extend ActionSupport get access to getText where you pass the key and receive localized text. No dark magic required.

// in an ActionSupport subclass
String label = getText("some.key")

In JSPs the Struts tag reads the same bundle via the s text tag

<s:text name="some.key" />

Enable locale switching

Add the i18n interceptor to your stack or to the specific action so a request parameter can change the user locale at runtime. The default parameter name is request_locale but you can choose a different name if it fits your routing better.

<interceptor-ref name="i18n" />

Send a request with the parameter request_locale set to fr US es or any supported locale and the framework will pick the appropriate properties file based on standard locale fallback rules. You can also rely on the Accept Language header from browsers if you prefer less user input.

Testing and debugging

  • Load a page then change the request_locale parameter to confirm the right bundle loads
  • Check that keys exist in all language files so fallbacks are predictable
  • Enable verbose logging for resource bundle loading if something refuses to behave

Quick recap and tips

Create ApplicationResources files with language suffixes. Configure Struts via the struts.custom.i18n.resources constant in struts.xml or struts.properties. Use getText in Java actions and the s text tag in JSP views. Add the i18n interceptor to allow users to switch locale with a request parameter.

Final tip Keep your keys tidy and your encoding consistent and you will avoid the kind of bugs that make you question all of your life choices.
seo_title: Use ApplicationResources for Struts 2 Localization That Works
seo_heading: Configure Struts 2 to load ApplicationResources for i18n and locale switching

title: Exception Handling with Struts 2 Annotations
description: Handle exceptions in Struts 2 with annotations for cleaner actions central error mapping and maintainable Java web apps
heading: Exception Handling with Struts 2 Annotations Guide
body:
Why use annotation driven exception handling in Struts 2

If you are tired of try catch soup spread across every action class then annotations are your new best friend. Annotation based exception handling keeps your action code focused on business logic and moves the unpleasant work of mapping exceptions to a single place that is easy to read and test.

This technique uses the Struts 2 exception interceptor together with @ExceptionMapping and @ExceptionMappings on actions or package level. The result is less XML clutter and fewer moments where you stare at a stack trace and ask yourself who broke production today.

What to wire up first

Short checklist that actually helps

  • Add the Struts 2 exception interceptor to your interceptor stack so framework level handling is available
  • Annotate actions or packages with @ExceptionMapping or @ExceptionMappings to map exception classes to result names
  • Create JSP or controller results that match the mapped result names like error or validationError
  • Log exceptions with context and run automated tests that simulate failure paths

Example mapping snippet

@ExceptionMapping(exceptionName="java.lang.Exception", result="error")
public class MyAction extends ActionSupport {
    // action code here
}

When the action throws an exception that matches a mapping the interceptor returns the named result and your view shows a friendly page instead of a stack trace. Yes this is the mild mannered adulthood of error handling.

Interceptor stack and configuration

Make sure your interceptor stack includes the exception interceptor. If the stack is missing the exception interceptor then annotations will look pretty but do nothing. Verify that your struts configuration loads the stack at startup and that the stack is used by your actions or packages.

Logging and diagnostics that do not suck

Log exceptions with a logger and include action name, parameters and a correlation id when available. A correlation id helps you trace a single request across logs and systems when things go sideways. Keep log messages factual and avoid dumping user secrets or full stack traces into user facing pages.

Best practices to avoid painful surprises

  • Prefer mapping specific exception classes rather than catching everything with java.lang.Exception. Specific mappings reduce accidental masking of bugs
  • Reuse a small set of error result pages so you do not accidentally expose implementation details in many places
  • Keep user facing messages friendly and concise and avoid showing stack traces in the UI
  • Write automated tests that simulate exception flows and assert that error pages hide sensitive information

Quick summary

Annotation based exception mapping in Struts 2 gives you centralized, readable, and testable error handling. Add the exception interceptor, map exceptions with annotations on actions or packages, define matching result pages, log with context and test the flows. Do that and your action classes can get back to doing what they were meant to do which is handling business logic instead of babysitting error plumbing.

Bonus tip keep a short list of result names and add correlation ids to logs so debugging feels slightly less like a ritual sacrifice.
seo_title: Struts 2 annotation based error handling for modern Java apps
seo_heading: Annotate actions and packages to centralize Struts 2 error responses

title: Apache Struts Debugging Tools Tutorial v2.5
description: Learn practical debugging tools and workflows for Apache Struts 2.5 to trace requests inspect parameters and diagnose common errors fast
heading: Apache Struts Debugging Tools Tutorial v2.5 Explained
body:
This tutorial shows how to use debugging tools for Apache Struts 2.5 to trace requests inspect parameters and diagnose common errors.

  1. Enable development mode and configure logging
  2. Activate debug interceptors and parameter dumps
  3. Attach an IDE remote debugger and set breakpoints
  4. Inspect the value stack and action properties
  5. Reproduce the issue and analyze logs and stack traces

Enable development mode and configure logging Use struts.devMode set to true in the configuration during local testing. Set the logging framework level to DEBUG for Struts packages so framework messages appear in log output. More verbose logs mean fewer wild guesses.

Activate debug interceptors and parameter dumps Turn on the debug interceptor provided by the framework or add a parameter dump interceptor to the stack. That displays incoming request parameters and provides a quick view of what reached the action versus what was expected.

Attach an IDE remote debugger and set breakpoints Start the server with remote debugging enabled and attach from an IDE. Place breakpoints in action execute methods and interceptor code to pause execution and inspect local variables and the call stack. This beats guessing based on logs alone.

Inspect the value stack and action properties Use value stack inspection to see current object graph and OGNL evaluations. Check action properties for unexpected nulls wrong types or misbound parameters. That often reveals mapping problems or missing converters.

Reproduce the issue and analyze logs and stack traces Try a minimal repro case while collecting logs and full stack traces. Look for root causes such as class cast exceptions missing resources or configuration mismatches. Trace from top of stack down to the first project class for the true culprit.

The tutorial covered practical steps for turning on verbose feedback tracing parameters using framework tools attaching a debugger inspecting the value stack and using logs to resolve common Struts 2.5 problems. Follow the sequence during local debugging to narrow down failures faster and with less drama.

Tip

Enable devMode only in development and add conditional logging around suspicious code paths. Create a minimal reproducible request so logs and breakpoints focus on the true failure rather than a giant noisy trace.

title: Struts Input Validation with Annotation Based Validators
description: Learn Struts input validation with annotation based validators for cleaner action classes and easy rule maintenance with examples and testing tips.
heading: Struts Input Validation with Annotation Based Validators
body:
If your idea of form validation is trusting the browser and crying later then this guide is for you. Struts2 lets you pin validation rules right next to the action properties using annotations. That keeps the rules readable during code review and prevents surprise bugs that show up in production like expired milk.

Why use annotation based validation in Struts

Annotations keep validation logic near the fields and methods they protect. That means less hopping between files during debugging and fewer forgotten checks hiding in obscure XML. It plays well with Java in MVC style web development and is a good fit for small to medium form sets.

Step by step workflow

Add annotations to fields or getters

Put validation annotations on the action class fields or their getters so rules travel with the code. Here is a minimal example for an email field that must not be empty and must look like an email.

@RequiredStringValidator(fieldName="email", message="Email required")
@EmailValidator(fieldName="email", message="Email format invalid")
public String getEmail() {
    return email;
}

Placing annotations on getters makes them visible in IDE inspections and during code review. If you prefer fields that works too. The point is proximity to business logic not where you like to type.

Enable annotation processing in Struts configuration

Tell Struts to scan action classes for validation metadata. Most projects just add the validator annotations library and flip a small config flag so the framework will pick up the annotations when actions are created.

Pick built in validators or write custom validators

Use the built in validators for common checks like required values, length, number ranges and regex matching. If your rules get weird or business specific write a custom validator class and reference it with the appropriate annotation. A custom validator typically extends FieldValidatorSupport and focuses on one rule so your action stays tidy.

Handle validation failures and show friendly messages

When validation fails add messages to the action error collection and return the input result that maps back to the original form page. User friendly messages and focusing the first invalid field improve UX and cut down on help desk tickets.

  • Use addActionError or addFieldError to attach messages to fields
  • Return the input view so the user sees the form again with errors preserved
  • Keep messages clear and polite so users do not get passive aggressive

Test rules with unit tests and manual checks

Automated tests catch regressions faster than manual QA or angry emails. Write unit tests for your action validation logic and add a few manual scenarios for edge cases. Adjust messages and error severity as user feedback arrives.

Best practices and tips

  • Prefer annotations for small to medium form sets because proximity improves readability and maintenance
  • Use custom validators for complex logic to keep action classes focused on flow not parsing
  • Keep error messages actionable. Tell the user what to do next not what they did wrong

In short, use Struts2 annotations to make form validation maintainable and predictable. You get fewer late night bug hunts, clearer code reviews, and forms that behave like they were tested by humans instead of feral raccoons.
seo_title: Clean Struts form validation with annotation based rules
seo_heading: Use annotations in Struts2 to keep validation close to your Java code

title: How to use Apache Struts interceptors tutorial
description: Compact tutorial on Apache Struts interceptors covering config custom interceptor creation and testing for request preprocessing and postprocessing
heading: How to use Apache Struts interceptors tutorial
body:
This tutorial shows how to add and use Apache Struts interceptors for request preprocessing and postprocessing in a Struts application.

  1. Understand interceptor purpose and stack
  2. Configure interceptor in struts.xml
  3. Create a custom interceptor class
  4. Apply interceptor to actions or packages
  5. Test and debug interceptor flow

Step 1 Understand that the interceptor role is to wrap action execution with common logic such as authentication logging timing and transformation of request and response data

Step 2 Open the Struts configuration file and declare interceptor and interceptor stack entries then reference that stack from an action or package mapping The configuration determines the execution order and parameters

Step 3 Implement a custom interceptor by extending com.opensymphony.xwork2.interceptor.AbstractInterceptor or implementing Interceptor Then override the intercept method and call invocation.invoke to continue the chain Remember to manage resources and handle exceptions

Step 4 Attach the interceptor stack to specific actions or to the entire package Use include and exclude patterns when certain actions must skip the logic This avoids surprising behavior when multiple stacks combine

Step 5 Run the application and trace logs to verify pre processing and post processing stages The usual suspects for bugs are wrong class names missing mapping and forgotten invocation.invoke calls Use breakpoints when the debugger feels like cooperating

Summary The tutorial walked through the concept of interceptors configuration of stacks creation of a custom interceptor attaching the interceptor to actions and basic testing strategies Following these steps gives consistent request handling without copy paste code across actions

Tip

Keep interceptors single purpose and small The less magic inside a single interceptor the easier the debugging When dealing with sensitive logic prefer explicit action checks instead of global interception

title: Apache Struts Unit Testing with JUnit Tutorial
description: Learn how to unit test Apache Struts actions with JUnit and mocks for fast reliable tests and better controller coverage.
heading: Apache Struts Unit Testing with JUnit Tutorial
body:
Why unit test Struts actions and not the whole server

Unit testing Apache Struts actions is like checking the engine before you drive the car into the ocean. It is faster and less tragic. Focused action testing with JUnit and Mockito keeps your controller logic honest without booting the full Struts container which is slow and fragile. You still get confidence that parameters are parsed validation rules run and service calls are made as expected.

Set up testing dependencies the fast way

Add JUnit and a mocking library such as Mockito to your build tool. If you use Maven enable a lightweight test profile so unit tests run quick and do not pull in heavy framework bits. If Struts test support classes are available include them so you can reuse any helpers for request simulation.

  • JUnit for test runner and assertions
  • Mockito for mocking services and collaboratos
  • Struts test support if your version provides it
  • Maven profiles to separate fast unit tests from slower integration tests

Write focused Action tests and keep them tiny

Test one action method at a time. Instantiate the action class directly set only the properties you need and call the method under test. Avoid starting a servlet container or Struts stack. Smaller tests mean less flakiness and faster feedback when a developer breaks something trying to be clever.

Typical test flow

  • Create the action under test and set request parameters or model fields
  • Mock service collaborators and stub responses you control
  • Call the action execute method or the specific action method
  • Assert the returned result name and any model or field changes
  • Verify interactions with services using argument captors when needed

Mocking request data and services without drama

Use Mockito to create mock services and to stub methods that would otherwise hit a database or network. For request parameters and session attributes either use light test helpers from Struts or supply simple POJOs that mimic what the action expects. The goal is isolation. If your test touches a real database or a web API it is not a unit test and your CI pipeline will hate you for it.

What to verify

  • The action returned the correct logical result name such as success or input
  • Important fields on the action or the model were set correctly
  • Service methods were called with expected arguments using verify and argument captors
  • No unexpected side effects like file writes or network calls occurred

Keep tests deterministic in continuous integration

Run your unit tests on every commit. Use Maven profiles to run only fast unit tests during CI and reserve slower integration tests for nightly runs. Avoid flaky tests by removing randomness controlling time and stubbing external systems. Tests that run quickly and consistently make refactoring feel less like a leap of faith.

When to write integration tests instead

If an automated test truly needs the full Struts container then label that test as integration and run it less frequently. Integration tests are useful but expensive. Keep your unit test suite focused on controller logic parameter handling validation rules and service interactions while saving end to end checks for a smaller integration suite.

Quick checklist to stop the bleeding

  • Add JUnit and Mockito and include Struts test helpers
  • Instantiate actions directly and avoid full container startup
  • Mock request parameters session attributes and service collaborators
  • Assert result names state changes and service interactions
  • Use Maven profiles and run fast tests in CI on every commit

Follow this pattern and your Struts2 action testing will be reliable fast and surprisingly pleasant. You will still encounter bugs but the tests will point to the problem instead of screaming at you from a stack trace that only a wizard could understand.

title: How to Integrate Struts and Ajax Tutorial
description: Learn how to integrate Struts and Ajax to add asynchronous calls in Java web apps for faster partial updates and clean JSON responses.
heading: How to Integrate Struts and Ajax Tutorial for Java Web Apps
body:
Practical Struts2 with Ajax for JSP asynchronous updates and JSON

Want parts of your JSP page to update without a full reload and without summoning ancient browser rituals? This guide walks you through integrating Struts and Ajax so your Java web app behaves like it knows what it is doing. You will see how to wire Struts2 actions to asynchronous requests, return JSON, and update DOM fragments while doing minimal ritual sacrifice to web.xml.

Quick overview

Here is the short version for impatient developers or anyone who enjoys skipping to the last page. You will:

  • Define Maven dependencies for Struts2 and the json plugin
  • Ensure the Struts filter is in web.xml
  • Create an Action that returns data for Ajax calls
  • Map the action in struts.xml and choose a json or stream result
  • Use fetch or jQuery to call the action and update a DOM fragment
  • Test with browser dev tools and server logs

Step 1 Setup project and dependencies

Use Maven or your build tool of choice. The important bits are struts2 core and the json plugin so you can return JSON without hand rolling serializers. A minimal Maven snippet looks like this.

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.apache.struts</groupId>
  <artifactId>struts2-core</artifactId>
  <version>2.5.x</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.apache.struts</groupId>
  <artifactId>struts2-json-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>2.5.x</version>
</dependency>

Also confirm web.xml has the Struts filter mapping. No magic here just a servlet filter that routes requests into the framework.

Step 2 Choose your Ajax method

You can use jQuery if you enjoy short code and mild nostalgia, or use the modern fetch API when you want fewer dependencies. Both talk HTTP which Struts understands perfectly.

// fetch example
fetch('/app/myAction.action', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ id: 123 })
})
.then(r => r.json())
.then(data => updateFragment(data))
.catch(e => console.error('Ajax failed', e));

Step 3 Implement a Struts2 Action

Implement a standard Action or extend ActionSupport. Read parameters, call your service layer, and expose getters so the json plugin can pick them up when serializing the response.

public class UserAction extends ActionSupport {
  private int id;
  private User user;

  public String execute() {
    user = userService.findById(id);
    return SUCCESS; // the json plugin will serialize getters
  }

  public void setId(int id) { this.id = id; }
  public User getUser() { return user; }
}

Step 4 Map action and choose result type

In struts.xml map the action name to your class and use the json result type when returning JSON. If you prefer manual control you can use a stream result and write to the HttpServletResponse.

<action name="user" class="com.example.UserAction">
  <result type="json"/>
</action>

Using the json plugin means getters become JSON properties. Keep payloads small and avoid sending entire object graphs unless you enjoy long responses.

Step 5 Build the JSP fragment and wire the call

In the JSP include the tiny script that triggers the Ajax request and updates a fragment. Update only the DOM nodes that need it to keep things snappy.

<div id="user-info">...</div>
<button id="load-user">Load user</button>

<script>
document.getElementById('load-user').addEventListener('click', function(){
  fetch('/app/user.action', { method: 'POST', body: new URLSearchParams({ id: 123 }) })
    .then(r => r.json())
    .then(json => {
      document.getElementById('user-info').textContent = json.user.name;
    })
    .catch(err => console.error(err));
});
</script>

Step 6 Test and debug the flow

Open the browser dev tools network tab and watch the request and response. Confirm content type is application/json when you expect JSON. Server side check logs for mapping problems or null pointers. If the json plugin is not serializing what you expect verify your getters and avoid circular references in model objects.

Troubleshooting tips

  • If you get 404 check action name and filter mapping in web.xml
  • If you get HTML instead of JSON ensure result type is json or you are writing the response manually
  • If JSON is empty verify your action populated fields before returning SUCCESS
  • Use the console to log the parsed JSON so you do not debug in the dark

Wrap up

Integrating Struts2 and Ajax is mostly predictable plumbing. Add the right dependencies, map the action, return JSON from the server, and let fetch or jQuery update the DOM. You get faster UI updates and less page reload drama. If anything breaks blame the network, then your code, and finally the person who suggested a clever database trick at 2 a.m.
seo_title: Make Struts and Ajax Play Nice in Your Java Web App Right Now
seo_heading: Practical Struts2 with Ajax for JSP asynchronous updates and JSON

title: How to Push an Empty Git Folder or Directory Example
description: Learn how to push an empty Git folder to a remote repository using a placeholder file and a few simple git commands for clean commits.
heading: How to Push an Empty Git Folder or Directory Example
body:
If you have ever stared at a fresh project and wondered why your carefully made folder is missing from the remote repo you are not alone. Git does not track directories that contain nothing that it cares about. That is by design and it saves everyone from committing clutter and regret. Here is a polite way to convince Git to keep the folder around without stuffing it with useless junk.

Why Git ignores empty folders

Git tracks files not folders. If a directory is empty Git will pretend it never existed. This helps keep the history meaningful but it also means that folder structure can vanish when you push. That is bad when the folder is a placeholder for future assets or an expected layout for other developers.

Use a placeholder file like .gitkeep

The usual trick is to add a tiny tracked file in the empty folder. The convention is a file named .gitkeep. It has no special magic in Git. It simply gives Git a reason to record the directory. You can create it from the command line or from your editor. Then commit and push like you always do.

mkdir myfolder
touch myfolder/.gitkeep
git add myfolder/.gitkeep
git commit -m "Add empty folder placeholder"
git push origin main

Yes it is a small lie that keeps the repo honest. Use .gitkeep to signal intent to other developers and to wonky CI scripts that expect a folder to exist.

Alternative with gitignore rules

If you prefer not to add dot files you can use a allow rule in your .gitignore to keep the folder structure while ignoring most files. This method requires a little care so that at least one tracked file remains in every folder you want to preserve.

# in .gitignore at the repo root
myfolder/*
!myfolder/.gitkeep

This tells Git to ignore everything inside myfolder except the .gitkeep file. It is neat when you want to keep folders but avoid accidental commits of temporary files or builds.

Developer tips and common gotchas

  • Pick a consistent placeholder name across the project so other developers know what to expect.
  • Do not add large binary files just to force a folder to exist. That is rude and pointless.
  • If a folder still does not appear check your branch and confirm the commit was pushed to the correct remote branch.
  • On GitHub the empty folder will show up once the placeholder file is pushed to the remote repository.

Troubleshooting

If you run git status and do not see the new file try running git add with the exact path. If the commit did not push double check the remote name and branch. Common commands that help are git remote -v and git branch -r. If you used a GUI sometimes the app filters dot files so the folder may look empty even though .gitkeep is present.

In short add a tiny tracked file like .gitkeep or use a careful gitignore rule then commit and git push. You will get the folder structure you need and your coworkers will stop yelling at you in the issue tracker. That alone is worth the tiny extra file.
seo_title: How to Make Git Track an Empty Folder and Push It to GitHub
seo_heading: Preserve empty directories in Git with .gitkeep and gitignore rules

title: What is .gitkeep in Git? Plus an example?
description: Quick explanation of .gitkeep why empty folders are ignored by Git and a practical example to keep directories tracked
heading: What is .gitkeep in Git Plus an example?
body:
Git is great at tracking files and terrible at feelings for empty folders. If your code expects a directory and it vanishes when someone clones the repo you get runtime errors and awkward blame emails. The humble file named .gitkeep is a tiny placeholder file that tells Git to track a folder that would otherwise be ignored because it is empty. It has no magical powers in Git and the name is purely a community habit for clarity in repo management and version control.

What .gitkeep actually does

Git does not track directories, only files. Put a file in a folder and that folder will be tracked. .gitkeep is just a small tracked file that makes an empty folder visible in the repository. The file name conveys intent so other contributors know that the folder is meant to exist even if it contains nothing yet.

Common use cases

  • Placeholder folders for logs or temporary uploads that will be created at runtime
  • Stubbing out project structure so new features have a home
  • Keeping example or template directories visible in small projects

Quick example you can type right now

mkdir logs
touch logs/.gitkeep
git add logs/.gitkeep
git commit -m "Add logs folder with .gitkeep"

That is literally it. No ceremony, no sacrifices, just a tiny file that keeps your folder from disappearing at the worst possible moment.

Alternatives and why you might prefer them

There are sane alternatives depending on how much hand holding you want to provide.

  • README in the folder. This explains why the folder exists and what should go in it. Good for clarity and future you.
  • .gitignore with a negation rule when you want to ignore everything except a placeholder file. Example for an uploads folder
# inside uploads/.gitignore
*
!.gitkeep

That pattern ignores all uploaded files while still letting the placeholder file be tracked. Use this when you want to keep the folder but not the noisy runtime files inside it.

Common mistakes and how to avoid them

  • Thinking .gitkeep is special to Git. It is not. Git treats it like any other file and it can be ignored or deleted just like any other tracked file.
  • Adding the placeholder to the wrong branch and wondering why it is missing in master. Add it where the folder belongs and merge or cherry pick as needed for repo management.
  • Having a global ignore rule that hides .gitkeep. If that is the case use a local negation rule in a .gitignore or pick a different placeholder name that your global ignore does not catch.

Tips and best practices for your repository

  • Prefer a README when the folder benefits from documentation. Prefer .gitkeep when you want the smallest tracked file possible.
  • Be consistent across the repo. Pick one approach and document it in CONTRIBUTING or README so new contributors do not guess.
  • Remember this is about intent. Files with names like .gitkeep help communicate that the folder is not an accident.

In short keep your repo tidy and your runtime folder structure predictable. Use .gitkeep for minimal footprints, use README when explanation helps, and use .gitignore negation when you want to ignore runtime clutter but not the folder itself. Now go forth and make your empty folders less lonely and slightly more useful in your git best practices workflow.

title: Pure JavaScript File Upload Example
description: Learn a compact pure JavaScript file upload example with drag and drop progress and server POST using FormData and XMLHttpRequest
heading: Pure JavaScript File Upload Example Guide
body:
This tutorial shows how to build a pure JavaScript file upload with drag and drop support progress bar and server POST

  1. Prepare minimal HTML
  2. Hook file selection and drop events
  3. Create FormData and send with XMLHttpRequest
  4. Show upload progress and handle server response

Step 1 Setup a file input and a drop zone so users have options and the page does not look like a toaster manual

< input type="file" id="fileInput" multiple> < div id="dropZone"> Drop files here< /div>

Step 2 Add listeners for change dragover and drop so the page accepts selected files or files flung with reckless abandon

const fileInput = document.getElementById('fileInput') fileInput.addEventListener('change', e => handleFiles(e.target.files)) const dropZone = document.getElementById('dropZone') dropZone.addEventListener('dragover', e => e.preventDefault()) dropZone.addEventListener('drop', e => { e.preventDefault() handleFiles(e.dataTransfer.files) })

Step 3 Build a FormData object append the file and send via XMLHttpRequest so upload progress can be measured without magic

function uploadFile(file) { const fd = new FormData() fd.append('file', file) const xhr = new XMLHttpRequest() xhr.open('POST', '/upload') xhr.upload.addEventListener('progress', e => { const percent = Math.round(e.loaded / e.total * 100) updateProgress(percent) }) xhr.addEventListener('load', () => { handleResponse(xhr.responseText) }) xhr.send(fd) }

Step 4 Show a friendly progress UI and handle server responses so users do not think the browser swallowed the file whole

Implement updateProgress to reflect percent in a bar and implement handleResponse to parse JSON or plain text from the server and show success or error messages

Summary of the flow Prepare a small HTML surface capture files from selection or drop pack files into FormData send with XMLHttpRequest track upload progress and handle the server response for user feedback

Tip

Use XMLHttpRequest upload progress for real time feedback and do not manually set multipart headers because the browser will manage boundaries correctly

body:

  2. Read the uploaded Part and validate incoming data
  3. Write the uploaded file to a safe server location

Create a JSP form

Use a plain HTML form with multipart encoding. Example form snippet shown for guidance

< form method="post" action="upload" enctype="multipart/form-data"> < input type="file" name="file" /> < button type="submit"> Upload< /button> < /form>

Declare a servlet

Annotate the servlet with a mapping and a multipart configuration so the servlet container will parse the request into Part objects

@WebServlet("/upload") @MultipartConfig

Read and validate

Call request.getPart("file") to retrieve the uploaded Part. Check file size and content type before any store action. Reject files that fail validation with a helpful message for the user.

Save the file

Use part.getSubmittedFileName to get a user file name. Create a server side file name that avoids collisions and directory traversal. Call part.write with a server path to persist the file.

Respond and handle errors

Return a friendly success page or JSON. Catch exceptions caused by IO or malformed requests and send a clear status and message so a developer does not have to play detective.

Summary of this tutorial shows how to create a form that posts multipart data and a servlet that receives, validates, and writes a file to disk while keeping common safety practices in mind

Tip
