  4. Update IDE project SDK
  5. Clean build and test

Check the runtime Java with a quick command and confirm the environment variable points to a full JDK rather than a JRE. Example command that reveals the runtime is java -version. Confirm the JAVA_HOME path points to a JDK 1.8 installation.

Edit the project pom xml to declare compiler properties so Maven does not guess legacy values. A compact properties block looks like this

< properties> < maven.compiler.source> 1.8< /maven.compiler.source> < maven.compiler.target> 1.8< /maven.compiler.target> < /properties>

If the project still complains add or update the maven compiler plugin configuration. This explicitly instructs Maven which Java language level to use during compilation.

Open the IDE project settings and select the correct JDK 1.8 for both project SDK and project language level. IDEs sometimes use a bundled JRE for running the editor while Maven runs from a different Java which causes the mismatch.

Run a full clean build from the project root so Maven picks up the changes. A common command is mvn clean install. Observe the compiler output for any lingering references to 1.5 and adjust pom or IDE settings if required.

Following these steps aligns Maven compiler targets Java home and IDE configuration so the compliance mismatch disappears and builds run using Java 1.8 instead of legacy 1.5 behavior.

Tip

Prefer defining Java level in a single place by using pom properties and ensure terminal and IDE share the same JAVA_HOME value. That prevents surprises when the build behaves like a magical time capsule.

title: Maven Compiler Plugin Java 8 Dependency Example
description: Configure Maven Compiler Plugin to compile Java 8 code and manage dependencies for stable builds and predictable compilation.
heading: Maven Compiler Plugin Java 8 Dependency Example Guide
body:
This tutorial shows how to configure the Maven Compiler Plugin to compile Java 8 code and manage dependencies for reliable builds.

  1. Add or update the Maven Compiler Plugin block in pom.xml
  2. Set the Java source and target to 1.8 or use the release parameter
  3. Declare any compiler dependencies such as annotation processors or alternate compilers
  4. Run a clean build and verify the compiled classes

Step 1 update the plugin section inside the project pom so Maven knows which compiler plugin version to use. A typical plugin block looks like this

org.apache.maven.plugins maven-compiler-plugin 3.8.1 1.8 1.8

Step 2 choose between explicit source and target values or the more modern release flag for consistent standard library linkage. Use the release parameter when the JDK supports that option for less surprise during compilation.

Step 3 add compiler dependencies when annotation processing or a specific compiler implementation is required. For example add an annotation processor artifact under the plugin or the project dependencies so the build can find generated code during compile phase.

Step 4 run a build to confirm that configuration and dependencies behave as expected. Use the command mvn clean compile and inspect the generated classes and any compiler warnings.

After completing those steps a Maven project will compile Java 8 sources with controlled compiler behavior and any required dependency support. The workflow keeps builds reproducible and avoids mysterious runtime surprises caused by mismatched compiler settings.

Tip

Prefer the release configuration when compiling for Java 8 if the JDK supports that flag. The release option pins standard library APIs rather than relying on separate source and target which can hide mismatches between JDK and target runtime.

title: Simple Spring Boot File Upload Example
description: Compact guide to add multipart file upload to a Spring Boot app with controller storage and quick testing tips
heading: Simple Spring Boot File Upload Example Guide
body:
This tutorial shows how to add multipart file upload support to a Spring Boot application using a controller that accepts MultipartFile and saves uploads to disk.

  1. Set up project dependencies and basic Spring Boot skeleton
  2. Configure multipart and storage properties
  3. Create a controller endpoint to accept MultipartFile
  4. Save uploaded files to a safe folder and validate size and type
  5. Test upload with curl or Postman

Step 1 Add the spring boot starter web dependency and, if needed, the servlet multipart support. The typical choice is spring boot starter web which brings the MVC plumbing and multipart support.

Step 2 Configure multipart limits and a storage path in application properties. Example property names look like spring servlet multipart max file size and spring servlet multipart max request size and a custom upload folder path for the saved file.

Step 3 Create a simple REST controller with a POST endpoint. Use an argument of type MultipartFile and annotation mapping like @PostMapping("/upload"). Validate the MultipartFile for emptiness and optional content type checks.

Step 4 Save the MultipartFile by calling transferTo or by streaming to a target path. Build a safe filename by using a UUID prefix or by sanitizing the original filename. Check the file size and reject files that exceed the configured limits.

Step 5 Test with curl or Postman by sending a multipart form data request to the upload endpoint. For curl use the form option and point to a local sample file. Verify the saved file appears in the configured folder and that the response contains the saved filename or an error message on failure.

This short workflow covers dependency setup controller creation property configuration file saving and manual testing. Follow validation and storage hygiene to avoid common pitfalls like overwriting files or allowing unsafe content.

Tip

Use UUID prefixed filenames and store uploads outside the classpath to prevent accidental execution of uploaded files. Add a whitelist of MIME types for extra safety.

title: Multiple Values Per Key in Java Maps Example
description: Learn how to store multiple values per key in Java Maps with list set patterns libraries and stream grouping for cleaner code and better performance
heading: Multiple Values Per Key in Java Maps Example
body:
This tutorial shows how to associate multiple values with a single key in Java Map structures using lists sets or third party multimaps for cleaner code and fewer surprises

  1. Pick the right value collection
  2. Use a Map of Collection with computeIfAbsent for safe adds
  3. Use a Set when duplicate values must be prevented
  4. Consider Guava Multimap or Apache commons for convenience
  5. Use streams to collect grouped values from a data source

Pick the right collection based on desired behavior. A List preserves insertion order and allows duplicates. A Set enforces uniqueness. A LinkedHashSet preserves insertion order while preventing duplicates. Choosing deliberately prevents later debugging grief.

Using a Map that maps to a Collection is the core pattern. Example usage map.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList()).add(value) This avoids null checks and reduces chances of missing initialization when adding values from multiple places

When duplicates are bad use a Set instead of a List. Use HashSet for raw speed and LinkedHashSet when order matters. Adding to a Set returns a boolean so duplicate attempts give immediate feedback without extra code

Guava Multimap and Apache MultiValuedMap encapsulate the map to collection pattern into a single API. Those libraries reduce boilerplate and provide helpers for common operations. Adopting a library pays off when multiple modules share the multimapping need

When starting from a stream use Collectors groupingBy combined with mapping to collect into lists or sets. That pattern turns a stream of records into a Map that maps to collections in one pass

Putting multiple values behind a single key is a common need across many applications. Choose collection type consciously use computeIfAbsent for manual maps or adopt a multimapping library for less code and clearer semantics. Use streams for bulk grouping and avoid ad hoc solutions that hide behavior

Tip

For high concurrency prefer concurrent maps with concurrent collection values or use atomic compute methods from concurrent map implementations to avoid lost updates. Wrapping a collection with synchronized methods often misses race conditions on map updates

title: Fix Eclipse's SerialVersionUID Warning Error
description: Quick guide to silence Eclipse serialVersionUID warnings by adding a field or suppressing the warning for Java Serializable classes.
heading: Fix Eclipse's SerialVersionUID Warning Error with a quick guide
body:
If Eclipse is nagging you about serialVersionUID like a coworker who just discovered code reviews you have options that do not involve dramatic rewrites or a ritual sacrifice of your build script. This guide shows how to quiet the warning by generating a stable id in the IDE adding a manual field or suppressing the message when serialization is accidental. Developer tips ahead with a wink.

Find the class that triggered the warning

Open the Java file with the warning. Eclipse flags classes that implement java.io.Serializable or that extend a serializable superclass. The warning appears because the compiler prefers an explicit serialVersionUID to reduce the risk of incompatible serialized forms later.

Use Eclipse Quick Fix to generate serialVersionUID

Place the cursor on the warning and press Ctrl 1. Pick Add generated serialVersionUID or Add default serialVersionUID. The generated value is derived from the class structure so it helps avoid spurious mismatch warnings when you refactor fields in predictable ways.

Why generated values matter

  • Generated ids reflect class details so Eclipse can keep you out of trouble when sensible refactoring happens
  • This is a low effort fix when you expect normal IDE driven edits and you want less editor noise

Add a manual serialVersionUID field when you need control

If you want to control compatibility between versions add a line like

private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L

Place it with other static fields. When you make a breaking change bump the numeric value to signal a new serialization version. This is the explicit and safest approach for objects that cross process boundaries or are stored long term.

Suppress the warning when serialization is accidental

If your class is only accidentally Serializable and you do not plan to persist or move instances use

@SuppressWarnings("serial")

on the class to silence the message. This avoids cluttering your class with a field you will never use. Only use suppression when you are confident serialization compatibility is not required.

Make the pragmatic decision based on how objects travel

If serialized forms are sent between services or persisted declare a meaningful serialVersionUID. For local ephemeral use suppress or accept the default generated id to reduce noise in the IDE. The choice depends on whether you value strict compatibility or minimal warnings.

Extra tool for the careful type

When in doubt run the serialver tool on a released class to obtain an explicit serialVersionUID for a shipped artifact. That produced value can be copied into your source so you know exactly what went out the door.

Recap and quick checklist

  • Identify the class with the warning
  • Use Eclipse Quick Fix and generate a serialVersionUID when you want low friction
  • Add a manual field when you need stable compatibility across versions
  • Use @SuppressWarnings("serial") when serialization is accidental
  • Use serialver on released code if you want a confirmed id

Follow these steps and Eclipse will stop yelling at you while your Java serialization stays predictable. You get less noise in the IDE and fewer mysterious InvalidClassExceptions later. Which sounds like a good bargain to me.
seo_title: Stop Eclipse serialVersionUID nags without breaking Java
seo_heading: How to add or silence serialVersionUID in Eclipse and stay sane

title: How Sass Variables Work
description: Learn how to declare use and manage Sass variables to write cleaner more maintainable stylesheets fast
heading: How Sass Variables Work for Cleaner Stylesheets
body:
This tutorial teaches how to declare and use Sass variables to make CSS maintenance less painful.

  1. Declare a variable
  2. Use a variable in a rule
  3. Override and use default values
  4. Understand scope and nesting
  5. Compile and test the output

Declare a variable Use a clear name for a variable and assign a value with an equals sign in examples below to avoid confusion with prose. Example in pseudo code shows intent not exact syntax

$primary-color = #3498db

Use a variable in a rule Reference a variable inside a property to avoid repeating raw values across a stylesheet. This makes global changes trivial and prevents hexadecimal fatigue

button { color = $primary-color }

Override and use default values A variable can be reassigned for themes or components. Use a default assignment when a fallback is desired so other files can override without conflict

$font-size = 16px

Understand scope and nesting Variables declared inside a block are local to that block. Global variables live at the top level and are available anywhere after declaration. Nesting rules determine which value takes precedence so declare carefully

Compile and test the output After changes run the preprocessor to generate CSS and check output for expected values. Inspect compiled stylesheet to confirm that variables produced the desired CSS

Sass variables save time and reduce mistakes by centralizing values for colors spacing and typography. Using descriptive names and predictable scope patterns helps teams move faster and break less

Tip

Use a consistent naming convention for variables such as prefix component names for overrides and keep global tokens in a single file for easy discovery

title: Quick Sass Mixins Example
description: Learn quick Sass mixin patterns to share styles accept parameters and keep styles DRY in a compact practical guide
heading: Quick Sass Mixins Example for Reusable Styles
body:
This tutorial shows how to write and use Sass mixins to share styles accept parameters and reduce repetition.

  1. Create a mixin
  2. Include the mixin in a selector
  3. Pass parameters to customize output
  4. Use defaults and simple logic to make mixins flexible

Create a mixin by naming a reusable block of styles. Use a descriptive name so later code reviewers do not rage. Example pseudo Sass syntax follows to keep punctuation levels low and focus on concept.

@mixin center display flex justify-content center align-items center

Include the mixin inside a selector using an include rule. This avoids copying style blocks across multiple rules and keeps style sheets DRY plus slightly less annoying to maintain.

.button @include center background blue color white

Pass parameters to mixins to create configurable patterns. Parameters turn a single mixin into many variations without rewriting code. Example shows a shadow mixin that accepts values.

@mixin box-shadow $x $y $blur $color box-shadow $x $y $blur $color .card @include box-shadow 0 4px 10px rgba(0,0,0,0.15)

Use default parameter values and simple conditional checks to provide sensible fallbacks. Defaults prevent callers from supplying every argument while conditionals allow optional behavior without clutter.

@mixin btn $bg blue $pad 8px background $bg padding $pad .btn-primary @include btn

Summary of the approach Create descriptive mixin names include mixins where styles repeat accept parameters for flexibility and provide defaults for nice developer ergonomics This keeps style code concise readable and reasonably pleasant to edit even on a Monday

Tip

Favor small single purpose mixins over giant catchall blocks Because reuse works best when the mixin does one predictable thing rather than trying to solve every future styling problem

title: Getting started with GitHub Pages
description: Quick guide to publish a website with GitHub Pages from repo to custom domain and Jekyll basics
heading: Getting started with GitHub Pages guide
body:
This tutorial teaches how to publish a static website using GitHub Pages from repository setup to a live site so readers can serve content with minimal fuss.

  1. Create a repository
  2. Add site content
  3. Enable GitHub Pages and choose a publishing source
  4. Pick a theme or add Jekyll
  5. Configure a custom domain and HTTPS
  6. Publish and verify

Create a repository on GitHub and name the repository according to preference. For a user site the repository name must match the username followed by .github.io. For a project site pick any name and expect a URL under the username domain.

Add site content by creating an index.html file or a Jekyll structure. Local workflow works fine. A typical flow is git add then git commit then git push -u origin main. No wizardry required.

Enable GitHub Pages from repository settings and choose a branch and folder such as main and /root or the gh-pages branch. The chosen branch becomes the publishing source for the site content.

Pick a theme from the Pages theme chooser or add Jekyll for templating and markdown. Jekyll supports layouts and plugins within allowed GitHub Pages constraints. A simple _config.yml will control basic site behavior.

Configure a custom domain by adding a CNAME file to the repository or set DNS records at the registrar. After DNS changes allow some time for propagation while GitHub provisions HTTPS. The Pages dashboard shows status and any DNS warnings.

Publish and verify by visiting the provided URL. Make small edits, push changes, and watch the repository trigger a deployment. If something breaks check the Pages log and the console output for helpful clues.

This guide covered repository creation, content placement, publishing source selection, theme or Jekyll setup, and custom domain configuration so a functional static site can be live on the web with predictable steps.

Tip

Use a CNAME file for custom domains and create an A record set or ALIAS depending on registrar. If HTTPS provisioning stalls try removing and readding the custom domain after DNS stabilizes.

title: Use Your Custom Godaddy Domain Name for Github Pages
description: Guide to point a GoDaddy domain to Github Pages using DNS A records and CNAME and enable HTTPS for a custom static site
heading: Use Your Custom Godaddy Domain Name for Github Pages Setup Guide
body:
If you bought a domain and you want it to proudly host your static site on GitHub Pages without throwing a tantrum, this guide will walk you through the parts that actually matter. You will make a tiny change in your repo add a DNS record at GoDaddy and wait for the internet to behave for a little while.

Prepare the GitHub Pages repository

Decide if your site is a user or organization page or a project page. For user and organization pages the URL looks like username.github.io. For project pages the repo name shows up in the URL and behavior is slightly different but the DNS steps are the same.

Two ways to tell GitHub which custom domain belongs to your site

  • Add a file named CNAME in the repository root with a single line that contains your custom domain for example mysite.com
  • Or enter the custom domain in the repository settings under GitHub Pages it will create the same mapping for you

Update DNS records at GoDaddy

Log in to your GoDaddy DNS panel and do two things. Add A records for the root domain and add a CNAME for the www host. GitHub Pages uses four IP addresses so add all four to reduce the chance of regional outages.

A 185.199.108.153
A 185.199.109.153
A 185.199.110.153
A 185.199.111.153

Then add a CNAME record

Host www points to username.github.io

Replace username.github.io with your GitHub Pages domain or the repository domain if this is a project page. The A records handle the apex root domain and the CNAME handles the www host which is what most browsers will use.

Enable HTTPS in GitHub Pages

Go back to the repository settings and enable GitHub Pages HTTPS. GitHub will provision a certificate for your custom domain automatically. This can take minutes or occasionally a few hours so pour yourself a beverage and refresh the settings page now and then.

If HTTPS does not appear

  • Check that your DNS changes have actually propagated using any DNS check tool
  • Make sure your CNAME file or custom domain entry in the repo matches exactly what you set at GoDaddy
  • If the root domain does not redirect to www you can set up forwarding at GoDaddy to send root traffic to www so the certificate covers the visible address

Test your site and tidy up

Open a browser and test both the apex domain and the www host. If one works and the other does not check your DNS records again and wait. If you prefer all visitors to end up at www set up a permanent redirect at GoDaddy or use a netlify style proxy if you need more control.

Common gotchas

  • For project pages remember the repository name affects the default URL so double check the target you put in the CNAME record
  • Do not remove the CNAME file from the repo after you add the domain GitHub uses that file to tie the domain to the site
  • Propagation takes time sometimes DNS updates are quick sometimes they are dramatic and slow like a sleepy sloth

That is it you are done unless the internet decides otherwise in which case troubleshooting will involve checking DNS TTL values matching names and patiently waiting. Congratulations you now have a custom GoDaddy domain serving your GitHub Pages site with HTTPS when the stars align.
seo_title: Point a GoDaddy Domain to GitHub Pages and Enable HTTPS
seo_heading: Set up GoDaddy DNS for GitHub Pages with CNAME A records and HTTPS

title: UiPath Certification Exam Objectives RPA Overview
description: Compact guide to UiPath RPA exam objectives covering Studio Orchestrator Robots REFramework debugging and best practices.
heading: UiPath Certification Exam Objectives RPA Overview
body:
Why this exam actually matters

UiPath certification is not a magic wand but it is a useful leak proof umbrella for your resume. The exam checks that you know the platform architecture and can build reliable automations that do not implode when a file goes missing or a selector decides to take a vacation. Study smart and treat repetitive tasks with the contempt they deserve.

Platform components you must know

Learn how the pieces fit together. These are exam gold and also the stuff you will use at work.

  • Studio for designing workflows and building activities
  • Orchestrator for deployments, queues, assets, schedules, roles and logs
  • Robots that run the processes on endpoints in attended or unattended modes

Practical tip

Deploy a small process to Orchestrator so you can watch jobs, push transactions to a queue and inspect logs. Nothing teaches faster than breaking and then fixing something in front of your own eyes.

Development fundamentals you should own

Expect questions on activities, variables, arguments and selectors. Be ready to explain when to use sequences versus flowcharts versus state machines and how to design reusable components that do not turn into a tangled ball of spaghetti.

  • Selectors and UiExplorer use wildcards and variables to handle dynamic UI elements
  • Arguments are for passing data between workflows. Variables live inside a workflow
  • Pick the right workflow type for readability and maintainability

Frameworks and transaction processing

The REFramework is the poster child for exam questions. Know how it moves through initialization, transaction fetching, processing and graceful shutdown. Learn how queues feed transactions, how retries are triggered and how logging keeps auditors from asking awkward questions.

  • Get Transaction Data and Process Transaction are core states to understand
  • Handle business rule exceptions separately from system exceptions
  • Use queues with retry and unique reference settings for resilient processing

Orchestrator features worth memorizing

Queues, assets, tenants, folders, roles and monitoring are common exam topics. Know how to create a queue, push a transaction, check the queue status and view logs. Understand role based access to argue why least privilege is not just buzzword friendly.

Debugging and exception handling techniques

Be comfortable with breakpoints, step into, step over and run to cursor. Use logs and screenshots for root cause analysis. Know Try Catch with Finally, Throw and Rethrow. Be ready to explain retry logic and business rule handling in plain terms.

Best practices and security

Learn why hard coded credentials are a crime against good automation. Use Orchestrator assets or the Windows credential store for safer deployments. Follow least privilege for service accounts and keep exception reporting clean and informative.

A study plan that does not suck

Make a small end to end project and then break it on purpose. That will teach you more than passive reading.

  • Build a simple invoice or data entry process with Studio
  • Use selectors that adapt to change and test with UiExplorer
  • Push transactions to Orchestrator queues and handle them with REFramework
  • Deploy and run using an unattended robot then inspect logs and retries
  • Practice debugging flows and handling business rule exceptions

Quick exam day checklist

  • Know Studio, Orchestrator and Robot roles
  • Understand REFramework states and queue processing
  • Be fluent with selectors, variables and arguments
  • Practice Try Catch patterns and retry strategies
  • Have one small project you can describe end to end

Study with purpose, build something that fails and then make it resilient. That is how you turn confusion into competence and survive the exam with your sanity intact.
seo_title: How to Master UiPath Certification and Real World RPA Skills
seo_heading: A no nonsense RPA study guide for UiPath exams and real projects

title: How to Install Tomcat 10 for Jakarta Development
description: Step by step guide to install Tomcat 10 for Jakarta EE development on Windows Linux and Mac with quick configuration and deploy tips
heading: How to Install Tomcat 10 for Jakarta Development
body:
This guide shows how to install Apache Tomcat 10 for Jakarta EE development on Windows Linux or Mac and how to configure Java and deploy a sample application.

  1. Download Tomcat 10
  2. Install Java
  3. Unpack and place server files
  4. Configure users and ports
  5. Deploy and start the server

Download Tomcat 10 Download the binary distribution from the Apache Tomcat mirrors and choose the core zip or tar archive that matches the operating system. Download the matching documentation and examples if moral support is desired.

Install Java Ensure Java 11 or later is installed and JAVA_HOME is set. Use the platform package manager or the vendor installer. Confirm Java by running java -version in a terminal window.

Unpack and place server files Extract the archive to a practical location such as a user home directory or a system level folder. Example commands include tar xzf apache-tomcat-10.x.tar.gz on Unix and extraction of the zip on Windows.

Configure users and ports Edit the configuration files in the conf folder to add a manager user and adjust HTTP port if a conflict exists. The user configuration lives in the users XML file and role names must match the manager and admin roles expected by the server.

Deploy and start the server Deploy a WAR by placing the file in the webapps folder or use the manager application after adding a manager user. Start the server with the startup script such as bin/startup.sh on Unix or bin\startup.bat on Windows. Check logs in the logs folder if the server grumbles.

This tutorial covered downloading Tomcat 10 installing a supported Java runtime unpacking the server files configuring access and ports deploying a simple application and starting the server for testing. Following these steps will produce a running Tomcat instance ready for Jakarta EE development and local testing without drama.

Tip

Tip Use a dedicated user account for the server process and avoid running the server as an administrator for improved security and fewer accidental deletions.

title: Install Eclipse IDE for Jakarta EE Dev
description: Quick guide to install Eclipse IDE for Jakarta EE development set up workspace add Jakarta EE tools and run a sample project
heading: Install Eclipse IDE for Jakarta EE Dev step by step
body:
Why this exists and who should read it

If you want an Eclipse IDE that actually understands Jakarta EE and lets you deploy to Tomcat Payara or WildFly without crying into your log files this guide is for you. It is short it is practical and it will get you from zero to a runnable Jakarta EE app with minimal drama.

What you need before we begin

  • Installed JDK that matches your application server and Jakarta EE version
  • Eclipse installer from eclipse.org and enough disk space to avoid surprises
  • Patience for one dialog box that asks about a workspace and your life choices

Download and run the Eclipse installer

Go to eclipse.org and grab the installer that matches your operating system and architecture. Pick the package that mentions Enterprise Java or Jakarta EE. If you pick the wrong package you will still fix it later but your coffee may go cold.

Install a compatible JDK

Jakarta EE runs on Java so install a JDK version supported by your app server. For example many modern Jakarta EE features work well on Java 11 or later but always check the server documentation for exact compatibility. Once installed run java -version to confirm that the JVM on your PATH is the one you intend to use.

Run the installer and choose the Jakarta EE tools

Launch the Eclipse installer and pick the Enterprise Java or Jakarta EE package. Default settings work for most developers. Accept the license choose a folder with enough space and let the installer do its thing. If it asks about additional components pick the Jakarta EE tooling and server adapters for Tomcat Payara or WildFly.

First launch and workspace choices

On first start Eclipse will ask for a workspace folder. Pick a clear folder now it will save you from dusty project metadata later. You can change this on future launches but avoid leaving projects scattered across your home folder unless chaos is your development strategy.

Add a server runtime in the IDE

Open the Servers view or go through Preferences to add a server runtime. Install the adapter for Tomcat Payara or WildFly if it is not already present. The server runtime lets you deploy debug and hot swap Jakarta EE applications straight from Eclipse without resorting to terminal rituals.

Create a new Jakarta EE project

  • Use the New Project wizard to create a Jakarta EE project
  • Select the Jakarta specifications you need such as Servlet or JAX RS and add an archetype or scaffold
  • Set the target runtime to the server you added and finish the wizard

Build and run to verify the setup

Run the server from the Servers view then deploy the new project. Check the Console and server logs for startup messages and make sure your servlet or JAX RS endpoint responds. If it does not respond check that the right JDK and server runtime are selected.

Quick tips and common fixes

  • Match your JDK version to the application server requirements to avoid mysterious runtime errors
  • Enable automatic updates in Eclipse to keep Jakarta EE tooling current
  • Set JAVA_HOME if a server adapter cannot find the JVM
  • If deployment fails check server logs and verify the server adapter is installed

That covers download installation workspace setup adding a server runtime and creating a Jakarta EE project to verify things work. Follow these steps and you will be ready for Jakarta EE development on Eclipse IDE with Tomcat Payara or WildFly without unnecessary suffering.

seo_heading: Quick Eclipse IDE workspace and server setup for Jakarta EE apps

title: How to Install Git
description: Step by step guide to install Git on Windows Mac and Linux with basic configuration and verification for developers
heading: How to Install Git Step by Step Guide
body:
This article teaches how to install Git across Windows Mac and Linux and how to perform basic configuration and verification so developers can start using version control.

  1. Choose installation method
  2. Run the installer or use a package manager
  3. Verify the installation
  4. Configure user name and email
  5. Generate and test an SSH key

Choose installation method based on the operating system and personal preference. On Windows download the official installer from git-scm dot com and follow the GUI prompts. On macOS use Homebrew with brew install git or use the installer from the same web page. On Linux prefer the native package manager with commands such as sudo apt update and sudo apt install git for Debian based systems.

Run the installer or invoke the package manager and accept sensible defaults unless there is a reason to tweak options. Yes clicking Next repeatedly is an acceptable life choice when the installer asks about line ending handling and SSH client selection. The package manager route is faster and less conversational than the GUI method.

Verify the installation by running the version command. Use git --version in a terminal to confirm Git presence. If the version returns a number then the environment is ready for configuration.

Configure a global user name and email to avoid anonymous commits. Execute git config --global user.name 'Jane Developer' and git config --global user.email 'jane@example.com'. Global settings apply to all repositories on the machine unless overridden inside a specific repository.

Generate an SSH key for seamless authentication with hosting services. Create a key with ssh-keygen -t ed25519 and add the public key to the hosting account. Test SSH access with ssh -T git@github.com or the equivalent for the chosen host.

This short guide covered selection of installation method running the installer or package manager verifying the Git installation basic global configuration and setting up SSH authentication so developers can push and pull without hand cramping.

Tip

Keep the global user email consistent with the account on the Git hosting service to ensure commits link to the correct profile. Use SSH keys for automation and avoid repeatedly entering credentials.

title: How to Set the Default Git Branch Name from Master to Main
description: Change default Git branch from master to main for new repositories and rename existing branches with simple commands and hosting updates.
heading: Set the default Git branch name from master to main
body:
If your repos still say master and you are tired of explaining yourself at meetups this git tutorial will show you how to make main the default for new repos and how to rename existing branches with minimal chaos. We will cover git config changes for future projects rename branch commands for existing repositories pushing the new branch to remotes and the hosting side of things on GitHub GitLab or Bitbucket. There will be a tiny amount of typing and a reasonable chance your CI will complain. That is normal.

Quick overview of what to do

Short version for impatient humans and machines

  • Set a global default so new repos start on main
  • Rename master to main locally in any existing repo
  • Push the new branch and update remote tracking
  • Update the default branch on your hosting platform
  • Search and update references in docs and CI

Set default for new repositories

Prevent future awkward renames by telling Git what to use when you run git init. This is a one time global setting that makes brand new repositories use main by default.

git config --global init.defaultBranch main

Now when you or your interns run git init the initial branch will be main instead of master. Nice and tidy.

Rename an existing branch

If a repo already uses master you can rename it locally then push the new name to the remote. Do this in the repository you want to change.

Rename the branch in your local workspace

git branch -m master main

If you were on master this command renames the branch to main. If you were not on master adjust the command accordingly or check out the branch first.

Push the renamed branch and set upstream

git push -u origin main

That publishes main to the remote and sets the upstream so future git push and git pull work without extra flags. You can delete the old remote branch if you want to be tidy.

git push origin --delete master

Update hosting platform default branch

Pushing main is not enough. Change the default branch setting in your hosting service so pull requests and new clones use the correct branch. On GitHub go to the repo Settings then Branches and change the default branch. On GitLab visit Repository settings and on Bitbucket check Branching model or repository settings depending on the UI. Every provider has a UI or API for this so pick whichever suits your automation style.

Fix references and CI

Search your repo for references to master in docs CI scripts and deployment configs and update them to main. Common spots to check include:

  • Continuous integration pipelines and YAML files
  • Deployment scripts and Dockerfiles
  • README badges and developer instructions
  • Automation and monitoring alerts that mention branch names

Run your test suite before merging anything. If CI has branch specific rules update them so builds keep working.

Bulk changes and automation

If you have many repositories automate the rename with a script or use the hosting platform API to change defaults in bulk. Be careful and run the script on a few repos first. Tests exist for a reason.

Checklist before you call it done

  • Global init.defaultBranch is set if you want new repos to use main
  • Local branch renamed and pushed with upstream set
  • Old remote branch removed if you chose to delete it
  • Hosting platform default branch updated
  • All CI and config references updated and tests passing

There you go. You have changed the default branch in git and migrated repositories from master to main like a responsible human. If anything breaks revert the file that broke it and blame your younger self. If you are changing lots of repos consider automating and add plenty of logging and backups before you go bulk renaming branches across orgs. Version control is for the living and the slightly regretful.

title: Change Git's Init Branch Name Default
description: Change the default branch name created by git init globally or per repo using git config or the git init -b option Learn commands and verification tips
heading: Change Git's Init Branch Name Default
body:
This tutorial shows how to change the branch name created by git init globally or per repository using simple git config commands and the newer git init -b option.

  1. Set global default branch name
  2. Set default for a single repository
  3. Use the init flag when creating a new repo
  4. Verify the configuration

Set global default branch name with git config --global init.defaultBranch main This saves a preference so every new repository created with git init will use main unless a repository override exists

Set default for a single repository by running git -C path/to/repo config init.defaultBranch main or run the command inside the repository without the -C flag This writes the option to the local config and avoids changing global behavior

Use the init flag when creating a new repo with a specific branch by running git init -b main This option is supported in recent versions of Git and overrides both global and local defaults for that initialization command

Verify default with git init temp-repo && cd temp-repo && git branch --show-current or inspect configuration with git config --get init.defaultBranch The branch name will appear when running git branch or by checking config values

Changing the default branch name helps align new projects with team conventions and avoids manual renaming after initialization This is handy when starting many repositories or when organization policy requires a specific default

Tip

Pick a default branch name and apply the global setting early Keep hosting service settings and CI configuration consistent with that choice to avoid surprises during automation

title: Use the latest Tomcat Version in Eclipse IDE
description: Learn how to run the newest Apache Tomcat inside Eclipse even when Eclipse flags the server as unsupported with a simple step by step guide.
heading: Use the latest Tomcat Version in Eclipse IDE without support warnings
body:
This tutorial shows how to configure Eclipse so the newest Apache Tomcat release can run inside the IDE even when Eclipse reports the server as unsupported.

  1. Download and unzip the latest Tomcat
  2. Install or enable the Tomcat server adapter in Eclipse
  3. Add a runtime by choosing the closest supported Tomcat version and point to the Tomcat folder
  4. Create a new server using the installed runtime and adjust settings if needed

Step 1 Download the Tomcat binary from the Apache site and extract to a stable folder on the development machine. Avoid temporary folders because deployments will be happier when the server lives somewhere persistent.

Step 2 Open Eclipse marketplace or the install new software dialog and get the Web Tools server adapters if the Servers view offers no options for Apache Tomcat. The server adapter bridges Eclipse and the Tomcat runtime.

Step 3 In Eclipse go to Preferences then Server then Runtime Environments and choose Add. If the literal newest Tomcat option is missing pick the closest lower supported version and set the home directory to the extracted Tomcat folder. Eclipse will accept the runtime even when the official adapter labels the version as unsupported.

Step 4 In the Servers view create a New Server and select the runtime added earlier. Configure ports and deployment options as desired. If a warning appears about unsupported status proceed anyway because most features will work normally with matching Java versions and correct library locations.

This process keeps the development workflow moving without waiting for an adapter update. Developers gain access to latest Tomcat fixes while preserving familiar Eclipse controls for debugging and hot deploy.

Tip

Tip Run the desired Java version for the new Tomcat from the server runtime settings. Mismatched Java versions cause more mysterious failures than unsupported labels do.

title: GitHub Pages HTML

body:

git init

git commit -m "Initial commit"
git branch -M main

title: Jekyll Markdown and GitHub Pages
description: Compact guide to use Jekyll with Markdown on GitHub Pages for a fast static site workflow and simple deployment steps.
heading: Jekyll Markdown and GitHub Pages Guide
body:
Why Jekyll and GitHub Pages actually make sense

If you want a fast static site without selling your soul to a complex CMS, Jekyll plus GitHub Pages is the sensible choice. You write in Markdown, Jekyll transforms it, and GitHub hosts the result for free. It is like magic, but the magician is a build step and you still need to remember to push your code.

Quick overview of the steps

This guide walks through repository creation, basic configuration, writing Markdown with YAML front matter, local testing with the Jekyll server, and pushing to GitHub Pages. If you need plugins, use GitHub Actions to build before publishing the final static site.

Create the repository and pick a branch

Make a new repository on GitHub. Choose a branch for Pages. main or gh-pages are common choices, pick one and stick with it unless you enjoy surprise downtime. Keep branch names consistent and avoid the tragic surprise of a site that refuses to publish because you pushed to the wrong branch.

Add a Jekyll config file

Create a file named _config.yml at the repository root. Put your basic site settings and theme in there. Many themes work out of the box on GitHub Pages, but if you need plugins that Pages does not allow, set up a build step with GitHub Actions and push the generated site to the Pages branch.

Write content in Markdown with front matter

Pages go in the root, posts go in _posts. Every page or post needs YAML front matter at the top, with three dashes lines before and after the block. Front matter tells Jekyll what layout to use and where to put the generated file. Keep front matter minimal when you can, and add metadata like layout and title for better site structure.

Test locally so you do not panic after a push

Install Jekyll and the needed gems, then run bundle exec jekyll serve or jekyll serve. This spins up a local server and shows your site at http://localhost:4000. Local testing saves time and spares you that embarrassing broken site moment after a push.

Deploy to GitHub Pages

Commit your changes, push to your chosen branch, then enable GitHub Pages in the repository settings and select the branch. If you are using the Pages build provided by GitHub, it will handle Jekyll for you unless you require unsupported plugins.

Use GitHub Actions when you need plugins or extra control

If you need plugins or want a custom build pipeline, configure GitHub Actions to run a full Jekyll build and then push the generated static site to your Pages branch. This gives you freedom to use third party gems while still using GitHub Pages for hosting.

Practical checklist

  • Create a GitHub repository and select a Pages branch
  • Add _config.yml with your site settings and theme
  • Put posts in _posts and pages in the root, each with YAML front matter
  • Run the Jekyll server locally to preview changes
  • Push to GitHub and enable Pages, or use Actions to build and deploy if you need plugins

Troubleshooting tips that actually help

If Pages reports build errors, check your front matter for formatting problems and confirm the branch is correct. If a theme behaves oddly, try a supported theme on GitHub Pages or move the build into Actions. For missing pages or 404s, verify file paths and permalink settings in the config.

Final note

Jekyll plus Markdown plus GitHub Pages gives you a lightweight static website that is easy to maintain and fast to serve. With a little local testing and a sensible workflow you can deploy a static site with minimal fuss and no dark rituals.

Reference Liquid objects in templates Use Liquid objects such as page and site inside layouts and includes. The page object exposes variables from front matter. The site object exposes collections posts and site wide settings.

title: GitHub Actions Bash Shell Commands
description: Learn to run Bash commands in GitHub Actions workflows with examples for error handling outputs and debugging.
heading: GitHub Actions Bash Shell Commands Explained
body:
This tutorial shows how to run Bash commands inside GitHub Actions workflows with practical tips for error handling passing outputs and debugging.

  1. Choose runner and shell
  2. Write multi line run steps
  3. Make scripts fail fast and handle pipes
  4. Pass data via outputs and environment
  5. Debug with logs and exit codes

Choose a runner that matches the target platform name and pick Bash when Linux behavior is required. Using the right shell avoids surprises from different shell builtins.

Write multi line steps by placing multiple commands in a single run block. Group related commands together to preserve environment changes between lines. Quoting and escaping reduce surprises with variables and special characters.

Fail fast by enabling strict modes at the start of scripts. For example use set -e to stop on first error and use set -o pipefail to catch failures inside pipelines. These two lines save hours of guessing why later steps fail.

Pass data between steps using the provided file based interfaces. For example write an output value with echo "name=foo" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT and export environment variables with echo "VAR=value" >> $GITHUB_ENV. That avoids fragile parsing of log lines.

Debug by printing useful context and checking exit codes. Use explicit echo lines for variables and consider running a small diagnostic command like bash -lc "env | sort | grep -i name" when tracking down environment surprises. Logs are the friend that does not sleep.

Recap The guide covered selecting the right runner and shell writing multi line run steps enforcing strict failure modes passing data between steps and pragmatic debugging practices to make workflows more reliable and less magical.

Tip

When debugging add a step that prints a compact snapshot of environment values and recent log files. That often exposes the cause faster than random edits to workflow files.

title: Run Shell Script in GitHub Actions Tutorial

Push the changes to the branch. The Actions tab shows the job log and any failing line numbers. Logs are the friend that tells what went wrong.

title: GitHub Actions Environment Variables
description: Quick guide to using environment variables in GitHub Actions for config and secrets with practical rules and examples
heading: GitHub Actions Environment Variables Guide
body:
Quick reality check

GitHub Actions environment variables are just key value pairs that your workflow uses for configuration and occasional chaos. They live at three levels, and yes the narrow ones win. Steps beat jobs and jobs beat the workflow. Treat secrets like sassy exes, do not broadcast them to the world or your logs will keep receipts.

How scopes and precedence work

  • Workflow level variables apply to every job unless overridden.
  • Job level variables are visible to all steps in the job and override workflow values.
  • Step level variables only last for that single run and beat job values.

If two variables share the same name, the one in the tighter scope wins. That means step changes do not magically carry into other jobs, and if you assume otherwise you will learn the hard way.

Set a variable during a run

If you need to set a value at runtime write it to the special file that the runner watches. Future steps in the same job will see it.

echo "MY_VAR=hello" >> $GITHUB_ENV
# later in another step
echo Hello ${{ env.MY_VAR }}

Secrets and safety

Sensitive values belong in the secrets context. Use the secrets namespace and avoid printing them unless you enjoy regret. Secrets are masked in logs, but only if you do not hand them to an unintended echo or debug print. Remember that values written to the environment file show up plainly unless you treat them as secrets.

# read a secret safely in a step
echo Hello ${{ secrets.MY_SECRET }}

The old workflow command that set environment variables was deprecated. The recommended pattern is either write to the $GITHUB_ENV file or declare things in your workflow YAML ahead of time. Pick one and be consistent.

Passing values between jobs

If you must get runtime output from one job into another use job outputs or upload artifacts. That requires an extra few lines and a smidge of patience, but it will not surprise you like hoping environment changes propagate across jobs.

Naming tips and common pitfalls

  • Use uppercase names with underscores, for example MY_VAR, to stay predictable.
  • Avoid names that collide with runner environment variables unless you enjoy debugging at 2 AM.
  • Do not print secrets to logs, even in debugging, because masking can be fickle when you pants the system.
  • Do not assume a step level change will show up in another job, because it will not.

Best practices to stop self sabotage

  • Prefer the secrets context for tokens and other sensitive data.
  • Use $GITHUB_ENV for dynamic values set during a run.
  • Keep variable scope as narrow as practical to reduce surprises.
  • Document variable purpose and expected lifecycle, so future you does not curse current you.

Follow these rules and your workflows will behave more like obedient pets and less like caffeinated raccoons. If something goes sideways read the logs carefully, check which scope your variable came from, and avoid echoing secrets into immortality.
seo_title: Manage GitHub Actions variables and secrets without leaks
seo_heading: Avoid secret spills and scope environment variables for reliable CI runs

title: Multi Step GitHub Actions Example
description: Compact guide to build a multi step GitHub Actions workflow for CI build test and deploy with practical steps and a useful tip
heading: Multi Step GitHub Actions Example explained
body:
If you like automating boring things and watching logs for entertainment then welcome to GitHub Actions land. This guide shows how to stitch lint build test and deploy into a single job so artifacts and workspace state behave like civilized adults. You will learn where to put the YAML how to pick a runner which steps to add and how to use cache and artifacts to avoid repeating the same slow chores every run.

Where the workflow file lives

Create a file under .github/workflows/ci.yml and GitHub will find it like a bloodhound that only cares about YAML. The file name is not sacred but the path is. Keep your automation in the repo so your CI is versioned and slightly less spooky.

Define a job and choose a runner

Give the job a clear name and set runs-on to something like ubuntu-latest. A single job is convenient when you want a shared workspace and easy artifact passing. Multiple jobs are fine for parallel work but then you start juggling artifacts and that is less relaxing.

Why keep steps small

Each step should do one thing. One step checks out code. One step runs lint. One step runs tests. One step builds. This makes logs readable and failures obvious. If a step fails you do not have to play detective for an hour to find the guilty command.

Example workflow snippet

Here is a minimal YAML example to get you started. Replace the commands with your actual lint build and test commands.

name: CI pipeline
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v3

      - name: Set up Node
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 18

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run linter
        run: npm run lint

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      - name: Build
        run: npm run build

      - name: Upload build artifact
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: build-output
          path: dist/

Share state with artifacts and use cache

Artifacts are the official way to move files between jobs or keep build outputs around for downloads. Use the upload and download artifact actions when you want to pass build results or test reports between runs or jobs.

Caching is your time saving friend. Cache package manager folders like node_modules or dependency folders for Maven and pip. Use the cache action to avoid reinstalling everything on every run. Cache keys based on lockfiles provide reliable invalidation.

Trigger and monitor

Push a branch or open a pull request to trigger the workflow. Visit the Actions tab and read the logs like a grumpy librarian. Steps include timestamps and stack traces when things blow up so you can fix the real problem instead of blaming the CI for being dramatic.

Troubleshooting tips

  • If a step fails look at the specific step logs first. They are rarely cryptic by accident.
  • If caching does not hit check your key and the paths. Missed cache is usually a path or key mismatch.
  • When artifacts do not appear verify the upload step ran and that the path exists on disk before upload.

Wrap up

This approach focuses on clarity and predictable artifacts. Use a single job when you want a shared workspace and simple debugging. Break into multiple jobs when you need parallel runs or matrix builds. Either way the essentials are the same specify your workflow YAML pick a runner add focused steps use cache and artifacts and then push to test. Now go automate something and enjoy the tiny victory of a green check mark.

seo_heading: Practical guide to lint build test deploy with artifacts and cache

title: GitHub Action Workflows on Mac, Windows and Linux
description: Learn to run GitHub Action workflows on macOS Windows and Linux runners for reliable cross platform CI and testing
heading: GitHub Action Workflows on Mac Windows and Linux
body:
This tutorial shows how to run GitHub Actions workflows across macOS Windows and Linux runners for cross platform testing and builds.

  1. Define a matrix strategy
  2. Pick appropriate runners
  3. Install dependencies and cache them
  4. Run tests and collect artifacts
  5. Inspect results and refine

Define a matrix strategy Use a matrix to declare combinations of operating systems language versions and other variables. The matrix reduces duplication and keeps the workflow concise while running multiple configurations in parallel.

Pick appropriate runners Choose hosted runners for convenience or self hosted runners for custom hardware. Hosted macOS runners are limited and have billing implications so plan job timing accordingly.

Install dependencies and cache them Install language runtimes and libraries early in the job. Add caching for package managers to speed up repeated runs and reduce pipeline duration.

Run tests and collect artifacts Execute the test matrix across each runner. Upload logs test reports and build artifacts so developers can inspect failures without rerunning the workflow locally.

Inspect results and refine Use the workflow UI to see which OS and which version failed. Narrow failures by adjusting environment variables or by adding debug steps that print system information and PATH contents.

This tutorial covered how to orchestrate cross platform CI using GitHub Actions. The focus included declaring a matrix strategy selecting runners optimizing dependency handling running tests and collecting artifacts for debugging. With these practices the workflow becomes faster clearer and easier to maintain while covering the combinations that matter most.

Tip

Run a single quick smoke test on every push while reserving full matrix runs for pull requests or scheduled jobs. That reduces wasted runner minutes and gives fast feedback to developers.

title: Java Artifacts in GitHub Actions Maven Build
description: Build and store Maven Java artifacts with GitHub Actions steps for packaging uploading and optional deployment from workflows
heading: Java Artifacts in GitHub Actions Maven Build
body:
If your goal is to turn Java code into deliverable jars without crying over merge conflicts every day then welcome to the land of CI with GitHub Actions. This guide walks through building Maven artifacts in a workflow then uploading or publishing them in a way your future self will thank you for. It is practical and mildly ruthless about mistakes.

Prepare the workflow

Create a YAML workflow under .github/workflows that checks out the repo and configures Java with actions/setup-java@v2. Keep credentials and GPG keys in repository secrets so the pipeline can authenticate when it needs to publish. Use the built in setup java cache or actions/cache to speed up dependency resolution and make your CI less fragile.

Run the Maven build

Use a non interactive Maven command to produce jars and modules in the target directory. A simple and reproducible command looks like this

mvn -B package

Use profiles to enable or disable tests or to change packaging. If you want to skip tests during a quick artifact build use the common flag -DskipTests=true. Keep your CI faithful to local builds so debugging is not a guessing game.

Upload artifacts for later steps

When you need to keep build outputs around for other jobs or for human retrieval use actions/upload-artifact. Point it at target/*.jar and give the artifact a predictable name. The action will hold files until you either download them from the workflow run artifacts tab or a later job picks them up.

Deploy to a Maven repository

When publishing provide a settings.xml that reads server credentials from secrets. In the workflow run mvn deploy to push to a Nexus server or to Maven Central staging. If your repository requires releases to be signed then sign artifacts with GPG and keep the passphrase and private key in secrets. Test deployment to a staging repository first so the real repo does not get sad.

What files and credentials to store

  • GPG private key and passphrase in repo secrets
  • Repository username and password or token in repo secrets
  • settings.xml that references those secrets at runtime

Verify and debug

Look at workflow logs for Maven output and artifact upload messages. Confirm uploaded files appear under the artifacts tab in the run. If a step fails reproduce it locally with the same Maven command and any needed environment variables. Local reproduction will save you from guessing and from blaming the CI runner for everything.

Tips to avoid later headaches

  • Use dependency caching with the setup java cache feature or with actions/cache to reduce build flakiness and speed up runs
  • Sign releases only when required and rotate credentials regularly for safer pipelines
  • Deploy to a staging repository before sending things to Maven Central
  • Give artifacts consistent names so automated downloads and later jobs do not fail spectacularly

Follow these steps to move from a simple package run to a reproducible publish pipeline that handles credentials signing and artifact storage. Your CI will do the heavy lifting and you can keep arguing about tabs versus spaces in peace.
seo_title: Automate Maven builds and publish Java artifacts on GitHub
seo_heading: CI workflow to package test sign and deploy Java artifacts to Maven

title: How to publish GitHub Actions artifacts example
description: Publish GitHub Actions artifacts step by step guide for upload download retention and reuse in workflows and jobs
heading: How to publish GitHub Actions artifacts example
body:
Overview

If your CI feels like a paper trail left in an office fire you are not alone. Artifacts are the polite way to keep build outputs alive after a job finishes. This guide shows how to upload artifact files from GitHub Actions, how to download artifact files later in the run, and how to think about retention and naming so your automation does not become a storage nightmare.

Create a workflow file

Start by adding a YAML file under the .github/workflows directory in your repo. Define when the workflow should run, and give jobs clear names so a future maintainer does not cry in the logs. Use descriptive job ids for clarity when you upload and download artifacts across jobs.

Upload an artifact with actions/upload-artifact

Add a step that uses the actions/upload-artifact action and point it at the build output directory or file you want to keep. The action packages the files and stores them as an artifact that survives past the job. The main knobs to set are the artifact name and the path to the files to keep.

What to include in the upload

  • Build results such as compiled binaries or archived packages
  • Test reports and coverage artifacts
  • Intermediate files that another job will consume

Download the artifact with actions/download-artifact

In a later job add the actions/download-artifact step and request the same artifact name. The files will be restored to the runner file system so tests or packaging steps can use them. This is the standard way to move files between runners without inventing a cloud storage solution for every branch.

Share artifacts across jobs and workflows

Within a single workflow it is common to upload in one job and download in another. That gives you simple job to job file handoff and keeps runners stateless. If you need to share artifacts across different workflows or across repositories you can use the artifacts API or attach files to a release. The API gives more control for longer term storage or cross repo consumption.

When to pick which method

  • Same workflow handoff use upload and download steps for speed and simplicity
  • Cross workflow or long term storage use the artifact API or a release for persistence

Naming and retention best practices

Bad names breed confusion. Pick descriptive artifact names that include branch, job name or run id so multiple builds do not step on each other. Control retention days to avoid surprise storage bills. Short lived artifacts keep costs down during normal CI cycles.

  • Include branch and run id in the artifact name to prevent overwrites
  • Set retention to a short safe value for everyday CI builds
  • Keep longer retention for releases or artifacts that must be audited

Example flow in plain English

Run tests and build in job A, upload the build artifacts with actions/upload-artifact, then run packaging or deployment in job B where you download the artifacts with actions/download-artifact. If you need to reuse outputs in another workflow publish via the API or attach to a release so the files persist beyond the normal retention window.

Quick checklist

  • Create a workflow under .github/workflows
  • Upload required files with actions/upload-artifact
  • Download them where needed with actions/download-artifact
  • Use stable naming patterns with branch and run id
  • Set sensible retention to manage storage costs

There you go. You can now pass build artifacts between jobs and workflows without melodrama. Treat names and retention like small acts of mercy for future you and your team.
seo_title: Publish and share GitHub Actions artifacts like a pro today
seo_heading: Upload download and manage build artifacts across workflows and jobs

title: Use Encrypted GitHub Actions Secrets in CI CD Workflows
description: Learn how to add encrypt and use GitHub Actions secrets so pipelines can access sensitive values securely and correctly.
heading: Use Encrypted GitHub Actions Secrets in CI CD Workflows
body:
If your CI CD pipeline treats secrets like party favors you will have a bad day. This guide shows how to add encrypt and use GitHub Actions secrets so workflows can access API keys tokens and other sensitive values without handing them to logs or attackers. Expect clear steps a few sarcastic asides and no nonsense about why the gh CLI is your friend.

Why GitHub Actions secrets actually matter

Secrets keep your infra from becoming public drama. If you push keys into logs they will be copied pasted and abused. Use repository level secrets for project specific values and organization secrets for shared credentials that cross projects. Treat secrets like teeth do not show them off unless you want trouble.

How to add a secret the easy way

Open repository settings or organization settings and add a new secret using the web UI. The UI performs encryption behind the scenes so the raw value never lives in plain text on GitHub servers. This method avoids extra steps and works for most use cases.

Quick CLI option

# set a secret with the official gh CLI
# gh will encrypt for you so you do not need to handle raw keys
gh secret set MY_SECRET -b"my super secret value"

When you must use the API

If you are automating secret creation with the API you must encrypt the secret value first using the target repository public key. That public key is provided by GitHub and you must use it with a libsodium style sealed box or a compatible library. The common pattern is to fetch the public key then encrypt and base64 encode the result before sending it in the API request.

If that sounds tedious use the gh CLI which handles the encryption for you and reduces human error.

How to reference secrets inside a workflow

In a job call the secret with the secrets context like ${{ secrets.MY_SECRET }}. You can pass that value to an environment variable or a command argument. Name the environment variable clearly so logs do not accidentally reveal the value.

Example usage notes

  • Prefer passing secrets to actions that accept an input that does not echo back the value
  • Avoid commands that print environment variables to logs
  • When calling external tools pipe the secret via stdin where possible

Testing without leaking

Run a dry job that echoes a placeholder value to confirm the secret path works. Replace real secrets with safe placeholders while iterating on workflow logic. Mask outputs and use conditional checks when a step might reveal sensitive content.

Common mistakes and how to avoid them

  • Storing secrets in code or plaintext files. That is not secure even if you think your repo is private.
  • Leaking secrets in logs by using echo or debugging commands that interpolate variables
  • Using unclear environment variable names which lead to accidental printing in logs
  • Sharing repository secrets when an organization secret would be better for rotation and auditing

Best practices summary

  • Use the web UI or gh CLI for most secret creation tasks
  • Encrypt manually only when automation requires the API and follow the public key encryption step with libsodium compatible libraries
  • Reference secrets with ${{ secrets.NAME }} and avoid printing them
  • Test using placeholders and mask outputs to prevent accidental exposure

Follow these steps and your GitHub Actions workflows will stop being a leaky faucet. Your ops team will sleep better and you will avoid having to explain how a token got into the wild.
seo_title: Stop Leaking Secrets in GitHub Actions Workflows Safely
seo_heading: Practical steps to encrypt and consume GitHub Actions secrets in CI CD pipelines

title: Lab 1 - Jenkins Configuration
description: Step by step guide to configure Jenkins for CI pipeline with user setup plugins and job creation
heading: Lab 1 - Jenkins Configuration Guide
body:
This tutorial teaches how to configure Jenkins for basic continuous integration tasks

  1. Install Jenkins
  2. Complete initial admin setup
  3. Install plugins
  4. Create users and credentials
  5. Connect source control and create a job
  6. Run a build and verify results

Install Jenkins by following platform specific instructions or run java -jar jenkins.war for a quick local lab. Expect a welcome page and a need to unlock the server with a generated password.

Complete the initial admin setup by entering the generated password and choosing an admin account. Choose strong credentials unless planning to host a carnival of broken builds.

Install plugins to add SCM support and pipeline features. The recommended plugin set covers common use cases. Add extra plugins only when absolutely necessary or when curiosity wins over common sense.

Create users and credentials next. Store SSH keys or tokens in the credential store. Jobs will use those entries to access repositories and remote systems without mailing a password to the console.

Connect source control by adding repository URLs to a new job or pipeline. For scripted pipelines provide a Jenkinsfile. For freestyle jobs configure build steps and post build actions.

Run a build and verify results by checking console output and build history. Fix failures by reading logs and adjusting credentials plugins or job configuration. Rerun builds until green or until deciding that red builds give character.
