title: Lab 2 - Jenkins Build Jobs
description: Hands on tutorial for creating Jenkins build jobs setting triggers and build steps for CI pipelines
heading: Lab 2 Jenkins Build Jobs Guide
body:
This tutorial teaches how to create and configure Jenkins build jobs including freestyle and pipeline jobs and how to trigger and run builds.

  1. Create a new job
  2. Configure source code management
  3. Define build steps or pipeline
  4. Set triggers and post build actions
  5. Run build and troubleshoot

Create a new job Visit the Jenkins dashboard and choose New Item. Pick a freestyle project for simple tasks or Pipeline for code defined pipelines. Give the job a name and proceed to configuration.

Configure source code management Select the Git option or other SCM provider. Add the repository URL credentials and branch specifier. Webhook setup in the repository can trigger builds automatically.

Define build steps or pipeline For freestyle jobs add build steps such as Execute shell for Maven or Gradle commands. For pipelines add a Jenkinsfile to the repository and reference that file. Example declarative snippet inside repository

pipeline { agent any stages { stage('Build') { steps { echo 'Building' } } stage('Test') { steps { echo 'Testing' } } } }

Set triggers and post build actions Use Poll SCM for scheduled checks or webhook based triggers for immediate builds. Add post build actions such as archive artifacts publish reports or send notifications to keep the team informed.

Run build and troubleshoot Use Build Now to start a run and open Console Output to see logs. Failed steps usually point to missing dependencies wrong paths or credential issues. Tweak steps run again and repeat until green.

The guide covered creating jobs configuring source control defining build actions setting triggers and checking build output. Following these steps turns a manual build process into an automated pipeline without needing to beg the server for mercy.

Tip

Store a Jenkinsfile in the same repository to keep pipeline code with source. That makes changes reviewable via pull requests and removes guesswork from job configuration.

title: Lab 3 - Advanced Jenkins Jobs
description: Advanced Jenkins job techniques for pipelines parameters credentials shared libraries triggers and testing to improve CI CD workflows
heading: Lab 3 Advanced Jenkins Jobs
body:
Quick summary for people who build pipelines

Welcome to the crash course in making Jenkins behave like an obedient robot instead of a haunted house. This guide covers multibranch pipelines for cleaner CI and CD, how to use parameters and credentials safely, when to pull common logic into a shared library, and how to avoid midnight pager parties with sensible triggers and tests. Read on for practical tips and a few sarcastic life lessons.

Design a multibranch pipeline that does the heavy lifting

Multibranch pipeline jobs are the reason you will stop babysitting branch jobs. Put a declarative Jenkinsfile next to your application code so each branch runs its own pipeline automatically. Versioning the pipeline with the repo keeps configuration consistent and avoids the old copy paste chaos.

  • Use declarative syntax for clarity and easier reviews.
  • Keep stages focused on build test and deploy.
  • Let branch indexing and branch source plugins discover feature branches and PRs automatically.

Why this matters for CI and CD

Multibranch setups reduce manual maintenance and make behavior predictable across branches. That means fewer surprises in production and fewer people loudly blaming the pipeline between sips of cold coffee.

Use parameters and manage credentials like a grown up

Parameters let you select environment feature toggles or build flags without editing the pipeline. For secrets use the Jenkins credentials store and avoid pasting secrets into jobs where curiosity and disaster can meet. In pipelines use the credentials binding features or relevant steps to inject secrets into the runtime instead of printing them into logs.

  • Define clear parameter defaults and validation where possible.
  • Limit credential scope to only the agents and steps that need them.
  • Never echo secrets into console output even if you are feeling brave.

Extract shared logic with a shared library for reuse

If you are repeating complex shell snippets or the same step sequences across repos it is time to move that logic into a shared library. Shared libraries keep your Jenkinsfiles small and make standardized behavior easier to enforce. Use global vars and helper steps to wrap common operations so pipelines read like a high level recipe rather than a horror script.

Configure triggers and notifications so humans can relax

Set up webhook triggers for push events and let scheduled builds handle periodic checks. For PRs rely on the branch source integrations so checks run when they need to. Add notifications to chat or email to inform teams when things fail or succeed. Notifications save time by stopping people from refreshing dashboards like anxious background processes.

  • Use webhooks from Git providers to trigger builds on push and PR activity.
  • Schedule cron style jobs for periodic tasks and maintenance checks.
  • Notify relevant channels on failure and on recovery to reduce noise.

Test and harden job configuration

Before you unleash a new pipeline into production run it through a linter or a disposable test job. Tools that validate pipeline syntax are your friend. Limit agent access and scope credentials to the minimal permissions required. Audit job definitions and plugin usage so changes do not cause surprise outages during peak hours.

  • Lint your Jenkinsfile locally or in a CI job that validates changes.
  • Use a sandbox or sample repository for experiments to avoid breaking production jobs.
  • Apply least privilege to agents and credentials and rotate secrets regularly.

Practical checklist to steal and use

  • Keep Jenkinsfile declarative and versioned with the app repo.
  • Use multibranch jobs so branches and PRs behave consistently.
  • Expose only the parameters you need and document them in the repo.
  • Store all secrets in the credentials store and inject at runtime.
  • Factor repeated work into a shared library for reuse and review.
  • Wire webhooks and targeted notifications to reduce manual checks.
  • Lint and test pipelines before granting them access to production resources.

Final tip

Keep a tiny sample repo devoted to pipeline experiments. That is the only place you should break things on purpose. It gives you a safe playground for new plugins or syntax and keeps your production Jenkins from staging its own reality show.

Follow these practices and your Jenkins pipelines will be more predictable and less dramatic. You will still get alerts at odd hours sometimes but at least they will be for real emergencies and not for a missing bracket in stage names.
seo_title: Build rock solid Jenkins pipelines for CI and CD automation
seo_heading: Practical multibranch Jenkins pipeline patterns with parameters and secrets

title: Lab 4 - Jenkins Template Jobs
description: Compact guide to building and using Jenkins template jobs for consistent CI workflows parameterized builds and reusable job definitions
heading: Lab 4 Jenkins Template Jobs tutorial
body:
If your Jenkins jobs look like a shrine to copy paste and chaos, templates are the sober friend you need. This guide walks through setting up Jenkins template jobs so builds stop making up their own rules and teams stop inventing unique ways to break pipelines.

Install plugins and tidy the server

Start by adding the Job DSL plugin or the Template Project plugin and make sure credentials for your source control are configured. A neat Jenkins matters because builds will not apologize for their behavior, they will just fail loudly.

Design a golden template job

Create a single golden job that contains common build steps, shared environment variables and post build actions. Use clear naming so humans on call do not have to play detective at 3 AM. Keep the template focused on shared concerns, not every special snowflake requirement.

Suggested template contents

  • Checkout steps and credential bindings
  • Build or pipeline stages that repeat across projects
  • Notifications and artifact publishing rules
  • Common environment variables and sensible defaults

Parameterize everything that varies

Replace hard coded values with parameters like REPO, BRANCH and BUILD_ARGS. Parameterized templates let many projects reuse one canonical config, and they prevent accidental copy paste therapy from becoming a career choice.

Instantiate child jobs from the template

Use Job DSL scripts or the template plugin to generate jobs from repository metadata or a small script. Generated jobs inherit pipeline steps, notifications and artifact rules so teams get predictable results instead of surprises.

Test templates and automate maintenance

Run sample builds, validate logs and verify artifacts. Store templates in source control and add automated validation so broken pipelines do not sneak into production. Treat templates like code and apply the same review and testing practices you use for applications.

Testing checklist

  • Run a full build with default parameters
  • Exercise parameter overrides and edge cases
  • Confirm notifications and artifact uploads
  • Run linting or validation as part of a CI job

Keep templates small and composable

Prefer tiny, focused template blocks that can be combined with parameter overrides. Small pieces are easier to review, easier to roll back and far less likely to become mysterious legacy magic.

Quick tips to avoid misery

  • Version templates in git for traceability and safe rollbacks
  • Document required parameters and sensible defaults
  • Automate validation so broken templates get caught early
  • Use Job DSL for programmatic generation when you have many projects

Templates will not make your team perfect, but they will reduce toil, enforce standards and speed onboarding. Do the work once and let Jenkins do the repeating, not your engineers.
seo_title: Make Jenkins template jobs enforce consistency and save time
seo_heading: Standardize CI pipelines with reusable Job DSL templates and parameters

title: Lab 5 - Non-Java Node Builds
description: Practical guide to building non Java nodes with cross compilation packaging and testing for embedded platforms from Lab 5
heading: Lab 5 Non Java Node Builds
body:
This tutorial teaches how to build non Java nodes for embedded platforms using cross compilation and packaging tools

  1. Install a matching cross toolchain
  2. Prepare source code and native dependencies
  3. Configure build scripts and flags
  4. Run cross compilation for the target
  5. Package the built node for deployment
  6. Deploy to target and run tests

Install a matching cross toolchain on the host machine so the compiler generates code for the target architecture rather than the host processor. Use a distro package or a vendor provided toolchain that matches CPU and libc choices for the target.

Prepare source code and native dependencies by collecting libraries and headers that the native module requires. Keep prebuilt binaries for the host separate from the ones used for the target platform.

Configure build scripts and flags to point to the cross compiler and sysroot. Override default compiler and linker variables inside build tools and package scripts so the correct architecture and ABI are produced.

Run cross compilation using the configured toolchain and verify output artifacts for correct architecture using file or readelf commands. Fix missing symbols by adding proper native libraries from the target sysroot.

Package the built node using the project packaging system. Include native libraries and a small loader that picks the right binary for runtime. Keep package layout predictable to make deployment simple.

Deploy to the target device and run basic tests to confirm the node loads native modules and communicates as expected. Use logging to catch ABI mismatches early and replace problematic binaries quickly.

Summary this Lab 5 style guide walked through a practical workflow to take non Java nodes from source through cross compilation packaging and deployment on embedded platforms

Tip

Match the toolchain libc and CPU variant to the target more than chasing the newest compiler. A perfect match saves hours of chasing mysterious runtime failures

title: Lab 6 - Jenkins Pipelines
description: Practical Lab 6 guide for Jenkins Pipelines with Jenkinsfile stages agents Blue Ocean and CI CD best practices
heading: Lab 6 - Jenkins Pipelines Practical Guide for CI CD
body:
Getting Jenkins and agents ready

Think of the controller as the project manager and agents as the overworked interns who do all the grunt work. Install the required plugins on the controller and register at least one agent node. The controller must have access to the code repository and the agent must have the right tools installed for your build, whether that is Maven for Java or whatever else your team insists on using.

Why keep the Jenkinsfile in the repo

Pipeline as code means your CI and CD definition lives alongside the application. That gives you version history a review trail and the ability to change build logic in a pull request without summoning the ancient Jenkins admin.

Write a clear Declarative Pipeline

Declarative Pipeline gives structure and predictable flow. Keep stages focused so failures are obvious and parallel work is possible. Here is a minimal example for a typical Java project that you can drop into your repo.

pipeline {
  agent any
  stages {
    stage('Checkout') {
      steps {
        checkout scm
      }
    }
    stage('Build') {
      steps {
        sh 'mvn -B package'
      }
    }
    stage('Test') {
      steps {
        sh 'mvn test'
      }
    }
    stage('Deploy') {
      steps {
        sh './deploy.sh'
      }
    }
  }
}

Manage credentials and environment safely

Never paste secrets into the Jenkinsfile like a caveman tattooing a password on a wall. Use the Jenkins credentials store and reference credentials by ID in environment blocks. That prevents secrets from ending up in logs and keeps third party access scoped to what it actually needs.

Checklist for secure setup

  • Store tokens and keys in the credentials store
  • Use scoped credentials for external services
  • Keep agent images trimmed to the tools you need
  • Restrict who can edit pipeline code through repo permissions

Run the pipeline and read the tea leaves

Trigger the job manually or wire up a webhook for automatic runs. When things fail the console log will be dramatic but brutally honest. Use the replay feature for quick iterative debugging when you do not want to push a new commit every five minutes.

Use Blue Ocean for visualization and troubleshooting

Blue Ocean does a handsome job of turning text into a flow chart that even managers can pretend to understand. It highlights failing stages and gives quick links to raw logs so you can find the broken command without scrolling through the whole build like a time traveler looking for clues.

Troubleshooting tips

  • If checkout fails confirm repository URL and credentials
  • If the build fails check that required tools are installed on the agent
  • If tests fail run them locally to isolate flaky tests from pipeline issues
  • If a deploy step fails verify environment variables and service access

Organize stages for speed and clarity

Split slow integration tests into their own stage and use parallel stages for independent work. A tidy stage layout improves visibility and helps you spot which piece of the pipeline decided to go rogue this time.

Keep learning and iterate fast

Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment are not set and forget projects. Treat your Jenkinsfile like production code. Use branch builds run frequent tests and refine your pipeline as your application evolves. When pipeline troubleshooting becomes a regular hobby you will know you are doing CI right.

Follow these steps and you will have a reliable Jenkins Pipelines setup with clear pipelines managed in a Jenkinsfile blue ocean visual feedback and sensible handling of credentials and agents. That is the technical bit done now go watch your first successful build and enjoy a small victory.
seo_title: Practical Jenkins Pipelines Guide for CI CD Reliability
seo_heading: Build test and deploy with Jenkinsfile and Blue Ocean visual flows

title: Lab 12 - Groovy Pipelines & Shared Libraries
description: Hands on guide to Groovy Jenkins pipelines and shared libraries for reusable CI CD code and cleaner Jenkinsfiles
heading: Lab 12 Groovy Pipelines and Shared Libraries
body:
If your CI server could sigh it would say thank you for building reusable pipeline code. This guide walks through building Groovy based Jenkins pipelines and authoring shared libraries that other teams can actually use without crying. We cover repository setup, library layout, global vars and helper classes, loading the library from a Jenkinsfile, testing locally, and versioning releases for safe consumption in CI and CD workflows.

Prepare the repository and Jenkins setup

Start by creating a Git repo for your shared library and make sure Jenkins can reach it. Enable the shared library integration in the Jenkins global configuration and add credentials if your repo is private. Put a simple Jenkinsfile in a reachable branch or repository so Jenkins does not sulk.

  • Enable shared library in Manage Jenkins under Global Pipeline Libraries
  • Provide repository URL and credentials if required
  • Keep a simple Jenkinsfile in a branch for manual testing

Library layout that keeps Jenkins happy

Jenkins expects a specific layout. At the root of the library repo create vars and src folders. Put simple global step wrappers in vars and full Groovy classes in src. Follow this structure and the loader will behave itself.

my-shared-library
  ├─ vars
  │  ├─ buildApp.groovy
  │  └─ notifySuccess.groovy
  └─ src
     └─ com
        └─ example
           └─ BuildHelpers.groovy

Global vars and helper classes

Keep global vars small and explicit. A typical global var is a file in vars that defines a call method which can accept a map. Use classes in src for heavier logic so you do not turn the var into a magical blob only you understand.

// vars/notifySuccess.groovy
def call(Map args) {
  echo "Notifying team about ${args.status}"
  def helpers = new com.example.BuildHelpers()
  helpers.sendNotification(args)
}

Write a Jenkinsfile that loads the library

You can load the library with the @Library annotation or by using the globally configured library name. Then call your global vars like simple functions. Both declarative and scripted pipelines can call into shared code, but keep style consistent across your org.

@Library('my-shared-library@master') _
pipeline {
  agent any
  stages {
    stage('Build') {
      steps {
        script {
          buildApp()
        }
      }
    }
    stage('Notify') {
      steps {
        script {
          notifySuccess(status: 'SUCCESS')
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

Create reusable steps that do one job

Design functions that do one thing and do it well. Small focused helpers are easier to test and less likely to become legacy folklore. Examples include buildApp, publishArtifacts, and notifySuccess. Avoid magic methods that only the author can reverse engineer at 3 a m.

Test the pipeline and library locally and in Jenkins

Do not push untested changes directly to a shared Jenkins server unless you enjoy surprise outages. Use a Jenkins sandbox, a pipeline runner, or a disposable Jenkins instance for validation. Unit test Groovy classes with standard frameworks like Spock or JUnit when possible. Integration test the Jenkinsfile against a test job.

Version and publish the shared library

Use tags or branches so consumers can pin stable releases. Semantic versioning works well in practice. Update the README with examples and usage notes so the adoption path is not a scavenger hunt. Keep a changelog so teams know when you broke them on purpose.

  • Tag releases for stable consumption
  • Document usage and examples in the repo
  • Provide migration notes for breaking changes

Final thoughts

Shared libraries bring order to pipeline as code when done right. Follow the structure, write focused steps, test before you deploy, and version your releases. Do that and your Jenkins pipelines will be more reliable, your teammates will thank you, and you can stop pretending global scripts are a good long term strategy.
seo_title: Master Jenkins Groovy pipelines with reusable shared libraries
seo_heading: A practical guide to creating Groovy shared libraries for Jenkins pipelines

title: Lab 8 - Jenkins Security
description: Hands on Jenkins security lab covering authentication authorization plugins and practical hardening steps for CI pipelines
heading: Lab 8 Jenkins Security Guide for Hardening Jenkins
body:
Why bother locking Jenkins down

If your Jenkins server is still running with default settings you are basically handing out keys to the kingdom with a ribbon on top. This guide walks through actionable Jenkins security steps that actually reduce risk while keeping your CI CD pipelines functional. You will learn how to enable authentication, limit permissions, install security plugins, harden agents and test the controls. No magic, no fake APIs, just solid hardening.

Start with access control basics

First things first, turn on security and create a real admin account that someone can remember without writing it on a sticky note. Default credentials are a hacker invitation and a great way to lose sleep. Use a strong password or integrate with centralized identity if you are in a grown up environment.

Pick the right security realm

Local user database is fine for labs and small teams. For enterprises use LDAP or OAuth providers for centralized authentication. This reduces credential sprawl and makes onboarding less of a ritual sacrifice to the config gods.

Choose an authorization model that fits your team

Prefer least privilege. Matrix security gives fine grained control, role based access with the Role Strategy plugin makes group management easier. Avoid giving blanket rights to anonymous users or developers who only need to run jobs. Trust but verify, then remove the trust.

Install and maintain security plugins

Plugins add protection, but they also add risk if they are stale or unnecessary. Install recommended plugins and keep them updated. Useful ones include the Role Strategy plugin, Matrix Authorization Strategy, Audit Trail or Logging plugins, and Configuration as Code for reproducible security settings. Remove unused plugins that only exist to collect dust and CVEs.

Harden agents and network access

Agents are a common weak spot. Enforce encrypted agent protocols, require agent authentication, and run agents behind private networks or VPNs. Use HTTPS for the Jenkins web interface and get a valid certificate so browsers stop yelling at you.

More network and CLI tweaks

  • Enable CSRF protection so bad requests do not act like good ones
  • Restrict CLI and script execution with whitelists and credentials policies
  • Disable unused endpoints and TCP ports that are only useful to troublemakers

Test your access controls like a skeptical developer

Log in as representative roles and try common workflows. Build jobs, change job config, trigger pipelines, and try to view credentials. If someone can do something they should not do, fix the policy. Repeat until the balance between security and developer sanity is acceptable.

Backup and rollback plans

Always backup the Jenkins configuration and credential stores before making changes and again after you are happy. If an authorization tweak breaks important pipelines you want to restore quickly, not ask a developer to reinvent the build script from memory.

Use configuration as code for consistency

Store security settings in configuration as code so changes are auditable and reproducible. This reduces the chance of configuration drift and makes onboarding new servers less terrifying.

Quick checklist for a reasonable Jenkins hardening

  • Enable security and create an admin account with a strong password
  • Use LDAP or OAuth for authentication where possible
  • Apply least privilege with matrix or role based authorization
  • Install and update security plugins, remove unused ones
  • Enforce HTTPS and CSRF protection, lock down CLI access
  • Harden agents with authentication and private networks
  • Test representative user journeys and backup configs
  • Manage settings with configuration as code

This is not about making Jenkins impossible to use. It is about closing the low hanging doors that attackers love, while keeping developer workflows intact. Follow these steps, add logging and audits, and sleep a little better tonight.
seo_title: Secure Jenkins for CI CD with real world hardening steps
seo_heading: Practical Jenkins security guide for authentication authorization and agents

title: Install Ubuntu 20 on VMWare Player in Less than 5 Minutes
description: Quick guide to install Ubuntu 20 on VMware Player using an ISO and VMware Tools for a fast and stable virtual desktop setup.
heading: Install Ubuntu 20 on VMWare Player in Less than 5 Minutes
body:
What you need before you start

Yes this is going to be fast and yes you can do it without crying. Gather these items first so you do not waste time rebooting the host into BIOS at three in the morning.

  • Ubuntu 20.04 desktop ISO 64 bit downloaded from the official Ubuntu site
  • VMware Player installed on the host machine
  • At least 8 GB free disk space and virtualization support enabled in BIOS or UEFI
  • A few minutes and a willingness to click the obvious buttons

Creating the virtual machine

Open VMware Player and choose create a new virtual machine. Point the wizard to the Ubuntu ISO you downloaded. Pick the typical or recommended settings unless you enjoy manual mysticism.

Hardware settings for a pleasant experience

  • CPUs: assign at least two cores to avoid slow motion typing
  • Memory: 4 GB minimum for a responsive desktop 8 GB if you want to run browsers and not weep
  • Disk: 20 GB or larger. Choose single file for a small performance win
  • Network: bridged when you test services on the network otherwise NAT is fine

Installing Ubuntu

Boot the VM and follow the installer prompts. Pick normal installation and check the option to install third party drivers if you plan to use proprietary Wi Fi or graphics. Create your user account and let the installer do the heavy lifting.

The installer will handle partitioning for you by default and will do the base software install. When it asks about updates choose the option that fits your patience level. You can skip updates now and run them after the first boot if you want to avoid a long initial wait.

Installing VMware Tools

After the first boot open the VMware Player menu and choose install VMware Tools or use the guest additions option. On Ubuntu the best practice is to install open vm tools from the package manager for integration that just works.

  • Open a terminal in the VM
  • Run sudo apt update and then sudo apt install open-vm-tools-desktop if you want clipboard and shared folder support
  • Reboot the VM to activate resized display and shared folders

Final tweaks and daily use

Run Software Updater to pick up kernel and security patches. Adjust display scaling and keyboard layout in Settings. Create a shared folder if you need easy file transfer between host and guest.

This setup is stable for development testing learning Linux or just pretending you are a sysadmin without real consequences.

Troubleshooting and quick tips

  • VM boots slowly Try increasing RAM or switching disk to a preallocated single file
  • No network Try toggling between NAT and bridged and check host firewall rules
  • Display issues Make sure open vm tools desktop is installed and reboot the guest
  • Want speed Enable hardware virtualization in the host BIOS or UEFI and make sure nested virtualization is off unless you are doing Inception level testing

If you followed the steps you now have Ubuntu 20 running in VMware Player with VMware Tools installed and basic settings tuned. Now go break something in a VM instead of a real machine and pretend it was intentional.

seo_heading: Step by step Ubuntu 20 VM setup with VMware Player for testers and learners

gem install jekyll bundler

title: How to build with Jenkins and Docker example
description: Compact tutorial to build Docker images with Jenkins pipelines run tests and push images for CI pipeline best practices and tips
heading: How to build with Jenkins and Docker example
body:
This tutorial shows how to use Jenkins pipelines to build Docker images run tests and push artifacts as part of a simple CI example.

  2. Install Docker and Jenkins on a host or VM
  3. Create a Jenkinsfile pipeline
  4. Use a Docker agent for builds
  5. Run pipeline and push image to registry

Prepare repository and Dockerfile

Place source code in a Git repo alongside a Dockerfile that declares the build steps. Keep layers small and cache friendly. A minimal local build command is docker build -t myapp . for quick testing.

Install Docker and Jenkins

Install Docker engine on the build host and install Jenkins as a service. Grant the Jenkins user access to the Docker socket or configure a Docker group so the Jenkins process can run container tasks without drama.

Create a Jenkinsfile pipeline

Write a declarative Jenkinsfile with stages such as checkout build test and push. Use the pipeline to run shell commands that build a Docker image and run unit tests inside a container if needed.

Use a Docker agent for builds

Configure an agent that runs builds inside a clean container. That keeps the build environment reproducible and avoids garbage on the host machine. The Docker plugin or Kubernetes plugin are common choices.

Run pipeline and push image to registry

Execute the pipeline to verify the image builds pass tests and then log in to a registry to push the image. Use credentials stored in Jenkins credentials store to avoid leaking secrets.

This workflow teaches how to combine Jenkins and Docker for reliable CI builds. The pipeline moves code from repository to built container images while ensuring tests run in a controlled environment. Follow the steps to set up local testing then move to a shared Jenkins server for team use.

Tip

Use image tags based on commit SHA or build number to avoid accidental overwrites and enable easy rollbacks when a deploy goes sideways.

title: Apache Ant & Jenkins Build Job Examples
description: Practical guide to creating Ant build files and configuring Jenkins build jobs for continuous integration and automation
heading: Apache Ant and Jenkins Build Job Examples
body:
This tutorial shows how to use Apache Ant and Jenkins to create and run build jobs for a Java project using simple examples and practical steps.

  1. Verify tools and environment
  2. Create a basic Ant build file
  3. Create a Jenkins job
  4. Add build steps and archive artifacts
  5. Run the job and inspect results

Step 1 Verify tools and environment. Confirm Java and Ant are installed by running java -version and ant -version. Confirm Jenkins is reachable on the chosen host and port.

Step 2 Create a basic Ant build file. Add a build.xml with targets such as clean, compile, and jar. Example target commands use javac and the jar task to produce a distributable artifact.

Step 3 Create a Jenkins job. Use a Freestyle project or a Pipeline job. For a Freestyle project select source control repository and set up a build step that calls ant clean jar. For a Pipeline place Ant commands inside a sh or bat step depending on the agent OS.

Step 4 Add build steps and archive artifacts. Configure post build actions to archive the generated jar or zip file. Set environment variables in the job to control behavior across branches and stages.

Step 5 Run the job and inspect results. Trigger a manual build or set up a webhook for push events. Review console output for any compilation errors and download archived artifacts for verification.

This companion guide walked through basic Ant file creation and Jenkins job configuration for continuous builds. Follow the steps to get a reproducible automated build that compiles code packages and stores artifacts for later deployment.

Tip

Use a dedicated build user on Jenkins agents and keep build.xml under source control. That provides reproducible builds and fewer surprises when dependencies change.

title: Declarative Jenkins Pipeline for Ant builds with Docker Exam
description: Practical guide to run Ant builds in a Declarative Jenkins Pipeline using Docker for consistent CI on agents and reproducible builds
heading: Declarative Jenkins Pipeline for Ant builds with Docker Example
body:
This tutorial shows how to create a Declarative Jenkins Pipeline that runs Ant builds inside a Docker container for clean and reproducible CI runs.

  1. Prepare Jenkins and agent with Docker support
  2. Create a Declarative Jenkinsfile
  3. Select or build an Ant Docker image
  4. Run build steps and archive results
  5. Add tests notifications and cleanup

Prepare Jenkins and agent with Docker support by installing the Docker plugin on the controller and ensuring Jenkins agents can run Docker commands or have Docker installed. The goal is to allow the pipeline to spin up a container when a job runs so the build environment matches across runs.

Create a Declarative Jenkinsfile stored in the source repository. Use the declarative pipeline block and define an agent that uses a Docker image. This keeps pipeline logic readable and portable for other team members who will inevitably ask questions at 2 AM.

Select or build an Ant Docker image that contains the desired JDK and Ant. Use an official Ant image or create a small Dockerfile that installs a specific JDK and Ant version. Tag the image clearly and push to a registry accessible by Jenkins agents.

Run build steps and archive results inside the pipeline. Invoke Ant targets for compile and test. Use stash and archive artifacts steps so build artifacts and test reports survive agent cleanup. That way the next person who breaks the build has evidence to present at standup.

Add tests notifications and cleanup. Publish JUnit results and send build notifications via email or chat. Use post blocks in the Declarative pipeline to always run cleanup steps so ephemeral containers do not linger.

This guide covered preparing Jenkins with Docker support creating a Jenkinsfile that runs Ant inside a Docker image running build and test steps and preserving artifacts and reports. The approach yields consistent builds across agents and reduces the classic developer blame game.

Tip

Pin the Docker image to a specific tag and include a simple verification stage that prints the Java and Ant versions. That prevents surprises when the image owner decides to upgrade the world without warning.

Prepare Maven project Create a standard Maven layout and add a pom.xml with groupId artifactId and version. Add JUnit tests so the pipeline has something to fail on and demonstrate test reporting.

Configure Jenkins server Install a JDK and add Maven under global tools. Create credentials for the source repository and set up a pipeline job or a Multibranch pipeline to scan a Git repository for branches.

Create Jenkinsfile Write a declarative pipeline that checks out code runs mvn clean package and archives the produced artifacts. Use sh on Unix agents or bat on Windows agents and set up post build steps to publish test results.

Cache Maven dependencies on build agents by using a shared local repository or mount a cache directory. That change can cut build time dramatically especially when many developers trigger frequent builds.

title: Example of a Jenkins Maven Integration Pipeline for Java Bui
description: Compact guide to create a Jenkins pipeline that runs Maven builds tests and archives Java artifacts for continuous integration
heading: Example of a Jenkins Maven Integration Pipeline for Java Builds
body:
Overview

If you want reproducible Java builds and a CI pipeline that does not scream at you at 3 AM then this is for you. This guide walks through a Jenkins pipeline that uses Maven to compile code run unit testing and produce artifacts ready for CD. It keeps things simple and predictable while adding just enough automation to make your future self proud or at least less annoyed.

What you need first

  • Jenkins installed on a supported version with the Pipeline plugin and Git plugin
  • Maven installed on a build agent or defined in Jenkins global tools
  • A source code repo with a pom.xml and some unit tests
  • Credentials with only the rights needed to clone and push artifacts

Configure Maven and Jenkins global tools

Point Jenkins at a known Maven installation via Manage Jenkins then Global Tool Configuration. Locking a Maven version keeps builds deterministic. If you prefer not to install Maven on every agent define a tool and let Jenkins handle it.

Create the pipeline job and connect source control

Create a pipeline job and give it access to your repository with a credential that only reads the code. Do not hand out admin keys to an automated job unless you enjoy incident reports.

Write a Jenkinsfile with clear stages

Use declarative pipeline syntax. A typical stage order is checkout compile test package and archive artifacts. Invoke Maven with goals like mvn clean verify or mvn clean package depending on whether you want integration checks.

Example stages

  • checkout code from Git
  • build with Maven using the configured tool
  • run unit tests and publish test reports
  • package and store artifacts in an artifact repository or archive with Jenkins

Handle credentials and artifacts

Add only the credentials you need to access the repository and artifact store. Use an artifact repository or the archiveArtifacts step so jars do not vanish into the void. Proper artifact storage prevents the mystery of where that release binary disappeared.

Run the pipeline and inspect results

Launch the job and watch the console output and stage view. Maven failures show up in the logs and test failures are visible in the test reports when you configure the JUnit or related reporting plugin. Fix the tests then run again unless your team likes surprise breaks.

Tips for less chaos

  • Use a small deterministic Maven settings file and lock dependency versions
  • Fail fast on tests so broken code does not slip through
  • Keep Jenkinsfile readable and keep stages focused
  • Use worker agents that match your production JVM if possible

Follow these steps and you get reproducible builds cleaner CI feedback and artifacts you can actually find. It is not magic but it saves time and improves developer sanity which is almost the same thing.

title: Warnings Next Gen Jenkins Plugin for Static Analysis
description: Guide to use Warnings Next Generation in Jenkins to parse static analysis tool output configure thresholds and publish clear reports
heading: Warnings Next Gen Jenkins Plugin for Static Analysis
body:
Why bother with Warnings NG in Jenkins

If your CI pipeline treats warnings like a polite suggestion then you are doing it wrong. The Warnings Next Generation plugin for Jenkins gives those nagging linter and compiler complaints a place in the light of day. It parses tool output, shows trends, and can fail builds when code quality goes on vacation.

Install and find the plugin

Go to Manage Plugins in Jenkins and install Warnings NG. Restart if Jenkins starts sulking. The plugin will appear in the list of installed plugins alongside other ambitious little utilities.

Configure parsers and patterns

Open Global Tool Configuration and add parsers for the tools you use. Give each parser a clear name so it does not pretend to be a different parser during a run. Test with a sample log so the parser does not act surprised when it sees real output.

  • Use built in parsers for common tools like Java compilers or popular linters
  • Create custom patterns for legacy tools or weird log formats
  • Keep names consistent with what you will reference in pipelines or jobs

Add static analysis to the build

Make sure your build writes warnings into console output or to report files. Most linters and compilers can emit either machine friendly formats or plain text logs that the plugin can parse. If the tool can produce reports prefer that over parsing messy console output, but parsing console output works when you are lazy or in a hurry.

Example pipeline snippet

pipeline {
  agent any
  stages {
    stage("Build") {
      steps {
        sh 'mvn clean verify'
      }
    }
    stage("Publish") {
      steps {
        warnings parserName 'Java'
      }
    }
  }
}

Publish warnings in freestyle and pipeline jobs

In freestyle jobs add the Warnings Next Generation publisher in the post build actions. In pipeline jobs add the warnings step as shown above. That step will collect parsed warnings and feed them into the Jenkins dashboard and change sets.

Quality gates and thresholds

Set thresholds to fail builds on new high severity warnings or to mark builds unstable when the warning trend heads uphill. Use differential analysis to focus reviewer attention on new issues introduced by the current change instead of punishing developers for sins committed before your time.

  • Fail on new high severity warnings when you want strict code quality
  • Mark unstable on rising trends when you need a gentle nudge
  • Use differential analysis to highlight new warnings only

Troubleshooting tips

If your parser misses things test with a known sample log and iterate on the pattern. Prefer structured reports when available. If the plugin shows more warnings than expected check that you are parsing the right file or console segment and that previous build artifacts are not being reprocessed.

Final thoughts on code quality and CI

Warnings NG will not fix your code for you, but it will point out where your code is crying for help. Integrate it into your Jenkins CI pipeline, tune parsers and quality gates, and use reports to turn noisy text into actionable dashboards. Your future self will send thanks and maybe fewer curses.
seo_title: Make Jenkins Catch Code Smells With Warnings NG Plugin
seo_heading: Collect and gate static analysis results in your Jenkins pipeline

title: Jenkins with PMD, FindBugs and CheckStyle Plugins Example
description: Configure Jenkins with PMD FindBugs and CheckStyle plugins to add static analysis to builds and publish issue reports for better code quality

This tutorial shows how to set up Jenkins to run PMD FindBugs and CheckStyle plugins to analyze Java code during continuous integration.

Install plugins in Jenkins Use Manage Plugins to search for PMD FindBugs and CheckStyle then install and restart if recommended. Plugin packages provide parsers and reporters that convert raw warnings into readable build artifacts.

Expect some noise at first and then enjoy progressively cleaner code because developers now get instant feedback during builds.

title: Jenkins Docker Pipeline Maven Build Example
description: Step by step guide to run Maven builds in Jenkins using Docker agents and pipeline for reproducible CI runs
heading: Jenkins Docker Pipeline Maven Build Example explained
body:
This tutorial shows how to configure a Jenkins pipeline that uses a Docker image to run Maven builds in a reproducible CI workflow.

  1. Prepare environment
  2. Create a Jenkinsfile that uses a Docker agent
  3. Checkout source and run Maven build
  4. Archive artifacts and publish results
  5. Run tests and clean up

Prepare environment means install Docker on the machine that will run pipeline agents and add the Docker plugin to Jenkins if missing. Also grant the Jenkins user permission to manage Docker so commands do not fail for reasons unrelated to actual code quality.

Create a Jenkinsfile that uses a Docker agent. A minimal example looks like this

pipeline { agent { docker { image 'maven 3 jdk 8' } } stages { stage('Checkout') { steps { sh 'git clone repo placeholder' } } stage('Build') { steps { sh 'mvn clean package' } } } }

Checkout source and run Maven build means use the standard checkout step and run Maven commands inside the Docker agent. Maven will run with the environment provided by the chosen image so builds stay consistent across hosts.

Archive artifacts and publish results means use archive step for binary outputs and JUnit publisher for test reports. That gives a neat history in the Jenkins UI and saves hours of squinting at console logs.

Run tests and clean up means fail fast on broken tests and remove temporary containers or volumes that might hog disk space or cause flaky runs. Caching Maven dependencies across builds speeds up the process so the build server does not cry every morning.

Summary recap of the workflow shows how Jenkins orchestrates a Docker based Maven build using a Jenkinsfile that defines agent steps stages and artifact handling. This pattern yields reproducible CI runs that behave the same on developer machines and pipelines.

Tip

Use a custom Maven settings file and a local repository cache mounted as a volume on the Docker agent to drastically reduce build time and network noise.

title: Jenkins GitHub WebHooks Example
description: Learn how to trigger Jenkins jobs from GitHub using webhooks. Setup plugins create job add webhook test trigger and secure payloads
heading: Jenkins GitHub WebHooks Example Guide
body:
This tutorial shows how to configure GitHub webhooks to trigger Jenkins jobs automatically and securely.

  1. Prepare Jenkins and plugins
  2. Create a Jenkins job and enable GitHub integration
  3. Add a webhook in the GitHub repository
  4. Trigger and test the webhook
  5. Secure webhook and troubleshoot

Prepare Jenkins and plugins Install the GitHub plugin and the GitHub Branch Source plugin from Manage Plugins on the Jenkins server. Add credentials for GitHub access and register a GitHub server under global configuration for smoother authentication.

Create a Jenkins job and enable GitHub integration Create a freestyle job or a pipeline job that uses the Git repository. Configure the Build Triggers section to accept GitHub hook triggers or use a Multibranch Pipeline for branch based builds. Point the SCM to the repository with proper credentials.

Add a webhook in the GitHub repository In the repository settings add a webhook with the Jenkins webhook endpoint path. Choose application slash json as the content type and paste a secret token that will also be entered on the Jenkins side for signature verification.

Trigger and test the webhook Push a change or use the Recent Deliveries panel on GitHub to resend a payload. Verify a new build appears in Jenkins by checking the job console output and the delivery logs on GitHub for HTTP response codes and response bodies.

Secure webhook and troubleshoot Use a shared secret and enable signature verification for the payload header named X-Hub-Signature-256. If webhook delivery fails confirm firewall rules allow traffic from GitHub and that the webhook endpoint is reachable from outside networks. Check credentials and SCM settings if the clone step fails.

This guide covered plugin installation, job setup, webhook creation, testing and basic security checks required to automate Jenkins builds from GitHub events. Following the ordered steps will deliver automated triggers and reduce manual build kicks while making debugging a bit less painful.

Tip

Use a tunnel service for local testing to expose the Jenkins server to GitHub and watch delivery logs on the repository. Always enable a secret and verify signatures to avoid accepting forged payloads.

title: Fix the Jenkins withMaven not found DSL pipeline error
description: Quick guide to resolve the Jenkins withMaven not found DSL pipeline error by installing the right plugin and configuring Maven tools
heading: Fix the Jenkins withMaven not found DSL pipeline error
body:
This tutorial shows how to fix the Jenkins withMaven not found DSL pipeline error by installing the Pipeline Maven Integration plugin and configuring Maven tools for pipeline builds.

  1. Install the Pipeline Maven Integration plugin
  2. Configure Maven in Global Tool Configuration
  3. Update pipeline syntax to use the withMaven wrapper
  4. Restart Jenkins and run the job
  5. Verify agent environment and plugin compatibility

Install the Pipeline Maven Integration plugin from Manage Plugins in Jenkins and perform a restart. This plugin provides the withMaven pipeline step that vanished and caused the error.

Open Manage Jenkins then Global Tool Configuration and add a Maven installation. Give the installation a clear name that the pipeline can reference. Configure automatic installer or point to an existing Maven on the agent.

Wrap build stages with the withMaven wrapper so the pipeline can find Maven and run lifecycle goals. An example declarative pipeline block follows.

pipeline { agent any stages { stage("Build") { steps { withMaven { sh "mvn -B -DskipTests clean package" } } } } }

Restart Jenkins after plugin changes and run the job. Check the console output for the presence of the withMaven step and for any errors about missing tools. Logs will show whether the wrapper loaded correctly.

Confirm that agents have a compatible Java version and that Maven is either on the PATH or configured as a tool. Also check that plugin versions match the Jenkins core version. Old or mismatched plugins are a favorite source of mystery failures.

Following these steps restores the withMaven DSL support for pipeline builds by ensuring the right plugin is installed and Maven is configured both in Jenkins and on build agents. The pipeline then has a reliable way to run Maven goals and collect reports.

Tip

If the withMaven step remains missing enable verbose plugin logs and check Manage Plugins for dependency gaps. Matching plugin versions to the Jenkins core saves a lot of debugging drama.

title: How to run Jenkins on AWS
description: Step by step guide to deploy Jenkins on AWS EC2 with security group setup installation and basic pipeline tips
heading: How to run Jenkins on AWS guide
body:
This tutorial shows how to deploy Jenkins on AWS using an EC2 instance security group configuration and a basic pipeline setup.

  1. Provision an EC2 instance
  2. Open network ports for SSH and Jenkins
  3. SSH into the instance and install Java
  4. Install and start the Jenkins service
  5. Unlock and configure the Jenkins server
  6. Optional hardening and persistent storage

Provision an EC2 instance using a current Ubuntu image with a sensible instance size. Choose a key pair for SSH access and pick a placement that makes the CI server reachable by the team.

Open network ports by editing the security group. Allow SSH from admin IP addresses and allow TCP port 8080 from trusted networks. Expose port 8080 to the public internet only if the Jenkins server will be behind authentication and monitoring.

SSH into the EC2 instance using the chosen key pair and the public IP address. Run package updates and install a modern Java runtime so the Jenkins service has a floor to stand on.

Install Jenkins from the package manager or use the jenkins war if a quick test is desired. Start and enable the Jenkins service so the server survives reboots.

When Jenkins first runs retrieve the initial admin password from the Jenkins home folder and complete the web setup. Install suggested plugins or pick minimal plugins for a tidy server. Create an admin user and configure credentials for source control access.

For production attach an EBS volume for job workspaces configure an IAM role for any AWS API access and consider an application load balancer with HTTPS termination for secure traffic. Backups of the Jenkins home folder avoid painful rebuilds.

Recap this tutorial covered launching an EC2 instance opening required ports installing Java and Jenkins starting the Jenkins service unlocking the web UI and planning for production readiness.

Tip

Use an IAM role for the EC2 instance rather than embedding AWS keys into the Jenkins server. That reduces secret sprawl and makes the Jenkins server behave like a grown up.

title: Run Bitnami Jenkins with AWS
description: Quick guide to deploy Bitnami Jenkins on AWS EC2 with SSH access security group setup and initial Jenkins configuration
heading: Run Bitnami Jenkins with AWS for quick EC2 deployment
body:
This guide teaches how to launch and run a Bitnami Jenkins stack on AWS using an EC2 instance and basic security settings.

  1. Choose a Bitnami Jenkins AMI and instance type
  2. Create key pair and security group allowing SSH and web ports
  3. Launch the EC2 instance and note the public IP
  4. SSH into the server and retrieve the initial admin password
  5. Finish Jenkins setup and create an admin user
  6. Optional add persistent storage and enable HTTPS

Choose a Bitnami Jenkins AMI and instance type Select the official Bitnami Jenkins image from the AWS marketplace. Pick an instance size that matches expected build load. Small teams often start with a t3.small and scale up later.

Create key pair and security group allowing SSH and web ports Make a key pair for SSH access and a security group that opens port 22 for admin access and port 8080 for Jenkins web UI. Add port 80 if the image uses HTTP on a standard port.

Launch the EC2 instance and note the public IP Start the instance and record the public DNS or public IP for remote access. Allow a minute or two for the stack to finish boot tasks that run on first launch.

SSH into the server and retrieve the initial admin password Use a command like ssh -i mykey.pem bitnami@PUBLIC_IP to connect. Find the initial Jenkins password in the Bitnami credentials file or Jenkins secrets path for example sudo cat /opt/bitnami/jenkins/jenkins_home/secrets/initialAdminPassword

Finish Jenkins setup and create an admin user Open the web UI at the public IP and port 8080. Use the admin password to unlock Jenkins then install suggested plugins and create the first admin account.

Optional add persistent storage and enable HTTPS Attach an EBS volume for build artifacts and configuration persistence. For HTTPS obtain a certificate using Certbot or use a load balancer with ACM to handle TLS termination.

This short tutorial covered launching the Bitnami Jenkins AMI on EC2 connecting via SSH retrieving the initial admin password completing the Jenkins setup and options for persistence and TLS protection.

Tip

Create an AMI snapshot after configuring Jenkins and plugins so future environments come preconfigured and boot faster. Backups and automated snapshots keep that precious pipeline history alive.

title: Install Jenkins on Windows 10 Fast
description: Quick guide to install Jenkins on Windows 10 with Java setup MSI installer and first admin configuration for CI CD.
heading: Install Jenkins on Windows 10 Fast Guide
body:
This guide shows how to install and run Jenkins on Windows 10 quickly and reliably.

  1. Install Java
  2. Download the Jenkins MSI
  3. Run the installer as administrator
  4. Unlock Jenkins using the initial admin password
  5. Install suggested plugins and create a user
  6. Verify the Jenkins service and open the web dashboard

Step 1 Install Java Java is a required runtime for Jenkins. Install a supported JDK or JRE version and confirm the JAVA_HOME environment variable points to the Java folder. A missing Java will make Jenkins sulk and refuse to start.

Step 2 Download the Jenkins MSI Grab the Windows MSI from the official Jenkins download page. Choose the LTS build for stability unless the goal is chaos and nightly surprises.

Step 3 Run the installer as administrator Right click and run with elevated privileges. The installer will set up a Windows service and default ports. Allow the installer through the firewall if prompted.

Step 4 Unlock Jenkins using the initial admin password After the first launch a file appears with an initial admin password under Program Files Jenkins secrets initialAdminPassword. Open that file and paste the value into the web setup to unlock the server.

Step 5 Install suggested plugins and create a user Use the suggested plugin set to get a practical CI platform quickly. Create the first admin user during setup and avoid using guessable passwords unless the goal is free curious visitors.

Step 6 Verify the Jenkins service and open the web dashboard Confirm the Jenkins Windows service is running and visit the dashboard at the local host URL shown by the installer. Start a simple freestyle job to confirm agents and pipelines can be created.

This tutorial covered Java preparation, MSI installation, unlocking Jenkins, plugin setup and basic verification steps required to have a working Jenkins instance on a Windows 10 machine.

Tip

Run Jenkins on a dedicated service account with the least privileges required and map the Jenkins home folder to a stable drive path to avoid permission surprises during builds.

title: Install a Jenkins War Example

heading: Install a Jenkins War Example for Local Server
body:
Why run Jenkins from a WAR

Because sometimes you want CI without the circus. Running Jenkins from the WAR file gives you a tiny, predictable server for testing pipelines and doing experimental DevOps tricks. It is not meant to be your production fortress, but it is perfect for local development, plugin testing, and pretending you know what continuous integration really means.

Get the Jenkins WAR file

Grab the latest jenkins.war from the official Jenkins download page or a trusted mirror. Drop the file into a folder that will become your Jenkins workspace so job data and config live in one predictable place. If you like backups and sanity set an environment variable named JENKINS_HOME to that folder before starting the server.

Start Jenkins with Java

Open a terminal and run the Java command to launch the WAR. Make sure Java 8 or newer is installed on your machine otherwise this will not work and you will have to admit defeat.

java -jar jenkins.war --httpPort=8080

The webapp will unpack itself and start a small HTTP server on the port you chose. If 8080 is taken pick another port number. The console will print logging and some helpful messages, including an initial admin password.

Unlocking and first setup

On first start Jenkins prints an initialAdminPassword in the console and also places the same file under secrets/initialAdminPassword inside your workspace. Copy that value into the browser unlock screen to move on to plugin selection and admin creation. No secret handshakes required.

Install plugins and create your admin account

Choose the recommended plugins for a minimal, CI friendly setup or pick individual plugins if you enjoy making careful choices. Create the first admin account and then configure global tools like JDK and Git so your jobs can actually build things. If your pipelines call for other tools add those in the global configuration as well.

Run Jenkins as a system service for longer runs

If you plan to leave Jenkins running for a while wrap the Java command with a service manager. On Linux use systemd and on Windows try NSSM or a similar wrapper. Point the service to java -jar /path/to/jenkins.war and set environment variables for JENKINS_HOME and JAVA_OPTIONS to keep things stable across restarts.

Practical tips for CI and DevOps sanity

  • Back up JENKINS_HOME regularly so your job configs do not disappear in a tragic spreadsheet accident.
  • Keep the WAR updated when new Jenkins releases arrive to get security fixes and features.
  • Use a separate port or firewall rules if you do not want random coworkers poking your test server.
  • For production grade servers switch to a packaged install or an official container image and add real security and persistence.

Follow these steps and you will have a lightweight Jenkins server suitable for rapid iteration on pipelines and CI development. It is quick, flexible, and perfect for those moments when you need to test a job without convincing the whole team to approve yet another server request. Now go break your pipeline in peace and fix it faster.

pipeline { agent any stages { stage('Build') { steps { echo 'Build started' } } } }

title: Install a Jenkins War Example
description: Quick guide to run a Jenkins WAR file with Java to start a local Jenkins server and access the web console
heading: Install a Jenkins War Example for a Local Jenkins Server
body:
If you want a no fuss Jenkins server for local testing or quick CI work then running the jenkins war file is the speediest option. This guide walks through the exact steps to get a Jenkins server up and serving web pages on localhost with minimal drama and just enough sarcasm to keep you awake.

What you need before you start

Keep this short and useful like a coffee run. You need Java installed and the jenkins.war file that you downloaded from the official Jenkins download page. A machine that can run Java is also helpful. That is it.

Run the war file with Java

Open a terminal in the folder that holds jenkins.war and run the server with a single command. This starts the embedded servlet container and boots Jenkins.

java -jar jenkins.war

If port 8080 is already occupied or you are trying to avoid a fight with another service then pass a simple flag to change the port.

java -jar jenkins.war --httpPort=8080

Yes that is all you need to get a server running locally. No Kubernetes, no cloud account, no mysterious plugins required up front.

Open the web UI

Point your browser to localhost on port 8080 to reach the Jenkins welcome screen. You will be asked for an initial admin password which is not printed on a sticker under your desk.

Find the initial admin password and unlock

The initial admin password lives in the Jenkins home folder. By default this is under a folder created in your user directory but you can control that with an environment variable that we will cover next.

cat JENKINS_HOME/secrets/initialAdminPassword

Copy the password into the unlock form in the web UI. Once Jenkins accepts it you can proceed to plugin setup and account creation.

Install suggested plugins and create an admin user

The easiest path is to install the suggested plugins. It gives you a sensible baseline for common CI and CD tasks without overwhelming your machine with optional extras. Follow the prompts to create the initial admin user. After that you have a working continuous integration server for local testing and small devops experiments.

Quick checklist for a reliable local server

  • Set JENKINS_HOME to a dedicated folder before launching the server so configuration and plugins persist across restarts
  • Use the httpPort flag if port 8080 is taken
  • Keep backups of JENKINS_HOME if you care about your build history
  • Run updates for plugins from the web UI not by guessing at random plugin files

Notes for devops and production thinking

Running the war locally is ideal for development and demos. For production deployments you will want a proper service wrapper, a dedicated JENKINS_HOME on persistent storage, and an actual reverse proxy or container orchestration platform that matches your release model for CI and CD. This guide keeps things simple so you can test jobs and pipelines without finger crossing or dramatic server rituals.

Summary and the parting gift

Download jenkins.war, run it with java -jar, visit localhost on port 8080, unlock with the password in JENKINS_HOME/secrets/initialAdminPassword, install suggested plugins, and create an admin user. Set JENKINS_HOME before you start if you want your configuration to survive a reboot or a moment of panic.

Now go create a pipeline and then try not to break the internet. You will be fine.

title: Jenkins Home Directory What is JENKINS_HOME and How to Set
description: Quick guide to JENKINS_HOME what the directory does and how to set the environment variable on Linux Docker and systemd
heading: Jenkins Home Directory What is JENKINS_HOME and How to Set
body:
JENKINS_HOME is the filesystem directory where Jenkins stores configuration plugins jobs builds and logs.

Default locations vary by install method. For package installs look under /var/lib/jenkins. For single user installs expect a hidden directory in the user home named .jenkins. Docker containers use a path inside the container that can be mapped to a host folder.

To set the environment variable for an ad hoc shell session run

export JENKINS_HOME=/var/lib/jenkins

To make the change persistent for a systemd service add an Environment line to the service override file or to the service unit. For example use systemctl edit jenkins and add a section with an Environment value matching the desired path. After saving run systemctl daemon reload and systemctl restart jenkins so the Jenkins process picks up the new directory.

For Docker use the environment flag and a volume mount to preserve data

docker run -e JENKINS_HOME=/var/jenkins_home -v /host/jenkins_home /var/jenkins_home jenkins

Permissions matter more than charm. Ensure the user running the Jenkins process owns the chosen directory and has read write access. Moves of an existing JENKINS_HOME require stopping the service copying data preserving ownership and restarting the service. Backups of the directory are lifesavers when a plugin update decides to play hardball.

Environment variable precedence follows process environment. A systemd or Docker environment setting will override a casual shell export that happens after service start. If the goal is predictable storage use an explicit environment setting in the service or container runtime and a dedicated host mount.

Tip

Pick a stable path outside temporary directories and set JENKINS_HOME in the service or container config rather than relying on transient shell exports. Back up that directory before experimenting with plugins.

title: Install Jenkins on Tomcat
description: Quick guide to deploy Jenkins WAR on Tomcat with clear steps for download deploy configure and run as a service
heading: Install Jenkins on Tomcat Guide
body:
Why run Jenkins on Tomcat at all

If you like control and tiny plumbing tasks then running Jenkins as a WAR inside Tomcat will make you happy. It is a valid option for a CI server when you want Tomcat features such as connection tuning or container managed threads while keeping Jenkins itself portable as a single file.

This guide will walk you through the safe steps to deploy the jenkins.war, configure context settings, set up a reverse proxy and TLS, and get the setup running as a service. Yes it will involve some copying of files and looking at logs. You can do it.

Prepare the environment

Requirements are simple and boring. Install a supported Java runtime like OpenJDK 8 or 11 and a Tomcat 8 or 9 install. Verify JAVA_HOME is set and make sure Tomcat runs as a dedicated user so you do not accidentally give your CI server root powers.

  • Java 8 or 11 installed and JAVA_HOME pointing at the runtime
  • Tomcat 8 or 9 deployed and configured for the right user
  • Disk space for plugins and builds in a secure JENKINS_HOME

Download the Jenkins WAR

Grab the latest jenkins.war from the official Jenkins site and place it on the server. Keep the filename exactly jenkins.war if you want Jenkins to appear at the default context path. If you rename it you will change the URL and confuse people.

Deploy the WAR to Tomcat

There are two easy ways to get the WAR into Tomcat. Either copy jenkins.war into the Tomcat webapps directory or use the Tomcat manager webapp to upload it. On restart Tomcat will unpack the WAR and create the jenkins context folder.

  1. Copy method example: cp jenkins.war /opt/tomcat/webapps/
  2. Manager method uses the Tomcat manager UI and an account with deploy rights

Configure context and security

Use a context XML file to tune thread pools session timeout and resource limits for the Jenkins webapp. Typical tweaks include maxThreads in your connector and a sensible session timeout so sessions do not pile up forever.

Set proper file permissions on JENKINS_HOME so the Tomcat user can write plugins and build artifacts. On first launch complete the setup wizard in the browser to create the initial admin account and install recommended plugins.

Suggested context items to review

  • JVM memory and GC settings for the Tomcat process
  • Connector maxThreads and connectionTimeout to match your load
  • Session timeout values and cookie security options

Reverse proxy and SSL

Front Tomcat with Nginx or Apache to serve traffic on standard ports and terminate TLS. Let the reverse proxy handle SSL so Tomcat can stay simple and not know about cert renewals. Make sure proxy headers are forwarded so Jenkins sees the real client IP and sets secure cookies when using HTTPS.

  • Configure X forwarded for headers so client IPs are preserved
  • Enable secure and http only cookie flags to harden sessions
  • Use a valid certificate from a trusted CA or a managed cert tool

Start Tomcat and verify Jenkins

Start or restart your Tomcat service and watch the logs such as logs catalytic file and catalina.out for plugin initialization messages. Access Jenkins on the host that runs Tomcat on port 8080 using a browser or access it through your reverse proxy on standard ports. Finish the setup wizard and install necessary plugins for your CI workflows.

Useful checks

  • Tail logs to confirm plugins loaded and no classpath errors appeared
  • Visit the initial admin unlock page to complete setup
  • Run a test job to confirm builds run and artifacts are stored in JENKINS_HOME

Run as a service and run book tips

Use your system service manager to run Tomcat under the dedicated user so it starts on boot and restarts on failures. Keep backups of JENKINS_HOME and your configuration and schedule plugin updates during maintenance windows because surprise plugin upgrades are how you lose weekends.

Troubleshooting quick hits

  • Permission denied errors usually mean wrong owner or file mode on JENKINS_HOME
  • 404 for the jenkins context often means the war was not unpacked or was renamed
  • Session or cookie oddities tend to be proxy header misconfiguration

There you go. Jenkins on Tomcat gives you a lean deployable WAR with Tomcat level controls and typical DevOps benefits. It is not shiny but it is reliable when configured correctly and not running as root. Now go deploy and try not to break anything important on the first attempt.
seo_title: Run Jenkins on Tomcat with WAR deployment and SSL setup for CI servers
seo_heading: Deploy and secure Jenkins WAR on Tomcat for Continuous Integration workflows

title: Jenkins Installer for Windows
description: Quick guide to install Jenkins on Windows using the MSI installer and get a running service with plugins and admin user
heading: Jenkins Installer for Windows Setup Guide
body:
Before you start

Yes you can install Jenkins on Windows and no it will not explode if you follow these steps. This guide uses the official MSI installer and assumes you want a stable CI CD server for your DevOps workflows. Quick checklist before we begin

  • Download the LTS MSI from the Jenkins website for production use
  • Make sure Java is installed and supported for your Jenkins version
  • Set the JAVA_HOME environment variable so Jenkins can actually find Java
  • Decide where JENKINS_HOME will live and plan backups

To verify Java run java -version and to check JAVA_HOME run echo %JAVA_HOME% in a command prompt. If those commands look sad fix Java first.

Run the MSI installer

Right click the MSI and choose Run as administrator. The wizard will ask for an install folder and optional components. Defaults work fine for quick tests, but for a production host pick a dedicated folder and a drive with space for build artifacts.

The installer will ask if you want Jenkins to run as a Windows service. Say yes unless you enjoy running processes manually. Pick a dedicated service account rather than Local System, so a compromised build does not hand the keys to the kingdom to an attacker.

Firewall and port notes

Confirm the listening port, commonly 8080, and open it in Windows Firewall. If corporate policy requires a different port pick one that does not clash with other services.

Unlock Jenkins and install plugins

After install point your browser to the host and port shown by the installer. The first page is the unlock screen. Retrieve the initial admin password from the file path displayed or from %JENKINS_HOME%\secrets\initialAdminPassword or the default install path C:\Program Files\Jenkins\secrets\initialAdminPassword. Copy that long string like it is the last coffee in the break room.

Choose Install suggested plugins to get a sensible base set for CI CD. That will pull in core plugins for pipelines, Git integration, and node management so you can start creating jobs faster.

Create an admin user in the setup wizard and store those credentials in a secrets store. No sticky notes, not even on your monitor.

Configure global tools and system settings

Go to Manage Jenkins and then Global Tool Configuration to point Jenkins at your Git executable and any JDK installations you want to use for builds. Set tool locations or let Jenkins auto install where appropriate. Configure agents and nodes if you plan to run distributed builds.

Post install hardening and tips

  • Run the service under a least privilege account and avoid using full administrator credentials
  • Enable automated backups of the JENKINS_HOME folder to preserve build history and plugin configs
  • Keep plugins updated and remove unused plugins to reduce attack surface
  • Record admin and service account credentials in a vault or secrets manager rather than a text file

This guide covered downloading the MSI, running it with admin rights, picking a safe Windows service account, unlocking Jenkins, installing suggested plugins, and creating an admin user. With Jenkins running you will have a Windows host ready to run builds and pipelines with reasonable defaults and clear next steps for hardening and scaling your CI CD system.

title: Jenkins Hello World Build Job Example
description: Step by step Jenkins Hello World build job tutorial for beginners showing how to create a freestyle job run a build and view console output
heading: Jenkins Hello World Build Job Example Guide
body:
If you just want to prove Jenkins can talk to an agent and print something other than an error message, this quick guide gets you from zero to Hello World. No magic required, just clicks, a tiny script, and the thrill of watching console output that actually contains the words you typed.

What you will do

We will create a freestyle build job that prints Hello World, run it manually, and inspect the console output. Then we will show a simple path to make it slightly less primitive by linking a repo or switching to a Pipeline with a Jenkinsfile for version controlled builds.

Step 1 Access Jenkins

Open the Jenkins web UI on your server host and port, for example http localhost 8080 if you are running locally. Log in using an admin or a regular account that has job create permissions. Yes you can use the GUI, no you do not need to sacrifice anything to get this working.

Step 2 Create a new job

Click New Item, give it a memorable name like Hello World or something cuter if you must, then choose Freestyle project and click OK. The freestyle job is simple and perfect for this learning exercise.

Step 3 Configure a build step

In the configuration page add a build step Execute shell for Linux agents or Add build step Windows bat for Windows agents. Type the simplest of all build scripts to prove the system works.

echo 'Hello World'

Save the job. This is the sort of happiness that comes from tiny, verifiable outputs. If you ever see that Hello World line in the console, you are officially in control.

Step 4 Run the build and view console output

  • From the job page click Build Now
  • Open the new build from the build history
  • Click Console Output to see the Hello World line printed with the rest of the build logs

Console output is how Jenkins talks to you when things work and when they do not. Look for the echo line, the exit code, and any agent warnings. If the build fails, read the log, address the problem, and celebrate when it succeeds.

Optional enhancements

When you are bored of manual builds, try these small improvements that scale much better than your patience.

  • Link a Git repository under Source Code Management to pull scripts from version control
  • Add triggers such as Poll SCM or Build periodically to automate runs
  • Convert the job to a Pipeline using a Jenkinsfile for version controlled build steps and better auditing

Minimal Jenkinsfile example

If you prefer code over clicking, put this Jenkinsfile in your repo root and create a Pipeline job instead of a freestyle job.

pipeline { agent any stages { stage('Hello') { steps { sh 'echo Hello World' } } } }

This declarative pipeline is readable, reproducible, and lives with your source like a responsible grown up. Use sh for Unix agents and bat for Windows agents.

Tips for moving forward

  • Prefer Pipeline for any build that needs to be repeatable across team members
  • Use a Jenkinsfile to keep build logic in the repository, not hidden in the UI
  • Wrap heavier scripts in executable files inside your repo to keep the UI tidy and the logs sane

That is it, you have a working Jenkins Hello World build job, console output that proves it, and a clear path to pipelines and CI maturity. Now go replace Hello World with a test suite and pretend this was always your plan.
