title: How to Delete AWS Secret Access Keys in IAM
description: Step by step guide to remove AWS secret access keys from IAM using the console and CLI to secure S3 EC2 and EKS access
heading: How to Delete AWS Secret Access Keys in IAM
body:
If your cloud credentials were a party guest they would be the one who never leaves. This guide shows how to kick old AWS secret access keys out of your IAM users and update whatever automation depends on them. We cover the console and the AWS CLI and we keep your S3 EC2 and EKS workflows intact while we do it.

Find keys and do a quick audit

First find the IAM user and list their access keys so you know what you are working with. This is the obvious step that somehow gets skipped by someone every time.

aws iam list-access-keys --user-name USERNAME

The command shows access key ids and statuses. Make a note of which keys are Active and which are Inactive before you touch anything.

Delete a key from the console

For humans who like buttons and reassuring dialogs use the AWS Management Console. Navigate to IAM then Users. Pick the target user and open the Security credentials tab. Find the access key and click Delete. Confirm the dialog. That is two clicks and the key is gone.

Delete or disable a key with the AWS CLI

If you prefer the command line or want to script this as part of an incident response follow these steps. If you want to be cautious disable the key first and then delete it after testing.

aws iam update-access-key --user-name USERNAME --access-key-id ACCESSKEYID --status Inactive
aws iam delete-access-key --user-name USERNAME --access-key-id ACCESSKEYID

Disabling first gives you a short window to see what breaks without permanently deleting the secret. That is useful if your CI pipelines are cursed with hard coded credentials.

When to disable first

  • If the key might be used by automation you can not instantly update
  • If you want a test period to confirm new credentials are working
  • If you are cleaning up after an incident and want to gather logs

Rotate keys for dependent applications

If a deleted key was in use by an app, pipeline or a developer workstation you must create a replacement and update every location where the key lived. That includes environment variables, CI secrets, container images with baked in credentials and developer machines.

aws iam create-access-key --user-name USERNAME

Save the access key id and secret access key securely. Do not paste them into Slack like a modern barbarian. Update your environment variables or credential files and test.

Quick test commands you can run to verify basic access for common services

  • S3 list test 
    aws s3 ls
  • EC2 simple check 
    aws ec2 describe-instances --max-items 1
  • EKS and kubectl usually require updating kubeconfig with the AWS credentials before testing cluster access

Verify removal and clean up stale credentials

Check local CLI configs and credential files. Common places to look are the AWS credentials file and any CI secret stores. On a developer machine check the file at ~/.aws/credentials and any environment variables that might be set. Remove stale entries and then run a simple API call with the intended profile to confirm the new credentials work.

Best practices to avoid future credential chaos

  • Prefer IAM roles and instance profiles over long lived access keys
  • Rotate keys regularly and automate rotation when you can
  • Apply least privilege to limit what a leaked key can do
  • Use MFA and temporary credentials for interactive users
  • Audit access keys with scripts or AWS Config to detect unused keys

Follow these steps and you will reduce the blast radius of a leaked key and make your cloud life less exciting in the worst possible way. If something breaks after deletion roll back to the disable first approach and trace where the old key lived. Then hunt down the hard coded credential and give it a stern talking to.
seo_title: Safely remove AWS secret access keys and rotate credentials
seo_heading: Step by step IAM key deletion and rotation for S3 EC2 and EKS security

title: AWS Parameter Store SSM with KMS SecureString & CLI
description: Store and decrypt SecureString parameters using AWS SSM Parameter Store KMS keys and AWS CLI commands for secure secrets management
heading: AWS Parameter Store SSM with KMS SecureString and AWS CLI
body:
If you like living dangerously but also want your secrets to survive an audit, this guide shows how to store SecureString parameters in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store with a customer managed KMS key and the AWS CLI. No mystical rituals required, just a few commands and the usual level of cloud paranoia.

Why use SecureString and a customer managed key

SecureString keeps values encrypted at rest and when transported. A customer managed KMS key gives you control over rotation, access auditing, and the satisfaction of telling security that yes you actually did think about key separation between environments.

Quick steps

  • Create or choose a customer managed KMS key per environment when you can
  • Create a SecureString parameter with the CLI
  • Grant SSM and KMS permissions to the right principals
  • Retrieve the parameter with decryption when needed
  • Follow best practices and automate rotation so you sleep at night

Create or pick a KMS key

Use a customer managed key to get audit logs and rotation control. Separate keys by environment to prevent someone from accidentally using dev keys in production and then explaining it in a blameless postmortem.

Store a SecureString parameter with the AWS CLI

Here is a minimal example. Replace names and values to match your setup.

aws ssm put-parameter --name /prod/db/password --value "SuperSecret123" --type SecureString --key-id alias/myAppKey

Grant SSM and KMS permissions

Two things must allow access to the secret. The KMS key policy must permit aws ssm to use the key when required. The IAM role or user that reads the parameter must have ssm GetParameter and kms Decrypt permissions. Check both key policy and IAM roles because both gate access.

Retrieve the secret with decryption

When you actually need the value, pull it with the CLI and request decryption. Do not echo it into logs unless you enjoy handing secrets to strangers.

aws ssm get-parameter --name /prod/db/password --with-decryption

Best practices so you do not regret things later

  • Name parameters to reflect environment and purpose for fast triage
  • Automate secret rotation and pair it with KMS key rotation when possible
  • Use parameter policies for automatic versioning and expiration to limit blast radius
  • Avoid printing secrets to logs or leaving them in shell history
  • Limit IAM principal scope and follow least privilege

This covered creating or selecting a KMS key, storing a SecureString parameter with the CLI, granting required permissions, retrieving a decrypted value, and operational tips for secret hygiene. Follow these and your pager will thank you, or at least be quieter.
seo_title: Encrypt and manage secrets in Parameter Store with KMS and CLI
seo_heading: Step by step guide to SecureString parameters and KMS key setup

title: How to Create an IAM User in AWS Management Console
description: Step by step guide to create an IAM user in the AWS Management Console with best practices for EC2 EKS and secure role assignment
heading: How to Create an IAM User in the AWS Console for EC2 and EKS Roles
body:
If you think creating an IAM user is thrilling you are emotionally healthy and slightly wrong. Still this job matters more than it looks and getting it right keeps your cloud from turning into a haunted data center. This guide walks you through creating an IAM user in the AWS Management Console and assigning permissions that actually follow least privilege for EC2 and EKS use.

Before you click create

Do not use the root account for day to day tasks. Root is for account setup and screaming on rare occasions. Sign in with a non root administrator when possible and open the IAM dashboard in the AWS Management Console. Have a plan for who owns the user and where credentials will live.

Quick checklist

  • Decide if this is a human or a machine
  • Pick console access or programmatic access for CLI and SDKs
  • Prefer groups and roles over one off policies
  • Enable MFA for privileged users
  • Store secrets in a vault not a sticky note

Step 1 sign in and start user creation

From the IAM console choose Users and then Create user. Use a clear username that hints at owner and purpose. For humans choose console access. For automation choose programmatic access so AWS will generate an access key pair for CLI and SDK usage.

Step 2 pick access type and intent

Console access gives a password and optional console permissions. Programmatic access gives an access key id and secret access key for aws cli and SDKs. If a workload will run on EC2 or in EKS prefer role based access instead of long lived keys. Use an instance profile for EC2 or IRSA for EKS pods where possible to avoid key management drama.

Step 3 assign permissions the smart way

Create or reuse groups with managed policies and add users to those groups. That reduces mistakes and makes audits less painful. Avoid attaching powerful policies directly to users. When EC2 instances or pods need AWS APIs prefer roles that can be assumed. Roles keep credentials short lived and auditable.

Step 4 review tags and least privilege

Double check the review screen. Confirm that policies match least privilege principles and do not allow unnecessary iam management unless absolutely required. Add tags to capture owner team or purpose for easier tracking and cost center drama control.

Step 5 save credentials and configure the CLI

Download the credentials CSV or copy the access key id and secret access key once. Do not paste keys into chat or a public gist. Store credentials in a secrets manager or vault. For quick CLI setup run aws configure and enter the keys when prompted. For automation use environment variables or the SDK credential mechanism that your tooling prefers.

Small but important security notes

  • Turn on MFA for privileged and administrative users
  • Rotate keys regularly and revoke keys when no longer needed
  • Use IAM Access Analyzer and the policy simulator to validate permissions before you push them into production
  • Avoid policies that allow full IAM management unless you enjoy surprises

Wrap up and practical tips

This covered the flow to create an IAM user in the AWS Management Console choose access type assign least privilege and configure CLI or SDK access. For EC2 and EKS prefer role based access where possible. If you are studying for the AWS Practitioner exam or just trying to keep your cloud secure these steps are exactly the kind of boring good habits that save your team from a data breach and yourself from long late night debugging sessions.

If you want a cheat sheet version here it is in plain form. Use non root admin accounts. Prefer groups and roles. Enable MFA. Store keys in a vault. Rotate and review. Be the kind of person the cloud deserves.
seo_title: Set up an AWS IAM user for EC2 and EKS access the smart way
seo_heading: Step by step IAM user creation with least privilege for CLI and console use

title: How to Create AWS IAM Admin Users in Console
description: Quick guide to create AWS IAM admin users in the AWS Management Console with best practices for permissions MFA and secure access
heading: How to Create AWS IAM Admin Users in Console
body:
So you need an AWS IAM admin user and you want to do it right without accidentally handing the keys to the cloud kingdom to a colleague who thinks MFA stands for Maybe Forgotten Auth. This guide walks you through creating an admin user in the AWS Management Console with sensible security, multi factor authentication, and fewer panicked ticket requests later.

Before you start

Make sure you are signed in with an account that already has permission to create users. Do not use the root account for daily work. That account belongs in a digital safe with dramatic music playing in the background. You will need access to the IAM service in the AWS Management Console and a plan for whether you want AdministratorAccess or a more careful least privilege setup.

Create the user in the console

  1. Open the AWS Management Console and navigate to IAM. This is where users, groups, and policies live and sometimes argue about who gets to change resource tags.
  2. Click Create user and choose console access. Give the user a clear user name so you do not need to play detective later.
  3. Decide whether the user needs programmatic access for the CLI or SDKs in addition to console access. If they do not need it do not enable it.

Attach permissions the right way

For full admin rights attach the managed policy named AdministratorAccess. If your security team breathes onto policies you will instead craft a custom policy that follows least privilege. In most real environments the right answer is specific permissions rather than broad access. Remember that AdministratorAccess is a nuclear option when you need it, not a default.

Enable MFA and enforce password rules

Turn on multi factor authentication for the new user. Configure a virtual MFA device such as an authenticator app or use hardware MFA if you are doing things old school and official. Set a strong password policy that requires complexity and rotation based on your company policy. Do not skip this step because it is invisible until it saves you from an account compromise.

Quick checklist

  • Sign in with an admin capable account not root
  • Create user with only the access needed for the job
  • Attach AdministratorAccess only when truly required
  • Enable MFA and apply a strict password policy
  • Revoke unused access keys and document credentials

Verify and tidy up

Log in as the new user to validate the experience and confirm the user can perform intended tasks. Rotate or revoke any unnecessary access keys and write down where credentials are stored and who is responsible for them. After setup put the root account into hibernation unless you enjoy emergency escalations at 2 a m.

Best practices and alternatives

  • Prefer creating an admin role and using temporary role sessions through IAM or AWS SSO instead of long lived admin users.
  • Adopt least privilege and break down AdministratorAccess into narrowly scoped policies where possible.
  • Use MFA for every privileged identity and monitor sign in activity with CloudTrail and AWS Config.
  • Document your access control process so new admins do not reinvent insecure habits.

Follow these steps and you will have an AWS IAM admin user that is useful instead of hazardous. You will also reduce the chance of wearing the cloud on fire while you explain how it happened. Good security is boring and reliable and that is what we are after.

title: AWS Batch Tutorial | Create Jobs Queues Fargate EC2 EKS
description: Learn to create AWS Batch jobs job definitions queues and use Fargate EC2 and EKS resources in a short practical tutorial
heading: AWS Batch Tutorial Create Jobs Queues Fargate EC2 EKS
body:
What this guide covers

Short version for people who like their cloud with a side of sarcasm. This article walks through AWS Batch basics so you can define jobs submit them to queues pick Fargate EC2 or EKS for compute and actually read the logs when things fail. We keep the facts accurate and the hand waving minimal.

Create a job definition

Think of a job definition as the recipe for your container. It tells Batch which image to run what command to invoke how many vCPU and how much memory to give the container and which IAM role to use for execution. Use environment variables for run time tweaks and mount points to attach data volumes. Revisions are supported so you can update settings without nuking older jobs.

  • Container image and command are required
  • Set vCPU and memory to match workload needs
  • Choose a retry strategy and exit code handling
  • Attach an IAM role so the job can talk to S3 CloudWatch and other services

Create job queues and attach compute environments

Job queues are where jobs wait for compute. Attach one or more compute environments to each queue and assign an order value to control priority. Use multiple queues when workloads need different priorities or compute types. Proper queue design makes job routing predictable which is a nice change from chaos.

  • Assign an order value per compute environment for priority
  • Route GPU jobs to EC2 environments that provide GPUs
  • Keep separate queues for latency sensitive jobs and batchy garbage collection

Choose your compute environment

Pick the compute type that matches your tolerance for control versus maintenance.

  • Fargate provides serverless container runs with no host management. Great when you want simplicity.
  • EC2 gives full control. Use custom AMIs spot instances or GPUs when you need performance or lower cost.
  • EKS is best if you already run Kubernetes and want to reuse tooling or service meshes.

Submit a job and track it

Submit jobs from the Console the AWS CLI or any supported SDK. Capture the returned job ID so you can track status or cancel things when they misbehave.

aws batch submit-job --job-name my-job --job-queue my-queue --job-definition my-job-def

Use parameters and container overrides to change commands environment variables and resource limits per run without creating a new job definition.

Monitor logs and manage retries

Send container logs to CloudWatch for troubleshooting. Configure retry attempts and map container or host exit codes to retry behavior so recoverable failures retry automatically while total meltdowns stop early. Autoscaling on your compute environment lets capacity grow with demand so the queue empties without manual babysitting.

Practical tips to keep your bill human sized

  • Use EC2 spot for non critical batch jobs to save cost
  • Right size vCPU and memory to avoid over provisioning
  • Set sensible retry limits to avoid runaway loops
  • Monitor CloudWatch metrics for queue depth and instance usage

Quick checklist before you hit run

  • Job definition has correct image command and IAM role
  • Queues use the right compute environments and order values
  • Compute environment matches workload needs Fargate EC2 or EKS
  • Logging and retries are configured and tested

There you go. Follow these steps and you can go from zero to running Batch workloads on AWS with Fargate EC2 or EKS while keeping control over cost and complexity. If something breaks read the CloudWatch logs tweak resources and try again. Repeat until it works or until you accept that the cloud has moods.

seo_heading: Step by step AWS Batch setup for job definitions queues and compute environments

title: Create an AWS API Gateway & Mock Responses
description: Configure API Gateway mock responses with mapping templates for quick testing and seamless Lambda integration without deploying backend code
heading: Create an AWS API Gateway and Mock Responses with Mapping Templates
body:
This tutorial shows how to configure AWS API Gateway to return mock responses using mapping templates for fast testing and to ease Lambda or backend integration later.

  1. Create an API resource and method in the API Gateway console
  2. Set the method integration type to Mock and define status codes
  3. Add response mapping templates for content type application slash json
  4. Test the method using the console or a simple curl call
  5. Replace the mock integration with Lambda or HTTP backend when ready

Step one is about scaffolding. Create a REST API or HTTP API then add a resource and an HTTP method. Naming things clearly now saves debugging time later when confusion ramps up.

Step two focuses on integration. Choose Mock as the integration type and declare response status codes that simulate production scenarios. API Gateway will return those codes without invoking backend services which speeds up development and reduces panic.

Step three covers mapping templates. Use mapping templates to shape mock response payloads and to populate headers. Use expressions like $input.path('$.message') to pull values from a simulated payload. Mapping templates act as glue between a request shape and the response shape so tests look realistic.

Step four is the part where tests happen. Use the API Gateway test console or run curl against the deployed stage endpoint to confirm status codes headers and body structure match expectations. Rapid feedback here prevents disasters in downstream systems.

Step five is the graceful swap. When the backend Lambda or HTTP service is ready change the integration type and reuse the mapping templates where useful. That saves time and keeps response contracts stable so clients do not explode.

Recap the flow performed here Create API resource choose Mock configure mapping templates test responses and swap to real backend when ready. That sequence gives reproducible tests and a safe path to production with fewer surprises.

Tip

When crafting mapping templates keep response contracts explicit and use example payloads that match client expectations. That makes the mock stage a reliable contract test before deploying backend code.

title: Create DynamoDB Tables for EC2 EKS API SNS SQS
description: Compact guide to create DynamoDB tables and connect database to EC2 EKS API Gateway SNS and SQS with practical steps and best practices
heading: How to Create DynamoDB Tables for EC2 EKS API Gateway SNS and SQS
body:
This tutorial teaches how to create DynamoDB tables and configure database access for EC2 EKS API Gateway SNS and SQS so services can read and write NoSQL records.

  1. Design keys and indexes
  2. Create the table
  3. Set IAM roles and policies
  4. Integrate with EC2 EKS API Gateway SNS and SQS
  5. Monitor capacity and optimize

Design keys and indexes

Choose a primary key that avoids hot partitions. Use a composite key when queries need range filtering. Add Global Secondary Indexes for alternative query patterns. Think like a database whisperer and avoid doom caused by a bad key choice.

Create the table

Use the console or AWS CLI to create a table with on demand billing for unpredictable traffic or provisioned capacity for tight cost control. Sample CLI command

aws dynamodb create-table --table-name MyTable --attribute-definitions AttributeName=Id,AttributeType=S --key-schema AttributeName=Id,KeyType=HASH --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST

Set IAM roles and policies

Grant least privilege to EC2 instances and pods in EKS via instance role or IAM role for service accounts. For API Gateway use an integration role or Lambda role that can access the table. For SNS and SQS grant publish and receive permissions where needed.

Integrate with EC2 EKS API Gateway SNS and SQS

From EC2 use SDKs to call DynamoDB. From EKS attach IAM roles to pods or use service account roles. For API Gateway use Lambda or direct integration to perform CRUD operations. For messaging use SNS to publish event metadata and SQS to queue processing tasks that update the table.

Monitor capacity and optimize

Enable CloudWatch metrics and set alarms for read write throttles. Use Auto Scaling for provisioned capacity or fine tune partition key design to balance throughput. Periodically review access patterns and remove unused indexes to cut costs.

This tutorial covered table design creation IAM setup integration with compute API and messaging services plus monitoring and tuning to keep production happy and bills reasonable.

Tip

Prefer PAY PER REQUEST while validating access patterns then switch to provisioned capacity with Auto Scaling after traffic stabilizes to save money without risking throttles.

title: How to Create an AWS S3 Bucket Amazon Web

heading: How to Create an AWS S3 Bucket Amazon Web

Step 2 Configure storage class versioning encryption and tags. Turn on server side encryption with AWS managed keys for basic compliance and enable versioning when accidental deletes are a real concern.

aws s3api create-bucket --bucket my-bucket-name --region us-east-1

aws s3api put-object --bucket my-bucket-name --key test.txt --body test.txt

Tip

title: AWS S3 Static Website Hosting
description: Quick guide to host a static website on Amazon S3 with bucket setup public access index document and optional CloudFront for speed and HTTPS
heading: AWS S3 Static Website Hosting Guide
body:
This tutorial shows how to host a static website on Amazon S3 by creating a bucket configuring public access enabling static website hosting uploading files and optionally using CloudFront for CDN and custom domain.

  1. Create an S3 bucket with a globally unique name
  2. Configure bucket policy and public access settings
  3. Enable static website hosting and set index and error documents
  4. Upload files and set correct MIME types and Cache Control
  5. Optional add CloudFront and configure DNS for custom domain
  6. Test using the S3 website endpoint and browser checks

Create a bucket that matches the desired domain or a friendly name. Choose a region close to the audience for lower latency.

Adjust block public access settings and add a bucket policy that grants public read to objects. Public access should be intentional and limited to static assets only.

In the S3 console enable static website hosting and set index document such as index.html and an error document. S3 provides a website endpoint for the chosen bucket.

Upload HTML CSS JS and image files and set Content Type metadata so browsers render files correctly. Set Cache Control headers to manage browser caching of assets.

For HTTPS and global performance add Amazon CloudFront and point DNS records to the distribution. Use an origin access identity or restrict bucket public access if CloudFront will serve files privately.

Test using the provided S3 website URL or the CloudFront domain. Verify the index page loads resources and that the browser console shows correct MIME types and status codes.

Summary recap Hosting a static website on S3 requires bucket creation policy tuning hosting enablement file uploads and optional CDN and DNS steps to deliver content to users fast and cheaply.

Tip

Set Cache Control per file for long lived assets and use versioned filenames for cache busting. For secure custom domains use CloudFront with an SSL certificate and origin access identity to keep the bucket non public while delivering content via HTTPS.

title: Create AWS SSL Certificates in Amazon Certificate Manager
description: Step by step guide to request an ACM TLS certificate validate via Route53 and serve an S3 static site over HTTPS using CloudFront and DNS updates
heading: Create AWS SSL Certificates in Amazon Certificate Manager with Route53 and S3
body:
This tutorial shows how to request a TLS certificate in AWS Certificate Manager validate the domain via Route53 and use the certificate to serve a static site from S3 over HTTPS using CloudFront.

  1. Request a public certificate in AWS Certificate Manager
  2. Validate the domain using DNS records in Route53
  3. Prepare the S3 bucket for static hosting
  4. Create a CloudFront distribution using the ACM certificate
  5. Update Route53 DNS with an alias to the CloudFront distribution

Request a public certificate Request a public TLS certificate for the apex domain and any subdomains such as www. Choose DNS validation and remember that CloudFront requires the certificate to live in the us east 1 region.

DNS validation in Route53 Choose DNS validation so AWS can offer CNAME records that map to the certificate validation endpoints. If the domain is managed in Route53 allow ACM to create the records automatically or copy the CNAME values and paste into the hosted zone.

Prepare the S3 bucket Create an S3 bucket named for the domain enable static website hosting or keep the bucket private and use an origin access control for CloudFront. Upload site files and set an index document and error page as needed.

Create CloudFront distribution Point the origin to the S3 bucket enable the alternate domain name field for the custom domain and attach the ACM certificate from us east 1. Set the viewer protocol policy to redirect HTTP to HTTPS and configure origin access control so the bucket does not need to be public.

Update Route53 DNS Create an A record with alias to the CloudFront distribution domain name or use an ALIAS record for the hosted zone. Wait for DNS to propagate and for the distribution to deploy because AWS likes to take a coffee break before rolling changes.

This guide covered requesting an ACM certificate validating domain ownership with Route53 preparing an S3 origin securing content with CloudFront and updating DNS so the site serves over HTTPS.

Tip

Pro tip Request the ACM certificate from the us east 1 region when planning to use CloudFront and prefer DNS validation so Route53 can add records automatically and save a few clicks and some mild frustration.

title: GitHub Pages Free Website Hosting How-To Guide
description: Step by step guide to host static HTML CSS and JavaScript on GitHub Pages for free with deployment and custom domain tips
heading: GitHub Pages Free Website Hosting How-To Guide
body:
This guide teaches how to host static HTML CSS and JavaScript on GitHub Pages for free with a simple repo based workflow and optional custom domain.

  2. Add static files
  3. Push changes to GitHub
  4. Enable GitHub Pages from settings
  5. Choose branch and folder for publishing
  6. Optional custom domain and CNAME
  7. Visit the live site

Create a repository Use the New repository button on GitHub and choose public for free hosting. For a user site name the repository username.github.io where username matches the GitHub account name. Project sites can use any repo name.

Add static files Drop in an index.html file plus CSS and JavaScript assets. Organize files in the repo root for simplicity. A single index.html in the root will serve as the homepage.

Push changes to GitHub Use a local git workflow or the web upload interface. Typical local commands are git init git add . git commit -m "Initial commit" and git push origin main after adding a remote URL from the new repo page.

Enable GitHub Pages from settings Open repository settings then find Pages. Select a publishing source such as the main branch and the root folder. Save choices and wait for the first build to finish. The build logs show any errors if the page fails to publish.

Choose branch and folder for publishing Project sites often use the gh-pages branch or the main branch. User and organization sites publish from the special username.github.io repo root. Selecting the correct branch prevents the wrong folder from being served.

Optional custom domain and CNAME Add a CNAME file with the domain name or enter the domain in the Pages settings. Configure DNS provider by creating the required A records or CNAME record depending on the domain setup. DNS changes may take a while to propagate.

Visit the live site Use the provided username.github.io URL or the custom domain after DNS propagation. Refresh caches if the latest changes do not appear.

This tutorial covered creating a repo adding static files pushing to GitHub enabling Pages choosing a publishing source and configuring an optional custom domain so a static HTML CSS and JavaScript site can be served for free from GitHub.

Tip

Use a simple index.html and keep assets in one folder for faster debugging. For automated builds add a GitHub Action to run tools and deploy the build to the chosen publishing branch.

title: Map Your Domain to GitHub Pages with GoDaddy
description: Step by step guide to point a GoDaddy domain to a GitHub Pages site with correct DNS records and HTTPS setup.
heading: Map Your Domain to GitHub Pages with GoDaddy
body:
Quick overview

Want your shiny static site on GitHub Pages to wear a custom domain from GoDaddy and look all professional with HTTPS That is doable and mostly painless if you follow the instructions and do not feed the DNS too much coffee

Prepare the GitHub Pages repository

Make sure your Pages site is published and serving content. For a user or organization site use a repository named username.github.io with the main branch published. For a project site either publish the gh-pages branch or the branch you picked in the Pages settings.

Push your built static site so GitHub actually has files to serve. No files means no site and a lot of awkward silence.

Create the CNAME file

In the repository root add a file named CNAME with only your custom domain on a single line for example www.example.com or example.com Commit and push it so GitHub Pages knows which domain to expect.

Update GoDaddy DNS records

Log in to GoDaddy and open the DNS manager for your domain. You will add either A records for the apex domain or a CNAME for the www hostname depending on how you want visitors to reach your site.

A records for the apex domain

  • Create A records for the root domain pointing to these GitHub Pages IPs
  • 185.199.108.153
  • 185.199.109.153
  • 185.199.110.153
  • 185.199.111.153

CNAME for the www hostname

If you prefer using www add a CNAME record for www that points to your GitHub Pages host for example username.github.io Save the record and try not to refresh the DNS page every five seconds

Wait for propagation and verify

DNS changes take a nap that can last from a few minutes to a few hours Accept it and check the status with tools like dig or online DNS checkers if you must be convinced faster.

Visit your custom domain in the browser and check the repository Pages settings for the green check that means GitHub validated the domain. If you see errors recheck your CNAME file and DNS entries for typos.

Enable HTTPS

Once GitHub validates the domain enable HTTPS in the Pages settings If you want all traffic to be secure check the enforce HTTPS option and GitHub will provision a certificate automatically. This usually happens without drama but it can take a few minutes.

Troubleshooting tips

  • If the apex domain is not resolving confirm all four A records are present and correct
  • If www does not work confirm the CNAME points to the correct username.github.io target and there is no conflicting A record
  • Use dig +short yourdomain to see what IPs are returned
  • Remember to push the CNAME file to the repo root otherwise GitHub will not claim the domain

That is it You prepared the repository added a CNAME updated GoDaddy DNS records waited for propagation and enabled HTTPS Now your static site is live on GitHub Pages with a custom domain and an SSL certificate without paying anyone a subscription fee for hosting

title: Tough AWS Solution Architect Pro Exam Question on EC2
description: Compact guide to EC2 placement groups and exam logic for AWS Solution Architect Professional level
heading: Tough AWS Solution Architect Pro Exam Question on EC2
body:
Welcome to the placement group jungle

If you thought AWS exams only tested your memory for obscure limits you are half right. Placement groups matter for real workloads and for Solution Architect certification questions because they control network performance and failure domains. This short guide will make you less likely to pick the wrong placement group and more likely to sound confident while doing it.

Why placement groups are even a thing

EC2 placement groups are AWS tools for deciding where your instances sit in the data center. That affects latency, throughput, and what dies when a rack gets dramatic. For High Performance Computing and tightly coupled apps you care about low latency and high throughput. For distributed systems you care about reducing blast radius when hardware goes bad. Exams love to mix those goals into one nasty little scenario.

The three placement group types and when to pick each

Cluster placement group

Cluster placement groups pack instances into a single availability zone to give you the shortest possible network paths and the highest throughput. This is the go to for HPC jobs and MPI driven clusters that act like one organism. Remember cluster cannot span multiple availability zones. If the question says single availability zone and low latency pick cluster.

aws ec2 create-placement-group --group-name exam-cluster --strategy cluster

Partition placement group

Partition placement groups split instances into logical partitions that minimize the blast radius when a physical failure happens. Partitions map to separate racks and hardware which helps keep parts of your system alive while other parts reboot. Partition placement works well for distributed data stores and larger fleets where you want some proximity but also fault isolation. Partition placement can span multiple availability zones in a region so double check the question.

Spread placement group

Spread placement groups put each instance on distinct hardware to maximize availability for a small set of critical instances. This is the safety first option when you have a handful of boxes that must not share a rack. Keep an eye on instance quotas and limits because spread groups are not meant for hundreds of instances. If the exam mentions a few mission critical servers and rack isolation pick spread.

Exam strategy that does not involve blind guessing

Exam writers like to hide the deciding detail in the middle of a verbose scenario. Here is a method that works and costs you minimal dignity.

  • Read the scenario and underline hard constraints on scratch paper. Single availability zone or cross availability zones will usually decide things.
  • If the question demands low latency inside one AZ pick cluster placement group.
  • If the question wants isolation across racks and reduced blast radius pick partition placement group.
  • If the question asks for a small number of independently placed critical instances pick spread placement group.
  • Always check quota and instance limits mentioned in the question because spread and cluster choices can be constrained by limits.

Quick cheats you can actually use without cheating

Write requirements as must have versus nice to have on your scratch paper. Mandatory items decide the winner. Optional items are tiebreakers. If the question forces a single availability zone and low latency the cluster answer usually wins. If it forces multi availability zone fault tolerance then partition is usually the correct compromise.

Parting tip for the Solution Architect exam and real life

Placement groups are technical and boring and also exactly the sort of thing that will ruin a distributed system when ignored. Use cluster for tight HPC jobs, partition for balanced fault isolation at scale, and spread for a few ultra critical instances. Read constraints carefully, call them out on your scratch paper, and move on before exam anxiety invents problems for you.
seo_title: Which EC2 placement group to pick for exam and real world
seo_heading: Practical guide to EC2 placement groups for exams and high performance

title: AWS Solution Architect Professional Blue Green AMIs EC2
description: Quick guide to blue green deployment with AMIs and EC2 for AWS Solution Architect Professional exam prep and real world deployment patterns
heading: AWS Solution Architect Professional Blue Green AMIs EC2
body:
If you like your deployments predictable and your downtime non existent then blue green with AMIs and EC2 is your friend and also your therapist. The idea is simple and ruthlessly efficient. You build a golden AMI from a configured instance then you spin up a fresh Auto Scaling group with a Launch Template. Test the new fleet. Swap traffic. Kill the old fleet. Everyone breathes again.

Core steps for AMI based blue green deployment

  • Create a golden AMI by baking your app runtime and configuration onto a build instance. Use automation tooling like Packer if you enjoy fewer surprises later on.
  • Store the AMI with clear version tags and metadata so rollbacks do not become archaeology projects.
  • Publish a Launch Template that captures instance type, IAM role, user data and other settings to avoid drift and guesswork.
  • Launch a new Auto Scaling group or EC2 fleet from the new AMI and attach it to a new ALB target group for isolation during validation.
  • Run smoke tests and integration tests against the new target group inside a private test subnet so you do not surprise customers with your debugging session.
  • Shift traffic to the new target group via ALB target group swap for an immediate cutover or use Route53 weighted records for a gradual rollout and confidence building.
  • Once healthy, scale down and terminate the old Auto Scaling group and archive the old AMI versions for audit and rollback purposes.

Why Launch Templates and Auto Scaling matter

Launch Templates keep instance settings consistent which makes life easier for you and harder for configuration drift. Auto Scaling groups give you automatic instance replacement and health checks so the system self heals while you sip coffee and watch CloudWatch graphs. Attach an ALB target group to each ASG to make traffic switching a simple registration change not a network engineering circus.

Testing and rollback playbook

Do your validation in isolation by registering new instances with a separate target group or running tests in a private subnet. That prevents accidental public exposure and keeps your incident inbox mercifully empty. Health checks on ALB target groups confirm readiness before traffic moves. If something goes sideways rollback is just a traffic reattach to the old target group or reweighting Route53 records back to the previous AMI fleet.

Gradual rollout and weighted traffic

If you are not bold enough for a full switch then use Route53 weighted records to shift traffic gradually. This buys you time to see how the new AMI behaves under real load while still keeping the old fleet as a rescue lane.

Automation and exam ready tips

  • Automate AMI baking and validation in CI so every AMI is a repeatable artifact and not a mystery snapshot.
  • Tag AMI versions and record Launch Template revisions to make rollbacks quick and auditable.
  • Mention Launch Templates, Auto Scaling groups, ALB target groups, AMI versioning and immutable infrastructure when answering exam questions on this pattern.
  • Focus on outcomes like zero downtime, quick rollback and immutability for both real world systems and exam checklists.

In short, bake a golden AMI, use Launch Templates to avoid drift, spin a new ASG and test it, then move traffic with ALB target group swaps or Route53 weights. Do that and your deployments will be boring in the very best way.

title: AWS DevOps Engineer Certification Exam Questions & Answers
description: Quick guide to API Gateway mapping templates Lambda integration and exam focused tips for AWS DevOps certification
heading: AWS DevOps Engineer Certification Exam Questions and Answers for API Gateway and Lambda
body:
This guide explains core exam topics for Amazon API Gateway Lambda integration and Velocity mapping templates with practical tips and short examples.

Focus areas that often appear on the exam

  1. Integration types and when to use proxy versus non proxy
  2. Velocity mapping templates for request and response transformation
  3. Permissions and execution roles for Lambda invoked by API Gateway
  4. Error mapping and status code control
  5. Testing and deployment stages and stage variables

Integration types Use proxy integration when full request context must reach the Lambda function with minimal transformation. Use non proxy integration when request or response must be transformed by a mapping template before arrival at the Lambda function.

Mapping templates Velocity templates transform JSON or form data before the Lambda function receives the payload. A minimal example to pass raw JSON looks like this

$input.json('$')

When exam questions ask about header mapping remember that header names appear in methods request context and mapping must reference those names explicitly. For query string parameters use the request method request querystring collection.

Permissions API Gateway needs permission to invoke the Lambda function. That permission is granted by adding an invoke permission to the Lambda resource policy for the API Gateway principal. Test questions often check knowledge of the resource policy and role difference.

Error handling Mapping templates can convert Lambda errors into custom HTTP status codes and bodies. Configure method response and integration response mappings so the client sees the intended status code and JSON body.

Exam tip for time pressed trainees Read the question for wording about proxy versus non proxy and look for mapping template snippets that expect VTL functions rather than raw JSON.

Tip

When practicing create one method with proxy integration and one method with non proxy integration. Compare incoming request context headers path parameters and body on each. That hands on contrast is the fastest route to spotting exam traps and passing with confidence.

title: AWS Machine Learning AI Specialty Exam Bedrock Sagemaker
description: Compact guide to tackle AWS ML and AI Specialty exam questions that involve Bedrock and Sagemaker with clear steps and exam friendly reasoning.
heading: AWS Machine Learning AI Specialty Exam Bedrock Sagemaker
body:
If you want to pass the AWS Machine Learning section without sweating into your keyboard this guide gives a pragmatic way to analyze exam questions that mention Bedrock and SageMaker. No hand waving, just a reliable checklist you can mutter under your breath during the test.

Start with the exam prompt

Read the question like it is the only thing stopping you from failing. Identify whether the primary need is model training, managed inference, data privacy, latency, or ongoing operations. Highlight words that point to managed foundation model inference, prompt based generation, batch pipelines, or custom training jobs.

Map requirement to service capabilities

Do not guess. Map the requirement to what each service actually offers so you can stop pretending you will remember later.

  • Bedrock is your managed foundation model playground. Use it when you need prompt based inference, quick generation, and minimal model maintenance. It is great for pay per inference scenarios and for teams that do not want to wrestle with training and infra.
  • SageMaker is the full MLOps toolkit. Use it when you need custom model training, hyperparameter tuning, distributed training, CI CD for models, or fine grained control over model deployment. SageMaker is the right pick if you need training pipelines, custom containers, or heavy model tuning.

Check security and data flow

Cloud security is not a magic checkbox. Verify these things in your head and mention them in your exam rationale so the grader knows you are not reckless.

  • Encryption at rest and in transit for any datasets or model artifacts.
  • VPC endpoints and network controls to avoid data leaving the private network unless required.
  • Least privilege IAM roles for training jobs and inference endpoints.
  • Data residency requirements and any needs for content filtering, user consent, or logging to satisfy compliance needs.

Consider cost and scalability

Stop treating cost like an afterthought. Estimate whether pay per inference with Bedrock or provisioned instances with SageMaker will be cheaper given the scenario. Think about burst traffic and autoscaling too. If the question mentions unpredictable spikes or extreme latency targets mention autoscaling, warm pools, or provisioned concurrency where applicable.

Trade offs you should call out

  • Control versus operational overhead. SageMaker gives more control but requires more management. Bedrock removes maintenance but gives up some control.
  • Latency and cost trade offs. Managed foundation models can be more expensive per request but simpler to operate. Provisioned instances can be cheaper at scale if you can manage them.
  • Data privacy. If the dataset cannot be shared outside your VPC or must stay in a region you might need a custom model on SageMaker rather than a managed foundation model.

How to write the exam answer

Keep it short and honest. One clear recommendation and one concise justification will beat a rambling essay every time.

  1. Recommend a service that matches the primary requirement from the prompt.
  2. Mention one security point and one cost or scalability note to back the choice.
  3. State any assumptions like expected data size, latency target, or compliance constraints.

Example answer pattern

Pick Bedrock when the need is quick prompt based generation with low ops overhead. Pick SageMaker when custom training, hyperparameter tuning, and full MLOps are needed. Then add one line about encryption and one line about cost to show you understand the trade off.

Quick recap and exam tip

The four question checks are clarify requirement, map to service capabilities, check security and data flow, and consider cost and scalability. Use this checklist like a tiny ritual before you bubble an answer.

When stuck pick the option that best matches the primary requirement and then write a single line about security or costs to support your choice. That one line often separates the confident candidate from the panicked one.

Good luck on the AWS AI Specialty exam. Use this method and you will sound like you know what you are doing even on questions that sound like they were written by a cryptic log file.

seo_heading: Decide fast for AWS AI Specialty questions using Bedrock or SageMaker

title: AWS Solution Architect Question Beanstalk EC2 Encryption
description: Quick guide to AWS exam concepts covering Beanstalk EC2 EBS IOPS EKS ECS S3 and encryption objectives with practical exam tips
heading: AWS Solution Architect Question Beanstalk EC2 Encryption
body:
Quick reality check

This is a short cheat style guide for AWS Solution Architect exam traps that like to hide inside Beanstalk, EC2 storage, and encryption questions. Elastic Beanstalk will spin up EC2 instances for the standard platform, not containers, unless the question explicitly says use containers or orchestration. Keep that tiny fact in your skull and move on.

Beanstalk and the container trick

If a stem mentions Beanstalk but then starts raving about pods, services, or kube this or kube that, pause. That is a prompt to pick EKS or ECS. If nothing in the question requires a container orchestration layer, assume Beanstalk means managed EC2 instances. That assumption will save you from choosing complicated answers that feel fancy but are wrong for the exam.

When to pick ECS or EKS

  • Use ECS or EKS only when the question explicitly calls for containers or container orchestration.
  • If the question mentions scaling containers, services, pods, or Kubernetes bits choose EKS or ECS.
  • If it says Beanstalk and nothing else about containers, assume EC2 instances.

EBS volume choices that do not lie

AWS loves throwing volume types at you like confetti. The mapping is simple if you are sober. Use gp3 for most workloads because you can increase baseline throughput and IOPS without changing volume size. Choose provisioned IOPS volumes, io1 or io2, when the scenario asks for sustained high IOPS or ultra low latency. And yes, instance store is ephemeral and will vanish when the instance dies, so do not pick it for persistent storage unless the question gives you a reason to be reckless.

Quick reference

  • gp3 for general purpose with tunable throughput and IOPS
  • io1 and io2 for heavy random IOPS and strict latency requirements
  • instance store for ephemeral local performance only

Match throughput and latency to volume type

Read the requirement. If the exam scenario mentions heavy random IOPS or low latency pick provisioned IOPS. If it only mentions steady throughput or mixed workloads gp3 is usually the right answer. The exam sometimes punishes cost heavy options, so if there is a cost tradeoff mentioned, weigh that when picking io1 or io2.

Encryption and key management without drama

Encryption questions test two axis, data at rest versus data in transit, and who owns the keys. Use customer managed KMS keys, CMK, when the scenario demands ownership, granular key policies, or cross account access control. S3 offers server side encryption options such as SSE S3 and SSE KMS, and you can also use client side encryption when the question explicitly requires client managed keys. Encrypted EBS snapshots stay encrypted when copied as long as you preserve or reassign the key properly. That is the little golden rule for snapshot questions.

Remember this

  • Pick CMK when the requirement is key ownership or custom policies
  • SSE KMS is the middle ground for S3 between usability and control
  • Client side encryption means the client manages keys outside of KMS
  • Encrypted snapshots remain encrypted if the key is preserved or rekeyed intentionally

Exam strategy cheat sheet

  • Map performance requirements to EBS types. High IOPS equals io1 or io2 unless cost is explicitly penalized.
  • Map security needs to KMS types. Ownership equals customer managed CMK.
  • When Beanstalk and containers show up together ask whether a container layer is required. Most times it is not.
  • Be suspicious of answers that suggest unencrypted backups or use instance store for durable storage. That is a trap with glitter.
  • Memorize defaults. Beanstalk uses EC2 by default. S3 offering SSE KMS is the safe middle ground.

Final exam tips that actually help

Practice with a few scenarios. Try ones that mention heavy random IOPS and ones that mention key ownership. State your reasoning briefly when a question asks for an explanation. If a scenario demands key ownership pick a customer managed CMK and say so. If it demands heavy random IOPS pick provisioned IOPS and call out io1 or io2. And if you see instance store in an answer for durable storage laugh quietly and pick the option that does not self sabotage.

Good luck. Treat the exam like a puzzle and not a trap filled with surprises. Keep the mappings in your head and you will stop getting seduced by the shiny new service named in the wrong question.
seo_title: Master Beanstalk EC2 storage and encryption for AWS tests
seo_heading: How to map EBS performance and KMS keys in Beanstalk exam scenarios

title: Transfer Domain Name to AWS Route53 from GoDaddy #techtarget
description: Step by step guide to transfer a domain from GoDaddy to AWS Route53 with unlock auth code DNS checks and approval
heading: Transfer Domain Name to AWS Route53 from GoDaddy Guide
body:
Quick summary

This guide walks you through moving a domain from GoDaddy to AWS Route53 while keeping DNS downtime to a minimum. You will unlock the domain, fetch the authorization code also known as the EPP code, request the transfer in Route53, approve any GoDaddy confirmations, and verify DNS and nameservers when the transfer finishes. Follow the checklist and you will avoid the usual hair pulling.

Prepare the domain at GoDaddy

Log in to your GoDaddy account and do the boring but essential prep work. If you skip this you will taste frustration.

  • Turn off domain lock so transfers are allowed.
  • Disable WHOIS privacy so the registrant email can receive approval messages.
  • Copy the authorization code from the domain management panel. This is the little string that makes the whole thing happen.

Check eligibility and contact details

Registrars and ICANN have rules that love to ruin your schedule. Make sure your registration is not stuck in a 60 day hold after a recent registration or transfer. Confirm the registrant email is accurate because the approval link will be sent there. If the email is wrong you will be on hold until you sort that out.

Request the transfer in AWS Route53

Open the Route53 console and choose transfer domain. Enter the domain and paste the authorization code. Select the contact settings and decide if you want to keep or turn off privacy protection under Route53. Route53 will present the required fees and the expected next steps.

Approve the transfer via GoDaddy confirmations

Watch the registrant email inbox for messages. Some transfers go through automatically while others need manual approval in the GoDaddy interface or via a confirmation link in email. If GoDaddy asks you to confirm the transfer, confirm it. It is not optional unless you enjoy delays.

Validate DNS and nameservers after transfer completes

When Route53 reports the transfer as complete do these checks right away. If Route53 will host your DNS create a hosted zone and import or recreate records before you switch nameservers. If you plan to keep DNS hosted elsewhere then leave the nameservers alone and skip creating a hosted zone for that domain in Route53.

  • Check that all important DNS records exist in the active DNS host.
  • Confirm nameservers are what you expect. If you moved registrar but keep an external DNS provider you may not need to change nameservers at all.
  • Lower TTL values ahead of transfer if you expect changes. Lower TTL reduces propagation surprises.

Troubleshooting and practical tips

  • If the transfer stalls confirm the registrant email and check the GoDaddy account notifications.
  • Remember ICANN transfer rules about the 60 day wait after registration or prior transfers.
  • Keep screenshots of settings so you can quickly recreate records in Route53 if needed.
  • Expect a small registrar fee with Route53. It is normal and covers the first year of registration renewal.

Final thought, patience helps. The technical parts are straightforward. The parts that make you sigh are usually email confirmation and registrar lock windows. Be methodical, and you will have your domain managed by Route53 with minimal fuss and only a little drama.

seo_heading: Domain transfer from GoDaddy to Route53 with DNS and nameserver checks

title: How to Transfer a Domain to AWS Route 53
description: Step by step guide to transfer a domain to AWS Route 53 with DNS checks authorization code and registrar settings for minimal downtime
heading: How to Transfer a Domain to AWS Route 53 Fast and Safely
body:
If you are looking to move a domain into AWS Route 53 without turning your website into a glitchy homage to dial up days you are in the right place. This guide walks through the domain transfer process from a third party registrar to Route 53 while keeping DNS intact and downtime minimal. Yes it requires paperwork and patience but it is a controlled kind of chaos.

Prepare your domain at the current registrar

Before touching the AWS console do a bit of boring prep work at the registrar that currently holds the domain. These steps save you from the classic transfer facepalm.

  • Remove the domain lock or domain lock setting. Many registrars call this registry lock or domain lock.
  • Disable privacy protection if it hides the admin email. Transfer approvals and authorization code emails go to the registrant contact.
  • Request the authorization code also known as the EPP code. You will need it to start the Route 53 domain transfer.

Do these now so you are not inboxing supplicants later.

Verify WHOIS and contact details

If the administrative contact email or phone number is outdated the transfer will probably fail. Update WHOIS data at the current registrar so the admin contact is reachable. Double check the email is not a dead alias or abandoned account.

Pro tip. Some registrars will reject transfer requests if WHOIS info looks too funky or privacy settings block verification emails. Fix that up front.

Decide how you will handle DNS and name servers

This is the important part for uptime. You have two solid options depending on how brave you feel.

  • Keep current name servers if you want zero DNS churn. Leave the existing DNS host in place, then transfer the registrar only. After the transfer you can create a hosted zone in Route 53 and copy records on your timetable.
  • Prebuild a Route 53 hosted zone if you prefer to switch quickly. Export your zone file or manually copy records into a Route 53 hosted zone ahead of time. Lower the TTL on key records a day or two before switching name servers to speed up propagation.

Lowering TTL values is your friend. Set TTL to a low value like 300 seconds well before the switch so DNS caches expire faster and changes show up quickly.

Initiate the transfer inside the Route 53 console

When you are ready log into the AWS console and go to Route 53. Choose the option to transfer a domain to Route 53 and follow the prompts. You will need to:

  • Enter the domain name.
  • Provide the authorization code you got from the current registrar.
  • Confirm contact details and accept the transfer fees.

Route 53 will contact the losing registrar as part of the process. Transfers often complete quickly but can take up to several days depending on the losing registrar and whether you need to approve the request via email.

Approve the transfer and confirm completion

Some registrars require an explicit approval step. Monitor the administrative contact email for approval messages and follow any instructions. If the transfer stalls check the registrar account for pending confirmations.

Once the transfer finishes verify the name servers and DNS records in Route 53. If you prebuilt a hosted zone compare records line by line to avoid missing A records MX records or TXT entries that can wreck email or verification flows.

After the transfer

  • Confirm WHOIS now reflects the new registrar and that privacy settings are configured as you want.
  • If you reduced TTL before the switch remember to raise it back to a reasonable default once everything looks stable.
  • Check propagation and DNS resolution with tools like dig or online DNS checkers to confirm global visibility.

Troubleshooting quick wins

  • No authorization code. Contact the current registrar support and ask for the EPP code. Be polite and persistent.
  • Transfer stuck. Verify admin email receipts and check for pending approvals at the losing registrar.
  • DNS not resolving after switch. Confirm name server records at the registrar match your Route 53 hosted zone NS records and that the hosted zone has the expected records.

Recap

In plain terms the process is this: unlock the domain and get the authorization code, verify WHOIS contact and email, decide whether to keep the old name servers or import records into Route 53, initiate the transfer in the AWS console and approve any required confirmations, then verify DNS and adjust TTLs. Follow these steps and you can move a domain to AWS Route 53 with minimal downtime and fewer hair pulling moments.

If you want a checklist version for copy paste say the word and we will make it gloriously simple and oddly satisfying.
seo_title: Move your domain to AWS Route 53 and avoid DNS downtime
seo_heading: Step by step domain transfer checklist for Route 53 with DNS tips

body:
This tutorial teaches how to publish a static website on GitHub Pages for free using a repository and simple Git commands.

Create a repository using a clear name. For a user page choose username.github.io as the repository name. For a project page any name works and the site will live under username.github.io slash repo name.

body:
If your team is moving to AWS and you want fewer surprises and more actual work done, this guide walks through migration planning and execution with a healthy dose of realism. No smoke and mirrors, just clear steps for discovery, strategy selection, execution, and ongoing cost optimization and security checks.

Assess the current estate

Start by inventorying applications, dependencies, and performance needs. Use discovery tools to map which services talk to what, collect current usage metrics, and gather cost and compliance requirements. That data will drive sensible migration planning and reduce the number of meetings where everyone blames the cloud.

  • Inventory apps, databases, queues, and external integrations
  • Capture performance baselines and peak usage patterns
  • Document compliance and cost constraints for each workload

Choose a migration strategy

Map each application to a strategy. Pick rehost for speed when you need to move fast, replatform when you want better long term value, and refactor when native cloud architecture pays off. This is migration planning in practice, not wishful thinking.

  • Lift and shift for quick moves with minimal code changes
  • Replatform to improve scalability or reduce operational toil
  • Refactor when cloud native benefits outweigh the effort

Prepare the AWS environment

Set up accounts and governance early so security and billing do not become a random scavenger hunt. Configure identity and access management, network segmentation, and basic monitoring before you flip production traffic. Apply tagging and cost allocation rules from day one so billing reports actually help you optimize spend.

Essentials to configure

  • AWS accounts and organizational units for isolation
  • IAM roles and least privilege policies
  • VPC design and network segmentation
  • Monitoring and centralized logging
  • Tagging and cost allocation policies

Execute the migration

Use an automated, staged approach and expect that at least one quirky dependency will require improvisation. Start with a proof of concept, move to a pilot cluster, then scale up. Run data replication and cutover tests, plan maintenance windows, and validate application behavior after traffic shifts.

  • Use automation tools for repeatability
  • Validate data replication and consistency under load
  • Document rollback criteria and runbooks so no one panics

Optimize and validate after migration

Once workloads run in AWS, tune instance types and storage tiers, enable autoscaling, and rightsize resources. Verify security posture with audits and penetration tests, and set up continuous monitoring and alerting. Review one full billing cycle for cost optimization opportunities like savings plans and reservations.

Best practices checklist

  • Start with a small low risk application to prove the pipeline
  • Keep stakeholders informed with a simple timeline and communication plan
  • Automate repeatable steps and codify runbooks
  • Measure and iterate on cost optimization and security posture

Migrations are rarely glamorous, but with solid migration planning and disciplined execution you can move to AWS with fewer emergencies and better cost control. Treat the move as a long term investment in reliability and security and you will get more than a change in hosting, you will get a better platform for the future.

title: hosting github pages
description: Quick guide to host a static site on GitHub Pages from repo setup to custom domain and publishing
heading: Hosting GitHub Pages guide
body:
If you want a free static site and you hate paying for hosting then GitHub Pages is the cozy little miracle you need. It will serve HTML CSS and static assets directly from a repo with almost zero drama. Below is a practical walkthrough that keeps the magic and skips the ceremony.

1 Create the repository

Use GitHub to make a new public repository or reuse an existing one. Public repos get free Pages hosting so you do not need to enter your credit card or perform a ritual. Private repos can also host Pages on paid plans but that is a different story.

2 Add your site files

Put an index.html at the root of the branch you will publish or in a docs folder if you prefer a tidy repo. Typical steps locally look like this.

git init
git add .
git commit -m "launch"
git branch -M main
git remote add origin git@github.com:yourname/yourrepo.git
git push -u origin main

Push the branch you intend to publish. If you use a docs folder you can keep the rest of your project in the same repo without chaos.

3 Choose the publishing source

In the repository settings open the Pages section and pick the publishing source. Common choices are the main branch root or the docs folder. Some folks use a gh-pages branch if they like extra complexity for no reason.

What happens next

GitHub Pages will build and serve the files from the selected branch or folder. A green check or a live site entry in the Pages settings confirms success. If you see an error check file paths branch selection and commit history before blaming DNS.

4 Add a custom domain if you want one

To use a custom domain add a plain text file named CNAME to the publishing branch containing only your domain name. Then update DNS at your registrar. GitHub supports either A records or a CNAME record depending on the setup.

  • Add a CNAME file with example.com on a single line if you want the root domain served.
  • Set an A record or a CNAME record at your DNS provider following GitHub guidance. DNS propagation timing depends on your provider mood and cache TTLs.

5 HTTPS and verification

Enable Enforce HTTPS in the Pages settings for secure connections. GitHub can provision an SSL certificate for your custom domain automatically in most cases. Wait a little if the certificate is still being issued.

Troubleshooting checklist

  • No index.html in the published path will result in a sad 404
  • Make sure you pushed the same branch you chose in the Pages settings
  • If custom domain fails recheck the CNAME file and DNS records
  • Look at the Pages build log in the settings for specific build errors

Final notes

This covers repository creation adding static files selecting a publishing source optional custom domain configuration and verification. Follow these steps and your static site will be live without hiring a wizard. If anything goes wrong try turning it off and on again then read the build log.

title: AWS Practitioner Certification Practice Exam
description: Practice exam walkthrough and study strategy for AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner Maximize score with active practice and focused review
heading: AWS Practitioner Certification Practice Exam Guide
body:
Quick strategy to treat a practice exam like real pressure

If you want to pass the AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner without crying into the exam portal, use a full length practice exam video and behave. That means one sitting, real time limits and no tab hopping. The point is to train timing, build stamina, and find the ideas that keep stealing your points.

Simulate real exam time

Set a timer for the official exam length and close everything except the video. Headphones help, coffee helps more, and snacks on the desk are allowed if they do not turn into distractions. Treat this run as both a knowledge check and a stress rehearsal.

Watch actively

Active watching beats passive replay. Pause before the answer and force yourself to call one. A reasoned guess counts as studying while a wild guess is just noise. If you answer wrong, do not immediately skip ahead. Use mistakes as a map, not a facepalm moment.

Log the recurring topics

Write down service access patterns, common security models, shared responsibility reminders and pricing basics. Those topics show up a lot on the exam. Keep a short running list so you do not relearn the same thing every session.

Cross check video explanations with official AWS docs

Video answers are fine but sometimes too neat. After a practice run, open the AWS exam guide and the relevant service pages. Official pages highlight nuances that short explanations skip and they will save you when a question tries to be annoying.

Retake and track weak areas

Mark domains where mistakes repeat and then focus study there. Do not just replay the entire video hoping for a different result. Make a plan that targets weak spots with short labs, focused flashcards and active recall practice.

Timebox practice runs and use active recall

  1. Run the full practice exam under timed conditions.
  2. Pause and answer each question without peeking.
  3. Log wrong answers and map each one to the exact AWS service or concept.
  4. Build a tiny hands on lab that demonstrates the concept in 10 to 20 minutes.

Build tiny hands on labs

Practical work fixes fuzzy memories. For example create a small IAM policy, launch a low cost EC2 instance and try S3 public bucket settings. The goal is not to become an architect in one lab. The goal is to convert abstract exam vocabulary into something your brain actually recognizes.

Final checklist for efficient exam prep

  • Schedule a timed practice exam at least weekly as you get closer to test day
  • Use active recall not passive watching
  • Map each missed question to a specific AWS service or concept
  • Create tiny labs to lock understanding
  • Repeat until you stop being surprised by the distractor answers

Follow this loop and the exam will feel less like a trap and more like a mildly stressful box checking exercise. You will still need to study, but you will also get better at spotting the exam writers clever tricks. Good luck and may your guesses be reasoned.

body:
Why pick AWS Bedrock for Amazon AI work

If you want a managed path to run GPTs and other LLMs without living in GPU dependency hell, AWS Bedrock is the adult supervision you did not know you needed. It gives developers API access to a marketplace of foundation models from multiple vendors and Amazon owned models. That means faster prototyping and fewer midnight production alarms when a model decides to be creative.

Core capabilities at a glance

  • Multi vendor model access for experimentation with GPTs and specialist LLMs
  • Private model customization and prompt engineering support for safer outputs
  • Integrated security identity and AI monitoring with existing AWS stacks
  • Deployments for inference with autoscaling to reduce operational overhead

Pick the right model for the right job

Model choice matters. Use smaller specialized models for embeddings and search when latency and cost matter. Save the big conversational GPT style models for tasks that need natural language generation and long context handling. Mixing model sizes is not cheating, it is smart engineering.

Customization without drama

Bedrock supports private customization, prompt templates and parameter tuning. Think of these as polite nudges for model behavior. Change the grain size of fine tuning, lock down prompt templates for consistency and tune temperature and top p when you want less hallucination and more reliability.

Security and AI governance that actually matters

Security and governance are not optional for Enterprise AI. Use encryption, strict access control and audit logs to meet compliance goals. Add validation checks and guardrails in the prompt layer for high risk outputs before routing generated content to customers. If you skip this step you will discover new and exciting ways to get fined.

Operational and cost playbook

AI cost optimization is a practical art. Track tokens per call and monitor usage patterns. Batch requests when possible and cache common responses to reduce repeated token spend. Choose the right instance size for production inference to avoid sticker shock. Monitor latency, error rates and cost together when selecting models for deployment.

Deployment tips for engineering teams

For teams that like vendor diversity and tight cloud integration, Bedrock offers operational leverage. For teams that want a one stop managed experience, Bedrock still reduces heavy lifting while keeping choices open. Prototype with small models for embeddings and larger models for generation. Measure latency, token cost and error rates early and bake those metrics into model selection before full scale deployment.

Quick checklist before going live

  • Choose model family for the use case
  • Prototype and measure latency and token costs
  • Apply encryption, access control and audit logging
  • Implement prompt guardrails and output validation
  • Monitor usage and optimize for AI cost optimization

In short, AWS Bedrock brings together the marketplace convenience of Amazon AI and the deployment controls enterprise teams need. Use the right models, add governance and keep an eye on tokens and infrastructure. Do that and your AI project will behave about 80 percent of the time.

title: How to Create an AWS Account | Free Tier
description: Step by step guide to sign up for an AWS account using the Free Tier with tips to avoid billing surprises and set basic security
heading: How to Create an AWS Account Free Tier
body:
If you are ready to poke at the cloud without accidentally paying a mortgage you are in the right place. This beginner guide walks you through how to create an AWS account and activate the AWS Free Tier while keeping billing alerts and basic security in place. Expect a few clicks and a tiny amount of patience.

Before you start

Quick checklist to save time and tears

  • Use a dedicated email for cloud accounts to avoid inbox chaos
  • Have a credit or debit card ready for identity verification
  • Keep your phone nearby for SMS or call verification

Step 1 Visit the AWS homepage and begin signup

Go to aws.amazon.com and click the Create an AWS Account button. Fill in an email you actually check and set a strong password. Yes we know you want to use your dog s name but do not.

Step 2 Add contact info and payment method

Enter your full contact details and add a credit or debit card. AWS requires a payment method for identity verification and to bill any usage outside the Free Tier. You will not be billed for eligible Free Tier use but the card stays on file.

Step 3 Complete phone verification

Provide a phone number and verify it via SMS or automated call. This step is mandatory and helps cut down on fake accounts. It takes a minute and then you can move on.

Step 4 Pick the Basic support plan

Choose the Basic support plan which is free. Paid plans exist if you like expedited human contact but the Basic plan is fine for learning and small projects.

Step 5 Confirm Free Tier eligibility and review limits

Activate the AWS Free Tier and check monthly limits for common services like EC2 compute hours, S3 storage, and RDS usage. The Free Tier is generous for testing, but heavy experiments will exceed limits and generate charges. Keep an eye on months when you run large workloads.

Step 6 Create IAM users and enable MFA

Do not use the root account for daily tasks. Create an IAM user with administrative privileges for day to day work. Enable MFA on the root account and on any IAM users with elevated access. MFA adds a second factor and prevents account takeover even when your password is weak or leaked.

Step 7 Configure billing alerts and budgets

Open the Billing console and set budgets that trigger email notifications. Configure billing alerts for amounts that would make you panic. If you want to be fussier you can create alarms for specific service usage in CloudWatch.

Practical billing alert tips

  • Set a low warning threshold so you get early notice
  • Create a hard threshold that sends multiple emails if crossed
  • Check usage reports weekly during experiments

Final notes for the wary explorer

This guide covered account signup payment verification support selection Free Tier review and basic security setup so a beginner can start using AWS safely. You will still make mistakes and that is fine. Keep budgets and billing alerts in place and treat the root account like a nuclear launch key. Now go provision something small and learn something valuable without ballooning your credit card statement.
