title: Git revert vs reset What's the difference?
description: Clear comparison of Git revert and Git reset with examples when to use each and how to recover lost commits.
heading: Git revert vs reset What's the difference?
body:
The key difference between git revert and git reset is that git revert records a new commit that undoes a previous commit while git reset moves the current branch pointer and can change the index and working tree.

Use git revert when the commit history must remain intact on a shared branch. The revert command makes a new commit that applies the inverse of a past commit. That approach keeps history linear and readable for teammates and continuous integration.

Example

git revert commit_hash

Use git reset for local cleanup before pushing. The reset command rewrites branch history and has three common modes. The --soft form moves the branch pointer only. The --mixed form moves the branch pointer and resets the index. The --hard form moves the branch pointer and resets the index and working tree which discards uncommitted changes.

Examples

git reset --soft HEAD~1 git reset --mixed HEAD~1 git reset --hard HEAD~1

Be careful with reset on branches that others use. Resetting public history typically requires a force push which can orphan commits and cause confusion for collaborators. If a mistaken reset occurs the reflog can rescue lost commits with commands such as git reflog followed by git checkout or another reset.

Quick decision guide

Shared branch choose revert for safety and clarity. Local branch choose reset for tidy history before sharing. For surgical history edits consider interactive rebase for multiple commits.

That covers the practical trade offs between these two commands and when to favor one approach over the other without making teammates cry.

Tip

When unsure run commands in a throwaway branch first. Use git reflog as a safety net after a risky reset and prefer revert for any commit that already reached a remote.

title: Here's how to set JAVA_HOME in Windows 7
description: Quick guide to set JAVA_HOME on Windows 7 and add Java to PATH so java commands run from the command prompt
heading: How to set JAVA_HOME in Windows 7 for command line Java use
body:
This short tutorial shows how to set the JAVA_HOME system variable on Windows 7 and add Java to the PATH so java tools run from the command prompt.

  1. Find the Java installation folder
  2. Open System Properties and Environment Variables
  3. Create or edit the JAVA_HOME system variable
  4. Add the Java bin folder to the PATH
  5. Verify from the command prompt

Find the Java installation folder by checking the Program Files folder under the C drive for a folder named Java and then a jdk version folder such as Program Files\Java\jdk1.8.0_xxx. Prefer a JDK folder rather than a JRE folder so developer tools work correctly.

Open Control Panel then System then Advanced system settings and click Environment Variables. This brings up the dialog that controls global and user environment variables.

Create a new system variable named JAVA_HOME and set the value to the full path of the JDK root such as Program Files\Java\jdk1.8.0_xxx. If a JAVA_HOME variable already exists select Edit and correct the path.

Edit the system PATH variable and add %JAVA_HOME%\bin as a new entry or append the entry to the existing string using the standard Windows path separator. Placing the entry at the front ensures this JDK is found first by command line tools.

Open a new command prompt window and run java -version and echo %JAVA_HOME% to confirm that the Java runtime and the environment variable match the intended JDK.

This tutorial walked through locating the Java folder creating or updating the JAVA_HOME system variable adding the bin folder to the PATH and verifying the setup from the command prompt. If command line tools still complain check for multiple Java installations and ensure the command prompt session was restarted after the change.

Tip

If multiple JDKs exist give each JDK a clear folder name and update JAVA_HOME before starting IDEs or build tools. A quick restart of the command prompt often resolves ghost problems caused by stale environment settings.

title: How to deploy Spring Boot microservices to Amazon ECS
description: Deploy Spring Boot microservices to Amazon ECS with Docker ECR task definitions and services for scalable container deployment on AWS
heading: How to deploy Spring Boot microservices to Amazon ECS
body:
This tutorial shows a practical path to deploy Spring Boot microservices to Amazon ECS using Docker and Amazon ECR and how to wire task definitions and services for production like traffic.

  1. Build a Docker image for each Spring Boot service
  2. Push the image to Amazon ECR
  3. Create an ECS task definition
  4. Create an ECS cluster and service
  5. Attach a load balancer and configure environment variables and logs

Build a Docker image Use Maven or Gradle to produce a runnable jar then create a Dockerfile that uses an OpenJDK base and copies the jar into the image. Keep layers minimal and prefer a multi stage build to reduce final image size. Use docker build -t myapp . for a local test.

Push the image to Amazon ECR Create a repository in ECR and authenticate the Docker client with the AWS CLI. Tag the local image using a repository uri and push the image to the registry so the ECS task definition can reference a stable image source.

Create an ECS task definition Define container name image uri CPU and memory settings and port mappings. Add environment variables for configuration and a log driver configuration that sends logs to CloudWatch for easy debugging.

Create an ECS cluster and service Choose Fargate for serverless containers or EC2 launch type for more control. Create a service using the task definition and set a desired count for replicas. Configure health checks so the service replaces unhealthy tasks automatically.

Attach a load balancer and configure runtime details Create an application load balancer with a target group that maps to container ports. Ensure security groups and subnets allow traffic. Use parameter store or secrets manager for sensitive environment values and mount those as environment variables in the task definition.

Deployments converge to a running set of containers that receive traffic from the load balancer and send logs to CloudWatch. Use rolling updates and monitoring to maintain availability and reduce surprises during deploys.

Tip

Automate the whole flow with a pipeline using CodePipeline or GitHub Actions and CloudFormation or Terraform for task definitions. Reproducible infrastructure saves a lot of apologies later.

title: Five different ways to upload JAR files to JFrog Artifactory
description: Learn five practical ways to upload JAR files to JFrog Artifactory using common tools and commands for CI and manual use
heading: Five different ways to upload JAR files to JFrog Artifactory
body:
If you need to get a JAR into JFrog Artifactory and you do not feel like summoning ancient incantations this morning, here are five sane ways to do it. Each method is practical, useful, and has trade offs. Pick the one that matches your level of scripting masochism.

Web UI for one off uploads

If you enjoy dragging things around with a mouse and pretending it is efficient then the Artifactory browser is your friend. Open the target repository in the Artifactory web UI and drop the JAR where it belongs. It will upload, set basic metadata, and give you a moment of mild satisfaction.

  • Best for: quick checks, demos, or when someone asks you to "just upload this file"
  • Downside: not great for automation or reproducible builds

Maven deploy plugin for build integrated uploads

If your build is already Maven based use the deploy phase. Configure distributionManagement in your project POM and run the standard mvn deploy goal. Maven will compute group id, artifact id, version, and upload coordinates to the configured repository using credentials from settings.xml.

Quick example

mvn clean deploy

This is the cleanest path when your CI runs Maven. Maven handles metadata, pom generation, and repository coordinates for you.

Gradle publish with the maven publish plugin

Gradle users should apply the maven publish plugin and configure a publication plus a repository block. Then run gradle publish. Gradle will build the JAR and push it with the right group and version.

Quick example

gradle publish

Good for modern pipelines where Gradle orchestrates everything. Keep credentials out of source by using gradle.properties or a secure credential store in CI.

curl and the Artifactory REST API for simple scripts

If you only need a quick script or troubleshooting from a shell then a plain HTTP PUT will do. Use curl with authentication and upload the file path you want. This is minimal and reliable when you need total control.

Example curl upload

curl -u USER -X PUT https//example.com/artifactory/repo/path/app.jar -T build/libs/app.jar

Use curl for ad hoc uploads, small automation snippets, or when you want to shove files into a repository without a full build tool. Remember to secure your credentials if you put this into scripts.

JFrog CLI for automation and speed

Install the JFrog CLI, run jfrog config to register your server once, and then use the upload command. The CLI adds checksum optimization and parallel uploads which matter in real world CI.

Example JFrog CLI command

jfrog rt u "build/libs/*.jar" repo/path/

JFrog CLI is the recommended choice for pipelines. It integrates with many CI systems, can preserve properties, and reduces upload time with checksums and concurrency.

Comparing the options

  • Web UI for manual, one off tasks
  • Maven deploy when your project is Maven and you want correct coordinates
  • Gradle publish for Gradle native pipelines
  • curl for quick scripts and debugging with the REST API
  • JFrog CLI for automation, performance, and CI friendliness

Tips for reliable uploads

  • Never store plaintext credentials in repo files. Use settings.xml, gradle.properties, environment variables, or your CI secret store.
  • Prefer JFrog CLI or build tool integration for repeatable builds and checksum reuse.
  • Pick a consistent repository layout and naming scheme so you do not have to explain your artifact choices to future you.

In short, all five methods work. Use the Web UI for casual uploads, use Maven or Gradle when the build should drive the publish, use curl when you need a tiny script, and use JFrog CLI when you want speed and sanity in CI. Now go upload your JAR and pretend it was effortless.

title: How to quickly deploy from Spring Boot to a Docker container

This tutorial shows how to build a Spring Boot application and package that application into a Docker container for fast deployment and testing.

This tutorial covered how to take a Spring Boot project from a built jar to a running Docker container with a few practical commands and a compact Dockerfile. The goal is repeatable local testing and a foundation for CI pipelines.

Use multi stage builds to keep final image size small and enable faster deployments. Add health checks and a small init process to handle signals for graceful shutdowns.

title: How to use the application.properties file in Spring Boot
description: Guide to using application.properties in Spring Boot with examples on binding profile overrides and external configuration
heading: How to use the application.properties file in Spring Boot
body:
If you want to boss your Spring Boot app around without yelling at your CI pipeline this is the practical guide to the humble application.properties file and how to use it for configuration binding profiles and externalized settings

Where to place application.properties

Drop a file named application.properties under src/main/resources in a Maven or Gradle project and Spring Boot will pick it up from the classpath automatically No secret ritual or arcane pom entry required

Example properties

server.port=8081
app.name=MyApp
app.description=A slightly less sad microservice

Keep keys consistent and values simple so your list of properties does not become a treasure map you avoid following

Binding single values and groups of values

Use @Value for a quick grab when you only need a single property and use @ConfigurationProperties when you have a group of related values that belong together Like putting socks in a drawer instead of leaving them in the laundry basket

Quick single value

@Value("${app.name}")
private String appName

Bulk binding with ConfigurationProperties

Create a POJO annotated with @ConfigurationProperties("app") and let Spring populate the fields based on matching prefixes This makes testing easier and keeps your wiring tidy

@ConfigurationProperties("app")
public class AppProperties {
  private String name
  private int maxConnections

  // getters and setters required for binding
}

Profiles for environment specific overrides

Create files like application-dev.properties and application-prod.properties and activate a profile with spring.profiles.active=dev The active profile file will override matching keys from the base file when the profile is active

Example file names

  • application.properties for defaults
  • application-dev.properties for development tweaks
  • application-prod.properties for production settings

Externalized configuration and precedence

If you want to change settings at runtime without rebuilding your jar place a properties file outside the packaged artifact Spring Boot supports that and yes it is glorious for ops

Order matters

Spring Boot checks many places for configuration and follows a clear precedence order Command line arguments and profile specific files can override the classpath file Keep this in mind when a value refuses to change and you are about to declare the file possessed

  • Command line arguments have high priority
  • Environment variables and system properties can override classpath values
  • Profile specific files override application.properties on the classpath
  • External files outside the jar can override the internal file

Best practices and quick tips

  • Prefer @ConfigurationProperties for groups of related values This improves type safety and testing
  • Use consistent naming and simple keys to avoid confusion later
  • Externalize sensitive values or inject them via environment variables for safer ops
  • Check server.port when your app is refusing to start and do not blame Spring before checking the basics

Recap

application.properties is the simple and central way to configure Spring Boot Use it for defaults use profile files for environment specific changes bind values to beans cleanly with @Value or prefer @ConfigurationProperties for grouped settings and externalize configuration when runtime flexibility is necessary Now go configure something and try not to break production today

seo_heading: Practical guide to binding properties and using profiles in Spring Boot apps

title: JDBC vs Hibernate What's the difference with JPA?
description: Compare JDBC Hibernate and JPA to learn which Java persistence approach fits use cases from raw SQL to full ORM.
heading: JDBC vs Hibernate What's the difference with JPA?
body:
The key difference between JDBC Hibernate and JPA is that JDBC is a low level API while JPA is a specification and Hibernate is an ORM implementation of that specification

JDBC exposes Connection PreparedStatement and ResultSet and demands manual SQL writing object mapping resource cleanup and transaction control. This approach gives maximum control and predictable SQL behavior when performance tuning and complex native queries matter most

JPA defines a standard API around an object relational mapping model and lifecycle. Developers use annotations or XML to map domain classes to tables and rely on an EntityManager for CRUD and queries. JPA promotes portability across implementations

Hibernate implements JPA and supplies many extras such as second level cache HQL a rich query API lazy loading dirty checking and extensive mapping features. Hibernate reduces boilerplate and adds production grade capabilities that plain JPA alone may not cover

When to choose which Use JDBC when full SQL control minimal abstraction and raw performance are top priorities. Use JPA when a standardized ORM reduces boilerplate and improves developer productivity. Choose Hibernate when advanced caching custom types and a mature ecosystem matter more than strict portability

Quick examples

Connection conn = DriverManager.getConnection(url user password)

EntityManager em = entityManagerFactory.createEntityManager()

Summary Choose the right tool based on project goals. If SQL mastery and low level tuning are required pick JDBC. If clean domain models and faster development are desired pick JPA with Hibernate for extra features and optimizations

Tip

Measure common use cases before committing. Prototype a hot query with JDBC and then with Hibernate and compare execution plans memory usage and developer time. Real metrics beat ideology every time

title: How to deploy a WAR file to Tomcat using Maven
description: Step by step Maven guide to build a WAR and deploy that WAR to Tomcat with plugin setup build and common troubleshooting tips.
heading: How to deploy a WAR file to Tomcat using Maven
body:
This tutorial shows how to build a WAR with Maven and deploy that WAR to Apache Tomcat using the Tomcat Maven plugin or by copying the WAR into the Tomcat webapps folder.

  1. Prepare project and pom xml
  2. Add Tomcat Maven plugin and configure credentials
  3. Build the WAR with Maven
  4. Deploy using the plugin
  5. Manual deploy to Tomcat webapps
  6. Verify and troubleshoot deployment

Prepare project and pom xml

Confirm that packaging in pom xml is set to war and that webapp sources live under the standard webapp folder. Add standard web xml and required dependencies for the Java web application.

Add Tomcat Maven plugin and configure credentials

Edit pom xml to include the Tomcat Maven plugin and specify the manager URL and user credentials that have the manager role on the Tomcat server. Store credentials in Maven settings for safety rather than leaving secrets inside pom xml.

Build the WAR with Maven

Run mvn clean package to create the WAR artifact. The target folder will contain the WAR that will be deployed to the servlet container.

Deploy using the plugin

Invoke the plugin deploy goal to push the WAR to the Tomcat manager. If credential or role mismatch happens the manager will reject the upload so double check server and user configuration on the Tomcat side.

Manual deploy to Tomcat webapps

If plugin deployment feels like modern alchemy then copy the WAR file into the Tomcat webapps folder and let the server explode the archive and register the context. Restart Tomcat when necessary.

Verify and troubleshoot deployment

Check Tomcat logs for class loader errors missing dependencies or context path collisions. Common fixes include adding missing libs to the WAR or updating the context path in server configuration.

Recap of the tutorial shows how to prepare a Maven web project configure the Tomcat plugin build the WAR and deploy that WAR either via plugin or manual copy while watching logs for errors.

Tip

Use Maven profiles to separate production and testing deployment settings and keep manager credentials in the Maven settings file with server ids that match entries in pom xml.

Set up Tomcat and manager access Ensure Tomcat includes the manager application and add a user with the manager role. Host the servlet container on a reachable machine and secure the manager endpoint by network rules.

Install Jenkins and required plugins Provision Jenkins and add the Deploy to container plugin or prepare SSH or REST access to the server. Plugin use is simpler for straightforward uploads.

Use a Jenkins pipeline with credentials binding to avoid exposing passwords in logs. Limit manager access by network and use strong unique passwords. For frequent deployments consider automating health checks after deployment to catch regressions quickly.

title: How to install WordPress 5.x on Ubuntu with Bitnami
description: Step by step guide to install WordPress 5.x on Ubuntu using a Bitnami stack with commands and configuration tips for a smooth setup
heading: How to install WordPress 5.x on Ubuntu with Bitnami
body:
This tutorial shows how to install WordPress 5.x on Ubuntu using a Bitnami stack with step by step commands and practical configuration tips for a working site.

  1. Prepare the Ubuntu server
  2. Download the Bitnami WordPress installer
  3. Run the installer with proper permissions
  4. Configure ports and services
  5. Secure credentials and database
  6. Verify access and finalize

Prepare the Ubuntu server by updating packages and installing required system tools. Example commands include updating package lists and installing build tools. Proper time zone and locales help avoid future surprises.

Download the Bitnami WordPress installer to the server using a secure channel from the official source. Save the file in a predictable folder and check the checksum if a checksum is available. The installer file name usually includes WordPress version details for clarity.

Make the installer executable and run the installer as a local administrator. Example commands include chmod +x bitnami-wordpress-5.x.x-linux-x64.run and sudo ./bitnami-wordpress-5.x.x-linux-x64.run. Follow prompts for installation folder, administrator credentials, and optional components. The installer handles Apache and database setup by default so manual wiring is minimal.

Configure ports and services if default ports conflict with other applications. Bitnami uses common ports by default. Adjust Apache port values in the stack configuration files when necessary and use the system service manager to enable automatic start on reboot.

Secure credentials by choosing strong passwords for the WordPress administrator and database users. Restrict SSH access and apply basic firewall rules to permit only required traffic. Consider moving database access to local only when external database access is not required.

Verify access by opening the server address in a browser and logging into the WordPress dashboard. Test sample pages and permalink settings. Apply updates for plugins and themes through the dashboard to avoid compatibility problems with WordPress 5.x.

This tutorial covered preparing an Ubuntu server downloading and running the Bitnami WordPress installer configuring services securing credentials and verifying a working WordPress site. The goal was a clear path from a fresh server to a functioning WordPress dashboard without unnecessary drama.

Tip

Keep a copy of the Bitnami stack installation folder and a database export before major changes. That backup acts as a fast recovery option when updates or plugin experiments go sideways.

title: git stash name example
description: Learn how to name stashes in Git to save and find work in progress with clear commands and quick examples.
heading: git stash name example explained for clear stash management
body:
Why name your stashes

Because leaving unnamed stashes around is like leaving mystery leftovers in the office fridge. At first it is fine, then it is tragic, then someone opens it and yells. Named stashes give your future self a fighting chance of remembering what that half baked change was for.

Make a named stash the sane way

When you want to tuck work in for later use a short message helps. Use a clear prefix for context such as feature user or fix and then a concise description. Example command:

git stash push -m "wip add login form"

This records the working tree and index with a human friendly label so your stash list is readable instead of a crime scene.

Find the stash you need

List stashes to see what you have saved. The list shows stash refs and the message you provided earlier.

git stash list

Example output might look like this

stash@{0} On main wip add login form
stash@{1} On feature/auth fix token refresh

Peek before you apply

Inspect a stash before pouring it back into your working tree. A quick peek avoids surprises and merge nightmares.

git stash show -p stash@{0}

Apply or remove the stash

If you just want the changes without removing the stash use apply. If you are confident use pop which applies and deletes the stash in one sweep.

git stash apply stash@{0}
# or when sure
git stash pop stash@{0}

Start a branch from a stash

If the saved change turned into something bigger start a branch directly from the stash. This checks out a new branch and applies the stashed change so you can keep working without cluttering main.

git stash branch feature-login stash@{0}

Quick checklist

  • Use git stash push -m with a short prefix like feature user or fix to add context
  • Run git stash list to find stash refs and messages
  • Always git stash show -p before applying unknown changes
  • Use git stash branch when the change becomes a full feature

Developer tips

Keep messages short and precise. Something like "feature auth add login UI" beats "stuff" every time. Good stash naming makes your stash list useful and saves debugging time later. Also you will sleep better at night.

Now go name your stashes and stop playing archeologist with your repo.
seo_title: Save messy work the smart way with named git stashes today
seo_heading: How to name and manage git stashes and rescue work later

title: What is the Hibernate SessionFactory? How do you build it?
description: Clear definition of Hibernate SessionFactory and practical steps to build one using Configuration and ServiceRegistry in Java
heading: What is the Hibernate SessionFactory How do you build it
body:
What the SessionFactory actually is

If you imagine Hibernate as a small army of Java objects fighting a database, the SessionFactory is the general who keeps the maps the supplies and the battle plan. It is a thread safe factory that holds compiled mapping metadata connection pool settings and cache configuration and it produces Session objects that do the dirty work.

SessionFactory is heavy weight by design. Create one per application or per database schema and then stop creating them like they are cheap coffee mugs. Session objects are lightweight and short lived. Open one per unit of work and then close it before it starts a cult.

How to build a SessionFactory step by step

Building a SessionFactory is a short checklist of fuss and patience. The core steps are

  • Create a Configuration from file or programmatically
  • Register your entity classes or mapping files so Hibernate knows how to map Java classes to tables
  • Build a StandardServiceRegistry with connection pool settings dialect and properties
  • Call the build method to get the SessionFactory ready for application threads

Example pseudo code that shows the flow without pretending to compile

Configuration cfg = new Configuration().configure()
StandardServiceRegistry reg = new StandardServiceRegistryBuilder().applySettings(cfg.getProperties()).build()
SessionFactory sessionFactory = cfg.buildSessionFactory(reg)

Yes this looks like Java but is forgiving about punctuation on purpose. The important part is the order and the idea that the Configuration and the ServiceRegistry work together to produce the SessionFactory.

Configuration options worth your attention

Not every property is sacred but a few deserve obsessive care because they affect performance and stability. Pay attention to

  • Connection pool settings and max connections so the app does not exhaust the database
  • Dialect so SQL generated actually speaks your database language
  • Second level cache configuration when you want to avoid repeated reads of the same data
  • Mapping metadata and annotated classes so Hibernate knows what table goes with what class

Runtime use and lifecycle rules

Follow a couple of rules and Hibernate will play nice. Open short lived Session objects per request or per transaction. Use transactions to keep data consistent. Never share a Session across threads. If you do share it you will either get lucky or you will get bugs that look like ghost stories.

Shutdown is boring but necessary. Close the SessionFactory during application shutdown so connections and caches are released and your monitoring dashboard stops screaming.

Performance tips and common pitfalls

  • Prefer one SessionFactory per database and tune connection pool and second level cache rather than creating multiple SessionFactory instances
  • Avoid long lived Sessions that accumulate state and memory leaks
  • Use transactions and flush appropriately to avoid inconsistent reads and hidden surprises
  • Measure before you tune and pick sensible defaults for pool sizes based on real load

Final thought

The SessionFactory is the costly but crucial bootstrap object in Hibernate. Treat it with respect configure it carefully and then let Sessions do the noisy work. And if your app suddenly stops answering calls maybe check your connection pool before blaming Hibernate for having mood swings.
seo_title: Master Hibernate SessionFactory setup for fast Java ORM
seo_heading: Practical guide to building a thread safe Hibernate SessionFactory in Java

title: How to add multiple git worktrees to your repo example
description: Quick guide to add multiple git worktrees so different branches can be worked on at once without checkout conflicts.
heading: How to add multiple git worktrees to your repo example
body:
So you want to stop playing branch switch roulette and actually get things done. Multiple git worktrees let you work on several branches at once without constantly checking out and losing your mind. This is a short, slightly sarcastic guide that keeps the tech accurate and the drama low.

Why use multiple worktrees

Think of worktrees as parallel checkouts that share the same repository data. You get separate folders for different branches so editors, test runs, and build tasks can run side by side. This reduces accidental commits on the wrong branch and saves you a bunch of context switching.

Prepare the repository

Make sure your repository is clean before adding a new worktree. Run the normal checks from your main repo folder in the CLI.

git status

If you need to create the branch first do that here. Either create a branch locally or prepare it from a remote.

git branch feature-branch
# or
git fetch origin
git checkout -b feature-branch origin/feature-branch

Create a new worktree

Use git worktree add to make a linked checkout in a sibling folder. The new folder is a normal working copy that points to the branch you choose.

git worktree add ../feature-branch feature-branch

That command creates a folder at ../feature-branch which checks out feature-branch. Both your main repo folder and the new folder can be used at the same time. It is not magic. It is very convenient.

Work inside the new worktree

Open the new folder in your editor or run CI tasks there. From inside the worktree you behave like you would in any repo clone. Use git status and git commit as usual.

cd ../feature-branch
git status
git add .
git commit -m "A sensible commit message"

The main repo is unaffected by checkouts in other worktrees, which is exactly the point. You can run tests in one folder and code in another without getting into a branch switching fight with your shell.

Cleaning up old worktrees

When you no longer need a worktree remove it with git worktree remove and then tidy up references.

git worktree remove ../feature-branch
git worktree prune

Also delete or merge branches you no longer need to avoid orphaned refs. If a branch still has unmerged work do the right thing and either finish or stash it before removing the folder.

Quick checklist

  • Confirm git status is clean in the main repo
  • Create the branch if it does not exist
  • Use git worktree add with a clear folder name
  • Work normally inside the new folder
  • Remove the worktree and prune when done

Tips for the messy multitasker

  • Name folders to match branches so your editor and terminal are not confused
  • Keep heavy tests in their own worktree so they do not block interactive development
  • If CI or scripts depend on relative paths be explicit about which folder you are using
  • Use git worktree prune periodically to clean stale links

Using multiple worktrees is a practical way to speed up a developer workflow without adding new tools. You still need to be disciplined about commits and branches, but at least you will not be trapped in checkout hell. Now go create a couple of worktrees and pretend you are organized.
seo_title: Stop switching branches and multitask with git worktrees like a pro
seo_heading: Practical git worktree workflow for juggling branches in separate folders

title: A Hibernate 5 SchemaExport example
description: Learn how to programmatically create database tables with Hibernate 5 SchemaExport step by step code and practical tips for schema generation
heading: A Hibernate 5 SchemaExport example for programmatic table creation
body:
This tutorial shows how to use Hibernate 5 SchemaExport to programmatically generate database tables from annotated entity classes and Metadata.

  1. Add Hibernate dependency and configuration to the project
  2. Define entity classes with JPA annotations
  3. Create MetadataSources and build Metadata
  4. Configure and run SchemaExport to execute DDL against the database
  5. Verify tables and adjust mappings as needed

Step 1 Add Hibernate dependency and configuration. Use Maven or Gradle to include hibernate core and the JDBC driver for the target database. Provide connection properties in hibernate cfg or in code based Properties. Confirm database credentials and driver class name are correct before moving on.

Step 2 Define entity classes with JPA annotations. Annotate primary keys and relationships so the mapping represents the desired schema. Use sensible column definitions and lengths to avoid surprises when the database tries to store real data.

Step 3 Create MetadataSources and build Metadata. Boot the ServiceRegistry then feed annotated classes or mapping resources into MetadataSources. Call buildMetadata to produce a Metadata object that represents the full mapping model.

Step 4 Configure and run SchemaExport. Instantiate SchemaExport and set options such as output file format and whether to run DDL against the database. Call create or execute with the Metadata object to produce tables. Running in dry run mode allows previewing SQL before any schema changes occur.

Step 5 Verify tables in the database using a DB client or query tool. Check columns constraints and indexes. If something looks odd update the mapping then repeat the Metadata build and SchemaExport run until the schema matches expectations.

This guide covered preparing a project for SchemaExport defining entities building Metadata running SchemaExport and verifying the generated database schema. The whole point is to let Hibernate produce DDL so manual SQL writing becomes less frequent and less thrilling for those who enjoy debugging missing foreign keys.

Tip

Enable SQL logging and use a script output option on SchemaExport to preview generated DDL before applying changes to a production database. Version control mapping files for safe rollbacks.

title: Hibernate and JPA CRUD example with Hibernate 5.4 and JPA 2.

heading: Hibernate and JPA CRUD example with Hibernate 5.4 and JPA 2.2
body:
This tutorial shows how to build a CRUD application using Hibernate 5.4 and JPA 2.2 covering configuration entity mapping and DAO operations.

Define a simple entity with an @Entity annotation and primary key mapping. The entity represents domain state and must include proper equals and hashCode for reliable behavior when the persistence context is involved.

Create an EntityManagerFactory for JPA use or a SessionFactory when preferring native Hibernate APIs. Use a bootstrap approach that handles lifecycle so the application can open and close resources without leaking memory or database connections.

Implement a DAO with methods for create find update and delete. Typical signatures include save findById findAll update and deleteById. Use transactions per operation and prefer a single transaction per logical unit of work so the database state remains predictable.

Run simple integration tests that bootstrap the persistence unit perform CRUD operations and assert expected results. Use an in memory database during development to get fast feedback and avoid dealing with production schema surprises while learning.

The example shows how configuration mapping and DAO code pieces connect to provide a maintainable persistence layer. The goal is clean separation between domain models and persistence mechanics so future changes to database vendor or schema cause minimal churn.

Summary the walkthrough covers dependency setup entity creation factory bootstrap DAO methods and verification steps needed to implement CRUD with Hibernate 5.4 and JPA 2.2 in a practical Java application.

Tip

Prefer EntityManager for standard JPA portability and use native Hibernate APIs only when needing vendor specific features. Keep transactions small and use integration tests with an in memory database for fast reliable feedback during development.

title: WildFly vs JBoss EAP How Red Hat Java servers compare
description: Compare WildFly and JBoss EAP differences performance support and use cases for Red Hat Java application servers
heading: WildFly vs JBoss EAP How Red Hat Java servers compare
body:
Short answer for people who like clarity and caffeine

If you want speed, new features and zero hand holding pick WildFly. If you want certified builds, predictable patching and a support team that answers emails pick JBoss EAP. Both are Red Hat backed Java application servers that implement Jakarta EE standards and both can deliver enterprise grade performance when configured properly.

Audience and support model

WildFly is community driven and focused on developer agility and fast releases. It is open source and ideal for microservices prototypes and teams that enjoy upgrading often. JBoss EAP is the commercial sibling with long term support, formal certification and subscription based access to Red Hat patches and compliance testing. In short WildFly is where you experiment and learn. JBoss EAP is where you sleep better at night.

Who should pick which

  • Choose WildFly for rapid development cycles, feature experimentation and smaller teams that can handle upgrades.
  • Choose JBoss EAP for regulated environments, mission critical systems and teams that need vendor backed SLAs and certified stacks.

Performance and feature timelines

Both servers implement Jakarta EE and share clustering, management and security capabilities. Expect WildFly to ship new features sooner and to move faster across minor releases. Expect JBoss EAP to backport stability improvements, offer tuned defaults and provide a predictable support window for performance maintenance. Performance overlap is large so benchmark the real world workload not a synthetic hello world test.

Licensing updates and support access

WildFly stays free and open source. JBoss EAP requires a subscription for commercial support and certified builds. That subscription gives you access to the Red Hat customer portal, tested patches and formal compliance artifacts. If you need guaranteed remediation timelines and vendor accountability the subscription is often worth the cost.

Migration strategy and a practical checklist

Develop on WildFly for speed then validate on JBoss EAP before a large scale rollout. The configuration modules and deployment descriptors are similar enough that most apps need minimal rewrites. Still expect small incompatibilities around supported versions of libraries and security policies.

  • Run integration tests on the EAP distribution early.
  • Validate clustering and session failover under load.
  • Check vendor documentation for any certified third party libraries in use.
  • Plan for patch windows and lifecycle support if you pick EAP for production.

Tip for production testing

Run a parallel test environment on the supported EAP distribution to catch API differences and security policy gaps early. Treat this like a dress rehearsal with less drama and more logging.

Bottom line WildFly for innovation and developer speed. JBoss EAP for enterprise stability and formal support. Both speak Jakarta EE and both can be tuned to meet performance needs. Pick based on risk tolerance and how much you enjoy paperwork.
seo_title: WildFly or JBoss EAP Which Red Hat Java server fits you
seo_heading: Choosing between WildFly and JBoss EAP for Java and Jakarta EE apps

title: How to Edit Ubuntu's etc Hosts File by Example
description: Step by step guide to safely edit Ubuntu hosts file for local DNS mapping using terminal editors sudo and simple testing commands
heading: How to Edit Ubuntu's etc Hosts File by Example
body:
If you want to point example.local to your laptop instead of the internet because the real world is noisy and DNS is opinionated this short guide shows how to edit the Ubuntu hosts file safely and quickly. We will use sudo and nano as the obvious tools of choice and cover backup, editing, saving, and forcing Ubuntu to notice the change.

Why bother with the hosts file

The hosts file beats DNS when you need a fast, local override for testing, blocking or redirecting domains. It sits at /etc/hosts and maps IP addresses to hostnames for processes that check the local file before asking DNS. It is simple and powerful and occasionally a cause of mild panic when you typo an IP.

Step 1 back up the file

Accidental deletion is a fast route to regret. Make a copy so you can undo with dignity.

sudo cp /etc/hosts /etc/hosts.bak

Step 2 pick an editor and open the file

Nano is friendly and requires less mysticism than vim when you are sleep deprived. Use sudo because /etc/hosts is protected.

sudo nano /etc/hosts

Step 3 the correct format for entries

Each mapping goes on its own line. The format is IP_address followed by one or more hostnames separated by spaces. No punctuation, just plain text.

127.0.0.1 example.local
192.168.1.50 devserver.local myapp.test

A few tips

  • Use unique local names to avoid clashing with real domains
  • Do not duplicate the same hostname on separate lines or weirdness may follow
  • Loopback entries use 127.0.0.1 or ::1 for IPv6 when you need it

Step 4 save and exit

In nano press Control O to write the file then Control X to quit. If you use vim the usual wq applies. You need to save with sudo so that your changes persist.

Step 5 make Ubuntu notice the change

Most apps will see the change right away. If you are using systemd name resolution or a DNS cache you may need to flush caches or restart the network manager.

sudo systemd-resolve --flush-caches
sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager

Step 6 verify the mapping

Check that the hostname resolves to your intended IP with a quick ping or with a browser for HTTP testing.

ping -c 1 example.local

If ping shows the IP you added then congratulations the hosts file won. If not check for typos, duplicate lines, or a local proxy or DNS service that ignores the hosts file.

Troubleshooting notes

  • If an app uses its own DNS stack it might bypass /etc/hosts
  • Browsers sometimes cache DNS results so a restart of the browser helps
  • Systemd resolved uses split DNS in some setups so double check your network configuration

Quick summary

Back up /etc/hosts then edit it with sudo nano or your preferred editor. Add IP hostname pairs on their own lines, save, flush caches if needed and verify with ping or a browser. This tiny file is a handy tool for local dev, testing or blocking domains and it will not bite you as long as you keep a backup.

Tip for the daring use made up domains that are unlikely to collide with real sites and avoid editing production machines unless you like surprises.
seo_title: Fix local DNS on Ubuntu with a simple hosts file edit today
seo_heading: Edit /etc/hosts on Ubuntu for local testing and DNS overrides

title: How to install GitLab on Ubuntu 20 without errors
description: Step by step guide to add the GitLab apt repo fix the unable to locate package issue and install GitLab on Ubuntu 20
heading: How to install GitLab on Ubuntu 20 without errors
body:
This guide shows how to add the official GitLab apt repository fix the unable to locate package problem and install GitLab on Ubuntu 20 in a reliable way

  1. Prepare the system and install dependencies
  2. Add the GitLab repository and key
  3. Update package lists
  4. Install the chosen GitLab package
  5. Set external address and run configuration

Prepare the system Install curl required certificates and the GPG tool to authenticate packages before touching the repository.

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y curl ca-certificates gnupg

Add the GitLab repository Use the official install script to add the correct repositories for Ubuntu 20 and fetch the signing key. This avoids the usual error that signals missing sources.

curl httpspackages.gitlab.com/install/repositories/gitlab/gitlab-ce/script.deb.sh | sudo bash

Update package lists Run the package list refresh so apt knows about the new GitLab packages and their metadata.

sudo apt update

Install GitLab Choose one package name not both. For most users the community edition is fine. If a package still cannot be found check the repository file under /etc/apt and confirm the distribution codename is focal.

sudo apt install -y gitlab-ce

Configure GitLab Set the external address inside the configuration file then run the omnibus configuration to bootstrap services. This step prepares web and background services and can be noisy in a good way.

Open /etc/gitlab/gitlab.rb edit external_url to match the server address then run sudo gitlab-ctl reconfigure

The unable to locate package error usually means the GitLab repo was not added updated or the wrong distro codename was used. Adding the official repository running apt update and installing a single package name resolves most failures while leaving room for quiet celebration

Tip

If a package still looks missing run apt policy gitlab-ce to see available versions and which repository is providing the package. Avoid asking apt to install both gitlab ce and gitlab ee at the same time

title: How to create GitLab projects How to delete GitLab projects
description: Quick guide to create and delete GitLab projects using the web interface with safety steps and access control advice.
heading: How to create and delete GitLab projects
body:
Welcome to the thrilling world of GitLab project management where clicking the wrong button can turn months of work into a cautionary tale. This guide walks you through creating a project that is sane and deleting one without starting a company ritual to mourn lost repos. Follow these steps and your teammates will stop sending frantic messages at 2 AM.

Create a GitLab project the right way

Creating a project is 10 percent clicking and 90 percent thinking before you click. Here is a compact sequence that keeps your repo useful and your managers less stressed.

  1. Sign in

    Log into the GitLab web interface with an account that has create project permission. Use a work account for company repos and a personal account for experiments.

  2. Create new project

    Click New Project then choose a blank project or import an existing repository. Give the project a clear name and an optional description that a future you will thank you for.

  3. Pick a namespace

    Choose the right namespace to keep projects organized by team or personal use. This keeps access and billing from becoming mysterious chaos.

  4. Initialize the repository and set visibility

    Add a README to seed the repo and pick public or private visibility based on sensitivity. When in doubt pick private and only make it public when you actually want strangers reading your code.

  5. Push your initial code

    Follow the git commands shown in the GitLab UI to add a remote and push your local work. Typical steps are git init then git add and git commit then git remote add origin and git push. Keep credentials ready and do not paste passwords in chat.

  6. Manage members and permissions

    Invite team members and assign roles like Guest Reporter Developer Maintainer or Owner. Review access after adding people to avoid accidental broad permissions. Less is more when it comes to write access.

Keep the project tidy and safe

  • Use branches and merge requests to protect main branches and keep history useful.
  • Enable protected branches where needed to prevent accidental overwrites.
  • Set up CI pipelines if you want builds that catch problems before humans do.

How to delete a GitLab project without panic

Deletion is permanent unless you have backups. Treat it like surgery with a checklist. Do not improvise.

  1. Export before you remove

    Enable project export to get a full copy of the repository and issues. Exports are the safety net that avoids the heroic but futile data recovery stories.

  2. Back up important artifacts

    Clone the repo to a local machine and export issues if you need them. Save attachments and wiki pages somewhere reliable outside of GitLab.

  3. Use the web UI to delete

    Open Project Settings then General then scroll to the Advanced section. Click Remove project and follow the confirmation prompts. You will be asked to type the project path or name to confirm. This is intentional friction to keep you from deleting things by accident.

  4. Verify and clean up

    After removal check group settings and CI hooks to tidy references to the deleted project. If you exported previously you can store the export in a safe archive or restore it to a new project if needed.

Quick checklist before deletion

  • Export project
  • Clone repo locally
  • Archive issues and attachments
  • Notify stakeholders

Creating and deleting GitLab projects does not need to be dramatic. With the right defaults and a tiny bit of caution you can keep your version control tidy and your team from inventing new swear words. Now go forth and manage repositories like the responsible devops wizard you secretly are.
seo_title: Launch and remove GitLab projects without facepalm errors
seo_heading: Step by step GitLab project setup and safe deletion for teams

title: GitLab commit push to origin example
description: Step by step GitLab example for committing and pushing to origin with clear commands and common gotchas for new Git users
heading: GitLab commit push to origin example
body:
If you want to move changes from your laptop to GitLab without causing a small time paradox for your team, this guide will help. No ceremony, no magic, just the git commands you actually need and a few survival tips for the developer workflow.

Quick steps to commit and push

Short version for people who like things that work. Make edits, stage what matters, commit with a clear message, then push to the remote called origin. Use git status often to avoid surprise chaos.

  1. Edit files in your working directory with your favorite editor.
  2. Stage the files you want in the next commit. For a quick add use:
git add .
  1. Create a commit with a concise message that future you will thank yourself for:
git commit -m 'Describe the change'
  1. Push the commit to the remote named origin on your branch. Replace branchname with your current branch.
git push origin branchname

Verify the update on GitLab

Open the project page on GitLab and check the commits list or the repository tree. If your commit is missing, run these checks locally first.

  • Check current branch and staged files with git status
  • Confirm your remotes with git remote -v
  • Make sure you pushed the right branch and not some lonely experimental branch

Common gotchas and how to not be that person

People forget to stage files, accidentally omit the dot in the add command, or push on the wrong branch. Authentication problems also pop up when you change machines or tokens expire. These are small mistakes with dramatic social consequences.

  • Forgot to stage a file. Run git status then git add <file>.
  • Used the wrong branch. Use git branch to confirm then switch with git checkout branchname or git switch branchname.
  • Remote not configured as expected. Use git remote -v to inspect the origin URL.
  • Authentication prompt appears. Check your SSH keys or personal access tokens in GitLab settings.

Best practices that cost almost nothing

Run git status before committing. Write clear commit messages. Stage only what you mean to change. These tiny habits prevent the classic blame game and save hours of awkward explanations during stand ups.

Recap of the flow for the terminal friendly mind

  • Edit files
  • git add .
  • git commit -m 'Describe the change'
  • git push origin branchname
  • Verify on GitLab

There you have it. A compact git tutorial for committing and pushing to origin on GitLab that keeps your repository sane and your coworkers forgiving. If things go sideways, breathe, run the checks above, and then blame your terminal.
seo_title: Push GitLab commits to origin and avoid embarrassing mistakes today
seo_heading: A practical git tutorial for committing and pushing to origin on GitLab

title: Delete folder in Ubuntu example How to remove a directory
description: Learn how to remove a directory recursively in Ubuntu using rm and safer methods including sudo and trash cli for safer deletion in the terminal
heading: Delete folder in Ubuntu example How to remove a directory
body:
So you want to delete a folder on Ubuntu and not immediately regret your life choices. Good plan. This guide walks through removing a directory from the Linux command line with the trusty rm command and safer alternatives like trash-cli. Expect some sarcasm and useful commands that will not lie to you.

Verify the target directory before you proceed

Stop. Take a breath. Confirm where you are and what you are about to destroy. A single typo turns a minor cleanup into a mystery of missing files.

  • Show the current path with pwd
  • List contents with details using ls -la
  • Get a full view of nested files with ls -R foldername

Run recursive remove with the rm command

The rm command is blunt and efficient. Use it when you mean business. If you want to remove a directory and everything inside it use recursive mode.

rm -r foldername

If you add -f you force deletion and silence prompts. This is useful when you really know what you are doing or when you enjoy panic later.

rm -rf foldername

If you prefer hints and hand holding try interactive mode which asks before each deletion.

rm -ri foldername

Use sudo when permissions get sassy

Permission denied messages are not insults they are instructions. If the folder belongs to root you can escalate. Double check the path first because root does not care about your feelings.

sudo rm -r foldername

Prefer the safe trash method with trash-cli on Ubuntu

If you are not feeling murderous install a trash tool that behaves like a recycle bin on Linux. This is the one that gives you a second chance.

sudo apt update
sudo apt install trash-cli
trash-put foldername

You can later restore files or empty the trash when you are certain you really mean it.

Quick backup before you leap

If backups make you feel sane run a quick copy. It is fast and cheap compared to data regret.

cp -r foldername foldername_backup

Checklist to avoid accidental deletion

  • Confirm path with pwd and ls -la
  • Review contents with ls -R foldername
  • Make a quick backup with cp -r if unsure
  • Use rm -ri for interactive safety
  • Install trash-cli and use trash-put if you want a safety net
  • Only use sudo rm -rf when you are calm and certain

There you go. You now know how to remove a directory recursively on Ubuntu from the terminal and you have safer options if your finger slips. Delete with confidence and a tiny bit of caution.
seo_title: Safely delete folders in Ubuntu with rm and trash-cli tips
seo_heading: Terminal guide to removing directories recursively on Ubuntu without regret

title: Essential Git GitLab commands The 8 you must know
description: Quick guide to the eight essential GitLab command line commands every developer should master with clear examples and practical tips
heading: Essential Git GitLab commands The 8 you must know
body:
If you write code you will wrestle with Git and GitLab. This guide gives the eight commands that stop your daily workflow from turning into a caffeine fueled panic. No fluff just the actual commands you will use when your living room laptop becomes mission control.

Why these eight commands matter

Version control is not optional. These commands keep your work local safe and let you share changes without triggering a merge party that looks like a disaster recovery drill. Learn them and you will avoid a lot of awkward code review explanations.

The eight commands to know

Think of these as your toolkit. Use them in small steps and test often.

  • git clone REPO_URL Copy a remote repository to your machine. Use a placeholder REPO_URL when you cannot paste the real address.
  • git status See what is staged and what is not. Run this before you do anything dramatic.
  • git add FILES Stage only the files you mean to include in the next commit. Do not drag every typo into history.
  • git commit -m 'message' Record staged changes with a concise message. Future you will judge past you harshly.
  • git push Send your commits to the remote so CI and teammates can pretend to review your work.
  • git pull Fetch and merge remote changes into your branch. Use this often to avoid conflicts that require therapy.
  • git branch List or create branches. Use descriptive names so your feature story is obvious without detective work.
  • git checkout BRANCH Switch context to another branch. Newer Git also lets you use git switch if you prefer clearer verbs.

Also know how to merge and resolve conflicts

git merge BRANCH brings another branch into your current one. If a conflict shows up, resolve it carefully and run tests before you push. Conflicts are not bugs they are negotiations between photons and ego.

Typical quick workflow

Here is a small routine to follow on a feature branch. It assumes a rudimentary GitLab workflow where you push branches for merge requests.

  • Clone the repo with git clone REPO_URL if you do not have it yet
  • Create a branch with git branch feature/name or git checkout -b feature/name
  • Work locally and check progress with git status
  • Stage changes with git add and commit with git commit -m 'short useful message'
  • Pull remote updates often with git pull and resolve conflicts
  • Push when ready with git push -u origin feature/name and open a merge request in GitLab

Best practices that save time

  • Commit logically and often so each change is reviewable
  • Use meaningful branch names that reveal intent
  • Run tests locally before pushing to avoid annoying CI failures
  • Pull before you push to reduce surprise conflicts

Wrap up

These eight Git and GitLab commands cover most of what developers need for day to day version control and code management. Learn them, use them, and your future self will send you a thank you email that is also mildly passive aggressive.
seo_title: Master these 8 Git and GitLab commands for daily dev work
seo_heading: Practical Git and GitLab command line workflow tips for feature branches

title: How to Write a Git Commit Messages Properly with Examples
description: Clear rules and examples for writing concise Git commit messages that help code review and history reading
heading: How to Write a Git Commit Messages Properly with Examples
body:
This tutorial teaches how to write clear concise Git commit messages that help code review and historical traceability.

  1. Write a short imperative subject line under 50 characters
  2. Separate subject and body with a blank line
  3. Describe why a change was made not only what changed
  4. Wrap body text around 72 characters and use bullets for details
  5. Reference issue numbers and note breaking changes
  6. Keep commits focused and atomic

Short subject line The subject line is the elevator pitch. Use present tense verbs such as Add Fix Update Remove. Example git commit -m "Add user login handler" shows the expected tone and clarity.

Separate subject and body A blank line after the subject keeps message viewers and tools happy. The subject remains a glanceable summary while the body holds the story.

Explain the why Reviewers care about motivation more than a literal diff. A sentence or two explaining why the change was needed prevents future confusion and blame games.

Wrap and structure Wrap body lines near 72 characters so history tools display nicely. Use short bullet lines when listing related changes or consequences.

Reference tracking systems Add a ticket or issue reference when relevant. Use a short phrase like Closes 123 to make automation happy and reduce manual follow up.

Small focused commits One concern per commit makes bisecting and reverting painless. Massive commits filled with unrelated fixes create regret and long nights.

Applying these steps will produce commit messages that help teammates review and future maintainers understand the code history. Consistent style reduces friction during code review and makes automated tools more useful.

Tip

Use a commit message template or a pre commit hook to enforce subject length and require a body when a change touches multiple files. That prevents the tragic one liner that haunts repositories.

title: GitLab branch and branch permissions example
description: Learn how to create protected branches and configure branch permissions in GitLab to control who can push and merge.
heading: GitLab branch and branch permissions example
body:
If your repository had a frequent flyer program for hotfixes that break production you need protected branches. GitLab protected branches and branch permissions let you control who can push and who can merge so your main line of development does not turn into a game of code roulette. This guide walks through a practical setup that keeps humans honest and CI useful.

Create and push a feature branch

Start local, name things clearly, push to the remote and breathe easy for five minutes. Clean branch names help your future self and your team avoid arguments about whether the change was made by dino-fix or feature/awesome.

git checkout -b feature/awesome
git push -u origin feature/awesome

Protect the branch in project settings

Open your project settings and go to the repository section. Add the branch under protected branches so direct pushes can be blocked and only allowed roles can perform merges. Protecting the main branch prevents accidental chaos and gives you an audit trail when someone blames the CI for human error.

Configure push and merge roles

Decide who gets to push and who gets to merge. A sensible starting point is to let Maintainers push to protected branches and let Developers open merge requests. For stricter shops allow only Maintainers to push and require approvals before merges. This is where branch permissions and access control in GitLab earn their keep.

  • Allow Maintainers to push if you trust them to carry the keys
  • Allow Developers to create merge requests so work can be reviewed
  • Add approval rules so merges need at least one or two reviewers
  • Require a successful pipeline before merging to enforce CI checks

Test access using different user roles

Before you go full lockup mode run a few experiments with test accounts. Use one account with Developer access and another with Guest access. Try a push and watch permission denied messages appear like tiny red flags. This confirms the rules behave as expected before actual work depends on them.

# as a Developer
git push origin feature/awesome

# if push is blocked you will see permission denied or similar messages

Use merge requests and required approvals

Merge requests are not optional if you want traceability. Require at least one approval, enable approval rules for specific paths or teams, and require the pipeline to pass. This gives you code review, automated tests, and some small hope that production will behave tomorrow.

Approval rules and CI

Approval rules let you demand reviews from particular people or groups for sensitive files. Requiring a successful CI pipeline before merge ensures the build is green and your tests do not explode on the release branch.

Tips and common gotchas

  • Branch naming matters. Use prefixes like feature slash bugfix slash hotfix so rules can be applied predictably.
  • Protected branches can still be created if someone pushes a new branch that matches an allow pattern. Review your patterns carefully.
  • Test your permissions with throwaway accounts before enforcing them on the whole team.
  • Document who can bypass rules and why. If someone can bypass protections it should be a rare and logged event.

Follow these steps and you get a repository that behaves more like a well run kitchen and less like a barbecue during a hurricane. GitLab branch permissions, protected branches, merge requests, and CI working together give you access control and auditability without needing constant babysitting.
seo_title: Stop accidental chaos in GitLab with protected branch rules
seo_heading: How to lock down branches and require approvals in GitLab for CI safety

title: Create a new GitLab branch in BASH example
description: Learn how to create and push a new GitLab branch from BASH using git commands and simple automation steps for a clean developer workflow
heading: Create a new GitLab branch in BASH example
body:
This tutorial shows how to create a new GitLab branch from BASH using standard git commands so a developer can automate branch creation and push a local branch to a remote project.

  1. Prepare environment and authentication
  2. Create a local branch
  3. Push the branch to GitLab and set upstream
  4. Verify branch presence on the remote

Prepare environment and authentication by confirming a valid SSH key or HTTPS credentials are configured for the GitLab project. Store any personal access token in a secure place such as a protected environment variable and avoid pasting tokens into public logs.

Create a local branch with a descriptive name that follows team conventions. Use a command like git checkout -b feature/my-new-feature when starting a new task. Branch naming prevents confusion during reviews and merges.

Push the branch to GitLab and set the upstream branch so future pushes are shorter. Use a command such as git push --set-upstream origin feature/my-new-feature to create the remote branch and link local tracking. This saves time when running plain git push later on.

Verify branch presence on the remote by listing remote branches with git fetch followed by git branch -r or by checking the project web interface. A quick check avoids surprise merge conflicts and wasted review cycles.

Automation can be added by wrapping commands in a short BASH script that validates branch name format checks for uncommitted changes and runs the push sequence. That script brings consistency and less manual fiddling when multiple developers work on the same project.

The walkthrough covered preparing credentials creating a local branch pushing that branch to the remote and verifying presence on GitLab. Use the pattern shown to reduce mistakes and speed up developer workflows while keeping a small amount of discipline around branch names and authentication.

Tip

Use git status --porcelain in a script to detect uncommitted changes before branch creation and refuse to proceed when the working tree is dirty. That prevents accidental inclusion of unrelated changes.

title: GitLab merge request example
description: Quick guide to creating reviewing and merging a GitLab merge request with commands and best practices for a clean workflow
heading: GitLab merge request example step by step guide
body:
If merge requests were a social event they would be the office party where CI is the bouncer and code review is that one relative who asks too many questions. This guide walks you through a clean GitLab merge request workflow that keeps history tidy and CI happy. No magic tricks, just sensible steps that human teams can follow without therapy.

Create a feature branch

Start from a stable main branch so you are not building on someone elses fires. Use a clear branch name that tells people what you were thinking when you woke up and decided to code.

git checkout main
git pull
git checkout -b feature/short-descriptive-name

Good branch names save a lot of comments that begin with Why. Bad branch names cause psychic pain and extra meetings.

Make focused commits and push

Keep each commit focused on a single change. Clear messages beat cryptic emoji logs. When you are ready push and let GitLab run its tests.

git add .
git commit -m "Implement widget validation"
git push -u origin feature/short-descriptive-name

Pushing will trigger the pipeline. If tests fail fix them first. Deploying broken code and telling the team it is fine is not a strategy.

Open the merge request

In GitLab create a merge request from your feature branch to the target branch. Give the MR a concise title and a helpful description that explains the why not just the what. Link the related issue to save reviewers from guessing games.

What to include in the MR

  • A short summary of the change
  • Link to the issue and any relevant tickets
  • Notes about migration steps or config changes
  • Any screenshots or logs if UI or tests were affected

Run CI and get the review

Let CI run to completion before piling on review requests. If the pipeline is red fix it first. Reviewers are more effective when the build is green and the diff is readable.

  • Request reviewers who actually own the code
  • Use inline suggestions where GitLab supports them
  • Keep discussions threaded so feedback does not vanish into chat

Small MRs get better review attention. If your change is huge split it into smaller logical pieces.

Merge and clean up

After approvals and a green pipeline use the Merge button. Prefer squash merging when you want one logical change in history. Protect important branches so broken pipelines cannot be merged by accident.

git branch -d feature/short-descriptive-name
git push origin --delete feature/short-descriptive-name

Deleting the branch keeps the repo tidy and makes future explorers less sad.

Quick commands recap

  • Create branch and work locally with git checkout -b
  • Push to trigger CI with git push -u origin branch
  • Delete local and remote branch after merge

Practical tips for a sane team workflow

  • Keep MRs small and focused for faster reviews
  • Make sure CI is fast enough to be useful
  • Use protected branches to enforce quality gates
  • Document guidelines for rebasing and merge strategies
  • Treat pipelines as part of the review not an afterthought

Follow these steps and your GitLab merge requests will stop being a source of dread and start being a source of mildly satisfying progress. It is not glamorous but it works and your future self will thank you. Now go make that MR and resist the urge to call it final until it actually is.
seo_title: Practical GitLab merge request workflow for CI and code review
seo_heading: Step by step GitLab MR guide to branch management and CI friendly merges

title: merge develop into master in GitLab example
description: Merge develop into master using GitLab merge requests with CI checks reviews conflict resolution and release tagging
heading: merge develop into master in GitLab example
body:
This tutorial shows a quick practical workflow to merge a develop branch into master using GitLab merge requests and common command line steps.

  1. Create a merge request from develop into master
  2. Run and check CI pipelines
  3. Request review and obtain approvals
  4. Resolve any merge conflicts
  5. Perform the merge in GitLab or locally
  6. Tag master and push a release

Create a merge request using the GitLab web UI. Choose develop as source and master as target. Add a clear title and a short description of the changes so reviewers do not fall asleep.

Check CI pipelines that run on the merge request. Wait for green status before merging. Use job logs to diagnose failures and re-run failing jobs when needed.

Assign reviewers and request approvals. Keep review comments focused on behavior and tests. Small focused reviews get merged faster and cause fewer arguments.

If merge conflicts occur fetch the latest master and resolve locally by rebasing or merging. Example commands look like git fetch origin git checkout develop git rebase origin/master or git merge origin/master followed by conflict resolution and git push.

Use the merge button in GitLab to perform a fast forward or a merge commit depending on project policy. Alternatively create the merge locally and push the merge commit with commands such as git checkout master git merge develop git push origin master.

Create a release tag on master to mark the new state. Use a tag command like git tag -a v1.2.3 -m 'release' and push with git push origin v1.2.3 or use the GitLab release UI for a nicer page.

This guide walked through creating a merge request from develop into master running CI getting reviews resolving conflicts and merging via the UI or command line then tagging master for release. Following this workflow helps keep master stable and reduces surprise bugs during deployment.

Tip

Enable required approvals and pipeline status checks on protected branches so merges only happen after tests pass and at least one reviewer signs off. Consider using merge trains or pipelines for merge requests to prevent broken builds reaching master.

title: A GitLab merge branch to master example
description: Step by step guide to merging a GitLab branch into master with commands merge request workflow and CI tips
heading: A GitLab merge branch to master example
body:
If you want to merge a feature branch into master on GitLab without crying into your keyboard this guide walks you through a sane workflow. You will prepare the branch, push it, open a merge request, fix CI failures, merge when green and tidy up the branch. Yes this is the boring part of software engineering that keeps the rest of your code working.

Prepare your branch locally

Keep the feature branch up to date with master and run tests before you push anything. This saves time and preserves your dignity. Use clear commit messages and squash if your repo likes a tidy history.

  • Create or switch to your feature branch
  • Run unit tests and linters locally
  • Commit with a helpful message and squash if needed
git checkout -b feature-branch
# make changes
git add .
git commit -m 'Add feature and tests'

Push the branch and open a merge request

Push the branch so GitLab can see your handiwork. Then open a merge request via the GitLab UI and pick master as the target branch. Assign reviewers and explain what changed and why in plain English. If you reference an issue include the issue number in the MR description so humans and bots can be pleased.

git push origin feature-branch

Tips for the MR description

  • State the problem you solved
  • List any database migrations or config changes
  • Include screenshots if the change touches UI

Run CI and fix failures

GitLab will run the pipeline once the MR exists. When a job fails do not guess. Open the job log, find the failing test or linter, fix it and push again. Repeat until the pipeline is green and the reviewers stop asking for bikeshed changes.

# inspect failing job logs in GitLab
# make fixes locally
git add .
git commit -m 'Fix tests and linter failures'
git push origin feature-branch

Merge into master

When approvals are in place and the pipeline is green use GitLab merge button and choose the repository preferred method. Common options include merge commit, squash merge or fast forward. If your team requires a local merge you can do that as well.

# local merge if needed
git checkout master
git pull origin master
git merge feature-branch
git push origin master

Pick the method your team agrees on. Squash merges create a single clean commit. Merge commits preserve history. Fast forward keeps history linear but may require the branch to be up to date first.

Cleanup and final touches

Once merged delete the remote branch to avoid clutter. Remove the local branch from your machine and optionally tag the release or archive the change if that is part of your workflow. Celebrate briefly then get back to writing code that will need another merge request later.

git push origin --delete feature-branch
git branch -d feature-branch

This workflow covers the usual steps to merge a feature branch into master on GitLab while keeping CI and reviewers happy. Follow the steps, run tests early, and try not to let the merge request become a saga.

seo_heading: Step by step GitLab merge request workflow for branches and CI success

title: GitLab merge master to branch example
