title: How to rename a GitHub repository in Git
description: Step by step guide to rename a GitHub repository and update local clones and remotes so pushes and pulls keep working.
heading: How to rename a GitHub repository in Git
body:
This tutorial shows how to rename a GitHub repository and update the local repository so the new name is used for future pushes and pulls.

  1. Rename the repository on GitHub
  2. Check redirection and locate the new clone URL
  3. Update the local remote URL
  4. Verify and update other clones and services

Rename the repository on GitHub by visiting the repository settings and changing the name field. GitHub will update the repository name while keeping a redirect from the old address for most requests.

Check redirection by viewing the repository page after the rename and by copying the clone URL shown on GitHub. Use the HTTPS or SSH clone option on the GitHub page and paste the value into the next command placeholder.

Update the local remote URL in each clone. Run git remote -v to see current remotes. Then run git remote set-url origin < new-remote-url> where the placeholder is the clone URL copied from the GitHub page. This command tells the local repository where to push and pull from now.

Verify the change with git remote -v again and perform a quick fetch with git fetch origin to confirm permissions and connectivity. Update any other clones on other machines the same way.

Remember to update external references such as continuous integration settings, webhooks, and documentation to point to the new repository name. GitHub redirects help for a period but external services are better served by direct links to the new name.

The steps covered a rename on the GitHub website followed by updating the local remote URL and verifying connectivity and external references. Follow these steps to avoid broken pipelines and confused collaborators and enjoy the tiny thrill of a cleaner repository name.

Tip

When copying the new clone URL paste the exact value into the set URL command to avoid typos. Consider running a test push from a throwaway branch to confirm permissions before relying on production pipelines.

title: How to Revert a Git Commit
description: Learn how to undo Git commits safely with revert reset and reflog examples and commands for shared and local branches
heading: How to Revert a Git Commit Guide
body:
Pick the right tool

Git gives you several ways to undo a commit. Some of them are polite and traceable. Some of them are blunt instruments that will make history look different and possibly anger your teammates. This short guide explains when to use git revert, git reset, and git reflog so you can undo commit mistakes without causing a merge conflict apocalypse.

Undo safely with git revert

If the branch is shared or public use git revert. It creates a new commit that undoes a previous commit while keeping the history intact. That means future humans can see what happened without guessing or blaming the nearest junior dev.

git revert <commit-hash>

Tips

  • Use a clear message so the why is obvious to whoever inherits your chaos.
  • If the commit touched many files you might need to fix conflicts during the revert.

Local cleanup with git reset

Want to rewrite local history because you are alone on the branch or you really know what you are doing Use git reset. There are two main flavors that matter here.

Soft reset when you want changes staged

git reset --soft HEAD~1

This moves the branch pointer back one commit but keeps your changes staged. Useful when the commit message sucked or you want to combine commits with a nicer message.

Hard reset when you mean it

git reset --hard HEAD~1

This will discard working tree changes and staged files. If that sounds terrifying it should. Make sure you really do not need the files before you run it.

Rescue mission with git reflog

If you accidentally nuked a commit with reset or a bad rebase then git reflog is your emergency hotline. Reflog records where HEAD has been so you can find the lost commit hash and bring it back from the void.

git reflog
# find the commit hash then
git checkout -b recover <commit-hash>
# or
git reset --hard <commit-hash>

Reflog is not permanent forever but it is usually enough to recover after a mistake that made you breathe loudly into a paper bag.

Sharing and pushing without grief

If you rewrote history on a branch that other people use coordinate before pushing. Prefer git push --force-with-lease over a blind force push. It reduces the chance you overwrite someone else s work but it does not make you morally blameless.

git push --force-with-lease origin your-branch

Rules of thumb

  • Use revert on public branches to keep version control honest.
  • Use reset for local tidy up when you are the only one affected.
  • Use reflog as the safety net after a dramatic mistake.

Recap and quick cheatsheet

Here are the git commands you will look up after you panic

  • git revert <commit> Creates a new commit that undoes the target commit. Good for shared branches and predictable history.
  • git reset --soft HEAD~1 Move the branch back but keep changes staged for rework.
  • git reset --hard HEAD~1 Destroy working tree changes. Use with extreme caution.
  • git reflog See recent HEAD positions and recover lost commits.
  • git push --force-with-lease Force push with a safety check when rewriting remote history.

Follow those simple rules and you will be a lot less likely to explain to your team why the repo timeline now looks like a crime drama. This mini tutorial is a practical git tutorial for undoing commits while keeping branch management sane and your coworkers only mildly annoyed.
seo_title: Undo a Git Commit Like a Grown Up Without Breaking History
seo_heading: Safe and risky ways to undo commits on public and private branches

title: git undo commits example
description: Practical guide to undo commits in Git using reset revert and reflog with safety notes and recovery tips for shared branches.
heading: git undo commits example guide
body:
If you broke the repo and blamed CI you are in good company. This guide walks through how to undo commits in git without turning your branch into a crime scene. We cover inspecting history, soft reset and hard reset, reverting pushed commits, recovering lost work with reflog, and when not to be a hero.

Inspect history first

Before you start swinging git reset around like a lightsaber run this command to see what you are about to mess with

git log --oneline

Find the commit hash you care about and breathe. Knowing the hash is half the battle and far less embarrassing than guessing.

Undo last commit but keep changes staged

Use soft reset when the commit message was tragic or you forgot a file. This moves HEAD back but leaves your index and working tree alone so you can fix things and recommit.

git reset --soft HEAD~1
# fix files or amend commit
git commit --amend

Good for cleaning up small mistakes on a branch that has not been shared yet.

Undo last commit and discard changes

When the previous commit is garbage and you want it gone from your working tree use a hard reset. Warning do not do this on a branch that other people use unless you enjoy awkward Slack messages.

git reset --hard HEAD~1

This rewrites history and updates your working tree to match the target commit.

Undo a commit that has already been pushed

For public history prefer a safe approach. Use git revert to create a new commit that undoes the changes. This keeps history intact and your teammates less annoyed.

git revert 
git push

If you are on a solo branch and must rewrite history you can reset then force push. Be prepared for consequences when other people have pulled the old commits.

git reset --hard 
git push --force

Recover a lost commit with reflog

Git keeps a log of where HEAD has been. If you accidentally nuked a commit you can often find it with reflog and bring it back.

git reflog
# find the lost commit hash
git reset --hard 
# or cherry pick the commit back onto your branch
git cherry-pick

Reflog is the safety net you forgot you had until you needed it.

Quick checklist for not breaking things

  • Prefer git revert on shared branches to avoid forced pain
  • Use git reset --soft when you just need to edit a commit
  • Use git reset --hard only when you know no one else depends on the history
  • Use git reflog to recover lost commits before you start panicking
  • Tell your team if you ever force push so they can reset their local branches

Undoing commits in git is not mystical. Inspect history first then pick the appropriate tool for the job. When in doubt play it safe and revert. When you are reckless and alone reset and force push. Either way do not forget to brew coffee and apologize if people notice the chaos.

title: Git clean up strategies
description: Practical Git clean up strategies to remove untracked files prune branches and optimize repository history for a cleaner workflow
heading: Git clean up strategies for tidy repositories
body:
This article teaches practical Git clean up strategies to remove unwanted files revive branches and keep history tidy.

  1. Inspect and stash changes
  2. Remove untracked files safely
  3. Clean up branches
  4. Rework local commits
  5. Compress repository and prune objects

Start with a quick inspection using git status and git diff to see the working tree. Use git stash push -m 'WIP' when changes should be set aside before any destructive action.

To remove untracked files run a dry run first with git clean -n -d then execute git clean -f -d when happy. The dry run shows what would be deleted so surprises are less likely.

Prune local branches that are merged into main with git branch --merged main then delete stale branches with git branch -d branch-name or force remove with git branch -D branch-name if the branch has diverged and deletion is intentional.

Rewrite local commit history carefully. Use git rebase -i HEAD~N to squash or reorder commits. Create a backup branch first with git branch backup to avoid heroic recoveries later.

Compress repository using git gc --aggressive --prune=now and prune remote refs with git remote prune origin. That reduces disk usage and speeds up operations on large repositories.

This guide covered quick inspections safe removal of untracked files pruning of local branches rewriting local history when needed and running garbage collection to keep a repository healthy and fast.

Tip

Always run dry run commands before destructive actions and create a lightweight backup branch. Scripts that run periodic git gc and prune unused refs prevent future mess and save developer time.

title: Easily rebase GitHub branches
description: Rebase GitHub branches fast and safely Learn commands to update feature branches resolve conflicts and push with confidence
heading: Easily rebase GitHub branches with git rebase
body:
Rebasing is the tidy roommate of Git. It makes your feature branch look like you used a time machine to avoid merge commits and awkward histories. This guide shows how to rebase a GitHub feature branch cleanly while avoiding common pitfalls and accidental data destruction.

What this tutorial covers

Fetch and update local refs, switch to your feature branch, rebase onto the target branch, resolve conflicts, and push the cleaned branch back to GitHub without annoying your teammates.

Quick safety checklist

  • Fetch remote changes first with git fetch origin
  • Confirm the target branch on the server is up to date
  • Do not rebase branches others are basing work on unless they like surprises
  • Prefer git push --force-with-lease over a plain force push

Step by step commands

  1. Fetch remote refs

    git fetch origin

  2. Switch to your feature branch

    git checkout feature-branch

  3. Rebase onto the target branch such as main

    git rebase origin/main

    If conflicts show up open the conflicted files, fix the issues, stage the fixes and continue.

    git add path/to/file
git rebase --continue

    If you realize you made a mess use this to go back

    git rebase --abort

  4. Push the updated branch safely

    git push --force-with-lease origin feature-branch

    This refuses to clobber new work that landed on the remote while you were rebasing. It is basically common sense in command form.

What happens on GitHub

Your pull request updates automatically and will show the cleaned linear history without extra merge commits. Reviewers get a nicer diff and you get bragging rights for a tidy commit graph.

Why force with lease matters

git push --force-with-lease checks that the remote ref is what you expect before forcing. If someone pushed while you were gone it refuses to overwrite them. Using this is like checking the living room for people before you throw out the couch.

When not to rebase

Do not rebase long lived branches or branches that others base work on. Rewriting public history will turn collaborators into confused detectives. If many people depend on the branch prefer a merge based workflow instead.

Pro tips

  • Use git rebase -i origin/main if you want to reorder or squash commits before pushing
  • Run tests locally before pushing after a rebase to avoid surprising CI failures
  • Prefer rebasing for local or short lived feature branches when you want a linear history

Follow these steps and you will have a cleaner commit graph and fewer merge noise headaches. If something goes sideways git rebase --abort will rescue you and the force with lease will protect other people from your mistakes.
seo_title: Keep your Git history neat with a safe GitHub rebase workflow
seo_heading: Step by step guide to rebase a feature branch on GitHub safely

title: How to Squash Git Commits
description: Step by step guide to squash Git commits for a cleaner history with safe force push tips and practical commands.
heading: How to Squash Git Commits for a Clean History
body:
Why squash commits at all

Short version the commit history is public and brutal and you should care. Squashing turns a messy stack of tiny commits into one tidy change that reviewers can actually read without crying. This keeps the branch history readable and spares your teammates from answering questions about that accidental debug print you forgot to remove.

Quick checklist before you start

  • Run git log --oneline to see your recent commits
  • Decide how many commits to fold together for the branch
  • Make sure you are okay rewriting history on this branch

Pick the commit range

Find the range you want to squash using git log --oneline. If you want to fold the last three commits use HEAD~3. If that sounds vague then count the commits first and be brave.

Start an interactive rebase

Run the interactive rebase to get a text editor that lets you tell Git what to do.

git rebase -i HEAD~3

The editor will list each commit with the default action pick in front. You will edit those lines to instruct Git how to combine them.

Choose squash or fixup

Change pick on the commits you want merged into the topmost commit to either squash or fixup. Use squash when you want to combine commit messages and tidy them up. Use fixup when the earlier message is useless and you want to discard it. Pro tip prefer fixup when follow up commits include the phrase fixup! Original commit message and you want Git to auto collapse messages.

Example edit

pick a1b2c3 add feature prototype
fixup d4e5f6 tweak tests
squash 7g8h9i small cleanup

Save and close the editor and Git will replay the commits with your chosen actions. If you used squash Git will open a second editor session to let you clean the combined message.

Edit the final commit message

When Git prompts you edit the commit message so it explains the change concisely. Keep a one line summary then an optional body for details. Be useful not poetic. A good message helps future you and your coworkers figure out why this change existed without spelunking through code.

Push the rewritten history safely

After a successful rebase push the branch. If this branch is shared use the safer force option.

git push --force-with-lease

That reduces the chance of stomping on someone else work compared to a blind force push. If you do accidentally overwrite something you will deserve the slightly awkward apology conversation.

Common gotchas and recovery tips

  • If the rebase encounters conflicts resolve them then run git rebase --continue
  • If you want to abort the whole operation run git rebase --abort
  • Always run git log --oneline before and after to confirm the history looks sane

Recap and best practices

  • Pick a sensible commit range using HEAD~N
  • Use interactive rebase with git rebase -i to squash or fixup commits
  • Clean up the final commit message so future humans can survive reading it
  • Push with git push --force-with-lease to avoid collateral damage

Now go forth and squash responsibly. Your repo will look better and your code reviews will be marginally less terrifying.
seo_title: Clean up your Git history by squashing commits like a pro
seo_heading: Interactive rebase tips for squashing commits and cleaning history

title: git rebase master to branch example
description: Step by step example of rebasing master onto a feature branch using git commands and conflict handling for a clean linear history
heading: git rebase master to branch example for a clean history
body:
If you want a feature branch that reads like a neat timeline rather than an archaeological dig then rebasing master onto your branch is your friend. This short git tutorial walks through the exact git commands and conflict resolution steps to update a feature branch with the latest master while keeping history linear and sane.

Quick checklist before you start

  • Make sure HEAD is on the feature branch you want to update
  • Fetch the latest master from the remote so you do not rebase against stale history
  • Know how to resolve conflicts and how to abort if things go off the rails
  • Plan to push with a non destructive force option like force with lease

Step 1 Check out your feature branch

Be on the branch you plan to rewrite. Rebasing works by replaying commits from the current branch on top of the target branch, so HEAD must point at the feature branch first.

git checkout feature-branch

Step 2 Fetch the latest master from origin

Do not skip this. git fetch origin updates your view of origin/master without changing any local branches. That is what you will rebase onto.

git fetch origin

Step 3 Rebase the feature branch onto origin master

While still on the feature branch run the rebase command. This rewrites your feature branch commits so they sit on top of the newest master commits.

git rebase origin/master

Conflict resolution and recovery

If a conflict appears git will pause and show which files need attention. Fix the files, stage them, and continue the rebase. If the universe conspires against you you can abort and go back to the state before the rebase.

# Resolve conflicts in your editor then
git add path/to/resolved_file
git rebase --continue

# If you decide the rebase was a terrible idea
git rebase --abort

Step 4 Push the rewritten branch safely

Because rebase rewrites commit history you need to update the remote branch with a forced push. Do not use plain force unless you enjoy causing grief. Use force with lease as a safety net that prevents stomping over someone else changes.

git push --force-with-lease origin feature-branch

Pro tips and common pitfalls

  • Do not rebase public history that others are building on unless everyone agrees
  • Prefer git rebase origin/master from the feature branch for fewer surprises
  • Use git status and git log to inspect where you are during a rebase
  • force with lease lowers the chance of clobbering teammates work but does not eliminate coordination needs

That is the recipe. Correct use of git rebase keeps your feature branch updated, your git history tidy, and your pull requests less dramatic. If things get messy remember git rebase --abort exists and your teammates will forgive you if you explain it with a little humility and a lot of coffee.

title: Git rebase to master example
description: Clear example showing how to rebase a feature branch onto master with commands conflict handling and safe push tips
heading: Git rebase to master example explained
body:
Why rebase at all

Rebasing a feature branch onto master keeps your project history neat and linear. It also applies the latest master changes to your branch so your work does not surprise reviewers or CI. If you enjoy tidy commit logs and fewer merge commits then this is the workflow for you. If you like chaos then skip this and enjoy merge commit soup.

Get ready before you touch anything

Make sure your working tree is clean. That means commit or stash local changes. Run git status on the command line and do not proceed if you have uncommitted work. You will thank yourself later.

Update the master branch

Switch to master and bring it up to date from origin. Fast forward only if possible. Example commands to run on the command line:

git checkout master
git pull --ff-only origin master

This ensures your feature branch will be replayed on top of the current master branch and not on stale history.

Rebase the feature branch

Switch back to your feature branch and start the rebase. Git will replay your feature commits on top of master which makes history linear and easier to follow.

git checkout feature-branch
git rebase master

When conflicts happen

Yes they will. Conflicts are a part of life and git. Open the conflicting files, resolve the differences, then stage the fixes and continue the rebase.

git add path/to/conflicted-file
git rebase --continue

If you decide this is not worth the pain you can go back to the state before the rebase with:

git rebase --abort

Push after rewriting history

Because rebase rewrites commits you must force push. Use the safer option to avoid stomping on someone else work.

git push --force-with-lease origin feature-branch

The --force-with-lease flag reduces the risk of overwriting remote changes. It is not magic but it helps.

Tips for polishing commits

  • Use interactive rebase to squash or edit commits with git rebase --interactive master. It is perfect when your feature has a dozen tiny fixup commits and you want to look professional.
  • Run your test suite after the rebase to catch integration problems early.
  • Communicate with teammates if you are rewriting a shared branch. Do not be the person who forces everyone to reset their branches without warning.

Common pitfalls to avoid

Do not rebase public branches without telling collaborators. If someone else has based work on the old commits you will cause pain. Avoid force pushing blind and prefer force with lease for a small layer of protection.

Quick checklist

  1. Clean working tree
  2. Update master with git pull --ff-only origin master
  3. Checkout your feature branch
  4. Run git rebase master
  5. Resolve conflicts with git add and git rebase --continue
  6. Push with git push --force-with-lease origin feature-branch

Follow this flow and you will have a tidy git history that is easier to review and bisect. Also you will annoy fewer teammates when you explain what happened in the pull request. Win win.

title: Git config file locations on Windows and Ubuntu
description: Quick guide to where Git stores system global and local config files on Windows and Ubuntu and how to view and edit each one
heading: Git config file locations on Windows and Ubuntu
body:
If your Git settings are acting like a confused thermostat you need to know where they live. This guide shows where Git reads configuration on Ubuntu and Windows and how to inspect and change system config global config and local config without making things worse.

Where Git reads configuration files

System config

System configuration applies to every user on the machine. On Ubuntu the file is /etc/gitconfig. On Windows look in the Program data area such as %PROGRAMDATA%/Git/config or in the Git install folder under Program Files. Modifying the system config usually requires administrator rights.

Global user config

The global user config affects one account and is what you use for your identity and sane defaults. On Ubuntu that file lives at ~/.gitconfig. On Windows the equivalent is %USERPROFILE%/.gitconfig. Put things here like user.name and user.email and your preferred merge and push defaults.

Local repository config

Repository specific settings live in the repo in .git/config. These values override global and system settings for that repository only. Use local config for repo specific remotes hooks and other rules you do not want in your dotfiles.

See which file set each value

If you are guessing where a setting came from stop guessing and run this command. It prints each key its value and the file that provided it.

git config --list --show-origin

That output tells you if the value came from system global or local config so you do not accidentally edit the wrong file.

Edit configs safely with Git commands

Manual file edits are allowed but you will be happier if you use Git commands that preserve syntax. The commands are simple and make it obvious where the change is being written.

  • git config --global user.name "Your Name" sets the global name
  • git config --global user.email "you@example.com" sets the global email
  • git config --local core.editor "code --wait" sets a repo only editor when run inside the repo
  • git config --system core.packages requires admin rights and changes the system config

If you must edit the file directly keep a backup copy and respect the ini like format used by Git. Broken syntax can make settings vanish mysteriously and that is not fun.

Troubleshooting checklist

  • Run git config --list --show-origin to find the source of a value
  • Change user name or email with git config --global not by editing the file unless you know what you are doing
  • If a value feels stuck check local then global then system in that order because of precedence
  • Back up your dotfiles before manual edits so you can undo without tears
  • Remember Windows paths for Git often live in Program Files or under the Program data environment variable and may need admin rights to change

Final tip

If a setting is misbehaving run the show origin command then fix the value with the matching flag like --local --global or --system so you know exactly where your change lands. Treat your Git config files like a fragile collection of tiny rules and keep backups in your dotfiles repository if you like living dangerously but safely.
seo_title: Find and fix your Git config files on Windows and Ubuntu fast
seo_heading: Track down global local and system Git settings on Windows and Ubuntu

title: Why you can't find the gitconfig file?
description: Find the missing gitconfig file learn where Git stores config and how to reveal and create global and system configuration files
heading: Why you can't find the gitconfig file explained
body:
Short answer when you are tired of searching

Git is not hiding your gitconfig as a prank. It just looks in three different places depending on what you asked it to do. There is repository level config under the repo, a user level file in your home or XDG config folder, and a system level file that the OS manages. Most missing file mysteries end with a shrug and the command that shows where settings actually come from.

Where Git looks for config files

  • Repository The one in your repo sits at .git/config and applies only inside that repo
  • Global or user Usually at ~/.gitconfig or under an XDG path at ~/.config/git/config
  • System Managed by the OS and found in system folders on Linux or under ProgramData on Windows

Why the file might not exist

If you never saved a global setting the global file may simply not exist. That is fine. Running a global set command will create it for you and then Git will stop nagging you about name and email.

Commands that tell the truth

Instead of spelunking through hidden folders use this command to see every setting and where it came from

git config --list --show-origin

The output shows the value and the file path or the word command line when the setting was provided via an environment variable or a CLI flag. That is the part that saves time and sanity.

How to create or edit your global file

To create or open the global config for editing use the safe command below

git config --global --edit

To set the minimum things you need to stop Git from nagging do this

git config --global user.name 'Your Name'
git config --global user.email 'email@example.com'

System level inspection

If you need to inspect the system wide values run

git config --system --list

Note that this may require administrator rights depending on your OS and where the system file lives.

Windows and Linux quirks

On Windows check your user profile folder for .gitconfig and look under ProgramData for system config. On Linux typical locations are in your home or under ~/.config/git/config when the XDG standard is in play.

XDG and why your file is hiding in plain sight

If the environment variable XDG_CONFIG_HOME points somewhere unusual Git will follow it and look there instead of the home folder. This explains a lot of mysterious locations and rogue dotfiles if you or some installer changed that variable.

Common traps and quick checks

  • Run git config --list --show-origin first and stop digging through hidden folders
  • If a setting shows as command line check for environment overrides or scripts that invoke Git
  • Remember that global file is created only when you write something at that scope

Parting tip

If your goal is to stop mysterious author errors set your name and email globally and move on with your life. For everything else the show origin command will point you straight to the file that actually mattered. Now go fix your dotfiles and blame the XDG standard with style.
seo_title: Where Git Keeps your gitconfig and how to stop hunting it
seo_heading: Locate the real gitconfig file on Linux Windows and XDG setups

title: How to Use the Git Config List Command Example
description: Learn how to use git config list to view and debug Git configuration across local global and system scopes with practical commands and tips
heading: How to Use the Git Config List Command Example
body:
This tutorial shows how to use the git config list command to inspect Git configuration across local global and system scopes and to debug where values come from.

  1. View all configuration entries with the list command
  2. Show the origin file for each entry
  3. Filter or fetch single keys
  4. Set or unset values in a specific scope
  5. Verify precedence among scopes

View all configuration entries Use the basic command to dump current configuration to the terminal. Example command

git config --list

The command prints key value pairs that apply to the repository or the environment. This is the first stop when a name or email looks wrong.

Show the origin file for each entry Add an option to see where each value came from. Example command

git config --list --show-origin

Because Git enjoys hiding surprises the origin flag reveals whether a value comes from system global or repository level files. That helps when a global setting overrides local expectations.

Filter or fetch single keys Use get or grep like tools to focus on a single setting. Example commands

git config user.email

git config --get-all user.email

These commands are the fast lane when only one configuration key matters during troubleshooting.

Set or unset values in a specific scope Use scope flags to control where a change lands. Examples

git config --global user.name "Jane Doe"

git config --local --unset user.name

Pick the correct scope to avoid surprising teammates with a global name change.

Verify precedence among scopes Remember that local repository configuration overrides global and system settings. Use the list and origin commands together to see the winning value and the file responsible.

Recap of the tutorial content The guide covered viewing all configuration values showing origins filtering single keys setting and unsetting values and checking scope precedence so that configuration surprises become less thrilling and more managed

Tip

Use the origin option when debugging to discover the exact file that defined a value and avoid chasing ghosts in the config files.

title: How to Remove and Delete Properties from Git Config
description: Compact guide to remove and delete properties from Git config using unset remove section and editing for local and global scopes
heading: How to Remove and Delete Properties from Git Config
body:
Why you might need to edit git config

Your git config is like that junk drawer everyone promises to fix. Over time values pile up, duplicates appear, and a bad email or leftover include causes odd behavior. This guide shows how to inspect, unset, and surgically remove sections from git config without nuking your workflow or your credentials.

Inspect current configuration before you touch anything

Stop. Look. Breathe. Find the exact key name you want to change so you do not accidentally remove the global user.email for every repo. Use these commands to inspect settings and where they come from.

  • git config --list shows active values across scopes
  • git config --list --show-origin shows which file provided each value
  • To limit scope run git config --local --list or git config --global --list

Unset a single property

When you need to replace or remove one setting use unset. Always specify scope so you do not surprise other repositories.

git config --local --unset user.email

If you run that inside a repo it affects only that repo. If you want to change user level settings add --global instead. Easy to test, easy to undo if you backed up wisely.

Unset all values for a key when duplicates haunt you

Sometimes a key has multiple entries and duplicates cause strange behavior. Use unset all to strip every occurrence.

git config --global --unset-all include.path

That will remove every include.path entry in the global file. Good for cleaning up cruft from copy paste sessions that seemed like a good idea at the time.

Remove a whole section if a feature is dead

If an integration or feature is gone remove the entire section. This is the nuclear option for related keys inside that section.

git config --remove-section branch.feature

Use this when multiple keys under the same section need to go. Think of it as tidying the whole folder instead of folding one sock.

Edit the config file directly when you need precision

For surgical edits or to remove comments open the config in a text editor. For global settings run:

git config --global --edit

For local repository edits open .git/config in your editor. You can also make a quick backup first to reduce regret later.

Quick backup tips

  • Local repo config backup cp .git/config .git/config.bak
  • Global config backup cp ~/.gitconfig ~/.gitconfig.bak

Checklist before you press enter

  • List active values and confirm origins with git config --list --show-origin
  • Prefer --local when testing changes to avoid breaking global preferences
  • Backup the file so rollbacks do not become a painful scavenger hunt
  • Reinspect with git config --list after changes

Common gotchas and how to avoid them

  • Removing a global credential like user.email can make commits look weird. Scope matters.
  • Duplicate entries can come from system, global, and local files. Use show origin to track them down.
  • Editing without a backup is a brave decision and a good way to learn how to apologize to your future self.

If you follow these steps you will be able to clean up git config like a pro and avoid accidental outages that cause panicked Slack messages. Or at least you will be able to blame configuration properly.
seo_title: Clean up Git config settings and safely remove old keys
seo_heading: When to unset a git config key and how to remove sections safely

title: How to set the Git user.name Property in Git Config
description: Quick guide to set Git user.name with git config for global and local repos and verify commit author
heading: Set Git user.name Property in Git Config
body:
This tutorial shows how to set the Git user.name property using git config for global and local repositories and how to verify the change.

  1. Check current name
  2. Set a global name
  3. Set a local name for a single repository
  4. Verify the configured values

Step 1 Check current name with a quick query. Run git config --list to see all configured values. For a focused check run git config user.name from inside a repository to view the local value that applies to that repository.

Step 2 Set a global name that will apply across repositories by default. Run git config --global user.name 'Your Name' to write to the global config file. This is handy when human readable commit authors are desired everywhere and no per repository override is needed.

Step 3 Set a local name when a repository needs a different author. From the repository folder run git config user.name 'Repository Name' to store the name in the repository config file. This local value will take precedence over the global value for that repository.

Step 4 Verify the change. Use git config --global user.name to check the global entry and git config user.name inside a repo to check the local entry. For a fast check of commit author on the last commit run git log -1 --pretty=format %an to display the author name recorded on the latest commit.

Choosing a clear user.name prevents mystery authors and awkward blame moments. Use single quotes in the shell if the name has spaces. If the wrong author was used on a commit there are ways to rewrite history but that is a slightly different conversation that includes force pushing and consequences.

Tip

Set both user.name and user.email together to avoid anonymous commit authors. Use global for daily work and local for special projects. If privacy matters use a throwaway name and a dedicated email for public repositories.

title: How to Set the Git Email Property in Git Config
description: Quick guide to set Git user email using git config for global and local scopes and fix commit author issues on repositories
heading: How to Set the Git Email Property in Git Config
body:
Why your Git email matters

Yes I know you would rather wrestle a merge conflict blindfolded than fiddle with config. Still your Git email is the part of the commit that tells the internet who to blame. If it does not match the address on GitHub or your company account your commits will show up as anonymous or get misattributed in web views and contributor graphs. This is a short practical git tutorial for developers who like tidy history and fewer awkward commit authors.

Quick check of the current email

Before you start changing things check what Git is currently planning to stamp on new commits. Run these commands from the command line while inside a repository or globally.

git config user.email
git config --global user.email
git config --list

The first command shows the email used by the current repository if one exists. The second shows your global setting for the whole machine. The third lists all effective settings. If nothing shows up Git will fall back to other metadata or leave the author looking like a ghost.

Set a global email for your machine

Use the global setting for your personal laptop or any machine where you want a single identity across projects. Run this once and forget it until you get a new machine.

git config --global user.email "name@example.com"

Replace name@example.com with the email you have registered on remote hosting services like GitHub. That keeps your commits linked to your online profile and prevents mysterious anonymous contributions.

Set a repository specific email

If you work on both personal projects and a job with strict attribution use a local repo setting to keep identities separate. Change into the repository folder and run this.

git config user.email "work@example.com"

This overrides the global value only for that project. Clean and professional if you want to keep personal and work commits from mingling.

Verify the configuration

After making changes confirm everything looks right with a quick list.

git config --global --list
git config --local --list

Seeing the expected user.email entry is far better than discovering wrong attribution after pushing to a shared repo and then explaining yourself to teammates.

Fix a recent commit author

If you just committed with the wrong email and have not pushed use the amend trick to fix the author information without rewriting the whole history.

git commit --amend --author="Your Name " --no-edit

This replaces the author on the most recent commit and keeps the commit message intact. Push force only if you need to update a remote and you understand the consequences.

Fix many commits when needed

If the error spans many commits you can do an interactive rebase or use a history rewrite tool. Common approaches include

  • git rebase -i HEAD~N to rewrite the last N commits manually
  • tools like git filter-branch or git filter-repo for bulk changes when you really need to rewrite history

Warning rewrite history only if you are the only one working on the branch or after you coordinate with collaborators. Breaking the shared history will trigger bad feelings and force pushes that look like an admission of weakness.

Practical tips and git tips for developers

  • Use the same email registered with GitHub to get proper author links and contribution counts
  • Use global for a personal machine and local for repo specific identities to keep personal and professional commits separate
  • Check configuration before big commits so you do not have to rewrite history later

Final thought

Setting the right git email is boring and important. Do it once and let Git do the tedious work of telling the world you wrote that code. If something goes wrong you now know how to inspect the config verify values and fix author data without summoning chaos.
seo_title: Fix your Git email so commits stop looking like mysteries
seo_heading: Set a global or local Git email that matches your GitHub profile

title: How to Configure Your Global Git Config Settings
description: Quick guide to set global Git config options like user name email default editor and signing keys so every repository behaves consistently
heading: How to Configure Your Global Git Config Settings for Every Repo
body:
Tired of surprise identities and broken commit signatures ruining your version control vibes? This friendly but slightly sarcastic guide shows how to set global Git config so your name email editor and signing behave across every repo on your machine. No ritual sacrifices required just a few command line git tweaks.

Quick check of your current global config

Before you start flailing at commands check what is already set so you do not clone someone else s identity by accident.

git config --global --list

If you see keys like user.name user.email or user.signingkey then you are halfway there. If not keep reading.

Set your name and email so commits look human

The commit author fields come from your global settings unless a repo overrides them. Use sensible values so your contribution history is not a mystery.

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

Tip Use the same public email for open source to avoid fragmented history. Use a private or obfuscated email for work or when you like privacy more than fame.

Pick an editor that will actually wait for you

Git occasionally asks you to write a commit message. Pick an editor that blocks until you are done so Git does not think you are a nihilist.

git config --global core.editor "code --wait"
# or for the minimalists
git config --global core.editor "nano"

Enable commit signing and set your GPG or SSH key

Signed commits are proof you are not a very convincing imposter. Configure signing with the key you actually control.

git config --global user.signingkey YOURKEY
git config --global commit.gpgsign true

If you use GPG follow your OS specific setup first then tell Git which key to use. If you use SSH based signing follow the provider s instructions for that workflow.

List verify and edit the global config manually

After you set things run the list command again and peek at the config file to confirm everything looks sane.

git config --global --list
git config --global --edit

Editing ~/.gitconfig directly is fine when you want to copy blocks between machines or add advanced settings. Just be careful with syntax and section names.

Common global keys worth knowing

  • user.name and user.email for identity
  • core.editor for your commit message editor
  • user.signingkey and commit.gpgsign for commit signing
  • pull.rebase if you prefer rebasing to merge commits

Troubleshooting quick hits

  • If commits show the wrong email check for repo specific config with git config --local --list
  • If signing fails ensure your key is available to your agent and that your Git and GPG versions are compatible
  • If your editor does not block try a different editor or add the appropriate wait flag

This is a short command line git tutorial that keeps your identity consistent across repositories and helps avoid squabbles about who actually wrote that rogue line. Follow these steps and your commit metadata will stop being a mystery novel.
seo_title: Set and Fix Global Git Config for Consistent Commits Fast
seo_heading: Make your Git user email editor and signing work across every repository

title: How to Set Your Username and Email in Git Config
description: Quick guide to set user.name and user.email in Git config for global and repository level commits and to verify or fix author information
heading: How to Set Your Username and Email in Git Config
body:
This tutorial gives a compact walkthrough for setting username and email in Git global and repository configuration so commits carry the correct author information with minimal drama.

  1. Set global username and email
  2. Set local username and email for a repository
  3. Verify configuration values
  4. Amend a recent commit author when needed

Set global username and email Use global configuration to apply name and email across all repositories on a machine. Run git config --global user.name "Your Name" and git config --global user.email "you@example.com" to set a default identity for commits.

Set local username and email To override the global identity for a specific repository run git config user.name "Project Name" and git config user.email "proj@example.com" inside the repository folder. Local values take precedence over global values which is handy for side projects or work accounts.

Verify configuration values Confirm current settings with git config --list for all values or query a single key with git config user.email to see which email will be stamped on new commits.

Amend a recent commit author If a recent commit used the wrong author correct the most recent commit with git commit --amend --author="Name < email@example.com> " and then force push if history rewriting is acceptable. For multiple commits use interactive rebase and rewrite author lines while being mindful that rewriting public history can annoy collaborators.

Summary of the steps covered includes setting global defaults configuring repository specific identity verifying active values and fixing a recent commit author. Proper configuration avoids confusing commit logs and reduces support messages about missing identity.

Tip

Use a consistent email that matches the host account to link commits to a profile. For multiple identities prefer global defaults plus repository level overrides or use conditional includes in the gitconfig to keep things tidy.

title: How to Show All Your Git Config Properties at Once
description: Quick guide to list every Git config property across local global and system scopes with commands examples and cleaning tips
heading: How to Show All Your Git Config Properties at Once
body:
Welcome to the thrilling world of Git config detective work. If your commits are acting like a rebellious ferret you probably want to know which config file is whispering bad ideas into your repository. This guide shows how to list every Git config property and where it came from so you can fix odd behavior without resorting to ritual sacrifice.

See all settings with one command

Open your terminal inside a repo and run the single command that saves time and dignity

git config --list --show-origin

That prints each config key with the path of the file that supplied it. You get the key name the value and the file path all on one line. No guesswork and no staring at three different dotfiles until your eyeballs blur.

Where values come from

Git reads settings from multiple scopes in this order of priority from most specific to least specific

  • Local which lives in .git/config inside a repository
  • Global which is your user level config usually at ~/.gitconfig
  • System which is for system wide defaults

The file path shown by the show origin output tells you which file to edit when a setting is misbehaving. If you see the same key in more than one place that explains a lot.

Filter the noise

If you only care about user or email settings or some cryptic credential helper use grep to narrow results

git config --list --show-origin | grep user
git config --list --show-origin | grep credential

On Windows use your shell search equivalent. This keeps the focus on the problem and avoids scrolling through unrelated decorations.

Edit or remove values

Change a value with the appropriate scope edit command

git config --global --edit
git config --local --edit

To delete a key run

git config --global --unset user.name
git config --local --unset core.editor

Manual editing of ~/.gitconfig is fine for brave humans who enjoy opening their dotfiles and pretending they know what they are doing.

Common troubleshooting tips

  • Run git config --list --show-origin before assuming Git is broken
  • Look for duplicate keys across scopes when behavior is inconsistent
  • Remember environment variables and conditional includes can also affect config

That is all you need to turn a confusing pile of settings into a readable list with file paths and values. Now go find the rogue entry that keeps rewriting your author name and get back to writing code or memes whichever pays the bills.

seo_heading: List Git settings from local global and system and fix surprising values fast

title: git reflog example
description: Practical guide to using git reflog to recover commits inspect history and reset branches safely
heading: git reflog example explained for commit recovery and history
body:
So you broke something, or deleted a branch, or performed an honest experiment gone wrong. Relax, git reflog is the time machine that lets you recover commits and pretend you always knew what you were doing. This short git tutorial walks through reading the reflog finding the commit you need and restoring work with git checkout and git reset in a way that does not make the rest of the team angry.

Read the reflog

Start with a quick inventory of recent moves in the repository. The reflog records where HEAD and branches have pointed. It is a local history of your repository state even after commits are detached or branches vanish.

git reflog

Scan the output for the entry that looks like your lost work. You will see references such as HEAD@{3} or a raw SHA. The numeric HEAD reference is handy when you do not want to copy a long hash or when you are reconstructing a chain of actions.

Create a recovery branch

Never move main or master around while you are still nervous. Make a temporary branch that preserves the commit you found. This is branch recovery best practice and it gives you a safe place to play.

git checkout -b recovered-branch HEAD@{3}

That command creates recovered-branch at the reflog entry and checks it out. You now have the lost commit saved on a branch that you can test or merge back calmly.

Reset or restore the target branch

If you want to move an existing branch pointer back to the recovered commit do it deliberately. A destructive option exists and it is named plainly.

git checkout target-branch
git reset --hard HEAD@{2}

Warning do not run the previous commands unless you are certain you want to discard uncommitted changes and the current tip of the branch. If you prefer not to overwrite anything use a merge or cherry pick from the recovered branch instead.

Safer alternatives

  • Merge the recovered branch into your target branch with git merge recovered-branch
  • Or cherry pick specific commits with git cherry-pick <sha>

Push recovered work and clean up

Reflog is local and not eternal. Push the recovered branch to the remote so your rescue does not depend on your hard drive continuing to behave.

git push origin recovered-branch

After you merge the recovered changes into the intended branch you can delete the temporary branch locally and on the remote.

git branch -d recovered-branch
git push origin --delete recovered-branch

Tips and common pitfalls

  • Push recovered work to a remote as soon as possible because reflog entries expire and git garbage collection will eventually clean up unreachable objects.
  • Use branches for recovery so you avoid accidental loss of main branch state.
  • Remember that git reset --hard will overwrite working files. If you are unsure create a branch and inspect the recovered commit first.
  • For small pieces of work a cherry pick is often less scary than a reset.

This is one of those git tips that feels like cheating. You get to undo mistakes learn a little about how HEAD works and rescue commits that would otherwise be gone. Use reflog for recovery not for daily navigation of your tree. Treat it like a map when you are lost, and push the salvage to a remote so the map does not evaporate overnight.
seo_title: Recover lost commits with git reflog and safe branch recovery
seo_heading: A practical git reflog guide for resetting checking out and rescuing work

title: git log and reflog compared
description: Understand differences between git log and reflog and learn when to use each for history inspection and recovering lost commits.
heading: git log and reflog compared for history inspection and recovery
body:
If you ever deleted a commit by accident and pretended not to panic this article is your therapy session. Git log and reflog both talk about history but they are gossiping about different things. One shows the public story your team sees and the other keeps your embarrassing personal browser history for when you need to recover that lost work.

What git log shows

git log walks the commit graph that is reachable from a branch or reference. That means it shows the history that is shared and pushed to remotes, the version control narrative your teammates can check. Use familiar options like --oneline and --graph to make that history readable instead of a wall of cryptic hashes.

Quick tips for reading history

  • Use git log --oneline --graph --all to see a compact view of all refs
  • Filter by author or message when you only need a specific thread
  • Remember git log shows reachable commits only, so it will not list commits you recently orphaned

What reflog does and why you need it

git reflog records local reference updates including HEAD moves, checkouts, rebases, resets and merges. This is not public history. Reflog is your personal safety net in the repository on your machine. It remembers where HEAD has been even when those commits are no longer reachable from a branch.

When to run reflog

  • If you ran a reset or an aggressive rebase and now regret it, run git reflog
  • If a commit seems vanished, reflog will show the recent hashes that pointed to it
  • When you are nervous, create a branch from a reflog entry instead of trying to recover straight into a main branch

Common commit recovery workflow

Here is the chill step by step approach that saves work and dignity. First list the reflog to find the hash you want. Then branch off that hash or move a branch back to it depending on what you want to do.

git reflog
# find the desired hash in the list
git checkout -b recover 
# or to move the current branch back
git reset --hard

Prefer creating a branch when you are unsure. That preserves the current state and prevents you from accidentally destroying work while trying to be clever.

Small but important warnings

Reflog entries are local and they eventually expire based on your repository garbage collection settings. Do not treat reflog as permanent backup. Push important branches to a remote or create tags to preserve commits across machines.

Extra survival tips

  • If you get stuck run git reflog before anything else
  • Create a short lived branch from the found hash so you can inspect changes safely
  • Use the reflog as a safety net not a long term archive

In short, use git log when you want the shared history and use git reflog when you need to rescue a lost commit or trace where HEAD has been. Both are useful tools, and knowing which one to run will save you time, tears, and a few panicked messages to your team.
seo_title: How to find lost commits fast with git reflog and git log
seo_heading: Practical git history and recovery tactics for lost commits and HEAD moves

title: git status command example
description: Learn how to read git status output stage changes and confirm commits with clear examples and commands for faster troubleshooting
heading: git status command example explained for beginners
body:
This guide teaches how to use the git status command to inspect repository state and decide the next steps.

  1. Run the command to view current state
  2. Understand untracked modified and staged categories
  3. Stage files for commit
  4. Commit staged changes
  5. Verify status after changes

Run the command to view current state Use git status in the repository root. The command prints branch name tracked changes and whether local history is ahead or behind the remote. This is the safest starting point before making changes.

Understand untracked modified and staged categories The output groups files into untracked modified and changes to be committed. Untracked files are new files that are not tracked by Git. Modified files are tracked but have changes in the working directory. Staged files are ready for the next commit.

Stage files for commit Use git add path/to/file to stage a single file or git add . to stage many files. Staging prepares a snapshot for the commit step. Think of staging as picking which changes deserve to live in history.

Commit staged changes Use git commit -m "short message" to record staged snapshots in the local repository. Commit messages should be concise and descriptive so future humans will thank the author.

Verify status after changes Run git status again to confirm that the staging area is clean and that the working directory has no unexpected changes. The command also reports whether pushes or pulls may be required to sync with the remote.

The tutorial showed how to run the status command interpret the three main output categories stage files commit changes and recheck status so that daily workflows cause fewer surprises.

Tip

Tip Use git status -s for a compact summary when dealing with many files and use clear commit messages to make the status output meaningful over time.

title: How the Git Working Tree Works by Example
description: Practical guide to how the Git working tree index and repository interact using clear example commands and explanations
heading: How the Git Working Tree Works by Example Explained
body:
This tutorial shows how the Git working tree the index and the repository interact using concrete commands and small examples.

  1. Initialize a repository and inspect status
  2. Create a file and observe the working tree
  3. Stage the file and inspect the index
  4. Modify the file and compare working tree and index
  5. Commit and examine the repository history

Start with a clean sandbox. Run git init then git status to see that the working tree has no tracked files yet. This step proves a repository starts empty and status will point out the lonely files.

Create a file named hello.txt and add some text. Run git status again to observe that the working tree contains an untracked file. The working tree reflects the current project files on the filesystem.

Stage the file using git add hello.txt then run git status --short or git ls-files --stage to peek into the index. The index acts as a staging area that records a snapshot ready for the next commit. Think of staging as a photo studio where files get their glamour shots taken before a public release.

Edit hello.txt and use git diff to compare the working tree with the index. Use git diff --staged to compare the index with the last commit. These commands clarify differences between the three states and prevent surprises when crafting commits.

Commit with git commit -m "add hello" and inspect history using git log --oneline. The repository holds the committed snapshots and the HEAD pointer moves with each commit. That completes the flow from working tree to index to repository.

The walkthrough demonstrated how changes travel from working tree to index to repository and how common commands reveal each state without drama or hand waving.

Tip

Use git status --porcelain for machine friendly output and git restore --staged to unstage changes without losing work.

title: git stash list example
description: Quick guide to using git stash list to view inspect and manage saved changes with practical commands and examples
heading: git stash list example how to view and manage stashes
body:
If your working tree looks like a thrift store after a tornado git stash list is the index card system that keeps the worst mess recoverable. This guide shows how to read the stash index inspect what was saved and bring changes back without causing a train wreck.

See what is stashed

Run the basic command to get a quick inventory of saved work. The output shows entries like stash@{0} followed by whatever message you gave when stashing. That gives you a scaffold for deciding what to restore and when.

git stash list

Inspect a stash before you touch it

If you are not sure what a stash contains do not wing it. Inspect the full patch to understand which files and hunks are involved. This helps you avoid applying changes that will conflict with recent work.

git stash show -p stash@{0}

The output is a full patch. Read it like a tiny horror story about your past self. If you only need a quick summary omit the -p flag to see filenames and stat info.

Reapply changes with apply or pop

Use git stash apply when you want the stash to survive after reapplying. Use git stash pop when you are lazy and want the stash removed in one go. Pop is convenient and slightly reckless when your working tree already has conflicts.

git stash apply stash@{1}
git stash pop

If conflicts happen resolve them like a responsible adult. If you are nervous apply a stash to a throwaway branch so main branches stay clean.

Name stashes so they mean something

Stop using the default cryptic messages. Give each stash a human readable note so you can find that WIP without playing detective later.

git stash push -m "WIP feature X"

Named stashes show up in git stash list as messages that actually help humans. It is a small mercy.

Remove stashes to avoid hoarding

When a stash is no longer useful drop it or nuking the whole stash list is an option for dramatic cleanup. Be careful you will not get those changes back unless they are committed somewhere.

git stash drop stash@{0}
git stash clear

Quick safe restore workflow

If you are unsure about applying directly try this safe sequence. It protects your main branch and gives you a place to tidy up rescued changes.

git checkout -b temp-restore
git stash apply stash@{0}
# review and commit the rescued changes
git commit -m "rescue work"
# switch back when ready
git checkout main

Alternatively use the built in helper to make a branch from a stash if you prefer fewer steps. That command creates a branch applies the stash and removes it if the apply succeeds.

Wrap up

Use git stash list as your quick map of deferred work. Inspect patches reapply or pop intentionally name stashes and drop the junk. Do this and your repo will stay livable and you will avoid tragic afternoons spent trying to remember what you were doing three stashes ago.
seo_title: Master git stash list to track and restore saved changes
seo_heading: How to inspect stash entries and safely apply or drop them in git

title: git stash untracked files example
description: Learn how to stash untracked files in git with clear commands and examples to keep new files safe when switching branches
heading: git stash untracked files example tutorial
body:
So you made new files while hacking on a branch and now Git is yelling at you. Relax and stash them like a responsible developer who also enjoys not breaking things. This guide shows how to stash untracked files safely and how to get them back when you need them again.

Check the working tree state

First stop panicking and run a status check. This way you see what Git thinks is changed and which files are untracked. No guessing allowed.

git status

Pick the stash mode

By default git stash only saves tracked changes. If you have new files you want to tuck away temporarily use the untracked flag. If you are hoarding ignored files use the all flag instead.

git stash push -u -m "WIP untracked"

To include ignored files use this instead

git stash push --all -m "WIP including ignored"

Which one should you use

  • Default stash saves tracked changes only when untracked files are irrelevant
  • -u includes new files that are not in .gitignore
  • --all hides everything including ignored files when you are cleaning up a messy sandbox

Create the stash with a message

Give the stash a message that future you can read without crying. Messages help when the stash list looks like a crime scene.

git stash push -u -m "WIP untracked"

The stash acts like a temporary commit reference so switching branches will not leave you with untracked file drama.

Inspect the stash

Before you reapply anything peek inside the stash to confirm it contains the files you expect.

git stash list
git stash show -p stash@{0}

Use the list output to identify the stash index you want. The show command will give a patch style preview so you are not guessing.

Restore or remove the stash

When you are ready to get your files back choose to reapply or reapply and delete.

git stash apply stash@{0}   # reapply but keep the stash
git stash pop stash@{0}     # reapply and remove the stash
git stash drop stash@{0}    # delete the stash if you are done

If there are conflicts Git will tell you. Resolve them like a human and continue. If something went wrong you can always look at the stash entry again or create a branch from it for a safer rescue.

Quick checklist

  • Run git status so nothing surprises you
  • Use -u to include untracked files and --all to include ignored files
  • Give stashes meaningful messages so future you does not scream
  • Use git stash show -p to verify contents before applying
  • Use apply if you want to keep the stash or pop if you want to consume it

There you go. Stashing untracked files is boring but effective. Do it often enough and your branches will stop ambushing you with mysterious new files. And if your stash list starts to look like a hoarder profile clean up with git stash drop when you are confident the work is saved somewhere better.
seo_title: Stash untracked files in Git without losing work or sleep
seo_heading: Practical steps to stash new and ignored files when switching branches

title: How to Use the Git Clean Command by Example
description: Practical git clean examples to safely preview and remove untracked and ignored files using dry run and force options.
heading: How to Use the Git Clean Command by Example
body:
If your workspace looks like a garage that someone else abandoned long ago you are in the right place. This short git tutorial shows how to preview and then remove untracked files and directories with git clean while avoiding the regret that comes from force deleting the wrong thing.

Preview before you nuke anything

Never skip the dry run. You get to see what git clean would remove without actually losing files. Pretend you are a cautious arsonist who likes to check the exits first.

Dry run example

Run a dry run at the repository root to list candidates for deletion. The output shows files and folders that git would remove.

git clean -n
or
git clean -nd

The -n flag means no changes are made. Add -d to include untracked directories in the preview.

When you actually want to remove files

When the preview looks safe use the force flag to perform the deletion. Git requires this explicit step so you do not accidentally erase your life work.

git clean -f
or
git clean -fd

Use -d to remove folders as well as files. The -f flag is required by design to discourage casual destruction.

Handle ignored files with care

There are two common ways to deal with ignored files. Lowercase x removes files that are excluded by .gitignore or other exclude rules. Uppercase X removes only ignored files that are not tracked. Both can be dangerous when build artifacts or local config files are present.

git clean -fdx
git clean -fdX

Think of these as the nuclear options. Use them only when you really want a pristine workspace and you have backups.

Interactive cleanup when you want to be choosy

Not sure which stray files are safe to lose Then use interactive mode to pick and choose. It prompts you for each candidate so you can play gatekeeper for your repo.

git clean -i

Safety tips that prevent sorrow

  • Commit or stash changes before running destructive commands. Backups are for the brave and the sensible.
  • Always run a dry run first so you know what will happen.
  • Add safe patterns to .gitignore for files you never want in version control.
  • Use local exclude rules for machine specific files you do not want to share.

Recap and quick commands

Here are the main git commands to remember for workspace cleanup and version control hygiene.

  • Preview what would be removed git clean -n or git clean -nd
  • Remove untracked files git clean -f
  • Include directories git clean -fd
  • Remove ignored or excluded files git clean -fdx or git clean -fdX
  • Run interactive selection git clean -i

Use these git commands with respect. Preview first, protect your work with a commit or stash, and only then let git clean do its job. Your future self will send you a thank you note, probably with fewer curse words.
seo_title: Git clean guide for safely removing untracked files and junk
seo_heading: Preview pick and purge untracked and ignored files with git clean safely

title: How to git clean Untracked Files with the fdx Switch
description: Learn to safely remove untracked and ignored files using git clean -fdx with a dry run and easy recovery tips
heading: How to git clean Untracked Files with the fdx Switch
body:
If your working tree looks like a yard sale and you want to restore order without sacrificing your precious uncommitted treasures here is how to use git clean -fdx without weeping later. This guide walks through a dry run preview backing up what matters performing the actual purge and verifying the result with a few safe steps and a dash of common sense.

Preview what would be deleted

Never trust a destructive command until you have seen its shopping list. From the repository root run a dry run to see candidate files without deleting anything.

git clean -ndx

The flags explained in plain English

  • -n shows a dry run so nothing is removed
  • -f forces the removal when you are actually ready
  • -d removes untracked directories as well as files
  • -x also deletes files that match ignore rules so ignored build artifacts do not survive

Back up anything you secretly care about

  • Copy files to a safe folder outside the repo

  • Make a zip of the working directory for maximum paranoia

Run the purge when comfortable

git clean -fdx

Exclude patterns if a file looks disposable but is not

If you want to protect certain files use the exclude option during the dry run to confirm behavior first.

git clean -e build/cache -ndx

Verify the cleanup

After the purge check the working tree and run another dry run to confirm nothing else is queued for deletion.

  • git status will show a clean working tree if you removed everything untracked
  • Run git clean -ndx again to verify there are no surprises left

Quick checklist before you hit enter

  • Did you run git clean -ndx and review the list
  • Did you back up any file that matters
  • Did you exclude patterns that should remain
  • Are you ready to lose ignored build artifacts and other untracked cruft

Summary in one sulky sentence git clean -ndx lets you preview what will be removed git clean -fdx actually removes untracked and ignored files and a quick backup or temporary branch will save you from the classic regret at 3 am. Proceed like a cautious vandal and you will survive intact.
