title: Difference between HashMap and Hashtable in Java
description: Quick guide on key differences between HashMap and Hashtable in Java covering synchronization null keys performance iteration and modern alternatives
heading: Difference between HashMap and Hashtable in Java Explained
body:
Quick verdict you can actually use

HashMap is the fast, unsupervised option that lets you store one null key and many null values. Hashtable is the older sibling that forces synchronization and rejects nulls. For real concurrent work use ConcurrentHashMap instead unless you enjoy hunting race conditions for fun.

Thread safety and synchronization explained without the panic

HashMap does not provide built in synchronization. That means if two threads try to update it at the same time bad things can happen like corrupted internal state or infinite loops when resizing. HashMap is fine for single thread scenarios or when you control synchronization externally.

Hashtable synchronizes its methods so every operation grabs a lock. That makes it thread safe in a crude way but also slow in highly concurrent usage. It is a legacy class that predates the modern Collections framework which is why it still exists in some dusty codebases.

Practical takeaway

  • Use HashMap for most single thread or externally synchronized code.
  • Do not reach for Hashtable for new code unless you are maintaining ancient libraries.
  • Prefer ConcurrentHashMap for scalable concurrent reads and writes.

Null keys and values and why Java cares

HashMap allows one null key and many null values. This is convenient but can bite you if you rely on null to mean missing. Hashtable throws a runtime exception if you try to insert a null key or null value. So if null handling matters pick accordingly.

Performance and iteration behavior

HashMap is faster in typical single thread scenarios because it avoids locking on every operation. Hashtable pays for method level synchronization on nearly every call which makes it slower under light loads.

Iterators from HashMap are fail fast and will throw ConcurrentModificationException when the map is modified during iteration by another thread. That is actually useful because it fails loudly so you can fix your concurrency bug.

Hashtable offers legacy enumerations that do not exhibit the same fail fast behavior which can hide concurrent modification bugs until they manifest as corrupted data.

Better alternatives for concurrency

If you need safe concurrent access with good throughput choose ConcurrentHashMap. It uses finer grained internal locking and modern techniques to scale much better than Hashtable or a synchronized wrapper. Another option is Collections.synchronizedMap with explicit external locking around iteration when you need it.

Example declarations without ceremony

Map<String Integer> hashMap = new HashMap<>()

Map<String Integer> hashtable = new Hashtable<>()

Map<String Integer> concurrent = new ConcurrentHashMap<>()

Which one should you pick

  • Pick HashMap for normal use where you control threading
  • Pick ConcurrentHashMap when multiple threads do frequent reads and writes
  • Avoid Hashtable unless you are stuck maintaining legacy code that cannot be changed

Final pro tip stop treating Hashtable as a default safe choice. It is a historical artifact that will slow you down and make your code look like it was written when phones were bricks. Use the right map and sleep better at night.
seo_title: HashMap vs Hashtable in Java pick the right map for threads
seo_heading: Deciding between HashMap Hashtable and ConcurrentHashMap for safety and speed

title: git stash changes
description: Quick guide to save list apply and manage uncommitted changes with git stash for safe context switching and tidy commits
heading: git stash changes guide
body:
Practical stash workflows for git on the command line and branches

If you ever need to abandon a half finished change without committing your sins to history git stash is the polite little dumpster that saves your work until you are ready to face it again. This guide covers the commands you actually use on the CLI and the decisions that keep your repo from becoming a graveyard of WIP.

Why stash exists

Sometimes you need to switch branches fast to fix something urgent and you do not want to commit a messy patch. Stash temporarily stores modified tracked files and optionally untracked files so you can switch context and come back later without polluting commit history.

Save uncommitted work

Want to park changes with a note so future you has some clue what was happening use:

git stash push -m 'WIP: refactor widget layout'

If you also want to stash untracked files add -u like this:

git stash push -u -m 'WIP including new test file'

The stash is stored in a stack so the most recent entry is stash@{0} and it behaves like a little time capsule.

Inspect stash list and contents

Do not blindly pop things unless you enjoy surprises. Check what is saved and why with:

  • git stash list to see entries and their messages
  • git stash show -p stash@{0} to peek at the diffs in an entry

This helps avoid applying the wrong stash to the wrong branch which is a special kind of chaos.

Apply or pop a stash

Two main options exist. Use apply to bring changes back while keeping the stash around. Use pop if you are confident and want the stash removed in one go.

  • git stash apply stash@{0} to reapply and keep the stash
  • git stash pop stash@{0} to reapply and delete that stash entry

If changes conflict treat it like a small merge and resolve files as usual with git add and git commit. Conflicts are annoying but honest.

Create a branch from a stash

When a stash deserves more than a temporary bin give it a proper home in a branch and rescue the work in one command:

git stash branch feature-from-stash stash@{0}

This creates the branch checks it out and applies the stash. It is the polite way to promote experimental work into a real branch without manual cherry picking.

Drop or clear stashes

Stash entries accumulate and then someone asks why disk space is weird. Keep the list tidy with these commands

  • git stash drop stash@{0} to remove one entry
  • git stash clear to wipe the whole stash stack if you are feeling ruthless

Quick tips and best practices

  • Use descriptive messages with git stash push -m 'short message' so future you does not stare at a list of cryptic timestamps
  • Prefer git stash branch when the stash contains work that should become a proper branch
  • Remember that stash stores tracked changes by default use -u to include untracked files
  • Think of stash as temporary not permanent backups and do not hoard entries for months

That covers the core stash workflows you will use on the CLI. Use stash to keep context switches fast and your commit history clean. And if you ever wonder what happened to that prototype in stash@{4} the answer is probably yes it is still there until you drop it or clear the stack.
seo_title: Master git stash for quick context switches and tidy history
seo_heading: Practical stash workflows for git on the command line and branches

title: git stash pop example
description: Learn how to use git stash pop to apply saved changes handle conflicts and keep the stash stack tidy with a practical example
heading: git stash pop example explained for developers
body:
So you made a dozen edits, broke nothing important yet and then a fire alarm called your name. Welcome to git stash pop the tool that lets you temporarily hide your half baked genius and then bring it back when the coast is clear.

Create a stash and keep your workspace sane

When you need to switch context fast use the stash to avoid committing junk. Run one of these commands to save your work:

git stash push -m "short description"
# or the shorthand
git stash

The working directory reverts to the last commit so you can switch branches or test a quick fix without your local chaos sabotaging everything.

Switch branches and do the thing you actually needed

Checkout a different branch or make the change that called you away. The stash sits on a stack until you decide you are ready to bring those changes back. No magic required and no judgment yet.

Bring the stash back with git stash pop

When you are ready to restore your changes run:

git stash pop
# to apply a specific entry
git stash pop stash@{n}

By default pop applies the latest stash and removes it from the stack. If something goes sideways and the stash did not drop run git stash drop stash@{n} to remove the stale entry manually.

What if there are merge conflicts

If your stash touches the same lines as the current branch you may see merge conflicts. Use the normal conflict resolution workflow. Typical steps look like this

  • Open the conflicted files and resolve differences
  • Stage the resolved files with git add
  • Create a commit with git commit to record the merged result

If you want to avoid applying and dropping the stash in one go you can use git stash apply instead of pop. That keeps the stash on the stack until you confirm everything worked.

Inspect and clean up leftover stashes

Use these commands to see what is hiding in the stack and to tidy up when stashes are no longer useful.

git stash list
# remove a single stash
git stash drop stash@{n}
# remove everything
git stash clear

Look at the stash list like a tiny archaeological record of your panic edits. Descriptive messages help a lot.

Pro tips for less regret

  • Make stash messages meaningful use git stash push -m "feature name or bug id" so the list tells a story
  • Prefer git stash apply if you are unsure about dropping the stash right away
  • If stash pop fails to drop the entry check stash@{n} and run git stash drop manually

This covers the full loop from saving changes to applying and resolving conflicts using git stash pop. Follow these steps and your developer workflow will be slightly less chaotic and slightly more heroic.
seo_title: Stop losing work with git stash pop and smarter stashing
seo_heading: Practical git stash pop workflow for handling stashes and merge conflicts

title: How to install UiPath Studio
description: Quick guide to download install and activate UiPath Studio with troubleshooting notes and first run tips for automation beginners and pros
heading: How to install UiPath Studio step by step
body:
Ready to build RPA or just curious what UiPath Studio looks like

If you want to install UiPath Studio and start automating boring tasks on Windows this guide will get you there without the usual panic. You will create an account download the installer pick the right profile install required packages and activate a license. Yes it is mostly clicks and yes it will work if you follow the steps.

Before you start

Quick checklist so nothing explodes later

  • Windows PC with admin access
  • An email for your UiPath account
  • Internet access to download the installer and license files
  • Some patience if this is your first RPA setup

Step by step install and setup

Follow these steps to install UiPath Studio and verify the core functionality. This works for the Community edition and for enterprise installs using a license key or Orchestrator based activation.

1 Create a UiPath account

Go to the official UiPath portal and sign up with a work or personal email. The Community edition is free for learning and small teams. Creating an account unlocks downloads and license options so do not skip this step unless you enjoy being blocked.

2 Download the Studio installer

From the portal download the latest stable Studio release for production use or grab a preview build if you like living on the edge. Save the installer somewhere obvious so you do not stage a frantic file hunt later.

3 Run the installer with admin rights

Right click run as administrator and follow the wizard. Say yes to any Windows prompts that ask to make changes. If you deny permission the installer will fail and then we will both pretend it was a mystery.

4 Choose a profile and optional packages

Select the profile that matches your needs. Studio Pro offers advanced functionality for enterprise developers while Studio is perfect for most automation tasks. Add common packages like UI Automation and Excel integration if you will automate user interfaces or spreadsheet work. You can add more later but picking the basics now saves time.

5 Activate your license

Pick the activation path that fits your situation

  • Community edition users follow the free activation flow from the portal
  • Enterprise users enter the license key or connect Studio to Orchestrator for centralized license management

License activation verifies your product and gives you access to enterprise features. If anything goes wrong contact your admin or UiPath support before throwing the laptop out a window.

First project sanity check

Open UiPath Studio and create a new project from a template. Familiarize yourself with the Designer panel the Activities panel and the Project panel. Run a simple Hello World or a text type automation to confirm runtime and packages are working.

Simple verify steps

  1. Create a sequence and add a Write Line or Message Box activity
  2. Run the workflow and confirm output appears
  3. Install any missing packages using the Manage Packages dialog

Troubleshooting notes that will save time

If the installer fails check that you ran it as administrator and that no antivirus blocked the process. If a package does not load try clearing the NuGet cache or reinstalling the package from Manage Packages. For licensing problems verify your key and make sure Studio can reach the activation servers if you are not using Orchestrator.

Final tips for beginners

  • Keep the installer and license emails in a safe folder so you do not hunt for them later
  • Start with simple automations to learn the Designer and Activities
  • Use the Community edition to practice before moving to an enterprise setup
  • Search UiPath documentation and community forum for samples and help

This tutorial covered account creation download installation profile selection license activation and first project creation so you can start building automations in UiPath Studio without losing your hair. Now go automate something tedious and feel slightly more like a wizard than a glorified clicker.

title: UiPath Studio Hello World Example
description: Quick Hello World tutorial for UiPath Studio showing how to create a project add a sequence use a message box and run the workflow
heading: UiPath Studio Hello World Example Tutorial
body:
If you want to feel like a wizard without actually learning magic then welcome to UiPath Studio Hello World land. This short tutorial walks a beginner through creating a Process project, adding a Sequence, and popping up a Message Box that says something human readable like "Hello World". It is friendly to humans and robots alike.

What you will build with UiPath Studio

A tiny automation that opens a Message Box during a run. The project uses a Process template, a single Sequence workflow in Main.xaml, and one Message Box activity. That is it. Minimal glory. Maximum learning.

Quick setup and steps

  1. Open UiPath Studio and pick Process from the start screen. Give the project a name such as HelloWorld and click Create to generate the workspace.
  2. In the Project panel open Main.xaml. If you prefer a fresh container create a new Sequence from the New menu. Sequences provide a linear flow that beginners can follow without drama.
  3. Open the Activities panel and search for Message Box. Drag the Message Box activity into your Sequence where you want the popup to appear.
  4. Select the Message Box activity and set the Text property to "Hello World" or any funny greeting that will not offend your laptop.
  5. Press the Run button in the ribbon to execute the workflow. A Message Box window should appear showing your greeting. Close the popup to finish the run and check the Output or Logs for any notes or errors.

Why use a Sequence in this tutorial

A Sequence gives you a straightforward linear flow that is easy to debug and understand. For a single Message Box the Sequence is efficient and low drama. When your life gets complicated you can explore Flowcharts and State Machines for more advanced workflows.

Beginner tips that do not make you look clueless

  • Prefer Write Line for background logging so your popup does not hog the show. Write Line writes to the Output panel and is great for tracing.
  • Use variables when you want dynamic messages. For example create a String variable greeting and set Message Box Text to greeting so you can change content without editing the activity every time.
  • Name activities clearly. "Message Box1" may be accurate but it will make your future self cry.
  • Run often and inspect the Output and Execution Logs. Errors exist to teach you humility and better automation design.

Quick recap and next moves

You created a Process project, added a Sequence to Main.xaml, dropped a Message Box into the flow, set its Text to "Hello World", and ran the workflow to see the popup. Congratulations on your tiny automation victory.

When you are ready to graduate from greeting pixels try replacing the Message Box with activities that read files, type into applications, or chain multiple sequences with arguments. The same fundamentals scale up, and your computer will learn to do boring work so you do not have to.

title: UiPath variables and input boxes example
description: Short guide to using UiPath variables and Input Dialog activities to capture user input and pass values through a workflow.
heading: UiPath variables and input boxes example for capturing user input
body:
Why user input matters in UiPath workflows

This short tutorial shows how to stop your robot from guessing and start asking. Use UiPath variables and the Input Dialog activity to get user input, sanitize it, and pass it along so the rest of your automation does not throw a tantrum. This is a practical guide for RPA developers who like predictable results and hate surprises.

What you will learn

  • How to create variables with the right data types and scope
  • How to wire an Input Dialog output into a variable
  • How to validate and parse user input with safe checks
  • How to use the value in an Assign activity and avoid silent failures

Set up variables the boring but important way

Create variables first and pick the right type. If the user will enter text use String. For numbers use Int32 or Double depending on the precision you need. Name variables so a future you or another human will not cry when reading the workflow. Examples include userName, quantity, or orderAmount.

Scope matters. If a variable is too narrow you will see missing value errors. If it is too wide you will run into accidental reuse. Keep scope as small as possible while still covering the activities that need the value.

Add an Input Dialog and bind the output

Drag an Input Dialog where interaction is required. Set a clear Title and Label so the user does not panic. In the Output field bind the result to the variable you created earlier. The dialog writes the text straight into that variable when the user clicks OK.

If you need a default value put one in the Input Dialog. That prevents blank submissions for quick tests and reduces the frequency of human error during demos.

Sample wiring

Input Dialog Output -> userInputString

Validate and parse user input like a responsible developer

Never trust human typed values. If you expect numbers use Int32.TryParse to convert safely. That returns a boolean success flag and an out parameter with the parsed value. For text use Trim to remove accidental spaces and a length check to reject tiny or massive strings.

  • Numbers example: Int32.TryParse(userInputString, out parsedInt)
  • Text example: userInputString = userInputString.Trim()
  • Simple guard: check for String.IsNullOrEmpty before processing

If parsing fails show a friendly message or loop the Input Dialog until you get something reasonable. Do not crash the workflow unless you enjoy digging through logs at 2 AM.

Use the value in actions

Once parsed and validated you can use the value in an Assign activity, an If condition, or pass it to an API call. Keep variable names explicit so the action is obvious. For example use totalItems = parsedInt or customerName = userName.

Debugging tips to stop guessing

  • Log the raw input and the parsed result with informative messages so you can follow the data flow
  • Use breakpoints and the Locals panel to inspect values at runtime
  • Watch for empty strings when scope is wrong or when the dialog was skipped in a test branch

Best practices for workflow design

  • Prefer explicit names and narrow scope to reduce scope related bugs
  • Validate early and often to avoid propagating bad data
  • Provide helpful prompts in the Input Dialog to reduce user confusion
  • Wrap risky sections in Try Catch and log exceptions with context for easier debugging

That is the essence of using UiPath Input Dialogs and variables to get predictable user input into your RPA automation. It keeps workflows readable, debuggable, and kinder to future you. Now go forth and automate with slightly less chaos.
seo_title: Make UiPath workflows friendlier with Input Dialogs and variables
seo_heading: Capture and validate user input in UiPath for robust RPA workflows

title: UiPath Read, Write and Filter CSV Files Example
description: Learn how to read write and filter CSV files in UiPath with clear steps and simple examples for reliable RPA data handling
heading: UiPath Read Write and Filter CSV Files Example
body:
This tutorial shows how to read write and filter CSV files using UiPath so a workflow can ingest transform and export tabular data without drama.

  1. Read the CSV into a DataTable
  2. Filter or transform the DataTable
  3. Write the result back to a CSV
  4. Add validation and error handling

Read the CSV

Use the Read CSV activity. Point the FilePath to the source file and store the result in a DataTable variable named table or whatever naming convention pleases the team. Use the delimiter setting if the file uses a separator other than comma.

Filter or transform the DataTable

Apply a filter with table.Select("Age > 30") to get rows matching a condition. Convert the result to a new DataTable with filtered = selected.CopyToDataTable() when needed. For column edits use a For Each row loop and assign values with row("ColumnName") = newValue.

Write the result back to a CSV

Use the Write CSV activity. Set the Input to the DataTable variable and provide a FilePath for the output. Choose overwrite behavior or move previous files to an archive folder if preserving history matters.

Add validation and error handling

Validate that the DataTable has rows before calling CopyToDataTable. Surround file operations with Try Catch to log access problems and to handle locked files or missing headers with grace.

Summary of the workflow reads a CSV into a DataTable filters or edits rows and then writes a clean CSV back to disk while including basic checks to prevent runtime surprises.

Tip

For consistent parsing specify a culture aware delimiter and trim whitespace from column values early. That prevents weird failures when source files come from different systems.

title: UiPath Keep Filter and Append CSV Example
description: Concise UiPath tutorial showing how to keep filtered rows and append them to a CSV for reliable automation and clean data flow.
heading: UiPath Keep Filter And Append CSV Example
body:
Quick overview

If you are automating CSV updates with UiPath in an RPA workflow and you want to keep only the good rows while appending them to an existing file without creating a duplicate mess this guide shows a tidy way to do it. We will use Read CSV, Filter Data Table in Keep mode and a safe append method so your CSV history stays intact and your boss stays calm.

What you will need

  • UiPath Studio and the CSV activities available in your package feed
  • A source CSV to Read CSV into a DataTable variable such as dtInput
  • A target CSV path to receive appended rows
  • Basic knowledge of DataTable operations in UiPath

Step 1 Read CSV and prep the DataTable

Use the Read CSV activity to load the source file into dtInput. Check encoding and headers while you are at it. If the column order or types are inconsistent normalize them now. Think of this step as grooming your data so it behaves later on.

Step 2 Apply the Keep filter

Drag a Filter Data Table activity and set it to Keep rows mode. Define the column conditions or a custom expression that matches the rows you actually care about. Send the output to dtFiltered. This removes the background noise and leaves only what matters.

Filter tips

  • Use exact column names to avoid silent mismatches
  • Trim and normalize case when you compare strings
  • For complex logic use a custom expression or a small LINQ query if you prefer

Step 3 Append the filtered rows to the CSV

You have two common options here. Use an Append To CSV activity from a known package if you have it. Or open a StreamWriter with append set to true and write rows manually. Either way make sure you do not write headers again if the file already exists. A quick check using System.IO.File.Exists will tell you whether to add the header line.

Header and format checklist

  • Write headers only when the file is new or empty
  • Match column order and data types between dtFiltered and the target
  • Escape commas and quotes the same way the target CSV expects

Step 4 Validate and dedupe

After appending read the target CSV back into a DataTable and compare row counts or key columns. If duplicates are a worry use a unique key column to remove repeats. A common pattern is to DataTable.Merge the new rows into the existing DataTable and then call DefaultView.ToTable(true) to get distinct rows. That keeps duplicates from stacking up like bad decisions.

Example dedupe flow

  • Read existing CSV to dtTarget
  • Merge dtFiltered into dtTarget using dtTarget.Merge(dtFiltered)
  • Create a distinct table with dtUnique = dtTarget.DefaultView.ToTable(true)
  • Write dtUnique back to CSV if you prefer a clean rewrite instead of append

Practical tips that save time

  • Normalize column names and order before appending to avoid misaligned rows
  • Use a consistent header list across pipelines in your RPA projects
  • Keep a unique key or hash column for easy dedupe checks
  • Log counts before and after append so troubleshooting is less painful

Final thoughts

This approach keeps your automation predictable. Read CSV into a DataTable, use Filter Data Table in Keep mode to isolate the rows you want, append carefully and validate with a dedupe step when necessary. Follow these steps and your CSV files will remain useful instead of becoming a forensic artifact for the next person who opens them.

If you want a canned example to paste into UiPath skip the drama and set up a small workflow with Read CSV, Filter Data Table, and Append To CSV or a StreamWriter write. Then add a quick validation read and a merge with DefaultView.ToTable(true) for peace of mind.

Now go automate something and let the computer handle the tedious parts. You do the clever stuff and the jokes about spreadsheets can wait until the build passes.
seo_title: Append CSVs in UiPath with Keep Filter and avoid duplicates
seo_heading: Step by step UiPath tutorial for filtering DataTable and appending CSV safely

title: Simple UiPath write to Excel example
description: Learn how to use UiPath Write Range to export data to Excel with Excel Application Scope and basic error handling
heading: Simple UiPath write to Excel example tutorial
body:
Quick summary

Want to shove a DataTable from UiPath into an Excel file and have it actually behave when you run it again tomorrow Not mystical black magic here just the Write Range activity inside an Excel Application Scope with a little common sense error handling

What you will build

An automated export that writes a DataTable to a workbook sheet while avoiding hardcoded paths and failing loudly but helpfully when the file is locked or missing

Prerequisites

  • UiPath Studio installed
  • Basic familiarity with DataTable and activities like Build Data Table Read CSV Read Range and Write Range
  • An Excel file to target or a path where the workflow can create one

Why follow these patterns

Because your future self and coworkers will thank you if you do not hardcode file paths or ignore AddHeaders. Also because explicit error handling stops silent failures that make scheduled jobs look mischievous

Step by step guide

Follow these steps and you will have a clean export that does not explode when Excel decides to be dramatic

  1. Create the project and the data

    Create a new process and either use Build Data Table to hand craft a sample DataTable or use Read CSV or Read Range to pull existing data. Name your variables clearly so debugging does not feel like archaeology.

  2. Use Excel Application Scope

    Drop Excel Application Scope and set the workbook path using a project argument or config variable. This prevents failures when you move the workflow to another machine or to Orchestrator.

  3. Prepare the DataTable

    Confirm column types match what you expect. Mismatched types cause fun little exceptions when Write Range meets reality. If you created sample data use Build Data Table and set column types explicitly.

  4. Add the Write Range activity

    Place Write Range inside the Excel Application Scope. Provide your DataTable variable set AddHeaders to True if you want the column names and leave Range empty to start at A1 unless you need an offset.

  5. Wrap with Try Catch

    Wrap the Excel Application Scope in Try Catch to handle common issues like file locked or missing file access. In the Catch log a friendly message and rethrow or handle according to your retry policy.

  6. Run and verify

    Execute the workflow and open the workbook to confirm the rows and columns appeared as expected. If headers are missing check AddHeaders and inspect the DataTable column names.

Suggested error handling and logging

  • Catch specific exceptions like IOException and display a clear log message that tells you which file path failed
  • Use retries or a friendly notification when the file is locked by a user or process

title: UiPath Remove Data Column Example
description: Learn how to remove a data column from a UiPath DataTable with clear steps alternatives and common pitfalls
heading: UiPath Remove Data Column Example
body:
So you have a DataTable full of secrets and unnecessary columns and you want to purge the excess without starting a small data rebellion. Welcome to the cheerful world of UiPath DataTable manipulation. This guide covers the visual Remove Data Column activity, code alternatives, and practical safety checks so your automation does not explode in front of stakeholders.

Prepare the DataTable

First things first, make the DataTable. You can build one with Build Data Table when you are feeling fancy, or read a sheet from Excel with Read Range when the spreadsheet gremlins are in charge. Name your DataTable variable something sensible like dt or dtSales, not columnSoup. Confirm the exact column name or index before you try to remove it. The platform will not be kind if you guess.

Quick sanity checks

  • Read Range into a DataTable variable for Excel automation and testing
  • Use dt.Columns.Contains("ColumnName") to check existence before removal
  • Work on a copy during development so you do not erase the original data forever

Use the Remove Data Column activity in UiPath Studio

This is the designer friendly option and the one your non coder colleagues will appreciate. Add Remove Data Column to your sequence and set the DataTable property to the target variable. For the Column property you can either put the column name as a string or use an index expression when you must rely on position. It is simple and visual and behaves predictably when you have the name right.

Example settings

  • DataTable: dtSales
  • Column: "Discount" or dt.Columns.IndexOf("Discount")

Code alternatives for more control

If you prefer code or need to do more advanced manipulation use Assign activities or Invoke Code to call DataTable methods. These are concise and avoid dragging extra activities into the workflow.

dt.Columns.Remove("ColumnName")
dt.Columns.RemoveAt(2)

To recreate a new table with only the columns you want use the DefaultView trick. This is handy when you need to drop many columns and care about performance and clarity.

dt = dt.DefaultView.ToTable(false, "KeepCol1", "KeepCol2")

Test and handle errors

Never remove columns in production without testing. Wrap risky operations in Try Catch so your robot can fail gracefully and give helpful logs instead of cryptic stack traces. Missing column errors and index out of range exceptions are common and entirely preventable.

Practical error handling

  • Check presence first with dt.Columns.Contains("ColumnName")
  • Use Try Catch around the Remove Data Column activity or around your Assign call
  • Log the exception message so you actually know what went wrong

When to prefer activities versus code

Use the Remove Data Column activity when you want readability and maintainability in UiPath Studio. Use code when you need loops, dynamic column lists, or better performance for large DataTables. Both approaches are valid. Your choice should be driven by who will maintain the process and how complex the column logic is.

Checklist before you hit run

  • Confirm column names or indexes exist
  • Test on a copy of the DataTable
  • Add Try Catch and logging for predictable behavior
  • Document the change so future you does not curse present you

That is the gist. Remove Data Column activity for the visual fans, dt.Columns.Remove and RemoveAt for quick code control, DefaultView.ToTable to rebuild tables with only the columns you actually want. Use checks and error handling to avoid runtime drama and keep your RPA workflows living their best life.

title: UiPath For Each Row Example
description: Quick guide to using UiPath For Each Row to iterate a DataTable handle data conversions and avoid common errors
heading: UiPath For Each Row Example for DataTable Looping
body:
Quick setup and why this matters

If you want your UiPath automation to behave like a reliable grown up and not like a spreadsheet that drank too much coffee last night then start with a tidy DataTable. Use Read Range for Excel inputs or Build Data Table for quick tests. A clear schema prevents surprise DBNull values and makes parsing less dramatic.

Step by step For Each Row basics

Add a For Each Row activity and point the DataTable property at the table you prepared. Name the loop variable something readable such as currentRow so your workflow reads like documentation and not like a cursed treasure map.

  • Read Range or Build Data Table to get a DataTable object
  • Place For Each Row in a sequence and set the DataTable property
  • Use a descriptive row variable name such as currentRow

Access cell values without crying

Prefer column names for clarity rather than numeric indexes. Both work but one reads well in three months when you are trying to remember what column 4 stood for.

currentRow("Name").ToString
currentRow(0).ToString

If a column might be DBNull handle it before parsing. Defensive code will save your weekend plans.

Dim price As Decimal
If IsDBNull(currentRow("Price")) Then
  price = 0D
Else
  price = Decimal.Parse(currentRow("Price").ToString())
End If

Convert numbers the smart way

Integer.Parse will work until it does not. TryParse gives you the option to survive messy data with dignity.

Dim age As Integer
If Integer.TryParse(currentRow("Age").ToString(), age) Then
  ' use age safely here
Else
  age = 0
End If

In UiPath you can do the same with Assign activities and variables. Wrap risky logic in a Try Catch activity if the data comes from sources that enjoy chaos.

Filter before you loop and save CPU and sanity

Looping a giant DataTable is fine if you like long waits and regret. Filter rows first with LINQ to reduce work. This is great for large tables or when you only need a subset of rows.

Dim filtered = myTable.AsEnumerable().Where(Function(r) Not IsDBNull(r("Status")) AndAlso r("Status").ToString() = "Active")
If filtered.Any() Then
  Dim reduced = filtered.CopyToDataTable()
End If

Note that CopyToDataTable will throw if filtered is empty. Handle that case or use safe checks.

Debugging and error handling that does not suck

  • Use Breakpoints in the loop to pause on suspicious rows
  • Add Log Message activities to print currentRow values so you can see why the robot is sad
  • Wrap parsing in Try Catch to capture bad data and continue processing

When a spreadsheet is actively trying to ruin your day use TryParse checks and default fallbacks. Column name usage improves readability and reduces accidental off by one horrors.

Recap and final tips

This guide covered preparing a DataTable, adding For Each Row, accessing values, handling nulls and conversions, filtering with LINQ, and basic debugging. The takeaway is simple. Be defensive. Prefer TryParse or Convert methods over blind parsing. Filter early to speed things up. And name your variables so future you does not rage quit.

One last pro tip. If you ever need to process millions of rows then consider batching, filtering, or leaving the computer to its quiet contemplation while you get coffee. A tiny bit of defensive coding saves many hours of debugging and a few tears.

title: Remove duplicate rows in Excel with UiPath Example
description: Learn how to remove duplicate rows from Excel using UiPath Read Range and DataTable techniques for clean automation
heading: Remove duplicate rows in Excel with UiPath Example
body:
Duplicates in Excel are like that one friend who shows up uninvited and never leaves. If you automate with UiPath you can evict those rows with minimal drama and no human judgment required. This guide walks through reading a sheet into a DataTable removing duplicate rows and writing the cleaned table back to Excel. Keep backups and a sense of humor.

What you need before you start

Make sure you have UiPath Studio with Excel activities and a basic workflow that can open the workbook. You will use Excel Application Scope Read Range DataTable methods and Write Range. The primary keyword to remember is DataTable since that is where the magic happens.

Step 1 Read the worksheet into a DataTable

Use Excel Application Scope and inside it place Read Range. Set the output to a DataTable variable named dt. If your sheet has headers check the property for headers. Leave the range blank to read the used range or specify a range if you want to limit the input.

Step 2 Option A use DataTable DefaultView ToTable to get distinct rows

This option is code light and fast. The trick is to specify the columns that determine uniqueness instead of trying to dedupe every cell in the row. For example use an Assign activity with the expression

dt = dt.DefaultView.ToTable(true, "Column1", "Column2")

Here true tells ToTable to keep only unique combinations of Column1 and Column2. If you need more key columns add them to the list. This method preserves only the first occurrence of each unique key combo so be careful if other columns contain important differing values.

Step 3 Option B use UiPath activities to remove duplicates

If you prefer visual activities try Remove Duplicate Rows or Filter Data Table. Configure the activity to match on the columns that define a duplicate. Filter Data Table can be used to keep rows that match a condition or to remove rows that match a duplicate pattern. The Remove Duplicate Rows activity is convenient when you only care about exact duplicates across chosen columns.

Example workflow with activities

  • Excel Application Scope open workbook
  • Read Range into dt
  • Use Remove Duplicate Rows or Filter Data Table to produce dtClean
  • Write Range to a new sheet or overwrite existing data

Step 4 Write the cleaned DataTable back to Excel

Use Write Range inside Excel Application Scope to save dt or dtClean to a sheet. You can write to a new sheet to keep the original file intact while testing. Always keep a backup until you are perfectly sure your logic does not eat important data.

Tips and gotchas that will save your career

  • Pick key columns that actually define uniqueness. Do not include noisy columns like timestamps unless you want to keep every row.
  • Test on a small sample before running on the full dataset to avoid accidental data loss.
  • If you need to preserve a specific row among duplicates add a sort step first so the preferred row appears first.
  • Use Write Range to a new sheet during testing so you have a safety copy.

Troubleshooting

If dt.DefaultView.ToTable returns fewer rows than expected double check that you listed the right columns. If activities fail check that headers are recognized and that the DataTable schema matches your expectations. Logging the row counts before and after the operation helps find where things went wrong.

That is all. You read the sheet you removed the duplicates and you wrote the clean table back. Throw a little celebratory confetti or just close the workbook and call it a day. Automation saved time and human sanity was preserved.

title: How to read Outlook email subjects in UiPath Studio example
description: Learn how to read Outlook email subjects in UiPath Studio using Read Outlook Mail Messages For Each and Subject extraction for automation workflows
heading: How to Read Outlook Email Subjects in UiPath Studio Example
body:
Why this matters and why you should care

If your automation needs to decide what to do based on email subjects then you do not need a miracle. You need UiPath Mail activities and a tiny bit of common sense. This guide will show how to fetch messages from Outlook and pull the subject text into your workflow without sending your robot into inbox purgatory.

What you will use

  • UiPath Studio with UiPath.Mail.Activities installed
  • Read Outlook Mail Messages activity to pull messages
  • A variable typed as IEnumerable(Of System.Net.Mail.MailMessage) or List(Of System.Net.Mail.MailMessage)
  • For Each set to TypeArgument System.Net.Mail.MailMessage
  • Log Message or Assign to handle the currentMail.Subject value

Step by step workflow

Follow these steps and pretend it was your idea all along. I will not judge.

  • Install the package Open Manage Packages and search for UiPath.Mail.Activities then install the version that matches your Studio. Compatibility complaints are normal and harmless so be annoyed briefly and move on.
  • Use Read Outlook Mail Messages Drag the activity into the sequence and set MailFolder to where your messages live. Set Top to a small number when testing so you do not fetch the entire internet. If you have multiple mailboxes set Account or Mailbox to the one you want. Use Filter to limit results when the inbox looks like a hoarder.
  • Store the output Create a variable of type IEnumerable(Of System.Net.Mail.MailMessage) or List(Of System.Net.Mail.MailMessage). Assign the Output property from Read Outlook Mail Messages to that variable.
  • Loop over messages Add a For Each activity and set TypeArgument to System.Net.Mail.MailMessage. Point the For Each to your variable. Inside the loop you will reference currentMail.Subject to get the subject line text.
  • Clean and validate Subjects can be messy. Use Trim to remove stray spaces and a regular expression when patterns matter. Wrap parsing logic in a Try Catch block to handle unexpected encodings or null values without crashing your whole run.
  • Log or route Send the cleaned subject to Log Message or store it in an Assign for downstream logic. From there you can route subjects to queues, files, or decision tables as needed.

Example checks to add inside the loop

  • Use If String.IsNullOrEmpty(currentMail.Subject) to skip blank subjects
  • Use currentMail.Subject.Trim to remove leading and trailing whitespace
  • Use System.Text.RegularExpressions.Regex.Match when you need to extract invoice numbers or dates

Troubleshooting and best practices

Here are practical tips that stop your robot from behaving like it had coffee for the first time.

  • When testing use the Top property to fetch a small sample before scaling to the whole inbox.
  • Use Filter expressions to reduce traffic and speed up tests. For example use a subject filter to pull only messages that matter.
  • Remember the output type is a MailMessage collection. The subject is available on each MailMessage as currentMail.Subject and it is a plain string.
  • Wrap parsing in Try Catch to handle odd encodings or missing headers without failing the entire job.
  • When moving to production consider handing subjects off to queues or files so auditing and retries are easier.

Final sanity check

Run the flow on a handful of emails first and confirm subjects are extracted and cleaned as expected. If the robot behaves, you win. If not, blame the inbox and then debug the filter and Try Catch blocks.

That is all you need to reliably read Outlook email subjects in UiPath Studio and route them where they belong. Go automate something boring and tell your coworkers you saved the company time and not that you just automated their email headaches.

title: UiPath Get Outlook Mail Messages Body Example
description: Learn how to extract email body text with the UiPath Get Outlook Mail Messages activity and feed that content into an automation workflow.
heading: UiPath Get Outlook Mail Messages Body Example
body:
Fast overview of reading Outlook bodies in UiPath

So you want to read the email body with UiPath and do clever things with it. Good news is the Get Outlook Mail Messages activity was made for that exact purpose. This mini tutorial walks through practical steps to fetch MailMessage objects from Outlook, extract the Body text, and keep your automation from repeating itself like a tired playlist.

Step 1 Place the Get Outlook Mail Messages activity

Drag Get Outlook Mail Messages into a Sequence or Flow. If you have more than one Outlook profile set the Account to the right mailbox. If you do not set Account UiPath will use the default Outlook profile and hope for the best.

Step 2 Configure filters and folder

Set MailFolder to Inbox or a subfolder and use Top to limit how many messages are returned. Toggle OnlyUnread to focus on new mail. These filters keep your run time sane and your errors fewer.

  • MailFolder is where UiPath looks for messages
  • Top limits the number of messages to fetch
  • OnlyUnread helps avoid reprocessing old mail

Step 3 Access the Body property in a loop

Use a For Each activity with the type argument set to System.Net.Mail.MailMessage or UiPath.Mail.MailMessage depending on your packages. Inside the loop read the Body property and stash it in a string variable for parsing or saving.

For Each mail As MailMessage In messages
    Dim bodyText As String = mail.Body
    ' parse bodyText or save it for later
Next

Yes that is the whole trick. MailMessage.Body contains the plain text or raw HTML that Outlook delivered. If the message is HTML treat it accordingly.

Step 4 Handle plain text and HTML safely

Not all bodies are equal. Some are plain text and cooperative. Others are HTML and dramatic. For HTML you can either strip tags with a simple regex or use an HTML parsing library to extract the real content. Save the raw Body first so you can debug later without re fetching messages.

  • Keep a copy of the raw body in a file or in a logging queue
  • Use a library for complex HTML parsing to avoid brittle regex hacks
  • Watch out for encoding quirks when non ASCII characters appear

Step 5 Handle errors and mark messages

Wrap the fetch and processing in a Try Catch so network blips and permission problems do not crash your whole robot. After processing use MarkAsRead or Move to archive the message. That prevents duplication and saves your future self from debugging why the same invoice keeps getting processed.

Tips and common pitfalls

  • Attachments are not in Body. Check the Attachments collection when you need files
  • HTML messages may contain inline images or encoded parts. Test with your messy real world examples
  • If you need structured data consider saving the body and running a separate parsing step so changes do not require re fetching mail

Wrap up

Reading the email body with UiPath and Get Outlook Mail Messages is mostly configuration and a small loop. The real work is in parsing messy human text and making sure you mark messages as processed. Do that and your automation will behave more like a reliable coworker and less like that one intern who never files anything.

title: UiPath Get Outlook Message Filter Example
description: Learn how to use UiPath Get Outlook Mail Messages with filter strings to fetch specific emails fast and reliably for automation workflows
heading: UiPath Get Outlook Message Filter Example
body:
Pull only the emails your robot actually needs

Yes I know you wanted every single email in the universe to be part of your workflow. That is not how efficient RPA works. Use the Get Outlook Mail Messages activity in UiPath to grab exactly the messages that matter. You still get to be clever and pretend the robot is thoughtful.

When to pick Get Outlook Mail Messages

Use this activity when Outlook is installed on the robot machine and you need access to the local mailbox. It returns a collection you can loop over and inspect. The output is meant to be stored in a variable typed as List MailMessage for downstream processing.

Key properties to set

  • MailFolder Set to Inbox or a named subfolder to limit the search area.
  • Top Use this during development to limit the number of items returned and keep your CPU from crying.
  • OnlyUnread Skip stuff that has already been handled by humans or other robots.
  • MarkAsRead Flip this when you want to prevent duplicate processing in future runs.
  • Filter A restriction string using Outlook field names to actually focus on relevant messages.

Filter syntax that does the heavy lifting

The Filter field expects Outlook restriction syntax. That means square bracket field names and operators like = LIKE and >=. It looks annoying but it works. Test your filters inside Outlook search first so you do not deploy something that returns everything or nothing.

[Subject] LIKE 'Invoice%'
[ReceivedTime] >= '2020-08-01'
[From] = 'vendor@example.com'
[Subject] LIKE 'Invoice%' AND [ReceivedTime] >= '2023-01-01'

Process the results without making network engineers cry

Store the activity output in a variable named messages and loop with a For Each activity. Each item is a MailMessage so you can inspect Subject From Body and ReceivedTime. Wrap your processing in a Try Catch to handle network blips parsing issues or other delightful surprises.

Practical tips that save time

  • During development use OnlyUnread and Top to limit workload and speed up iteration.
  • Validate filter strings directly in Outlook search before you deploy to production.
  • Use clear date formats like yyyy-MM-dd when filtering by ReceivedTime to avoid locale drama.
  • Combine filters with AND to reduce false positives and make your automation look smarter than it is.

Example flow summary

  1. Drag Get Outlook Mail Messages into a sequence.
  2. Set MailFolder Top OnlyUnread and MarkAsRead as needed.
  3. Build a Filter string and test it in Outlook search.
  4. Save output to a List MailMessage variable named messages.
  5. For Each message in messages inspect fields and handle the email inside a Try Catch.

Filtering reduces processing time and keeps your RPA focused on the emails that count. Follow these tips and your robot will stop playing inbox archaeologist and start doing actual work.

title: Download Gmail attachments with UiPath Studio Example
description: Step by step guide to download Gmail attachments using UiPath Studio with Gmail scope filters message retrieval and file saving best practices
heading: Download Gmail attachments with UiPath Studio Example
body:
Why this workflow matters

If you like repetitive inbox fishing and manual save dialogs then this tutorial is not for you. If you prefer machines doing boring work so humans can do slightly more interesting things then welcome. This guide shows a compact UiPath Studio workflow that connects to Gmail, finds messages with attachments, and saves those files to disk with basic error handling and reliable file naming.

What you will use

  • UiPath Studio and the Gmail activities pack
  • Gmail Scope with OAuth credentials for secure access
  • Get Mail Messages to fetch targeted emails
  • Looping and file activities like Save Attachments, Write File, or Write Bytes
  • Try Catch for file and IO handling and basic logging

Overview of the flow

High level steps that your nice obedient robot will follow

  • Authorize the Gmail account with the Gmail Scope activity and OAuth credentials
  • Configure Get Mail Messages with query filters to limit the hits
  • Loop through the returned list with For Each and process each mail
  • Save attachments to disk while preventing filename collisions and logging the result
  • Use Try Catch to trap IO problems and move tricky messages to a review folder

Authorize Gmail access the right way

Use the Gmail Scope activity and supply OAuth client credentials. Grant permission only for what you need such as reading messages and accessing attachments. Store credentials in Orchestrator assets or Windows Credential Manager so the robot is not babysitting a password in a notes file.

Build a focused Get Mail Messages query

Filters are your friend. Configure Get Mail Messages to reduce noise and runtime by using filter values like from, subject, hasAttachment true and maxMessages. Tight queries make your workflow faster and less likely to accidentally download someone else s vacation photos.

Loop and extract attachments

Return value of Get Mail Messages is a list of MailMessage objects. Use For Each over that list. Inside the loop you have two reasonable options

  • Use the built in Save Attachments activity which handles simple cases
  • Or iterate the Attachments collection and use Write File or Write Bytes for more control over filenames and encoding

Filename strategy

Name files so they never collide and so you can trace them back to the message. Prepend a timestamp or include the message id and the sender. For example use a format like yyyyMMdd_HHmmss_sender_filename.ext or include the MailMessage MessageId. Check if a file exists before writing to avoid overwrites.

Error handling and retries

Wrap disk operations in Try Catch to catch permission and IO exceptions. When something fails move the message to a review label or folder and write a log entry with the message id, sender and the target path. That makes post mortem less painful than guessing which email caused the crash.

Run and verify

Execute the workflow in Studio and watch the Output panel for logs. Inspect the target folder to confirm saved files. If attachments are missing tweak your query filters or add additional logging for message headers and attachment names to pinpoint the problem.

Troubleshooting tips

  • If OAuth fails check client id and redirect settings and confirm the Gmail API is enabled in your Google project
  • If messages are not returned simplify the query to return everything and then narrow it once you see what the robot can access
  • If file writes fail verify folder permissions and free disk space
  • Log message id and saved path on success to speed up later investigation

Security and best practices

Keep credentials out of plain files. Use Orchestrator assets or Windows Credential Manager. Avoid storing long lived tokens in the workflow. Log enough to debug but not so much that you leak attachments to logs. Limit Gmail permissions to only what the robot needs.

Final notes and small victories

This workflow is compact but practical. It uses standard UiPath activities like Gmail Scope, Get Mail Messages, Save Attachments and file operations nested in robust Try Catch blocks. Configure IMAP connection in UiPath Studio

Server imap.gmail.com Port 993 Secure True User user@example.com Password yourPassword

Use Get IMAP Mail Messages activity

Drag the Get IMAP Mail Messages activity into your workflow and point it at your account. Set the Folder property to Inbox or whatever folder you actually care about. Use Top to limit the number of messages returned when testing, and set OnlyUnread to True if you want to avoid reprocessing the same emails over and over.

Practical settings to avoid chaos

  • Folder set to Inbox or Archive, depending on your flow
  • Top set to a reasonable number for testing, for example 50
  • OnlyUnread True to skip old messages while you iterate

Filter and loop messages

Get IMAP Mail Messages returns a list of MailMessage objects. Use a For Each activity typed to System.Net.Mail.MailMessage to loop the collection. Inside the loop filter by subject, sender, or date so your workflow only touches relevant emails. Filtering in the loop is simple and robust when you do not want to rely on server side rules.

Example filter ideas

  • Check message.Subject for keywords like invoice or signup
  • Use message.From.Address to allow only specific senders
  • Compare message.Headers or message.Headers.Item when you need advanced checks

Download attachments and process content

If message has attachments, call Save Attachments and give a folder path. Prefer a structure that adds timestamps or message id fragments to filenames to avoid overwrites. After saving you can hand files off to OCR, data extraction, or whatever downstream process keeps your business moving.

Naming and storage tips

  • Include a timestamp in the filename to avoid collisions
  • Store attachments in a dedicated folder per run or per sender
  • Scan for expected file types before handing to parsers

Clean up and handle errors

Mark processed messages as read or move them to an archive folder so the next run does not repeat work. Wrap network calls in Try Catch and log failures. Add retry logic for transient IMAP errors and backoff between attempts. Proper logging makes debugging less painful when servers act up.

Suggested fault handling

  • Try Catch around Get IMAP Mail Messages to catch network failures
  • Move or mark messages after successful processing to avoid duplicates
  • Retry a few times on transient errors with a delay between attempts

Final checklist

  • Mail activities package installed in UiPath Studio
  • Credentials stored securely and tested
  • Get IMAP Mail Messages configured with sensible Top and OnlyUnread settings
  • For Each loop with filtering and Save Attachments where needed
  • Try Catch and retry logic for robustness

That covers connecting to an IMAP server in UiPath, fetching messages, filtering by criteria, handling attachments, and adding basic error handling. Build the workflow step by step, test with a limited message set, then scale up when you are no longer afraid of your inbox.

title: UiPath Do While Number Guesser Game Challenge Project
description: Build a Do While number guesser in UiPath using loops variables input validation and feedback for practice and learning automation concepts
heading: UiPath Do While Number Guesser Game Challenge Project Guide
body:
Overview

Want to build a tiny game that teaches you loops variables and input handling while making your coworkers wonder if you are avoiding real work This Do While number guesser in UiPath is the perfect practice project for RPA beginners It shows random number generation loop control input validation and friendly failure modes all in one neat package

What you will build

A simple console style interaction using Input Dialog that asks the user to guess a number between 1 and 100 The workflow keeps running until the guess matches the secret number and then shows how many attempts it took

Core variables and setup

  • targetNumber as Integer this is the secret number
  • guessedNumber as Integer the parsed user guess
  • rawInput as String the exact text the user typed
  • attemptCount as Integer starts at 0 and increments on valid guesses

Generate the secret with a Random instance for realistic randomness For example use an Assign activity with new Random().Next(1, 101) to get a value from 1 to 100

Build the loop

Use a Do While activity that continues while guessedNumber <> targetNumber The nice thing about Do While is it runs at least once which is perfect for asking the first guess

Inside the loop

  • Show an Input Dialog and store the response in rawInput
  • Try to parse rawInput into guessedNumber inside a Try Catch block to avoid crashes from messy typing
  • If parsing fails or the number is out of range show a friendly message and skip incrementing attemptCount
  • If parsing succeeds compare guessedNumber with targetNumber
  • Use If activities to display Guess higher or Guess lower messages for guidance
  • When the guess is valid increment attemptCount to track performance

Validation and error handling

Bad input happens often and you should be prepared If parsing throws a FormatException catch it and show a helpful message Keep parsing inside Try Catch to prevent the workflow from exploding If you prefer a more defensive style you can use Int32.TryParse in an expression where supported

Also enforce the allowed range Check that guessedNumber is between 1 and 100 and tell the user when they wander off the map

End game and reporting

When guessedNumber equals targetNumber the Do While loop ends Then use a Message Box to congratulate the user and display attemptCount Keep the tone upbeat or sarcastic depending on how many attempts they needed

Tips for a cleaner workflow

  • Use descriptive names like targetNumber guessedNumber and attemptCount so future you does not cry
  • Keep parsing inside Try Catch to prevent unexpected crashes from creative typing
  • Increment attemptCount only when a valid numeric guess is made to keep stats honest
  • Break complex logic into small workflows for readability and reuse

Summary

This project covers variable setup random number generation loop structure user interaction comparison logic validation and result reporting in UiPath It is a compact practice task that reinforces Do While loops and basic RPA patterns while giving you a small victory to show off

title: Fix Git clone's fatal setting SSL certificate error
description: Quick guide to fix Git clone fatal setting SSL certificate error by checking CA trust adjusting Git settings or using a safe temporary bypass
heading: Fix Git clone's fatal setting SSL certificate error with simple steps
body:
This guide shows how to fix Git clone fatal setting SSL certificate error by checking certificate trust and adjusting Git or system certificate settings.

  1. Diagnose the error source
  2. Use the system CA bundle
  3. Test with a temporary verify bypass
  4. Install a custom certificate or update CA store

Step 1 Diagnose the error by reproducing the problem and reading the full error message from the Git client. The message often indicates whether the remote certificate chain failed validation or if a corporate proxy replaced certificates.

Step 2 Use the system CA bundle so the Git transport layer trusts the same authorities as the operating system. Point Git to a known CA file with a command such as git config --global http.sslCAInfo /path/to/ca-bundle.crt or configure the curl backend on systems that require that step.

Step 3 Test with a temporary verify bypass when troubleshooting only. Run git -c http.sslVerify=false clone https //example.com/repo.git to confirm that certificate validation is the blocker. Do not leave global verification disabled on development machines or servers because that disables certificate validation completely and opens a security hole.

Step 4 When the problem stems from a private certificate authority add the CA certificate to the system trust store or to a custom bundle referenced by Git. On Linux copy the PEM to the distro trust directory and update the trust database. On Windows import the certificate into the trusted root store for the user or machine.

Recap of the approach is simple diagnose the error decide whether the OS trust store or a custom bundle must be used avoid permanent verify bypass and then add the missing CA to the appropriate store so future clones succeed without hacks.

Tip

When working behind corporate proxies capture the server chain with an SSL debug tool and add only the missing CA certificate to the trust store rather than turning off verification.

title: UiPath Try Catch Finally Tutorial
description: Learn UiPath Try Catch Finally to handle errors cleanly and ensure proper cleanup in automation workflows with practical steps and tips
heading: UiPath Try Catch Finally Tutorial for Robust Error Handling
body:
If your UiPath automation has ever face planted because a file was missing or a UI selector went on vacation you are not alone. Try Catch Finally is the tiny insurance policy that stops your robot from flailing in front of users. This guide shows how to wrap risky actions in a safety net and keep your RPA projects behaving like they were tested by a human who drinks coffee.

Why Try Catch Finally matters in RPA

Exception handling is the difference between an automation that recovers and one that becomes a cryptic error in a log never to be seen again. Use Try Catch Finally to catch exceptions handle errors gracefully and guarantee cleanup so resources are not left open or temp files are not piling up like bad decisions.

What each part does

  • Try area. Put the risky actions here. Think file IO web requests and selector based UI operations.
  • Catch blocks. Handle specific exception types such as System.IO.IOException or UiPath.Core.SelectorNotFoundException. This avoids swallowing real bugs while still recovering from expected hiccups.
  • Finally block. Code here runs no matter what. Close apps release resources and remove temp files here so the next run does not inherit your mess.

Step by step in UiPath

  1. Drag the Try Catch activity from the Activities panel into your sequence or flowchart. This gives a container for error handling and keeps the workflow from crashing on the first failure.
  2. Place actions that may fail inside the Try area. Common examples include reading or writing files making HTTP calls and interacting with selectors. Isolate risky operations so the rest of the workflow stays calm.
  3. Add one or more Catch blocks and pick specific exception types like System.IO.IOException or UiPath.Core.SelectorNotFoundException. In each catch implement targeted recovery logic logging or an alternate flow so important failures are not hidden.
  4. Use the Finally block to run guaranteed cleanup. Close applications release resources and delete temporary files so no ghost processes haunt future runs.
  5. Run scenarios that force different failures and observe behavior. Use logs breakpoints and the UiPath debugger to verify handlers execute and that cleanup always runs.

Practical tips and best practices

  • Prefer specific exception types instead of catching System.Exception everywhere that is how you avoid hiding bugs and keep logs meaningful.
  • Add retry logic inside Catch blocks for transient failures like network blips. Backoff and a few retries will save many runs.
  • Log clear messages including context variables so future maintainers understand what went wrong without guessing.
  • Keep the Try block focused. If it gets long split it up so each risky operation is handled where it makes sense.
  • Use Finally for cleanup only. Avoid putting recovery logic there because it runs even when you have not handled the problem yet.

Debugging and validation

Force failures deliberately during development. Breakpoints and test cases where file access fails network calls are blocked or selectors change will show if your Catch handlers and Finally cleanup behave as expected. Check logs for the sequence of events and make sure retries and alternate flows actually take effect.

Wrap up

Try Catch Finally is a small pattern that makes UiPath workflows far more resilient. Add it thoughtfully use specific exception types and keep your cleanup reliable. Follow these steps and your automation will fail less often and be easier to troubleshoot when it does. And yes your future self will thank you much more than the person who suggested skipping error handling to save five minutes.

seo_heading: Practical exception handling in UiPath workflows for reliable automation

title: UiPath Exception Handling Example
description: Learn UiPath exception handling with try catch finally rethrow and logging for more robust workflows
heading: UiPath Exception Handling Example Guide
body:
Quick note before you panic

This short guide will help you stop your UiPath workflows from dying mysteriously and make them actually tell you why they crashed. We cover where errors usually hide, how to catch them with Try Catch, how to log useful context, and when to clean up or rethrow. It is practical, accurate, and slightly sarcastic.

Identify risky activities

Start by admitting the obvious. Activities that do IO, call external systems, or parse messy inputs are the usual troublemakers. Think HTTP requests, file reads, database calls, and fragile string parsing.

  • UI automation steps that depend on timing or selectors
  • Network calls that can fail for reasons outside your control
  • Parsing user supplied data or third party files

Wrap actions with Try Catch

Use the Try Catch activity around a sequence that can throw. The Try area is your normal logic, the Catch area is the emergency room. This prevents the whole workflow from aborting and gives you a chance to do a graceful recovery.

Use specific catch blocks

Do not catch everything with a blanket System.Exception. Catch specific types like System.Net.WebException, System.FormatException, or System.UnauthorizedAccessException when appropriate. Specific catches let you handle each problem correctly and avoid hiding critical failures that need human attention.

Log context and decide recovery

Logging is not optional. Use Log Message or a structured logging approach to record the exception message, stack trace, and business context such as invoice number or user id. After logging decide whether to retry, continue with a safe default, or escalate by throwing a new exception.

  • Include business keys so support teams can find the incident
  • Record the activity name and input parameters when possible
  • Choose retries only when the failure is transient

Finally and Rethrow

Use Finally for cleanup tasks like closing applications or releasing resources. When you need to escalate, use Rethrow to preserve the original exception details so debugging is not a guessing game. Rethrow keeps the crime scene intact for whoever is on call.

Testing and iteration

Create unit style scenarios and negative tests that simulate network failures, malformed data, and permission errors. Robust exception handling evolves with test feedback, so make small changes and repeat. If a pattern fails once in production, add a test for it and sleep better at night.

Practical best practices

  • Fail fast for unrecoverable errors so problems are detected early
  • Use targeted retries for intermittent failures only
  • Keep logging consistent and searchable for incident triage
  • Document escalation rules so human teams know what to do

Follow these patterns and your UiPath workflows will fail less loudly and give better diagnostics when they do. Your support team will appreciate the breadcrumbs, and your boss will appreciate the fewer angry emails. That is what good exception handling looks like in RPA.

title: UiPath Nested If Then Else Example
description: Learn to build nested If Then Else workflows in UiPath with step by step guidance and practical tips for handling multiple conditions
heading: UiPath Nested If Then Else Example Guide
body:
Why nested If in UiPath still matters

Yes nested If blocks can look like a tiny paper hurricane in your Studio designer, but they are still a useful tool for compact conditional logic in RPA. Use them when you need quick branches like grade tiers or multi stage approvals. This guide will show a practical way to build nested If Then Else logic in UiPath without making your future self cry.

Prepare variables and sample data

Start with meaningful variable names. I am not kidding. Use names like score or status so debugging does not turn into a séance to summon the original author. Create a few sample records to validate edge cases such as 80, 81, negative values, and unexpected strings.

Add the primary If activity

Drop an If activity and set the main condition. For example score > 80 for a passing threshold. The Then branch runs when the expression is true. The Else branch covers everything else including dramatic failures and mildly inconvenient results.

Nest a secondary If for finer checks

Inside a Then or Else branch you can add another If activity to refine the decision. For example use nested checks for grade tiers like:

if score > 95 then assign grade A
else if score > 80 then assign grade B
else assign grade C

This pattern is perfect for multi stage approvals or cascading status rules. But do not let nesting go beyond two or three levels or the flow turns into a labyrinth.

Logging and readable expressions

Keep expressions short and explicit. Add Log Message activities in each branch so you record which path fired. That saves time when the process goes sideways at 3 AM. Example logs help you and your team trace behavior during tests and production runs.

Testing and default handling

Run tests with boundary numbers and oddball values. Include a default Else branch that handles unexpected inputs so the workflow behaves predictably instead of silently failing. Handle nulls and invalid types explicitly and log a friendly error message that humans can understand.

When nested If becomes a code smell

If you see more than two nested levels ask yourself if Switch or a separate workflow would be clearer. Extract complex branches into small reusable workflows and invoke them. That keeps the main flow tidy and helps with unit testing and reuse in other automations.

Quick checklist for readable nested If logic

  • Use descriptive variable names like score and approvalStatus
  • Keep expressions short and clear
  • Add Log Message activities to every branch
  • Test edge cases and invalid inputs
  • Refactor into Switch or separate workflows when complexity grows

Wrap up and best practices

Nested If Then Else is a legitimate tool in UiPath Studio for compact conditional logic in RPA. Be pragmatic and keep things readable. If the flow becomes a nested horror show then refactor into a Switch or modular workflows. Follow these best practices and your UiPathTutorial readers will thank you while your future self stops yelling at the monitor.

title: UiPath Logging Example
description: Practical UiPath logging techniques for debugging monitoring and exception tracking in workflows with clear examples and quick tips
heading: UiPath Logging Example for Debugging and Monitoring
body:
If your UiPath workflows are tiny and perfect you can stop reading now and go meditate on your incredible luck. For the rest of us logging is the difference between fixing problems in minutes and crying into a stack trace for hours. Here is a pragmatic guide to logging in UiPath that keeps your automation observable without filling Orchestrator with useless fluff.

Pick the right activity and message

Use the Log Message activity where the action actually matters. A good log entry explains what happened and includes the relevant variables. Think less cryptic note to future you and more helpful breadcrumb to the person doing the debugging.

  • Write concise messages that include context like workflow name step name and id
  • Prefer structured text that can be parsed by Orchestrator or a log shipper
  • Avoid logging secrets or personal data while still giving enough context

Use sensible log levels

Match severity to the event. The standard LogLevel values are your friends.

  • LogLevel.Information for normal but useful runtime details
  • LogLevel.Warning for odd but recoverable situations
  • LogLevel.Error for things that broke and need attention
  • LogLevel.Trace for verbose traces used during deep debugging

Write Line for development and then prune

Write Line prints to the Studio Output panel and is great while you are building flows. Just remember to remove or reduce these before shipping to production or you will be the reason Orchestrator retention runs slow and people hate you.

Log exceptions with detail

Inside Catch blocks log the exception message and the full stack trace so the root cause is visible. A typical pattern is to log the exception using the message and a full dump so troubleshooting has context and a breadcrumb trail. Use ex.Message and ex.ToString() in your log text.

Example format

Try a simple convention like

WorkflowName StepName id=123 status=failed error="{ex.Message}" trace="{ex.ToString()}"

Check Studio Output and Orchestrator

Watch the Studio Output during runs for quick feedback and rely on Orchestrator for centralized log aggregation filtering and retention. Configure retention policies to balance compliance with storage costs and set filters so only relevant levels are kept long term.

Correlation and consistency

Standardize message formats and pass a correlation id across queues and processes using Add Log Fields or custom properties. Consistent fields make searching and debugging less painful and let you stitch a distributed execution into a single story.

Final tips that will make future you clap

  • Keep messages meaningful not mysterious
  • Log enough context but not sensitive data
  • Use levels deliberately to avoid log noise
  • Use Write Line for development and clean up before production

Do these things and when the robot inevitably misbehaves you will spend minutes not hours finding the culprit. Or at least you will have better notes for the apology email.
