title: How to use UiPath Select Folder to get all files
description: Quick UiPath guide to select a folder and retrieve all files from a directory using Directory.GetFiles and a For Each loop
heading: How to use UiPath Select Folder to get all files from a directory
body:
This tutorial shows how to use the UiPath Select Folder activity to pick a folder and retrieve all files from that directory and subfolders using a simple workflow.

  1. Select Folder using the Select Folder activity and capture output as folderPath
  2. Get files using Directory.GetFiles or Directory.EnumerateFiles and store into an array variable
  3. Loop files with For Each to process each file
  4. Optionally filter by extension or use SearchOption.AllDirectories for recursion
  5. Log results or pass file paths to downstream activities

Step 1 Select Folder Use the Select Folder activity from the UIPath activities panel. Assign the selected path to a string variable named folderPath. No need to guess folder names like a detective.

Step 2 Get files Use a Assign activity to call the System IO method. Example code can be

files = Directory.GetFiles(folderPath, "*.*", SearchOption.AllDirectories)

For large directories consider

filesEnumerable = Directory.EnumerateFiles(folderPath, "*.*", SearchOption.AllDirectories)

Step 3 For Each loop Use a For Each activity over the files array or enumerable. Set the type argument to String and process each file path. Typical operations include reading content moving files or logging names.

Step 4 Filtering and recursion Use the search pattern argument to limit extensions such as "*.pdf" or use LINQ to filter the array before processing. Use SearchOption.AllDirectories for recursive search or SearchOption.TopDirectoryOnly for single folder scanning.

Step 5 Use results Store results in a Data Table log file names or pass file paths into other workflows for processing. Remember to handle permissions and locked files with Try Catch activities.

This workflow provides a simple and reliable way to let a user pick a folder and have the automation gather every file for processing. The approach works well for small to medium datasets and scales better when using the enumerable pattern for large repositories.

Tip

Prefer Directory.EnumerateFiles for very large folders because the enumerable yields paths on demand and reduces memory usage compared to getting a full array first

title: Introduction to PDF Text Extraction with UiPath
description: Learn how to extract text from native and scanned PDFs using UiPath with practical steps for parsing and saving structured data.
heading: Introduction to PDF Text Extraction with UiPath
body:
This tutorial shows how to extract text from PDFs using UiPath with practical methods for native and scanned documents and for turning raw text into structured data.

  1. Create a UiPath project and install PDF and OCR packages
  2. Use Read PDF Text for native PDF files
  3. Use Read PDF With OCR for scanned images inside PDFs
  4. Parse raw text and extract fields with regex or string methods
  5. Save results and add error handling and logging

Step one sets up the workspace. Create a new process and add UiPath.PDF.Activities plus an OCR provider such as Tesseract or Google Cloud Vision. Package versions matter so pick one that matches the robot runtime.

Step two covers native PDFs. Use Read PDF Text activity and choose the path to the PDF file. The activity returns a plain string that often contains line breaks and headers that need trimming.

Step three handles scanned PDFs. Use Read PDF With OCR and select a suitable OCR engine. OCR will not be perfect and may require image preprocessing or DPI adjustment to improve recognition accuracy.

Step five shows output and resilience. Write extracted data to CSV or a database. Add Try Catch blocks to log failures and create a fallback path for manual review when parsing confidence falls below a threshold.

This workflow provides a practical starting point for automating document intake. The approach covers both native and scanned PDFs and offers parsing strategies that scale from a handful of files to batches that would otherwise make humans cry.

Tip

When OCR quality looks flaky try increasing image DPI running a despeckle filter or switching OCR engines. Store raw OCR confidence scores and route low confidence results to manual validation to avoid garbage in the final dataset.

title: UiPath Anchor Base Tutorial
description: Learn UiPath Anchor Base activity to find elements reliably using anchors and relative selectors for robust automation workflows
heading: UiPath Anchor Base Tutorial Guide for Reliable Selectors
body:
Why Anchor Base matters

If your UiPath automation feels like it is held together with duct tape and wishful thinking then Anchor Base is your new best friend. Anchor Base helps you find elements that move around like they pay rent by the week. This is essential for selectors that fail when windows resize or when the UI decides to rearrange itself for dramatic effect.

Getting your project ready

Open UiPath Studio and create a sequence or flowchart. Keep the real application visible while you work because tweaking selectors without the app is like tuning a piano with oven mitts. Add logging to make selector debugging less mystical and more data driven.

Place the Anchor Base and understand how it works

Drag the Anchor Base activity from the activities panel into your designer. Think of it as a little rescue team with two roles. One role is the anchor element that is stable and predictable. The other role is the action that targets the element that moves. The container keeps the two linked so your automation can find the target relative to the anchor.

Pick a solid anchor

Good anchors are labels, icons, or static text that rarely move. Strong anchors reduce reliance on fragile absolute coordinates and stop your selectors from breaking when someone tweaks the page layout. If an element appears in multiple places avoid using it as the only anchor.

Use Find Relative to locate the target element

Inside Anchor Base use the Find Relative activity to indicate the target. Choose the direction and offset that match the layout. For example if the input field is to the right of a label pick direction Right and test different offsets until the selector consistently hits the right control. This is literally why Anchor Base exists to rescue selectors that would otherwise fail.

Tune selectors and validate

Open the selector editor and inspect attributes. Use wildcards for dynamic parts and prefer stable attributes like automation id or meaningful names when available. Avoid overly greedy patterns that match multiple elements. Log selector values during debug runs to see what changes across screens and window sizes.

  • Use wildcards such as star or question mark for session ids and timestamps
  • Test selectors in different resolutions and DPI settings
  • Add retry scopes with sensible timeouts to handle transient UI delays

Edge cases and extra tricks

For non standard controls consider combining OCR with anchors to read text when native selectors are useless. Screen scraping can help but expect more false positives. When controls are truly stubborn use a mix of anchor based finding, OCR, and targeted clicks rather than blind hard coded coordinates.

Quick checklist before you run

  • Anchor is unique and stable
  • Find Relative direction and offset tested
  • Selectors use stable attributes and minimal wildcards
  • Retries and timeouts handle slow UIs
  • Logs capture selector values for debugging

Recap

Place an Anchor Base, pick a solid anchor, use Find Relative to target moving elements, and then refine selectors for stability. Add retries and consider OCR for weird controls. Follow these steps and your Robotic Process Automation will stop being haunted by broken selectors and you will sleep a little better at night.

title: UiPath Data Scraping Example
description: Learn UiPath Data Scraping wizard to extract web tables to Excel with selectors and retry strategies for reliable automation
heading: UiPath Data Scraping Example Guide
body:
Quick warning and a tiny pep talk

If you like hunting for missing cells and debugging brittle selectors at 2 AM then this guide may be a gentle insult to your lifestyle choices. For everyone else here is a clear path to use the UiPath Data Scraping wizard to pull structured web tables into a DataTable and write them to Excel without losing your mind.

Prepare the page and project

Open UiPath Studio and create a new Process. Navigate to the target web page in a browser that supports selectors. If the page layout is stable your life will be easier. If it is not stable then expect tunnel vision and lots of trial runs.

Checklist

  • Use a supported browser and enable UiPath extensions
  • Choose a page where the table structure is consistent across rows
  • Open the Design tab to find the Data Scraping wizard

Use the Data Scraping wizard

Launch the Data Scraping wizard from the Design tab. Click the first cell or element to define the pattern. Then select a second example so the wizard can confirm the pattern detection. The preview shows extracted rows so you can validate the pattern before wiring any logic.

Configure columns and cleaning

Adjust which columns to keep and set basic data types when available. If the site is messy plan to clean strings after extraction rather than assuming perfect input. Removing unwanted columns now saves grief later.

Set output to a DataTable variable

Choose a DataTable as the output. Give that variable a clear name such as extractedTable or scrapedData. Clear naming saves debugging time and reduces caffeine dependency.

Handle pagination and repeated extraction

If the target table spans pages use the pagination option built into the wizard. If that does not work use a loop that clicks the Next button and repeats extraction. Either approach ends with a DataTable that accumulates rows across pages.

Pagination patterns

  • Try the wizard pagination option first
  • If the wizard misses the button use a Click activity inside a While or Do While loop
  • Make sure to detect the last page to avoid infinite loops

Selectors and UiExplorer tips

For dynamic selectors inspect elements with UiExplorer. Use anchor or relative selectors when possible to keep targets stable across runs. Avoid brittle absolute paths. When in doubt prefer attributes that do not change between page loads.

Process or export the DataTable

You can either iterate rows with For Each Row to do row by row processing or export the full DataTable at once with Write Range from the Excel Activities. If you do Write Range use Excel Application Scope or the Workbook activities depending on whether you need Excel on the machine.

Error handling and logging

Wrap network sensitive steps and selector interactions in Try Catch. Log meaningful messages that explain what failed and why. A good log message is worth more than ten frantic reruns.

Practical error handling tips

  • Catch Element Not Found and Timeout exceptions separately so you can decide to retry or skip
  • Use Retry Scope for flaky clicks
  • Save partial results to disk if a long extraction is interrupted

Final checklist before running

  1. Variable names are clear and descriptive like extractedTable
  2. Selectors are tested and anchored where needed
  3. Pagination logic is verified on edge pages
  4. Try Catch covers network and selector issues
  5. Write Range or Workbook Write Range is configured with the correct sheet and file path

This guide covered the Data Scraping wizard workflow from selecting columns through exporting to Excel while handling pagination and dynamic selectors. Go run the job and try not to blame UiPath for every minor website change. If things break you can always blame the site and then fix the selector.

title: Text Data Extraction in Multiple PDF files with UiPath Examp
description: Learn how to extract text from many PDF files using UiPath with a step by step workflow that saves results for analysis.
heading: Text Data Extraction in Multiple PDF files with UiPath Example
body:
If you have a folder full of PDFs and zero desire to copy and paste for the rest of your life this workflow will rescue you. This friendly UiPath tutorial shows how to loop through multiple PDF files extract searchable and scanned text and save structured data for later analysis. Expect Read PDF Text for boring digital PDFs and Read PDF With OCR for the ones that still look like they were printed in 1997.

What the workflow does and why you should care

Short version The robot finds PDFs in a folder reads each file extracts fields with Regex or string logic and writes rows to a spreadsheet. It also logs problems so your human coworker can pretend to be surprised at how easy automation is.

Prerequisites and packages

Create a new UiPath project and add the packages you actually need rather than guessing. Install UiPath.PDF.Activities for Read PDF Text and UiPath.OCR.Activities for scanned documents. Add any OCR engines such as Tesseract or Microsoft OCR depending on your environment.

High level steps

  1. Gather PDF file paths into an array using Directory.GetFiles or similar.
  2. Loop through files with a For Each activity using TypeArgument String.
  3. Use Read PDF Text for searchable files and Read PDF With OCR for scanned pages.
  4. Parse the extracted text with Regex or string methods to get fields like invoice numbers dates and totals.
  5. Append results to CSV or Excel with Append Range or Append CSV.
  6. Wrap work in Try Catch and log failures with Log Message so you can blame the file not the robot.

Gather PDF files

Use an Assign activity to set a variable such as pdfFiles to Directory.GetFiles(folderPath, "*.pdf") so the workflow ignores random junk on your desktop. Make folderPath a configurable argument so you do not need to rebuild when somebody moves the files.

Loop through the files

Drop in a For Each activity and set TypeArgument to String. Each item will be a file path. Use Read PDF Text for normal PDFs. Switch to Read PDF With OCR when pages are scanned and choose the OCR engine and scale to improve accuracy.

Extract fields with Regex or simple parsing

Once you have the page text store it in a variable and run Regex or string methods. Example Regex for an invoice number might be

Dim invoicePattern As String = "Invoice\s*#\s*(\d+)"

Adjust patterns for dates totals or vendor names. If text quality is poor try OCR scale or language settings first before writing heroic parsing code.

Save results

Collect one row per file or one row per document line depending on your analysis needs. Use Append Range to add rows to an Excel sheet or Append CSV for a simpler append only file. Use consistent column order so downstream reports do not get dramatic.

Error handling and logging

Wrap read and parse logic in Try Catch. On exception log the file path and the message with Log Message so you can filter the execution log later. Optionally move bad files to an error folder for manual review.

Tips that save time and sanity

  • Make folder paths and output files configurable arguments.
  • Test with a small sample set before letting the robot loose on thousands of files.
  • Keep OCR only for files that need it to save runtime and avoid random mistakes.
  • Use conservative Regex patterns and then relax them as you learn what the data looks like.

There you go An automated UiPath flow that reads many PDFs handles both searchable and scanned documents and produces CSV or Excel output with error logs. Now go automate something boring and come back with coffee.

title: UiPath Remove or Delete Empty Rows Example
description: Quick UiPath guide to find and delete empty Excel rows using DataTable filtering and activities for cleaner automation workflows
heading: UiPath Remove or Delete Empty Rows Example
body:
Why bother removing empty rows in Excel for RPA

If your automation is anything like mine it will encounter blank rows and pretend everything is fine until it silently fails or produces sad looking reports. Cleaning empty rows early means your UiPath process will stop negotiating with Excel and actually do work. This tutorial covers DataTable techniques and alternative row deletion tactics so you can remove rows reliably and avoid brittle filters that cry in production.

Prepare your project and load the sheet

Use the Read Range activity from the Excel or Workbook package to pull the sheet into a DataTable. Store it in a descriptive variable like dt. Yes the name matters. If you name it dataTableThatDoesEverything you are asking for future confusion.

Fast and clean method using DataTable filters

The cleanest approach uses the DataTable Select method and CopyToDataTable so you filter out empty rows without loop gymnastics. This is ideal when a key column indicates whether a row is blank.

Dim rows As DataRow() = dt.Select("Not (ColumnName Is Null Or ColumnName = '')")
If rows.Length > 0 Then
    dt = rows.CopyToDataTable()
Else
    dt = dt.Clone()
End If

Notes that matter in real life

  • Replace ColumnName with the column you actually care about.
  • Check rows.Length before calling CopyToDataTable() because that method will throw if there are zero rows.
  • For multiple column checks build a filter expression like Not (Col1 Is Null Or Col1 = '' ) And Not (Col2 Is Null Or Col2 = '' ) or loop and test the combined condition.

Alternative method using a reverse loop

When emptiness is complex or mixed types mess with Select expressions you can delete rows while iterating from the bottom to the top. This prevents skipping rows when deletion shifts the index. It is old school but reliable.

For i = dt.Rows.Count - 1 To 0 Step -1
    Dim row As DataRow = dt.Rows(i)
    If String.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(Convert.ToString(row("ColumnName"))) Then
        dt.Rows.RemoveAt(i)
    End If
Next

If you prefer using UiPath activities use For Each Row with a counter and Delete Row or use Delete Range in Excel. Always iterate from bottom to top and test on a copy first.

Write the cleaned table back to Excel

Use the Write Range activity to save your cleaned DataTable. Overwrite the original sheet or write to a new sheet if you want a quick rollback plan. After writing use AutoFit or run a macro to tidy column widths because stakeholders judge success by how neat the spreadsheet looks.

Quick checklist for reliable automation

  • Read Range into dt
  • Prefer DataTable filter and CopyToDataTable for speed and clarity
  • Handle zero result sets before calling CopyToDataTable
  • Use a reverse loop when filter logic is too messy for Select
  • Write Range and AutoFit the sheet
  • Run the process on a sample file before production

Final thoughts

Cleaning empty rows is one of those small RPA wins that makes the rest of your automation behave. Use DataTable filters for elegance and reverse loops for stubborn edge cases. With these patterns your UiPath workflows will stop being offended by blank cells and start solving real problems.

title: UiPath Data Scrape PDFs into Excel Example
description: Compact UiPath guide for scraping tables from PDFs and exporting to Excel with practical steps and quick tips.
heading: UiPath Data Scrape PDFs into Excel Example
body:
So you have a PDF full of tables and the patient art of manual copy paste is not on the menu today. This guide walks through a reliable UiPath workflow that extracts table data from PDF pages and writes it to an Excel workbook. Expect practical tips on Read PDF Text versus Read PDF With OCR, the Data Scraping wizard, cleaning a DataTable, and using Write Range inside Excel Application Scope.

What you need before you start

Create a new UiPath process and add the usual suspects for PDF and Excel support. Install UiPath.PDF.Activities and UiPath.Excel.Activities if they are not already in your project. Clear, consistent naming of variables and activities will save you from future regret.

Choose the right PDF read method

If the PDF has selectable text use Read PDF Text for speed and accuracy. If the pages are scanned use Read PDF With OCR and pick an OCR engine that matches the document language such as Tesseract or Microsoft OCR. OCR is slower and messier but it works when there is no selectable text.

Use the Data Scraping wizard to capture the table

Open a PDF viewer that UiPath can interact with and launch the Data Scraping wizard. Click the first visible cell in the table and then click the second cell so the wizard can detect the repeating row pattern. The wizard often gets the structure right and outputs a DataTable for you to work with.

Set the wizard output

  • Assign the result to a DataTable variable. Name it something obvious like extractedTable so your workflow reads like documentation.
  • If the table spans multiple pages configure pagination in the wizard so it extracts every visible page.

Clean and convert the DataTable

Once you have a DataTable do some light cleaning. Trim whitespace from strings. Convert numeric columns with Convert.ToInt32 or use Int32.Parse when the format is consistent. An Assign inside a For Each row loop or a short Invoke Code can handle most fixes. Example approach in a For Each row workflow:

  • row("Price") = row("Price").ToString.Trim
  • row("Quantity") = Convert.ToInt32(row("Quantity").ToString.Trim)

If dates are messy use DateTime.Parse or TryParse to avoid runtime surprises. Keep everything defensive and log when conversions fail so you can inspect the bad rows later.

Write the results to Excel

Wrap an Excel Application Scope around a Write Range activity to persist the DataTable to disk. During testing overwrite an existing sheet so you do not end up with a folder of mystery files. Use Write Range to write the full DataTable including headers and confirm the sheet looks sane after a run.

Troubleshooting and tips

  • If the Data Scraping wizard fails because the PDF viewer is uncooperative try Read PDF Text and parse the plain text with regex or string splitting to reconstruct rows.
  • If OCR gives you funky characters try a different engine or preprocess the PDF to improve contrast and resolution.
  • Log the row count of your DataTable after extraction so you can detect missing pages quickly.
  • When working with large PDFs consider batching pages to avoid memory pain and long debug cycles.

Run and verify

Run the workflow and open the workbook. Verify column alignment and a few converted values. If a number looks like a phone number you probably parsed the wrong column. If the whole sheet is empty check that the wizard captured the right table area and that the PDF viewer was in the expected state when you ran the robot.

This process covers the core RPA moves for scraping PDF tables into Excel with UiPath while keeping your sanity intact. The main tools are Read PDF Text or Read PDF With OCR for reading, the Data Scraping wizard to build a DataTable, a bit of cleaning with Trim and Convert.ToInt32 or Parse, and Write Range inside Excel Application Scope to save the output. Now go automate and let the robot do the boring work.

title: How to create and build a DataTable in UiPath Example
description: Build and populate a DataTable in UiPath using Build Data Table Add Data Column and Add Data Row with clear step by step examples
heading: How to create and build a DataTable in UiPath Example
body:
If you are automating things with UiPath and you need a tidy table of data instead of chaos then this guide is for you. Follow along and learn how to create a DataTable variable, populate it with Build Data Table or Add Data Row, and then process or export it like a civilized RPA developer.

Why bother with a DataTable in UiPath

DataTables are the polite way to handle row and column data in UiPath. They play nicely with Read Range and Write Range, they let For Each Row do the heavy lifting, and they save you from string parsing nights that ruin your weekend.

What you will need

  • UiPath Studio with basic activities available
  • A variable of type DataTable, for example dt
  • Build Data Table, Add Data Column, Add Data Row, For Each Row, Write Range and Output Data Table activities

Step 1 Create the DataTable variable

Create a variable of type DataTable and name it dt or something equally reasonable. This gives the rest of your workflow a place to park the table so you do not have to guess where the data went.

Step 2 Define columns with Build Data Table or Add Data Column

You have two main choices. Use the Build Data Table activity and use the visual designer to add column names and data types. The designer saves a neat schema so the rest of your workflow does not get confused. Or add columns at runtime with Add Data Column if incoming data has unpredictable fields. Dynamic columns are handy and also spice up debugging a little.

Step 3 Add rows with Add Data Row or import in bulk

For individual entries use Add Data Row. In the Properties panel use the ArrayRow property for a single row example like this

ArrayRow = { "Alice", 30 }

For bulk loads use Read CSV or Read Range and assign the result to dt. That saves you from manual looping and from inventing new ways to break things.

Step 4 Process rows with For Each Row

Use For Each Row in dt and then reference columns by name like row("Name").ToString. Use Assign activities to transform values and Write Line or Log Message while debugging. Here is a typical access pattern

For Each row In dt
  name = row("Name").ToString
  age = CInt(row("Age"))
Next

Keep an eye on nulls and empty strings. A null will happily crash your workflow if you do not handle it first. Defensive coding is not glamorous but it keeps your job from being a panic show.

Step 5 Output or export the DataTable

When you are done choose Write Range to send dt to Excel. If you just want a quick text snapshot use Output Data Table and then Write Line to print the table to the console. Both options are valid depending on whether you like spreadsheets or like to stare at log windows.

Quick checklist for a working DataTable flow

  • Create a DataTable variable named dt
  • Define columns with Build Data Table or Add Data Column
  • Populate rows with Add Data Row or Read Range
  • Loop with For Each Row and transform or validate values
  • Export with Write Range or Output Data Table as needed

Common pitfalls and how to avoid them

  • Column name typos cause runtime errors so copy paste names when possible
  • Type mismatches will blow up conversions so validate or use Try Catch in risky places
  • Null values will surprise you so check for DBNull.Value before calling ToString

That is the gist of building and using DataTables in UiPath for reliable automation. Follow these steps and you will have a clean DataTable driven workflow that plays well with Excel and the rest of your RPA world. If you want a ruthless optimization tip then stop manually adding thousands of rows one at a time and use Read Range when possible. Your future self will send you a thank you email that is mostly relieved emoji.

title: Add Rows to DataTables in UiPath
description: Learn practical ways to add rows to UiPath DataTables using Add Data Row and VB expressions for reliable automation
heading: Add Rows to DataTables in UiPath Efficiently and Correctly
body:
Why adding rows feels like soldering without goggles

If you work in RPA you have met DataTables and you have cursed them. They are useful and they will punish you if types do not match. This guide gives a compact, slightly snarky walkthrough for safely adding rows to a UiPath DataTable while keeping your automation alive and your logs readable.

Start with the right schema

Build Data Table when you need a new schema. Read Range if you want to steal the structure from an Excel sheet. Choosing the correct column types up front prevents those delightful runtime errors about Cannot convert value to integer. Use DataTable.Clone when you want the schema only and not the baggage of rows.

Quick checklist

  • Use Build Data Table for controlled schemas
  • Use Read Range to import the sheet and its types
  • Validate column types before adding rows to avoid surprise casts

Fast path Add Data Row for simple inserts

If your row data arrives as an array or object array use the Add Data Row activity. Set the ArrayRow property to a new Object array that follows the column order. This is lazy and glorious for simple inserts and for designers who avoid manual VB code.

ArrayRow = New Object() { nameValue, CInt(ageValue), DateTime.Parse(dateValue) }

Match the order of values to the columns and convert types with CInt or DateTime.Parse when needed. Mapping by index is brittle so prefer it only for quick, predictable sources.

Create a DataRow when you want control

When you need per column logic create a DataRow object and populate columns by name. This avoids column order surprises and makes conversions explicit. Typical flow in UiPath Studio looks like this.

newRow = dt.NewRow()
newRow("Name") = nameValue
newRow("Age") = CInt(ageValue)
dt.Rows.Add(newRow)

You can also use the Add Data Row activity and pass the DataRow in the DataRow property. This method is explicit and helps when you are merging from multiple sources with different orders.

Merging and persisting results

Want to combine tables or write back to Excel Use Merge to preserve schema and get smarter merging behavior. ImportRow brings a single DataRow from another DataTable while preserving row state. When you are ready to output use Write Range to push the DataTable to Excel for downstream consumers.

Merge tip

  • Use dt.Merge(otherDt) when schemas match or when you want to keep the original column types
  • Use ImportRow when you need to move specific rows and keep row metadata

Common traps and how to avoid them

  • Type mismatch errors. Convert explicitly with CInt CDate or DateTime.Parse before adding values
  • Column order changes. Address columns by name to make your workflow forgiving
  • Silent truncation. Verify string lengths and numeric ranges in a validation step

Final words of robotic wisdom

Add Data Row is your quick and clean option. DataRow creation with dt.NewRow and dt.Rows.Add is your power move for complicated logic. Merge and ImportRow are the proper tools when combining sources. Follow these steps and your automation will stop throwing tantrums and start behaving like the obedient RPA citizen it pretends to be.

title: How to Save UiPath DataTables to Excel Example
description: Step by step guide to export UiPath DataTable objects to Excel using Write Range and Excel Application Scope with examples and tips
heading: How to Save UiPath DataTables to Excel Example
body:
If your UiPath robot could talk it would beg you to stop breaking Excel files. Here is a practical and slightly snarky guide to saving DataTable objects to Excel using Excel Application Scope and Write Range while avoiding the usual RPA pitfalls.

Prepare the DataTable like a responsible automation citizen

Make sure the DataTable has the rows and columns you want. Use Build Data Table when you need test data or use Read Range to pull data from a source. Validate column names and types before you write anything. Mismatched columns are the silent gremlins of automation.

Quick checklist before you write

  • Confirm column names match the destination sheet
  • Trim or sanitize strings to avoid weird Excel formatting
  • Keep a copy of the DataTable for quick retry logic

Open the workbook with Excel Application Scope

Excel Application Scope manages the Excel process so you do not end up with orphaned instances and locked files. Use it to open or create the workbook, and always let the scope close naturally so Excel stops being clingy.

Write Range for full table writes and Append Range for adding rows

Inside the Application Scope use Write Range when you want to replace or create a sheet. Set the DataTable property to your variable and turn AddHeaders to True when the first row contains column names. If you only want to add rows to an existing sheet use Append Range or read the sheet to find the last used row and then call Write Range starting at the appropriate cell.

How to find the start row without guessing

  • Use Read Range to pull the existing sheet into a DataTable and get its Rows.Count
  • Compute the next start row as existingRows plus header offset
  • Call Write Range with a starting cell like A plus the computed row

Align columns to keep Excel from doing improv

Make sure DataTable column order and names match the worksheet layout. If they do not match Excel will shift data like it knows better. If you need strict placement, specify the start cell and keep AddHeaders consistent.

Save and verify like you mean it

Close the Excel Application Scope and then use Read Range or reopen the file to confirm the write worked. Add simple log messages after successful writes so you can blame logs instead of crying in the support channel.

When Excel is not installed use Workbook activities

If your robot runs on a machine without desktop Excel use Workbook activities to read and write xlsx files. They are less chatty about COM objects and do not require Excel to be present.

Performance tips and best practices

  • For very large DataTable objects consider exporting to CSV first for speed and disk friendliness
  • Only convert to XLSX when you need formatting or formulas
  • Log the row counts and sheet names you wrote for easier debugging
  • Use Try Catch around file operations to handle locks and retries gracefully

Following these steps will get your DataTable out of UiPath and into Excel with fewer surprises. Use Excel Application Scope, choose Write Range or Append Range intentionally, validate your columns, and verify the output. Do that and your automation will be slightly less dramatic than usual.

title: How to use UiPath Append Range with Excel Example
description: Step by step guide to using UiPath Append Range with Excel to add rows without overwriting data and fix common problems
heading: How to use UiPath Append Range with Excel Example
body:
If you enjoy watching Excel fights with your robot then this tutorial is for you. Welcome to the gentle art of appending rows with UiPath, where the goal is to add data to a sheet without bulldozing what is already there. We will keep things practical and funny in equal measure, while staying true to how UiPath activities actually behave.

When to append rows and not overwrite

Use Append Range when you want new records to land below existing rows and not replace headers or previous data. If your goal is to refresh a range entirely use Write Range instead. Append Range works with a System.Data.DataTable as input, and it plays nicely with both Excel Application Scope and the Workbook activities.

Prepare the DataTable

Make sure your source data is a DataTable. You can build one from scratch with Build Data Table or load one from a file using Read Range. The important part is that column names match the target sheet headers or you will get misaligned cells and missing values. UiPath treats the columns by name when mapping headers, so spelling matters.

Choose the workbook approach

Pick Excel Application Scope when you need the Excel app for features like macros or COM specific actions. Use Workbook activities when Excel is not installed or when you want faster unattended runs. Workbook activities avoid Excel interop overhead and reduce the chance of COM lockups, which can save you from late night firefighting.

Configure the Append Range activity

  • Place Append Range inside the chosen scope or call the Workbook Append Range directly.
  • Set the DataTable property to your DataTable variable. UiPath expects a System.Data.DataTable object.
  • Set the SheetName string exactly as it appears in the workbook. Case and spelling must match in some contexts.
  • Leave StartingCell blank to append after the last used row. If you set it then data will be written at that address instead.
  • Toggle AddHeaders based on whether the destination sheet already has headers. If headers exist set AddHeaders to false to avoid duplicating them.

Tip about headers

If your DataTable has a header row and the target sheet does not, enable AddHeaders. If the sheet already has a header row then disable AddHeaders to keep things tidy.

Run verify and common fixes

Run the workflow and open the workbook. New rows should appear below existing data. If nothing shows up check these usual suspects.

  • No rows in DataTable. Confirm your Read Range or Build Data Table actually produced rows.
  • Sheet name mismatch. Double check the sheet name string for typos and case sensitivity.
  • File locked by another process. Close other Excel instances or related apps. If necessary terminate stuck processes carefully.
  • Duplicate rows. Validate your source filtering or use a unique key to prevent repeats.
  • Performance problems with large volumes. Batch your writes or prefer Workbook activities to reduce Excel interop overhead.

Safe large volume trick

When appending thousands of rows write them to a temporary sheet first and then move the block to the final sheet. Doing the heavy write in one place reduces repeated lookups for the last used row and lowers the chance of conflicts during concurrent runs. You can move the block using Read Range and Write Range or by copying ranges inside Excel when you need atomic moves.

Quick checklist before you press run

  • DataTable is not empty and columns match the target sheet headers.
  • Correct workbook approach selected for unattended performance or Excel features.
  • Append Range has DataTable, SheetName, and StartingCell configured as intended.
  • AddHeaders is set according to whether headers exist on the sheet.
  • Verify file locks and duplicates before scheduling unattended runs.

There you go. Append Range is straightforward once you avoid the usual traps. Now go automate, and try not to make Excel cry.

This tutorial covered extracting text from PDF with UiPath parsing that text into structured fields and writing the result into an Excel workbook for downstream use. The steps form a repeatable pattern that replaces manual copy paste and scales to batches of documents.

title: UiPath Invoice Processing Demo
description: Step by step demo for building UiPath invoice processing using Document Understanding OCR validation and export for faster accounts payable automation
heading: UiPath Invoice Processing Demo Guide
body:
Quick confession and what this guide does

If you are tired of feeding invoices to a black hole and getting vague promises of automation, welcome. This article walks through a practical UiPath invoice processing workflow using Document Understanding and OCR. You will get a repeatable plan to convert messy PDFs into structured data for accounts payable while keeping humans in the loop so the robots do not stage a revolt.

What you need before you start

Short list of essentials that stop the project from becoming a weekend horror show

  • Representative invoice samples with varied layouts and vendors
  • A UiPath project with Document Understanding packages and OCR dependencies
  • A chosen OCR engine that balances accuracy and cost
  • A plan for a Machine Learning Extractor or templates for consistent suppliers
  • Access to a Validation Station for human review when confidence is low

Step 1 Gather a real world set of invoices

Collect invoices that reflect actual chaos. Different layouts, scanned photos, multi page invoices, missing totals and odd fonts all help the extractor learn the ways invoices try to ruin your month end.

Step 2 Create the UiPath project and add the right packages

Start a new project and install Document Understanding and any OCR packages you need. Organize your workflows so ingestion, processing and export are separate. This helps later when you need to swap an OCR engine or add a sanity check before export.

Step 3 Pick and configure OCR and extractor

Choose an OCR engine that fits your accuracy needs and budget. Some engines are cheap but noisy. Some are accurate but expensive. For structured suppliers use templates. For varied vendors use a Machine Learning Extractor. Apply image pre processing like deskewing, noise removal and contrast fixes to boost recognition rates.

Step 4 Train and validate the extractor

Label training documents and run training cycles until field level accuracy is acceptable. Track metrics such as precision, recall and confidence per field. If a critical field like total amount is unreliable then fix the training data or add rules rather than hoping for miracles.

Step 5 Add human in the loop with Validation Station

Set up a Validation Station for low confidence fields. Route questionable results to accounts payable specialists who can confirm or correct values. Log reviewer corrections so you can retrain the model and slowly reduce human hours rather than writing them off.

Validation workflow tips

  • Set confidence thresholds per field so only risky values go to review
  • Present side by side image snippets with the extracted field for fast decisions
  • Store reviewer corrections to improve future training cycles

Step 6 Export mapped data and handle exceptions

Map extracted fields to your ERP, CSV output or a database. Implement exception handling for unreadable pages, missing totals and mismatched line items so the bot does not crash during month end. Log exceptions with enough context to reproduce the issue.

Operationalize and measure success

Put monitoring in place. Track throughput, error rate and the human review ratio. Use field level confidence to drive routing decisions. Keep a retraining cadence based on new samples from exceptions and reviewer logs. That is how you go from a fragile prototype to a resilient automation.

Common pitfalls and how to avoid them

  • Training on too few layouts leads to brittle models. Add diversity early.
  • Blindly trusting OCR without validation creates costly errors. Always surface low confidence data for human review.
  • Failing to log corrections means you miss easy wins for retraining.

Final notes on workflow design

Design your UiPath workflow with modular steps so you can swap OCR engines or tweak the Machine Learning Extractor without rewriting everything. Keep the Validation Station visible to accounts payable teams so they feel like collaborators rather than babysitters. With a solid Document Understanding pipeline and sensible exception handling you can turn chaotic invoices into structured data that your systems actually use.

Automation is not magic. It is hard work wrapped in clever code. Follow these steps and you will save time, reduce errors and keep the human experts for things that actually need human judgement.

title: UiPath Set Reading Order to Inferred for Adobe
description: Quick tutorial on setting Adobe reading order to Inferred so UiPath extracts PDF text more reliably for automation and document understanding
heading: UiPath Set Reading Order to Inferred for Adobe PDF extraction
body:
Why bother with reading order

If your PDFs look fine to humans but throw a tantrum when UiPath tries to extract text, the reading order is probably the culprit. Changing Adobe Acrobat reading order to Inferred often makes text flow more sane for automation, accessibility tools, OCR and downstream document understanding. Think of it as teaching a stubborn document to behave around robots.

What this fixes

  • Misplaced text fragments and scrambled line order
  • Problems with multi column layouts and floating images
  • Better results for UiPath Read PDF Text and Read PDF With OCR

Step by step instructions

  1. Open the PDF in Adobe Acrobat Pro. Acrobat Reader will not let you edit reading order so do not waste time with it.
  2. Open Tools then Accessibility and launch the Reading Order panel. The panel shows visual blocks and a menu for how logical flow is inferred from layout.
  3. Select Inferred reading order and apply it to the document. This tells Acrobat to guess structure from page layout and tags so assistive tech and UiPath get a more consistent sequence.
  4. Save the PDF using Save or Save As so the new reading order becomes embedded. If you skip this UiPath will read the old structure and you will curse quietly into your coffee.
  5. Test in UiPath. For searchable PDFs use Read PDF Text, for scans use Read PDF With OCR. Point the activity to the saved file and run extraction on a few representative pages before you hit production.

Troubleshooting and tips

If text still comes out wrong, try the Make Accessible action in Acrobat to add tags then reapply the Inferred option. For scanned pages use a stronger OCR engine or higher DPI settings and rerun the inferred reading order. Sometimes manual tagging is the only thing that will make a complex layout behave, so reserve that for the stubborn documents.

Quick checklist before rollout

  • Confirm file saved after applying inferred reading order
  • Run UiPath extraction on sample pages, not just one lucky page
  • Document your approach so automation runs stay predictable

Bottom line, using Adobe inferred reading order is a fast, low drama trick to improve PDF extraction for UiPath automation and accessibility. It will not magically fix every layout but it fixes enough to save you time and irritability. Now go fix those PDFs and pretend it was always part of the plan.

title: How to Maximize Document Windows in a UiPath Sequence
description: Quick guide to maximize document windows in a UiPath sequence for more reliable selectors and predictable automation.
heading: How to Maximize Document Windows in a UiPath Sequence
body:
Attach and maximize document windows in UiPath for stable selectors

If your UiPath workflow sometimes clicks on the wrong window like it is playing pin the tail on the wrong donkey, maximizing the app window first will calm the chaos. This guide walks through a practical approach to make UI automation more predictable by using Attach Window or Use Application Browser together with the Maximize Window activity. You will keep your selectors honest and your logs readable.

Why maximize the window at all

Maximizing reduces variability. When a window is maximized the UI structure and element positions are more consistent across screen resolutions and monitor setups. The Maximize Window activity talks to the UI framework directly which makes it less fragile than blasting keystrokes at the keyboard and hoping for the best.

In plain terms this means fewer mysterious failures and less digging through logs at 2 AM wondering why the automation decided to interact with a settings dialog instead of the document.

Step by step workflow

  1. Attach to the correct window

    Start with Attach Window or Use Application Browser and target the main document window. Make sure your selector scopes only the window you want. If your target is a browser tab prefer Use Application Browser for more reliable handling.

  2. Apply the Maximize Window activity

    Drop Maximize Window inside the Attach or inside the Use Application Browser container. This makes subsequent activities operate on a consistent UI layout. It is less likely to fail when users move the window between monitors or change resolution.

  3. Stabilize selectors for the maximized state

    Update selectors after maximizing. Some attributes change when a window grows. Use wildcards for volatile parts, prefer stable attributes like automation id or class, and use anchors for nearby stable elements.

  4. Add verification checks

    Follow Maximize Window with Element Exists or Wait For Element on a UI element that only appears or stays stable in the maximized state. These checks confirm the window reached the right state before you try clicking or typing.

  5. Test across environments

    Run the sequence in different screen resolutions and with multiple monitors attached. Log the existence of the window and key selector matches so failures are easier to trace and look less like random gremlins sabotaging your automation.

Quick checklist to avoid the usual traps

  • Always attach to the correct window or browser instance before maximizing
  • Do not rely on long blind delays. Use Wait For Element and Element Exists instead
  • After maximizing, revalidate selectors and add wildcards where attributes change
  • Log window state and selector outcomes to make debugging pleasant and fast

Selector hygiene that actually helps

Selectors are like eyewitness testimony. They are reliable when the witness is coherent and not wearing sunglasses. Prefer stable attributes such as automation id or accessible names. Remove dynamic indexes that will move when a dialog appears. Use anchors to find elements relative to stable neighbors.

If a selector works in a small window but breaks after maximize you probably depended on a layout specific attribute. Update the selector to match the maximized DOM or UI tree structure and retest.

Troubleshooting and fallbacks

If Maximize Window fails to take effect try these things. First confirm your Attach Window actually targeted the app you think it did. If focus is the problem try Activate within the same scope. If automation still misbehaves capture UI screenshots or use Highlight to visually confirm what the robot sees.

As a last resort and only when necessary consider a targeted hotkey sequence to maximize the window. That is less reliable than the Maximize Window activity but it can be a pragmatic fallback in legacy cases.

Summary and recommended practice

Use Attach Window or Use Application Browser to point at the right app. Maximize the window with the Maximize Window activity. Update selectors for the maximized layout. Verify success with Element Exists or Wait For Element. Test in multiple monitor and resolution setups and log results. Follow that routine and your automation will misbehave far less often and you will have fewer angry emails to explain.

Final checklist

  • Attach Window or Use Application Browser first
  • Apply Maximize Window next
  • Rework selectors for the maximized state
  • Use Element Exists or Wait For Element to verify
  • Test with many resolutions and monitor setups

seo_heading: Attach and maximize document windows in UiPath for stable selectors

title: How to use UiPath Hotkeys Example
description: Learn a compact UiPath hotkeys tutorial to send keyboard shortcuts select targets and speed up automation workflows
heading: How to use UiPath Hotkeys Example for faster automation
body:
Quick summary for the impatient

Tired of manual clicking and pretending your mouse is productive Great news You can teach UiPath to press keys for you and it does not complain. This guide shows how to use UiPath hotkeys and keyboard shortcuts inside UiPath Studio so your automation behaves like a grown up app.

What this covers

  • Choosing between Send Hotkey and Type Into
  • Capturing stable selectors and avoiding flaky behavior
  • Using modifiers like Ctrl and Alt and when to add delays
  • Tips to improve reliability and productivity

Step by step workflow

Step 1 Set up the sequence and open the target app

Create a new sequence in UiPath Studio and launch or attach to the application you want to automate. No drama here just a sequence and an app window. If the application needs an initial login or splash screen wait for it to be ready before you start sending keys.

Step 2 Pick the right activity

Use Send Hotkey for single keyboard shortcuts and small combos. Use Type Into when you need to send full strings. Send Hotkey is lean and focused for productivity tasks like Ctrl C and Enter while Type Into handles text input without assuming your target app knows the difference between polite and rude typing.

Step 3 Capture a reliable UI element

Indicate on screen to get a selector. If the selector is brittle capture a larger parent element or use an anchor element. Attach the activity to a parent window with Attach Window or Attach Browser when possible. Bad selectors are the leading cause of dramatic midnight debugging sessions.

Step 4 Choose keys and modifiers

Select the key in the activity dropdown and add modifier keys like Ctrl, Alt, or Shift with the checkboxes. For combos say Ctrl plus C instead of trying to type control characters by hand. Avoid embedding long wait sequences unless the app is genuinely slow.

Step 5 Tune reliability

Enable SimulateType or SendWindowMessages in Send Hotkey when the target supports them. These modes are less needy about focus and often skip the focus drama. When the app takes a breath add a short Delay or a small wait for element ready before the hotkey. Surround critical sends with logging so the next person looking at logs does not need a crystal ball.

Troubleshooting checklist

  • If a hotkey fails try clicking the element first or use Focus then send the hotkey
  • If selectors fail expand to a parent element and add attributes that are stable across runs
  • Switch to Type Into for text only tasks when Send Hotkey is not suitable
  • Use short debug runs with logs around hotkey calls to isolate timing issues

Best practices and final tips

Prefer Send Hotkey with SimulateType for modern apps when possible. Avoid hard coded long delays. Use targeted waits and element checks instead. Keep your selectors honest and stable and your logs friendly enough to explain what happened without an apology.

There you go A pragmatic UiPath hotkeys tutorial that will cut repetitive clicks and raise your automation productivity. If things still fail blame the app not your clever robot and then fix the selector.

This tutorial shows a practical UiPath workflow that moves files between folders with variable driven paths and simple error handling for reliable automation.

  4. Test the workflow

Step 1 Prepare variables and folder paths

Create clear string variables such as sourcePath and destinationPath. Use absolute paths to avoid surprises. Check existence with Directory.Exists before attempting any move. This avoids the common rookie mistake of sending the robot on a wild goose file chase.

Step 2 Use the Move File activity

Drag the Move File activity into the sequence. Bind the Activity properties to the variables created earlier. For overwriting use a conditional check and a Delete activity if replacing a file is desired. The Move File activity performs the actual transfer with minimal fuss.

Run the workflow with sample files and edge cases such as missing folders and locked files. Observe logs and refine path checks and exception handling until behavior matches expectations. Manual testing avoids deploying a tantrum prone robot.

The workflow described moves files reliably between folders while handling the usual problems that appear when working with file systems. Following the four steps yields a maintainable approach that scales from simple tasks to larger automation chains.

Tip

Use dynamic timestamps in destination file names to avoid collisions when the source may contain duplicate names. That keeps history and prevents accidental overwrites without complicated logic.

title: How to UiPath Move Invoices to a New Directory After Process
description: Move processed invoices with UiPath using folder variables For Each Move File and basic error handling to keep invoice folders tidy and auditable
heading: How to UiPath Move Invoices to a New Directory After Processing
body:
If you like piles of invoices overflowing into your inbox then stop reading now. For the rest of us who prefer tidy folders and robots that do the boring heavy lifting here is a practical UiPath workflow to move invoices from an incoming folder to a processed archive with audit friendly logging and sane error handling.

Setup folders and variables

Create two folders on a file share or local disk. One is the incoming folder where new invoices land. The other is the processed folder where files go after validation. Add an optional quarantine folder for the oddball files that scream for human attention.

Define clear variables such as inFolder and processedFolder and verify that the robot has read and write permission. If the robot cannot touch the files you will learn patience and how to explain permissions to IT.

Get the file list

Use Directory.GetFiles(inFolder) or UiPath activities that list files to get a snapshot of new invoices. This avoids hard coding paths and makes re runs less tragic.

Iterate with For Each

Feed the file list into a For Each activity. For Each gives you a tidy loop per file name so you can apply extraction validation and movement logic without copying the same logic into 17 places.

Process and validate invoice data

Run your extraction steps here. That may be native selectors text extraction or an OCR step when the PDF is a noisy scan. Validate key fields such as invoice number date and total before you move anything. If validation fails log the reason and consider moving the file to the quarantine folder for manual review.

  • Check invoice number presence and format
  • Verify date is within expected range
  • Confirm total matches line item sums when possible

Move files and avoid collisions

When the invoice passes validation use the Move File activity to relocate it to the processed folder. To avoid accidental overwrites append a timestamp or a GUID to the file name. For example use Path.Combine(processedFolder, Path.GetFileNameWithoutExtension(file) + "_" + DateTime.Now.ToString("yyyyMMddHHmmss") + Path.GetExtension(file)) as the destination path.

This gives you traceable file names for auditors and saves you from the existential sadness of replaced invoices.

Handle errors and log actions

Wrap processing for each file in a Try Catch activity. On exception log the error at the proper level and move the problematic file to the quarantine folder for human review. Silent failures are the worst kind of failure so keep logs verbose enough to troubleshoot but not so verbose that everyone cries.

Make sure your logs include file name action taken timestamp and failure reason when applicable. That will make post mortems less dramatic.

Workflow checklist

  • Create incoming processed and optional quarantine folders
  • Define variables like inFolder and processedFolder and test permissions
  • List files with Directory.GetFiles or UiPath file activities
  • Loop with For Each and extract invoice data
  • Validate fields then Move File on success
  • On error log and move file to quarantine using Try Catch

Summary and audit tip

This pattern keeps the incoming folder clear and builds an auditable processed archive for downstream reporting. Use timestamps or transaction ids in file names to avoid collisions and to make traceability friendly for auditors and humans alike. If you want extra credit add a small CSV or database entry with file metadata for quick search and reporting.

Now go forth and automate. Your future self will thank you and your accountant will stop sending passive aggressive emails.

title: UiPath OCR Image Example
description: A compact guide to using UiPath OCR to extract text from images using Tesseract and Microsoft OCR for better RPA data capture
heading: UiPath OCR Image Example Extract Text from Images
body:
If your scanner hates you and your PDFs are a cryptic mess then welcome to UiPath OCR land. This guide walks through using UiPath OCR activities to read image text with engines like Microsoft OCR and Tesseract and then clean the output so your RPA bots stop making bad guesses out loud.

Set up project and install OCR packages

Open Manage Packages and grab Microsoft OCR and Tesseract. Add the packages to your project and import any namespaces you need so the activities show up without drama. Yes this is boring but yes it matters.

Add an image and pick an OCR activity

Use Read Image Text for a file input or OCR Read Text when you are targeting a screen region. For flaky layouts use an Anchor Base so your robot can find stuff even when the universe decides to shuffle the page.

Configure the OCR engine and tweak options

Microsoft OCR is handy when language support and cloud parity are priorities. Tesseract is the offline option and it is great if you want to train for weird fonts or avoid sending data anywhere. Adjust scale and language settings to help with low resolution images and bad scans. If your image is tiny then scale up before recognition. If it is noisy then increase contrast and denoise first.

Run the workflow and inspect the output

Execute the workflow and check the output variable in Locals or the Logs. Expect junk from noisy images and treat confidence scores as the moral compass of OCR. Low confidence means human review or a retry with different settings.

Post process and validate text

Clean extracted strings with regex and trimming to remove stray whitespace and artifacts. Use confidence thresholds and pattern matching to decide whether a result is reliable. Route questionable results to a human reviewer or retry with a different engine and preprocessing steps.

Practical checklist to improve accuracy

  • Preprocess images by scaling up and increasing contrast
  • Remove background noise or shadows before reading
  • Use zones and templates for repetitive documents to reduce errors
  • Consider training Tesseract for unusual or proprietary fonts
  • Log confidence scores and example images to track failure modes

That is the setup. Pick your engine, wire up Read Image Text or OCR Read Text, run a test, and clean the output with regex and filters. Follow these steps and your automation will get better faster than blaming the robot for bad scans.

title: How to Process Scanned Image Invoices with UiPath Example

heading: How to Process Scanned Image Invoices with UiPath Example
body:
This tutorial shows how to extract structured data from scanned image invoices using UiPath and OCR so the workflow can turn messy pixels into usable fields.

  1. Create a UiPath project and add Document Understanding and OCR packages
  2. Preprocess scanned images to improve OCR accuracy
  3. Configure an OCR engine and read text from the image
  4. Extract fields using anchor based methods templates or regex
  5. Validate extracted data and export to Excel or a database

Step 1 Create a project using Studio. Add UiPath.DocumentUnderstanding and an OCR package such as Tesseract or Google Cloud OCR. Dependency management saves a lot of future hair pulling.

Step 2 Preprocess images by converting to grayscale resizing to 300 DPI and applying thresholding. Deskewing and noise removal dramatically improve OCR accuracy so the extractor does not invent random numbers.

Step 3 Configure the OCR engine and use Read PDF with OCR or Read Image Text activities. Choose an engine based on language and budget. Always test with a handful of representative invoices rather than gambling on a single sample.

Step 4 For extraction use Anchor Base or Document Understanding classifiers. Regex is handy for invoice numbers and totals. Example regex that avoids punctuation traps is Invoice\s+No\s*([A-Z0-9\-]+). Templates work well when vendor formats are stable.

Step 5 Use Validation Station to confirm extracted fields when accuracy is not perfect. Export a DataTable to Excel with Write Range or push records to a database for downstream processing.

The workflow in this tutorial turns scanned images into validated structured data using common UiPath building blocks. The process improves with better sample documents and iterative tuning of OCR and extraction rules.

Tip

Boost OCR accuracy by standardizing incoming scans to 300 DPI performing deskewing and limiting character sets for known fields. A small whitelist beats endless regex chain fighting random PDFs.

title: OCR with UiPath and Google Cloud Vision Example
description: Learn how to integrate UiPath with Google Cloud Vision for reliable OCR extraction from images and PDFs in a simple example workflow.
heading: OCR with UiPath and Google Cloud Vision Example
body:
If you want UiPath to read text from PDFs and images so your bot can pretend it understands paperwork, this guide walks through a practical setup with Google Cloud Vision. You will get the essentials for project and credential setup, UiPath integration choices, and tips to improve text recognition quality without crying into your logs.

Create a Google Cloud project and secure credentials

Start like a normal adult who cares about security. In the Google Cloud Console create a project and enable the Vision API. Create a service account and download the JSON key file. Then move it to a locked down folder or better yet store a reference to it as a secure asset in UiPath Orchestrator or as an environment variable. Grant only the permissions needed for Vision API so nothing extra is wandering around with keys it does not need.

Install UiPath packages and decide how to call the API

You have two sensible options in UiPath. Use the UiPath.Web.Activities package and the HTTP Request activity for full control, or keep it simple and use packaged activities if your environment provides them. Either way store the credentials out of plain workflows. Secure assets or environment variables are your friends.

Why the HTTP route is useful

  • Works with the raw Vision API endpoints for images and document OCR
  • Easy to base64 encode image content and send a JSON request
  • Gives you explicit control over language hints and batch sizing

Build the workflow to send images and PDF pages

Read each image or render PDF pages to images. For simple jobs use the images:annotate endpoint with an array of requests. For large or multi page PDF jobs use the async batch file endpoints or the recommended document OCR workflow to avoid timeouts. Convert each image to base64 and include it in the request body.

Example request body for a single image:

{
  "requests": [
    {
      "image": { "content": "BASE64_IMAGE_DATA" },
      "features": [ { "type": "DOCUMENT_TEXT_DETECTION" } ],
      "imageContext": { "languageHints": ["en"] }
    }
  ]
}

Use language hints and batch requests

Language hints help when documents contain non English text. Put likely languages in imageContext to nudge the model. Also batch multiple pages in one call when possible to reduce orchestration overhead and round trips. But do not cram too many pages into one request if you want predictable latency and cost.

Parse the JSON response and map fields

The Vision API returns structured JSON. Look for fullTextAnnotation for multi line extraction and textAnnotations for individual blocks. Use boundingPoly or boundingBox data to build positional logic like "find the amount near the bottom right" or "extract the header field". Map extracted strings into DataTable rows or variables in UiPath for downstream processing.

Practical parsing tips

  • Check fullTextAnnotation.text for a simple combined result when you just need raw text
  • Inspect pages and blocks if you care about structure or layout
  • Use the vertices in boundingPoly to compute regions and proximity for field matching

Error handling and reliability

Add retries for transient network issues and for quota responses. Implement exponential backoff rather than hammering the API like it owes you money. Log request IDs and response snippets for debugging but do not dump raw credentials or full document text into public logs.

Improve OCR accuracy with preprocessing

Recognition improves when the input looks reasonable. Common preprocessing steps that actually help include deskewing, cropping to the content area, increasing contrast, converting to black and white for high noise scans, and removing speckle. Test different settings on a representative sample set and keep notes. Hand tuning often beats blind faith in default settings.

Cost and quota awareness

Run tests on a small sample first and monitor Vision API quota and billing. Batch where reasonable but avoid making huge blind runs. Alerts for cost spikes save budgets and job owners from angry emails.

Quick checklist before you run end to end

  • Create project and enable Vision API in Google Cloud
  • Make a service account and store the JSON key securely in Orchestrator or env vars
  • Install UiPath.Web.Activities and prepare HTTP Request calls or use available activities
  • Encode images as base64 and use DOCUMENT_TEXT_DETECTION for OCR tasks
  • Include languageHints when needed and use batch requests prudently
  • Parse fullTextAnnotation and use bounding boxes for positional extraction
  • Add retries, logging, and preprocessing like deskewing and contrast adjustment
  • Monitor quota and cost to avoid surprises on the invoice

If you follow these steps the bot will extract text from most PDFs and images without staging a rebellion. If it fails, turn up preprocessing or add a human in the loop for edge cases and then blame the scanned original.

seo_heading: Step by step UiPath automation with Google Vision API for PDF and image OCR

title: Fix GitHub support for password authentication error fast
description: Fast guide to fix GitHub support for password authentication was removed error by switching to personal access tokens or SSH and updating Git settings
heading: Fix GitHub support for password authentication error fast
body:
This guide shows how to fix the GitHub 'support for password authentication was removed' error by switching to a personal access token or SSH key and updating local Git settings.

  1. Choose between personal access token or SSH key
  2. Create a personal access token on GitHub if using HTTPS
  3. Update the repository remote to use the new credential method
  4. Configure a credential helper so frequent prompts disappear
  5. Test a push and pull to confirm success

Step 1 Choose a method based on comfort level. A personal access token is quick and familiar for HTTPS workflows. SSH keys require one time setup and avoid typing credentials later.

Step 2 On GitHub open Settings then Developer settings then Personal access tokens and generate a token with repo scope. Copy the token now because GitHub will not show the token again. Use the token instead of a password when Git asks for credentials.

Step 3 Update the local repository remote. Run git remote set-url origin NEW_REMOTE where NEW_REMOTE is the URL selected from the repository page. For HTTPS use the repository HTTPS URL. For SSH use the SSH URL provided by GitHub after key setup.

Step 4 Configure a credential helper so the token does not need to be entered every time. Use git config --global credential.helper store to save credentials on disk or git config --global credential.helper cache for a temporary cache. Pick the helper that fits the level of security desired.

Step 5 Test by running git push origin main or git pull. If authentication fails check token scopes or ensure the SSH public key is added to the GitHub account.

Recap choose personal access token or SSH key then update the remote and configure a credential helper to stop the password authentication error from blocking repository operations.

Tip

Generate a token with only the minimum scopes required. Treat the token like a password and rotate tokens periodically to reduce risk and maintain sanity.

title: Maven GitHub and Eclipse How to get a Maven project
description: Step by step guide to import a Maven project from GitHub into Eclipse using Git integration and Maven build commands for a clean setup.
heading: Maven GitHub and Eclipse How to get a Maven project
body:
Why this exists and why you will thank me later

If you ever stared at Eclipse while it stared back at you and wondered why dependency errors feel like a secret society initiation, this guide will save your sanity. We will clone a Maven repo from GitHub, import it into Eclipse with EGit and M2E, and get the build running without sacrificing your coffee break. Primary keywords covered include Maven, GitHub, Eclipse, EGit, M2E, Java, and importing Maven projects.

Before you start check your toolbox

  • Make sure Eclipse has the EGit and M2E plugins installed. If they are missing you will get charming errors and a longer debug session than you wanted.
  • Confirm Java JDK is installed and set in your PATH, and that Maven is available if you like running things from the terminal.
  • Decide where you will keep your local clone. Pro tip do not create pointless local branches just to prove you can, unless you enjoy pain.

Step by step workflow

The steps are simple but precise. Follow them and Eclipse will behave like a competent coworker for once.

1. Clone the repository

Use the Eclipse menu File > Import > Git > Projects from Git > Clone URI. Paste the HTTPS or SSH URL from GitHub and follow the prompts. If you already cloned locally, point Eclipse to the folder instead. Remember the repository on GitHub is the canonical source of truth so avoid random local experiments without a branch.

2. Import as a Maven project

Go to File > Import > Maven > Existing Maven Projects and select the cloned repository folder. Eclipse will read the pom.xml and build the project model that powers dependency resolution and launch configurations. If Maven warns about a missing parent pom, check the repository structure and relative paths in the pom

3. Refresh Maven dependencies

Right click the project and choose Maven > Update Project or run mvn clean install in a terminal. Maven will download libraries and run the compile phase. If something fails check the effective pom and the repository settings.xml if you use private artifact repositories.

Configure Java runtime and build path

Open Project Properties > Java Build Path and make sure the installed JRE or JDK matches the source and target levels declared in the pom. The most common mystery compile failure is a Java version mismatch. Fix that here and in Window > Preferences if needed.

Run, test and iterate

  • Run your app with the Run menu or by invoking Maven goals from the Run Configurations.
  • Run tests locally with mvn test or with Eclipse test runners.
  • If dependencies still act up check Project > Maven for lifecycle mappings or plugin versions that need updating.

Commit and push like a responsible human

Use EGit to commit and push changes with Team > Commit and Push or from the repository view. Write commit messages that explain why you broke things and how you fixed them. Future you will appreciate the effort and your teammates will stop leaving passive aggressive comments in code.

Troubleshooting quick hits

  • Build failures after import: run mvn clean install and read the topmost error, not the stack trace waterfall.
  • Missing dependencies: check Maven repositories and your settings.xml for credentials to private repos.
  • Wrong Java level: update Project Properties and ensure Eclipse points to the correct JDK installation.
  • M2E lifecycle warnings: adjust plugin versions or add appropriate lifecycle mappings if the plugin is not supported out of the box.

Wrap up

Importing a Maven project from GitHub into Eclipse is mostly boring but necessary. With EGit and M2E installed and a sensible Java and Maven setup you can clone, import, build, test and push changes without too much drama. Follow the steps, keep your repo the single source of truth, and write commit messages like a civilized developer.
