title: Developer vs DevOps Engineer What's the difference?
description: Clear comparison of Developer and DevOps Engineer roles responsibilities tools and career paths for engineers seeking practical clarity fast
heading: Developer vs DevOps Engineer What's the difference?
body:
If you like writing features that users actually click and curse at in equal measure then developer work is your jam. If you enjoy keeping things on the rails so those features do not explode at 2 a m then DevOps engineering might be your kind of chaos control. Both jobs are noble and both come with their own late night drama.

Core difference in plain language

Developers focus on product and user facing functionality. They build APIs, UI components, business logic and unit tests. DevOps engineers focus on delivery and reliability. They design CI CD pipelines, manage infrastructure as code with tools like Terraform, and tune monitoring so the on call person sleeps a little more often.

Goals and success metrics

  • Developer goals include feature velocity, code quality and user metrics such as retention or conversion.
  • DevOps engineer goals include deployment frequency, mean time to recovery and system uptime.

What each role does day to day

Think of developers as architects of features. They write code in Node, Python, Java or whatever framework your product worships. They review pull requests and debug business logic. The DevOps engineer draws the map that gets that code to production. They write automation for CI CD platforms, configure Kubernetes clusters, manage cloud resources and set up observability with Prometheus, Grafana or ELK style stacks.

Common tools you will actually use

  • Developer toolkit git, unit and integration tests, web frameworks like Spring or Express, local dev environments.
  • DevOps toolkit CI CD platforms, Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform for infrastructure as code, cloud provider APIs and monitoring tools.

Where the lines blur and careers get interesting

Most teams do not have a magic wall between code and infrastructure. A developer who learns basic CI CD and a bit of Terraform becomes eight times more annoying in meetings and also much more useful. A DevOps engineer who can read application code will fix production puzzles faster and go home before sunrise sometimes.

Overlap that pays off

  • Automating deployments makes developers faster and happier.
  • Reading code helps DevOps engineers reduce incident toil.
  • Cross training boosts deployment quality and reduces all nighters.

How to choose your path if you like options

Pick developer work for product driven problems, user experience and algorithmic challenges. Pick DevOps work for orchestration, automation and systems scale puzzles. Both paths reward curiosity, solid debugging skills and the ability to admit when you broke production and then fix it quietly.

Practical tip to learn both

Start a tiny project that forces you to touch both worlds. Build a simple web app, host it on a cloud provider, write infrastructure as code with Terraform, and wire a CI CD pipeline to deploy to Kubernetes or a managed platform. Add basic observability so you can see what is actually happening in production and practice rolling back a bad release. Doing this will teach feature design and deployment patterns faster than any job description.

In short, if you like building user facing magic go developer. If you prefer making the magic reliable and repeatable go DevOps engineering. If you like both you will be very employable and mildly sleep deprived in equal measure.
seo_title: Should you pick Developer or DevOps Engineer for your career
seo_heading: What Developers and DevOps Engineers actually do day to day in teams

title: Tomcat vs JBoss Which Application Server Should You Choose?
description: Compare Tomcat and JBoss to choose the best Java application server for performance features memory and deployment needs.
heading: Tomcat vs JBoss Which Application Server Should You Choose?
body:
If you are wrestling with Tomcat and JBoss WildFly the decision really comes down to scope and how many enterprise toys you want built in. Tomcat is a lean servlet container that excels at serving WARs and handling HTTP requests and servlets with minimal fuss. JBoss WildFly is a full Java EE application server with built in EJB support JMS capabilities clustering and an administrative console for people who enjoy clicking through options late at night.

Quick reality check

Short version for the impatient humans and CI pipelines:

  • Tomcat is best for microservices stateless web apps and most Spring Boot deployments where startup time and memory footprint actually matter.
  • JBoss WildFly is best when you need Jakarta EE features distributed transactions message driven beans or heavy middleware integration.

What each server actually gives you

Do not confuse a servlet container with a full application server. Tomcat focuses on JSP servlet APIs and HTTP request processing. That keeps things fast and light. WildFly provides the full Java EE toolkit including EJBs transaction managers JDBC resource adapters and JMS messaging. That means more features but more moving parts and more configuration to love or loathe.

Why pick Tomcat

  • Fast startup and lower memory usage which is great for autoscaling and fast CI runs.
  • Simple deployments and straightforward logging for most web apps and Spring Boot services.
  • Smaller attack surface and fewer admin consoles to babysit.

Why pick JBoss WildFly

  • Built in Java EE stack for legacy apps that expect EJB JMS distributed transactions or advanced clustering.
  • Richer management and monitoring tools useful at enterprise scale and for complex integration scenarios.
  • Vendor support and certifications when compliance matters more than startup time.

Performance and operations matter more than fanboy claims

Raw benchmarks are useless without context. Performance depends on configuration JVM tuning and workload shape. For simple servlet based workloads Tomcat often wins on latency and throughput. For enterprise workloads involving distributed transactions or messaging WildFly may be heavier but functionally necessary. Always profile with representative traffic rather than trusting random blog charts.

How to pick without regret

Do this instead of flipping a coin:

  1. List required features such as EJB JMS XA transactions clustering or simple servlet handling.
  2. Prototype both servers in Docker with a realistic workload and your production JVM settings.
  3. Measure response time memory usage startup time throughput and error rates.
  4. Consider operational preferences like ease of deployment CI pipeline speed and available expertise.

Example use cases

  • Use Tomcat for microservices API gateways simple web front ends and most Spring Boot apps.
  • Use JBoss WildFly for legacy Java EE applications complex transactions and systems that need integrated middleware.

Final word

Match the server to the job. If you want speed and small footprint pick Tomcat. If you need a certified Java EE stack and enterprise services pick JBoss WildFly. And if you are still unsure go build a tiny proof of concept with Docker measure real metrics and let the data make the annoying choice for you.
seo_title: Tomcat or JBoss For Java apps pick based on features and scale
seo_heading: When to choose Tomcat for microservices and when to use JBoss WildFly

title: How to use the JDK's javap command by example
description: Practical guide to using javap to inspect Java class files and bytecode with examples and useful flags for debugging and learning
heading: How to use the JDK's javap command by example practical guide for Java developers
body:
Why you should care about javap

If you write Java then sometimes the JVM will behave like a vending machine that ate your change. javap is the tiny disassembler that helps you figure out what the compiler actually put into the class file. It is part of the JDK and it will show you signatures fields and bytecode instructions so you can stop blaming the framework and start blaming the code you wrote last week.

Quick setup and first commands

Make sure you have the JDK installed and a compiled class file to inspect. No need for a complex example. A one method class will do nicely.

javac HelloWorld.java

Then run the basic disassembly to list public signatures and method descriptors.

javap HelloWorld

The output shows the class name fields and method headers. This is the fastest way to confirm what the compiler emitted for method signatures and visibility.

Useful flags to reveal the juicy bits

When you want more detail use the following flags. They are the difference between guessing and knowing.

  • -c show bytecode instructions for each method
  • -private include non public members
  • -v verbose output for the constant pool and attribute details

Example command that I actually use when chasing odd behavior.

javap -c -private -v HelloWorld

How to read bytecode without crying

Every bytecode line lists an opcode and its operands. Look for patterns like loads stores invokes and returns. Those map back to source constructs such as variable reads writes method calls and returns. When you see synthetic methods or weird bridge methods you are looking at compiler generated plumbing not your craftiness.

Keep an eye on the constant pool in verbose mode. Class names method refs and string literals live there. If something is missing or misreferenced you will find it in this table before the JVM raises a fuss at runtime.

Common things to check

  • Method descriptors to verify binary compatibility
  • Access flags to confirm visibility
  • Line number tables to map bytecode back to source lines
  • Synthetic markers to find compiler generated members

Using javap for debugging and build validation

javap is not a debugger replacement but it is a fast sanity check. Use it to confirm that method signatures match what libraries expect to avoid NoSuchMethodError surprises. Use it to spot accidental generated members that change your public API. And when performance mysteries arise compare the bytecode generated with different compiler options to see what optimizations took place.

Tips and troubleshooting checklist

  • Run javap -c -v ClassName and compare the bytecode against source line numbers
  • Look for invokespecial and invokevirtual to understand call dispatch
  • Check the constant pool for unexpected constant entries
  • If things look wrong recompile with debug info enabled and check the line table

Wrapping up

javap gives you a microscope for class files. It helps with debugging bytecode analysis and certifying that your compiled classes match your intentions. If your code ever behaves like it has a mind of its own run javap and you will often see who is really to blame.
seo_title: Inspect Java class files with javap for quick troubleshooting
seo_heading: A practical javap guide to read bytecode and inspect class files

title: How to use JarSigner to Sign Java JAR files digitally
description: Step by step guide to sign Java JAR files using jarsigner and keystore best practices for secure distribution and verification
heading: How to use JarSigner to Sign Java JAR files digitally Step by Step
body:
Step by step JAR signing with jarsigner keytool and keystore best practices

If you ship Java code and expect users or platforms not to freak out, sign your JARs. This guide walks through creating or using a keystore, generating a keypair, signing with jarsigner, verifying the result, and adding a timestamp for long lived trust. All without wizardry, but with a touch of sarcasm for flavor.

Why sign a JAR in plain human terms

Signing proves two important things. First, who published the JAR. Second, that nobody sneaked in malicious changes after the build. If either of those matters to you, which it should, signing is a non optional step in secure deployment and code signing workflows.

Create or reuse a keystore and keypair

If you do not already have a keystore, create one. The keystore holds the private key that you should guard like a tiny digital crown. The keypair represents the publisher identity that gets attached to the JAR.

keytool -genkeypair -alias myalias -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -keystore mykeystore.jks -validity 365

Pick a clear alias and a secure password. Use a real identity and contact email if this is for production, because some platforms and users will check the certificate chain.

Sign the JAR with jarsigner

Once you have a keystore and a keypair, tell jarsigner to add a digital signature. This attaches certificate data and a signature to the JAR which prevents undetected tampering.

jarsigner -keystore mykeystore.jks myapp.jar myalias

Pro tips that do not cost extra but will save you pain later

  • Choose a modern signature algorithm like SHA256withRSA when creating keys or certificates.
  • Keep the private key offline or in a secure vault whenever possible.
  • Use a dedicated signing key rather than reusing a general purpose one.

Verify the signature before you ship

Never assume. Always verify. This is the safety check that confirms the signature and the certificate chain are valid after your build pipeline does whatever it does to your files.

jarsigner -verify -verbose -certs myapp.jar

If verification fails, stop and investigate. The error messages are usually blunt and unhelpful, but they do help.

Timestamping for kicking certificate expiry in the teeth

A timestamp proves when the signature was applied, so the signature can remain valid even after the certificate expires. Use the -tsa option with jarsigner and a trusted timestamp authority when longevity matters.

jarsigner -keystore mykeystore.jks -tsa TSA_URL myapp.jar myalias

Replace TSA_URL with a timestamp authority URL provided by your CA or a trusted provider. If you omit timestamping your signed JAR may stop validating once the signing certificate expires.

CI automation and secure key handling

Automate signing in CI pipelines to avoid human error, but do not shove your keystore into plain text repository land. Use environment protected secrets, vault storage, or a hardware signing service.

  • Store keystore passwords in CI secret storage.
  • Use ephemeral signing agents or hardware security modules if available.
  • Audit who can access signing keys and rotate them if a leak is suspected.

Quick checklist before distribution

  • Keystore exists and is protected
  • Keypair generated with a secure algorithm
  • JAR signed with jarsigner
  • Signature verified with jarsigner verify
  • Timestamp applied if you need long term validity

There you go. Signed JARs, happier users, and fewer frantic support tickets. If you want even less drama look into automated signing workflows with proper secret management and a hardware trust anchor. Your future self will thank you, or at least file fewer incident reports.
seo_title: Sign Java JARs with JarSigner and prevent nasty tampering
seo_heading: Step by step JAR signing with jarsigner keytool and keystore best practices

title: scrumbut
description: Quick guide to scrumbut meaning signs and fixes for Agile teams struggling with half baked Scrum practices
heading: scrumbut explained for Agile teams
body:
Call it scrumbut if you like. That little word is the polite cover story for a team that kept the Scrum label but ditched the parts that make Scrum useful. You still get the look and feel of ceremonies and charts but not the feedback loops or the shared discipline that actually deliver value. This is the classic Agile anti pattern where the costume stays but the soul walks out the door.

What scrumbut looks like

Signs are obvious to anyone who stopped nodding and started watching. Common indicators include skipping retrospectives or standups, holding sprint reviews that feel like status meetings, and measuring finished tasks instead of learning. Roles are fuzzy, artifacts are half implemented, and teams proudly claim they are doing Scrum while missing most of the mechanisms that force improvement.

  • No regular retrospective or retrospectives that are theater
  • Daily standups reduced to email updates or skipped entirely
  • Sprint reviews turned into stakeholder status sessions with no real feedback
  • Output metrics like story counts or hours trumping outcome metrics like cycle time and customer satisfaction
  • Confused roles and rituals that exist on paper but not in practice

Audit your team process to find the Frankenstein bits

If your process feels like a Frankenstein project then do a quick audit. List ceremonies roles and artifacts and mark which ones are present and which ones are performed in name only. You will find the gaps fast. That gives you a real answer to the question are we doing Scrum or did we make something else and keep the label.

  1. List ceremonies like planning daily standup sprint review and retrospective
  2. Check roles like Product Owner Scrum Master and the Development Team
  3. Inspect artifacts like the backlog increment and the definition of done

Pick one practice to restore

Change overload is a morale killer. Pick the single practice that will increase transparency the fastest. That is usually the daily standup or the sprint review. Restore it for two weeks as an experiment and watch what happens. Keep changes small and observable so you can tell if the fix helps or simply makes the meeting longer.

Measure outcomes not just activity

When teams obsess over task completion they avoid hard questions about value. Switch the conversation to outcome metrics like cycle time quality and customer feedback. Track cycle time to see flow problems. Track defect rates or test coverage to monitor quality. Track direct customer feedback or a simple satisfaction signal to measure real impact.

  • Cycle time and lead time to reveal bottlenecks
  • Quality signals like production defects and acceptance pass rates
  • Customer feedback and usage metrics rather than completed story count
  • Short team pulse checks for morale and confidence

Use honest language and a pragmatic path back to continuous improvement

If your workflow evolved into something other than Scrum call it by that name. Polite pretending only slows down improvement and creates confusion later on. Decide if you want pure Scrum a hybrid or a different lightweight Agile approach and then pick practices that match that decision. Be deliberate and avoid ritual worship.

Two week experiment

Run a two week experiment restoring one missing Scrum practice and compare customer feedback and team morale before and after. Keep the experiment time boxed and measurable. If the metrics improve you have evidence for broader change. If not you learned something useful and can try a different lever.

Bottom line do not let the name Scrum be a synonym for doing whatever was easy that week. Scrumbut is fixable if you stop pretending and start measuring. Small honest steps lead back to real Agile continuous improvement and a team that actually delivers value.
seo_title: Scrum or Scrumbut Which one is actually helping your team
seo_heading: Spot scrumbut early and get your Agile rituals to actually work

title: Top 5 Reasons Youll Love Jakarta Servlet 6.0
description: Five clear reasons to upgrade to Jakarta Servlet 6.0 and modernize Java web apps with better APIs performance and migration ease
heading: Top 5 Reasons Youll Love Jakarta Servlet 6.0
body:
Practical migration tips for Jakarta Servlet 6 and modern HTTP apps

Jakarta Servlet 6.0 modernizes the servlet API while keeping the programming model you secretly enjoy. The big moves are sensible and boring in a good way. If you like clearer APIs and fewer legacy traps then this update is a welcome cleanup crew for your web code base.

What changed with Servlet 6

Short version, because your backlog is merciless. Key changes you need to know about are listed below and none of them are imaginary.

  • Package rename to the jakarta namespace to align with Jakarta EE and future compatibility
  • Removal of deprecated cruft so the API is smaller and less confusing
  • Improved HTTP and async handling for more predictable high concurrency behavior
  • Lighter defaults that behave better in cloud and container environments
  • Better tooling and migration guides which make upgrading less heroic

Why these changes matter

The jakarta namespace move is a one time migration pain that unlocks long term compatibility and community momentum. Removing long deprecated bits means fewer surprises during maintenance. Async improvements mean your threads behave more predictably under load. And yes, cloud friendly defaults translate to faster startup and fewer deploy time mysteries.

Migration checklist you can actually follow

Do these things in order to keep your hair and your production environment intact.

  • Inventory dependencies and map them to jakarta names first so you find namespace issues early
  • Pick a servlet container or app server that supports Servlet 6 and run tests there
  • Update imports in your code base and rebuild to catch compile time breaks
  • Run integration tests under a container to surface runtime class loading or dependency conflicts
  • Check third party libraries and frameworks for jakarta updates before cutting a release

Common gotchas

  • Libraries that still use the old javax namespace will fail at runtime
  • Servlet filters and listeners with package mismatches are easy to miss
  • Some build scripts and CI images need updating to a Servlet 6 compatible runtime

Performance and async behavior

Servlet 6 improves the async request flow so asynchronous processing is less fiddly. That means better throughput when you are juggling many concurrent connections. Keep using AsyncContext and async listeners but expect fewer weird edge cases and more predictable behavior under load.

Cloud and container friendliness

The API changes favor smaller footprints and smarter defaults which helps microservices and cloud runtimes. Faster startup and fewer surprises during deployment are practical wins. Frameworks and servers will do a lot of the heavy lifting so your app code can stick to business logic and not servlet plumbing.

Quick plan before you hit the upgrade button

  • Map dependencies to jakarta names first and fix those issues before anything else
  • Run your test suite in a container that supports Servlet 6 to catch runtime problems
  • Stage the rollout if you can and keep a rollback plan handy

In short, Jakarta Servlet 6.0 is a tidy evolution. You will have some migration work to do but the payoff is clearer APIs, better async and HTTP handling, and friendlier behavior in cloud environments. Do the prep work, run container tests, and enjoy the less legacy filled future. You deserve the peace of mind and maybe a small celebratory beverage afterwards.
seo_title: Why Servlet 6 in Jakarta EE Will Actually Make Your Life Easier
seo_heading: Practical migration tips for Jakarta Servlet 6 and modern HTTP apps

title: s3 bucket temp
description: Compact guide to temporary S3 buckets and presigned URLs for short lived uploads downloads and cleanup
heading: s3 bucket temp guide for temporary storage and presigned URLs
body:
This tutorial shows how to create temporary S3 buckets and presigned URLs for short lived uploads and downloads.

  1. Create a temporary bucket and add lifecycle rules
  2. Configure access controls and minimal permissions
  3. Generate presigned URLs for upload or download with an SDK or CLI
  4. Test access then clean up resources

Create a bucket with a clear name that signals temporary use. Use a lifecycle rule to expire objects after a short period and to remove the bucket when empty. This avoids turning cloud storage into a digital attic full of old logs and receipts.

Grant the minimal permissions needed for the task. Create a role or user that only has put and get access for the specific prefix. Avoid wildcard permissions that would grant broad access across other buckets.

Generate presigned URLs when a temporary client side upload or download is required. A presigned URL can expire after a chosen number of seconds. Example CLI style command for reference use with an SDK command if required

aws s3 presign my-temp-bucket/path/to/object --expires-in 3600

Test the presigned URL from a browser or curl alternative that does not require additional credentials. Confirm that upload and download work within the expiry window and that requests beyond expiry fail with an appropriate error.

When the temporary workflow is done remove objects and the bucket. Automated lifecycle rules handle most of the cleanup but a final manual removal step ensures no leftover resources and no surprise bills.

This guide covered creating a temporary bucket adding lifecycle rules configuring tight permissions generating presigned URLs and testing and cleaning up. The goal is temporary safe transfers without long term storage baggage.

Tip

Set presigned URL expiry to the shortest practical window and use lifecycle rules to remove objects automatically. Short expiry reduces risk and lifecycle rules reduce bill shock.

title: install nginx ubuntu
description: Quick practical guide to install Nginx on Ubuntu with commands firewall checks and basic configuration for a working web server
heading: How to Install Nginx on Ubuntu
body:
So you want a web server that does not complain and mostly behaves. This Ubuntu nginx install guide walks you through a tidy, repeatable setup for a Linux web server with systemctl and ufw. No magic, no demons, just commands that work.

Before you start

Assume you have an Ubuntu machine and a user with sudo powers. This is for a basic production ready server setup that devops folks and hobbyists both will find useful. We will cover installing nginx, enabling the service with systemctl, opening the firewall with ufw, verifying the default page, and editing nginx config for custom sites.

Install and enable Nginx

First update the package index so apt does not surprise you with ancient dependency drama.

sudo apt update
sudo apt install nginx -y

Then start nginx and enable it so it comes back after reboots. This is the systemctl way which avoids ritual sacrifice.

sudo systemctl start nginx
sudo systemctl enable nginx

Open the firewall for HTTP traffic

If ufw is active allow traffic to port 80. If you prefer named profiles use ufw allow "Nginx Full" but the minimal rule is fine for a start.

sudo ufw allow 80

Verify the server is serving requests

Check locally with curl or from another host if you opened ports on a cloud firewall. The default nginx page is boring but comforting.

curl -I http //localhost

A 200 or 301 status means nginx is awake. If you see problems check the service status which is annoyingly useful.

sudo systemctl status nginx

Edit site configuration

For a custom site edit the default server block or create a new file under sites available then enable it with a symlink in sites enabled. Keep server names and root paths tidy and avoid accidental overlaps.

sudo nano /etc/nginx/sites-available/default
# or
sudo nano /etc/nginx/sites-available/example.com
sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/example.com /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/

Test configuration and reload safely

Always validate the nginx configuration before applying changes. This prevents outage and the inevitable blaming of DNS.

sudo nginx -t
sudo systemctl reload nginx

Troubleshooting tips

  • Check error logs at /var/log/nginx/error.log for useful grumbling.
  • Use sudo journalctl -u nginx to see recent service messages.
  • If ufw is blocking traffic verify status with sudo ufw status.

Next steps for production

Now that your basic server is running consider HTTPS with Certbot, tuning worker processes for traffic, and hardening headers. This sequence gives you a reliable Nginx on Ubuntu install that is easy to maintain and simple to extend for real world deployments.

If you hit a snag remember to breathe and read the logs. Nginx is mostly cooperative once you stop yelling at it.
seo_title: Set up Nginx on Ubuntu with systemctl ufw and secure defaults
seo_heading: Quick Ubuntu Nginx server setup guide for devs and small sites

title: filezilla ftp nginx
description: Step by step guide to connect FileZilla to an NGINX served FTP setup with user creation passive mode and file permission tips
heading: FileZilla FTP NGINX setup guide for secure file transfer
body:
This tutorial shows how to configure the FileZilla client to connect to an NGINX hosted FTP service for secure file transfers.

  1. Prepare the server
  2. Create FTP user and set permissions
  3. Configure passive mode and firewall
  4. Set up FileZilla client
  5. Test transfer and troubleshoot

1 Prepare the server

Install a lightweight FTP daemon that works alongside NGINX on the same host. Use a packaged FTP server that supports virtual users and chroot. Adjust the NGINX configuration if NGINX is serving web content from the same directories to avoid permission clashes.

2 Create FTP user and set permissions

Create a dedicated user account for FTP access. Set ownership and strict permissions on upload directories so the FTP account can write while the web service can only read where necessary. Avoid using a global root account unless adventure is the goal.

3 Configure passive mode and firewall

Enable passive mode ranges in the FTP daemon configuration and open those ports on the server firewall. Add the server public address to the passive mode settings so the client can establish data connections through NAT and corporate routers.

4 Set up FileZilla client

In the client add a site entry with the server address username and password. Select passive mode in transfer settings and a secure transfer type if the daemon supports TLS. Save the site for repeated use and avoid typing credentials every time like a caveman.

5 Test transfer and troubleshoot

Upload a small file and check web access if the files are meant to be served by NGINX. If directory listing fails verify firewall rules passive ports and user permissions. Consult server logs for authentication or connection errors.

Summary This guide walked through preparing the server creating a user configuring passive mode and firewall settings setting up FileZilla and running tests to confirm successful transfers

Tip

Use explicit FTP over TLS when supported and match the passive port range with firewall rules for fewer headaches later

title: How to create and run a script in Ubuntu
description: Learn how to create make executable and run a script in Ubuntu using the terminal with simple commands and examples
heading: How to create and run a script in Ubuntu step by step
body:
Welcome to the tiny miracle known as shell scripting. You will type once and make the computer do the same thing forever while you pretend this was always your plan. This guide shows how to make a script in Ubuntu that actually runs, without relying on black magic or clipboard copy rituals.

Create the script file

Open a terminal because this is a terminal tutorial. Create a file with your favorite editor or the lazy command line tools. Examples that will not judge you:

nano hello.sh
# or
touch hello.sh && nano hello.sh

Save the file and move on. You will come back later and edit it like a responsible adult.

Add a shebang and your commands

The first line tells Linux which interpreter to call when you run the file. Use a portable shebang so your script behaves on systems that are not trying to make your life difficult.

#!/usr/bin/env bash

# a tiny script
echo "Hello World"

Put any real work on following lines. Loop, call other programs, or just print witty one liners to keep morale high.

Why use /usr/bin/env bash

On some systems bash lives in different places. This version asks the system to find bash for you. It makes your script more portable across different Linux distros and developer machines.

Make the file executable

Files need permission to be run. Changing permissions is not a dark art, but the command looks impressive which helps at parties.

chmod +x hello.sh

This sets the execute bit for the owner so the kernel will allow the file to run as a program. If you want to be cautious use a more precise mode like 755 or 700.

Run the script

There are two common ways to run your script. One treats the file as a program and the other calls the interpreter explicitly.

  • Run from the current directory with a path
./hello.sh
  • Invoke the interpreter directly
bash hello.sh

If you want to run the script by name from anywhere add its folder to PATH or move the script into a directory that is already in PATH like /usr/local/bin if you have permission. Be careful with PATH or your machine may start doing things you did not expect.

Debugging and safety tips

When things go wrong the terminal will tell you. Read the error messages. They are blunt but usually correct. For safer scripts add a defensive option near the top.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e

set -e stops the script on the first command that fails. It makes debugging less mysterious and prevents cascading failures that turn small problems into sunday level disasters.

Common gotchas

  • Forgot the shebang and the script still runs with bash hello.sh but not with ./hello.sh
  • Permissions not set so the kernel refuses to run it
  • Expecting a program that is not installed on the host

Recap and next steps

Create a file, add a shebang and your commands, make it executable, then run it. Congratulations you now have a tiny automation that replaces repetitive typing and gives you a suspiciously large amount of control over a pile of silicon. Next try passing arguments, reading from files, or putting your script in PATH to feel like you have conquered at least part of the system.
seo_title: Make a runnable Ubuntu script and run it from the terminal today
seo_heading: Step by step bash script guide for Ubuntu users who want automation

title: Configure GitHub SSH Keys
description: Practical guide to generate add and test an SSH key for secure GitHub access without fuss
heading: Configure GitHub SSH Keys Guide
body:
Yes this is another guide about SSH keys because typing your password every time you push is so 2008. Follow these sane steps to create a key pair add it to your GitHub account and stop authenticating like a caveman.

Generate your SSH key

Pick a modern algorithm and do not reuse ancient keys. Ed25519 is the current cool kid. If you are forced to support fossilized systems use RSA with a large key size.

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"
# fallback if absolutely needed
ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "your_email@example.com"

Accept the default file path unless you want multiple keys for different machines. If you like passphrases use one. It makes you slightly more secure and slightly more committed to your future self.

Start the SSH agent and add your private key

The agent keeps your unlocked key in memory so you do not need to type the passphrase every five minutes. Magic but safer.

eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

On Windows with the built in OpenSSH you can use PowerShell to start the agent

Start-Service ssh-agent
ssh-add $env:USERPROFILE\.ssh\id_ed25519

If you run PuTTY use Pageant and create keys with PuTTYgen. Same idea different toolchain.

Copy the public key and add it to GitHub

The public key is safe to share it is the part GitHub needs to know that your machine is you.

cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

Copy the output then go to GitHub Settings under SSH and GPG keys and click New SSH key. Give the key a helpful name like work laptop or home desktop so future you does not have an identity crisis.

Test the SSH connection

Now prove to the internet that you own the key and can receive merciless praise from GitHub.

ssh -T git@github.com

You may be prompted to confirm the host fingerprint. Say yes if the fingerprint matches what GitHub documents. A successful reply will mention your GitHub username and confirm authentication by SSH key.

Switch your repo remote to SSH

If your repo still uses HTTPS change it to SSH so pushes and pulls use the key instead of typing your password into the void.

git remote set-url origin git@github.com:username/repo.git
# verify
git remote -v

Now push and pull as usual. If things break check which key the agent has loaded and whether the public key on GitHub matches the private key on your machine.

Quick extra tips

  • Set file permissions to keep private keys private: chmod 700 ~/.ssh and chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.
  • If you manage several keys use a config file at ~/.ssh/config to map keys to hosts and identities.
  • Label keys clearly on GitHub so you can revoke a lost laptop without wrecking all your setups.

That is it. You generated a key started the agent added the public key to GitHub tested the connection and switched your repo to SSH. You will now type fewer passwords and gain a small boost in developer dignity.
seo_title: Stop Typing Passwords Add SSH Keys to GitHub Like a Pro
seo_heading: A practical guide to SSH keys for GitHub on Windows macOS and Linux

title: How to use GitHub with SSH Keys on Windows 10
description: Set up SSH keys on Windows 10 for secure GitHub access Learn key generation agent setup and testing for password free Git operations
heading: How to use GitHub with SSH Keys on Windows 10
body:
This tutorial shows how to generate an SSH key on Windows 10 add that key to a GitHub account and use the key for secure Git operations without typing a password every push.

  1. Install Git and open a Unix style shell
  2. Generate an SSH key pair
  3. Start the SSH agent and add the private key
  4. Copy the public key to GitHub
  5. Test the connection and switch repository remotes to SSH

Install Git for Windows and use Git Bash or enable the Windows OpenSSH client. The shell provides the familiar ssh tools needed for the rest of the steps. Yes that means fewer surprises when following commands shown online.

Generate a strong key with a command like ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com" and follow prompts to save the file under the default path. If older systems demand RSA use a modern key type for better security.

Start the SSH agent and add the private key with commands such as eval "$(ssh-agent -s)" and ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519. The agent keeps the key unlocked for the session so that repeated pushes do not require typing a passphrase over and over.

Expose the public key with cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub | clip and paste the clipboard contents into the GitHub account settings under SSH keys. Use a clear title so the key can be identified later when managing multiple machines.

Verify the setup with ssh -T git@github.com and look for a welcome message. After confirmation switch repository remotes to the SSH address shown on GitHub and push to confirm password free access.

This guide covered installation key generation agent usage public key registration and connection testing so that Git operations use SSH keys instead of repeated passwords.

Tip

Use a passphrase on the private key and rely on the SSH agent for convenience. A passphrase protects the key if the machine is compromised and the agent prevents repeated typing during active sessions.

title: Create and Configure GitLab SSH Keys
description: Quick tutorial on generating SSH keys and adding the public key to GitLab for secure push pull and CI access
heading: Create and Configure GitLab SSH Keys for Secure Access
body:
This tutorial shows how to generate an SSH key pair and register the public key with GitLab for secure push pull and pipeline access.

  1. Generate an SSH key pair
  2. Add the public key to GitLab profile
  3. Start SSH agent and add the private key
  4. Optional configure SSH client for multiple accounts
  5. Test connection and use with repositories

Generate an SSH key pair

Run a modern key generator for better security and less drama. Example for an Ed25519 key

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"

Press Enter to accept default path unless a custom path is needed. Use a passphrase for extra protection or leave blank for automation environments.

Add the public key to GitLab profile

Copy the public key content and paste into the GitLab web console under Profile Settings SSH Keys. On a Unix like machine use

cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

Give a clear title so future you does not panic when scanning a list of keys.

Start SSH agent and add the private key

Use the SSH agent to cache the private key for the session. Typical commands are

eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"

ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

On Windows use the OpenSSH agent service or a GUI key manager depending on preference.

Optional configure SSH client for multiple accounts

Create a config file to pick the right key per host. Example content

Host gitlab.com User git IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

This prevents accidental use of the wrong account when juggling personal and work keys.

Test connection and use with repositories

Verify that GitLab recognizes the key with a test connection

ssh -T git@gitlab.com

Successful authentication will prompt a welcome message. After that add SSH remotes and push or pull as usual.

Recap The guide covered generating an SSH key pair adding the public key to a GitLab profile loading the private key into an SSH agent optionally configuring the SSH client and testing the connection. Following these steps gives a secure and convenient way to access GitLab repositories and pipelines without password prompts.

Tip

Use distinct keys per machine or role and give descriptive key titles in GitLab. That makes revocation painless when a laptop goes on an unexpected vacation.

title: JavaScript and Node.js File Upload Example
description: Step by step guide to implement file uploads with JavaScript and Node.js using Express and multer with practical production tips
heading: JavaScript and Node.js File Upload Example Guide
body:
This tutorial shows how to add a file upload feature using JavaScript on the client and Node.js on the server in a practical way.

  1. Set up an Express server and install multer
  2. Create a minimal HTML form for the client
  3. Implement the upload route and middleware
  4. Validate and store uploaded files
  5. Serve or process uploaded files after storage

Set up an Express server by installing Express and multer. Use multer as middleware to parse multipart form data. Keep configuration simple during development and plan a storage strategy for production storage locations.

Create a minimal HTML form that posts to the upload route and uses enctype multipart slash form data. Use a single file input and progressive enhancement for nicer UX. On the client use Fetch API for AJAX uploads or a plain form submit when a simple flow is desired.

Implement the upload route with multer middleware. Example route can accept a single file field named file. Access the uploaded file from the request object and inspect file metadata such as originalname mime type and size. Respond with JSON or a redirect depending on the application flow.

After storage serve files through a static route for simple apps or generate signed URLs when using cloud buckets. For processing run image resizing transcoding or antivirus scans as part of a background task so the upload response remains fast.

Recap of the tutorial content explains how to wire up client HTML JavaScript and a Node.js Express route with multer perform validation and choose a storage plan that matches expected traffic and security needs.

Tip

title: jdbc
description: Compact guide to JDBC for Java developers connecting to relational databases and running safe queries
heading: jdbc explained for Java database access
body:
JDBC is a Java API for connecting Java applications to relational databases.

JDBC provides standard interfaces for drivers connections statements and result sets. A vendor supplied driver handles protocol details and the API handles query execution transaction control and result processing. The typical workflow is short and predictable. Follow these steps for a reliable integration.

  1. Load or rely on the driver
  2. Open a Connection
  3. Create a PreparedStatement
  4. Execute query or update
  5. Process the ResultSet
  6. Close resources or use try with resources

Load the driver by including a JDBC driver jar on the class path and letting the driver register automatically. Opening a Connection uses a URL user name and password managed by the driver manager or a connection pool. PreparedStatement provides parameter binding which prevents SQL injection and often improves performance. Executing a query returns a ResultSet which moves forward row by row while methods extract typed values. Closing resources matters more than most developers admit. Use try with resources for automatic cleanup and prefer a connection pool for production to avoid expensive open close cycles.

Here is a terse conceptual snippet showing the flow

Connection conn = DriverManager.getConnection(url username password) PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement("select id name from users where email = ?") ps.setString(1 email) ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()

Loop the ResultSet and map columns to domain objects. Handle SQL exceptions by logging enough context to debug without leaking secrets. For transactions use setAutoCommit false commit and rollback explicitly through the Connection. For modern applications prefer lightweight libraries or micro ORM layers to reduce boilerplate and to centralize error handling.

JDBC remains the low level bridge between Java and SQL databases. Mastering driver choice connection management prepared statements and resource cleanup will save hours of debugging and a few production incidents.

Tip

Always use PreparedStatement for user supplied values and use a connection pool such as HikariCP for production to cut latency and improve reliability.

title: networking lab
description: Hands on guide to build a small networking lab for testing routing switching and troubleshooting with virtual devices and lightweight tools
heading: networking lab guide for hands on practice
body:
Why build a networking lab at home

If you want to learn routing switching packet tracing or just prove to yourself you can break and fix a network without HR noticing this is the place. A small lab gives you a safe playground to test BGP OSPF VLANs and packet captures without bringing down the production network or your self esteem.

Plan a tiny topology that still teaches big lessons

Keep it small and mean. Start with two routers one switch and two hosts. That setup covers IP addressing basic routing and VLANs while leaving room for dramatic failure scenarios. Sketch the topology on paper or in a whiteboard app so you only change things when you mean to.

Basic topology ideas

  • One subnet with two routers for route selection experiments
  • One switch with two VLANs to learn switching and trunking
  • Introduce a Linux host for packet tracing and scripting

Choose virtualization or cheap physical kit

GNS3 and EVE NG are great if you like GUIs and snapshots. Raspberry Pi and thrift store switches work if you want real packets and a mess on your desk. Virtualization saves desk space and coffee stains. Physical gear gives you the satisfying crunch of a cable being unplugged while you panic.

Assign IPs and configure interfaces

Consistency is your friend. Pick a scheme and stick to it. Use clear subnets and name interfaces so your future self can read the config without the need for therapy.

ip addr add 192.168.1.10/24 dev eth0
ip link set eth0 up

On routers you can use static routes for clarity or run a simple routing protocol for realism. OSPF is a friendly intro and BGP can be saved for when you like chaos with paperwork.

Routing and switching basics to practice

Practice static routes first then add OSPF or RIP. Configure VLANs on the switch and test inter VLAN routing through a router on a stick or a layer 3 switch. Observe MAC tables and ARP caches to learn how packets get around.

Test connectivity with packet tracing tools

Ping and traceroute are old but gold. For actual packet level proof use tcpdump or Wireshark. Capture the traffic and read it like a crime scene report for packets.

ping 192.168.1.20
traceroute 192.168.2.20
tcpdump -i eth0 -nn -w capture.pcap

In virtual labs GNS3 and EVE NG both support live packet captures. Use them to watch packets take scenic routes you did not authorize.

Troubleshooting workflow that does not involve guesswork

When traffic stops follow a checklist. Check interface states IP addresses routing tables ACLs and firewall rules. Then capture traffic to confirm whether packets arrive and where they die.

  1. Verify interfaces are up and have correct IPs
  2. Check routing tables and next hops
  3. Look at ACLs or firewall rules that might block traffic
  4. Use tcpdump or Wireshark to follow packet paths

Document changes and use snapshots

Keep a short log of commands you change and take snapshots if using virtual devices. Snapshots let you roll back fast and save your pride. If a change goes bad restore and try again with less confidence.

Quick lab recipe to get started

  • Set up two routers and one switch in GNS3 or EVE NG
  • Create two hosts on separate VLANs and assign IPs
  • Configure static routes then swap to OSPF
  • Capture traffic with tcpdump and analyze in Wireshark
  • Introduce a fault and practice troubleshooting with your checklist

Final tips that actually help

Start small take snapshots name interfaces and keep a lab log. Use virtualization for speed and physical gear when you need real wires. Learn packet tracing early because reading a pcap is like reading tea leaves that tell you why your network sneezed.

Now go build a lab and break it on purpose. That is the point of learning.

seo_heading: Step by step virtual networking lab with GNS3 EVE NG and Linux tools

title: Performance
description: Concise guide to measuring and improving web performance with practical metrics and fixes for faster user experiences
heading: Performance Guide for Faster Apps and Pages
body:
Understanding web performance in plain terms

Performance is not a religion and it is not a sport where the loudest fan wins. It is how fast your site responds and how much battery, CPU and developer dignity it consumes while doing so. Good performance improves conversions, saves server money and keeps users from throwing their phones across the room.

Stop chasing vague feelings and start tracking real numbers that match real user goals. The right metric depends on your product. A blog needs content to show fast. A complex single page app needs to be interactive quickly. Both deserve measurable targets and real user monitoring.

Key metrics to track

  • Time to First Byte TTFB measures server responsiveness for the initial request
  • First Contentful Paint FCP shows when something useful appears on screen
  • Largest Contentful Paint LCP captures when the main content is visible
  • Time to Interactive TTI tells when the page is actually usable
  • Cumulative Layout Shift CLS tracks unexpected layout jumps that annoy humans

Practical fixes that actually move the needle

Do not guess. Measure first and then change one thing at a time. Use lab tools to run controlled experiments and field tools to see what real people on real devices experience. Here are the usual suspects that help more than corporate buzzwords.

  • Inline minimal critical CSS and delay non essential styles so the browser can paint sooner
  • Defer or async non critical scripts and split code so first time visitors do not get the entire app dumped on their device
  • Compress images, serve modern formats like WebP or AVIF and use responsive images to avoid shipping huge payloads
  • Cache aggressively on the client and at the edge to cut round trips and reduce TTFB
  • Use a CDN so assets come from places closer to your users
  • Profile CPU usage and layout thrash to find hotspots rather than blaming random libraries

Testing and monitoring that do not lie

Combine lab testing with controlled throttling and field collection from real users. Lighthouse and lab tools are great for reproducible benchmarks. Real user monitoring or RUMs reveal issues that only show up on slow networks or older phones. Use both to catch different classes of problems.

Automate your checks. Run performance tests in CI and capture metrics from production. When you get alerted about a regression you can fix it before the marketing team tweets about the slowness.

Performance budgets and team sanity

Set a budget for things like bundle size or LCP and make builds fail when the budget is exceeded. It is a blunt instrument but it keeps regressions honest and launches less embarrassing. Budgets help teams make trade offs instead of piling features until the page collapses under its own weight.

Quick checklist for the impatient

  • Pick one metric that maps to user goals and measure it
  • Run lab tests for controlled comparisons and collect field data for reality checks
  • Compress and modernize images and split JavaScript
  • Cache and use a CDN to reduce latency
  • Set a performance budget and automate it in the build pipeline

Tip Start with a single meaningful metric such as LCP for content heavy pages or TTI for interactive apps. Measure on real devices, enforce a budget and automate checks so nobody is surprised at launch day.
seo_title: Speed Secrets for Web Performance that Actually Boost Conversions
seo_heading: Practical page load metrics and frontend optimization for real users

title: threads
description: Quick guide to threads for developers covering concepts race conditions synchronization and best practices
heading: threads explained for developers
body:
Threads are like tiny chaotic interns that share the same memory space. They promise speed and parallelism but bring surprises when you are not watching. If you care about concurrency without spontaneous data corruption then this guide will help you steer clear of the usual disaster movies.

What a thread actually is

A thread is a lightweight sequence of instructions that runs inside a process. Multiple threads can run concurrently which can improve throughput for IO bound work or help exploit multiple cores for CPU bound tasks when the runtime allows real parallelism. But sharing memory makes communication fast and bugs theatrical.

Key properties to remember

  • Context switching cost matters. Too many threads and the OS will spend more time swapping than doing real work.
  • Shared memory is convenient and dangerous. Race conditions happen when access is not coordinated.
  • Synchronization works but adds complexity and the delightful possibility of deadlock.

Common problems and how to avoid them

Race conditions occur when two threads read and write the same data without coordination. The cure is synchronization such as locks mutexes and atomic operations. That prevents corruption while introducing new risks like lock contention and deadlocks.

Practical tips

  • Prefer a thread pool over spawning raw threads for each task. A thread pool controls thread count and reduces context switching overhead.
  • Use higher level concurrency frameworks or task queues when they exist. They handle lifecycle scheduling and pooling with much less drama.
  • Keep critical sections small. Lock less do more outside the lock.
  • For CPU bound work consider separate processes if your language has a global interpreter lock. Threads will sit there politely while the GIL eats CPU time.
  • For IO bound work threads are often the better choice because they can wait on IO without wasting a whole process.

Lifecycle and shutdown

Production code needs more than a cute example. Handle exceptions lifecycle and graceful shutdown. Use timeouts and join operations to avoid orphaned threads and leaked resources.

Thread t = new Thread(runnable)
t.start()
t.join(timeout)

If a thread pool exists use it. If you must manage threads manually then have a controlled shutdown path and stop accepting new work before waiting for threads to finish.

Diagnostics and performance

Profiling and tracing usually reveal where threads block and where locks become bottlenecks. Look for long hold times on locks hot spots caused by busy waiting and thread thrash from too many context switches.

Summary checklist

  • Use thread pools and task queues instead of raw thread management.
  • Pick processes for CPU bound tasks if your runtime limits parallelism.
  • Prefer threads for IO bound workloads.
  • Protect shared mutable state with synchronization but keep critical sections tiny.
  • Profile trace and measure before assuming more threads will help.

Threads are powerful when used carefully and chaotic when treated like a magic trick. Respect context switching mind your synchronization and you might actually ship code that behaves in production.
seo_title: How to tame threads for fast and sane concurrent code
seo_heading: Practical multithreading tips to avoid race conditions and deadlocks

title: Apache Reverse Proxy Configuration Example
description: Quick hands on guide to configure Apache as a reverse proxy with ProxyPass ProxyPassReverse virtual host and basic security tips
heading: Apache Reverse Proxy Configuration Example Guide
body:
This tutorial gives a high level overview of how to configure Apache as a reverse proxy to forward client requests to backend servers in a safe and predictable way.

  1. Enable required modules
  2. Create a virtual host or update an existing one
  3. Add ProxyPass and ProxyPassReverse rules
  4. Harden proxy rules and add headers
  5. Restart Apache and test requests

Enable required modules Load mod_proxy mod_proxy_http and mod_proxy_balancer as needed on the server. Those modules perform the heavy lifting for forwarding and balancing traffic. On many systems a2enmod is the helper command that saves typing.

Create a virtual host Configure a virtual host block that listens on port 80 or 443 depending on presence of TLS. The virtual host becomes the face that clients connect to while backend servers remain hidden behind that face.

Add ProxyPass rules Use ProxyPass and ProxyPassReverse to map a public path to a backend server or pool. Preserve the Host header when needed by enabling ProxyPreserveHost. Keep mapping rules minimal and predictable to avoid accidental open proxies.

Harden and add headers Deny access to local resources that should not be proxied. Add headers such as X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto so backend servers receive useful client information. Consider limiting allowed methods and adding basic authentication for admin paths.

Restart and test Reload or restart Apache and perform a few manual requests from curl or a browser. Check response headers and backend logs to ensure forwarded requests carry expected host and client data. If using TLS verify certificate chain on the public interface while backend communication can remain plaintext on a trusted network.

The guide covered enabling proxy modules crafting a virtual host mapping public paths to backend servers adding basic security headers and checking behavior after a restart. This provides a reliable starting point for running Apache as a reverse proxy without surprises or accidental open doors.

Tip

Run simple curl checks that print response headers and backend content to confirm proxy rules and forwarded headers match expectations before announcing the new entry point to users.

title: Run Apache in Docker Example Host Your Website
description: Learn how to serve a local website using the official Apache httpd Docker image with a bind mount and port mapping
heading: Run Apache in Docker Example Host Your Website from Local Files with Httpd Image
body:
Why run Apache in Docker

Want to serve a simple site without turning your laptop into a permanent server pit of despair This approach uses the official Apache httpd image so you get a real web server without building an image every time you change a line of HTML

What you need before you start

  • Docker installed and working on your machine
  • A terminal and just enough patience to type commands
  • A folder called site with an index html file inside it

Step by step guide

Create the document root

Make a folder named site and drop an index html file in there This is the document root that Apache will serve so avoid creating a nested maze unless you like solving puzzles

Run the Apache container

Start a container with a bind mount so edits on your host show up instantly in the container This keeps your dev workflow fast and annoying free

docker run -d -p 8080->80 -v ./site->/usr/local/apache2/htdocs httpd

What that does in plain English It runs httpd detached maps host port 8080 to container port 80 and mounts your local site folder into the Apache document root

Open the site in a browser

Point your browser to localhost on port 8080 to see the index page If nothing shows up check that the container is running and that you did not pick a port that is already occupied

Live editing and workflow tips

Edit files inside your local site folder and refresh the browser Changes appear immediately because of the bind mount This is great for prototyping and horrible for forgetting to commit changes

  • Want fast feedback Use your editor of choice and keep the container running
  • Need to make a lot of changes Consider using a local build step or a live reload tool on top of this setup

Troubleshooting common annoyances

Container exits or fails

Run docker ps -a to see status and docker logs with the container id to read what went wrong Logs are your friend unless you enjoy guessing games

Port conflicts

If port 8080 is taken pick another high numbered port and update the run command accordingly

Permission denied when files do not appear

If new files do not show up check file ownership and permissions on the host Make the site folder readable by your user or use a safer folder on the host

Why this method is nice for dev

No need to build an image for every tiny edit The container runs a stock Apache httpd image and your local files are mapped in so you get a fast feedback loop while keeping the container clean and disposable

Quick checklist

  • Create site folder and add index html
  • Run the container with port and volume mapping
  • Open localhost on the chosen port to test
  • Edit files and refresh to see changes
  • If problems arise check docker ps -a and docker logs

If you want to graduate from this toy setup later you can build a custom image with your assets and configuration But for hacking on HTML CSS or templating this keeps things quick and mercifully simple
seo_title: Host your local website with Apache in Docker without drama
seo_heading: Quick local web development with Apache httpd inside a Docker container

title: Docker Compose Example with Apache
description: Learn how to run Apache with Docker Compose using a simple compose file for fast local development and testing
heading: Docker Compose Example with Apache
body:
This tutorial shows how to run Apache in a container using Docker Compose and a minimal compose file for quick local development.

  1. Create a docker compose file for the Apache service
  2. Select an Apache image and configure ports
  3. Mount web content via a volume for live edits
  4. Start containers with docker compose up and view logs

Tip

title: Differences Between Docker Compose and Dockerfile
description: Quick comparison of Docker Compose and Dockerfile with practical guidance on when to build images and when to orchestrate services for development and depl
heading: Differences Between Docker Compose and Dockerfile
body:
If Dockerfile and Docker Compose were people one would be a grumpy sous chef and the other would be a party planner who insists everyone share a playlist. Both are essential, and neither will fix your broken CI pipeline by themselves. Here is a clear and slightly rude guide to when to build images and when to wire containers together.

What each file actually does

Dockerfile defines how an image is built. It lists the steps to install dependencies copy files and set the default process. Think of it as a recipe that produces an image you can store in a registry and reuse in CI pipelines or production.

Docker Compose uses a YAML file to describe how one or more containers run together. It declares services networks and volumes and handles environment variables port mappings and simple scaling. Compose is the script that starts the whole ensemble so your web app can talk to its database without existential angst.

Typical workflow that does not make your life worse

  • Build an image from Dockerfile using a build command like docker build -t myapp .. That creates an image with layers and configuration baked in.
  • Declare services in a compose file named docker-compose.yml and describe the web database and other pieces. Keep the wiring and runtime settings there.
  • Start everything with docker-compose up for development or simple deployments. It brings up networks volumes and the linked containers in one shout.

Quick example without a cliff note

Build step example above creates the image. Compose step example starts the stack. No magic is happening here just sensible separation of responsibilities.

When to choose Dockerfile

  • Use Dockerfile when you need a reproducible image that CI can build and push to a registry.
  • Pin dependencies optimize layer order and set the default process in the Dockerfile.
  • Use multi stage builds to keep final images small and avoid shipping your build tools with the app.

When to choose Docker Compose

  • Choose Docker Compose when multiple containers must work together and orchestration needs are light.
  • Compose is great for local development testing and simple multi container deployment setups.
  • Keep runtime concerns here like environment files port mappings and volume mounts rather than baking them into the image.

Practical tips and common traps

  • Keep build concerns in the Dockerfile and runtime wiring in Compose. If you mix them you will regret it later.
  • Do not bake runtime secrets into an image. Use environment files or a secret manager to handle sensitive values.
  • Use multi stage builds to avoid giant images that waste bandwidth and soul.
  • Remember that Compose is not a full orchestration solution for large production clusters. For heavier orchestration you want a system like Kubernetes or another orchestrator that handles scaling health checks and scheduling.

Takeaway for sleep deprived devops humans

Dockerfile builds the image and stores the repeatable steps that make it possible to reproduce a build. Docker Compose wires containers together at runtime and makes multi container development tolerable. Use both wisely and your deployments will be less tragic and somewhat predictable.
seo_title: When to Use Dockerfile Versus Docker Compose for Containers
seo_heading: Make images and run services the right way with Dockerfile and Compose

title: Differences Between Docker Run and Docker Compose Compared
description: Compare Docker Run and Docker Compose and learn when to use each for single containers or multi service stacks
heading: Differences Between Docker Run and Docker Compose Compared
body:
The key difference between Docker Run and Docker Compose is that Docker Run manages single containers from the command line while Docker Compose defines and runs multi container applications using a YAML file.

Think of Docker Run as a quick one off command for testing an image. Use Docker Run when launching a single service or when trying a new image. Example command docker run --name web nginx will start an nginx container with a simple name.

Think of Docker Compose as a blueprint for full stacks. Use Compose when coordinating multiple services database cache and web server or when configuring shared networks and volumes. Compose reads a file named docker compose yaml and brings all services up with a single command such as docker compose up -d.

Key practical differences

  1. Scope Docker Run focuses on a single container while Docker Compose orchestrates multiple containers
  2. Configuration Docker Run relies on command line flags while Compose stores configuration in a YAML file for reproducibility
  3. Networking Docker Run often needs manual network setup while Compose creates a network so services can talk to each other by name
  4. Scaling Docker Run needs repeated commands while Compose supports scaling copies of a service with a single flag

Pick Docker Run for quick experiments and one off tasks. Pick Docker Compose for local development environments and simple multi service deployments. When growth demands more advanced scheduling and resilience consider moving from Compose to a dedicated orchestration platform but remember that Compose remains a low friction way to model and share application topologies.

Tip

Keep Compose files under version control and use environment variable files to avoid leaking secrets. Use Compose for reproducible local stacks and switch to orchestration platforms only when scaling needs actually require that move.

title: Difference Between Rows vs Columns Explained Quickly
description: Quick explanation of how rows differ from columns in spreadsheets and databases so data becomes clearer and less confusing.
heading: Difference Between Rows and Columns Explained Quickly
body:
If your spreadsheet once betrayed you by summing the wrong thing do not blame the format. Rows and columns are simple creatures that get misunderstood when people try to be clever. This guide will explain the orientation role and typical operations for rows and columns so you can stop blaming pivot tables for your mistakes.

What is a row and what is a column

Think of a row as a single record. It runs left to right across a table and usually describes one entity like a customer an order or an event. A column runs top to bottom and stores the same attribute across many records like name date amount or status.

Quick visual rules

  • Rows run horizontally. Look left to right to see a single record.
  • Columns run vertically. Look top to bottom for an attribute.
  • Column headers sit at the top and become the field names used in formulas and queries.

Why the difference matters in spreadsheets and databases

Aggregations like sum average and count operate on columns. Filters searches and edits usually target rows. In Excel you might select a column to total sales. In SQL you will select specific columns in the SELECT clause and filter rows with WHERE to find particular records.

Examples that do not lie

Spreadsheet example:

Name    Age    Email
Alice   30     alice@example.com
Bob     42     bob@example.com

SQL example that follows the same idea

SELECT name email FROM customers WHERE id = 123

Indexes keys and performance

Columns define attributes that you often aggregate or index. Rows should have a unique identifier like a primary key for safe joins and lookups. Adding an index on a column speeds up row lookups in SQL tables but it does not change the orientation. Indexing is about access speed not about turning rows into columns.

Common mistakes and how to avoid them

  • Accidental transposes when copying data. If the data flips orientation your calculations will scream.
  • Summing rows instead of columns. Double check which axis your formula is using.
  • Pivot table confusion. The most likely culprit is swapping rows and columns not a mystical spreadsheet gremlin.

Design tips that save your future self

  • Choose columns for consistent attributes and rows for individual records.
  • Freeze column headers in Excel to keep context while scrolling.
  • Add a unique row identifier for safe joins and reliable lookups in databases.

Rows tell the story. Columns provide the facts. Keep that in mind and your charts will stop lying to you and your SQL will stop making you cry.

seo_heading: Practical guide to rows columns and indexing in spreadsheets and SQL

title: Setup an Apache Load Balancer Example
description: Compact guide to configure an Apache load balancer using mod proxy modules with commands testing tips and monitoring advice
heading: Setup an Apache Load Balancer Example Guide
body:
This tutorial teaches how to configure an Apache load balancer using mod_proxy and mod_proxy_balancer to distribute HTTP requests across backend servers.

  1. Prepare backend servers
  2. Enable required Apache modules
  3. Create the balancer configuration
  4. Secure the balancer manager
  5. Test and monitor the setup

Prepare backend servers by installing a simple web service on each host and confirming health with a browser or curl. Use distinct ports or hostnames for each backend so the load balancer can target multiple endpoints.

Enable required Apache modules with a single command that does the heavy lifting. Run a2enmod proxy proxy_balancer proxy_http lbmethod_byrequests and then restart the Apache service with systemctl restart apache2. This adds the proxy and balancing functionality so the server can accept and route traffic.

Create the balancer configuration inside a virtual host file. Define a named balancer block and add backend members inside that block. Use ProxyPass and ProxyPassReverse directives to point a public path to the named balancer block. The named block groups backend servers and controls load distribution and session affinity.

Secure the balancer manager by restricting access to the management interface. Place a manager location behind authentication and limit access to admin networks. The balancer manager provides runtime controls for removing members and changing load methods so exposing that interface to the world would be rude.

Test and monitor by sending traffic to the public virtual host and watching backend logs. Use curl with simple requests and watch the load shift across backends. For more visibility enable status pages and log health probe results. Monitoring tells the honest truth about stability or lack of grace under pressure.

Recap of the tutorial steps covers preparing backends enabling modules creating a balancer configuration securing the manager and validating the setup with tests and monitoring. Follow those steps and the Apache load balancer will carry more traffic than any single server wants to admit.

Tip

Use a dedicated health check endpoint on backend servers and have the balancer probe that endpoint frequently. That avoids serving broken pages and keeps traffic flowing to healthy hosts only.

title: Install & Setup PHP and Nginx on Ubuntu Linux with FPM
description: Step by step guide to install PHP and Nginx on Ubuntu and configure PHP FPM for fastcgi processing and testing.
heading: Install and Setup PHP and Nginx on Ubuntu Linux with FPM
body:
Why this guide exists and who should read it

If you want a lean web server on Ubuntu that speaks PHP without hiccups, you are in the right place. This practical tutorial walks through installing Nginx and PHP FPM on Ubuntu, configuring Nginx to hand PHP requests off to FPM, and verifying that everything actually works. Expect clear commands, a few sarcastic comments, and no baffling magic.

Quick checklist before you begin

  • Ubuntu server or VM with sudo access
  • Basic familiarity with the terminal
  • About 10 minutes and a tiny bit of patience

Step by step install and configure

1 Update the base system

Updating first avoids the classic dependency drama that shows up when you try to install things on old packages. Trust me, this saves time and pillow punching.

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

2 Install Nginx and PHP FPM

Install the web server plus the PHP fastcgi manager and the common MySQL extension if you need it for databases.

sudo apt install nginx php-fpm php-mysql -y

PHP FPM runs PHP separately from Nginx which keeps the site snappier and more stable under load.

3 Configure Nginx to pass PHP to PHP FPM

Edit a server block in /etc/nginx/sites-available or modify the default file. The important bits are enabling index.php and forwarding .php files to the FPM socket or TCP port.

# typical minimal server block
server {
  listen 80;
  server_name example.com www.example.com;
  root /var/www/html;

  index index.php index.html index.htm;

  location / {
    try_files $uri $uri/ =404;
  }

  location ~ \.php$ {
    include snippets/fastcgi-php.conf;
    fastcgi_pass unix:/run/php/php-fpm.sock;
  }
}

Replace the socket path with the one on your system for your PHP version. If PHP FPM runs on another host use fastcgi_pass ipaddress:9000 instead of a unix socket.

Always test Nginx syntax before reloading.

sudo nginx -t
sudo systemctl reload nginx

4 Test PHP in the browser

Create a small phpinfo file in the web root to confirm PHP is being processed by FPM. Do not leave this file online forever, it is an open invitation for nosy scanners.

echo '<?php phpinfo(); ?>' | sudo tee /var/www/html/info.php
# then visit http://your-server/info.php

When you see the PHP info page you know Nginx and PHP FPM are talking to each other like civilized services.

5 Restart and verify services

If something was changed or you installed a new PHP version restart services and check statuses.

sudo systemctl restart php*-fpm nginx
sudo systemctl status nginx
sudo systemctl status php*-fpm

Adjust the php service name if you target a specific version like php7.4-fpm or php8.1-fpm.

Tips and best practices

  • Prefer Unix sockets for local FPM communication as they are usually faster
  • Switch to TCP when the FPM process is remote or inside a container
  • Remove the phpinfo page after testing so you do not leak configuration details to strangers
  • Use nginx -t after edits to avoid syntax errors that take down your site

Next steps and hardening suggestions

Once PHP and Nginx are talking you can deploy your app. Consider TLS, fail2ban, proper permissions, php ini tuning, and a caching layer for better performance. This is a functional server setup guide, not a fortress design guide, so plan additional hardening before going public.

There you go, a working Ubuntu Nginx and PHP FPM setup that should handle your app without whining. Now go break it in a staging environment and fix what you find.
