seo_heading: Ubuntu Nginx and PHP FPM server setup for fastcgi and app hosting

title: How to Install Tomcat 10 on Ubuntu 22
description: Step by step guide to install Apache Tomcat 10 on Ubuntu 22 with systemd setup and basic security tips
heading: How to Install Tomcat 10 on Ubuntu 22 Server
body:
This tutorial shows how to install Apache Tomcat 10 on Ubuntu 22 and run Tomcat as a systemd service with basic security and a quick test.

  1. Update packages and install Java
  2. Create a Tomcat user and download Tomcat
  3. Set permissions and move Tomcat files
  4. Create a systemd service for Tomcat
  5. Start service and test deployment
  6. Apply simple security steps

Step 1 Update package index and install a supported Java runtime. Tomcat 10 runs well on Java 11 or later. Use commands like sudo apt update and sudo apt install openjdk-11-jdk and confirm Java with java -version.

Step 2 Create a dedicated user for Tomcat and download the Tomcat binary. A service user reduces risk from running as root. Example commands include sudo useradd -r -m -U -d /opt/tomcat -s /bin/false tomcat and then download the latest Tomcat 10 tarball to /tmp and extract to /opt/tomcat.

Step 3 Adjust ownership and permissions so the tomcat user owns the installation. This prevents accidental access from other users. Typical commands are sudo chown -R tomcat tomcat /opt/tomcat and a careful permission mask on configuration and bin directories.

Step 4 Create a systemd unit file to manage the Tomcat service. Point the ExecStart to the Tomcat startup script and set the user and group to tomcat. After adding the unit file reload systemd with sudo systemctl daemon-reload.

Step 5 Enable and start the service and verify health. Use sudo systemctl enable --now tomcat and check status with sudo systemctl status tomcat. Test deployment by placing a WAR file in the webapps folder and accessing the default port usually 8080.

Step 6 Apply basic security measures such as locking down manager and host manager apps with strong passwords and limiting network exposure with a firewall rule. Consider running Tomcat behind a reverse proxy for TLS termination.

This guide covered package preparation, Java installation, user setup, file permissions, systemd integration, service launch and basic hardening for Tomcat 10 on Ubuntu 22. Follow the steps in order and test each change before moving on to production.

Tip

Use a reverse proxy like Nginx to terminate TLS and protect the Tomcat manager with IP allow lists. That adds a layer of defense without changing application code.

title: How to configure Nginx Reverse Proxy Servers Tutorial
description: Step by step Nginx reverse proxy guide from install to SSL and testing for reliable backend routing and headers
heading: How to configure Nginx reverse proxy servers tutorial
body:
This tutorial shows how to set up an Nginx reverse proxy to route traffic to backend services.

  1. Install Nginx
  2. Create a server block
  3. Configure proxy settings and headers
  4. Test connectivity
  5. Enable SSL
  6. Reload and enable on boot
  7. Check logs and troubleshoot

Install Nginx Use the distribution package manager to install Nginx and enable the service. Start the service and confirm the web server responds on port 80. No rocket science required unless the server hates you today.

Create a server block Place a server block file under /etc/nginx/sites-available and create a symlink in sites-enabled. Set a proper server_name value for the domain that will receive public traffic. That domain will be the face that clients see while backend services remain hidden.

Configure proxy settings and headers Add a location block that forwards requests to a backend pool or upstream group. Preserve client context by setting headers such as X-Real-IP X-Forwarded-For and Host. Use upstream blocks to list backend hosts for simpler proxy lines and optional load distribution.

Test connectivity Use a simple HTTP request from another host or local curl command to verify that the domain returns content from the intended backend. Watch response headers for correct forwarding and expected status codes. If the response is wrong the server block may point to the wrong backend name or port.

Enable SSL Obtain a certificate from a trusted authority or use an automated tool for certificate issuance. Configure a listen directive for port 443 and reference the certificate files in the server block. Redirect plain HTTP to HTTPS so browsers get a secure connection without manual complaint.

Reload and enable on boot Validate Nginx configuration with the built in test command and then reload the service to apply changes. Enable the service so the reverse proxy survives reboots. That keeps the proxy online even when the universe tries to reboot the host.

Check logs and troubleshoot Review access and error logs under /var/log/nginx for clues when responses misbehave. Common culprits include wrong upstream addresses missing headers and firewall rules blocking backend ports.

The steps above provide a clear path from a fresh server to a functional Nginx reverse proxy that forwards traffic securely and preserves client information. Follow the order to avoid surprises and make small tests after each change to catch mistakes early.

Tip

Use an upstream block with backend hostnames and health checks from a process monitor. That reduces manual edits when scaling services and gives quick insight when one backend becomes grumpy.

title: Setup Login to Tomcat Manager without 401 403 errors
description: Quick guide to configure Tomcat Manager and avoid 401 and 403 errors when logging in to the Manager web interface
heading: Setup Login to Tomcat Manager without 401 403 errors
body:
This tutorial shows how to configure Tomcat and log in to the Manager web application without 401 or 403 errors.

  1. Add a manager user to tomcat users XML
  2. Restart the Tomcat server
  3. Verify Manager webapp and security constraints
  4. Check network binding and connector settings
  5. Access the Manager page and authenticate

Step one Edit the conf slash tomcat users dot xml file and add a role and a user entry for the manager GUI. Use a strong password and avoid using a default account that invites trouble.

< role rolename="manager-gui" />

< user username="admin" password="StrongPass123" roles="manager-gui" />

Step two Restart the Tomcat server so the new user and role take effect. A restart forces the authentication realm to reload configuration files.

Step three Confirm that the Manager webapp is enabled and that web xml or context xml does not block the manager GUI from the desired host. Some distributions restrict the manager by default to local requests only.

Step four Check connector attributes and firewall rules. If the server is bound to a specific address or a proxy is in front of the server the Manager may deny access with a 403. Confirm that the connection comes from an allowed address.

Step five Open a browser and go to localhost slash manager slash html on the server host or use the proper host name and port. Enter the admin credentials created in the first step to log in.

Following these steps resolves most 401 and 403 responses when attempting to use the Tomcat Manager. If errors persist check Tomcat logs for authentication realm messages and review any reverse proxy rules that may alter authentication headers.

Tip

Restrict Manager access to trusted hosts by using a remote address valve in the Manager context and keep the manager user out of production code repositories

title: How to add a new project to an existing GitHub repository
description: Step by step guide to add a new project into an existing GitHub repository using local Git commands branches and basic workflows
heading: How to add a new project to an existing GitHub repository
body:
If you need to drop a brand new project into an existing GitHub repository and survive to tell the tale this guide will get you there without breaking the commit history or making reviewers cry. We will use plain git commands and a sensible git workflow to clone or reuse a local copy create a project folder work on a feature branch stage and commit push and open a pull request and handle reviews.

Prepare your local copy

If the repo is not on your workstation clone it. If it is already present skip this step and go make coffee.

git clone REPO_URL
cd repo-folder

If you already have the repo locally then just change into the repo root and update from remote if you want to be polite to your future self.

cd path/to/repo
git fetch
git checkout main
git pull

Create the project folder and add files

Make a directory and drop your source files docs and configuration in there. Use a starter template if that speeds things up. Remember to add or update README and .gitignore if needed.

mkdir new-project
cd new-project
# create files or copy a template
# example touch main.py README.md

Create a feature branch

Branching keeps the main branch tidy and gives reviewers a sane diff to look at. Pick a descriptive branch name that hints at what you added.

git checkout -b feature/new-project

Names like feature/new-project bugfix/fix-build or docs/add-guide are simple and useful. Short lived branches win the popularity contest with reviewers.

Stage and commit thoughtfully

Stage only what belongs in this change. Small focused commits help reviewers and your future self when debugging. Use clear commit messages and split the work if it helps explain intent.

git add new-project
git commit -m 'Add new project with initial files'
# or make multiple commits for separate concerns
# git add fileA
# git commit -m 'Add core module'
# git add fileB
# git commit -m 'Add tests and docs'

If the repo runs continuous integration run the tests locally before you push. That way CI does not become your project's first fan club meeting.

Push and open a pull request

Push the feature branch to the remote then create a pull request on GitHub for code review. Give the PR a useful title and description link any relevant issues and explain setup steps or migration notes if needed.

git push origin feature/new-project

On GitHub open a pull request from your branch into main and request reviewers. Address review comments with follow up commits and squash or rebase if your team prefers a tidy history.

Merge and follow up

When the PR is approved and CI is happy merge using the repository workflow. After merging pull main locally and delete your feature branch both locally and on the remote to avoid future confusion.

git checkout main
git pull
git branch -d feature/new-project
git push origin --delete feature/new-project

Quick recap and tips

  • Clone or use your local repo and stay up to date with main
  • Create a dedicated feature branch with a descriptive name
  • Stage only related files and commit in small logical steps
  • Push the branch and open a pull request for review
  • Run tests and update CI config or docs if needed
  • Delete stale branches after merging to avoid mystery branches later

If you follow this sequence your git history will stay readable and your teammates will thank you or at least not leave passive aggressive comments in PRs. That is basically a win.
seo_title: Add a new project to a GitHub repo and keep history tidy
seo_heading: Step by step Git workflow for adding a project to an existing repo

title: How to Add & Upload a New Project to an Existing GitLab
description: Step by step guide to add and upload a new project to an existing GitLab repo with Git commands SSH key tips and push verification.
heading: How to Add and Upload a New Project to an Existing GitLab
body:
So you built something useful or at least interesting and now you want to upload that mess to a GitLab repository. Good. This guide walks you through the tidy and boringly reliable steps to add a new local project and push it to an existing GitLab repo. No ceremony, no GUI acrobatics, just Git commands that actually do what they claim.

What you will do

Quick run down of the plan so you can pretend you knew it all along

  • Create a project folder and add files
  • Initialize a local repository with git init
  • Add a remote that points to the existing GitLab repository
  • Stage files, commit, and git push to the remote
  • Optionally set up ssh keys so you never type a password again

Step 1 create the project folder and files

Make a directory for your work and add whatever belongs there. Code, docs, or a single README that explains why this exists are all acceptable. Missing files will not ruin your day.

mkdir my-project
cd my-project
# add your code and other files here

Step 2 initialize a local Git repository

Turn that folder into a Git repository with one small magic spell. Then stage and commit the initial snapshot.

git init
git add .
git commit -m 'Initial commit'

Step 3 add the remote that points to the existing GitLab repo

Tell your local repo where the remote repository lives. Replace remote-url with the URL you get from the GitLab project page. Keep the name origin unless you have a reason to be dramatic.

git remote add origin remote-url

Step 4 push the code with git push

If your default branch is main push like this. If the remote uses master or another branch name adapt accordingly. The -u option links your local branch to the remote branch so future pushes are simpler.

git push -u origin main

What if the remote already has commits

If the remote repo is not empty you might need to pull or fetch first and reconcile histories. Typical pattern is to fetch then merge or rebase. Do that politely and avoid forcing things unless you truly know what you are doing.

Step 5 verify and protect

Open the GitLab project page and confirm your files arrived intact. Consider enabling branch protection and required merge requests if this is a team repository. Protecting branches is the adult thing to do in DevOps workflows.

Optional make pushing painless with ssh keys

Generate an SSH key so Git stops asking you for passwords like it has amnesia. Then copy the public key into your GitLab profile under SSH keys. After that git push will be quieter and slightly kinder.

ssh-keygen -t ed25519
# then copy the contents of ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub into GitLab profile under SSH keys

Recap and tips

We covered creating a local project folder, running git init, adding a remote with git remote, committing with git commit, and pushing with git push. You also learned how ssh keys can reduce friction. These are foundational Git and GitLab tasks useful in everyday DevOps work. Now go upload that project and pretend you always had a plan.

seo_heading: From folder to remote in five sane commands for GitLab repositories

title: Create Bitbucket App Password Fix Git Auth Errors
description: Step by step guide to create a Bitbucket app password and fix fatal invalid credentials and authentication failed errors when using Git
heading: Create Bitbucket App Password Fix Git Authentication Errors
body:
If your Git push or pull turns into a saga about invalid credentials you probably need a Bitbucket app password and a small cleanup ritual. This guide walks you through creating a dedicated app password in Bitbucket setting minimal scopes clearing stale local credentials and using the new secret with Git. It is short it is practical and it will save you from yelling at your terminal at 2 AM.

Why use an app password

App passwords are small scoped secrets that work with HTTPS Git operations and replace using your main account password. They are safer because you can pick minimal permissions and revoke them without touching your whole account. If someone finds an old token you do not have to cancel your life or reset your main password.

How to create an app password in Bitbucket

  1. Sign in to your Bitbucket account and open personal settings then app passwords.
  2. Click to create a new app password and pick a clear label so future you does not scream at the terminal while trying to remember why an ancient token exists.
  3. Select minimal scopes that match the work you will do. For basic push and pull choose repository read and repository write. For pull request tasks add pull request permissions.
  4. Copy the generated app password now because Bitbucket will not show it again. Store it in your password manager if you are feeling responsible.

Clear cached credentials before you test

Most invalid credentials errors come from cached secrets that refuse to die. Remove those old entries and Git will prompt you to enter the new app password.

Windows

Open Credential Manager then look for entries related to bitbucket and remove them. After that Git will ask for fresh credentials on the next network operation.

macOS

Open Keychain Access and search for bitbucket or the name of your remote. Delete any matching items so cached secrets stop sabotaging you.

Linux

Common helpers store credentials in a file or in your keyring. Try these checks and fixes

  • Unset a global credential helper with a command like git config --global --unset credential.helper
  • Remove a credentials file if you used one for convenience by deleting the file named .git-credentials in your home folder
  • If you use a desktop keyring check its entries for bitbucket related secrets and remove them

Use the app password with Git

When Git prompts for a password enter the app password instead of your account password. Keep using your Bitbucket username as the username. If you use a credential helper allow it to store the new app password for fewer awkward prompts later.

git pull
git push origin main

Troubleshooting steps if authentication still fails

  • Double check you used the correct Bitbucket username
  • Confirm the app password scopes include the action you attempted like repository write for pushes or pull request access for PR tasks
  • Make sure you cleared every cached credential on your machine so an old secret does not get reused
  • Verify your remote is using HTTPS remotes not SSH because app passwords only work with HTTPS authentication
  • Confirm the app password has not been revoked or expired and that two factor on your account is handled by using app passwords

Recap and final tips

Create a dedicated Bitbucket app password pick minimal scopes clear stale local credentials then supply the new app password when Git asks. Test with a simple pull or push and if you still see invalid credentials repeat the cleanup steps and check the scopes. Your main account password survives and your logs and old gists stay less dramatic.
seo_title: Stop Git authentication failures with Bitbucket app passwords

title: How to install Java on Ubuntu with apt
description: Step by step guide to install Java on Ubuntu using apt with commands to verify and configure default Java runtime and JDK
heading: How to install Java on Ubuntu with apt guide
body:
This is the short and slightly snarky guide to installing Java on Ubuntu with apt. You will get a working JDK and runtime without the drama. This tutorial works on Ubuntu and other Debian based Linux systems that use the apt package manager. We cover updating the package list, installing OpenJDK or the default JDK, verifying the runtime and compiler, and managing multiple Java versions on the command line.

Update apt and prep your system

First let the package manager know what is new. This keeps you from installing ancient packages that feel like antiques.

sudo apt update

Optionally upgrade stuff if you enjoy long waits and system improvements.

sudo apt upgrade -y

Install a JDK with apt

Most people are fine with the default JDK package. If you need a specific OpenJDK release pick it instead for compatibility with legacy builds or picky CI systems.

  • Default JDK install for most use cases
sudo apt install default-jdk
  • Install OpenJDK 11 for older projects
sudo apt install openjdk-11-jdk

The package manager will fetch the runtime and the compiler components. No magic spells required.

Verify Java and javac

Check both the runtime and the compiler so you do not discover version mismatch at build time while staring at the error logs at 2 AM.

java -version
javac -version

The output tells you which Java runtime and compiler are installed. If they disagree then you might want to fix that before your build system attempts a mutiny.

Set or switch the default Java

If you have multiple Java installs use the Debian alternatives system to pick a default on the system path. This is the proper way to avoid a Java version yard sale.

sudo update-alternatives --config java

Pick a number from the list. Repeat for the compiler if needed.

sudo update-alternatives --config javac

Remove an unwanted version

When a JDK has outlived its usefulness remove it to keep the system tidy and free of ancient leftovers.

sudo apt remove openjdk-11-jdk
sudo apt autoremove

Extra tips for people who like options

  • Use apt search openjdk to browse available JDK packages in the repositories.
  • If you switch JDKs often consider SDKMAN for user level JVM management and faster switching without sudo.
  • If you plan to use Oracle builds check the license and any third party repository terms before adding them to apt.

Quick recap

Update apt, pick a JDK package, verify java and javac, and use update alternatives to manage multiple versions. Follow these steps and your Ubuntu machine will have a reliable Java runtime and compiler ready for development or production. Also you will avoid at least one late night debugging session caused by a version mismatch.
seo_title: Install Java on Ubuntu with apt the smart and clean way

title: Fix the 'Expected a Step on Line' error in Jenkins
description: Quick guide to fix the Expected a Step on Line error in Jenkins pipelines with simple syntax checks and plugin updates for fast CI recovery
heading: Fix the Expected a Step on Line error in Jenkins pipelines
body:
This guide shows how to fix the Expected a Step on Line error in Jenkins pipelines by correcting pipeline syntax and missing step blocks.

  1. Identify pipeline type
  2. Validate Jenkinsfile syntax
  3. Ensure stages contain a steps block
  4. Use proper step commands such as sh or bat
  5. Update plugins and test the job

Identify pipeline type by checking whether the Jenkinsfile uses declarative or scripted style. Declarative style requires a top level pipeline and explicit stages and steps. Scripted style looks more like plain Groovy code and follows different rules.

Validate Jenkinsfile syntax by using the built in pipeline syntax tool or by running a linter. Missing brackets or misplaced blocks often trigger the Expected a Step on Line complaint from the parser.

Ensure stages contain a steps block because a stage that directly contains shell commands without a steps wrapper will cause the parser to complain. Place commands inside steps to satisfy the declarative validator.

Use proper step commands such as sh or bat for shell execution. A common mistake is pasting raw commands where a step name is required. Replace loose script fragments with proper step calls so the pipeline parser sees a valid step entry.

Update plugins and test the job after fixes. Old pipeline plugins or syntax validators can produce confusing errors. Refresh the plugin set and rerun the job to confirm the problem went away.

The outcome should be a Jenkinsfile that the parser accepts and a pipeline that runs without the Expected a Step on Line error. The workflow includes identifying style type validating syntax wrapping commands in steps using proper step names and confirming environment and plugins are current.

Tip

When stuck paste the smallest failing Jenkinsfile into the pipeline syntax validator and remove parts until the error goes away. That narrows the culprit faster than blaming the CI server for being dramatic.

title: Docker and Docker Compose on Ubuntu How to setup
description: Quick guide to install configure and use Docker and Docker Compose on Ubuntu for reliable container workflows
heading: Docker and Docker Compose on Ubuntu How to setup
body:
This guide shows how to install configure and use Docker and Docker Compose on Ubuntu for local container workflows.

  1. Install Docker engine
  2. Enable user permissions and start the service
  3. Install Docker Compose
  4. Create a docker compose file
  5. Run and manage containers

Install Docker engine Follow standard package steps to get the Docker engine from Ubuntu repositories for a quick start. Example commands include

sudo apt update

sudo apt install -y docker.io

sudo systemctl enable --now docker

Enable user permissions and start the service Add a non root user to the Docker group so interactive workflows do not require elevated rights. After the group change perform a logout and login or reboot.

sudo usermod -aG docker $USER

Install Docker Compose Install the compose tool for multi container definitions so orchestration becomes readable and repeatable. On many Ubuntu releases the compose package is available via apt.

sudo apt install -y docker-compose

Create a docker compose file Create a docker compose file named docker compose.yml that declares services networks and volumes for the application. Keep definitions small to start and test a single service first.

Run and manage containers Use the compose command to bring up the stack and view logs and status. Typical commands include

docker compose up -d

docker compose ps

The tutorial covered installation of the Docker engine user configuration installation of Docker Compose and a basic workflow to define and run services with a compose file so local container development becomes efficient and reproducible.

Tip

For production like testing run the Docker engine on the latest stable kernel and pin image tags to avoid surprises. Keep backups of compose files and use version control for changes.

title: Nginx Load Balancer Example Setup and Config
description: Step by step Nginx load balancer setup for distributing HTTP traffic with upstream groups health checks and reload testing
heading: Nginx Load Balancer Example Setup and Config Guide
body:
This tutorial shows how to set up NGINX as a simple HTTP load balancer that distributes requests across multiple backend servers.

  1. Install NGINX
  2. Create an upstream group
  3. Configure a server block for proxying
  4. Add health and timeout settings
  5. Test and reload

Install NGINX on a Debian or Ubuntu host with package manager commands. Choose a system with at least two backend servers ready to serve web content. No black magic required and no need to summon ancient daemons.

Create an upstream group inside the main NGINX config or a site file. Define a logical name for the backend pool and list backend server IPs or hostnames. Optionally assign weights and failure settings to influence load distribution and graceful failover.

Configure a server block that listens on port 80 or 443 and uses proxy directives to forward requests to the upstream group. Preserve important headers like host and client IP for accurate logs and application behavior. Use proxy buffering and timeout tuning to match application needs.

Add passive health controls by setting max_fails and fail_timeout for backend servers. For active health probes consider NGINX Plus or an external health check solution. Configure reasonable connect and read timeouts to avoid holding connections to slow backends.

Test configuration syntax with the NGINX test command and then reload the service gracefully so that worker processes pick up the new configuration without dropping existing connections. Verify load distribution by curling the load balancer multiple times and checking backend logs or a response header that reveals server identity.

Recap of the tutorial shows how to install NGINX create an upstream pool configure proxying tune health and timeouts and perform safe testing and reloads so the load balancer can start sharing traffic across backends with minimal drama.

Tip

Enable keepalive connections between NGINX and backend servers to reduce connection overhead. Monitor backend response times and use weights to steer traffic during maintenance windows.

  4. Run the container with port mapping and mounted config

Prepare the Nginx configuration by defining server blocks that proxy pass requests to backend services by name or address. Use upstream blocks for multiple backends and health checks as needed. Avoid overly complex rewrites unless a demand exists.

Create a Dockerfile based on the official Nginx image. Copy the custom Nginx configuration into the image and include any required static assets. Keep layers tidy to reduce image size and cache busting to a minimum to avoid slow builds.

Build the image with a descriptive tag. Choose a tag that reflects the role and version of the proxy. Keep continuous integration pipelines in mind and store the image in a registry if multiple hosts will pull the image.

Run the container with host port mapping to container port numbers and mount the configuration file or directory so configuration changes survive container replacement. Use a restart policy and name the container for easy management. Label the container for monitoring tools and service discovery.

Add certificates by mounting a directory with PEM files or by integrating with an ACME client on another container. Ensure Nginx has proper paths and that permissions allow reading certificate files.

This guide covered building a custom Nginx image for reverse proxy use running a container with mapped ports mounted configuration and an approach to TLS

Tip

Use health checks and graceful reloads for zero downtime deployments. Keep configuration modular and versioned so rolling back becomes boring and easy.

title: How to Open a Java JAR File in Windows
description: Quick guide to open and run Java JAR files on Windows including installing Java file association and using the command line
heading: How to Open a Java JAR File in Windows Guide
body:
This guide shows how to open and run Java JAR files on Windows using both the graphical method and the command line.

  1. Install Java runtime
  2. Associate JAR files with the Java launcher
  3. Run the JAR by double click or from a command prompt
  4. Troubleshoot common errors

Download a Java runtime from Adoptium or Oracle and install either the JRE or the JDK depending on development needs. After installation run java -version in a command prompt to confirm a working Java runtime is present on the machine.

To associate the JAR file type with the Java launcher right click the JAR choose Open with then Choose another app and point to the Java runtime executable. For graphical programs pick javaw.exe to avoid a stray console window. Check Always use this app to open .jar files to make double click launch behavior permanent.

The command line method gives more control for logs and debugging. Open Command Prompt change directory to the folder that contains the JAR and run java -jar MyApp.jar. For GUI only applications use javaw -jar MyApp.jar to suppress the console window.

Common errors include no main manifest attribute and version mismatch messages. Open the JAR with any archive tool and inspect META-INF/MANIFEST.MF to ensure a Main-Class entry exists. If a version mismatch appears install the matching Java major version or adjust the build target. For permission related errors run the command prompt as administrator or right click the file and unblock from Properties.

This tutorial covered installing a Java runtime associating JAR files with the Java launcher and running JARs either by double click or via the command line plus basic troubleshooting steps to fix typical problems. Follow these steps and launching a JAR on Windows will be less like witchcraft and more like mild system administration.

Tip

Set JAVA_HOME and add the Java bin folder to PATH for consistent command line behavior. Create a small batch file that runs java -jar with logging redirected to a file to capture startup errors without staring at an empty console window.

title: How to run a Java JAR file on Windows 10
description: Quick guide to run a Java JAR file on Windows 10 using command prompt or double click with clear commands and common fixes
heading: How to run a Java JAR file on Windows 10
body:
This guide shows how to run a Java JAR file on Windows 10 using the command prompt and when double clicking will work.

  1. Check Java installation
  2. Open a command prompt in the folder with the JAR
  3. Run the JAR with the java command
  4. Double click when possible
  5. Associate JAR files with Java runtime

Step one confirm that Java is installed and on the system path. Run java -version in a command prompt. If no version appears download a JDK or JRE from a trusted distributor and install that package.

Step two open a command prompt in the folder that holds the JAR file. Use File Explorer then type cmd in the address bar or use Shift plus right click and select Open command window here for older Windows versions.

Step three run the application with this command java -jar myapp.jar replacing myapp.jar with the real file name. If the application needs console output use java -jar directly. If the manifest lacks a Main Class use jar tvf myapp.jar to inspect contents and confirm an entry point.

Step four try double clicking the JAR file for a GUI only application. Some packages use javaw.exe which suppresses a console window. If double click does nothing the JAR may require command line arguments or a console session.

Step five associate the JAR extension with the Java runtime by right clicking a JAR file then choose Open with then Choose another app then Browse to the Java bin folder and select javaw.exe. Set Always use this app when prompted. That makes double click behavior predictable.

This short tutorial covered checking Java, running a JAR from the command prompt using java -jar, why double click may fail and how to associate JAR files with the Java runtime for easier launching.

Tip

If an application needs admin rights run the command prompt as administrator. If the JAR needs libraries place dependency jars in the same folder or use a shaded fat JAR to avoid runtime missing class errors.

title: Fix Java's 'Could Not Find or Load Main Class' Jar error
description: Quick guide to diagnose and fix the Could Not Find or Load Main Class error when running a jar file on the command line
heading: Fix Java's 'Could Not Find or Load Main Class' Jar error
body:
This tutorial shows how to diagnose and fix the Could Not Find or Load Main Class error when running a jar file from the command line.

  1. Check the jar manifest for a Main Class entry
  2. Confirm a proper main method exists
  3. Verify package path matches class location
  4. Inspect the jar contents for compiled classes
  5. Run with the correct java command and classpath
  6. Check Java version and duplicate classes

Check the jar manifest by listing files inside the archive with a tool such as jar tf myapp.jar. Open the manifest with jar xf myapp.jar META-INF/MANIFEST.MF and confirm a Main-Class line exists and points to the fully qualified class name.

Confirm a public static main method exists with the standard signature public static void main(String[] args). The JVM needs that exact signature to start the application.

Verify package declarations in source match the folder layout inside the jar. For example a class declared as package com.example.app must appear in com/example/app inside the jar.

Inspect the jar to ensure compiled class files are present and not missing due to a misconfigured build. Use jar tf myapp.jar and look for .class files in the expected locations.

Run the application with the correct command. For an executable jar use java -jar myapp.jar. For classpath launches use java -cp myapp.jar com.example.app.Main and provide the fully qualified main class name.

Check Java runtime version compatibility and avoid having duplicate classes on the classpath that shadow the desired main class. Conflicting jars can cause the JVM to pick the wrong class or fail to load the declared main class.

Recap of the tutorial steps The workflow is to confirm the manifest points to the right class confirm the main method exists verify package layout confirm compiled classes are packaged run with the correct java command and check for version or classpath conflicts

Tip

If the manifest keeps getting overwritten inspect the build tool configuration. Maven and Gradle need explicit manifest entries in the jar task. Fixing the build script saves a lot of future grumbling.

title: How to Install and Configure the Nginx Proxy Manager
description: Step by step guide to install and configure Nginx Proxy Manager on a Docker host for reverse proxy and SSL management
heading: How to Install and Configure the Nginx Proxy Manager
body:
If you want a mercifully simple way to manage reverse proxies and SSL on your server without learning ancient arcane rituals this guide is for you. We will install Nginx Proxy Manager on a Docker host run a database and request LetsEncrypt certificates so your sites can stop yelling insecure in the browser.

Prepare the host

Keep it boring and secure. Update packages and install Docker and Docker Compose. Either assign a static IP or reserve a DHCP lease so your server does not move like it has commitment issues. Open ports 80 and 443 on the firewall so LetsEncrypt can reach your machine. Create one folder for persistent Nginx Proxy Manager data and one for the database files.

Compose the services

You need a docker compose file that runs the Nginx Proxy Manager image plus MariaDB or another supported database. Map persistent volumes for the proxy manager data and the database storage. Map ports for the admin web UI and for HTTP and HTTPS so LetsEncrypt can complete certificate challenges.

  • Use clear volume paths and keep credentials in a safe place
  • Set the admin UI port to 81 by default if you want the usual layout
  • Use MariaDB as the database and set reasonable passwords and user names

Start containers and verify services

Run docker compose up -d and watch the logs with docker logs for the proxy manager container. You should see database migration messages and a successful startup. If a service fails to start check permissions on the data folders and confirm the database is reachable from the proxy manager container.

Initial web UI setup

Open a browser to your server address on port 81 to reach the admin UI. The default account is a known quantity so change the email and password immediately. Configure global settings such as default contact email for certificate registration and pick a preferred challenge method for LetsEncrypt.

Add proxy hosts and request SSL

When adding proxy hosts you will specify the external domain name and the internal service address and port where your backend listens. Choose the forward scheme that matches the backend and enable WebSocket support when needed. Use the LetsEncrypt option to request certificates and verify that ports 80 and 443 are accessible from the internet for the HTTP challenge. If you prefer not to open ports use the DNS challenge with your DNS provider.

  • Map domain names to internal services with care
  • Enable WebSocket support for apps that require live updates
  • Use DNS challenge if you cannot open ports to the wider internet

Troubleshooting tips that actually help

Container fails to start

Check folder ownership and file permissions first. Containers cannot work magic on files they cannot read. Confirm the database container is healthy and reachable from the proxy manager container.

LetsEncrypt certificate request fails

Make sure ports 80 and 443 are forwarded from your router and not blocked by cloud provider security rules. If the HTTP challenge keeps failing switch to a DNS challenge with your DNS provider and provide the correct credentials in Nginx Proxy Manager.

UI or apps return 502

Verify the internal service address and port for the proxy host. Check that the backend app is listening on the expected port and that the correct forward scheme is selected.

Backup and maintenance

Keep a copy of your data and database folders off the host so you can recover when Murphy pays a visit. Restart containers with docker compose up -d after changes and watch logs for errors. Consider automating updates if you enjoy risk management with reduced manual labor.

That is it. You now have a manageable reverse proxy with SSL that plays nicely with Docker and LetsEncrypt. If anything breaks remember it is almost never Nginx Proxy Manager fault and usually either permissions or network plumbing.

seo_heading: Practical Docker guide for reverse proxying with Nginx Proxy Manager and SSL

title: How to format a Java double with printf example
description: Learn how to format a Java double using printf format specifiers for precision width and grouping for clean console output
heading: How to format a Java double with printf example
body:
This tutorial shows how to format a Java double using printf and format specifiers for readable numeric output on the console.

  1. Choose a format specifier
  2. Set precision and width
  3. Apply flags for grouping and sign
  4. Print the number

Choose a format specifier by picking the pattern that matches the desired presentation. Use %f for standard decimal notation use %e for scientific notation and use %g for compact selection between the two.

Set precision and width to control decimal places and field alignment. A precision of two is written as %.2f and a width of eight with two decimals becomes %8.2f. The precision rounds the number and the width pads the output for neat columns.

Apply flags for grouping and sign to make numbers human friendly. A comma flag groups thousands as in %,.2f. A plus flag forces a sign in front of positive numbers as in %+8.2f. Flags may be combined for tidy results.

Print the number using the standard console method. Example usage with a sample value looks like this code sample double value = 12345.6789 System.out.printf("Formatted %,.2f", value) This prints a rounded grouped value such as 12,345.68 according to the chosen pattern.

The guide covered how to pick a specifier how to set precision and width how to add flags and how to call the printf method to produce clear numeric output on the console.

Tip

Use a specific locale for predictable decimal separators when running code on different systems. Example usage is System.out.printf(Locale.US, "%,.2f", value) This forces a period as the decimal marker and comma for grouping which helps when parsing or comparing output across environments.

title: Use the Java Console Class for User Input
description: Learn how to use the Java Console class to read lines and secure passwords handle parsing and fallback for terminal input
heading: Use the Java Console Class for User Input
body:
Welcome to the thrilling world of terminal input in Java where users type things and programs pretend to be surprised. This guide shows how to get a Console instance with System.console, read lines with prompts, accept secure passwords with readPassword, parse numeric input safely, and fall back to Scanner when the JVM is stuck inside an IDE.

Get a Console instance

The Console class is your friendly terminal sidekick when running from a real shell. Call System.console and save the result. If you get null you are probably running inside an IDE console that is not a real terminal.

Console console = System.console();
if (console == null) {
    // No console available. Fall back to Scanner or fail gracefully.
}

Read a line with a prompt

Use readLine to prompt for text. It prints the prompt then waits. Handle a null return which means end of stream or a detached terminal.

String name = console.readLine("Enter name ");
if (name == null) {
    // User closed input or stream ended
}

Read a password securely

readPassword returns a char array so characters do not echo to the terminal. That is better than watching someone type a password and becoming an unsafe witness.

char[] pw = console.readPassword("Password ");
if (pw == null) {
    // input closed
} else {
    // use password in memory as char[] only
    // zero it out after use
    java.util.Arrays.fill(pw, '\0');
}

Do not convert the char[] to String unless you enjoy leaving secrets in the immutable string pool. Zeroing the array with Arrays.fill is polite security hygiene.

Parse and validate numeric input

Console gives you text. Your job is to turn it into a number that does not throw a tantrum at runtime. Read a line then use parsing with try catch for NumberFormatException and prompt again when validation fails.

int age = -1;
while (age < 0) {
    String line = console.readLine("Age ");
    if (line == null) {
        // handle end of input
        break;
    }
    try {
        age = Integer.parseInt(line.trim());
    } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
        console.printf("Please enter a valid number\n");
    }
}

Fallback when Console is not available

If System.console returns null use Scanner as a fallback for basic input in IDEs and other noninteractive environments. Scanner is fine for simple input but it does not provide secure masked password entry.

java.util.Scanner sc = new java.util.Scanner(System.in);
String line = sc.nextLine();
// No masked password support here

Tips and gotchas

  • System.console is often null in IDEs and some build tools. Test in a real terminal for full behavior.
  • Always check for null from readLine or readPassword. Streams get closed and people are unpredictable.
  • Prefer readPassword for secrets and zero the char[] after use.
  • Wrap parsing in try catch and loop until you get sensible input or a polite EOF.
  • Scanner is a practical fallback but does not mask passwords and may change tokenizing behavior compared to Console.

There you go. With System.console and a sensible fallback you can handle user input reliably. It is not glamorous work but someone has to trust the program with user typing. Do it cleanly and do not leave passwords lying around in String objects.
seo_title: Read terminal input in Java with Console and fallback safely
seo_heading: Get secure terminal input with System.console and a Scanner fallback

title: Java Double Brace Initialization of Lists and Sets Explained
description: Clear explanation of Java double brace initialization for lists and sets with pros cons examples and safer modern alternatives
heading: Java Double Brace Initialization of Lists and Sets Explained
body:
Double brace initialization creates an anonymous subclass with an instance initializer block that adds elements to a collection.

Example usage

List list = new ArrayList() {{ add("one") add("two") }}

The pattern looks neat and compact while allowing inline population of a collection during construction. The first brace starts an anonymous subclass the second brace opens an instance initializer block with calls to add

  1. Benefits
  2. Drawbacks
  3. Safer alternatives

Benefits

Quick literal like syntax with minimal boilerplate and useful for small examples or test code where clarity matters more than robustness

Drawbacks

Creates an anonymous inner class which carries a hidden reference to the enclosing class and increases class count. Serialization can behave unexpectedly and performance may suffer due to extra class creation. The subclass also prevents use of some optimization and can complicate stack traces

Safer alternatives

Use factory methods for compact and clear collection creation. For immutable small lists use List.of with explicit elements. For mutable lists use new ArrayList and Collections addAll or Arrays asList when appropriate

Example modern alternatives

List immutable = List.of("one", "two") List mutable = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList("one", "two"))

When reading legacy code and encountering the double brace pattern expect an anonymous inner class and check for subtle issues like unexpected serialization keys or a leaked outer class reference

For production code prefer explicit construction or factory methods for readability safety and predictable behavior

Tip

Prefer factory methods for small collections to avoid hidden subclasses and surprising serialization behavior while keeping source code easy to maintain

title: How to import the Java Scanner

  4. Close the Scanner when done

Add the import statement Use the import line at the top of a Java file so the compiler recognizes the Scanner class from the standard library. Example use looks like this

import java.util.Scanner

scanner.close()

title: How to use the Java Scanner next & nextLine methods
description: Learn when to use next and nextLine with Scanner in Java and how to avoid common newline problems when reading string input from console
heading: How to use the Java Scanner next and nextLine methods for string input
body:
If your console input code ever returns an empty string and makes you question your life choices then welcome. This short guide explains how the Java Scanner next and nextLine methods behave, why the newline bug shows up, and how to stop it from wrecking your user input. It is a practical input tutorial for Java developers who want predictable String input and fewer head scratches.

Quick recap of how Scanner reads things

The Scanner class reads tokens and lines from System.in for console input. Keep one Scanner and reuse it. Close it when the program is done to free resources. Here are the two methods you care about.

  • next reads the next token separated by whitespace. Perfect for single words or tokens. Example: String word = scan.next().
  • nextLine reads the remainder of the current line including spaces until it sees a newline character. Use it for full lines like addresses. Example: String line = scan.nextLine().

Why the newline bug happens

Numeric reads such as nextInt() and nextDouble() read the number but do not consume the newline that ends that line. The newline stays in the input buffer. If you call nextLine() next, it immediately reads that leftover newline and returns an empty string. That empty string is not a ghost from beyond reality, it is the remainder of the line you never finished.

Minimal example that causes trouble

Scanner scan = new Scanner(System.in);
System.out.print("Enter age: ");
int age = scan.nextInt();
System.out.print("Enter name: ");
String name = scan.nextLine(); // often returns empty string

After nextInt() the input buffer still contains the newline. The nextLine() that follows consumes that newline and gives you an empty string for name. Congratulations you just read nothing.

How to fix it and stop crying

The usual pattern is simple and boring. After any numeric or token read that does not consume the whole line call one extra nextLine() to discard the rest of that line. Then call nextLine() again to read the real line you want.

  • Read number or token
  • Call scan.nextLine() once to clear the newline
  • Call scan.nextLine() to get the actual user input line
// correct pattern
Scanner scan = new Scanner(System.in);
System.out.print("Enter age: ");
int age = scan.nextInt();
scan.nextLine(); // discard leftover newline
System.out.print("Enter name: ");
String name = scan.nextLine();

// now name contains the full line including spaces

Rules of thumb and developer tips

  • Use next for single token String input and nextLine for full line String input.
  • When mixing numeric reads and line reads always add a discard nextLine() after the numeric call to avoid the newline bug.
  • Keep one Scanner instance for System.in and close it at the end of main. Closing is polite and avoids resource warnings.
  • If you need more control try BufferedReader with readLine or java.io.Console for richer console input features, but Scanner is fine for most small programs.

Common gotchas to watch for

Sometimes the input appears to skip prompts when you run tests or paste multiple lines into the console. That is usually the leftover newline effect again. If you are getting unexpected empty strings check the sequence of reads in your code and insert a discard nextLine() where appropriate.

Wrapping up

Remember this simple mantra: next for tokens, nextLine for lines, and throw away the sneaky newline after numeric reads. Follow these rules and your console driven Java programs will stop surprising you with empty strings and awkward null humor. You are welcome.
seo_title: Fix the Java Scanner newline bug and master next and nextLine
seo_heading: Avoid empty string surprises when mixing nextInt and nextLine in Java

title: How to use the Java Ternary Operator by Example
description: Quick guide to the Java ternary operator with clear examples and best practices for concise conditional expressions
heading: How to use the Java Ternary Operator by Example
body:
This tutorial shows how to use the Java ternary operator for concise conditional assignments and expressions

  1. Learn the syntax and purpose
  2. Use the operator for simple assignments and returns
  3. Mind types and evaluation order
  4. Avoid deep nesting and prefer clarity
  5. Try examples and refactor for readability

Learn the syntax and purpose

The ternary operator offers a one line alternative to an if else block. The operator evaluates a boolean condition then yields a value for true or a value for false. Think of the operator as a tiny inline decision maker

Use the operator for simple assignments and returns

Use the operator when a single expression chooses between two values. For example a max comparison or a conditional message works great with the operator. Avoid using the operator for complex logic that belongs in a method

Mind types and evaluation order

The chosen values must be type compatible. Primitive and reference conversions follow the usual Java rules during assignment. Also the condition expression evaluates first then one of the two branches evaluates next so watch for side effects

Avoid deep nesting and prefer clarity

Nesting multiple ternary operators can create a small maze that future maintainers will love to hate. Use parentheses sparingly and prefer a named method when branching logic grows beyond one line

Try examples and refactor for readability

Start with short examples that show typical uses such as selecting a default value or formatting a message. Rewrite long chained expressions into readable helper methods when needed

Summary of the tutorial shows the operator as a compact tool for simple conditional expressions. The operator shines for brief choices and falls short when logic complexity grows. Use the operator with awareness of types and readability

Tip

When readability matters more than line count prefer an if else block or extract a method. Use the ternary operator for tidy decisions and avoid nesting that requires a map and a torch to debug
