title: Multiversion Concurrency Control MVCC Explained
description: Clear practical guide to MVCC for databases Learn how multiversion concurrency control prevents conflicts and improves isolation
heading: Multiversion Concurrency Control MVCC Explained
body:
If your database could talk it would say two things. One it loves MVCC for saving it from lock fights. Two it hates old row versions cluttering up disk like forgotten takeout boxes. Multiversion concurrency control or MVCC is the neat trick that keeps many versions of a row so readers do not have to stand in line while writers do their thing.

What MVCC actually does

MVCC stores a bit of history with each row so every transaction sees a stable snapshot of the database. Instead of overwriting data on update the database appends a new version. Timestamps or transaction ids tell the engine which version a transaction can read. The outcome is higher read concurrency and fewer transactions throwing tantrums over locks.

Basic visibility rules

  • Read snapshot means a transaction sees the newest version whose timestamp is at or before the transaction start.
  • Write new version means updates append a fresh row version and leave old versions for in flight readers.
  • Visibility and cleanup means once a version is no longer needed it can be removed by garbage collection or vacuum.

Why long running transactions are trouble

Long running transactions are the usual villain when it comes to version bloat. If someone starts a read and then sips coffee for an hour every update will pile up older versions the vacuum process cannot reclaim. That extra baggage costs disk, index bloat, and slower queries. The good news is this is predictable and fixable. The bad news is you will still have to explain to your team why you killed that beloved immortal query.

Practical differences between PostgreSQL and MySQL

Both PostgreSQL and InnoDB in MySQL use MVCC but they implement it differently. PostgreSQL tracks xmin and xmax metadata per tuple and relies on a visibility map and autovacuum to reclaim space. InnoDB uses undo logs and transaction ids to provide read consistency. Snapshot isolation and repeatable read play out differently between systems so test your workload before assuming behavior is identical.

Common pros and cons

  • Pros. High read concurrency, fewer blocking reads, and better overall throughput for mixed workloads.
  • Cons. Storage overhead from multiple versions, potential bloat, and the need to tune garbage collection or autovacuum.

Tips and tuning that actually help

Yes you can ignore version bloat until it bites you but here are sensible steps to stay ahead.

  • Monitor long running transactions and idle in transaction sessions. They are the usual suspects behind bloat.
  • Tune autovacuum or your garbage collector so cleanup runs often enough but not so often it wastes CPU.
  • Use HOT updates in PostgreSQL friendly schemas when possible to avoid index churn.
  • Design indexes and schema with snapshot isolation in mind. Snapshot isolation avoids many classic anomalies but does not make poor schema design invisible.

Quick experiment for your dev server

Try this on a test box. Start a long running read transaction that selects a lot of rows. While that transaction is open run many concurrent updates on the same table and watch the version count grow with a monitoring query or by checking table size. The observation is obvious and motivating. Tune your vacuum or garbage collector and rerun the test to see the difference.

MVCC is not magic. It is a careful tradeoff between read consistency and storage cost. Use it to avoid unnecessary locking and learn to manage the cleanup. Your database will be faster and you will have fewer angry deadlocks to mediate at 3 a m.
seo_title: MVCC Explained for Developers Who Hate Locking and Bloat
seo_heading: How multiversion concurrency control gives consistent reads without heavy locks

title: What's the Difference Between Forward and Reverse Proxies?
description: Learn the core difference between forward proxy and reverse proxy and when to use each for privacy caching load balancing and security
heading: Difference Between Forward and Reverse Proxy Servers
body:
The key difference between a forward proxy and a reverse proxy is who each serves and how the proxy presents clients and servers to one another.

Think of a forward proxy as a user cloak and a reverse proxy as a server bouncer. A forward proxy sits between client devices and the wider web. Users route requests through a forward proxy to hide origin IP addresses apply access rules or cache frequent requests to speed up browsing from the user side.

  1. Forward proxy

    A forward proxy accepts requests from clients and forwards those requests to external servers. Common uses include privacy filtering content control and client side caching. Enterprise networks and privacy conscious users love forward proxies for hiding client identity and enforcing usage policies.

  2. Reverse proxy

    A reverse proxy stands in front of one or more web servers and receives incoming client traffic first. That proxy can load balance traffic terminate secure connections cache responses and shield backend servers from direct exposure. Web operators use reverse proxies to improve performance and to centralize security handling.

Key practical differences to remember are endpoints and control. A forward proxy protects clients and controls what clients can reach. A reverse proxy protects servers and controls what clients see when they reach a service. Both can cache and both can log traffic but logs serve different goals depending on whether the target is client or server side.

Picking a proxy depends on goals. Want to hide user origin or restrict outbound access choose a forward proxy. Want to scale services secure certificates and distribute load choose a reverse proxy. Deploy both if a network needs strong client side control and hardened server side delivery while avoiding duplicated effort.

Tip

When testing pick a simple scenario and monitor headers and logs. That practice reveals which proxy changed headers who saw client IP and how caching altered response times so the right proxy choice becomes obvious fast.

title: Quick Introduction to Java JShell Tutorial
description: Learn Java JShell basics fast with commands examples and tips for interactive Java REPL use
heading: Quick Introduction to Java JShell Tutorial for Fast REPL Learning
body:
Why bother with JShell

Think of JShell as a sandbox for Java where you can try ideas without committing to a full project and without waiting for the slow compiler to hold your hand. It is a REPL that helps you verify behavior, debug tiny pieces, and feel clever in under a minute.

Start JShell and stop pretending you like builds

Open a terminal and type this to start a session

jshell

The prompt will let you type expressions and declarations and get results right away. No build files required. No mysterious maven errors to decode.

Run quick expressions and check assumptions

Want to confirm a value or try a library call Just type it at the prompt

jshell> 3 + 4
jshell> Math.sqrt(16)

Immediate feedback means fewer silly mistakes make it into the codebase.

Declare variables and small snippets

JShell accepts declarations and small methods so you can prototype logic step by step

jshell> int x = 5;
jshell> String s = "hello";
jshell> System.out.println(s + " world");

Keep snippets focused. Test one assumption at a time and you will find the bug before it multiplies.

Save your session and load it later

If your session becomes glorious and you want to keep it use the save command to persist the history

/save demo.jsh
/open demo.jsh

Save gives you a tiny script of the good bits. Open lets you reload that work in a new shell and pretend you planned everything.

Handy REPL commands to know

  • /vars list current variables so you stop guessing what you declared
  • /list show the snippets in this session
  • /help get command info when you forget the obvious
  • /exit leave the REPL and return to civilization

Workflow tips for prototyping and debugging

Use JShell as an experiment loop. Try small pieces first. If a test fails break it down into simpler snippets and run those. The REPL makes it easy to isolate the bad behavior without the drama of a full test suite.

A tiny checklist to get the most from JShell

  • Start JShell to quickly verify behavior
  • Run expressions and library calls to check results
  • Declare variables and small functions to prototype logic
  • Save sessions with /save and reload with /open
  • Inspect state with /vars and /list

JShell reduces friction and gives you a fast feedback loop for interactive Java exploration. Use it to validate ideas, debug tiny problems, and avoid the long compile and run ritual when you only want to check one thing. Now go try Math.sqrt and enjoy being right more often.
seo_title: Master quick Java experiments with JShell REPL in minutes
seo_heading: An interactive guide to JShell for faster Java prototyping and testing

title: Chrome Color Picker from Image
description: Quick tutorial on using Chrome Developer Tools color picker to sample and copy colors from any image for web design and CSS
heading: Chrome Color Picker from Image Tutorial for Web Design
body:
Why bother with the Chrome color picker

Because guessing is for phonies and mood boards. If you want the exact hex that makes a logo pop or a background feel sinister in a tasteful way you need pixel level truth. Chrome Developer Tools has a built in color picker and eyedropper that will hand you the exact color from any image open in a tab. No uploads, no magic, no guessing.

What you will need

  • Chrome browser on your computer
  • An image or webpage open in a Chrome tab
  • Basic comfort with keyboard shortcuts and not panicking

Quick steps to sample a color

  1. Open the image or page in Chrome. Drag and drop into a tab if you want to skip hosting drama.
  2. Open Developer Tools. Press Ctrl Shift I on Windows or Cmd Option I on Mac. Yes that many keys are intentional.
  3. In the Styles panel find a CSS rule with a small color square. That square is the gateway to the picker.
  4. Click the color square to open the color picker. Then click the eyedropper icon labeled "Pick color from page". Your cursor will turn into a tiny crosshair.
  5. Move the crosshair over the image and click the pixel you want. The hex color will appear in the color input box. Click the hex code to copy it or press Ctrl C or Cmd C.
  6. Paste the hex into your stylesheet variable or design tool and admire your newfound precision. For example #34A853 looks nice and confident in many palettes.

Where to paste the color

Drop the hex into a CSS rule a variable or a design palette. Example CSS fix if you are feeling tidy

:root {
  --brand-color: #34A853;
}

.button {
  background: var(--brand-color);
}

Tips and troubleshoot moves

  • Zoom in on the page before sampling if the image is compressed or noisy. Bigger pixels are less traitorous.
  • If the color tool samples the wrong pixel move the cursor slowly. The crosshair is unforgiving when you rush.
  • Sample from an image opened in its own tab when possible. Background images and overlays can get in the way.
  • Remember that displayed color can vary by monitor calibration. The hex is accurate to the image data not to your screen's drama.

Quick troubleshooting

If the eyedropper is grumpy check that the Styles panel is focused and that the color square actually opened the picker. Sometimes a stray extension or a weird site style can hide things. Reloading the tab or opening the image in a fresh tab usually fixes the issue.

There you go. Fast color sampling, less squinting, more exact hex values. Use it for prototypes production or petty design triumphs. Now go pick a color and pretend you planned it all along.
seo_title: Extract perfect hex colors from images in Chrome Developer Tools
seo_heading: Sample exact pixel colors with the Chrome eyedropper for web design accuracy

title: Single Responsibility Principle in Java (SOLID Principles Tu
description: Learn how to apply Single Responsibility Principle in Java for cleaner classes and easier maintenance with practical steps and examples.
heading: Single Responsibility Principle in Java SOLID Principles Tutorial
body:
This tutorial teaches how to apply the Single Responsibility Principle in Java to keep classes focused and maintainable.

  1. Identify responsibilities in a class
  2. Extract responsibilities into separate classes
  3. Define clear interfaces for each role
  4. Prefer composition over monolithic classes
  5. Refactor with tests to verify behavior

Step one requires reading the code and naming the reasons for change for a given class. If a class handles business logic and logging then two responsibilities exist and clarity is missing. Naming responsibilities forces a decision.

Step two moves each responsibility into a dedicated class. For example move order validation into OrderValidator and persistence into OrderRepository. The original class becomes a coordinator instead of a kitchen sink.

Step three uses interfaces to express expectations. An interface such as PaymentProcessor defines a contract so that replacements and testing become trivial. Contracts prevent surprise behavior.

Step four uses composition to assemble behavior from small pieces. Inject OrderValidator and PaymentProcessor into OrderService rather than adding more methods to OrderService. Composition encourages reuse and reduces coupling.

Step five introduces tests before and after refactor. Unit tests safeguard business rules while refactor reduces duplication and improves readability. Tests give permission to change with confidence.

Following these steps yields classes that are easier to reason about and easier to test. The Single Responsibility Principle is not a rigid law but a design compass that points toward simplicity and maintainability. Expect fewer merge conflicts and less mysterious bugs when responsibilities are explicit rather than buried in large classes.

Tip

Look for reasons to change as the quickest smell detector. If a change in logging causes edits in a business class then a split is overdue. Small focused classes make debugging less tragic and future work less heroic.

title: Git Fetch vs Git Pull? Which one should you choose?
description: Fast clear guide to choosing between git fetch and git pull Learn when to inspect remote changes and when to update local branches safely
heading: Git Fetch vs Git Pull Which One Should You Choose
body:
The key difference between git fetch and git pull is that fetch only downloads remote refs and objects while pull downloads and integrates those changes into the current branch.

Use fetch when wanting to inspect remote changes without touching the working branch. Use pull when ready to bring the working branch up to date in one command. Pull equals fetch plus merge by default. Pull can be configured to rebase instead of merge for a cleaner history.

Common commands

  1. git fetch origin downloads updates from origin
  2. git pull origin main downloads and merges remote main into local main
  3. git pull --rebase origin main downloads and rebases local commits on top of remote main

Why prefer fetch sometimes A fetch first approach lets a developer review changes before merging and avoids surprise conflicts. Fetch followed by a manual merge or rebase gives full control over conflict resolution. Pull is convenient for fast updates when the team agrees on integration style.

One note on fast forward merges and automatic updates If the local branch has diverged then pull will attempt a merge or rebase which can create conflicts. If the local branch is behind then pull often fast forwards. Fetch leaves those decisions for the developer and keeps the working branch untouched until a deliberate merge or rebase occurs.

The choice depends on workflow preferences and risk appetite. Conservative developers fetch inspect and then merge. Fast moving workflows pull and resolve as needed.

Tip

Prefer a fetch first approach when working on shared branches. After fetch run git log origin/main..main or use a diff to see remote changes before merging. That habit reduces surprise conflicts and protects local work.

title: How to Install the Java 21 JDK Early Access Edition
description: Step by step guide to download verify and install Java 21 JDK Early Access with environment setup and simple verification commands
heading: How to Install the Java 21 JDK Early Access Edition Guide
body:
This guide shows how to download verify and install the Java 21 JDK Early Access edition on Windows macOS and Linux with environment setup and basic checks.

  1. Download a build
  2. Verify checksum
  3. Install or extract
  4. Set JAVA_HOME and update PATH
  5. Verify installation
  6. Cleanup

Download a build

Choose an official early access source such as the OpenJDK early access page or vendor preview downloads. Pick the package that matches system architecture and preferred format like tar gz or msi or zip.

Verify checksum

Always validate the archive before running any binaries. Use a checksum tool such as sha256sum or shasum with the provided digest file for confidence that the download was not corrupted or tampered with.

Install or extract

On Linux and macOS extract the archive with standard tar commands and move the folder to a system location reserved for software. On Windows run the msi installer or unzip and move the folder to Program Files using administrative privileges.

Set JAVA_HOME and update PATH

Define a JAVA_HOME environment variable that points to the jdk 21 folder. For shells edit the profile file and add an export line with the full path to the jdk 21 directory. For Windows use the system environment variables UI to create JAVA_HOME and add the jdk bin folder to the Path entries.

Verify installation

Run java -version and javac -version to confirm the expected Java 21 build is active. If output shows a different release check shell profile order or system Path entries to ensure the new JDK is preferred.

Cleanup

Remove the downloaded archive to free space and keep the machine tidy. Keep the extracted JDK folder in place for development and toolchains to reference.

The procedure covered downloading verification installation environment setup and simple verification so a developer can start using Java 21 JDK Early Access without guessing where things belong or why commands fail.

Tip

Use a version manager for Java when juggling multiple JDKs. That avoids manual Path wrestling and delivers clean switches between stable releases and early access builds.

title: Hibernate and JPA3 Configuration and Setup
description: Compact guide to configure Hibernate with JPA3 for Java projects covering dependencies persistence unit entities and runtime tips
heading: Hibernate and JPA3 Configuration and Setup Guide
body:
This tutorial shows how to configure Hibernate with JPA3 for a Java project using Maven or Gradle and how to wire entities persistence unit and runtime properties for a working ORM setup.

  1. Add dependencies and choose provider versions
  2. Configure persistence properties or persistence xml
  3. Create entity classes and mapping annotations
  4. Manage EntityManagerFactory and transaction handling
  5. Run an integration test and enable SQL logging

Add dependencies and choose provider versions

Declare hibernate core version 6.x and jakarta persistence api 3.x plus a JDBC driver in the project's build file. Optionally add a connection pool such as HikariCP for production grade performance. Use the build tool to lock versions for reproducible builds.

Configure persistence properties or persistence xml

Provide a persistence unit via METAINF persistence xml or supply properties programmatically. Typical property names include jakarta.persistence.jdbc.url equals your database connection string jakarta.persistence.jdbc.user equals username jakarta.persistence.jdbc.password equals password and jakarta.persistence.schema-generation.database.action equals update or create. Set the correct hibernate.dialect class for the database in use.

Create entity classes and mapping annotations

Annotate domain classes with @Entity @Id and mapping annotations for relationships. Prefer explicit column mappings for clarity and use generated value strategies that match the chosen database. Validate mapping at build time with a schema generation pass when helpful.

Manage EntityManagerFactory and transaction handling

Obtain an EntityManagerFactory via jakarta.persistence.Persistence or rely on container integration for Jakarta EE or Spring managed beans. Use EntityManager and EntityTransaction for manual transaction boundaries or integrate a transaction manager from the chosen framework for declarative control.

Run an integration test and enable SQL logging

Write a small test that boots the persistence unit persists a sample entity and queries back results. Enable SQL visibility with hibernate.show_sql equals true and hibernate.format_sql equals true to inspect generated SQL and catch mapping errors quickly.

This guide covered dependency selection provider compatibility configuration of persistence properties entity mapping and a simple run test to validate the setup. The goal is a repeatable and transparent Hibernate and JPA3 configuration that behaves predictably across environments.

Tip

Prefer explicit properties over implicit defaults during initial setup and enable SQL logging for debugging. Watch for package name changes from javax to jakarta when migrating and align Hibernate version with Jakarta Persistence 3 compatibility.

title: Hibernate and JPA 3.x CRUD Operations Example
description: Step by step guide to implement CRUD with Hibernate and JPA 3.x including setup entity mapping configuration and basic CRUD code samples.
heading: Hibernate and JPA 3.x CRUD Operations Example Guide
body:
This tutorial shows how to implement CRUD operations using Hibernate and JPA 3.x in a simple Java project.

  1. Project setup and dependencies
  2. Define entity and mapping
  3. Configure persistence and EntityManager
  4. Implement create read update delete methods
  5. Test operations and handle transactions

Step 1 Project setup and dependencies explains which libraries to include. Use Jakarta Persistence API and a matching Hibernate release that supports JPA 3.x. Choose Maven or Gradle and add the core ORM and JDBC driver for the database.

Step 2 Define entity and mapping covers creating a plain Java class annotated with persistence annotations. Annotate primary key and any relationships. Keep mapping simple for CRUD focus.

Step 3 Configure persistence and EntityManager shows how to wire persistence unit configuration or use a Spring Boot datasource. Create an EntityManagerFactory or let the container manage one for cleaner code.

Step 4 Implement create read update delete methods demonstrates basic usage. Use entityManager.persist(entity) to create and entityManager.find(EntityClass, id) to read. Use merge for updates and remove for deletes. Always manage transactions around these calls.

Step 5 Test operations and handle transactions recommends writing simple unit tests or a main runner to exercise each CRUD method. Verify SQL logs to confirm expected queries and watch for lazy loading surprises.

The guide walked through the essentials from adding dependencies to running CRUD calls. The goal is reusable patterns rather than clever one offs so the code can be adapted to real applications.

Tip

Enable SQL logging during development to see generated statements and catch mapping mistakes early. Use optimistic locking version fields for safer concurrent updates.

title: You first Java AWS Lambda function in less than 5 minutes
description: Build and deploy a Java AWS Lambda function fast with Maven handler setup and AWS Console deployment tips for a quick serverless start
heading: Create your first Java AWS Lambda function in under 5 minutes
body:
This tutorial teaches how to create a minimal Java AWS Lambda function and deploy using Maven and the AWS Console in under five minutes.

  1. Create a Maven project
  2. Add the Lambda handler class
  3. Build the deployment package
  4. Create the function in the AWS Console
  5. Test the deployed function

Create a Maven project

Use a simple Maven archetype or a favorite IDE to start the project. Add aws-lambda-java-core to the pom.xml as a dependency so the runtime knows how to call the handler. No wizard hat required.

Add the Lambda handler class

Write a handler that implements the proper interface and accepts a request object. For example use public class Handler implements RequestHandler< Map< String,Object> , String> and return a short string response. Name the handler class exactly as declared when creating the function in the console.

Build the deployment package

Run mvn package to produce a shaded jar or a simple jar depending on dependency needs. The jar must contain the handler class and all required classes for the runtime to execute the function.

Create the function in the AWS Console

Open the Lambda console choose Java as runtime and upload the jar. Set the handler value using the fully qualified class name followed by the handler method name. Adjust memory and timeout to reasonable defaults for fast cold starts.

Test the deployed function

Use the built in test tool or invoke via AWS CLI to send a sample payload. Check logs in CloudWatch for printed messages and stack traces. Fix any classpath or dependency problems and redeploy.

The tutorial covered creating a Maven based Java project adding a Lambda handler building a jar deploying that package in the AWS Console and testing the result to confirm a working serverless function.

Tip

Use small dependencies and keep the handler simple to reduce cold start time. If the function needs many libs consider using provisioned concurrency or move heavy work to background tasks.

title: How to enable Java 21 preview features
description: Guide to enable Java 21 preview features on JDK command line Maven and Gradle so developers can compile run and test new language features
heading: How to enable Java 21 preview features step by step
body:
This guide shows how to enable Java 21 preview features on the JDK command line and in Maven and Gradle so developers can compile and run new language features safely.

  1. Install JDK 21
  2. Compile with preview flags
  3. Run with preview flags
  4. Configure Maven for compile test and run
  5. Configure Gradle for compile test and run

Step 1 Install a Java 21 build from a vendor or build one from source. Use the same JDK binary for compilation and runtime to avoid surprising failures.

Step 2 Compile source with the Java compiler flags that enable preview features. Example command

javac --enable-preview --release 21 MyClass.java

Step 3 Run classes with the matching runtime flag so preview behavior is preserved.

java --enable-preview MyClass

Step 4 For Maven add the preview flag to the maven compiler plugin compilerArgs and set release to 21. Also add the same flag to surefire or failsafe argLine so unit tests run with preview behavior.

Step 5 For Gradle append the preview flag to compileJava options compilerArgs and set jvmArgs for run and test tasks so program execution and tests use the preview runtime.

Using preview features requires the matching compile and run flags and a clear plan for migration. Keep preview usage isolated in feature branches and use feature toggles for experiments in shared repositories. Remember that preview APIs and syntax can change between JDK updates so frequent retesting is prudent.

Tip

Use continuous integration jobs that install the exact JDK 21 build used locally. Add tests that fail fast when preview flags are missing so code does not accidentally land on a different JDK without the required flags.

title: How to create AWS Lambda functions in Python
description: Build deploy and test AWS Lambda functions using Python with practical steps for handler packaging deployment and monitoring
heading: How to create AWS Lambda functions in Python step by step

This tutorial teaches how to create deploy and test AWS Lambda functions using Python in a few practical steps.

  4. Test monitor logs and tweak configuration

Step 1 Create a Lambda function and set an execution role using the AWS Console for a quick start or the AWS CLI for automation. Grant basic Lambda execution permissions and any service specific policies for access to resources like S3 or DynamoDB.

Step 2 Write the handler in Python and keep the function focused on a single responsibility. A minimal handler looks like this in principle def lambda_handler(event context) return 'hello from lambda' Avoid bulky dependencies in the handler module to speed up cold starts.

Tip

title: Import a Gradle Project from GitHub
description: Quick guide to import a Gradle project from GitHub into Android Studio or IntelliJ with Gradle wrapper and dependency tips
heading: Import a Gradle Project from GitHub step by step
body:
Why this exists and who will enjoy it

You found a Gradle project on GitHub and you want it to run in Android Studio or IntelliJ IDEA without a week of grieving. This guide walks through the pragmatic steps to import a Gradle project from GitHub and get past the usual hurdles. Expect Gradle, build.gradle files, the Gradle Wrapper, dependency management and a little version control drama.

Get the repo into your IDE

Clone or open the repository

Use the IDE VCS menu or run git clone from a terminal if you like the smell of vintage commands. Newer IDE versions can open a GitHub URL directly. Either way you want a local copy that the IDE can point at.

Pick the correct project root

Point the IDE at the folder that contains settings.gradle or the main build.gradle file. If you point at a random submodule you will get missing project errors and a healthy amount of swearing. The right root means the IDE sees the multi module or single module setup and imports modules correctly.

Use the Gradle Wrapper and set the JVM

Prefer the Gradle Wrapper from the repo

Always prefer the Gradle Wrapper that comes with the repository. The wrapper guarantees a consistent Gradle version for everyone on the team. If you force a different Gradle version you will be the reason someone opens an issue later.

Match the Gradle JVM to the project expectations

If the project needs a specific Java version set the IDE Gradle JVM accordingly. Android Studio and IntelliJ IDEA provide a Gradle JVM setting in the project settings. Using the wrong JVM leads to compiler errors that look mysterious but are 100 percent avoidable.

Sync, resolve dependencies and watch logs

Trigger a Gradle sync or refresh the Gradle project. Keep an eye on the dependency resolution log. If a dependency fails check repository URLs and credentials first. Private registries require credentials or tokens and will fail noisily.

  • If dependency resolution fails try running ./gradlew dependencies from a terminal for clearer logs
  • Add or fix repository entries in build.gradle or settings.gradle rather than guessing
  • Check for version conflicts and missing artifacts in the Gradle output

Build or run the project

Use the IDE run configurations or run ./gradlew build from a terminal. Address compiler messages and missing resources one by one like a patient bug wrangler. If you get Android specific issues check the Android SDK and platform versions in the project settings.

Troubleshooting tips that actually help

  • Private dependencies often fail because of missing credentials. Check your gradle.properties or IDE credential settings.
  • Network or proxy issues can block dependency downloads. Try running the wrapper on the command line to see full logs and stack traces.
  • Multi module projects may have settings in settings.gradle that change included paths. Confirm the include statements match the repo layout.
  • When in doubt run ./gradlew clean build and read the output. It tells you what broke and often why.

Recap

Steps in plain English

  • Clone or open the repo in Android Studio or IntelliJ IDEA
  • Select the folder with settings.gradle or the main build.gradle file
  • Use the Gradle Wrapper and set the correct Gradle JVM
  • Sync and resolve dependencies and check the logs
  • Build or run and fix compiler messages and missing resources

If dependency resolution still fails run the Gradle wrapper from a terminal to get full log output and add missing repository entries to build.gradle or settings.gradle rather than guessing. Now go forth and import. Try not to blame Gradle for everything.
seo_title: Bring a Gradle project from GitHub into Android Studio fast
seo_heading: Open a cloned Gradle repo in IntelliJ IDEA or Android Studio and get it building

title: Quickly run a Spring Boot JAR file at the Command Line
description: Run a Spring Boot JAR from the command line fast with clear steps common flags and quick troubleshooting tips
heading: Quickly run a Spring Boot JAR file at the Command Line
body:
If you just want to start a Spring Boot JAR from the command line and move on with your life, this guide will get you there fast and with minimal hair loss. We will cover building the artifact, the usual java -jar dance, runtime flags, background runs, and the common fails that turn a quick test into a full on investigation.

Build or get the runnable JAR

If you are using Maven or Gradle you need a runnable Spring Boot artifact not a plain library. With Maven run the package phase and with Gradle build the bootJar task. Then check the output folder for the file name to use in the next step.

mvn package
./gradlew bootJar
# find the artifact in target or build libs

Start the app with java -jar

Use the Java launcher like a civilized person and avoid copying random scripts from the internet. The basic command is straightforward.

java -jar myapp.jar

On Unix systems a Spring Boot build may produce a launchable JAR that runs as an executable file. If so set execute mode and run it directly.

chmod +x myapp.jar && ./myapp.jar

Apply JVM and Spring Boot flags and run in background

Memory and config flags are your friends. Use JVM flags to control heap and use Spring Boot command line properties to change port or profile. For background runs use a real process manager or nohup rather than hoping your SSH session will stay alive forever.

java -Xmx512m -jar myapp.jar --server.port=8081 --spring.profiles.active=dev
# increase logging if you need more clues
java -Xmx512m -jar myapp.jar --logging.level.root=DEBUG
# background run with nohup
nohup java -jar myapp.jar > app.log 2>&1 &

Prefer a process manager for reliability

For anything beyond quick testing use systemd or another init system to make sure the app restarts and logs are captured. A tiny service file is less drama than babysitting a background PID.

[Unit]
Description=My Spring Boot service
After=network.target

[Service]
User=appuser
ExecStart=/usr/bin/java -Xmx512m -jar /opt/myapp/myapp.jar
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Troubleshooting without panicking

If the app refuses to start check the obvious first. A missing JDK is the most common silly mistake. Make sure java runs on the host and the JAR is an executable Spring Boot artifact rather than a library produced by a wrong build step.

  • If you see a bind exception for the port, pick another port with the server.port flag or stop the other service using that port.
  • If configuration seems wrong pass active profiles on the command line using the profile flag.
  • When logs are sparse increase the logging level with the logging flag and inspect stdout or the configured log file for stack traces and root causes.

Quick checks

  • Run java -version to confirm the JVM is present
  • Open the JAR with jar tf to confirm it is Spring Boot style and contains a main class
  • Use netstat or ss to find port conflicts if the app exits with a bind error

Production tips that do not require a ritual sacrifice

For reliable deployment use a system service and central logging. Capture stdout to files or forward logs to a collector so you do not have to ssh and ask a developer to paste a stack trace. Add health checks and a restart policy so the platform can handle hiccups while you enjoy coffee.

Follow these steps to quickly run Spring Boot JARs from the command line and avoid the common traps that turn a five minute test into a debugging saga.

title: How to login to DockerHub with an Access Token
description: Quick tutorial to authenticate to DockerHub using a personal access token and the docker login command for secure CI and scripting
heading: How to login to DockerHub with an Access Token
body:
So you want CI to push and pull from DockerHub without humans typing passwords at 3 a.m. Good plan. Personal access tokens let automation act like a responsible adult instead of a password-hoarding raccoon. This guide shows how to create a DockerHub token then use it with docker login so scripts, CI pipelines, and sleepy developers can all get along.

Why use a personal access token for DockerHub

Passwords belong to people. Tokens belong to machines and can be treated like expendable tiny keys. Benefits include:

  • Least privilege control by giving only the scope you need
  • Easy rotation without changing your main account password
  • Cleaner audit and easier revocation when someone leaves or an automation goes rogue

Create a personal access token in DockerHub

Open your DockerHub account settings and create a personal access token. Give it a clear name that explains what the token does and limit the scope to the minimum required. If you name a token something cryptic like "token123" you will regret it three months from now when you have to remember why it exists.

Best practice for token naming and scope

  • Name it by pipeline or service for quick identification
  • Grant the least privileges needed for pushing or pulling
  • Treat the token like a password and rotate it regularly

Login with the Docker CLI without leaking secrets

Never put tokens on the command line where shell history and process lists can spy on you. Use the password standard input option of docker login instead. Example:

echo 'MY_TOKEN' | docker login -u myusername --password-stdin

The CLI will hand off credentials to the configured credential helper when one is present. On a production host use a credential store or helper that encrypts or isolates secrets instead of letting them sit in a plain file.

Verify the authenticated session

After login run a simple pull or perform an action the token is supposed to allow:

docker pull hello-world

If the command succeeds your token is working. If it fails the error usually tells you whether authentication failed or the token lacks the right permissions.

Use tokens safely in CI and automation

Do not commit tokens to repositories. Instead store them in your CI secret store or platform secret manager and inject them at runtime. Example CI pattern:

  • Save token in pipeline secrets
  • In the job echo the secret and pipe to docker login using --password-stdin
  • Remove any temporary files and avoid printing the token to logs
# pseudo steps in a CI job
# assume SECRET_TOKEN is stored in the CI secret manager
echo "$SECRET_TOKEN" | docker login -u "$DOCKERHUB_USER" --password-stdin
# push or pull images
docker push myorg/myimage:tag

Credential helpers and where secrets live

The Docker CLI delegates to the credential helper configured on the host. If a helper exists your secrets usually end up in that helper. If not they go into the local config file. For production runners prefer a secure helper or a host that integrates with your platform secret service.

Rotation and least privilege

Rotate tokens on a schedule and revoke unused ones. Give tokens exactly the rights they need. If you only need to pull set the token to pull only. If you need to push create a token scoped accordingly. Think of tokens like disposable keys that expire or get changed before someone uses them as a coaster.

Quick recap

Create a personal access token in DockerHub. Pipe the token into docker login with --password-stdin to avoid exposing it. Verify with a pull or the relevant action. Store the token in your CI secret store and rotate and limit scope frequently for better security. You now have CI that behaves and a slightly lighter sense of dread about credentials.

title: Push a Spring Boot app to Dockerhub
description: Step by step guide to build a Spring Boot jar create a Docker image and push the image to Docker Hub with practical commands and tips
heading: Push a Spring Boot app to Dockerhub for quick deployment
body:
This tutorial shows how to build a Spring Boot jar create a Docker image and push the image to Docker Hub so the app can run anywhere.

  1. Build the Spring Boot jar
  2. Create a Dockerfile
  3. Build the Docker image
  4. Login to Docker Hub
  5. Push the image to Docker Hub

Build the Spring Boot jar using the chosen build tool. For Maven use

mvn clean package

The build step produces a jar in the target folder. Keep track of the jar name and location for the Dockerfile copy step.

Create a Dockerfile that copies the jar and runs the Java runtime. Keep the Dockerfile minimal and add a .dockerignore file to avoid copying unnecessary files.

Build the Docker image with a tag that matches a Docker Hub repository name on the local machine for easier push. Example command

docker build -t username/spring-boot-app .

The build will produce an image stored locally. Use small base images and consider multi stage builds to reduce image size when preparing a production image.

Login to Docker Hub from the command line before pushing. Use the CLI login flow to authenticate with the Docker Hub account.

docker login

After authentication push the local image to Docker Hub so other hosts can pull the image. Example push command

docker push username/spring-boot-app

Pushing uploads the image layers to Docker Hub where the repository becomes the source for deployments and CI pipelines. Tagging strategies help manage versions and rollbacks.

Summary of the tutorial The guide covered building a Spring Boot artifact creating a Docker image authenticating to Docker Hub and pushing the image to a repository for distribution and deployment

Tip

Use a .dockerignore file to exclude target and local config files and use automated builds in the Docker Hub or a CI pipeline to avoid manual pushes when scaling releases

title: Introduction to Spring Boot Tutorial for 2023
description: A compact Spring Boot guide for 2023 covering setup dependencies REST controllers and running a local app.
heading: Introduction to Spring Boot Tutorial for 2023
body:
This tutorial teaches how to set up a Spring Boot project create REST endpoints manage dependencies and run a local application using current best practices for 2023.

  1. Initialize a project
  2. Choose dependencies and build tool
  3. Create main application and controller
  4. Run and test locally
  5. Package and deploy

Step 1 Initialize a project Use Spring Initializr to pick a group name artifact name and one or two starter dependencies. Choosing minimal starters avoids dependency sprawl and mysterious runtime surprises.

Step 2 Choose dependencies and build tool Pick Maven or Gradle and add web starter plus data or security if needed. Keep dependency list focused on features required for the project scope.

Step 3 Create main application and controller Add a class annotated with @SpringBootApplication and a simple REST controller using @RestController and @GetMapping to expose an endpoint. Thin controllers and clear service layers make maintenance less painful.

Step 4 Run and test locally Start the application with Maven or Gradle and use curl or a browser to hit the endpoint. Example command for Gradle is gradle bootRun. Add unit tests for controller behavior and integration tests for full request flow.

Step 5 Package and deploy Build a runnable jar and deploy to a cloud target or container. Use profiles for configuration and avoid hard coded values in source code.

The tutorial covered project bootstrap dependency selection basic controller creation local execution and packaging for deployment. Following these steps gets a lean Spring Boot application into production ready shape with less ceremony and fewer surprises.

Tip

Start with minimal starters then add dependencies as features are required. Use devtools for fast reload during development and profile driven configuration for safe deployments.

title: How to run your Spring Boot JAR file from the command line
description: Quick guide to build run and manage a Spring Boot JAR from the command line including background run and basic runtime options
heading: How to Run Spring Boot JAR from the Command Line
body:
This tutorial shows how to build package and run a Spring Boot JAR from the command line and how to manage background execution and logs.

  1. Build the JAR
  2. Navigate to the JAR folder
  3. Run the application with java
  4. Run in the background and capture logs
  5. Pass runtime options and environment variables

Build the JAR

Use Maven or Gradle to produce a runnable artifact. Typical commands are

mvn clean package or ./gradlew bootJar

The packaged file usually lands in target or build/libs and will have a name like myapp.jar.

Navigate to the JAR folder

Change the working directory to the folder that contains the JAR before running commands. Example

cd target

Run the application with java

Start the application with the Java launcher

java -jar myapp.jar

Use Spring Boot properties to override defaults on the fly

java -jar myapp.jar --server.port=8081

Run in the background and capture logs

For a quick background run use nohup and redirect output to a file

nohup java -jar myapp.jar > app.log 2>&1 &

Check the running process and stop when needed using standard process commands

ps aux | grep myapp.jar then kill PID

Pass runtime options and environment variables

Set JVM options and Spring profiles on the same line for simplicity

SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod JAVA_OPTS="-Xmx512m" java $JAVA_OPTS -jar myapp.jar

This setup covers typical development and light production needs without orchestration tools.

The guide explained how to build a Spring Boot JAR locate the artifact run the application handle background execution capture logs and pass runtime options.

Tip

For serious production use prefer a process manager like systemd or a container platform. A managed service provides automatic restarts log rotation and clearer lifecycle control which saves time and prevents angry wake up calls.

title: How to Containerize Spring Boot applications
description: Step by step guide to containerize Spring Boot apps using Docker best practices for small images fast startup and reliable deployment
heading: How to Containerize Spring Boot applications for Docker
body:
This tutorial teaches how to containerize a Spring Boot application for Docker based deployment and best practices for small images and fast startup.

  1. Build a reproducible executable jar
  2. Create a multi stage Dockerfile
  3. Tune JVM and environment variables
  4. Build the image
  5. Run the container locally
  6. Push the image to a registry

Step 1 Produce an executable jar with Maven or Gradle and enable the Spring Boot plugin to get a single artifact. That artifact contains application classes and dependencies so the container only needs one file to run the app.

Step 2 Use a multi stage Dockerfile so the build stage assembles the jar and the final stage uses a slim runtime image. This approach keeps the image small and avoids shipping build tools into the runtime image.

Step 3 Configure JVM memory and startup flags using environment variables so the container can adapt to different hosts. Use a small heap and enable server mode for faster startup when running in containers.

Step 4 Build the image with a clear tag name and a reproducible build process. Example command to run from project root

docker build -t myapp_latest .

Step 5 Run the container locally to verify health and logs. Map the application port and test endpoints from a browser or curl. Example run command

docker run -p 8080 8080 myapp_latest

Step 6 Push the image to a registry for CI CD pipelines or shared deployment. Use authenticated registries and immutable tags to avoid surprise rollbacks.

The guide covered how to prepare a Spring Boot jar craft a minimal Docker image tune runtime settings build and run the container and publish the image for deployment. Follow the steps to get predictable images faster builds and fewer surprises when moving from developer laptop to production.

Tip

Use layered jar or build tools that produce a dependency layer and an application layer so small code changes only update the top layer and push times become delightfully short.

title: Fix Docker Hub Invalid Username or Password Error with an Ac
description: Fix Docker Hub invalid username or password errors by using an access token and updating login and CI credentials to restore push and pull access
heading: Fix Docker Hub Invalid Username or Password Error with an Access Token
body:
This tutorial shows how to fix Docker Hub invalid username or password errors by using an access token.

  1. Create an access token on Docker Hub
  2. Use the token with the docker login command
  3. Update CI and local credential stores
  4. Verify push and pull operations
  5. Revoke old password or token if compromise is suspected

Step 1 Generate a Docker Hub access token from the account security page. Pick a descriptive name so a later audit does not turn into a guessing game.

Step 2 Authenticate using the token instead of a password. A quick command example follows.

echo "ACCESS_TOKEN" | docker login --username USERNAME --password-stdin

Provide the Docker Hub username and stream the access token via password standard input. This avoids exposing the token on the command line history and keeps logs cleaner than a confession.

Step 3 Replace stored passwords in continuous integration pipelines and local credential managers with the new access token. Most CI systems accept a secret named DOCKERHUB_TOKEN or similar.

Step 4 Perform a docker push and docker pull against a repository that requires authentication. Successful operations confirm that credential change solved the invalid username or password error.

Step 5 If the previous password was compromised or if credential reuse was present revoke the old password and unused tokens. That prevents awkward follow up messages from the security team.

This short workflow swaps a fragile password based login for a token based approach and restores registry access with minimal fuss and fewer mysterious failures during CI runs.

Tip

Use separate tokens for human developers and automated systems. Rotate tokens regularly and store tokens in a secrets manager so credential leaks become a rare and solvable event.

title: What should a successful HTTP PUT operation return?
description: Practical guidance on what a successful HTTP PUT should return after success including status codes headers and body choices for REST APIs
heading: What should a successful HTTP PUT operation return for REST APIs?
body:
A successful HTTP PUT should clearly tell the client whether the resource was created updated or accepted for later processing.

PUT is idempotent. The same request repeated should not create multiple resources unless the server decides otherwise and documents that behavior.

  1. 201 Created Use when the server created a new resource that the client did not already address. Include a Location header that points to the new resource and optionally return the new representation in the response body.
  2. 200 OK Use when the server updated an existing resource and returns the updated representation. This is handy for clients that want an immediate canonical view of the resource after the change.
  3. 204 No Content Use when the server applied the update and there is nothing useful to return. This keeps traffic small and honest.
  4. 202 Accepted Use for asynchronous processing when the update is queued and not yet applied. Provide a Location header or another way for the client to check status later.

Headers matter more than most people admit. Include ETag for optimistic concurrency control. Use Content Location when the returned representation comes from a different URL than the request target. Consistent use of headers prevents heroic guesswork by client developers.

Avoid sending conflicting signals like a 200 OK and an empty body unless the goal is confusion. If the client needs the full updated representation for display or caching return it. If the client only needs acknowledgement prefer 204 No Content and save bandwidth.

Design a predictable rule for PUT responses and document that rule. Predictability is the friend of stable clients and fewer support tickets.

Tip

Pick one primary successful response for PUT across the API and stick with that choice. Consistency beats cleverness when multiple client libraries rely on the same server behavior.

title: Git reset hard vs soft What's the difference?
description: Clear comparison of Git reset hard vs soft with examples and guidance for when to use each command in your workflow
heading: Git reset hard vs soft What's the difference?
body:
Welcome to the one minute tutorial where we explain how to politely or brutally rewind your git history. If you want to undo commits without panicking, understanding the difference between git reset --soft and git reset --hard will save your keyboard and possibly your job.

Quick comparison

Short version first since attention spans are short. git reset --soft moves HEAD to another commit but leaves the index and working tree alone. git reset --hard moves HEAD and then makes the index and working tree match that commit exactly which discards uncommitted changes. One is a gentle nudge the other is a nuclear option.

What git reset --soft does

Use this when you want to rewrite history but keep the work you already made. The last commit is undone but the files stay staged. This is great when your commit message was tragic or when you want to squash the last commit into a different one.

git reset --soft HEAD~1

After that command the changes from the undone commit will be in the index so you can edit files or recommit with a cleaner message.

What git reset --hard does

This one erases the messy bits. HEAD moves to the specified commit and both the index and working tree are reset to match. Uncommitted changes are removed. No refunds.

git reset --hard HEAD~1

Use when you want to restore the repo to a known clean state or when a bad experiment needs to be wiped from existence. Warning do not use this if you might want to recover unstaged work.

When to use which

  • Choose git reset --soft when you need to undo and rework commits but want to keep the code handy for editing and recommitting.
  • Choose git reset --hard when you want the working tree to match a past commit exactly and you are sure uncommitted work can be discarded.
  • If you are not sure create a branch or stash first to preserve the work.

Safety chores before you reset

Git gives you ways to be less reckless. Create a branch if you might want to go back. For quick safety stash changes with git stash so nothing goes missing. If you already pushed commits and need to rewrite history communicate with your team before you force push.

git branch savepoint
git stash push -m "temp save"

Examples in a real workflow

Say you made a commit but realized the message is wrong or you want to combine it with other changes. Use git reset --soft HEAD~1 to uncommit but keep changes staged. Make edits and run git commit again. If you accidentally created garbage in the working tree and just want to start over use git reset --hard HEAD to make your tree match the last commit.

Final takeaways and git tips

Remember these rules of thumb for version control survival. Soft moves only the commit pointer and keeps your work. Hard moves the pointer and resets files which removes uncommitted changes. When in doubt branch or stash first. These are common git commands that will improve your git workflow once you stop treating them like magic curses.

Now go fix that commit message or blow away the failed prototype depending on your mood and your backup plan.

title: How do you say idempotent?
description: Quick guide to pronouncing idempotent with phonetic cues tips and context for programmers and mathematicians
heading: How do you say idempotent Pronunciation Guide
body:
Quick guide to saying idempotent without sounding like you guessed

The safe bet is to stress the third syllable and say something that sounds like eye dem POH tent when you want to be taken seriously. That is the common American pattern and the one dictionaries show as the careful form. If you prefer phonetics the standard transcription is /ˌaɪdɛmˈpoʊtənt/ which you can read slowly and then move on with your life.

Three compact ways people actually say it

  • eye dem POH tent which is the clear, stressed third syllable version
  • id em POH tent a clipped casual variant you will hear in standup meetings
  • eye dem puh tent a sloppy version that gets laughs and confusion in equal measure

Common mispronunciations and how to dodge them

People sometimes push the stress to the wrong syllable or swap the vowel sounds. If you put the stress earlier you sound unsure. If your squad looks baffled say the phonetic form slowly and then follow with a short example. That anchors both sound and sense.

The concept matters more than the accent

In mathematics an idempotent function satisfies f of f of x equals f of x for every x in its domain. A concrete everyday example is the floor function floor of floor of x equals floor of x. In linear algebra an idempotent matrix P satisfies P times P equals P which is a fancy way to say applying the same operation twice does not change anything after the first application.

What idempotent means for APIs and servers

In web development and API design idempotent means repeated requests with the same parameters leave the server state unchanged after the first request. This is why GET and PUT are considered idempotent in HTTP semantics. DELETE is idempotent in principle if deleting the same resource repeatedly ends up in the same state. POST is not idempotent by default which is why you do not blindly retry it without thought.

Why you should care in ops and engineering

  • Retries become safe when an endpoint is idempotent
  • Clients and load balancers can be simpler and less brittle
  • Testing and debugging are easier when behavior is predictable

Quick usage lines for code reviews

Drop any of these when someone looks like they might escalate to a flame war

  • "This endpoint is idempotent so safe retries are allowed"
  • "Mark the database operation idempotent to prevent duplicate rows"
  • "PUT is idempotent here so repeated requests should be harmless"

Final tip that actually works

If you are unsure speak the phonetic form slowly then use the term in a one line example. Context helps teammates remember both the sound and the meaning. Say it confidently and move on to the bug that actually matters.
seo_title: Say idempotent like a developer who actually knows things
seo_heading: How to pronounce idempotent confidently in meetings and reviews

title: PUT vs POST What's the difference?
description: Short clear guide to the practical differences between PUT and POST for REST APIs with idempotency and usage tips
heading: PUT vs POST What's the difference?
body:
If you are designing an API and you do not want clients to accidentally summon duplicate users or corrupt your database with bad retries then knowing the practical difference between PUT and POST is the ticket. Short version in plain human terms Put is idempotent and targets a known resource URI. Post is non idempotent by default and targets a collection or action where the server usually picks the new id or runs a process.

Idempotency and why you should care

Idempotency is the boring but heroic property that lets clients retry requests without chaos. If a PUT request succeeds once then sending the exact same PUT again should not change the server state beyond the first success. Repeatability is the whole point. POST on the other hand will often create new resources or trigger additional side effects when repeated, unless you build protections like idempotency keys.

Examples that do not lie

PUT /users/123
payload { name: "Ada Lovelace", email: "ada@example.com" }

POST /users
payload { name: "Alan Turing", email: "alan@example.com" }

With PUT the client is saying store this exact representation at /users/123. With POST the client is saying create something under /users and server will usually assign an id or perform some processing.

Response patterns and common status codes

  • 201 Created when a POST or sometimes a PUT results in a newly created resource and the server supplies the new location header
  • 200 OK when an update returns the updated representation
  • 204 No Content when an update succeeded and the server has nothing to return
  • 400 Bad Request for malformed input and 409 Conflict when creation collides with an existing resource

When to pick PUT

  • Client controls the final URI or the resource id and wants safe retries
  • Full replacement semantics are acceptable or desired for that resource
  • You want predictable behavior when network problems force a retry

PUT is your careful librarian who will replace the book on the exact shelf you name. If you own the key or id, use PUT.

When to pick POST

  • Server should assign ids or generate the resource location
  • You are creating subordinate resources under a collection endpoint
  • The operation is more like submit and process than replace

POST is the eager intern who drops new entries into the pile and asks the server to decide where they belong. If you want server side id allocation or side effects that are not safe to repeat then POST fits.

About PATCH and partial updates

PATCH exists for partial updates and can be implemented to be idempotent but it is not guaranteed by the spec. Use PATCH when you want to change only parts of a representation and you do not want to send the whole object in every request. Be aware that some PATCH implementations are tricky to get right when concurrent edits happen.

Practical tips for real world API design

  • If retry safety matters prefer idempotent methods like PUT or implement idempotency keys for POST calls
  • Return appropriate status codes so clients can make smart decisions about retries
  • Use consistent resource design so developers do not guess whether an endpoint creates or replaces
  • Document whether POST endpoints are safe to retry or whether they require an idempotency token

In the end choose the method that matches who owns the id and how safe you need retries to be. And if you still feel nostalgic for chaos you can always let every POST do double duty and call it a feature. But do not blame the client when the database cries.
seo_title: Choose PUT or POST for REST APIs without breaking things
seo_heading: How PUT and POST differ in idempotency resource design and retries

title: The HTTP verbs
description: Quick guide to HTTP verbs GET POST PUT DELETE PATCH HEAD OPTIONS and how to use safe and idempotent methods in APIs
heading: The HTTP verbs explained for developers
body:
If you treat HTTP methods like fortune telling you are doing it wrong and your logs will hate you. This guide gives the short version with real examples and a little sarcasm to keep you awake. You will learn what GET POST PUT PATCH DELETE HEAD OPTIONS and TRACE really mean and when to use each one so your API does not surprise anyone at 3 a m.

Common HTTP methods and what they do

GET

GET retrieves a resource without changing server state. It is safe and cache friendly. Use GET for reads and for things where repeating the request must not mutate data.

GET /users
GET /products/42

POST

POST creates or submits data. It usually changes server state and is not idempotent. If you make the same POST twice you often get two resources unless the server deduplicates for you.

POST /users
body contains new user data

PUT

PUT replaces a resource or creates it when absent. It is idempotent which means repeated identical PUT calls should leave the server in the same state as one call.

PUT /users/123
body contains full user representation

PATCH

PATCH applies a partial update. Patch semantics depend on your patch format so it may or may not be idempotent. Use PATCH when you only need to tweak a few fields and you want to avoid sending the whole object.

PATCH /users/123
body contains only the fields to change

DELETE

DELETE removes a resource. DELETE is idempotent in the sense that deleting something twice leaves the server in the same final state. Do not confuse idempotent with safe.

DELETE /users/123

HEAD

HEAD is like GET without the response body. Handy for metadata checks and for caches that want headers without the payload.

HEAD /products/42

OPTIONS

OPTIONS asks the server which methods are allowed on a resource. It is useful for CORS handshakes and for tooling that wants to know supported verbs.

OPTIONS /users

TRACE

TRACE echoes back the received request for debugging. Most production servers disable it for security reasons so do not rely on it being available.

Safe and idempotent explained without math

Safe methods do not change server state. GET and HEAD are safe. That means you can repeat them without worrying about accidental writes.

Idempotent means repeating the same request results in the same server state as doing it once. PUT and DELETE are idempotent. POST typically is not. PATCH depends on your patch design.

Status codes that play nice with verbs

When a POST creates something return 201 to say the resource was created. When an action succeeds but there is no body to return use 204 which keeps responses tidy and avoids wasted bandwidth.

Choosing the right verb without losing your mind

  • Does the request change server state If no use GET or HEAD
  • Is this creating a resource Use POST
  • Is this a full replacement Use PUT
  • Is this a small tweak Use PATCH
  • Is this removing something Use DELETE
  • Need to know allowed methods Use OPTIONS

Quick tips

  • Favor semantic verbs over transport level tricks so clients and caches behave predictably
  • Think about idempotency when designing retries and error handling
  • If unsure ask whether repeating the request should do extra work That question saves hours of debugging and angry emails

Follow those rules and your API will be calmer than your error logs. Break them and you will get a front row seat to weird bugs that only appear in production on a Friday. Happy coding and try not to POST things by accident.
seo_title: HTTP methods explained for mortals and confused API developers
seo_heading: How to pick GET POST PUT DELETE PATCH and keep your API sane

title: How to say Udemy?
description: Short guide to pronouncing Udemy with phonetics stress and quick practice tips for confident speech
heading: How to say Udemy correctly
body:
Stop pretending the spelling tells you everything. The brand name Udemy is one of those words that looks like a spelling contest but behaves like a spoken word. This quick guide will get you saying Udemy clearly and confidently so you do not sound like you invented a new app mid sentence.

What the proper pronunciation sounds like

The short version is YOO duh mee. Stress the first syllable and keep the middle syllable reduced to a schwa like sound. If you like phonetics the pattern is roughly /ˈjuːdəmi/. Say it slowly at first then smooth it out into conversation.

Break it into three parts

  • YOO This is the stressed syllable. Think of the word "you" and say it with a confident vowel.
  • duh A reduced syllable, like the schwa sound in about. Do not over pronounce this part.
  • mee Short and clear. Keep the vowel pure and finish cleanly.

Practical speaking tips for English pronunciation

Here are a few language tips that actually work with brand name pronunciation and online courses references.

  • Listen to a native speaker for rhythm and vowel quality. Use an audio clip from the official site or a trustworthy source.
  • Record yourself saying short phrases instead of isolated words. Examples include "I took a Udemy course" and "Find a Udemy class." Phrases lock in natural rhythm faster.
  • Compare your recording to the native example and tweak stress and vowel length until it feels natural.

Quick practice routine

  1. Say the three syllables slowly: YOO, duh, mee.
  2. Link them together with smooth motion while keeping the stress on YOO.
  3. Repeat short phrases and record once you stop laughing at yourself.
  4. Use the article a before Udemy because the initial Y sound is a consonant sound, not a vowel sound. Say a Udemy class, not an Udemy class.

Final notes on brand name pronunciation and confidence

Pronouncing Udemy correctly is mostly about stress and vowel quality. This matters more than memorizing spelling tricks. Treat the middle syllable as a shrug, keep the first syllable bright, and finish with a clean mee. With a little practice you will sound like someone who knows what an online course is and not like a confused spell checker.

Now go practice, record, compare, and then use your new powers for good. Or at least for enrolling in more online courses you will enthusiastically start and never finish.
seo_title: Say Udemy Like a Pro and Stop Mangling Brand Names
seo_heading: Master Udemy pronunciation with simple syllable tips and practice routines
