body:
If you want your git pushes and pulls to stop acting like their own indie project assume responsibility and set an upstream. This short guide walks through setting a tracking branch so your developer workflow does not require ritual incantations every time you push.

Why set an upstream at all

Think of an upstream as the GPS for your branch. Without it git will still work but you will type more, make mistakes, and maybe accidentally push a Frankenbranch to origin. Setting an upstream makes branch management predictable and reduces version control drama.

Step 1 Create a local branch

Start a feature or fix with a local branch. You can create and switch in one move if you like efficiency.

git checkout -b feature-branch

Step 2 Push and set the upstream

Send the branch to the remote and tell git to remember where future pushes and pulls belong. This is the one command that saves keystrokes and sanity.

git push -u origin feature-branch

The -u flag sets origin/feature-branch as the tracking branch so plain git push and git pull will work from now on.

Step 3 Verify tracking status

Want proof that your branch is no longer wandering alone in the void use one of these commands.

  • git status -sb shows a short status and the tracking branch
  • git branch -vv lists local branches with their remote trackers and how far they are ahead or behind

Step 4 Change upstream when needed

If a remote branch got renamed or you need to point at a different branch there is no need to delete and recreate anything. Update the tracking target with this command.

git branch -u origin/other-branch feature-branch

You can also use the equivalent long form if you prefer explicit commands.

git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/other-branch feature-branch

Step 5 Use tracking for day to day work

Once upstream is set use simple commands and move on with your life.

  • git pull to fetch and merge from the tracking branch
  • git push to push to the tracking branch

This avoids accidentally pushing to the wrong remote branch which is the true developer hazard.

Quick tips and common gotchas

  • If git push complains about no upstream and you thought you set one run git branch -vv to inspect the mapping
  • If you want new branches to track a remote automatically consider setting a sensible push default in your config
  • Renaming a local branch does not change the remote. Rename first then update the upstream or push the new name with -u

Troubleshooting

If you get merge conflicts after pulling it is because history diverged. Resolve the conflicts then commit and push. If you need to rebase remember to force push carefully and only when you know what you are doing.

Following these lightweight rules for setting upstreams keeps branch management less annoying and makes collaboration less of a guessing game. Now go push something useful and try not to break prod.
seo_title: Set Git upstream the right way for smoother branch management
seo_heading: How to connect a local branch to a remote tracking branch in Git

title: GitHub URL Example | Learn how to use GitHub URLs & Git
description: Learn how to read GitHub repository URLs and use Git to clone branch and push changes with clear examples and common gotchas
heading: GitHub URL Example Learn how to use GitHub URLs and Git
body:
This tutorial shows how to read GitHub repository URLs and use Git to clone create branches and push changes without mystery.

  1. Open the repository page on GitHub
  2. Identify the URL parts that matter
  3. Decide on HTTPS or SSH for cloning
  4. Clone the repository locally
  5. Create branch make changes and push back

Open the repository page on GitHub

Navigate to the repository in a browser and look at the address bar. The visible address often reads like github dot com slash owner slash repo and that is enough to reference the project for many tasks.

Identify the URL parts that matter

Domain owner and repository name are the core pieces. Paths after the repository name indicate a file or folder and branch names can appear in the URL. Knowing where the branch name lives helps avoid surprising downloads of the wrong branch.

Decide on HTTPS or SSH for cloning

HTTPS is simple and uses a username and password or personal access token. SSH uses a key pair and is more convenient for frequent pushes. Choose the method that matches local credential setup.

Clone the repository locally

Copy the clone URL shown on the GitHub page. Example notation without protocol is github dot com slash owner slash repo dot git. Then run a clone command from the command line using Git and the chosen URL method.

Create branch make changes and push back

Make a feature branch using a clear name then add commit messages that explain changes. Push the branch to the remote and open a pull request on GitHub for code review.

This tutorial covered how to parse a GitHub URL how to choose a clone method and the basic flow from clone to push. The goal is to make URL anatomy boring so actual development can be fun again.

Tip

When copying a clone URL prefer SSH if a key pair is already configured. That avoids repeated prompts and saves precious typing energy.

title: Generate GitLab SSH Keys & setup SSH on GitLab
description: Step by step guide to generate SSH keys and configure SSH on GitLab for secure push and pull access and painless authentication
heading: Generate GitLab SSH Keys and setup SSH on GitLab
body:
Why bother with SSH keys

Short version You can stop typing your password and avoid awkward merge conflicts with your own credentials. SSH keys give Git and GitLab a polite but firm handshake that says I am who I claim to be without a password. Developers and DevOps people use this for secure Git authentication and to keep workflows smooth.

Check for existing keys in your .ssh folder

Before you become heroic and generate another key pair check if you already have one. Overwriting a working key is a neat way to lock yourself out of other servers.

ls -al ~/.ssh

Look for files like id_ed25519 and id_ed25519.pub or id_rsa and id_rsa.pub. If you see them you can reuse or backup instead of making a mess.

Generate a modern SSH key pair

Use ed25519 unless you have a legacy reason not to. It is smaller faster and secure enough to make dinosaurs jealous.

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your.email@example.com"

When prompted pick a file name or accept the default. Add a passphrase if you want defense in depth. Remember the private key must stay private and never be uploaded to GitLab or pasted into a random forum.

Add the private key to the SSH agent

The SSH agent remembers your private key so you do not type the passphrase for every push. That is the whole point of the agent.

eval $(ssh-agent -s)
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

The first command starts the agent for the session and the second adds your private key. On some systems the agent is provided by the OS so these steps may already be covered.

Copy your public key safely

The public key is a single line and it is what you paste into GitLab. Do not try to trim it or it will stop working and you will cry quietly.

cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

Copy the entire line that starts with ssh-ed25519 and ends with your email. That entire string is the public key GitLab needs to identify your machine.

Add the public key to GitLab

No admin rights required This is a per user setting. Open GitLab in your browser sign in and go to your user settings then find SSH Keys in the menu. Paste the key into the key field give it a descriptive title like Home Laptop or CI Runner and save.

  • Use a title that tells you which machine the key belongs to
  • Do not paste the private key anywhere ever

Test the SSH connection

Now for the tiny adrenaline rush run the test command and accept the host fingerprint if prompted. If you use a self hosted GitLab replace gitlab.com with your instance domain.

ssh -T git@gitlab.com

A successful response will say something friendly and confirm your account name. If it fails you will get useful errors to debug.

Troubleshooting tips

  • Permissions matter Make sure your private key file is only readable by you for extra drama free security with chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
  • Check what keys the agent knows with ssh-add -l
  • Verbose SSH output helps run ssh -v -T git@gitlab.com to see why it is angry
  • If Git still prompts for a password check your remote URL It should be an SSH url like git@gitlab.com:group/project.git rather than an HTTPS url

Final notes

Using SSH keys replaces password based pushes and makes authentication smooth and script friendly. Keep your private key secret use a passphrase for extra safety and add a new key for each machine so you can revoke one without burning the whole house down.

Happy pushing and may your merges be merciful.
seo_title: Create Secure SSH Keys for GitLab and Stop Typing Passwords
seo_heading: Step by step GitLab SSH key setup for secure Git push and pull

title: How to Generate GitHub SSH Keys
description: Quick guide to create SSH keys for GitHub add the public key to the account and test secure git access from a local machine
heading: How to Generate GitHub SSH Keys Step by Step
body:
This tutorial shows how to generate SSH keys for GitHub and set up secure git access from a local machine.

  2. Generate a new SSH key pair
  3. Add the private key to the ssh agent
  4. Add the public key to the GitHub account

Step 1 Check for existing SSH keys in the default SSH folder. Use the list command to inspect the directory and avoid overwriting a working identity.

ls -al ~/.ssh

Step 2 Create a strong modern key. ed25519 is recommended for most users. Run the key generation command and follow the prompts. Provide an email for the comment and a passphrase for extra protection.

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"

Step 3 Start the ssh agent and add the private key so the system can use the key without repeated passphrase prompts.

eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"

cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

Following these steps creates a key pair adds the private key to the local agent uploads the public key to the GitHub account and verifies secure access for git operations. That protects code pushes pulls and other git interactions from password prompts and reduces the chance of credential leaks while keeping developer life slightly less annoying.

Tip

Prefer ed25519 for small fast keys and protect the private key with a strong passphrase. Use an SSH config file to manage multiple keys per host and store backups of public keys in a safe place rather than repeating guesswork later.

title: How to Undo a Pushed Git Commit - Reset & Revert a Git Commi
description: Learn how to safely undo a pushed Git commit using reset or revert and avoid breaking shared history.
heading: How to Undo a Pushed Git Commit Reset and Revert After Push
body:
This guide teaches how to undo a pushed Git commit using reset and revert while keeping repository history safe and collaborators sane.

  1. Assess the situation and choose reset or revert
  2. Use git revert to create a new reversing commit
  3. Use git reset and force push only for private branches
  4. Push changes and communicate with team members
  5. Verify repository state on remote

Assessing the situation means checking whether the problematic commit has been shared with others and whether the remote branch must keep a stable history.

For shared branches use the revert approach to avoid rewriting history and causing surprise merge conflicts. Example command

git revert

For private feature branches where rewriting history is acceptable perform a reset on local branch and then force push. Example commands

git reset --hard

git push --force

When using force push explain the reason to team members and consider using safer options like force with lease to reduce risk of clobbering someone else work. Example command

git push --force-with-lease

After any undo operation verify the remote branch with a fetch and log check to confirm the desired history. Example commands

git fetch origin

git log --oneline origin/

The goal is to pick the least disruptive method for the scenario and then apply that method cleanly with clear communication to avoid confusion.

Recap The tutorial explained how to decide between revert and reset how to execute the chosen approach and how to push and verify changes while keeping teammates informed.

Tip

When unsure choose revert because creating a reversing commit preserves history and avoids angry notifications from teammates who enjoy blaming others for lost work.

title: Why Java Uses static & final for Constants
description: Clear explanation of why Java uses static and final for constants with examples scope memory and practical guidance
heading: Why Java Uses static and final for Constants Explained
body:
If you have ever cursed at a bug that turned out to be a constant that lied to you then welcome to the club. Java constants are simple in theory and sneaky in practice. Using static and final together gives you a single, immutable reference at class level that plays nice with the JVM and your CPU cache when you do it right.

What static means in plain English

static makes a member belong to the class instead of to each object. The JVM puts that single value in the method area so many instances do not each carry their own copy. That is memory friendly and faster for lookups when you avoid creating pointless duplicates.

What final actually prevents

final stops reassignment of the variable reference or primitive value. For primitives and String literals the compiler often treats the value as a compile time constant and performs inlining. That inlining is a performance win but it has a catch when the constant is public.

Example that everyone has seen

public static final int MAX = 100

Other classes that compile against a public static final primitive or String may bake the literal into their bytecode. That means changing MAX in the original class and redeploying it might not change behavior in already compiled consumers. Surprise bug incoming.

Final on objects does not freeze the object

Declaring a List as final only prevents reassigning the list variable. Items can still be added or removed unless you take extra steps. If you want a truly immutable collection prefer immutable factories or return an unmodifiable view from accessors.

Thread safety and class initialization

Java gives a useful guarantee during class initialization for static final primitives and String constants. The JVM ensures they are visible safely across threads once initialization completes. For more complex objects assigned at initialization you may still need explicit synchronization or use immutable data structures to avoid subtle concurrency issues.

Practical rules of thumb for sane constants

  • Use uppercase names to signal intent and keep the code readable
  • Prefer private static final for anything that might change later and expose a stable accessor instead
  • Do not make mutable collections public and final. Wrap them with Collections.unmodifiableList or return a defensive copy from getters
  • Be cautious with public static final primitives and strings because of compile time inlining across modules
  • Prefer immutable collections or factory methods when you need a constant complex object

Quick checklist before you hit commit

Keep constants private when possible. Use static to share one copy and final to prevent accidental reassignment. Remember that final does not make object state immutable. Consider the JVM inlining behavior before you publish a value across modules. And when in doubt return an unmodifiable view or a defensive copy and sleep a little easier at night.

Follow these tips for better JVM memory use reduced surprises from inlining and clearer code design. Your future self will thank you or at least send a sarcastic emoji.
seo_title: How to Declare Java Constants That Won't Betray You at Runtime
seo_heading: Best practices for Java constants memory inlining and thread safety

title: How to Unstage a File in Git Remove from Staging Index
description: Learn how to unstage a file in Git using git restore and alternatives so the file is removed from the staging index before commit
heading: How to Unstage a File in Git Remove from the Staging Index
body:
So you accidentally staged a file and now commit is judging you silently. Relax, Git will not exile you. This guide shows how to unstage a file while keeping your edits intact. We will use modern commands and mention the older method for those working with ancient Git relics.

Quick status check

Before you start playing surgeon with the staging index run git status. That neat command tells you which files are staged and which are merely sulking in the working tree. Knowing what is staged helps avoid heroic mistakes.

Unstage a single file with git restore

If you want to move a file out of the staging index but keep your edits in the working directory run:

git restore --staged path/to/file.txt

This removes the file from the index but leaves your changes where they belong. You can keep editing or stage only the hunks you actually want to commit.

Why this works

The index is just a snapshot waiting to become a commit. git restore --staged tells Git to reset that snapshot for the target file back to the last commit while preserving the working copy. Your changes are safe and not magically erased.

Legacy method for old Git versions

If you are stuck on an old Git that does not know about restore use the trusty classic:

git reset HEAD path/to/file.txt

It does basically the same job for the index and works fine. Nobody will shame you for using it while your environment refuses to upgrade.

Unstage everything at once

When your staging area looks like a trash bin and you want to start over run:

git restore --staged .

That removes all files from the staging index in one go. Be careful if you only meant to keep a handful of files staged. This is the nuclear option for cleanup.

Verify the result

After running any unstage command check with git status again. Staged files should have vanished and your target files will appear under changes not staged for commit or untracked depending on their prior state.

Quick tips and workflow ideas

  • Use git add -p to stage hunks when you want fine grained commits.
  • If you want to discard changes from the working tree instead of unstaging use the appropriate git restore options carefully.
  • Keep your commits focused. Staging only what belongs together makes life easier for future you and everyone else on the project.

There you go. Unstaging files is a tiny bit of Git hygiene that prevents messy commits and awkward explanations in PRs. Do it, then sip coffee and fake confidence.
seo_title: Take files out of Git staging without losing your changes
seo_heading: Practical ways to remove files from Git staging in a few steps

title: How to Convert a Java String to int or long Type
description: Quick guide to parse Java strings to int and long with safe parsing examples NumberFormatException handling and practical tips
heading: How to Convert a Java String to int or long Type
body:
This tutorial shows how to convert a Java String to int and long safely and efficiently

  1. Use Integer.parseInt or Long.parseLong for direct conversion
  2. Wrap parsing in try catch to handle bad input
  3. Use Integer valueOf when a boxed type is required
  4. Specify a radix when parsing non decimal numbers
  5. Provide a safe try parse helper to avoid throwing exceptions

Step 1 Use Integer.parseInt and Long.parseLong when input is trusted and performance matters

int n = Integer.parseInt(str)

long l = Long.parseLong(str)

Step 2 Protect parsing with try catch when input may be malformed NumberFormatException will be thrown for invalid digits or overflow

try { int n = Integer.parseInt(str) } catch (NumberFormatException e) { // handle invalid number }

Step 3 Integer valueOf returns an Integer object and may use caching for small values Use when an object is required or when relying on autoboxing

Integer boxed = Integer.valueOf(str)

Step 4 Specify a radix for hexadecimal or other bases Parsing with a radix prevents mistaken conversions for non decimal input

int hex = Integer.parseInt(str, 16)

Step 5 Implement a safe helper when throwing exceptions is undesirable A small helper can return an OptionalInt or a default value and avoid log spam and CPU cost from exceptions

Integer safeParse(String s) { try { return Integer.parseInt(s) } catch (NumberFormatException e) { return null } }

Summary recap The article covered direct parsing methods error handling boxed conversions radix parsing and a safe helper pattern for robust code When parsing from external sources validate input and prefer safe parsing when performance of exception handling matters

Tip

Prefer parseInt when a primitive is needed Use a try parse helper or a library method when input is untrusted Exceptions are expensive so avoid throwing them in normal control flow

title: My Video
description: Fast guide to extract the main idea from a one minute video and turn that into a concise summary with practical steps.
heading: My Video Explained
body:
Stop guessing and start summarizing

This micro tutorial walks through a fast way to turn a one minute video into a tidy video summary that actually helps people. No mystical skills required. You will watch actively mark timestamps identify the main claim condense it to one sentence and add two supporting bullets. This method is perfect for note taking content extraction and quick social copy when you do not have time for a dissertation.

Why this matters for visual learning and productivity

Short clips are everywhere and memory is lazy. A crisp summary saves future you from clicking back through the clip and pretending you remember what was said. Use this for description writing tweets internal notes or a quick micro tutorial pack. The goal is clarity not heroic coverage.

Step by step workflow

1 Watch actively

Play the clip with focus and mute distractions. Look for repeated phrases and emphasis because presenters tend to repeat the important bit like a stuck record. When you hear something that sounds like a thesis pause or jot a quick note.

2 Mark timestamps and cues

Write down seconds where key phrases appear or where visuals change. A few time marks save a lot of guessing later and make citation painless. This is the difference between a useful summary and a vague memory that sounds impressive but means nothing.

3 Identify the main claim

Ask what the presenter wants viewers to remember. Pull out the central noun and verb that carry the message. If you can say the claim in the time it takes to sip coffee you are on the right track.

4 Condense to one sentence

Combine the main claim with a clarifying phrase. Keep the sentence short enough to fit on a sticky note and long enough to actually help someone. This single line is your headline for the clip.

5 Create two supporting bullets

One bullet should name a quick fact or example from the clip. The other should suggest a next step for an interested viewer. Together they give evidence and action which makes a summary useful for readers and searchable for you.

Quick example

  • Main sentence The presenter recommends batching similar tasks to reduce context switching.
  • Bullet one Quick fact Batching saved the team two hours a week in the demo.
  • Bullet two Next step Try grouping similar small tasks into one 30 minute block tomorrow.

Pro tip for speed

If a transcript is available search for repeated nouns and verbs and highlight those lines. That approach finds the backbone of the message faster than heroic guessing. It also makes content extraction and summary writing much faster when you are doing high volume note taking for learning or productivity.

Final notes and use cases

Apply this to one minute reels micro tutorials and classroom clips. The process scales well so creativity remains the only real bottleneck. Use the compact summary as a description a tweet or an internal note and stop wasting time rereading footage you already watched.

Go forth summarize and bask in the small but mighty glory of neat notes.

seo_heading: A simple workflow to capture the claim add timestamps and write two bullets

title: Git Stash Tutorial
description: Learn git stash commands and workflows to save uncommitted changes and switch branches safely
heading: Git Stash Tutorial Save and Restore Uncommitted Changes
body:
If you like switching branches and then instantly regretting life choices, git stash is your emotional support tool. This guide shows how to stash work without committing, restore it when needed, and avoid the drama of lost changes. Think of stash as a temporary shelf for uncommitted changes while you go explore other branches or chase a bug.

Stash the stuff you are not ready to commit

To tuck away tracked changes and staged files use:

git stash push -m 'short message'

If you also want untracked files to come along add the untracked flag:

git stash push -u -m 'include untracked files'

This clears your working tree so you can switch branches without dragging your half finished masterpiece along. Use brief meaningful messages so your future self does not scream later.

See what you saved

Want to inspect the stack of saved work

git stash list

Each entry looks like stash@{0} with your message. If you enjoy chaos skip messages, otherwise document what you were procrastinating on.

Bring changes back to life

Two ways to restore a stash

  • Reapply but keep the stash for later: 
    git stash apply stash@{0}
  • Reapply and remove it from the stack: 
    git stash pop

If conflicts show up handle them like a responsible developer by resolving and committing. Stash will not do the tough emotional work for you.

Create a branch from a stash

If your stash belongs on its own branch use the dedicated command. This makes a branch that starts with the stashed changes and checks it out.

git stash branch my-feature stash@{0}

This is cleaner than patching things by hand and works well when an experiment becomes real work.

Remove stuff you no longer want

When the stack looks like a thrift store clear what you do not need.

  • Drop a single stash: 
    git stash drop stash@{1}
  • Wipe the entire stash list: 
    git stash clear

Be careful with clear unless obliteration is your idea of housekeeping.

Quick workflow tips and developer tricks

  • Prefer git stash branch when the changes need isolated development rather than applying into a messy workspace.
  • Use short messages that say what problem you were solving so you do not have to open a time machine later.
  • Stash is great for switching context fast but do not use it as permanent storage. Commit when the work is real.

Recap

Git stash lets you save uncommitted changes, list entries, reapply with apply or pop, create a branch from a stash, and delete stashes when they are no longer useful. It keeps your workflow flexible and saves you from the classic broken build panic. Use it wisely and with tiny amounts of dignity.
seo_title: Master Git Stash to Save Uncommitted Changes and Switch Branches
seo_heading: Practical git stash workflow to keep uncommitted changes safe and tidy

title: Rename a Git Branch
description: Quick guide to rename a Git branch locally and update the remote with safe commands and practical tips.
heading: Rename a Git Branch safely and quickly
body:
Renaming a Git branch is the kind of small maintenance task that can turn into a surprise party for your CI and teammates if you do it wrong. Do it right and it is quick, tidy, and rarely dramatic. This guide shows a safe sequence for renaming a branch locally and on the remote while keeping upstream tracking and history intact.

What you are trying to do

Goal is simple. Rename the branch on your laptop, push the new name to the remote, tell your local branch which remote branch to track, remove the old remote name so no one gets confused, and prune any stale references. If a pull request exists keep it open and update the branch reference on your hosting service when possible.

Rename the local branch

If you are checked out on the branch use this command to rename it on your machine

git branch -m new-name

If you are not on that branch run this instead

git branch -m old-name new-name

Both variants are safe and simple. The local branch name changes without rewriting commits or history.

Push the new branch to the remote

Send the fresh name to the remote repository so others can see it and CI can find it

git push origin new-name

If you get a rejection because the remote already has a branch with that name you will need to coordinate with whoever created it or choose another name. Do not force push unless you know exactly what you are doing.

Set upstream tracking for the new branch

Tell Git which remote branch your local branch should push and pull from

git push --set-upstream origin new-name

After this push and pull behave normally with no extra flags.

Delete the old branch name from the remote

Once the new branch exists on the remote remove the old name to avoid stale references and confusion

git push --delete origin old-name

Only delete the old remote when you are sure no one still needs it. If you are on a team mention the rename in your usual channel to avoid surprise breakage in open work.

Prune stale references and tidy local repos

Clean up any leftover refs in your local clone

git fetch -p

This prunes deleted remote branches from your local remote tracking namespace and keeps listings honest. Ask teammates to run the same command or to perform a fresh fetch if they see odd behavior.

Troubleshooting and common gotchas

  • If you renamed a branch that has an open pull request check the hosting service UI to see if the PR preserves history or if it needs the branch field updated.
  • If CI fails after the rename double check branch filters and webhooks on your CI provider.
  • If you accidentally pushed the new name before coordinating with the team you can recreate the old name from new-name and push it back while you fix the mess.

Quick checklist

  1. Rename local branch with git branch -m
  2. Push new-name to origin
  3. Set upstream with git push --set-upstream origin new-name
  4. Delete old remote branch with git push --delete origin old-name
  5. Run git fetch -p and tell your team about the rename

Tip Use clear descriptive branch names and announce renames in your team channel. If a pull request exists try to keep the PR open and update the branch reference on your hosting service when possible so you do not lose discussion or CI history.
seo_title: Rename your Git branch without breaking your team's flow
seo_heading: Step by step branch rename in Git with remote updates and cleanup

title: How to download and install Git
description: Quick guide to downloading installing and configuring Git on Windows macOS and Linux with verification commands
heading: How to download and install Git on Windows macOS and Linux
body:
This tutorial shows how to download and install Git on Windows macOS and Linux and perform basic configuration and verification so version control starts behaving.

  1. Choose the correct installer for the operating system
  2. Run the installer or use the package manager
  3. Configure global user name and email
  4. Verify installation with simple commands
  5. Optional pick a GUI or enable shell integration

Choose the correct installer by visiting the official Git website or by using a trusted package manager. Windows users will likely want the Git for Windows package. macOS users can get Git from Homebrew using brew install git if convenience wins. Linux users should prefer the distribution package manager for stable integration.

Run the installer and follow prompts. Windows installers will offer options for the default editor and PATH behavior. Accepting sensible defaults usually avoids confusion. For macOS the installer package will guide the process. Linux commands such as sudo apt update && sudo apt install git provide a fast route on Debian based systems.

Configure Git identity with two global commands so commits carry a name and contact. Use git config --global user.name "Your Name" and git config --global user.email "your_email@example.com". These commands prevent anonymous commit drama and keep contribution history tidy.

Verify installation by running git --version in a terminal or command prompt. Initialize a test repository with git init then check status with git status to confirm basic functionality. If the version command returns a number then Git is present and ready.

Optional choices include using a graphical client for a gentler learning curve or enabling shell integration for nicer prompts and credential helpers. GUI options like GitHub Desktop or other clients are available for those who prefer point and click over command line poetry.

This guide covered downloading running the installer or package manager configuring user identity and verifying that Git works on major desktop platforms so a developer can start tracking code with confidence.

Tip

Use an SSH key for painless authentication. Generate a key with ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com" and add the public key to the code hosting profile to avoid repeated password prompts.

title: Git Log Graph Tree Command
description: Quick guide to using git log graph tree command to visualize commit history as a branch shaped graph on the command line
heading: Git Log Graph Tree Command explained
body:
This tutorial shows how to use the git log graph tree command to visualize commit history on the command line.

  1. Run a basic graph
  2. Make output compact and readable
  3. Include all refs and branches
  4. Customize the format for clarity

Run a basic graph

Use a simple command to get the ASCII graph view of commit history. This gives a quick branch map that saves several furious guesses.

git log --graph --oneline

Make output compact and readable

Add decoration and one line formatting to see branch names tags and short messages without scrolling forever.

git log --graph --oneline --decorate

Include all refs and branches

Show remote branches and all refs when curiosity about non local branches is required. This avoids missing that ghost commit.

git log --graph --oneline --decorate --all --branches --remotes

Customize the format for clarity

Use a pretty format to color hash and author and show relative time for quick scanning. Colors may look fancy but developers actually use the extra context.

git log --graph --pretty=format="%C(yellow)%h %Creset%s %C(green)(%cr) %C(bold blue)<%an>" --all

Replace the format string with fields that match personal taste. Shorter hashes and concise messages tend to work best when reviewing a messy merge history.

This tutorial covered how to produce a branch shaped visual of commit history how to compact output how to include all refs and how to customize display for faster reasoning about changes. The commands shown make the command line feel less like a punishment and more like a useful map.

Tip

Pipe the output through a pager with line numbers for copy pasting commit hashes to other tools. Example use of a pager makes sharing a specific commit faster and reduces the chance of selecting the wrong hash.

title: Rename Master Branch to Main on GitHub
description: Quick guide to rename master branch to main on GitHub with steps to update local clones CI and collaborators
heading: Rename Master Branch to Main on GitHub Guide
body:
This tutorial shows how to rename the master branch to main on GitHub while updating remote settings and local clones.

  1. Rename default branch on GitHub
  2. Update branch protection rules and settings
  3. Update local clones and set new upstream
  4. Update CI and deployment references
  5. Notify collaborators and clean up old branch

Step 1 Use the repository settings on GitHub to change the default branch from master to main. For command line lovers run gh repo edit --default-branch main to set the new default.

Step 2 Review branch protection rules and update any rules that referenced master. Confirm required status checks and required reviewers now apply to the main branch name.

Step 3 On each developer machine run git fetch origin then git branch -m master main then git checkout main and git push -u origin main. Optionally remove the old remote branch with git push origin --delete master. Those commands keep local history and set the proper upstream.

Step 4 Search CI configuration files deployment scripts and automation for references to master and update to main. Remember that YAML pipeline files and environment settings often contain branch names that block deployment.

Step 5 Tell the team what changed and provide the commands above. A short message prevents confusion and avoids the classic blame game about missing commits.

Renaming master to main on GitHub is mostly a configuration and communication task. Change the default branch on GitHub update protections update local clones push the new branch update CI references and inform collaborators to avoid surprises.

Tip

Run a grep or the repository search for master before and after the rename to catch hidden references in docs CI and scripts. A quick check saves debugging time and awkward deploy failures.

title: Change Git Branch Master to Main Locally and Remotely
description: Quick guide to rename a Git branch from master to main on local repo and on remote including commands cleanup and tips
heading: Change Git Branch Master to Main Locally and Remotely
body:
Why move master to main now

You want to rename the primary branch in Git from master to main and not set off a chain reaction of failed builds, confused teammates, and angry deploys. Good news, this is mostly administrative surgery and not dark magic. The commands are short and predictable, and I will walk you through them with minimal moralizing and a healthy dose of sarcasm.

Rename the local branch

Do this while you have no uncommitted chaos. The local rename is just a pointer update and it keeps your working tree intact.

git branch -m master main

If you were on master this moves you to main and renames the branch. If you had local work, nothing spooky happens. If you were not on master, run the same command to rename the branch name only.

Push the new branch and set upstream

Make sure the remote knows about main and that your local main is linked to it for future pushes and pulls.

git push -u origin main

This creates origin/main and sets your local main to track it, so you can git push and git pull like a civilized developer.

Remove the old remote branch

Leaving origin/master around only serves to confuse humans and tooling. Remove it from the server once main exists.

git push origin --delete master

Yes this is permanent on the remote unless you have backups. If your CI or CI history depends on origin/master, update those first.

Update the remote head and hosting default branch

Tell your remote what the default branch is so web views and clones point to the right place. The following syncs the remote head.

git remote set-head origin -a

After that change the default branch setting on your hosting provider like GitHub or GitLab using the web UI. This cannot be done purely from local Git in all hosts, so open the project settings and select main as default. Doing this avoids surprises when people open the project page or create new clones.

Refresh other clones and CI settings

Other developers and CI agents need a quick update so they do not accidentally recreate master. Share these exact steps.

git fetch origin
git branch -u origin/main main
git remote set-head origin -a

If someone still has a local master branch they can either delete it with

git branch -d master

or rebase their work onto main if they have unmerged changes.

Search for hard coded references

Grepping for master is your friend. Update CI files, deploy scripts, documentation, and automation that mention master by name. The exact command depends on your tools, but a simple repo wide search will find most of them.

Quick checklist before you celebrate

  • Rename local branch with git branch -m master main
  • Push new branch and set upstream with git push -u origin main
  • Delete origin master with git push origin --delete master
  • Run git remote set-head origin -a and change default branch in the host UI
  • Update CI, deploy scripts, submodules, and documentation that mention master
  • Tell teammates to git fetch and remove or rebase local master

Parting words

This process is short and reversible if you think ahead. The biggest risks are outdated CI, missed references, or sleepy teammates. Communicate the change, run a quick search for references to master, and be ready to help anyone who clings to the old name like a nostalgic relic. The result is a cleaner repo and fewer confusing defaults for new contributors.
seo_title: Rename master to main in Git without breaking remotes
seo_heading: Step by step guide to renaming master to main and updating remotes

title: GitHub Personal Access Token How To Create Use
description: Step by step guide to create and use GitHub personal access tokens with fine grained permissions for secure automation and API access
heading: GitHub Personal Access Token How To Create Use
body:
Why use a fine grained PAT

Personal access tokens let automation act on your behalf without handing over your whole account. Fine grained PATs let you pick which repositories and permissions matter so your CI runs like a well behaved guest instead of a wrecking ball.

How to create a fine grained token

Step one Log into GitHub then click your avatar then Settings then Developer settings. Under Developer settings pick Personal access tokens and choose Fine grained token. Yes the menu is nested like an onion and you will cry for security reasons.

Step two Select the exact repositories or organizations the automation needs. Assign the minimum permissions required. If you are tempted to grant everything imagine explaining that to your future self.

Step three Set an expiration that matches the automation lifespan. Short lived tokens mean less cleanup after something inevitably goes sideways.

Step four Generate the token and copy it immediately. GitHub shows the secret once and then hides it forever. Store that string in a vault instead of a sticky note stuck to your monitor.

How to store and use the token

Do not commit tokens to git. That is not a negotiation. Use a secrets manager or an encrypted vault for storage.

  • Local use Set the token in an environment variable like export GITHUB_TOKEN=your_token_here or configure a git credential helper so your credentials stop shouting at the terminal.
  • CI systems Add the token to your pipeline secrets and reference the secret in workflow configuration. That keeps tokens out of logs and out of human error territory.
  • API calls Use the token for authentication when calling the GitHub API. Most SDKs and HTTP clients accept a token parameter so follow your client docs for authentication details.

Classic tokens versus fine grained tokens

Classic tokens still exist for legacy tools but fine grained tokens offer safer, repo level control. If a tool does not support fine grained tokens consider a service account or a dedicated machine user with tight permissions.

Best practices for PAT security

  • Rotate tokens regularly so an old secret does not haunt you.
  • Grant the least privilege needed for the task.
  • Use expirations and automate rotation when possible.
  • Audit token usage and revoke anything unused or suspicious.

Quick recap

Create a fine grained PAT in Developer settings. Scope it to the minimum repositories and permissions. Set a short expiration and stash the token in a secrets manager. Use environment variables or credential helpers for local work and CI secrets for pipelines. Repeat these steps like a ritual and sleep a little easier.
seo_title: Set Up a Fine Grained GitHub PAT for Secure Automation Today
seo_heading: Quick guide to GitHub personal access tokens with fine grained scopes for CI

title: Change the Remote Git URL with Set Remote Origin
description: Quick guide to change a Git remote URL using git remote set-url origin and verify the change with git remote -v
heading: Change the Remote Git URL with Set Remote Origin Guide
body:
If your repository is gossiping with the wrong server it is time to update the origin and regain control. This concise git tutorial walks through inspecting the current git remote, using git remote set-url origin to update the remote url, and verifying connectivity with fetch and push tests. No drama required but a little sarcasm is included free of charge.

Check what your repo is currently talking to

First, confirm the current remote url so you do not overwrite something important by accident. In your CLI run

git remote -v

The output shows names like origin and their fetch and push urls. This is your safety check. If you see an address you do not expect then pause and breathe before changing anything.

Set the new remote url

To update the origin use the set url command with either an SSH or HTTPS address. Replace the example url with your actual repository address.

  • SSH example
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:username/repo.git
  • HTTPS example
git remote set-url origin https://github.com/username/repo.git

If you are switching protocols remember to update credentials or SSH keys to avoid authentication surprises. If your project uses a different remote name then replace origin with that name.

Verify the change

Run git remote -v again to confirm the origin url matches your intended address. If it does not look right double check for typos and the correct protocol.

Test connectivity without committing to a push

Before pushing actual work run a fetch or a dry run push to confirm permissions and network access.

  • Fetch to see if the remote responds
git fetch origin
  • Dry run push to check authentication and refs
git push --dry-run origin your-branch-name

If fetch succeeds you have basic connectivity. If the dry run reports the ref updates you will be able to push for real without a surprise outage.

Troubleshooting checklist

  • If git prompts repeatedly for credentials consider enabling credential caching on your OS or using a credential helper
  • If you switched to SSH but get permission denied then ensure your public key is added to the remote server and your agent is running
  • If the url looks wrong copy it straight from the remote host web UI to avoid subtle typos
  • If you have multiple remotes or submodules verify each one as needed

Recap and quick commands

In short follow these steps to change a remote url in git and verify it works

  1. Inspect current remote with git remote -v
  2. Set the new url with git remote set-url origin <new_repo_url>
  3. Verify with git remote -v and test with git fetch or git push --dry-run

This keeps your version control tidy and your push privileges intact. If Git keeps nagging about passwords consider switching to SSH keys for fewer prompts and less grumbling. Now go update that origin and pretend you meant to do it all along.

title: Java Constructors Tutorial
description: Learn Java constructors with clear guidance on default constructors parameterized constructors and constructor chaining for better object creation
heading: Java Constructors Tutorial Explained for Beginners
body:
Why constructors matter in Java

Constructors are the tiny dictators that set initial state for your objects. Get them right and your code behaves like a civil society. Get them wrong and you spend the afternoon debugging nulls as if they were a personality defect. This guide covers default constructors, parameterized constructors, constructor chaining, overloading, and access control so your objects start life with dignity.

What a constructor actually is

A constructor is a special method whose name matches the class and that does not declare a return type. Its job is simple and sacred initialize fields and enforce any invariants the class expects before the object is handed out to the rest of the program.

Default constructor rules

If you write no constructors the Java compiler gives you a no argument default constructor for free. If you add any constructor the free one disappears and you get to decide what default state looks like. That is where explicit default constructors earn their keep.

public class Person {
    private String name;
    private int age;

    public Person() {
        this.name = "unknown";
        this.age = 0;
    }
}

Use a custom default constructor when you need sane defaults or when other constructors are present and you still want a zero argument creation path.

Parameterized constructors and final fields

Parameterized constructors accept values at creation time so the object starts life complete. Prefer clear parameter names and assign final fields when those values should never change after construction. Final fields make your classes safer and your future self happier.

public class Config {
    private final String host;
    private final int port;

    public Config(String host, int port) {
        this.host = host;
        this.port = port;
    }
}

Best practice

  • Validate inputs in the constructor to avoid broken objects.
  • Keep constructors focused on initialization not heavy logic.
  • Use final for fields that should not change after creation.

Constructor chaining with this()

Constructor chaining means calling one constructor from another using this parentheses. It reduces duplication and keeps initialization paths consistent. Yes it is slightly less magical than a spell but much more maintainable.

public class Box {
    private int width;
    private int height;
    private int depth;

    public Box() {
        this(1, 1, 1); // sensible tiny box
    }

    public Box(int size) {
        this(size, size, size);
    }

    public Box(int width, int height, int depth) {
        this.width = width;
        this.height = height;
        this.depth = depth;
    }
}

Call this only as the first statement in a constructor. Use it to centralize validation and defaulting logic in the most general constructor.

Overloading and access control

Offer multiple constructor signatures to support different creation scenarios. Keep the core initialization logic in a single place and have other constructors delegate to it. Use access modifiers to control who can construct what. A private constructor is a polite way to say you want to manage creation with a factory or a builder.

public class Connection {
    private String url;
    private int timeout;

    private Connection(String url, int timeout) {
        this.url = url;
        this.timeout = timeout;
    }

    public static Connection createDefault() {
        return new Connection("http example com", 5000);
    }
}

Factories and builders are your friends when construction gets complex. They keep constructors simple and move optional parameters out of the constructor signature.

When to use a builder

  • Many optional parameters that would bloat constructors
  • Immutable objects with many configuration options
  • Fluent, readable creation syntax is important

Quick checklist for healthier constructors

  • Give objects sane defaults or provide explicit constructors
  • Prefer final fields for required state
  • Use this chaining to reduce repeated code
  • Validate inputs early to avoid fragile objects
  • Use access control, factories, or builders for complex creation

Constructors are boring to write but invaluable to get right. Treat them like the bouncers at the club of your class keep the riffraff out and let only valid state through. Do that and your Java beginners will thank you later when bugs are mercifully absent.
seo_title: Master Java object creation with smart constructors and chaining
seo_heading: How to write clear default and parameterized constructors in Java

title: Complete Java Records Tutorial
description: Compact guide to Java records covering syntax constructors validation and use cases for immutable data classes
heading: Complete Java Records Tutorial Guide
body:
This tutorial teaches how Java records provide compact syntax for immutable data carriers and how to use records in real code.

  1. Define a record
  2. Use constructors and compact constructors
  3. Accessors equals hashCode and toString
  4. Add validation and custom methods
  5. Use pattern matching and deconstruction

Define a record

Declare a record with the record keyword and a component list. Example record Point(int x, int y). That declaration creates a canonical constructor and component accessors without boilerplate code.

Constructors

Use the canonical constructor when parameter types need to be explicit. Use a compact constructor to validate or normalize parameters without repeating types. Example compact form record Person(String name, int age) { Person { if(age < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("age must be positive") } }

Accessors and generated methods

Each component gets a public accessor named after the component. Generated equals and hashCode follow component order. Generated toString is concise and useful for debugging.

Validation and custom behavior

Records accept additional methods and static factories. Add validation in a compact constructor or add helper methods for derived values. Avoid adding mutable fields in a record design aimed at immutability.

Pattern matching and deconstruction

Records work well with pattern matching by structure. Use the accessor names when deconstructing values in switch expressions and pattern contexts for clearer code.

Summary paragraph that recaps the tutorial content and practical benefits of adopting records for simple domain models. Records reduce boilerplate generate sensible methods and encourage immutable design while allowing customization when needed.

Tip

Prefer records for simple data carriers that represent state without mutation. When validation or complex invariants are required use a compact constructor or static factory and keep business logic in separate classes.

title: Java Tic Tac Toe Game Tutorial
description: Step by step Java Tic Tac Toe guide covering game logic GUI event handling and win detection for a playable console or Swing version
heading: Java Tic Tac Toe Game Tutorial Build a Playable Version in Java
body:
If you want a Tic Tac Toe program that does not feel like a one night coding regret then this guide will get you there. You will use Java and solid OOP to build a board model game controller and a simple UI. Along the way you will add basic AI win detection and event handling so the program actually behaves like a game and not a random number generator with feelings.

Plan the board and the rules

Start with a clear mental picture of the 3 by 3 grid. Represent the board with a two dimensional array or a single array of nine cells. Define constants or an enum for EMPTY X and O so you never have to guess what a magic integer was supposed to mean when you read your code at 3 am.

Model classes to keep the mess tidy

Separate concerns. Make a Board class that stores cell state and checks for wins. Make a Player class that holds marker type and move logic. Make a GameController class that validates moves enforces turns and coordinates game flow so UI code can stay gloriously simple.

Move handling and win detection

When a player attempts a move validate the coordinates check the cell is empty and then apply the move. After each successful move scan rows columns and both diagonals to detect three in a row. If no moves remain declare a draw. Keep the logic small and testable so debugging does not feel like punishment.

Win detection checklist

  • Check each row for identical non empty markers
  • Check each column for identical non empty markers
  • Check the two diagonals for identical non empty markers
  • Track move count to determine a draw

Build a user interface that does not lie to you

Choose console prompts for the fast route or Swing for a simple GUI. For a Swing UI use a grid of JButtons and attach ActionListener instances that call methods on the GameController. Update button labels and enable states based on the model state and avoid putting model logic in your UI classes. That is how you keep event handling simple and testable.

Console game tips

Print the board after every move ask for row and column input validate the input and then call the same controller methods you would from the Swing interface. This lets you reuse core game logic between the two front ends.

Add an AI opponent without selling your soul

Start with random moves to get something playable. Then graduate to a minimax strategy to make the opponent competent. Minimax is a recursive search that evaluates terminal positions as win loss or draw and chooses moves that maximize the AI outcome while assuming the human plays optimally. Implementing minimax on a 3 by 3 board is small enough to finish before you lose interest.

AI implementation notes

  • Random AI is fine for quick testing
  • Minimax will make the AI unbeatable if implemented correctly
  • Prune or add memoization if you want to be fancy but it is optional for this scale

Testing and packaging

Write unit tests for move validation and win detection using JUnit. Test edge cases like attempts to play off the board and attempts to play on occupied cells. Unit tests save you from future embarrassment when a minor refactor breaks the rules.

Finally package the app as a jar for the console version or include the Swing UI classes for distribution. Add a simple README explaining how to run the console game and how to launch the Swing window.

Final thoughts

This project is a perfect playground for OOP event handling and AI basics in Java. You get a clean Board class clear win detection and a GameController that keeps the UI honest. Build the console game first then wire up Swing once the core logic is stable. After you finish you will have a compact Tic Tac Toe program that demonstrates design principles and actually beats at least some humans.

So you want a MySQL database that behaves long enough to do real work. Good choice. This guide walks you through a no-nonsense MySQL install and basic configuration on Windows macOS and Linux with just enough snark to keep you awake. Follow along to download packages start the server create a test database and run basic hardening with mysql_secure_installation.

Download and install MySQL

Pick your platform and follow the command that looks least like sorcery. Use official packages for stability and package managers for efficiency.

Windows

Grab the MySQL Installer from the official site and run the wizard. Choose a developer or production profile depending on whether you want a playground or something that will actually be maintained.

macOS

Homebrew fans use this single line and then go make coffee while the system does the work.

brew install mysql

Linux

On Debian based systems run these commands as a user with sudo privileges.

sudo apt update
sudo apt install mysql-server

Configure root user and authentication

During setup pick a strong password for the root account. Prefer native password authentication for compatibility with most client tools. If this is just for testing in an isolated VM you can relax rules temporarily but do not do that on a network facing host.

  • Avoid weak passwords unless you enjoy surprises
  • Choose authentication that matches your client libraries
  • Document the credentials so you do not lock yourself out three days later

Start the MySQL service

Use the system service manager that matches your OS. If you installed with a package manager the service usually registers itself automatically.

  • systemd systems run
sudo systemctl start mysql
  • On macOS with Homebrew use
brew services start mysql

Test connection and create a sample database

Make sure the server is actually listening and that credentials work. Use the mysql client and create a tiny database and table to confirm read write and privilege behavior.

mysql -u root -p
CREATE DATABASE test_db;
USE test_db;
CREATE TABLE users (id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100));
INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES ('Alice');
SELECT * FROM users;

If those commands run without existential despair you have a working MySQL database ready for development or light production use.

Secure the installation with mysql_secure_installation

This script is your friend. Run mysql_secure_installation to remove anonymous users disallow remote root login and drop test databases. It is the small amount of work that prevents large amounts of regret.

sudo mysql_secure_installation

Follow the prompts to set or confirm the root password and to remove risky defaults. If you answer yes to the sensible options you will lock down the server enough for most simple deployments.

Notes on common pitfalls and tips

  • If a client library complains about authentication try switching to native password plugin for compatibility
  • Remember to open necessary ports in your firewall only if you intend remote connections
  • Keep backups and test restores because the person who forgot backups is always very confident until the data disappears

That covers the essentials of MySQL install database setup and basic MySQL configuration for beginners. You now have a running SQL server a sample database and the basic hardening steps in place. Go build something useful and try not to put production secrets in a file named password.txt on your desktop.

title: SOLID Liskov Substitution Principle
description: Clear explanation of Liskov Substitution Principle with example failures and practical fixes for robust object oriented design and cleaner inheritance.
heading: SOLID Liskov Substitution Principle Explained
body:
Liskov Substitution Principle states that objects of a superclass must be replaceable with objects of a subclass without changing program correctness.

When a subclass breaks expectations calling code sees surprises. That leads to bugs test failures and unhappy developers. The principle protects contracts between types so polymorphism behaves like a promise not a prank.

Classic failure example

class Bird method fly return "flying" end class Penguin extends Bird method fly raise CannotFlyException end

This pattern shows a subclass that violates a base class contract by refusing a capability that callers expect. Forcing a penguin to inherit a flight feature is a design smell that will make maintenance painful.

How to fix

Prefer abstractions that express behavior rather than concrete species. Split interfaces for flying and non flying roles. Use composition when a role cannot be shared across all subclasses.

  1. Keep method contracts stable across the hierarchy
  2. Do not strengthen preconditions in subclasses
  3. Do not weaken postconditions in subclasses
  4. Write tests that verify the base class contract against subclasses

Applying these practices keeps hierarchies predictable and code easier to refactor. A good hierarchy promises behavior and then keeps the promise. The Liskov rule saves time and reduces surprises by aligning design with real capabilities rather than hopeful inheritance.

Tip

Design by behavior not by concrete class. If a subclass cannot honor the base class contract create a new abstraction or use composition. Add contract tests that run against the base type to catch violations early.

title: SOLID Liskov Substitution Principle Explained?
description: Clear guide to the Liskov Substitution Principle in SOLID with examples and practical rules for safer object oriented design and fewer surprises.
heading: SOLID Liskov Substitution Principle Explained
body:
What Liskov actually wants from your objects

The Liskov Substitution Principle lives in the SOLID family and pretends to be polite. In plain terms it says a subtype must behave like the base type so client code does not get existential dread. If you swap in a subclass and things explode or produce surprising results then congratulations you found an LSP violation.

Three short rules to save future you

  • Do not strengthen preconditions for a subtype
  • Do not weaken postconditions for a subtype
  • Preserve invariants set by the base type

Those are the behavioral contracts that matter more than matching method names. Method signatures alone are like a costume without the manners. Polymorphism and subtyping are built on promises not on syntax.

Classic example that still ruins interviews

The rectangle and square story is boring but useful. A Rectangle has setWidth and setHeight. A Square inherits and forces width and height to match. Client code that expects independent setters sees broken behavior. That is the textbook LSP fail and it smells like bad inheritance.

class Rectangle
  width
  height
  setWidth(w)
  setHeight(h)

class Square extends Rectangle
  setWidth(w)
    set both width and height to w
  setHeight(h)
    set both width and height to h

Design moves that calm the chaos

If your subtype cannot accept the same inputs or guarantee the same outcomes then stop and rethink. Here are practical strategies that actually work in real OOP code.

  • Prefer composition over inheritance when behavior differs. Composition lets you reuse code without lying about contracts.
  • Program to interfaces that declare behavior not implementation. Interfaces make expectations explicit and keep subtyping honest.
  • Keep behavioral tests that exercise lists of base type instances with subclass objects. Those tests are boring and they save lives on Fridays.

How to test substitution without drama

Write substitution tests that run the same scenarios against base type objects and subclass objects. If outcomes vary then you either have a bug or a bad inheritance decision. Example checks include inputs accepted, outputs produced, and invariants maintained across operations.

Quick checklist before you inherit

  • Does the subtype accept the same inputs under the same conditions
  • Does it guarantee the same results and side effects
  • Does it preserve the base type invariants

Why this matters for clean architecture

Following LSP leads to fewer runtime surprises and clearer contracts. That means easier refactoring and components that actually play nicely together in your clean architecture. It also cuts down on the kind of code smells that creep in when inheritance is used as a lazy shortcut.

In short if your subclass is lying about what it can do prefer composition or pick a different abstraction. Your future self will thank you and your stack traces will be less dramatic.
seo_title: Stop Inheritance From Breaking Your Code With Liskov Principle
seo_heading: Practical LSP checks for OOP design that prevent nasty code smells

Before you start

It covers the installer the Java runtime and the basic workflow for creating and running a Spring Boot app.

Step 1 Download the STS installer

Choose the Spring Tools distribution that matches your preferred editor. For the full Eclipse experience pick the STS package. If you use IntelliJ or VSCode grab the matching extensions from their marketplaces. The downloads page usually offers platform bundles so pick Windows Mac or Linux based on your machine and your desire to feel productive.

Step 2 Pick a compatible Java runtime

Use a supported JDK such as Java 17 or Java 21 depending on your project needs. Mismatched runtime versions are the most common source of avoidable headaches. Set your JAVA_HOME and make sure the IDE preferences point at the same JDK you plan to use at runtime.

Step 3 Run the installer and choose workspace and features

Launch the installer and accept the license like an adult. Pick a workspace folder that you have write permissions for and avoid system directories that will make life miserable. If the installer lets you add Spring related plugins take the ones you need and skip the novelty extras. Restart when asked because the computer is not psychic.

Step 4 Integrate Spring support into Eclipse IntelliJ or VSCode

Each editor has its own sweet spot for Spring support.

  • For Eclipse use the STS plugins from the Eclipse marketplace. They bring starter wizards and live tooling for Spring projects.
  • For IntelliJ rely on the built in Spring features or add the Spring Assistant plugin if you prefer extra hand holding.
  • For VSCode install the Spring Boot extension pack from the extensions view. It gives quick project creation and debugger hooks.

After installing extensions restart the IDE and confirm the Spring menus and wizards appear. If they do not show up try reloading the window or checking the plugin installation log.

Step 5 Create a Spring Boot project and run the app

Use the New Spring Starter Project wizard in your IDE and pick sensible dependencies like web and data. Generate the project and import it into the IDE workspace. You can run the application from the IDE run configuration or build and run it with your build tool. Using the IDE run button is the fast path for development.

Common troubleshooting

  • JDK mismatch. Verify the JDK configured in IDE preferences matches the JDK you use to run the app.
  • Plugin oddness. Clear workspace caches or reload the IDE if plugin updates behave oddly.
  • Dependency failures. Check your build file and update versions or refresh the project dependencies.
  • Permissions and paths. Make sure your workspace has write access and that long path names are not sabotaging you on Windows.

Wrap up tip: if the IDE still refuses to behave uninstall and reinstall only after you have cooled down. STS 2024 works well with modern JDKs and the main effort is matching runtimes and installing the right extensions for Eclipse IntelliJ or VSCode. Now go make a SpringBoot app and try not to break production on day one.

title: Advanced Spring Boot Restful APIs Tutorial Build Web App
description: Learn to build advanced Spring Boot RESTful APIs covering controllers services repositories DTO mapping error handling testing and security for a full web
heading: Advanced Spring Boot RESTful APIs Tutorial Build Web App
body:
Welcome to the pragmatic Spring Boot crash course

If you want a REST API that does not self combust in production then you are in the right place. This guide walks through a sane workflow for Spring Boot projects while throwing in real world tips and a dash of sarcasm. We cover project setup, data access with Spring Data JPA, DTO mapping, Controllers and Services, exception handling, testing and deployment. No useless bells and whistles unless they actually help you ship code.

Project setup and dependencies

Start with Spring Initializr or a Maven setup that will make your future self grateful. Add Spring Web, Spring Data JPA, Lombok if you like fewer getters, Spring Security, and either H2 for local experiments or PostgreSQL for pretending your app is serious. Dependency management saves you hours of dependency hell and invites fewer midnight debugging sessions.

Suggested starter stack

  • spring-boot-starter-web for Controllers and REST handling
  • spring-boot-starter-data-jpa for repositories and ORM
  • Lombok to reduce boilerplate if your team agrees to it
  • spring-boot-starter-security for auth and authorization
  • H2 for quick local runs and PostgreSQL for production

Domain model and data access

Define JPA entities that mirror your business domain and keep relationships meaningful. Use indexes for queries you actually run. Repositories in Spring Data JPA let you focus on queries not setup. Avoid leaking your entities to the outside world unless you enjoy breaking clients when you refactor.

DTOs and mapping

DTOs protect your database schema from curious API consumers and give you a stable contract for clients. Map DTOs to entities in the service layer. You can use MapStruct or manual mapping. MapStruct gives compile time safety and fewer mapping bugs. Manual mapping is fine for tiny projects or people who enjoy typing.

Service layer and business logic

Put business rules in services so controllers stay thin and readable. Services handle transactions and reduce duplication. Throw well typed exceptions when business rules fail so your exception handling can translate them into clear API responses.

Controllers and request handling

Use REST controllers to map DTOs to domain objects and return proper HTTP status codes. Use @RequestMapping and @Valid on incoming payloads to keep routing predictable and validation automatic. Keep controllers focused on request and response logic and delegate work to services.

Validation and centralized exception handling

Add a @ControllerAdvice to centralize exception handling and convert exceptions into consistent API error responses. Provide meaningful HTTP status codes and error messages that help clients and do not leak secrets. Validation failures should map to 400 level responses with field level details when possible.

Testing strategies

Write unit tests for services and controller slices. Add integration tests that exercise the full web layer. Use MockMvc or TestRestTemplate for integration tests so regressions are caught before CI yells. Tests are not optional if you want to sleep at night.

What to test

  • Service logic and edge cases
  • Controller request validation and response codes
  • Integration flows with MockMvc or TestRestTemplate
  • Security rules to ensure endpoints are protected

Security and auth

Secure endpoints with Spring Security using JWT for stateless APIs or session based auth if that matches your architecture. Configure CORS and role based authorization to match your client needs. Remember security is not a checkbox, it is ongoing maintenance and occasional screaming.

Packaging and deployment

Package as an executable jar or containerize with Docker and run on a cloud provider or a humble VM that everyone forgets about. Add health checks and externalize configuration with Spring profiles and environment variables. Automate builds and deploys so your deployment pipeline does not depend on ritual sacrifices.

Final thoughts

Follow this flow from project creation through validation, error mapping, testing and security and you will end up with a REST API that teams can maintain without losing all hope. Keep controllers lean, services authoritative, DTOs stable, and tests comprehensive. Repeat until your CI pipeline stops screaming and you can actually enjoy feature work again.
