title: The difference between Controller vs RestController in Sprin
description: Quick guide to Controller versus RestController in Spring with examples and clear rules for choosing the right annotation for views or APIs
heading: Controller vs RestController in Spring explained
body:
The key difference between Controller and RestController in Spring is that Controller returns view names by default while RestController returns response bodies as JSON or text by default.

Controller is the classic choice for server side rendered pages. Methods typically return a view name such as return 'index' and the view resolver picks a template such as Thymeleaf. When a JSON response is needed on a single method the developer can add @ResponseBody on that method and Spring will convert the return value using message converters.

RestController is a convenience wrapper that combines @Controller and @ResponseBody so every handler method returns a response body by default. That behavior makes the annotation ideal for REST APIs single page application backends and any scenario where JSON or plain text is the primary product.

Both annotations play nicely with content negotiation request mappings and response status handling. Spring chooses a message converter based on the return type and accepted media types. If a method returns an object Spring will serialize to JSON or XML when a matching converter exists.

If mixing view rendering and API endpoints in the same controller feels tempting the better practice is separation. Use one controller for templates and another RestController for API responses. That approach reduces accidental surprises and keeps request handling predictable.

For a quick rule of thumb choose Controller when rendering templates and choose RestController when building API endpoints. The annotation choice saves a lot of boilerplate and prevents missing @ResponseBody mistakes that lead to baffling errors.

Tip

When migrating a controller to an API first check for methods returning view names. Add a new RestController for JSON endpoints or apply @ResponseBody only to specific methods to avoid breaking existing templates.

title: Spring Boot H2 Console JDBC URL for Embedded H2 Databases an
description: Configure the Spring Boot H2 console JDBC URL for embedded H2 databases and DataSource setups with clear examples and tips
heading: Spring Boot H2 Console JDBC URL for Embedded H2 Databases and DataSources Configuration
body:
Overview

If you want to stare at a friendly web UI while your in memory database quietly judges your SQL, the H2 console is your friend. This guide shows how to enable the Spring Boot H2 console and how to pick the correct JDBC URL for embedded H2 and for DataSource based setups. The goal is to stop the classic cannot connect drama and get you back to writing questionable queries.

Enable the console

First rule of H2 club is do not forget to turn the console on. Add this to your application properties so Spring Boot will actually expose the web UI during development.

spring.h2.console.enabled=true
spring.h2.console.path=/h2-console

If you omit those lines nothing will show up and the console will sulk silently.

Set up DataSource properties

Tell Spring Boot what database to connect to. For simple apps or tests use an embedded URL. For more realistic setups use a file based URL or a TCP URL for clients and pools. Example properties that are copy friendly follow.

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:mydb
spring.datasource.driver-class-name=org.h2.Driver
spring.datasource.username=sa
spring.datasource.password=

# File based development example
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:file:./data/mydb

# External TCP example for a separately running H2 server
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:tcp://localhost/~/test

Note that username sa with an empty password is the convenient default. You may want to change that before committing code, unless your goal is embarrassment.

Pick the right JDBC URL pattern

  • In memory Use jdbc:h2:mem:mydb for quick tests and demos. Data lives in the running JVM and disappears when the process ends.
  • File based Use jdbc:h2:file:./data/mydb for local dev that survives restarts. Files live on disk and are visible to other tools.
  • TCP or external Use jdbc:h2:tcp://host/~/dbname when H2 runs independently or when a connection pool expects a full network style URL.

Match URL to runtime mode

Spring Boot treats embedded URLs differently than externally provided DataSources. If your URL is jdbc:h2:mem it assumes embedded lifecycle. If you hand a container or pool a full TCP URL it assumes external lifecycle and pooling behavior. Mix those up and you get subtle failures like an empty web console or connections that refuse to appear.

Accessing the console

Open the path you configured for the console in your browser, for example http://localhost:8080/h2-console. Enter the JDBC URL and credentials that match spring.datasource properties. If the console rejects the connection check the exact URL string. A single missing prefix or wrong mode will make H2 frown.

Troubleshooting checklist

  • Is spring.h2.console.enabled set to true in the active profile
  • Does the JDBC URL match the runtime mode you want
  • Did a different profile override spring.datasource.url at startup
  • Is your security config blocking access to the console path
  • Are you using an embedded URL while the console expects a TCP server or vice versa
  • Is the driver class correct and available on the classpath

Developer tips

When in doubt start the app with debug logging and grep for the resolved JDBC URL and driver. Spring Boot merges multiple property sources and the final resolved values are what actually matter. Debug logging will show the exact URL that the DataSource ended up using and save you a bunch of wild guesses.

Also remember this is a development convenience. Do not enable the H2 console on public production endpoints unless you enjoy handing strangers an SQL prompt and a free show.

If you follow these steps you will either get the H2 console running or learn a new way to be mildly annoyed by configuration. That is growth.

seo_heading: How to configure JDBC URLs for embedded H2 and DataSource setups

title: Spring Boot Console App with CommandLineRunner

body:
This short tutorial shows how to create a Spring Boot console application that runs startup logic via CommandLineRunner and accepts command line arguments.

  1. Create a Spring Boot project
  2. Add a CommandLineRunner implementation
  3. Parse command line arguments
  4. Run and test locally
  5. Package for distribution

Step 1 Create a project using start.spring.io or an IDE. Choose Java and the Spring Boot version desired. Add no extra web framework when the goal is a console application. Maven or Gradle both work fine.

Step 2 Add a class that implements CommandLineRunner. The application class can implement the interface or a separate bean can do so. Place startup logic inside the run method so the runner executes after the Spring context is ready.

Step 3 Parse command line arguments with plain Java or use Spring Boot support for binding. For simple flags check the args array. For more complex parsing consider a library such as picocli for better ergonomics and help output.

Step 4 Run the application from an IDE or the command line. Use mvn spring-boot run or java -jar target app jar. Pass arguments to observe runtime behavior and verify that expected tasks run during startup.

Step 5 Package the application into an executable jar using Maven or Gradle. The jar can be distributed to other machines or used in CI jobs where console based tools are preferred over web services.

Example minimal class

@SpringBootApplication public class App implements CommandLineRunner { public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run(App.class, args) } @Override public void run(String... args) throws Exception { System.out.println("Hello from CommandLineRunner") } }

Summary This guide covered project setup creating a CommandLineRunner bean handling command line arguments running locally and packaging a console focused Spring Boot artifact. The process gives a clean way to run startup tasks without a web layer and plays nicely with CI and CLI workflows.

Tip

If command line parsing grows awkward adopt a dedicated parser such as picocli and register a bean that delegates work to tested services. That keeps the runner thin and test friendly.

title: Swagger UI Tutorial for REST API Developers
description: Learn Swagger UI for documenting testing and exploring REST APIs using OpenAPI to speed development and improve developer experience
heading: Swagger UI Tutorial for REST API Developers Guide
body:
If you build or maintain REST APIs you will be grateful for Swagger UI and also mildly suspicious of anything that promises magic. Swagger UI makes your OpenAPI file useful instead of just another YAML graveyard. This guide walks through the practical bits you need to document test and share APIs without losing your mind.

Why Swagger UI actually matters

Swagger UI turns an OpenAPI definition into an interactive documentation page. That means developers can read models see example requests and click a button to fire real requests from their browser. It reduces guesswork speeds onboarding and prevents the ancient ritual of reading three different READMEs to figure out one endpoint.

Create an OpenAPI spec

Write an OpenAPI 3 file in YAML or JSON that describes your paths parameters schemas responses and servers. Keep the spec in source control and treat it like tests. You can author it by hand use Swagger Editor or generate parts from annotations in your code. Whatever you do make sure schemas match reality or the UI will look like a narwhal in a penguin costume.

Serve Swagger UI

You have options depending on how much effort you want to expend. For a quick demo point a browser at the Swagger UI CDN and load your spec URL. For production or nicer integration host the Swagger UI distribution on a static server or embed it in your frontend assets. If you run Node add middleware like swagger-ui-express to serve docs alongside your API backend and avoid awkward CORS dance moves.

Load the spec into the UI

Configure Swagger UI to fetch the spec URL or embed the JSON directly in the init options. Confirm that paths parameters and models render correctly and that example values make sense. If models are missing double check references and schema names in your OpenAPI file.

Try endpoints from the UI

Use the Try It Out control to submit real requests from the browser. Provide authentication headers query parameters and request bodies to validate behavior. Inspect response payloads headers and status codes to diagnose issues quickly. This is a great shortcut for manual testing API demos and convincing teammates that the server is not trying to ruin their day.

Customize and secure the docs

Tweak theme layout and default display through the Swagger UI configuration and optional plugins. You can hide operations mark examples as deprecated or reorder tags for readability. For security protect the docs route with authentication or serve a read only public copy for discovery while keeping private endpoints on a locked path. Remember that documenting a private endpoint does not make it public by default unless you hand someone the URL and a password.

Quick checklist for a usable API docs page

  • Author OpenAPI 3 spec and store it in the repository
  • Validate the spec with Swagger Editor or CLI tools
  • Host Swagger UI via CDN static files or swagger-ui-express for Node
  • Load the spec URL and verify model rendering
  • Use Try It Out with auth headers and real payloads
  • Protect the docs route if your API is not public

Summary wise here is the deal. Write a correct OpenAPI 3 spec host Swagger UI near your API let users run Try It Out and lock down access where needed. Do that and onboarding will be faster bug reports will be clearer and you will spend less time explaining why the request body is an octopus instead of JSON.
seo_title: Get Swagger UI Working for Your REST APIs Without Tears
seo_heading: Author OpenAPI specs and host Swagger UI docs for testing and onboarding

Project setup and dependencies

Service layer and transactions

Controllers DTOs and REST

CRUD operations and testing

Deployment and best practices

Final notes

This is a pragmatic guide to building a maintainable Spring Boot application with Spring MVC Spring Data and JDBC. Keep layers separated write tests and use migrations and pooling to survive production. If you follow these patterns your app will be boring and reliable which is the nicest kind of success.

title: What's the difference between Spring Boot and Spring MVC?
description: Clear comparison of Spring Boot and Spring MVC with use cases setup differences and when to pick each framework for Java web projects.
heading: What is the difference between Spring Boot and Spring MVC
body:
Pick your fighter. On one side we have Spring MVC, the focused web framework that teaches you how the plumbing actually works. On the other side we have Spring Boot, the cheerful package that brings the plumbing preinstalled and says go build something useful already. Both live in the Spring Framework family and both are solid choices depending on whether you want control or convenience.

What each tool does well

Spring MVC is the web layer expert. It handles controllers, request mapping, view resolution and the usual HTTP dance. Use it when you want fine grain control over servlet configuration or when your app must deploy to a shared servlet container.

Spring Boot is opinionated setup plus runtime. It wires auto configuration, starter dependencies and an embedded server so you can ship an executable jar and run it with java -jar app.jar. If you like health checks, metrics and a short feedback loop, Boot will make you feel very productive.

Key differences at a glance

  • Setup and dependencies. Spring MVC needs explicit dependency management and server wiring. Spring Boot gives starter dependencies and auto configuration so you write less boilerplate.
  • Packaging and runtime. Spring MVC apps commonly become WAR files for external servers. Spring Boot makes executable jars with an embedded server for single command startup.
  • Opinion vs control. Spring Boot is opinionated for fast results. Spring MVC is granular for deep customization and complex container setups.

When to pick Spring MVC

Choose Spring MVC when you need precise control over the web layer. Typical reasons include legacy enterprise constraints that require WARs, custom servlet container integrations or when learning core framework behavior is the goal. Spring MVC forces you to see the moving parts and that knowledge pays off when debugging subtle issues.

When to pick Spring Boot

Choose Spring Boot when you want to build REST API microservices quickly or prototype without wrestling with configuration. Boot is great for production services that benefit from built in health checks, logging and metrics. It also has starter dependencies that simplify dependency management across Spring projects.

Migration path and practical tips

  • To migrate a Spring MVC module into Boot add spring boot starter web and switch packaging to an executable jar. You will reduce configuration code and gain operational features with little ceremony.
  • If you need the best of both worlds use Spring MVC patterns inside a Spring Boot project. You keep control of controllers and view resolution while enjoying Boot conveniences.
  • Remember that Boot abstracts internals. Learn core Spring MVC concepts if you expect to debug complex framework behavior later.

Final verdict with a tiny reality check

If speed to working code matters and you are building microservices or REST APIs go with Spring Boot. If your environment demands custom servlet containers or you need to be the person who understands every spring bean lifecycle detail pick Spring MVC. Either way you are using Java and the Spring Framework so try not to fight it too hard and enjoy the fact that both options are widely supported in production.
seo_title: Choose Spring Boot or Spring MVC for APIs and microservices
seo_heading: A practical guide to Spring Boot and Spring MVC for Java web apps

title: What is MVC? Model View Controller Explained
description: Clear explanation of MVC pattern for developers and learners. Learn roles of Model View Controller and how separation simplifies web apps.
heading: What is MVC Model View Controller Explained
body:
If your codebase feels like a mystery novel written by a committee that never met, MVC can stop the plot twists. Model View Controller is an architecture pattern that splits responsibilities so your app behaves and your team does not need daily standup therapy.

Why MVC still matters

Separate concerns means fewer merge conflicts and less accidental logic living in templates. The pattern is not a religion. It is a pragmatic way to keep state validation and business rules in one place, keep presentation focused on rendering, and let controllers choreograph without turning into the villain of the story.

What each piece actually does

Model

The Model owns data and business rules. Use plain classes or your ORM models to validate, persist, and enforce invariants. This is where you write code that is testable and not hiding in a template or a view helper. Think of the model as the single source of truth that can be exercised with unit tests instead of black magic.

View

The View renders the user interface. Keep templates minimal and focused on presentation. Push computations into helpers, partials, or presenter objects so designers and front end developers can work without accidentally becoming business analysts.

Controller

The Controller handles requests and user input. It should validate parameters, call the model or services, and decide which view to render. Do not let controllers become fat beasts that do database work formatting and business logic all at once.

Typical request flow

  1. Controller receives a request and parses parameters
  2. Controller asks the model or a service to read or update data
  3. Model performs validation and persistence and returns a result
  4. Controller picks the appropriate view or response format and renders it

Benefits and common pitfalls

  • Benefits include clearer separation of concerns and easier testing
  • Teams can work in parallel on UI and business logic without stepping on toes
  • Pitfalls include fat controllers and views that leak business rules
  • A model that still has UI logic is not a model, it is a shape shifting problem

Practical tips to avoid pain

  • Keep controllers thin and move business rules into models or dedicated service objects
  • When views start to contain logic extract helpers, partials, or presenters
  • Write unit tests for models and service objects and integration tests for controllers
  • Use background jobs for heavy lifting and avoid blocking request threads
  • Refactor boundaries as complexity grows instead of piling on hacks

MVC is simple in theory and useful in practice. It will not solve every scaling problem and it will not make meetings shorter, but it will keep business logic where tests can find it and views where designers can tweak without breaking the app. Follow the pattern, write tests, ship features, and try not to cry when a legacy controller resurfaces.
seo_title: How MVC Keeps Your Code Sane and Teams Shipping Faster
seo_heading: Practical MVC patterns for cleaner backends and smoother frontends

title: How Spring XML Configuration Works by Example
description: Compact guide to Spring XML configuration schemas beans XML files and how Spring Boot loads XML based config for Java apps
heading: How Spring XML Configuration Works by Example
body:
This article teaches how to configure Spring using XML schemas beans XML files and how Spring Boot interacts with XML configuration.

  1. Read XML schemas and namespaces
  2. Declare beans and properties
  3. Wire dependencies and scopes
  4. Load XML into an application context or Spring Boot
  5. Test and migrate to modern configuration when ready

Read XML schemas and namespaces Learn which namespace matches desired features. Common namespaces cover core beans context and aop. Schema locations tell the Spring parser what rules to apply and validate configuration against the chosen schema.

Declare beans and properties Define classes as beans with an id and a class name. Example XML in a compact form looks like this

< bean id="myService" class="com.example.MyService" />

Wire dependencies and scopes Inject dependencies using constructor args or property tags. Choose singleton prototype request or session scope depending on lifecycle needs. Use dependency injection to avoid newing up objects all over the codebase like a confused cowboy.

Load XML into an application context or Spring Boot Use ClassPathXmlApplicationContext in plain Spring or register XML locations in Spring Boot via spring.config.location or an XML based ApplicationContext initializer. Spring Boot tends to prefer Java config but XML remains supported for legacy modules.

Test and migrate to modern configuration when ready Write unit tests that load a minimal XML context and assert bean wiring. When comfortable replace pieces with @Configuration classes and component scan to reduce verbosity and gain compile time safety.

This tutorial covered reading schemas declaring beans wiring dependencies loading XML in an application context and strategies for testing and migration. The goal was to demystify old school XML configuration and show how Spring Boot can still cooperate with XML driven setups without drama.

Tip

Prefer small focused XML files per module and enable schema validation during tests. That catches typos faster than runtime errors and keeps legacy XML manageable while migrating to Java config.

title: What is Inversion of Control?
description: Clear explanation of Inversion of Control with examples benefits and common patterns for developers seeking cleaner decoupled code
heading: What is Inversion of Control Explained
body:
Stop letting your framework play puppet master

Inversion of Control or IoC is the design idea where the framework calls the shots and your code supplies the parts. Think Hollywood principle dont call us we will call you. The framework decides when to construct components run behavior and manage lifecycles while your application provides concrete implementations. You will see this in Dependency Injection service locator style registries framework callbacks and lifecycle hooks across frameworks like Spring Framework and Angular.

Dependency Injection is the polite option

Dependency Injection or DI gives modules their dependencies through constructors setters or factory methods so code does not new up things deep inside. This makes dependencies explicit and keeps tests sane. Prefer constructor injection for required collaborators and use interfaces so you can mock cleanly.

  • Constructor injection makes dependencies visible and test friendly
  • Setter injection fits optional features or late configuration
  • Factory methods work when creation requires extra logic

The service locator is the sneaky option

The service locator pattern asks a registry for a service at runtime instead of constructing one directly. It can cut down on long parameter lists but it also hides who depends on what. Use this pattern sparingly because debugging can become a treasure hunt when components grab services from a global like registry.

Framework callbacks and lifecycle hooks

Callback hooks let the framework call your code at specific moments such as startup shutdown or plugin events. These are great for initialization tasks and extension points. Keep callbacks small document them well and avoid stuffing complex logic into lifecycle methods to prevent surprising behavior.

Benefits and trade offs

  • Benefits include looser coupling easier testing and centralized lifecycle management
  • Trade offs include extra indirection and the risk of hidden dependencies when auto wiring is overused
  • Pick the approach that fits team workflow codebase size and future maintainability

Practical rules to avoid accidental chaos

Prefer explicit constructor injection for required dependencies and keep wiring visible in module configuration. Use a lightweight container only when wiring is complex. In Spring Framework use annotations and configuration judiciously. In Angular prefer constructor injection for services so components stay easy to test.

function main(service) {
  service.execute()
}

IoC is your friend when you want decoupled code and better tests. It stops being fun when everything is auto wired and no one knows where things come from. Use DI for clarity reserve service locators for special cases and keep lifecycle callbacks focused. Your future self will thank you or at least curse less during debugging.
seo_title: Why IoC Matters in Modern Apps and How DI Saves Your Sanity
seo_heading: Practical guide to Inversion of Control and dependency strategies

title: Dependency Injection and Inversion of Control in Spring
description: Learn DI and IOC patterns in Spring and Spring Boot with practical examples and annotation based configuration for clean and testable Java apps
heading: Dependency Injection and Inversion of Control in Spring Tutorial
body:
If you like writing code and not wiring up everything by hand like a medieval artisan, welcome to Dependency Injection and Inversion of Control in Spring without the boring lecture. This guide walks through how the Spring Framework and Spring Boot take responsibility for creating and connecting your objects so you can focus on business logic and not on who calls new.

What IoC and DI actually mean

Inversion of Control, or IOC, is the polite way to say your framework runs the show. Dependency Injection, or DI, is the mechanism where the framework hands the right bits to your classes. Together they reduce coupling and make unit tests less tragic.

Why care

When Spring manages your dependencies, you get easier testing, clearer responsibilities, and less glorified singleton soup. Your application classes declare what they need and the container provides it. No more secret constructors or mysterious static methods.

How to declare beans without crying

You have options depending on how nostalgic you are. Use Java config with @Configuration and @Bean if you like typesafe wiring. Use component scanning with @Component, @Service, @Repository, and @Controller if you prefer convention over configuration. XML is still supported for the people who enjoy suffering on purpose.

  • Java config with @Configuration and @Bean for explicit wiring
  • Component scanning with @Component family for quick setup
  • XML if you miss the 2000s

Annotations and autowiring without the mystery

Spring uses annotations like @Autowired and @Qualifier to wire dependencies. Autowiring by type is usually fine. If Spring finds multiple candidates use @Qualifier to pick one. Pro tip, prefer constructor injection because it makes dependencies obvious and helps testing. Field injection is convenient and lazy if you like brittle tests.

Constructor injection example idea

Declare dependencies in the constructor. The container will supply them. Your class is now easier to test with plain Java constructors and mocks.

Bean scope and profiles to avoid shared state nightmares

Spring Beans default to singleton scope which means one instance per container. Prototype scope creates a fresh instance each time. Use prototype when you need independent state, and singleton when you actually want shared services. Profiles let you switch implementations for development, testing, and production. Use profiles to avoid logging into production databases from your dev machine unless you enjoy chaos.

Testing with the container and mocks that behave

Spring Boot provides test slices like @WebMvcTest to start only the parts you need and @SpringBootTest when you want the whole enchilada. Use @MockBean to replace external dependencies with mocks during tests. Keep unit tests small and fast and leave full integration tests for CI where you can watch failures slowly blossom.

Testing tips

  • Slice the context to speed up tests
  • Use constructor injection so you can pass mocks easily
  • Mock external services and keep integration tests for real wiring

Practical wiring patterns

Assemble small services with clear interfaces. Let Spring build the object graph. Favor composition over static methods. Use @Qualifier for ambiguous beans and named @Bean methods when you need human readable identifiers. Keep configuration classes focused and readable so future you does not curse past you.

Conclusion

Dependency Injection and Inversion of Control in Spring and Spring Boot are not mystical powers. They are solid, practical patterns that make Java apps easier to test and maintain. Configure beans with Java config or annotations, prefer constructor injection, mind your scopes and profiles, and test with slices and mocks. Do that and your app will behave more like a cooperative organism and less like a pile of duct taped services.
seo_title: Make Spring do the heavy lifting with dependency injection
seo_heading: How to wire Spring Beans and use DI for cleaner and testable Java apps

title: How does a HashMap Work Internally?
description: Concise guide to how Java HashMap stores and accesses key value pairs with hashing collision handling resizing and performance tips
heading: How does a HashMap Work Internally?
body:
Quick anatomy of a HashMap

Think of a Java HashMap as a fancy apartment building for key value pairs. The building is an array of buckets. Each bucket can hold a linked list of entries or, if things get dramatic, a balanced tree. Each entry keeps the key, the value, the cached hash, and a pointer to the next entry in that bucket.

The hash and the index math you should not ignore

Java computes a hash from your key and then scrambles it a bit in Java 8 to mix high bits into low bits using a trick like h ^ (h >>> 16). The final array slot is found with a mask such as (n - 1) & hash where n is the table length. That mask only behaves well when n is a power of two which is why HashMap sizes are powers of two by design.

Collision handling that goes from sad to dramatic

When two keys land in the same bucket you get a collision. Then one of three things happens:

  • If the bucket is empty a new node is stored there.
  • If there are a few nodes they form a linked list and each lookup walks the list comparing the stored hash and then calling equals when needed.
  • If the list grows too long and the table is large enough the list is converted into a red black tree for faster lookups. In Java 8 the treeify threshold is 8 and the minimum table size for treeify is 64. If the table is too small HashMap will prefer to resize instead of treeifying.

How put actually works without the marketing copy

To put a key value the map computes the hash and index. If there is no node at that index a new node is inserted. If nodes exist the code walks the chain comparing the hash first and then calling equals on the key. If a matching key is found the value is replaced. If not found the new entry is appended or the bin is treeified when the chain length crosses the threshold.

When size exceeds capacity * loadFactor the map resizes to a larger table and redistributes entries. Resizing is the expensive party trick so picking a sensible initial capacity and load factor saves you from paying the toll often.

How get actually finds your stuff

Get computes the same hash and index and then scans the bucket. For small lists it just walks and compares. For treeified buckets it does a tree lookup which gives you logarithmic time in that bucket. In the common case with well distributed hashes get is effectively constant time.

Performance pitfalls and real world tips

  • Bad or identical hashCode implementations cause many collisions and drop you from O(1) to O(n). Fix your hashCode or change keys.
  • Avoid mutable keys after insertion. If you change a key field that affects hashCode you will lose the entry like a magician who forgot the trick.
  • Tune initial capacity and load factor if you know the size to avoid frequent resizing.
  • HashMap is not thread safe. Use ConcurrentHashMap for multi threaded access instead of relying on hope.

Key takeaways to look clever in code reviews

  • Provide a solid hashCode and a correct equals to keep operations fast.
  • Prefer immutable keys when possible.
  • If you see many collisions consider a different hashing strategy or increase initial capacity.
  • Remember Java 8 specifics like the treeify threshold of 8 and the power of two table sizes for the index mask.

There you go. You now understand the apartment hierarchy, the bickering between linked lists and trees, and why resizing is the expensive landlord who shows up at midnight. Use that knowledge and your HashMap will behave, mostly.
seo_title: What really happens inside a Java HashMap during collisions
seo_heading: Deep dive into HashMap internals with hashing collisions and resizing tips

title: How Spring Boot Auto Configuration Works
description: How Spring Boot auto configuration works with @EnableAutoConfiguration explained with conditionals and customization options for smarter bean wiring
heading: How Spring Boot Auto Configuration Works
body:
How Spring Boot auto configuration shows up and starts making guesses

Spring Boot auto configuration tries very hard to be helpful and sometimes it succeeds. The short version is this. When you enable auto configuration via @EnableAutoConfiguration the framework uses an import selector that asks SpringFactoriesLoader to read META-INF/spring.factories and load candidate auto configuration classes. Those candidates are ordinary @Configuration classes with gatekeepers on the door that check the environment before they register beans.

Conditional annotations that actually matter

The most common guards are @ConditionalOnClass and @ConditionalOnMissingBean. The first one checks if a library or type is on the classpath. The second one checks if you already provided a bean that does the job. If either check fails the auto configuration politely stays home.

For feature toggles use @ConditionalOnProperty to flip things on or off without editing code. For test scenarios use @ImportAutoConfiguration to load only the pieces you want in that test. Those are safe and explicit ways to avoid surprise wiring.

Which configuration wins when beans fight

Auto configuration is modular and opinionated. When several configurations could provide the same bean Spring Boot uses ordering hints like @AutoConfigureAfter and the order implied in spring.factories to decide who wins the bean tug of war. If you need to change which provider wins you can either supply your own bean of the expected type or tweak ordering with annotations.

Common ways to opt out or override

  • Exclude globally with the property spring.autoconfigure.exclude or by passing exclude to @SpringBootApplication or @EnableAutoConfiguration
  • Define a user bean with the same type so @ConditionalOnMissingBean stops the framework bean from being registered
  • Use @ConditionalOnProperty to gate an auto configuration behind a property you control
  • In tests import only what you need with @ImportAutoConfiguration

Troubleshooting checklist when Spring guesses wrong

If Spring registers a bean you did not expect here is a quick checklist that will save you time and tears.

  1. Enable debug logging for org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure and watch which auto configuration classes ran and which conditions passed
  2. Open the relevant auto configuration class and read the condition annotations to see why it ran
  3. Look in META-INF/spring.factories to see the candidate list and implied ordering
  4. Decide if you want to provide your own bean or exclude the auto configuration class
logging.level.org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure=DEBUG

A few practical examples

If DataSourceAutoConfiguration initializes a DataSource you do not want one of two things usually helps. Either provide a DataSource bean of your own so @ConditionalOnMissingBean short circuits the auto configuration, or exclude the auto configuration class explicitly in your application entry point.

@SpringBootApplication(exclude = {org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class})

For feature flags the pattern looks like this

@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "feature.x.enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = false)
public class FeatureXAutoConfiguration { ... }

Final honest advice

Spring Boot does a lot of clever guessing so you can write business logic instead of wiring code. When the framework makes a baffling guess look at the auto configuration class and the debug log first. That is almost always faster than blaming your IDE and yelling at the console.

Auto configuration is driven by spring.factories metadata, guarded by conditional annotations, and influenced by ordering hints. Learn those three things and you will stop being surprised.

If you still want revenge try reading the source code for a weekend. It will make you either wiser or more humble and both outcomes are acceptable.
seo_title: Understand Spring Boot Auto Configuration Without Losing Your Mind
seo_heading: Why ConditionalOnClass and ConditionalOnMissingBean Decide Your Beans at Startup

title: What is Dependency Injection?
description: Clear and practical explanation of dependency injection for developers. Learn benefits types and patterns for cleaner testable code.
heading: What is Dependency Injection What Developers Need to Know
body:
Why bother with dependency injection

Dependency injection is the polite way of telling your objects to stop making friends on their own. Instead of each class reaching into the void to assemble its own collaborators you hand those collaborators to the class from the outside. The result is less hidden coupling and more predictable code when you are writing unit tests or swapping implementations that do not suck.

Core idea in plain English

Give objects what they need instead of letting them build it secretly. This moves responsibility for wiring to a single place often called a container or composition root. Business logic gets to stay focused on business logic and not on object plumbing.

Key benefits

  • Better decoupling so you can swap implementations like a sane adult
  • Easier unit testing because tests can inject fakes or spies
  • Clearer separation of responsibilities which reduces future surprises

Common injection styles

There are a few practical ways to inject dependencies. Each has trade offs and yes you will be judged by your choice in code reviews.

Constructor injection

Pass required dependencies through the constructor at creation time. This is the most common style and it makes dependencies explicit and effectively immutable. Use this for the things your class cannot function without.

Setter injection

Provide optional collaborators via setters. This works well for optional or late bound dependencies and lets you change behavior after creation. Use it sparingly or tests will have too many moving parts.

Interface injection

Have the consumer implement an interface that accepts a dependency. Less common today but useful when you need a formal contract for injection.

What a composition root looks like

The composition root is the place where construction and wiring happen. Keep it small and obvious so you do not have to go spelunking through the codebase to see who gets what.

class Logger {
  log(message) {
    console.log(message)
  }
}

class UserService {
  constructor(logger) {
    this.logger = logger
  }

  createUser(name) {
    this.logger.log('create ' + name)
  }
}

const logger = new Logger()
const userService = new UserService(logger)

DI and tests living their best lives

Because you do not instantiate dependencies inside the class you can hand tests fake or spy implementations. No need to mess with global state or convoluted setup. This improves test readability and reduces flakiness.

When to reach for a framework

Frameworks and IoC containers can help manage object lifecycle and scope but the principle stands with or without them. Start with simple wiring in a composition root and only add a container if the complexity is real and painful.

Practical tips

  • Prefer constructor injection for required collaborators
  • Use setter injection for optional collaborators that may change
  • Keep your composition root small and obvious to avoid surprises
  • Use dependency injection to support SOLID principles and easier unit testing

In short dependency injection is not magic or software worship it is a disciplined way to decouple code so you can test and change it without crying in production logs. Embrace the wiring and your future self will send you a polite thank you note.
seo_title: Dependency injection explained for humans and unit tests
seo_heading: How dependency injection makes your code testable and less dramatic

title: Stop Using Setter Injection Constructor Injection is Better
description: Why constructor injection is better than setter injection in Spring Boot Learn benefits like immutability clearer dependencies and easier testing
heading: Stop Using Setter Injection Constructor Injection is Better in Spring Boot
body:
If your codebase still treats setter injection like a charming shortcut you can get away with forever, relax and enjoy the chaos. Setter injection is tempting because it looks neat and simple, but it also makes missing dependencies sneak up on you during runtime and in unit tests. Constructor injection forces required dependencies up front which makes life easier for humans and tools alike.

What actually differs between setter injection and constructor injection

Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit at creation time. Required services show up as constructor parameters and can be declared final which helps with immutability and prevents accidental mutation. Setter injection puts wiring in methods which can be called or not called which turns certain fields into optional time bombs.

Short example that proves the point

public class OrderService {
  private final PaymentService paymentService

  public OrderService(PaymentService paymentService) {
    this.paymentService = paymentService
  }
}

public class OrderServiceWithSetter {
  private PaymentService paymentService

  public void setPaymentService(PaymentService paymentService) {
    this.paymentService = paymentService
  }
}

The first version will not compile in the land of runtime surprises because the dependency must be supplied when creating the instance. The second version lets nulls and tests that forget to wire things cause subtle failures.

Why developers actually like constructor injection

  • Dependencies are explicit which helps code reading and IDE navigation
  • Fields can be final which supports immutability and predictable behavior
  • Unit testing is simpler because a test can construct the class directly with mocks or fakes
  • Frameworks like Spring Boot and the Spring Framework play well with this pattern

Use cases for setter injection that are legit

Setter injection is not evil in every situation. Use it when a dependency is truly optional or when wiring must be changed after construction for a very good reason. For example you might inject an optional callback or a performance tuning hook that is fine to be absent during tests.

Tips for optional wiring

  • Prefer Optional injection or nullable fields that are explicitly handled
  • Document why the setter is optional so the next engineer does not assume it is safe to leave out

What about Lombok and ceremony

If you hate typing constructors more than most people hate meetings, Lombok can help. An annotation such as RequiredArgsConstructor generates the constructor so you keep constructor safety without a pile of boilerplate. That keeps code concise while preserving immutability and explicit wiring.

Cyclic dependencies and the polite ways to fix them

Yes constructor injection can expose design smells like cycles. When that happens do not reach for setter injection as a duct tape solution. Consider these options instead

  • Refactor responsibilities so the cycle disappears
  • Introduce a factory or builder to break the direct dependency graph
  • Use lazy wiring or provider interfaces when a true runtime break is needed

Practical DI best practices for Spring Boot and Java

  • Prefer constructor injection for mandatory dependencies
  • Mark fields final to enforce immutability and make tests predictable
  • Use setter injection only for genuinely optional services and document why they are optional
  • Leverage Lombok to reduce boilerplate while keeping constructor based wiring
  • When you encounter cycles refactor rather than masking the problem with setter wiring

In short if you want fewer surprises in production and happier unit testing, use constructor injection in your Spring Framework and Spring Boot projects. Setter injection is fine for optional cases, but treating it as the default is a fast track to bugs that look innocent and behave nasty.
seo_title: Choose constructor injection for safer Spring dependency wiring
seo_heading: Why constructor injection wins for Java Spring Boot and testable code

title: How to Clone a Repository from GitHub
description: Step by step guide to clone a GitHub repository using Bash and VS Code with branch tips and common fixes
heading: How to Clone a Repository from GitHub Using Bash and VS Code
body:
Why this matters and when to care

You found a repo you want to poke at, tweak or pretend you understand. Cloning a repository from GitHub brings a copy to your local machine so you can run code tests edit files and push changes back when you are feeling brave. This guide walks through the git clone command using Bash and how to open the project in VS Code without summoning chaos.

Grab the clone URL from GitHub

Go to the GitHub repo page and click the Code button. Pick HTTPS if you like typing usernames and passwords now and then. Pick SSH if you prefer configuring keys once and avoiding password prompts forever or until you forget your passphrase.

Copy options you will actually use

  • HTTPS example
    • https://github.com/user/repo.git
  • SSH example
    • git@github.com:user/repo.git

Open a terminal in the folder you want the repo to live

Use your file manager or a Bash command like cd to move to the directory where you want the project folder. If you want to keep your life tidy make a projects folder and go there.

Run the clone command

Use the URL you copied and run the clone command. The default creates a folder named after the repository.

git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git
# or for SSH
git clone git@github.com:user/repo.git

If you want a different local folder name add it at the end of the command like this

git clone URL my-local-name

Clone a specific branch when you are picky

If your task needs a particular branch you can do it in one step or two.

  • One step using the branch flag
    • git clone -b branch-name URL
  • Two steps if you already cloned
    • git checkout branch-name

Open the project in VS Code

Once the clone finishes open the folder in VS Code. From the terminal run

code repo

or use the editor menu and choose Open Folder. VS Code will detect common tooling and may suggest extensions to install which is perfect unless you enjoy ignoring helpful prompts.

Troubleshooting and helpful tips

  • Set up SSH keys to avoid repeated password prompts. After you add a key to your GitHub account test it with ssh -T git@github.com
  • If authentication fails check that your SSH key is loaded and that the remote URL matches the protocol you intended
  • Use git remote -v to verify the origin URL and git remote set-url origin URL to fix it
  • If you see Permission denied publickey the usual culprit is a missing or unloaded SSH key

Quick checklist before you start committing to the void

  1. Copy HTTPS or SSH URL from GitHub
  2. Open a Bash terminal in the desired parent folder
  3. Run git clone with or without the -b flag
  4. Open the folder in VS Code using code or the GUI
  5. Confirm remotes and authentication if anything smells off

There you go. You cloned the repo and opened it in your editor without summoning polite chaos. Now go edit something useful or at least make a tiny typo commit and call it progress.
seo_title: Get a GitHub repo on your machine with Bash and VS Code
seo_heading: Clone a GitHub repo locally and open it in VS Code like a pro

title: Master Spring Profiles in Spring Boot
description: Guide to Spring Profiles in Spring Boot covering active profiles profile properties include annotation and Environment usage
heading: Master Spring Profiles in Spring Boot for Active Profiles and Properties
body:
If you ever wanted different settings for local hacks and production nightmares this guide will help you tame Spring profiles in Spring Boot without melodrama. You will learn how to name profile specific properties files how to activate a profile how to gate beans with an annotation how to compose profiles and how to handle properties at runtime and in tests. Also a tiny reminder to keep secrets out of source control unless you like late night incident responses.

Profile specific properties files

Name files using the familiar convention application-dev.properties and application-prod.properties and watch Spring Boot do its overlay magic. Spring Boot reads application.properties first and then overlays the active profile file so values in a profile file replace defaults quietly and predictably.

  • Keep common defaults in application.properties
  • Put environment overrides in application-dev.properties or application-prod.properties
  • Use application-local.properties for short lived experiments that never see CI

Activate a profile

Choose the active profile with a property or a command line flag. For example set spring.profiles.active=dev in a properties file or start your app with the flag --spring.profiles.active=prod. CI pipelines and containers can inject this value per deployment so your app boots with the right configuration for that stage.

Use the @Profile annotation for conditional beans

If a bean should only exist in development give it a profile annotation. Annotate configuration classes or individual beans with @Profile("dev") to ensure they only load when that exact profile is active. This keeps debug helpers out of production and avoids wiring that would make ops grumble.

Example concept in plain terms

@Configuration
@Profile("dev")
public class DevConfig {
  @Bean
  public MyService devOnlyService() {
    return new DevOnlyService()
  }
}

Compose profiles with spring.profiles.include

If several profiles share the same settings avoid copy paste. Put shared values in a common profile and include it from other profile files with spring.profiles.include=common inside a profile file. This merges properties so the common values apply followed by the environment specific overrides.

Access properties at runtime with Environment

Inject the Spring environment and call env.getProperty("my.property") when you need a value at runtime. This is handy for feature gates or conditional logic that depends on configuration and lets you keep properties tidy instead of scattering system checks around the codebase.

Testing with @ActiveProfiles

In tests simulate an environment by annotating the test class with @ActiveProfiles("test"). That makes Spring load the matching profile file and any beans annotated for that profile. Use this to run integration tests with test friendly overrides and to ensure beans wired for production do not sneak into test runs.

Quick testing checklist

  • Add application-test.properties with test values
  • Annotate tests with @ActiveProfiles("test")
  • Keep test secrets out of repo by using environment variables or a vault

Security and deployment tips

Do not store secrets in profile files that live in source control. Use environment variables a secrets manager or a vault and combine those with a minimal profile specific overlay at deployment time. Remember that profiles control what Spring wires and what properties are visible so a misconfigured profile can leak surprises at runtime.

Final notes

Spring profiles are simple but powerful. Name your files clearly activate the right profile for each stage use @Profile to keep beans separated use spring.profiles.include to reduce duplication and use the Environment object and @ActiveProfiles to make runtime logic and tests reliable. Do this and your configuration will be predictable and at least slightly less likely to ruin someone's morning.
seo_title: Make Spring Boot profiles work across dev test and prod
seo_heading: Practical spring profiles guide with env tricks and test tips

title: Spring Boot Properties & Configurations 10x Devs Must Know
description: Essential Spring Boot properties and configuration practices for Java and Kotlin developers to ship safer and faster applications.
heading: Spring Boot Properties & Configurations 10x Devs Must Know
body:
Why these settings matter

If you are tired of apps that behave like rebellious teenagers in production then welcome. This guide walks through the Spring Boot properties and configuration patterns that actually save time and reduce hair loss. We cover file locations and precedence, profiles, datasource and JPA settings, server port quirks, logging, actuator safety, Jackson naming, and the proper way to bind config for tests and deployment in Java and Kotlin projects.

Where to put application files and which one wins

Spring Boot looks for application.properties or application.yml on the classpath. You can also add files named application-dev.yml or application-prod.yml to separate environment specifics. Order of precedence matters. If you pass something on the command line or an environment variable it usually wins during emergencies when you want to fix things without opening the code base.

Quick precedence cheat sheet

  • Command line arguments
  • Environment variables
  • Application properties or YAML on the classpath
  • Defaults inside the jar

Profiles and profile specific files

Use spring.profiles.active=dev to enable a set of properties for an environment. Layer profiles rather than scattering conditionals everywhere. Profiles make your deployments act like grown ups and let you test production like you actually plan to run it.

Datasource settings and secrets

Use spring.datasource.url spring.datasource.username and spring.datasource.password for connections. Do not commit credentials to source control. Prefer environment variables or a secrets manager. If you use Spring Data, keep the datasource config tight and avoid magic that only works on your laptop.

JPA schema management that will not surprise you

Control JPA schema behavior with spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto. In production use validate or none. For local testing use update or create only when you enjoy losing data. Treat ddl-auto as a development convenience not a deployment strategy.

Server port and multiple apps

If two apps fight for port 8080 set server.port=8081 or whatever number you like. Containers make this less of a drama but being explicit still helps during local debugging and CI runs.

Logging without redeploying

Toggle logging with keys like logging.level.org.springframework=DEBUG and prefer environment overrides for quick fixes. Centralized logging on deployment remains a superior long term plan.

Actuator exposure and safety

Expose only what you need by setting management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info and lock down sensitive endpoints with proper auth and network rules. Actuator is awesome when you secure it and dangerous when you treat it like a status page for nosy people.

Jackson naming and serialization

Tune JSON with spring.jackson.property-naming-strategy=SNAKE_CASE or the strategy your clients expect. Most of the time you do not need custom serializers. Match the client convention and move on with your life.

Use configuration binding the right way

@ConfigurationProperties is your friend when grouping related settings. It beats scattering @Value annotations like confetti. Binding makes validation and testing far less painful and reads better in Java and Kotlin code.

Externalized config and deployment patterns

Remember the predictable override order. Command line flags and environment variables are the best friends of CI pipelines and containers. For many services at scale consider a config server or centralized management so ops teams stop yelling at developers during deployments.

Simple deployment checklist

  • Keep secrets out of source control and use env variables or a vault
  • Use profiles for environment differences and test them
  • Validate JPA schema in production and avoid automatic updates
  • Limit actuator endpoints and secure the management port
  • Prefer @ConfigurationProperties over scattered @Value usage

Follow these patterns and your Spring Boot apps will be faster to develop and less likely to surprise you at 3 AM. If they still misbehave at least you will have better logs and a plan for blaming the right configuration file.
seo_title: Master Spring Boot configuration for safer Java and Kotlin apps
seo_heading: Practical Spring Boot properties and YAML tips for real world deployments

title: Spring Boot application.properties How it Works
description: Clear guide to Spring Boot application.properties and YAML showing how profiles and active config merge for Java Kotlin and Graal
heading: How Spring Boot application.properties Works for Profiles and YAML
body:
If your Spring Boot app ever behaved differently in production than it did on your laptop then welcome to the club. Spring Boot reads configuration from a bunch of places and merges them together. That is efficient and convenient until it is not. This guide explains the lookup order and merging behavior so you can stop blaming mysterious stack traces and start blaming your own config with confidence.

Where Spring Boot looks for configuration

Think of property sources like a stack of sticky notes. The top note wins when the same key appears more than once. The common sources arranged from low priority to high priority are

  • Default properties packaged in the application jar
  • Profile specific files like application-dev.properties or application-dev.yml
  • Main files such as application.properties or application.yml inside the jar
  • External files placed in a config folder next to the jar or other external locations
  • Environment variables and system properties
  • Command line arguments which take the top prize when there is a tie

Files with a profile suffix override the main configuration when that profile is active. Use spring.profiles.active=dev or set the environment variable SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE in containers and CI to activate a profile.

Merging behavior that saves pain

Spring Boot usually merges values instead of replacing entire objects. That means you can override a single property under a nested object without reworking the whole block. This is great for sharing defaults across environments and applying small tweaks for dev or prod.

Example

If you have a nested config object in YAML or properties and you only override the inner field in a profile file then Spring will merge the change rather than throwing away the rest.

YAML, native image caution and language parity

YAML is supported and great for structured settings. But if you build a GraalVM native image then resource scanning and profile activation can behave differently. Make sure you include property files in the native image resource list and run profile activation tests as part of the native build pipeline.

Kotlin and Java applications use the same configuration model. Your Kotlin code does not get a VIP pass. The same rules apply across languages running on the JVM or as a GraalVM native image.

When you need to override the default lookup order

If your team needs configuration outside of the jar or wants explicit control over where Spring Boot looks for files use these properties

  • spring.config.location to specify exact locations that Spring Boot should load
  • spring.config.additional-location to add extra places without replacing the defaults

These are handy in containers and when configuration must live on a mounted volume or central config server.

DevOps friendly checklist

  • Supply the profile via environment variable or command line for reliable CI and production behavior
  • Use the Actuator environment endpoint during development to inspect the final merged property set
  • Keep secrets out of properties files and prefer a secrets manager where possible
  • Include configuration tests in your pipeline especially when building GraalVM native images

Final thought. Configuration is a superpower until it is a landmine. Learn the precedence and merging rules and you will debug faster and stop inventing new swear words at 3 AM. Now go find that rogue property and put it out of its misery.

title: How to Install Node JS on Windows 10/11

This tutorial walks through installing Node.js on Windows 10 and 11 and verifying npm and npx so React ExpressJS and Angular projects can run without drama.

  2. Run the installer and accept default options
  3. Enable Add to PATH and install optional tools as needed
  4. Verify Node and npm versions from a terminal
  5. Update npm globally if a newer version is desired
  6. Create a quick test app with npx to confirm workflow

Step one get the official installer from nodejs.org and choose the LTS build for stability. Picking the LTS build spares future headaches when libraries decide to act up.

Step two run the downloaded installer as an administrator and follow the GUI prompts. Accepting defaults is fine for most developers unless a custom setup is required.

Step three make sure to check Add to PATH so the Node.js runtime becomes available from any terminal session. Optional tools for native modules can be installed when asked but those are only needed for specific packages.

Step six try a quick scaffold such as npx create-react-app my-app to validate that package execution via npx works. Successful project creation proves that Node.js npm and npx are ready for development.

This guide covered downloading the Node.js installer choosing sensible defaults enabling PATH verification updating npm and running a test project. Following these steps turns a fresh Windows machine into a developer friendly Node environment in minutes while keeping things pleasantly boring and stable for real work.

Use the LTS release for production work and install Windows build tools only if native module compilation fails. That keeps the system lean and reduces future version mismatches.

title: Advanced Spring Data & JDBC Tutorial #SpringBoot
description: Learn advanced Spring Data and JDBC techniques with JdbcTemplate and JPA for MySQL and PostgreSQL in Spring Boot projects
heading: Advanced Spring Data and JDBC Tutorial for Spring Boot
body:
Quick truth about this guide

If you are tired of mystical ORM promises and want tools that actually do the job, welcome. This guide walks through Spring Boot database access using JdbcTemplate and Spring Data JPA while staying useful for both MySQL and PostgreSQL users. Expect concrete advice on setup, transactions, testing, migrations and speed tweaks that do not rely on witchcraft.

Project setup and dependencies

Add the JDBC and JPA starters and the appropriate driver for your database. Use Spring profiles to switch between MySQL and PostgreSQL so your dev laptop does not sabotage production. Typical artifacts are spring boot starter data jdbc, spring boot starter data jpa, and the MySQL or PostgreSQL driver on your classpath. Keep your dependency versions aligned with the Spring Boot bill of materials and you will sleep better.

JdbcTemplate in the wild

JdbcTemplate is your friend when you want explicit control. Use RowMapper or NamedParameterJdbcTemplate for readable queries and safer parameter binding. Manual mapping gives predictable performance and avoids invisible lazy loading surprises from ORMs.

Typical patterns

  • Single row mapping with a RowMapper for clear conversions from result set to domain object.
  • Named parameters to keep long queries maintainable and to avoid positional chaos.
  • Batch updates for bulk operations to avoid chatty database behavior.

When to prefer JdbcTemplate

  • Complex joins or heavy batch workloads that need tuned SQL.
  • When you need predictable prepared statement and batching behavior.
  • When ORM generated SQL is slower than your willingness to accept.

Spring Data JPA and repositories

Use JPA and repository interfaces when you want domain centric models and quick CRUD scaffolding. JpaRepository gives derived queries, pagination and a lot of convenience. Annotate entities with @Entity and choose fetch strategies explicitly to avoid N plus one problems.

Custom implementations and derived queries

  • Derived finder methods are great for simple filters and paging.
  • Provide custom repository implementations when you need a mix of ORM convenience and handcrafted SQL.
  • Use projections for narrow read models to reduce data transfer overhead.

Transactions and error handling

Spring transaction management is mature and reliable. Annotate service methods with @Transactional and think carefully about propagation and isolation. Common settings you will see are Propagation REQUIRED and Isolation READ_COMMITTED. Handle transient database errors with retries or compensating actions rather than swallowing exceptions and hoping for the best.

Practical notes

  • Keep transactions short and focused to reduce lock contention.
  • Avoid long running work inside a transaction, especially network calls.
  • Test transactional behavior in integration tests to catch surprises early.

Testing and database migrations

Integration tests are the only kind that will prove your database assumptions. Use Testcontainers to run real MySQL or PostgreSQL in CI or H2 for lightweight checks if your SQL is simple. Migration tools like Flyway or Liquibase keep schema changes predictable and ensure your tests use the same migrations as production.

Test strategies

  • Use Testcontainers for integration tests that need realistic behavior.
  • Run migrations as part of test setup so the schema stays honest.
  • Keep unit tests for logic and integration tests for data access and transactions.

Performance tuning and indexing

Before blaming the database, measure query plans. Use EXPLAIN to see what the planner does and add indexes based on evidence not paranoia. Batching, prepared statements and tuned fetch sizes can make huge differences for large data sets. When you hit complex reporting or analytic queries consider raw SQL using JdbcTemplate rather than trying to force JPA to be something it was not designed to be.

Checklist for faster queries

  • Inspect query plans and address full table scans where they are unnecessary.
  • Batch updates and reads to reduce roundtrips and JDBC overhead.
  • Create targeted indexes and monitor their impact on write performance.

Decision guide and final tips

Prefer JdbcTemplate for heavy batch operations and finely tuned queries. Prefer JPA for rich domain models that benefit from entity relationships and automatic dirty checking. Always measure with real data and your production like configuration before picking a side. If you must gamble pick the one you can debug at 2 a m.

Now go implement your repository with confidence and a little contempt for cargo cult development. Measure query plans, write good tests with Testcontainers or H2, and let Flyway or Liquibase keep schema drift from turning your database into a mystery novel.

seo_heading: Practical Spring Data patterns for MySQL and PostgreSQL in Spring Boot apps

title: React Hello World App for Beginners #javascript #reactjs
description: Quick step by step guide to create a React Hello World app using Node and VS Code with commands and tips for beginners
heading: React Hello World App for Beginners using Node and VS Code
body:
Why we bother with Hello World

If you are starting front end development or just learning React and JavaScript the Hello World app is the ritual. It is tiny and useless in the market but huge for your confidence. This short tutorial shows how to scaffold a project with Node and create react app then open it in VS Code and see that glorious heading show up in the browser.

What you need before you begin

  • Node and npm installed from the official Node website
  • VS Code or your favorite editor that does not judge your folder names
  • A terminal and a little patience for installing packages

Create the starter project

Open a terminal and run the scaffolding command that does all the heavy lifting. This uses create react app under the hood so you do not have to configure a bundler yourself.

npx create-react-app hello-world

That will create a hello-world folder with everything you need for a development server that hot reloads as you change code.

Open the project and inspect the files

Launch VS Code in the project folder. The main source code lives in src. The app entry point is src/index.js and the page shell has a root div in public/index.html. You do not need to memorize all files yet. Focus on src/App.js to render something visible.

Edit App to render Hello World

Function components are concise and modern so use one. Replace the existing component with a simple header to prove the app is alive. Here is a minimal example for src/App.js.

import React from 'react'

function App() {
  return (
    

      
Hello World

      
This is your first React component doing its job

    

  )
}

export default App

Start the development server and admire the result

Run the dev server with your package manager. It launches a local server with live reload so you can edit and instantly see changes.

npm start

Open a browser at http://localhost:3000 and confirm the Hello World message is displayed. Congratulations you have completed the classic first step in web development.

Optional build for production

When you are ready to deploy run the build command to create optimized static assets. Then serve those files from a static host or a platform like Netlify or Vercel.

npm run build

Where to go next

With this foundation you can explore component props state routing and more advanced front end patterns. The Hello World app is tiny but the lessons stick. Try passing props to a child component or add a bit of state just to prove the mental model works.

If something breaks first time do not panic. Read the terminal output fix the dependency or restart the dev server. Programming is part puzzle and part coffee consumption. Keep going and build something a bit more ambitious than a heading next time.

title: Spring Boot Actuator Full Tutorial
description: Practical guide to enable and configure Spring Boot Actuator for monitoring metrics health endpoints and security in a Spring Boot application.
heading: Spring Boot Actuator Full Tutorial Guide
body:
This tutorial teaches how to add and use Spring Boot Actuator for monitoring metrics health endpoints and management functions of Spring Boot applications.

  1. Add the Actuator dependency
  2. Expose and configure endpoints
  3. Secure management endpoints
  4. Collect metrics and custom health checks
  5. Integrate with monitoring backends

Add the Actuator dependency

Start by adding the dependency named spring-boot-starter-actuator to pom.xml or build.gradle. That gives access to a suite of ready made endpoints for metrics and health that save time and reduce the need for handcrafted status pages.

Expose and configure endpoints

Configure endpoint exposure in application properties using keys such as management.endpoints.web.exposure.include and management.endpoint.health.show.details. Choose a sensible set of endpoints to expose to avoid accidental leakage of internal details to the world wide web.

Secure management endpoints

Protect endpoints with Spring Security or network rules. Map actuator endpoints to a restricted path under /actuator and require authentication for sensitive endpoints like shutdown and env. Default openness is useful for demos and dangerous for production.

Collect metrics and custom health checks

Use Micrometer for metrics export. Add custom meters with MeterRegistry and implement HealthIndicator for bespoke health checks. Custom checks give operational teams signals that matter beyond CPU and memory numbers.

Integrate with monitoring backends

Push metrics to Prometheus Grafana or other backends by adding the corresponding Micrometer registry. Endpoint scraping or push gateways can be chosen based on infrastructure and scale requirements.

This tutorial covered enabling Actuator adding basic configuration securing management endpoints collecting custom metrics and integrating with monitoring backends. Following these steps results in operational visibility and fewer surprise outages while keeping the developer life slightly less chaotic.

Tip

Expose only needed endpoints in production and use role based access for management paths. If observability budget is tight focus on request metrics error rates and a single meaningful custom health check.

title: Create a Custom Spring Boot Actuator Endpoint Tutorial

Create a class annotated to become an Actuator endpoint. A minimal example uses the endpoint annotation and one read operation. Example annotation usage is shown here for clarity

@Endpoint(id = "custom")

@ReadOperation

Spring Boot will pick up a component scanned endpoint class when the class is a Spring bean. Mark the class with a stereotype or register the bean manually when component scanning does not apply.

Enable exposure through application properties so the endpoint is reachable via HTTP. A typical property line looks like management endpoints web exposure include equals custom comma health comma info. The specific property for enabling the endpoint can be management endpoint custom enabled equals true.

Test the endpoint with curl or a browser by calling the management context path plus the endpoint id. If the management server port differs include the port. Secure the endpoint using Spring Security by restricting actuator endpoints to authorized roles and by enabling HTTPS when needed.

The tutorial covered dependency setup class creation registration exposure and basic security considerations. The custom endpoint provides a lightweight way to expose application specific data or operations without polluting public APIs.

Tip

Prefer ReadOperation for safe queries and UseOperation for actions that change state. Keep payloads small and avoid exposing sensitive data through the custom endpoint unless access is strictly controlled.

title: Actuator Metrics in Spring Boot Examples
description: Learn how to enable and expose CPU memory and thread metrics with Spring Boot Actuator for easy monitoring and troubleshooting.

This tutorial shows how to enable and expose CPU memory and thread metrics in Spring Boot using Actuator and Micrometer for basic monitoring.

  1. Add dependencies to the project

Add dependencies to the project

Include spring-boot-starter-actuator and a Micrometer binder such as micrometer-registry-prometheus in the build. Maven users add the dependencies in pom.xml and Gradle users add them in build.gradle. This gives the application the metrics plumbing which does most of the heavy lifting.

Register Micrometer metrics backend

Wire a backend such as Prometheus by adding the registry dependency and leaving the default meter names. Micrometer auto config supplies metrics like jvm.memory.used and thread metrics under jvm.threads. No heroic coding required.

Query metrics from the endpoints

Request endpoints such as /actuator/metrics/jvm.memory.used or /actuator/metrics/jvm.threads.live. For CPU usage check platform specific meters or use OS binders from Micrometer for process CPU metrics.

Secure and tune metric collection

Control who can see metrics by securing actuator endpoints with Spring Security and by filtering which meters are registered to avoid noise. Adjust meter reporting frequency using registry settings to reduce overhead.

Summary of the tutorial topic This guide covered dependency setup configuration to expose metrics registering a backend how to query common CPU memory and thread metrics and basic security and tuning tips for production use

Tip

Enable only the specific meters and endpoints needed for monitoring to reduce runtime overhead and avoid exposing sensitive operational details to the public.
