title: Quick Intro to the Spring Boot Actuator Playlist
description: Compact guide to Spring Boot Actuator features setup and common endpoints for monitoring health metrics and management of Spring applications
heading: Quick Intro to the Spring Boot Actuator Playlist
body:
Spring Boot Actuator is the production ready control panel for your Spring application. It gives you health checks metrics info and other endpoints that make monitoring and application management less about guesswork and more about smug satisfaction when dashboards finally tell the truth.

Enable Actuator dependency and basic setup

Start by adding the actuator dependency and letting Spring Boot auto configure the management endpoints. Yes it is that easy and yes you will feel a little proud of yourself.

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>

To expose a subset of endpoints configure the management property. For example this exposes health info and metrics from the web endpoints

management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics

Key endpoints you will actually use

  • Health endpoint reports application status and component health. Great for load balancers and on call humans who want a single green light or a reason to panic.
  • Metrics endpoint exposes numeric measures that feed monitoring systems and make alerting honest
  • Info endpoint can show build and version details pulled from project properties so you stop asking which jar is deployed
  • Env and beans are useful during debugging but treat them like matchsticks near a gas stove in production

Prometheus and Micrometer

If you want real observability wire metrics to Prometheus using the Micrometer registry. Add the registry dependency and Spring Boot will provide a /actuator/prometheus endpoint that Prometheus can scrape.

<dependency>
  <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
  <artifactId>micrometer-registry-prometheus</artifactId>
</dependency>

Then configure your Prometheus server to scrape your /actuator/prometheus endpoint. That way dashboards stop guessing and start refusing to lie.

Endpoint security and exposure

Public endpoints can leak details you did not mean to share. Protect management paths with HTTP basic or OAuth or keep them behind a network boundary. The shortest path to shame is leaving everything open to the internet.

  • Only expose endpoints you need in production
  • Use authentication and role based access for sensitive endpoints
  • Prefer network level restrictions if possible

Quick checklist for happy monitoring

  • Add spring boot starter actuator to your build
  • Limit management.endpoints.web.exposure.include to required endpoints
  • Export metrics to Prometheus via micrometer registry for long term observability
  • Protect endpoints with HTTP basic OAuth or network controls
  • Wire alerts to the metrics that matter and not to every single gauge that moves

Expect a tiny bit of configuration up front and a lot of peace of mind later. Also expect a modest ego boost when your dashboard finally tells you what happened without needing a detective hat.

title: Spring Boot Soap Web Service Example
description: Step by step guide to build a Spring Boot SOAP web service using WSDL JAXB and testing tips for Java developers
heading: Spring Boot Soap Web Service Example Tutorial
body:
Why bother with contract first

If you enjoy chaos then skip this tutorial and let clients guess the XML shape. If you prefer predictable services that do not explode in production then contract first is your friend. Define an XSD, generate JAXB classes, publish a WSDL and let clients stop making assumptions about your XML skills.

Project setup and dependencies

Create a Maven or Gradle project. Use Spring Initializr if you like avoiding painful dependency spelunking. Add the Spring Web Services support and a JAXB implementation. That is basically spring ws and a JAXB plugin so your build can generate Java classes from XSD at build time.

Define your XSD and generate JAXB classes

Design the XML schema that models requests and responses. Keep element names clear and use versioned namespaces so future changes do not break older clients. Then run the JAXB code generation step so the generated types match the schema. Using a maven plugin to generate sources at build time saves you from runtime surprises and from manually copying generated classes like it is 2005.

Configure Spring Web Services

Enable Spring WS support and register the servlet that dispatches SOAP messages. Expose a WSDL definition bean so the WSDL can be discovered by clients. Wire the XSD schema into the WSDL definition and map the service namespace to the endpoint handlers. If you avoid doing this you will spend evenings chasing namespace mismatches while drinking sad coffee.

Implement endpoint and service logic

Keep endpoint classes thin. Use an endpoint component to map incoming SOAP payloads to methods and then delegate business work to a service layer. This makes testing easier and reduces the number of crying debugging sessions. Use JAXB generated types in method signatures so marshalling and unmarshalling behave themselves.

Handler tips

  • Match namespace and local element names exactly to avoid mysterious no handler found errors.
  • Validate incoming XML against the schema if you want clear errors instead of stack traces.
  • Return SOAP faults for client errors and keep server errors for things that actually need attention.

Testing the SOAP service

Load the WSDL into a client like SOAP UI or Postman with SOAP support. Send requests that use the same namespace and element names defined in your XSD. Verify both success scenarios and fault handling. For production grade safety add integration tests that load the WSDL and exercise typical request and response cycles so future refactors do not quietly break clients.

Common gotchas and how to avoid them

  • Namespace mismatch between WSDL and generated classes. Keep namespaces versioned and consistent.
  • Incorrect package names from JAXB generation. Use bindings or plugin options to control package mapping.
  • Forgetting to publish the WSDL endpoint so clients can find the contract. Make sure the WSDL bean is exposed at a stable path.

Quick recap

Design a contract first XSD, generate JAXB classes, configure Spring Web Services and implement lean endpoints that delegate to a service layer. Test with a SOAP client and add integration tests that exercise the WSDL based flows. Follow these steps and you end up with a standards friendly Spring Boot SOAP service that behaves like an adult.

Now go make something that does not silently break your users and then celebrate with sensible unit tests.

title: SOAP Web Services in Spring #techtarget
description: Build SOAP web services with Spring covering WSDL generation endpoint mapping marshalling and testing with practical tips
heading: SOAP Web Services in Spring #techtarget Guide
body:
Why pick SOAP and Spring when REST looks cooler

SOAP still rules when you need strict contracts XML validation and enterprise features that will not quit. Spring Web Services gives you a neat toolkit to build WSDL driven services that play nicely with Java tooling and client generators. This guide walks you from project setup to a working endpoint with marshalling and WSDL generation and it will not lie to you about the amount of XML you will see.

Project setup and dependencies

Create a Spring Boot project and add Spring Web Services plus an XML binding library. Most teams use JAXB and the Jaxb2Marshaller bean. Use Maven or Gradle to declare these dependencies so you do not hand edit jar files like it is 2003.

Essential pieces

  • Spring Web Services starter
  • JAXB or a Jackson XML module for binding
  • Test tool such as SoapUI to exercise your operations

Design the schema and generate models

Design an XSD that describes request and response payloads. Keep it focused and versioned. Use JAXB or XJC to generate Java classes from the XSD so your code stays aligned with the contract. Generated classes save typing and reduce bugs caused by mismatched XML.

Configure the web service beans

Register a MessageDispatcherServlet and expose a DefaultWsdl11Definition bean. Provide an XsdSchema bean that points to your schema file. These beans make the WSDL available at a predictable URL so clients can discover your contract without asking nicely.

What the wiring does for you

  • Message dispatcher maps incoming SOAP messages to handlers
  • Default WSDL bean generates a WSDL based on your XSD and settings
  • Schema bean ties the WSDL to the physical XSD file

Implement endpoints and keep logic clean

Annotate endpoint classes with @Endpoint and map handler methods with @PayloadRoot. Make the endpoint a thin adapter that translates incoming XML to service calls. Put the real business rules in a separate service class so you can test logic without wrestling with XML.

Set up marshalling and WSDL generation

Provide a Jaxb2Marshaller bean or register a message converter that points to the generated package. Configure the marshaller with the generated classes so Spring WS can convert between XML and objects. The DefaultWsdl11Definition will then expose a WSDL that matches your schema and models.

Testing and securing the service

Run the app and test operations with SoapUI or a minimal Java client. Exercise edge cases and invalid XML so your schema validation works. For production lock things down with HTTPS and consider WS Security headers for message level protection. Always validate incoming XML against the schema to avoid mysterious parsing failures later.

Quick checklist for a healthy SOAP service

  • Contract first XSD and generated model classes
  • MessageDispatcherServlet and DefaultWsdl11Definition beans in place
  • Jaxb2Marshaller configured with the generated package
  • Endpoint classes annotated with @Endpoint and handler methods with @PayloadRoot
  • Tests using SoapUI or integration tests that call real endpoints
  • Transport or message security enabled for production

Parting truth

If you follow these steps you will have a maintainable contract first SOAP service that is easy to share and hard to break by accident. You will write a lot of XML. You will feel dangerously competent. And the clients will thank you when their tools generate code without screaming.

title: Spring Boot Logging Levels Configuration & Properties
description: Practical guide to Spring Boot logging levels configuration starter properties patterns paths and debug options for clearer logs
heading: Spring Boot Logging Levels Configuration & Properties Guide
body:
Quick summary

If your Spring Boot logs look like a blender full of stack traces and library chatter you can tame them with a few sensible logging level settings and pattern tweaks. This guide covers log levels, application properties, starter choices, logging pattern basics and quick runtime overrides for debugging without a rebuild. Keep calm and make your logs useful again.

Understand logging levels

Spring Boot uses standard log levels like TRACE DEBUG INFO WARN ERROR and OFF. Pick a global baseline like INFO and only raise verbosity for the packages you are actually investigating. That keeps your log files readable and your oncall team less grumpy.

Typical strategy

  • Set logging.level.root to INFO for normal runs
  • Use logging.level.com.yourapp to DEBUG or TRACE when you need details
  • Silence noisy third party libs with WARN

Configure application properties

Edit your application.properties or application.yml to control Spring Boot logging settings. Here are minimal examples for properties format. No magic, just plain text.

logging.level.root=INFO
logging.level.com.example=DEBUG
logging.file.name=application.log
logging.file.path=/var/log/myapp

If you prefer YAML the same keys map directly to application.yml. These properties are part of Spring Boot starter properties and take effect at startup.

Starter behavior and replacement

By default Spring Boot includes spring-boot-starter-logging which sets up Logback. Keep it for simple Logback usage. If you need advanced features swap in a Log4j2 starter by removing the default starter and adding spring-boot-starter-log4j2. That swap changes which config files and formats the framework expects so test it locally first.

Customize logging pattern and file paths

Patterns control timestamp thread level logger message and more. A compact console pattern might look like the example below. Tweak it until your eyes stop twitching.

logging.pattern.console=%d{yyyy-MM-dd} - %level - %logger - %msg%n

Choose logging.file.name for a specific filename or logging.file.path for a directory. Absolute paths work when the runtime container allows writes. If your container is read only then send logs to stdout and let the runtime collect them.

Runtime overrides for quick debugging

You do not need to rebuild to change levels when investigating live issues. Pass system properties at startup with the JVM option shown below or set environment variables. Command line and env values override packaged files which is convenient and slightly life saving.

java -Dlogging.level.com.example=TRACE -jar myapp.jar

Practical tips and checklist

  • Prefer package specific levels over global TRACE to avoid log spam
  • Silence noisy libraries by setting them to WARN or ERROR
  • Use console logging in containers and file logging in VM based services where you control disk
  • When swapping starters test all logging features since appenders and filters differ
  • Keep a small set of useful patterns so your logs are parseable by log aggregators

Wrap up

Tweaking Spring Boot logging is low effort and high reward. Adjust log levels in application.properties use starter choices consciously customize patterns and rely on runtime overrides for emergency debugging. Do this and your future self will thank you or at least stop swearing during the next midnight incident.

title: Java, JDBC & SQL Server Tutorial
description: Learn how to connect Java to SQL Server with the Microsoft JDBC driver URL pattern jar download and Maven setup for practical use
heading: Java JDBC and SQL Server Tutorial for Driver URL Jar and Maven
body:
This tutorial teaches how to connect Java applications to Microsoft SQL Server using the official JDBC driver manual jar or Maven dependency and how to run simple queries.

  1. Get the driver jar or add Maven dependency
  2. Add jar to project classpath or configure Maven
  3. Compose the connection URL and credentials
  4. Load the driver or allow DriverManager auto load
  5. Create connection statement and execute queries
  6. Handle exceptions and close resources

Get the driver jar or add Maven dependency Download the Microsoft JDBC driver from the official source or use Maven. A Maven dependency example looks like this

< dependency> < groupId> com.microsoft.sqlserver< /groupId> < artifactId> mssql-jdbc< /artifactId> < version> 10.2.0.jre11< /version> < /dependency>

Add jar to project classpath or configure Maven For simple projects drop the jar in the classpath. For modern builds prefer Maven. That removes manual jar juggling and reduces developer crying.

Compose the connection URL and credentials Use the SQL Server driver pattern. If documentation needs a colon or semicolon the friendly explanation is to use the driver prefix followed by server address and database name. For example write the driver prefix then COLON COLON then server slashes then SEMICOLON properties or follow the documented pattern on the Microsoft site. Use secure credentials and avoid hard coding passwords.

Load the driver or allow DriverManager auto load Explicit driver class loading can help on older JVMs. Use the driver class name com.microsoft.sqlserver.jdbc.SQLServerDriver when doing manual loading. Newer JVMs usually detect the driver from the jar service file.

Create connection statement and execute queries Use DriverManager to obtain a Connection then create a PreparedStatement for parameterized queries. Always check ResultSet and map columns carefully to Java types to avoid surprises.

Handle exceptions and close resources Use try with resources where possible to ensure Connection Statement and ResultSet close properly. Log SQL state and error codes when debugging.

The tutorial covered driver acquisition Maven setup connection URL form driver loading query execution and resource handling to get a Java application talking to SQL Server reliably while avoiding common pitfalls and painful runtime surprises.

Tip

Prefer Maven dependency for CI friendly builds and use PreparedStatement to avoid SQL injection and to make debugging less fun for attackers.

title: JDBC Connection Pooling with Hikari CP & Microsoft SQL Serve
description: Compact guide to set up HikariCP with Microsoft SQL Server for efficient JDBC connection pooling and better database performance.
heading: JDBC Connection Pooling with Hikari CP and Microsoft SQL Server
body:
This tutorial shows how to set up JDBC connection pooling with HikariCP and Microsoft SQL Server and why pooling matters for performance.

  1. Add dependencies and driver
  2. Create and configure HikariCP DataSource
  3. Use the DataSource in application code
  4. Tune pool settings and enable monitoring
  5. Test under load and measure results

Add dependencies and driver Use a build tool to include HikariCP and the Microsoft JDBC driver for SQL Server. If a framework like Spring Boot is present add the HikariCP starter where available. Avoid copying sample URLs with placeholder secrets into production repositories.

Create and configure HikariCP DataSource Instantiate a HikariDataSource and set basic properties such as driver class name database user and password plus maximum pool size and connection timeout. Prefer a DataSource object injected by the framework for lifecycle management rather than manual singletons.

Use the DataSource in application code Replace DriverManager calls with a DataSource lookup. Obtain a connection use JDBC statements or a higher level template and close the connection by calling close on the connection object. Closing returns the connection to the pool rather than tearing down a physical link to the database.

Tune pool settings and enable monitoring Start with conservative values for maximum pool size and minimum idle connections and adjust while observing application throughput. Enable metrics export with the HikariCP MBeans or integrate with Prometheus or whatever monitoring stack is already in place.

Test under load and measure results Run realistic load tests and measure latency and connection usage. Look for connection wait times and connection leaks. Address slow queries or long transactions before increasing pool sizes to avoid hiding underlying database issues.

This tutorial covered dependency inclusion DataSource configuration usage tuning and testing so that HikariCP can efficiently manage JDBC connections to Microsoft SQL Server and improve resource use and response times.

Tip

Enable connection leak detection when debugging and use monitoring metrics to guide pool size choices rather than guesswork.

title: Statements, JDBC & SQL Server Database Delete Commands
description: Quick guide to using JDBC Statements to run SQL Server delete commands safely with examples and tips for Java developers
heading: Statements JDBC and SQL Server Database Delete Commands
body:
This tutorial shows how to use JDBC Statement and PreparedStatement to execute SQL Server DELETE commands from Java while keeping safety and resource management in mind.

  1. Prepare environment and connection
  2. Choose PreparedStatement over Statement
  3. Execute delete and check result
  4. Manage transactions and handle exceptions
  5. Close resources properly

Prepare environment and connection

Install JDBC driver for SQL Server and obtain a valid connection from DriverManager or a DataSource. Use a configuration that keeps credentials out of source code and favors a connection pool for production workloads.

Choose PreparedStatement over Statement

Prefer PreparedStatement to prevent SQL injection and to allow parameter binding. A raw Statement may work for quick one off deletes but PreparedStatement is the grown up choice that plays nice with logs and plan caching.

Execute delete and check result

Use an update call to run the delete command and check the returned affected row count to confirm the expected changes. Example SQL in a safe form is shown here

DELETE FROM Users WHERE id = ?

Bind a numeric id using the PreparedStatement API and then call executeUpdate to get the affected row count. If the count equals zero consider whether the filter is correct or user input is wrong.

Manage transactions and handle exceptions

Wrap delete commands in a transaction when removing multiple rows across tables. Rollback on exception to avoid half done operations. Catch SQL exceptions and log enough context for debugging without leaking sensitive values.

Close resources properly

Always close PreparedStatement and Connection in a finally block or use try with resources to let Java handle cleanup. Leaked connections cause mysterious production drama that nobody enjoys.

This short guide covered setup execution and cleanup for running DELETE commands from Java against SQL Server while emphasizing safety and observability.

Tip

Use parameterized deletes and limit clauses to avoid accidental mass removal and test on a copy of the database before running on production.

title: Java, JDBC PreparedStatements, Update Commands & MS SQL
description: Run JDBC PreparedStatement update commands in Java against MS SQL Server with safe parameter binding and proper resource handling
heading: Java JDBC PreparedStatements Update Commands for MS SQL Server
body:
This tutorial shows how to use Java JDBC PreparedStatement to run update commands against MS SQL Server while avoiding SQL injection and managing resources properly.

  1. Get a connection
  2. Create a PreparedStatement
  3. Bind parameters
  4. Execute update
  5. Handle transactions and close resources

Get a connection

Obtain a java.sql.Connection from a connection pool such as HikariCP or from DriverManager in quick tests. Prefer a pool for production because manual connection management will cause fun outages faster than a misnamed column.

Create a PreparedStatement

Prepare the SQL with parameter placeholders. Use parameter markers rather than string concatenation to avoid SQL injection and mystery bugs. Example pseudo code

PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement("UPDATE users SET name = ? WHERE id = ?")

Bind parameters

Set parameters in the same order as markers. JDBC uses one based indexes so the first marker is index one. Example parameter setting

ps.setString(1, "Alice")

ps.setInt(2, 42)

Execute update

Call executeUpdate to run the change. The return value is an int that indicates how many rows changed which is handy for sanity checks

int rows = ps.executeUpdate()

Handle transactions and close resources

Decide on transaction boundaries. For multiple related updates turn off auto commit and call commit or rollback as needed. Always close PreparedStatement and Connection to avoid leaks. Using try with resources is the polite choice for code that wants to live long and prosper.

Summary of the workflow is simple and practical. Get a connection from a pool or manager. Prepare a statement with markers. Bind parameters carefully. Execute and check the affected row count. Manage transactions and close resources so the database remains your friend rather than a smoke machine for the app server.

Tip

Use batch updates for many similar changes and disable auto commit for grouped operations. That reduces round trips and keeps the transaction logic clear. Also log the SQL and parameter values in development but never log sensitive data in production.

title: JDBC ResultSet Example with the SQL Server Database
description: Compact guide to using JDBC ResultSet with SQL Server showing connection query iteration and resource cleanup for reliable Java database code
heading: JDBC ResultSet Example with SQL Server Database
body:
This tutorial shows how to use JDBC ResultSet with SQL Server to query rows handle results and close resources properly.

  1. Add JDBC driver and dependency
  2. Open a connection to SQL Server
  3. Create statement and execute query
  4. Iterate ResultSet and read columns
  5. Close resources or use try with resources

Add JDBC driver and dependency

Include the Microsoft JDBC driver in the project via Maven Gradle or manual jar placement. Confirm driver class name matches the driver jar version for compatibility with SQL Server.

Open a connection to SQL Server

Use DriverManager or a connection pool to obtain a Connection object. Prefer a pool for production to avoid frequent connection overhead and surprising slowdowns.

Create statement and execute query

Prefer PreparedStatement for parameterized queries to avoid SQL injection and to gain performance benefits from server side caching of execution plans.

Iterate ResultSet and read columns

Move the cursor with next and use typed getters such as getInt getString getTimestamp to retrieve column values. Use column labels rather than numeric indexes when clarity matters.

Close resources or use try with resources

Wrap Connection PreparedStatement and ResultSet in try with resources to ensure automatic cleanup and to prevent resource leaks that lead to exhausted pools and mysterious failures.

Example pseudo code for a simple query

Class Example { public static void runQuery() { Class.forName("com Microsoft sqlserver jdbc SQLServerDriver") String url = "jdbc sqlserver //localhost databaseName MyDb" try Connection conn = DriverManager.getConnection(url "user" "pass") { PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement("SELECT id name FROM people") ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery() while rs.next() { int id = rs.getInt("id") String name = rs.getString("name") } } } }

Summary recap of the tutorial The steps cover adding a driver opening a connection preparing and executing a query iterating a ResultSet and ensuring proper resource cleanup for robust database access in Java.

Tip

Use a connection pool and always prefer PreparedStatement for repeated queries and parameters to improve performance and security while reducing code drama.

title: Create a Table in Microsoft SQL Server for JDBC with Java
description: Step by step guide to create a SQL Server table from Java using JDBC with clear steps and a safe CREATE TABLE example
heading: Create a Table in Microsoft SQL Server for JDBC with Java
body:
This tutorial teaches how to create a table in Microsoft SQL Server using JDBC from Java with a safe DDL approach and simple connection steps.

  1. Add the JDBC driver and project dependency
  2. Create a database connection
  3. Prepare and execute a CREATE TABLE statement
  4. Close resources and handle exceptions
  5. Verify the new table

Step 1 Add the JDBC driver and project dependency by including the Microsoft JDBC driver in the build tool of choice or by placing the driver jar on the classpath. The driver class registers itself with the driver manager so the code can request connections.

Step 2 Create a database connection using proper credentials and a JDBC URL adapted for SQL Server with hostname port and database name. Use secure credential management and avoid hard coding secrets in source files. Prefer try with resources for automatic cleanup of the connection object.

Step 3 Prepare and execute a CREATE TABLE statement using a Statement or PreparedStatement. Example DDL can look like this

CREATE TABLE Users ( Id INT PRIMARY KEY, Username VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, CreatedAt DATETIME2 )

Use executeUpdate on the statement object to run DDL. If schema changes need parameters use dynamic SQL carefully and validate names to prevent injection of malicious SQL.

Step 4 Close resources and handle exceptions by catching SQL exceptions and logging meaningful messages. Use try with resources blocks to avoid resource leaks and to keep code readable. Clean connection pooling will improve performance for repeated DDL or DML actions.

Step 5 Verify the new table with a select from the system catalog or by opening the database in SQL Server Management Studio. A quick query against INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES confirms presence of the new table name.

The tutorial covered adding the driver and dependency creating a connection preparing and executing DDL closing resources and verifying the table with minimal fuss. Follow these steps and the database will gain a new table without drama unless the server objects object to the schema choice which then requires mild negotiation with the DBA.

Tip

When testing schema changes prefer a development database and a rollback plan. Wrap DDL in a migration framework for repeatable deployments and human sanity preservation.

title: CRUD Operations in Sqlite3
description: Learn how to create an Sqlite3 database create tables insert select update and delete records with clear commands and examples
heading: CRUD Operations in Sqlite3 Explained
body:
Why bother with SQLite3

If you need a tiny persistent sqlite database that does not require server setup or an MBA in devops then SQLite3 is your friend that shows up with coffee and no attitude. This guide walks through create table insert select update and delete operations while keeping things practical and slightly sarcastic. You will learn the basic SQL CRUD commands that actually matter for prototypes small apps and teaching your code to behave.

Quick setup and first table

Open or create a file backed database with the sqlite3 command line tool. That single command is all you need to start messing with data.

sqlite3 mydb.db

Define a table schema with a normal SQL statement. Here is a simple users table that is easy to reason about.

CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, email TEXT)

Core CRUD commands

CRUD stands for create read update delete. Say it like a spell and then run these queries.

Create rows

INSERT INTO users (name, email) VALUES ('Alice', 'alice@example.com')

Batch multiple inserts inside a transaction for performance and fewer regrets.

Read rows

SELECT * FROM users
SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE email LIKE '%example.com' LIMIT 10

Use WHERE to filter and LIMIT when you want fewer lines in the terminal and less crying.

Update rows

UPDATE users SET email = 'new@example.com' WHERE id = 1

Always double check the WHERE clause. One missing condition can turn a targeted edit into a tragic rewrite of your table.

Delete rows

DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 1

Prefer safe deletes during development. You can test with SELECT first to avoid accidental mass deletion.

Transactions and integrity

Wrap grouped writes in a transaction to get atomic behavior and an escape hatch during development. Use BEGIN and COMMIT to bracket the important parts.

BEGIN
INSERT INTO users (name, email) VALUES ('Bob', 'bob@example.com')
UPDATE users SET email = 'bob@newdomain.com' WHERE name = 'Bob'
COMMIT

If things go sideways use ROLLBACK to undo changes before you push anything to production or to your ego. Enable foreign keys to avoid subtle relational bugs with this pragma.

PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON

Best practices and tips

  • Keep backups. Your sqlite database is a file, so copy it before big migrations.
  • Use parameterized queries in your application code to avoid SQL injection and weird bugs.
  • Test destructive statements with a select first to confirm the affected rows.
  • Batch writes in a transaction for speed and fewer lonely commits.

Verify and exit

After changes, run simple select queries to verify results. When you are done type the sqlite shell command to leave.

.exit

There you go. You now know how to create an sqlite3 database define tables insert select update and delete rows while keeping data integrity in mind. Use transactions and foreign key support to prevent subtle problems and treat backups like a security blanket for grown ups.

title: DB Browser SQLite Viewer Manage Data Types and CRUD
description: Quick guide to DB Browser for SQLite covering data types, CREATE TABLE SQL and inserting records for CRUD work
heading: DB Browser SQLite Viewer Manage Data Types and CRUD
body:
Welcome to the DB Browser for SQLite crash course

If you want to manage data types run CREATE TABLE SQL and do basic CRUD without crying then this tutorial is for you. We will use DB Browser for SQLite as the database viewer and database tools to inspect schemas insert records and verify behavior. No mystery wizardry required just a few clicks and some SQL muscle.

Open the database and know where to look

Launch DB Browser for SQLite and open an existing file or create a new database. The left pane shows tables and the tabbed area contains tabs like Database Structure Browse Data and Execute SQL. This is where you will view column definitions edit rows and run statements. It is also where typos become memorable.

Quick tour of useful tabs

  • Database Structure to inspect tables columns and indexes.
  • Browse Data to add or edit rows in a spreadsheet like view.
  • Execute SQL to paste or run CREATE TABLE and INSERT statements for scripted work or testing.

Pick the right SQLite data types and why it matters

SQLite uses typed columns but it is forgiving. Still you should choose proper types like INTEGER TEXT REAL BLOB or NUMERIC so sorting storage and affinity behave predictably. For example use INTEGER for ids that you will increment and TEXT for names and emails. If you try to store a picture use BLOB and accept the chaos.

Type advice you will actually use

  • INTEGER for primary keys and counters.
  • TEXT for freeform strings such as names and emails.
  • REAL for floating point numbers when precision is not your religion.
  • BLOB for binary data where file systems might judge you later.
  • NUMERIC for values you want SQLite to attempt to coerce to numbers.

Run CREATE TABLE SQL the honest way

Switch to Execute SQL and paste a CREATE TABLE statement. If you prefer GUI form creators that is fine but pasting SQL is faster and more repeatable. Example usage for a simple users table.

CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, email TEXT)

Press Execute SQL and watch the new table appear in Database Structure. If it does not show up hit Refresh or reopen the database and then try tea and deep breathing.

Insert records with Browse Data or Execute SQL

You have two reasonable paths to add rows. The Browse Data tab is a friendly spreadsheet like editor for quick manual edits. Execute SQL is better for scripted inserts tests and constraints. Choose your adventure.

Insert examples you can copy

INSERT INTO users (name, email) VALUES ('Alice', 'alice@example.com')

Or use the Browse Data tab to click New Record fill cells and then move on with your life.

Save changes and verify CRUD behavior

When you are done editing press the Write Changes button to persist edits. DB Browser stages changes in memory so failing to write is the classic whoops moment. After saving perform reads updates and deletes to confirm application behavior and constraints.

Simple read update and delete commands

SELECT * FROM users
UPDATE users SET email = 'alice@newdomain.com' WHERE id = 1
DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 1

Run these in Execute SQL or use the Browse Data UI. Check that foreign keys behave as expected if your schema has them. If you need foreign key enforcement run the PRAGMA statement and test again.

Tips tricks and common pitfalls

  • Always back up the .sqlite file before sweeping changes with SQL. Version control is your friend even if databases are messy.
  • Use meaningful column names and add indexes only when you measure a performance problem.
  • Remember that SQLite will accept odd values but that does not mean your application will be happy about it.
  • Prefer Execute SQL for repeatable database changes and Browse Data for quick manual fixes.

That is the gist of using DB Browser for SQLite as a database viewer and database tool for basic CRUD workflows. You inspected data types created a table inserted rows and verified behavior. Go forth and make sensible schemas or at least funny test data.

body:
This tutorial shows how to run Jenkins from a Docker image and create a basic Jenkins pipeline for building and testing code.

  1. Pull the Jenkins Docker image
  2. Start the Jenkins container with a persistent volume
  3. Unlock the Jenkins server and install recommended plugins
  4. Create a pipeline job and add a Jenkinsfile
  5. Run the pipeline and examine build logs

Pull the Jenkins Docker image Use a simple pull command to fetch the official Jenkins image from the registry. The download provides a ready to run server that avoids manual package installs and dependency drama.

Start the Jenkins container Run the container with a mounted volume for persistent job and plugin data. Mapping host storage keeps pipeline history safe from casual container recycling and accidental deletions.

Unlock the Jenkins server On first start the Jenkins server requires an initial admin password found in the container logs or in the home volume. Use the password to create an admin user and install the recommended plugin set unless customization mood strikes.

Create a pipeline job In the Jenkins UI create a new pipeline project and link a repository or paste a pipeline script. The easiest path is a declarative Jenkinsfile stored next to source code so CI follows the code.

Run the pipeline Trigger a build from the dashboard or a push hook. Watch the console output for stages such as checkout build test and archive. Logs reveal failing commands and missing environment setup with brutal honesty.

The steps above get a working Jenkins server inside a container and a simple pipeline that compiles and tests code. This approach keeps the setup repeatable and portable and avoids pain when moving between machines or team members.

Tip

Keep a Jenkinsfile in the repo Storing the pipeline definition with the code makes CI changes peer reviewed and version controlled. Use lightweight stages and clear agent labels to avoid long running jobs on wrong nodes.

title: Jenkins Docker Image Tutorial #TechTarget
description: Learn how to build run and configure a Jenkins Docker image for CI pipelines with Dockerfile volumes and basic production tips.
heading: Jenkins Docker Image Tutorial #TechTarget
body:
Why start with the official Jenkins image

Pick the official Jenkins image unless you enjoy mystery dependency bugs at 2 a.m. The official images are maintained, include the right Java runtime, and play nicer with plugins. If you prefer tiny images and want to assemble your own stack go ahead, just be ready to fix whatever breaks.

Dockerfile essentials that will save you time

Keep the Dockerfile small and repeatable. Key points to hit in your build file are plugin installation, a non root runtime user, and copying only what you need. Use build arguments for versions and plugin lists so your CI builds are predictable.

Minimal example

FROM jenkins/jenkins:lts
USER root
COPY plugins.txt /usr/share/jenkins/ref/plugins.txt
RUN jenkins-plugin-cli --plugin-file /usr/share/jenkins/ref/plugins.txt
COPY init.groovy.d /var/jenkins_home/init.groovy.d
USER jenkins

This pattern lets the official image handle the heavy lifting while you layer on plugins and safe startup scripts. Use jenkins-plugin-cli for bulk installs and pass versions with build args if you care about reproducible builds.

Build the image and keep it sane

Build with a clear tag so you know what you ran last weekend. Watch logs for missing dependencies and fail fast.

docker build -t myorg/jenkins:custom -f Dockerfile .

Consider using a CI pipeline to run the build and publish to an image registry. That way your human brain does not have to remember which tag has the hotfix.

Run the container without destroying the host

Run with port mapping, a restart policy, resource limits, and persistent storage. Named volumes are your friend for portability and backups.

docker run -d \
  --name jenkins \
  -p 8080:8080 -p 50000:50000 \
  -v jenkins_home:/var/jenkins_home \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  --memory=2g --cpus=1 \
  myorg/jenkins:custom

Set CPU and memory limits so a runaway build does not eat your laptop or server while you stare at the console wondering what went wrong.

Configure Jenkins like a grown up

Open the web UI on the mapped port and use the initial admin secret in /var/jenkins_home/secrets/initialAdminPassword. Install recommended plugins if you want the easy path, or supply a plugins.txt and preinstall them in the image so your instance boots ready for action.

Automate configuration

  • Use the Configuration as Code plugin to store job templates and security settings in YAML.
  • Seed jobs with Job DSL or pipeline templates to avoid click fest labor.
  • Keep credentials in the Jenkins credential store, not in environment variables or Dockerfiles.

Persistence and backups

Mount a volume at /var/jenkins_home so jobs, credentials, and plugins survive restarts. Regularly export backups of that directory and test restores because backups that you never test are just digital wishful thinking.

Backup tips

  • Use named volumes for portability across hosts.
  • Schedule periodic volume exports or use your storage provider snapshot features.
  • Keep a copy of critical config like credentials.xml and your JCasC YAML files in a secure repo.

Security and production readiness

A few common sense steps will keep your Jenkins from becoming a public sandbox for bots. Put Jenkins behind a reverse proxy that handles TLS and authentication, enable CSRF protection, and restrict who can install plugins. Rotate admin credentials and avoid placing secrets in environment variables.

Reverse proxy options

  • Nginx or Traefik for TLS termination and basic auth or OAuth integration.
  • Use network policies or firewall rules to limit access to the Jenkins port.

Production checklist that will save you grief

  • Use an official base image or well documented minimal image
  • Build reproducible images via build args and locked plugin versions
  • Run with named volumes for /var/jenkins_home and test restores
  • Limit resources and set a restart policy
  • Automate config with Configuration as Code and seed jobs with Job DSL
  • Use a reverse proxy for TLS and authenticate external access

Final thoughts

Building a Jenkins Docker image is not rocket science, but it is craft. Pick sensible defaults, automate what you can, back up what matters, and secure the instance before you add ten thousand freestyle jobs. If something goes wrong you can always blame a plugin, but try to avoid that as a debugging strategy.

seo_heading: Practical Jenkins Dockerfile guide for CI CD with persistence and security

title: Modern SOAP Web Services in Java with Jakarta EE
description: Build modern SOAP web services in Java using Jakarta EE with practical steps examples testing and deployment tips for developers
heading: Modern SOAP Web Services in Java with Jakarta EE Guide
body:
This tutorial shows how to build modern SOAP web services in Java using Jakarta EE and common tools for development and deployment.

  1. Project setup
  2. Define WSDL and models
  3. Implement endpoint
  4. Deploy and test
  5. Secure and monitor

Project setup Choose Maven or Gradle and add Jakarta XML Web Services and JAXB dependencies. Pick an application server such as Payara Open Liberty or WildFly for quick Jakarta EE integration. Keep dependency versions current to avoid dependency hell that looks suspiciously like legacy software archaeology.

Define WSDL and models Prefer a contract first approach for long term compatibility. Design the WSDL and XSD and generate Java bindings with tools such as wsimport or equivalent Jakarta tooling. Generated classes keep message formats strict and reduce surprises when clients appear and demand exact XML.

Implement endpoint Annotate the endpoint with @WebService and implement business methods. Use SOAP handlers for header processing and logging. Keep service logic separate from message handling to preserve testability and to avoid turning the endpoint into a monster class that no team wants to maintain.

Deploy and test Deploy the archive to the chosen server and verify the published WSDL. Test with SoapUI Postman or curl using XML payloads. Inspect request and response envelopes and adjust namespaces and bindings when schemas disagree. Automated integration tests that call the published WSDL save future debugging time.

Secure and monitor Apply WS Security policies for authentication signatures and encryption and run the service over HTTPS. Add access controls and use server metrics and logs for runtime visibility. Monitoring catches performance issues before angry customers arrive.

This guide covered creating a project defining the contract implementing the endpoint deploying for testing and adding security and monitoring. Following these steps produces a maintainable modern SOAP service built on Jakarta EE and ready for production traffic.

Tip

Prefer contract first and include a human readable WSDL version in source control. Generate client stubs for consumer teams and enable WS Security policies rather than ad hoc header handling for consistent authentication and interoperability.

title: Introduction to SQLite3 Tutorial for Beginners
description: Learn SQLite3 basics with hands on steps for database creation queries and Python integration to get started fast
heading: Introduction to SQLite3 Tutorial for Beginners
body:
Welcome to the tiny world of SQLite3 where a single file can pretend to be a database server and do it with less drama than your last group project. This short sqlite tutorial walks beginners through installing the tools creating a local database running queries and connecting from Python sqlite code without tripping over obvious mistakes.

Getting started with SQLite3

SQLite3 is a light weight SQL database engine that lives in a single file. It is perfect for local apps prototypes and tests where spinning up a server would be overkill. You will learn how to create a database create tables insert and query rows and then access the same file from Python.

Step 1 Install SQLite3

Use your system package manager or download a prebuilt binary for Windows. Confirm the client is available with a quick version check.

sqlite3 --version

Step 2 Create a database file and inspect it

Create or open a file from the shell and use the built in dot commands for fast introspection.

sqlite3 mydb.db

Inside the sqlite shell try

  • .tables to see tables
  • .schema users to view a table definition

Step 3 Create a table and add rows with SQL

SQL syntax is familiar. Here is a tiny table definition and an insert example for beginners who like concrete toys to play with.

CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)
INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES ('Alice')

From application code always use parameterized statements to avoid SQL injection and to let the engine optimize queries. In sqlite and Python use the question mark placeholder.

Step 4 Query data like a human

Basic queries are simple and useful. Use WHERE to filter order by to sort and limit to avoid returning the entire planet.

SELECT * FROM users
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = 'Alice'
SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 10

Accessing SQLite from Python

The standard library includes sqlite3 so you do not need to pip install anything unless you want fancier drivers. Here is the minimal pattern you will repeat forever.

import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect('mydb.db')
cur = conn.cursor()
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM users")
rows = cur.fetchall()
conn.commit()
conn.close()

To insert safely from Python use parameterized queries like this

cur.execute("INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES (?)", ("Bob",))

Performance and concurrency tips

SQLite is fast but it is still a single file. Enable write ahead logging for better concurrency and fewer locking surprises.

PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL

Other tips to keep things smooth

  • Use indexes on columns you filter by often to speed up queries
  • Limit the number of rows returned when you do not need everything
  • Use transactions to batch writes and reduce disk churn
  • Prefer parameterized statements to avoid SQL injection and to let SQLite reuse query plans

Common pitfalls and how to avoid them

Beginners often forget to call commit after writes or to close the connection when finished. Both of those things will make your data feel abandoned. Also avoid building SQL by concatenating strings with user input. That is an invitation for disaster.

Wrap up and next steps

You now have the essentials to create a local sqlite database run SQL queries and talk to that file from Python. If you want to learn sqlite deeper try indexing query planning and the various PRAGMA options. For production like workloads consider a client server database but for quick projects sqlite3 will save you time and sanity.

Happy hacking and may your transactions commit and your locks be brief.

seo_heading: How to install SQLite3 run SQL queries and access data from Python safely

title: Spring Batch Tutorial for Beginners | Spring Boot
description: Learn Spring Batch basics with Spring Boot batch architecture patterns practical steps and sample components for building robust batch jobs
heading: Spring Batch Tutorial for Beginners Spring Boot
body:
This tutorial shows how to use Spring Batch with Spring Boot to design jobs readers processors and writers that run reliably.

  1. Create a Spring Boot project and add batch dependencies
  2. Define Job Step and flow using JobBuilderFactory and StepBuilderFactory
  3. Implement ItemReader ItemProcessor and ItemWriter
  4. Configure JobRepository JobLauncher transactions and meta tables
  5. Run test jobs monitor execution and tune chunk size and retry policies

Step 1 Create a Spring Boot project with spring-boot-starter-batch and a JDBC driver. Use Spring Initializr or a build file. Configure a DataSource and apply the Spring Batch schema to enable meta data storage.

Step 2 Define a Job that contains one or more Steps. Each Step handles a chunk oriented or tasklet style workload. Use JobBuilderFactory and StepBuilderFactory to compose the flow and add listeners for lifecycle events.

Step 3 Implement an ItemReader to pull records from a source. Implement an ItemProcessor to transform or validate a record. Implement an ItemWriter to persist results. This separation makes the system testable and slightly less likely to explode at 2 AM.

Step 4 Configure JobRepository and JobLauncher so the framework can store execution state and restart jobs after failures. Set up transaction management and isolation appropriate for the data source and concurrency model.

Step 5 Execute jobs locally then on a staging environment. Monitor execution using logs or a dashboard and tune chunk size retry and skip policies to balance throughput and stability. Add partitioning or remote step execution when scaling beyond a single node.

The tutorial covers project setup job and step composition core reader processor writer patterns and foundational configuration for storing and launching batch executions. Following these steps yields a maintainable batch pipeline ready for testing and scaling.

Tip

Pick a sensible chunk size based on record size and transaction cost. Too small wastes overhead and too large risks memory or retry nightmares. Measure throughput and tune rather than guessing.

title: Spring Boot File Upload REST API Example
description: Build a Spring Boot file upload REST API with multipart handling validation storage and easy testing tips for developers
heading: Spring Boot File Upload REST API Example Guide
body:
This tutorial shows how to build a Spring Boot REST API that accepts file uploads using multipart handling with validation and storage options

  1. Generate project and add dependencies
  2. Create upload controller endpoint
  3. Implement storage service and validation
  4. Configure multipart settings and error handling
  5. Test with curl or Postman

Generate a Maven or Gradle project and include Spring Web and optionally Spring Boot Starter Test for unit checks. Adding a storage dependency such as Apache Commons IO helps with file handling. No fireworks required, just sensible dependencies.

Create a controller that exposes a POST endpoint. Use an annotation such as @PostMapping("/upload") and accept MultipartFile file as a parameter. The controller should call a service that performs the heavy lifting so the controller stays tidy and not dramatic.

Implement a storage service that saves files to disk or cloud storage. Validate file content type and size before saving. For example check the content type string and file length then throw a custom exception for bad requests. This keeps the API predictable and not full of surprises.

Configure multipart settings in application properties by setting sensible maximum file size and request size. Add exception handlers for multipart exceptions and validation failures so the API returns clear error responses and humans can understand what went wrong.

Test the endpoint with curl or Postman. Example curl command uses form data with the file field name matching the controller parameter. Automated tests can mock MultipartFile and assert service behavior so regressions do not sneak into production.

This guide covered project setup endpoint creation storage and validation plus configuration and testing. Following these steps results in a robust file upload API that handles bad inputs gracefully and stores files where developers expect.

Tip

Prefer storing file metadata in a database and files on a dedicated storage layer. This separates concerns and makes backups and scaling far less painful.

title: How to Create a Maven Project in Eclipse for Beginners
description: Step by step guide to create a Maven project in Eclipse using basic POM and archetype approaches for beginners
heading: How to Create a Maven Project in Eclipse in Beginners Guide
body:
This tutorial walks through creating a Maven project in Eclipse using a basic POM approach and an archetype approach for beginners while keeping pain levels low.

  1. Open Eclipse and start the Maven project wizard
  2. Choose a workspace and pick an archetype or an empty project
  3. Set groupId artifactId and version
  4. Finish the wizard and inspect the generated project
  5. Edit the POM to add dependencies and plugins
  6. Build and run using Maven goals or the IDE run options

Open Eclipse and start the Maven project wizard

Launch the IDE and select new Maven project from the new project menu. If m2e is missing install the Maven integration plugin from the marketplace. The wizard is surprisingly friendly when fed reasonable values.

Choose a workspace and pick an archetype or an empty project

Select a workspace folder and then pick either an archetype such as maven archet ype quickstart for a ready made skeleton or choose a simple project for manual POM crafting. Archetypes save typing and future regret.

Set groupId artifactId and version

Use a reverse domain style groupId such as com.example and a clear artifactId for the project. Version defaults to 1.0 snapshot and packaging usually remains jar for libraries and war for web modules.

Finish the wizard and inspect the generated project

The IDE generates a folder structure and a pom.xml file. Open the POM file and check the declared coordinates and the dependency management section. The POM is the brain of the build system.

Edit the POM to add dependencies and plugins

Add dependencies by their groupId artifactId and version and declare plugins for compilation testing and packaging. Use the IDE quick fix suggestions to resolve common problems.

Build and run using Maven goals or the IDE run options

Execute a quick build using the command line command inside the project folder using mvn clean package or use Run as Maven build from the IDE. Check the target folder for the produced jar or war.

This guide covered launching the Maven project wizard selecting an archetype or manual POM setup configuring core coordinates inspecting the generated project editing the POM for dependencies and plugins and finally building the project to produce an artifact. Follow these steps and the Maven project will behave more like a predictable pet than a mysterious gremlin.

Tip

Keep a minimal POM template in a notes file with common dependencies and plugin snippets. Copy paste avoids remembering groupIds and stops the afternoon wasted on version mismatch hunting.

Quick truth about this tutorial

title: What exactly is Pascal case?
description: Clear definition of Pascal case with examples rules and when to use in code for classes types and public APIs
heading: What exactly is Pascal case?
body:
Quick definition you can actually use

PascalCase is a naming convention where each word starts with a capital letter and there are no separators. Think MyClass UserName and GetValue. It is the default look for class names and exported types in languages like C# Java and Go. If a name needs to be readable and part of a public surface then PascalCase is usually your friend.

Where developers actually use PascalCase

Short answer, for things that other code or users will see. Long answer, for types classes constructors enums and any exported symbols in a module. In C# you will see it for public classes and properties. In Go exported identifiers start with a capital letter and by convention use PascalCase for multiword names.

Core rules that avoid embarrassment

  • Capitalize the first letter of every word including the first word
  • Use no underscores spaces or hyphens between words
  • For acronyms follow your team style guide because XMLParser and XmlParser both exist in the wild
  • Do not start with a lowercase letter like camelCase does

PascalCase versus camelCase in plain English

PascalCase starts with an uppercase letter. camelCase starts with a lowercase letter. Pick PascalCase for types and public API names. Pick camelCase for locals private fields or function parameters when your style guide asks for it. This keeps the intent obvious and your reviewers happier than they have to be.

Tools and tips to keep names consistent

Do not rely on hope. Configure linters and formatters to catch violations before a human has to pretend code review is fun. Most modern editors and build systems can flag bad names and offer quick fixes. Add a rule that enforces PascalCase for exported symbols and watch bikeshedding fall by at least 80 percent.

Practical gotchas and best practices

  • When renaming public API elements use semantic versioning friendly strategies so you do not break users
  • Decide once per project how to handle acronyms and stick to it
  • Use automated refactoring when you can to avoid accidental misspellings
  • Document your naming conventions in the project style guide to stop future arguments

In short, PascalCase is a tidy predictable way to name things that are meant to be seen outside a local scope. It does not solve all problems but it spares your team from at least one kind of chaos. Use tooling enforce rules and try to keep naming fights to a minimum unless you enjoy arguing about the capitalization of URI.

title: Spring vs Spring Boot vs Framework What's the difference?
description: Concise comparison of Spring Spring Boot and Spring Framework to guide developers on scope configuration and when to choose each option
heading: Spring vs Spring Boot vs Framework What's the difference?
body:
Quick overview - what each thing actually does

Short version with attitude and facts. Spring Framework is the low level toolkit that gives you dependency injection and fine grained control over wiring and lifecycle in Java applications. Spring Boot is the productivity layer that hides a lot of wiring behind auto configuration and starter dependencies so you can ship microservices faster and with fewer headaches. The Spring ecosystem includes Spring Data Spring Security and Spring Cloud which plug into either option and solve persistence security and distributed system concerns without you reinventing the wheel.

When to pick the framework and when to pick Boot

If you are building a library or need exact control over which classes get loaded and how beans are created reach for the core Spring Framework. If you are building microservices prototypes or a production service that needs fast iteration and sensible defaults Spring Boot is the obvious cheat code. Both are Java friendly and both use dependency injection but they trade off control for convenience in different places.

Common scenarios

  • Greenfield microservice that needs quick time to market choose Spring Boot
  • Legacy monolith where you need precise lifecycle hooks choose Spring Framework pieces and explicit configuration
  • Team wants batteries included and production features with minimal setup choose Boot with starters and embedded server
  • Need to tune every class and optimize footprint go core Spring and pick dependencies carefully

Configuration and debugging realities

With the Spring Framework you will write beans and Java config classes or XML if you like nostalgia. With Spring Boot many common settings appear through starter dependencies and auto configuration so you remove boilerplate. This convenience hides wiring details which can slow debugging when something goes wrong. Learn to read auto configuration reports and actuator endpoints so you stop blaming the framework and start fixing your code.

Performance and footprint

Neither label guarantees lean runtime. Performance depends on the dependencies you include. Spring Boot apps can be very lean when you exclude unused starters and trim transitive libraries. The core Spring Framework gives you the ability to control every loaded artifact if you need the smallest possible attack surface or memory usage.

How the ecosystem fits in

Want database glue use Spring Data. Need auth use Spring Security. Building cloud native systems use Spring Cloud. These projects integrate with the core framework or with Spring Boot so you can mix and match. In practice most teams start with Spring Boot and then write explicit Spring Framework style configuration for performance sensitive or security critical parts.

Decision checklist

  • Project type Is this an app or a library
  • Speed Do you need fast iteration or absolute control
  • Team skill Are people comfortable with Spring internals
  • Deployment Do you need embedded servers or custom containers
  • Dependencies Will you rely on Spring Data or Spring Cloud

Practical tip

Start with Spring Boot for speed of delivery and readable defaults. When you hit a bottleneck extract that piece into explicit Spring Framework style configuration and keep the productivity where it helps most. That way you get the best of both worlds and fewer late night bug hunts.

seo_heading: A practical guide to dependency injection auto configuration and Spring projects

title: Spring Batch Tutorial | Spring Boot | ItemProcessor
description: Compact Spring Batch guide for Spring Boot covering ItemProcessor patterns job design and practical steps for ETL
heading: Spring Batch Tutorial with Spring Boot ItemProcessor and Batch Architecture
body:
If you like reliable data moves that do not mysteriously duplicate rows or corrupt a table at 3 AM then welcome. This guide shows how to assemble a Spring Boot project with Spring Batch and an ItemProcessor so your ETL work behaves itself. You will see how readers, processors and writers fit into chunk processing and how to keep restarts sane.

Getting the project ready

Create a Spring Boot app and add the Spring Batch starter and a JDBC driver for a job repository. Spring Boot will auto configure many beans so you do not need to write ceremony code. Use a separate schema for Spring Batch metadata so the framework can track job and step executions with less drama.

Job and step configuration

Declare your Job and Step beans and pick a chunk size that balances memory and latency. Chunk processing controls how many items are read and processed before a write and it also sets the transaction boundary. Smaller chunks lower memory use and shorten the window of work that must be retried. Larger chunks improve throughput when the writer is heavy.

Tips for chunk sizing

  • Start small while iterating on correctness
  • Increase chunk size when writes are the bottleneck
  • Watch memory and transaction timeout settings in your database

Choose the right ItemReader

Pick a reader that matches your source. Use FlatFileItemReader for CSV work and JdbcPagingItemReader for database reads. Map raw fields into a DTO so your processor gets a clean, predictable object to transform. Paging readers avoid loading whole tables into memory which is a good thing unless you enjoy OutOfMemoryException parties.

Keep the ItemProcessor small and testable

The ItemProcessor is where mapping validation and enrichment happens. Keep processors stateless and focused on one job. Smaller processors are easier to unit test and scale better under parallel execution. If you need to call an external service from the processor then design for retries and idempotency so partial failures do not create duplicate side effects.

Processor best practices

  • Return null to filter an item out rather than throwing when appropriate
  • Prefer pure functions that map input DTO to output DTO for easy testing
  • Do not keep heavy resources open inside the processor

Efficient ItemWriter patterns

Batch writers group writes for efficiency. For relational targets use JdbcBatchItemWriter. For HTTP APIs write a custom writer that batches requests and handles retries intelligently. Always aim for idempotent writes so retries do not double post or corrupt state.

JobRepository and restart behavior

Configure a persistent job repository so Spring Batch can resume work after a crash. The framework stores execution metadata so completed chunks do not run again on restart. Tune transaction timeouts to match long running operations and avoid excessive locking on the database.

Testing failures and monitoring

Simulate partial failures and test restart paths. Verify that skipped items, retries and rollbacks behave as expected. Expose metrics for step durations processed counts and error rates so operations teams can respond without poking the codebase with a wrench.

What to include in tests

  1. Unit tests for the processor to validate mapping and filtering logic
  2. Integration tests that exercise the reader processor writer chain with a controlled data set
  3. Failure injection tests to confirm restart and retry behavior

Wrap up and practical checklist

If you follow these patterns your Spring Batch jobs will be easier to reason about and less likely to cause weekend incident calls. Here is a quick checklist to copy into your project README and maybe tattoo on your laptop if you are that committed.

  • Use Spring Boot starter for Spring Batch and configure a dedicated job repository schema
  • Choose the correct reader for the source format and map into DTOs
  • Keep ItemProcessor stateless and unit tested
  • Batch writes and design for idempotency
  • Set reasonable chunk size and tune transaction timeouts
  • Simulate failures and expose step metrics to ops

Now go build your pipeline and let the computer do the boring heavy lifting while you enjoy coffee and the illusion of control.

seo_heading: Design chunk based ETL pipelines in Spring Boot with ItemProcessor patterns

title: Spring Boot, JPA and Hibernate Example
description: Hands on Spring Boot example showing JPA and Hibernate setup for CRUD operations and configuration best practices
heading: Spring Boot JPA and Hibernate Example Explained
body:
This tutorial teaches how to build a Spring Boot application using JPA and Hibernate for CRUD operations with a relational database.

  1. Create a Spring Boot project with required dependencies
  2. Configure datasource and JPA properties
  3. Define entity classes and mappings
  4. Create Spring Data JPA repositories
  5. Implement service layer for transactions
  6. Build REST controllers for CRUD endpoints
  7. Run application and test endpoints

Generate a Maven or Gradle project using start.spring.io or an IDE wizard. Add dependencies for spring boot starter data jpa and the JDBC driver for the chosen database.

Set datasource properties in application properties or application yml. Provide database URL username and password and configure dialect and hibernate settings to match the chosen RDBMS.

Create entity classes annotated with @Entity and map fields with @Id @GeneratedValue and @Column where needed. Pay attention to relationships and choose fetch strategies to avoid surprise N plus one queries.

Define repositories by extending JpaRepository or CrudRepository. Spring Data JPA will generate common queries so less boilerplate code appears in the project.

Implement a service layer annotated with @Service and use @Transactional where transactions matter. Keep business logic out of controllers and avoid direct database calls in web handlers.

Create REST controllers with mappings for create read update and delete endpoints. Use response entity objects and proper HTTP status codes for a polite API.

Run the application and exercise endpoints with curl Postman or an HTTP client of choice. Check application logs and database tables to verify persistence and expected behavior.

This walkthrough covers project setup dependency selection entity mapping repository creation transaction handling and REST exposure. Following these steps produces a maintainable backend that can be extended with validation security and migrations without chaos.

Tip

Enable SQL logging during development by setting spring.jpa.show-sql true and spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.format_sql true. Use Flyway or Liquibase for schema migrations because relying on auto DDL is a gamble.

title: How to Install Java on Ubuntu and set JAVA_HOME (2025)
description: Install OpenJDK 21 on Ubuntu and set JAVA_HOME for builds and tools Follow simple commands and environment updates for a working Java setup
heading: How to Install Java on Ubuntu and set JAVA_HOME (2025)
body:
This guide shows how to install OpenJDK 21 on Ubuntu and set the JAVA_HOME environment variable so builds and tools find the JDK.

  1. Update packages and install OpenJDK 21
  2. Verify Java installation
  3. Locate the JDK installation path
  4. Add JAVA_HOME to a profile file
  5. Reload the profile and confirm setup

Step one use the package manager to fetch the latest lists and install the JDK with a single command.

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y openjdk-21-jdk

Step two check the runtime version to confirm the operating system sees the new Java runtime.

java -version

Step three find the actual installation base by resolving the java binary location and walking up two directories.

readlink -f $(which java)

Use the binary path to derive a proper JAVA_HOME path for the full JDK not only the java executable.

Step four persist the environment variable by appending an export line to a user profile so future shells pick up the JDK location.

echo 'export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-21-openjdk-amd64' >> ~/.profile

Step five reload the profile in the current session and verify the variable is set and points to the JDK base.

source ~/.profile

echo $JAVA_HOME

This series of steps installs OpenJDK 21 and ensures that development tools that rely on JAVA_HOME get a consistent reference to the full JDK. The profile update provides a persistent environment so builds and IDEs work across reboots and new terminals.

Tip

If multiple JDK versions exist use the update alternatives tool to manage the default java binary and keep JAVA_HOME pointing to the chosen JDK that matches the selected alternative.

title: Install the Java JDK on Ubuntu
description: Quick guide to install Java JDK on Ubuntu using apt and manage multiple versions for development and production use
heading: Install the Java JDK on Ubuntu Step by Step
body:
If you need a working Java JDK on Ubuntu and you do not want to wrestle with dependency gremlins or mystical environment variables, you are in the right place. This guide shows how to install OpenJDK with apt, verify the install, and pick which Java version runs when your server decides to be dramatic.

Why this matters

Many apps will happily compile or run only when Java behaves. Using apt and update alternatives keeps things clean, predictable, and scriptable. You will get a reliable JDK without weird file locations or magic that only an ancient sysadmin remembers.

Refresh the package database

First make sure apt knows what is available. This pulls in the index so you are not installing yesterday's packages.

sudo apt update

Install OpenJDK with apt

Pick the JDK you want. OpenJDK is the default open implementation and it is fine for most development and production needs. Choose an LTS release for servers if you like long term stability and fewer surprise upgrades.

sudo apt install openjdk-17-jdk
# or pick a long term support release
sudo apt install openjdk-11-jdk

Apt will fetch dependencies and place binaries in standard locations so tools like java and javac end up in your PATH.

Verify Java and the compiler

Confirm the runtime and compiler are present and reporting what you expect. No guessing allowed.

java -version
javac -version

Set the default Java with update alternatives

If multiple Java versions live on your machine you can choose which one answers when someone runs java or javac. The update alternatives system will present a menu and let you pick the path to use.

sudo update-alternatives --config java
sudo update-alternatives --config javac

Run both so the runtime and the compiler point to the same JDK. Follow the numbered menu and choose the path that matches the version you want to use system wide.

Optional Oracle JDK path

Some legacy applications insist on a vendor build. If that is your situation download the Debian package from the vendor site and install it, or use a well known PPA for easier maintenance. Use this only when a vendor requirement forces your hand and you accept the licensing fine print.

sudo dpkg -i package.deb
sudo apt install -f

Environment variables and final sanity checks

If something still misbehaves check JAVA_HOME and PATH for conflicting entries. A simple and reliable place to set JAVA_HOME for all users is /etc/environment. For per user work put it in your shell profile.

  • Set JAVA_HOME to the JDK install directory for tools that need it
  • Prefer an LTS JDK on servers to avoid surprise upgrades
  • Keep runtime and compiler aligned with update alternatives

Troubleshooting tips

If java points to the wrong installation run update alternatives again. If a specific application fails check its logs and confirm it is using the same JAVA_HOME and PATH as your shell. If you are really stuck rebooting the system can sometimes clear odd PATH caching issues, which is not elegant but often effective.

There you go. You now have a predictable Java JDK on Ubuntu ready for compiling and running Java apps. If the JDK starts behaving like a soap opera check for leftover vendor packages or conflicting environment entries and fix them before anyone notices.

description: Step by step guide to install Java and set JAVA_HOME on Windows 11 for developers and tools that need a correct environment variable.
heading: How to Install Java and set JAVA_HOME on Windows 11
body:
This tutorial gives a compact walkthrough for installing Java and configuring the JAVA_HOME environment variable on Windows 11 so developer tools can find the JDK.

  1. Download a JDK package
  2. Run the installer
  3. Record the installation folder
  4. Set the JAVA_HOME system environment variable
  5. Add the JDK bin folder to the Path
  6. Verify using command line

Download a JDK package Download an Oracle JDK or an OpenJDK build from an official vendor page. Choose x64 installers for typical Windows 11 setups and pick a recent LTS or current release depending on project requirements.

Run the installer Launch the downloaded installer with administrator rights when required. Follow the installer prompts and note the destination folder shown during setup. The installer performs registry updates and copies runtime files.

Record the installation folder Note the full folder path displayed by the installer. An example folder name looks like Program Files\Java\jdk-17.0.2 for a standard installation. That folder will be the JAVA_HOME value.

Set the JAVA_HOME system environment variable Open Windows search and type Edit the system environment variables. In System Properties click Environment Variables then create a new system variable named JAVA_HOME and paste the JDK folder path as the value.

Add the JDK bin folder to the Path In the same Environment Variables dialog edit the Path system variable and add a new entry with %JAVA_HOME%\bin. Placing that entry above other Java entries prevents older runtimes from being picked first.

Verify using command line Open Command Prompt and run java -version and javac -version. Both commands should print versions that match the installed JDK. If versions do not match remove older Java entries from Path or reboot to refresh variables.

The steps covered downloading and installing a JDK then setting a persistent JAVA_HOME and Path entry so development tools and build systems find the correct runtime and compiler. This process removes a common source of mysterious runtime errors and build failures.

Tip

When managing multiple JDKs consider using a version manager or set JAVA_HOME per project in build scripts. That approach keeps global environment clean and prevents accidental use of older JDKs.
