title: How to Abort Git Merge Conflicts
description: Quick guide to abort a messy Git merge and restore a clean working tree fast and safely
heading: How to Abort Git Merge Conflicts Safely and Fast
body:
This guide shows how to abort a Git merge that produced conflicts and return the repository to a clean state.

  1. Check merge status
  2. Abort the merge
  3. Preserve or stash local changes
  4. Reset if the index or working tree is confused
  5. Prepare branches and retry the merge

Check merge status Use git status to see which files are conflicted and which files are staged. The status output tells which branch is merging and lists conflicted paths in plain English. This saves guesswork and dramatic scrolling.

Abort the merge If the merge is unwanted or desperate then run git merge --abort. This command attempts to roll back to the state before the merge started and restores the index and the working tree. The abort command works when the merge recorded a merge head.

Preserve or stash local changes If local edits need saving use git stash push -m "WIP before abort" or stage important files with git add then stash. Stashing prevents data loss and keeps the working tree clean for the abort command.

Reset if the index or working tree is confused When git merge --abort fails consider git reset --hard HEAD to force the working tree back to the last commit. Only use the hard reset when sure about discarding unstashed edits.

Prepare branches and retry the merge Update both branches with git fetch and consider rebasing feature work with git rebase origin/main before merging. Cleaner history reduces future conflict carnage.

Recap The steps covered how to inspect a merge, run the abort command, stash local work, and use reset when necessary so recovery is predictable and safe.

Tip

Keep frequent small commits and use git stash for ephemeral work. Smaller changes mean fewer conflicts and less drama when abortion becomes necessary.

title: How to Merge Git Commits
description: Quick guide to merging Git commits using interactive rebase squash amend and safe force push for a tidy commit history
heading: How to Merge Git Commits Step by Step
body:
This tutorial shows how to combine Git commits for a cleaner history using interactive rebase squash and careful pushing.

  1. Inspect the commit history
  2. Create a backup branch
  3. Run an interactive rebase to squash or fixup commits
  4. Amend messages and resolve conflicts
  5. Push changes safely to the remote

Use git log --oneline to see recent commits and decide which commits belong together. Think of the branch history as a public record that deserves neat handwriting.

Create a snapshot with git branch backup or git checkout -b backup before rewriting history. This step prevents a small mistake from turning into a dramatic git therapy session.

Start an interactive rebase with a range such as git rebase -i HEAD~3. In the editor change pick lines to squash or fixup for the commits that should merge into one. Squash combines messages followed by an opportunity to edit while fixup skips message edits and silently merges.

If conflicts appear run git status to see affected files then stage fixes with git add and continue using git rebase --continue. To adjust the final commit message use git commit --amend after the rebase completes.

After the branch history looks tidy push with care. Use git push --force-with-lease when rewriting a branch that others might have checked out. This option reduces the chance of accidentally overwriting teammate work.

Recap The process covers inspecting history creating a backup performing an interactive rebase to squash or fixup commits resolving conflicts amending the final message and pushing safely. The goal is a concise and readable commit history that does not embarrass future maintainers.

Tip

Prefer small frequent commits during development then squash before merging to main. Communicate rewrites to teammates and use --force-with-lease not plain force to avoid surprise lost work.

title: How to Git merge one branch into another
description: Step by step guide to merging one Git branch into another safely with commands conflict tips and best practices for clean history
heading: How to Git merge one branch into another safely
body:
If merging branches makes you reach for the coffee or the emergency chocolate then this guide is for you. We will walk through the safe, boring and effective way to merge one Git branch into another with minimal chaos and a dash of sarcasm.

Prepare the repo and save your dignity

Before you start merging things that will haunt your team for weeks run a quick sync and inspection. That reduces surprises and keeps your coworkers from forming a riot club.

git fetch origin
git status
git log --oneline --graph --decorate

Confirm your working directory is clean. If it is not then either stash, commit, or make peace with your local changes before proceeding.

Switch to the branch that should receive the changes

The branch you want to update is the branch you must be on. Use one of these commands depending on your Git version and mood.

git switch target-branch
# or
git checkout target-branch

Double check with git status that there is nothing uncommitted. Proceed only if the tree is clean or intentionally dirty in a way you understand.

Merge the source branch and choose your history style

Now perform the actual merge. For a clear merge commit that shows the moment you brought two histories together use the no fast forward option. If you prefer a linear history let Git fast forward when possible.

# preserve a merge commit for history and debugging
git merge --no-ff source-branch

# or allow a fast forward when it is safe and simple
git merge source-branch

When conflicts appear stay calm and resolve them

Yes conflicts will happen. Git will mark the files and put conflict markers right where the fun is. Open the files, resolve the differences and then tell Git you fixed them.

  1. Edit the files with conflict markers and choose the correct changes
  2. Mark changes as resolved with git add
  3. Complete the merge with git commit if you used a normal merge or git merge --continue if you are in a special flow

Run your tests and a quick build to make sure nothing exploded. Fix what broke and repeat if needed.

Share the merged branch with remote and avoid surprising your team

When the local branch is merged and verified push it back up to the remote.

git push origin target-branch

If the push is rejected because the remote has diverged then do not force push without communicating. Prefer opening a pull request or coordinating with the team. If you must rewrite history use force with lease and say sorry in the commit message.

git push --force-with-lease origin target-branch

Quick troubleshooting checklist

  • Did you fetch and inspect the history with git log --graph --oneline --decorate before merging
  • Are you on the correct target branch
  • Is your working directory clean
  • Did you run tests after resolving conflicts
  • Did you coordinate before rewriting remote history

Best practices to avoid future pain

Use feature branches and pull requests for team work. Keep changes small and frequent. Prefer a merge commit when you want a clear record of integration and prefer a fast forward for trivial updates. And remember that communication beats force pushing every time.

Follow the prepare switch merge resolve push pattern and you will merge with fewer surprises and fewer passive aggressive Slack messages.
seo_title: Merge Git branches without drama and with fewer conflicts
seo_heading: Step by step guide to merging branches with conflict handling and best practices

title: How Git no-ff Merges Work
description: Learn how Git no-ff merges preserve history create merge commits and affect rebasing and workflow in a compact technical guide
heading: How Git no-ff Merges Work Explained
body:
Think of a Git no-ff merge as the developer equivalent of signing a receipt when you hand over a car. You could just slide the keys and trust people, or you can make a merge commit and document who did what and when. Use it when you want the record to show a feature as a single logical unit instead of letting the main branch quietly absorb your changes with a fast forward.

What a no-ff merge actually does

Normally if main has not moved since you branched off, Git will fast forward and move the main pointer to your feature tip. No fuss and no extra commits. The --no-ff option forces Git to create a merge commit even when a fast forward would be possible. That merge commit ties the feature branch together in the commit graph and gives you a neat join point you can point at when things go sideways.

Why teams ask for merge commits

  • Auditability It's easier to say "this whole feature landed in one place" when a merge commit names the feature.
  • Rollbacks Reverting a single merge commit rolls back an entire feature in one go, which beats trying to pick apart a wall of tiny commits.
  • Review context PRs that result in a merge commit keep discussion and metadata tied to a clear point in history.

When a no-ff merge is overkill

If you are fixing a typo or doing a trivial refactor, a fast forward keeps history linear and tidy. Merge commits can clutter the log for tiny changes. Pick battles. For long lived branches and complex features the tradeoff usually favors a no-ff merge.

How rebase changes the picture

If you rebase your feature branch onto the latest main then a normal merge will often fast forward and avoid a merge commit. If you still want that single join point use git merge --no-ff feature and Git will oblige and create the merge commit anyway. In short, rebase affects whether a fast forward is possible but it does not stop you from forcing a merge commit.

Commands that actually help

Here are the practical bits to run when you need to inspect or enforce history.

git log --graph --oneline --decorate

# Force the merge commit and inspect before finalizing
git merge --no-ff --no-commit feature

# The usual forced merge
git merge --no-ff feature

Using --no-commit lets you review the staged merge and edit the message. Merge messages are your chance to explain the who what and why, so try not to write a haiku.

Practical policy for teams

Pick a policy for your git workflow and enforce it with pull request checks. If your team wants merge commits for auditing set rules that require them. If you prefer a tidy linear history require fast forwards or rebasing. Consistency saves time and arguments at 3 am.

Quick decision guide

  • Long lived feature or audit required: use --no-ff.
  • Tiny fix or trivial change: prefer fast forward or rebase and merge.
  • Need to review the merge before it lands: use --no-ff --no-commit.

In the end Git gives you both tools. Use no-ff when you want a clear merge commit to capture a feature in one place. Use fast forward when you like clean lines and are not afraid of small, quiet histories. Either way try to agree as a team so your git history does not look like a crime scene.
seo_title: Force a merge commit in Git and keep your history actually sane
seo_heading: When to use git no-ff merges for clearer commits and safer rollbacks

title: What is a Fast Forward Merge in Git?
description: Quick guide to fast forward merges in Git Learn how Git moves branch tips when no divergent commits exist and when to avoid linear history
heading: What is a Fast Forward Merge in Git?
body:
Fast forward merge at a glance

A fast forward merge moves the target branch pointer forward to the feature branch when there are no divergent commits. In plain terms that means Git does not make a merge commit and the history stays perfectly linear. It is neat it is cheap and sometimes it hides the fact that work happened on a separate branch.

How to run a fast forward merge

If the branch you want to merge from is strictly ahead of the branch you are on Git will simply advance the pointer. Example commands that do the job are below.

git checkout main
git merge feature

If you want to force a merge commit even when a fast forward is possible use this.

git merge --no-ff feature

If you want to make sure a merge only happens when it can be fast forwarded use this instead.

git merge --ff-only feature

Pros and cons without the marketing fluff

  • Pros Linear history that is easy to read with tools like git log and git bisect. Fewer merge commits cluttering the graph.
  • Cons You lose an explicit record that the work was grouped on a branch. That can make auditing reverting or understanding context later more annoying.

When to use fast forward merges

Use fast forward when the change is trivial or a single commit that does not need its own identity. Think small fixes documentation updates and tiny tweaks where the branch exists only to isolate a momentary thought.

When to avoid fast forward merges

If a feature branch represents a unit of work that you might revert cherry pick or inspect later keep the branch visible in history. In that case create a merge commit so the branch remains a named grouping.

Practical team guidance

  • Decide on a convention and stick to it. Inconsistent merges lead to a history that looks like the aftermath of a party.
  • Enforce merge commits when branch level traceability matters. Many pull request systems let you require merge commits so features stay obvious.
  • Use git merge --no-ff for PR merges when you want a clear unit in history. Use git merge --ff-only when you want to be strict about keeping history linear.

Reverts and auditing made slightly less painful

A merge commit gives you a single handle to revert an entire feature. Fast forward merges scatter the commits into the main line so reverting a whole feature may require multiple steps. If your team needs clean revert paths prefer merge commits.

Final thought

Fast forward merges are a tidy option that keep history linear but they are not a universal good. If you care about traceability prefer merge commits or enforce a PR workflow that creates them. If you mostly want a clean log for tiny fixes then fast forward is your friend. Pick a policy tell the team and stop blaming Git when history gets weird.
seo_title: Fast forward merge in Git explained and when to force a merge
seo_heading: Why your Git history changes with fast forward merges and how to manage it

title: Remove and Revert Uncommitted Git Changes & Files
description: Quick guide to discard uncommitted Git changes and remove untracked files safely using git restore git reset and git clean
heading: Remove and Revert Uncommitted Git Changes and Files for Git users
body:
If your working tree looks like a science experiment gone wrong and you need to remove uncommitted changes and stray files fast but safely this guide is your rescue rope. It walks through how to revert tracked edits use restore and reset unstage changes remove untracked files with git clean and fully reset the working tree when you accept total loss of local edits.

Revert tracked file edits with git restore

When a tracked file has local edits you do not want to keep run git restore path/to/file. That command throws away working tree modifications for a tracked path and makes the file match the index or the last commit depending on state. If you are on an older Git version use the legacy form git checkout -- path/to/file which behaves the same for this purpose.

Remember that this loses local changes unless you stash or commit them first. If you might need the work later stash it with git stash push -m "save before restore".

When you only want to unstage files

If you accidentally added files to the index but still want them in the working tree use git restore --staged path/to/file or the older form git reset HEAD path/to/file. That moves the changes out of the staging area while keeping the edits available to edit or readd.

Remove untracked files and directories with git clean

When junk files clutter your repo like build artifacts or editor backups use git clean to remove them. Start always with a dry run to preview deletions with git clean -n. If the preview looks safe run git clean -f to remove untracked files.

To also remove untracked directories add the directory flag and run git clean -fd. Use these commands carefully because recovery is not automatic once the files are deleted.

Tips for git clean safety

  • Run git clean -n before any destructive command.
  • Add frequently recreated paths to .gitignore to avoid repeat cleanups.
  • Use backups or a stash for important but temporary files.

Reset the working tree to the last commit when you mean it

If you want a full rollback and do not care about losing local changes use git reset --hard HEAD. This resets the index and working tree to match the last commit. It is powerful and destructive and should be used only after confirming there is nothing worth keeping.

Quick developer workflow checklist

  • If you might need changes later stash them with git stash push.
  • Unstage mistakes with git restore --staged or git reset HEAD.
  • Preview deletions with git clean -n and then run git clean -f or git clean -fd if you also need directories removed.
  • When you want a full wipe use git reset --hard HEAD with eyes wide open.

This practical tutorial keeps version control tidy without heroic guesswork. Treat these commands like hammers use them when needed and always do a dry run or stash first if you value your work. If you break something at least you will have learned something useful while panicking briefly.
seo_title: How to Safely Discard Uncommitted Git Changes and Junk Files
seo_heading: Practical git restore reset and git clean tips for removing uncommitted changes

title: Discard local changes and untracked files in Git repo
description: Quick guide to discard local changes and remove untracked files in a Git repo using git reset git clean and safe previews.
heading: Discard local changes and untracked files in Git repo
body:
So your working tree looks like a crime scene and you want everything wiped clean without crying later. Here is a no nonsense guide to inspect the repo, discard tracked changes, and remove untracked files while giving you a chance to double check like a sensible human.

Inspect the repository state

Before you do anything dramatic run a status check. This will show modified tracked files and any untracked files that might be important or junk.

git status

Look at the output. If you see files you actually care about stash or commit them first. This step avoids the classic facepalm when you lose that one change that mattered.

Reset tracked changes safely

If you are sure the last committed state is the one you want then reset the index and working tree. This will remove all modifications to tracked files, yes even the ones you thought were clever.

git reset --hard HEAD

That is the hard reset. It will restore files to the last commit and discard local edits to tracked files. If you are unsure stash first.

Use stash as a safety net

If you want to be dramatic but not careless run this before any destructive command.

git stash push -m "wip"

Preview and remove untracked files

Untracked files are those extra files Git does not manage. Maybe build artifacts or temporary nonsense. Always preview before deleting.

git clean -n

The -n flag shows what would be removed. If the list looks safe then run the actual cleanup. If there are directories include the -d flag.

git clean -fd

Remove ignored files if you must

Sometimes you need to remove generated or ignored files too. Preview with:

git clean -nx

If that list is acceptable run the real command. Warning this removes ignored files as well.

git clean -fdx

Verify a clean working tree

One last sanity check after the operations to confirm nothing was left behind.

git status

The output should report a clean working tree and no untracked files. If it does not match your expectations check stashes, backups, or your own tears before trying more drastic measures.

Quick checklist

  • Run git status and inspect changes
  • Stash anything you might need with git stash push -m "wip"
  • Run git reset --hard HEAD to restore tracked files
  • Preview deletions with git clean -n
  • Remove untracked files with git clean -fd
  • Optionally remove ignored files with git clean -fdx after preview
  • Run git status again to confirm a clean working tree

These steps cover the common version control tasks when you want to discard changes and remove untracked files. Follow the previews first, stash if unsure, and breathe. You will survive and your repo will be tidy again.
seo_title: Reset a Git repo fast and remove untracked files safely
seo_heading: Return a messy Git working tree to pristine status and lose nothing

title: Introduction to Lambda Expressions in Java
description: Learn Java lambda expressions with clear syntax examples and best practices for functional interfaces and streams
heading: Introduction to Lambda Expressions in Java Guide
body:
This tutorial covers Java lambda expressions with practical examples and best practices for functional interfaces and streams.

  1. Understand functional interfaces
  2. Learn lambda syntax
  3. Apply lambdas with collections and streams
  4. Handle type inference and common errors
  5. Practice with short examples

1 Functional interfaces Functional interfaces define a single abstract method that accepts parameters and returns a result. Annotate with @FunctionalInterface for clarity. Example interface form looks like interface Adder { int add(int a, int b) }

2 Lambda syntax A basic lambda expression looks like (a, b) -> a + b Single parameter form looks like x -> x * x Types can be declared explicitly when needed using (int a, int b) -> a + b

3 Apply lambdas with collections and streams Common usage is in stream pipelines for filtering mapping and terminal actions. Example usage looks like list.stream().filter(x -> x % 2 == 0).map(x -> x * 2).forEach(x -> System.out.println(x)) This pattern reduces boilerplate that anonymous classes would bring

4 Type inference and common errors Java performs target typing to infer parameter types. Overloaded methods and complex generics can confuse type inference. When compilation fails provide explicit parameter types or add a cast for the lambda expression

5 Practice examples Compare strings by length using (s1, s2) -> s1.length() - s2.length() Create a runnable using () -> System.out.println("Hello") Try converting common anonymous classes to lambdas for faster feedback during learning

This guide covered how to read and write lambda expressions how functional interfaces form a target type and how to use lambdas with streams and collections for cleaner code and less ceremony

Tip

Prefer short clear lambda bodies. When a lambda grows beyond a single expression extract a named method for readability and easier debugging

title: Tomcat vs Apache What's the difference?
description: Compare Apache HTTP Server and Apache Tomcat roles performance and when to use each for Java web applications
heading: Tomcat vs Apache What's the difference
body:
Quick reality check

If your app is pure static files then Apache HTTP Server will be the sprinter you want. If your app runs Java servlets or JSP then Tomcat is where the Java magic happens. Yes this is obvious. No you did not need a PhD to get here but the deployment choices will still haunt you if you ignore them.

What each project actually does

Apache HTTP Server is a general purpose web server that excels at serving HTML CSS images and dealing with TLS and caching. It has a mature module system and plays nicely as a public facing endpoint. Tomcat is a servlet container and application server that implements servlet and JSP specs and runs Java web apps packaged as WAR files. Think of Tomcat as the place your Java code takes a nap then wakes up to process requests.

Roles in plain English

  • Apache HTTP Server: static content delivery TLS termination caching and request routing with modules like mod_proxy
  • Tomcat: executes Java servlets and JSP handles session state and Java specific lifecycle concerns

Common production patterns

The most used pattern is to put Apache HTTP Server in front as a reverse proxy and let Tomcat sit behind it handling the dynamic Java work. That gives a neat separation of concerns and lets each tool do what it does best. Use mod_proxy or mod_proxy_ajp or mod_jk to connect the two depending on your needs and comfort with connectors.

Why put Apache in front

  • TLS termination at the edge for simpler cert management
  • Caching and compression to reduce load on the JVM
  • Serving static assets fast and cheaply
  • Access controls and request filtering with mature modules

Why Tomcat still matters

Tomcat runs your Java web apps and implements servlet APIs so it is required when server side Java code must run. Performance and stability on Tomcat is tied to JVM tuning thread pool sizes and garbage collection behavior. Monitoring thread usage and GC metrics will save you from midnight panic sessions.

Performance and tuning tips

  • Tune Tomcat connector threads and JVM heap sizes for expected concurrency
  • Watch garbage collection pauses and tune the GC strategy for your workload
  • Let Apache serve many static assets and cache responses to lower load on Tomcat
  • Consider using an AJP connector when latency matters but know the security implications and configuration details

Configuration differences you will actually deal with

Apache HTTP Server uses plain text config files and a modular approach. Tomcat uses XML based server and web descriptors plus WAR deployments. Neither is mystical. Both will bite you in slightly different ways when configs drift between environments.

Security and deployment notes

Keep the public surface small. Use Apache to filter and log traffic at the edge and let Tomcat be internal if possible. Keep JVM and Tomcat versions patched. Monitor logs for slow servlets and avoid running everything as root even if you are very confident.

Decision checklist

  • If you serve mostly static content or need a hardened frontend choose Apache HTTP Server
  • If you need servlet APIs or JSP choose Tomcat
  • If you want both use Apache as a reverse proxy with mod_proxy or mod_jk in front of Tomcat

Parting advice with a wink

Do not try to make Tomcat a static file server unless you enjoy confusing performance graphs. Do not expose Tomcat directly to the internet unless you have a good reason and proper hardening. Use the right tool for the job and sleep a little better. If things go wrong blame the configs not the coffee.
seo_title: When to Use Apache HTTP Server or Tomcat for Java Web Apps
seo_heading: Choose a reverse proxy or servlet container for Java web architecture

title: Jenkins Tomcat WAR Deployment
description: Step by step guide to configure Jenkins to build a WAR and deploy to Tomcat using pipeline and common plugins
heading: Jenkins Tomcat WAR Deployment Guide
body:
This tutorial walks through using Jenkins to build a WAR file and deploy that artifact to an Apache Tomcat server using a pipeline and common plugins

  1. Prepare Tomcat and Jenkins
  2. Create a Jenkins job or pipeline
  3. Build the WAR using Maven or Gradle
  4. Archive and deploy the WAR to Tomcat
  5. Verify deployment and enable rollback

Prepare Tomcat and Jenkins by ensuring Tomcat runs on a reachable host and that the Tomcat manager credentials are available in Jenkins credentials store. Install the Deploy to Container plugin when a GUI approach is preferred or prepare a script for a remote copy when automation feels more honest.

Create a Jenkins job or pipeline that checks out source from version control. For a pipeline use a simple Jenkinsfile that runs build steps and exposes the WAR as a pipeline artifact. For freestyle jobs configure build steps and post build actions to archive the artifact.

Build the WAR using a build tool. For Maven run the package goal using a build agent that has Java and Maven installed. For Gradle run the build task and confirm the WAR appears in the expected target or build libs folder.

This guide covered preparing servers and credentials creating a Jenkins job building a WAR archiving the artifact deploying to Tomcat and verifying and handling rollback. Follow these steps and expect fewer surprises than when guessing where a missing dependency hid itself

Tip

Use Jenkins pipeline declarative stages and store Tomcat credentials in the credentials store. Add a quick health check stage that fails the pipeline when the application does not respond to avoid promoting broken deployments

title: How to Resolve Git Stash Pop Conflicts
description: Fix Git stash pop conflicts step by step and recover changes safely with merge tools stash branches and recovery commands
heading: How to Resolve Git Stash Pop Conflicts and Recover Changes
body:
If you ran git stash pop and suddenly your codebase looks like a crime scene you did not sign up for this guide will help. You will learn how to apply stashes safely resolve stash conflicts and get back to writing code instead of soothing merge markers.

What happened and why you should care

git stash pop tries to apply the top stash and then removes it from the stash list. That is handy until it hits changes that conflict with your working tree. Then you get merge conflicts inside files and a choice between messing things up or doing the right thing. This is normal in version control and recoverable most of the time.

Quick checklist for resolving stash conflicts

  • Run git stash pop and do not panic
  • Use git status to see conflicted files
  • Edit files to remove conflict markers and pick the correct code
  • Stage resolved files with git add
  • Commit the resolution or preserve the stash if you want to try again

Step by step

Run the command that caused the chaos

git stash pop

If stash pop fails you will see merge conflicts. Run git status to get the exact list of problem files.

Open files and resolve merge markers

Open each conflicted file and look for the familiar markers. Remove the markers and pick the lines that belong together. If you prefer a visual helper use git mergetool to avoid finger stabbing.

Stage and confirm

When you are happy with edits stage them with git add and confirm a clean index with git status. If everything looks good create a commit to record the resolution.

git add path/to/file
git commit -m 'Resolve stash conflict'

Keep the stash and test first

If you do not want the stash removed use git stash apply instead of pop. That applies changes but leaves the stash in place so you can retry or inspect later.

git stash apply

Use a stash branch to avoid pain

If the stash touches many files create a branch from the stash and resolve there. This keeps your main branch pristine while you do the messy work.

git stash branch fix-stash

Git recovery tricks when things go missing

If stash pop looked like it worked but some changes are unaccounted for check git reflog for recently referenced commits or run git fsck --lost-found to locate dangling objects. Often you can recover blobs or commits and revive your work.

Best practices so you do not have to read this again

  • Give stashes a message with git stash push -m 'describe change' so you know what you shoved into the void
  • Use git stash apply when you want to test without dropping the stash
  • Create a stash branch for big or risky changes
  • Run git status often it is the one trustworthy friend you have in git land

Stash conflicts are annoying but fixable. Follow the steps to resolve conflicts stage your changes and either commit or preserve the stash. Keep stash branch and git recovery commands in your toolbox and you will survive the drama with your code mostly intact.
seo_title: Fix git stash pop conflicts and recover lost changes fast
seo_heading: Practical git stash pop conflict fixes and stash branch recovery tips

title: Developer vs DevOps Engineer What's the difference?
description: Compact guide comparing developer and DevOps engineer roles responsibilities tools skills and career paths for engineers and managers.
heading: Developer vs DevOps Engineer What's the difference?
body:
Pick a side if you like drama. Or read this and realise most teams do both jobs while stealing each others snacks. In plain terms a developer writes the app and a DevOps engineer makes sure the app actually reaches users and stays alive when traffic spikes or someone pushes bad code at 2 a.m.

Core difference

Developers focus on product problems and application logic. That means feature design code quality tests and keeping users from rioting over a broken button. DevOps engineers focus on deployment automation reliability monitoring and the plumbing that keeps services online when things go sideways. One builds the toy. The other makes sure the toy does not explode on launch day.

Tools and the daily toolbox

Yes there is overlap and no you do not need a magical degree to get started. But the day to day toolsets are different and telling.

  • Developers often live in language specific frameworks local testing tools debuggers and IDEs. Think unit tests integration tests and code review rituals.
  • DevOps engineers work with CI CD pipelines containers Docker or OCI images orchestration platforms like Kubernetes cloud providers and observability stacks for logs metrics and traces.
  • Both need Git and basic scripting but the emphasis changes from feature velocity to deployment safety and operability.

Goals and priorities that actually matter

Developers aim for clear maintainable features shipped on schedule. DevOps engineers aim for fast safe releases predictable environments and less pager noise at 3 a.m. Good teams measure both feature delivery and operational health so nobody is surprised by either users or oncall rotations.

Metrics that teams pay attention to

  • Deployment frequency and lead time for changes
  • Mean time to recovery MTTR and incident counts
  • Change failure rate and system uptime

Skills you actually use on the job

Recruiters will hand you long lists of buzzwords. Here is what really matters.

  • Developers need strong programming skills testing practice design thinking and familiarity with the codebase.
  • DevOps engineers need scripting system administration networking automation and a solid sense of how services behave in production.
  • Both benefit from knowledge of cloud platforms Kubernetes CI CD pipelines automation and observability.

Collaboration and culture

Blame is for bad coffee machines. Teams that align goals metrics and incentives ship faster and have fewer outages. Developers who code with deployability in mind help DevOps engineers sleep. DevOps engineers who understand app architecture avoid useless roadblocks. Shared responsibility is the real magical process improvement.

Career paths and what to expect

Paths cross a lot. A developer can move toward platform engineering SRE or cloud architecture if they like infrastructure and automation. A DevOps engineer can grow into site reliability engineering platform work or specialize in cloud native operations. The market rewards people who can bridge feature creation and delivery pipelines without crying.

Practical career advice and a short checklist

  • Learn basic Linux and a CI CD tool first.
  • Automate repetitive tasks and add monitoring to every service.
  • Get comfortable with containers and at least one orchestration platform like Kubernetes.
  • Practice scripting and read up on networking and observability.
  • Understand cloud fundamentals and explore SRE principles for operational thinking.

If you enjoy writing features and occasional chaos become a developer. If you enjoy taming chaos with automation and coffee become a DevOps engineer. If you enjoy both then congrats you are either the glue everyone relies on or the reason the oncall rota exists. Either way cross training pays off and fewer teams regret that choice.
seo_title: Developer or DevOps Engineer Which career fits you best
seo_heading: How developers and DevOps engineers share the workload in real teams

title: Tomcat vs JBoss Which Application Server to Choose?
description: Compare Tomcat and JBoss for Java deployment Learn differences in features performance architecture and when to choose each server
heading: Tomcat vs JBoss Which Application Server to Choose
body:
Tomcat servlet container or WildFly Java EE server Which one fits your stack

If you are squinting at the Tomcat vs JBoss debate and wondering which server to invite to your deployment party you are not alone. One is lean and fast and prefers doing one thing well. The other brings the whole toolbox and occasionally a consulting bill. Here is a pragmatic comparison that keeps the facts straight and the drama light.

What each server actually is

Tomcat is a focused servlet container and HTTP server for Java. It handles servlets JSP and the usual web app plumbing very well. Developers reach for Tomcat for web front ends microservices and Spring Boot style deployments where resource efficiency matters.

JBoss is the old name you probably use when you mean WildFly or Red Hat JBoss EAP. It is a full Java application server that implements enterprise APIs like EJB JMS transactions clustering and management features out of the box. If your app wants built in enterprise services you will notice the difference quickly.

Feature set and ecosystem

  • Tomcat gives you servlet and JSP support plus optional security and session management add ons. It is modular and small by default.
  • WildFly JBoss bundles Java EE or Jakarta EE APIs along with an admin console management CLI and clustering features. It is designed for larger enterprise use cases.

Memory footprint and startup time

Tomcat typically consumes less memory and boots faster. That makes it a popular choice for containerized microservices and dense VM packing. WildFly JBoss starts with more services enabled which means more RAM and a longer startup time but also fewer external dependencies when you actually need EJB or JMS.

Operational complexity and deployment

Deploying to Tomcat is usually straightforward. Fewer moving parts means fewer surprises when the app goes live. WildFly JBoss brings powerful admin tools and a steeper learning curve. If you like clicking through admin consoles or automating complex subsystems you will appreciate it. If you prefer minimal ops work choose Tomcat and be smug about it.

Containerization and microservices note

For microservices and Spring Boot style apps embedded Tomcat is a natural fit. The small footprint helps with fast scaling and CI pipelines. If your microservice suddenly needs distributed transactions or JMS you can either add libraries or graduate to a full application server.

Performance in the real world

For raw servlet throughput Tomcat often has the edge thanks to its lighter runtime. When enterprise services are used heavily WildFly JBoss can outperform because it implements those APIs natively and optimizes them under load. The correct answer is to benchmark with representative workloads and then pretend the numbers validate your existing bias.

When to pick which

  • Choose Tomcat for simple web apps microservices resource constrained deployments and when you want fast startup and low memory usage.
  • Choose WildFly JBoss for legacy Java EE systems complex transactional workflows when you need built in messaging clustering or enterprise APIs to reduce custom code.

Quick migration and testing tips

  • Start with Tomcat if you are unsure. It is easier to add services than to remove them from a packed application server.
  • Benchmark CPU memory and response times with realistic loads not just hello world tests.
  • If you need vendor support consider JBoss EAP from Red Hat rather than the community WildFly build.
  • Automate configuration and use health checks logs and metrics so your ops team does not have to rely on mythic knowledge.

Final verdict without the sermon

If you need a nimble servlet container for a modern microservice architecture pick Tomcat. If your project leans on Jakarta EE enterprise APIs or needs tightly integrated messaging transactions and clustering pick WildFly JBoss. And if you still cannot decide flip a coin but run a benchmark first so the coin has supporting data.

Keywords to keep in your search history include Tomcat JBoss WildFly application server servlet container Java deployment performance microservices and comparison. You are welcome and good luck with the configuration files.
seo_title: Choose Tomcat or JBoss With Real World Tradeoffs and Tips
seo_heading: Tomcat servlet container or WildFly Java EE server Which one fits your stack

title: How to use the JDK's javap command by example
description: Practical guide to using the JDK javap command with examples to inspect class files methods and bytecode for debugging and learning
heading: How to use the JDK's javap command by example for class and bytecode inspection
body:
A compact tutorial showing how to use the JDK javap command to inspect class files methods and bytecode.

  1. Compile Java source
  2. Run javap with basic flags
  3. Read disassembled bytecode
  4. Use verbose and private details for deep inspection

Step 1 compile source using the standard compiler example command javac MyClass.java This produces MyClass.class which is the target for analysis

Step 2 run basic listings with commands such as javap MyClass to see public signatures and javap -p MyClass to include private members Use javap -c MyClass to show disassembled bytecode

Step 3 inspect bytecode to understand method behavior Look for opcodes like aload_0 invokespecial and return Method descriptors describe parameter and return types which helps map source level code to generated instructions

Step 4 enable deep inspection with javap -v MyClass This reveals the constant pool and detailed attributes and can be noisy Use javap -l -c MyClass to include line number tables which help match bytecode to source lines

For classes inside jars provide a classpath argument such as javap -classpath lib.jar com.example.MyClass The command works well for quick debugging verifying compile outputs and learning how the compiler transforms source

The tutorial covered compiling a class running javap with common flags reading opcode output and using verbose details to dig deeper The goal is to make class file inspection part of a regular debugging and learning workflow without magic

Tip

When confused use a decompiler alongside javap The decompiler gives readable source and javap shows exact bytecode and constant pool This combo makes surprising compiler behavior less mysterious

title: How to use JarSigner to Sign Java JAR files digitally
description: Learn how to sign Java JARs with JarSigner and keytool for code integrity trust with concise commands to create keystore sign and verify
heading: How to use JarSigner to Sign Java JAR files digitally
body:
This tutorial shows how to sign a Java JAR file using keytool and jarsigner to provide integrity and trust.

  1. Create a keystore and keypair
  2. Sign the JAR with jarsigner
  3. Verify the signed JAR
  4. Optional timestamping and distribution

Create a keystore and keypair

Generate a signing key using keytool so the keystore holds a private key and public certificate. Example command

keytool -genkeypair -alias mykey -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -keystore mykeystore.jks -storepass changeit -keypass changeit -dname "CN=Dev"

Sign the JAR

Apply a digital signature to the JAR using jarsigner. The signature binds the code to the signer and helps users and systems trust the binary.

jarsigner -keystore mykeystore.jks -storepass changeit -keypass changeit myapp.jar mykey

Verify the signed JAR

Always verify after signing to confirm the signature is valid and certificates chain correctly. Use verbose mode for details.

jarsigner -verify -verbose -certs myapp.jar

Optional timestamping and distribution

Add a timestamp using the -tsa option with a timestamp server URL so the signature stays valid after key expiry. Use separate signing keys for development and release builds to keep things tidy.

Signing a JAR is not magic just a few commands that prove provenance and protect integrity. Keep passwords and private keys secure and automate signing in build pipelines to avoid human error.

Tip

Store signing keys in a secure location such as a hardware token or CI secret store. Test verification on a clean machine to catch missing cert chain issues before distribution.

title: scrumbut
description: Quick guide to scrumbut signs causes and fixes for teams claiming to follow Scrum while bending rules and skipping ceremonies
heading: scrumbut explained how to fix Scrum problems
body:
Scrumbut is the practice of claiming to follow Scrum while omitting or changing core Scrum rules to suit convenience.

Common warning signs include phrases such as we do Scrum but no retros we do Scrum but no timebox and we do Scrum but no product owner. Those phrases are the bureaucratic equivalent of rearranging deck chairs and calling that Agile.

Consequences are lower predictability poor feedback loops and diluted team accountability. Promises to stakeholders become vague and long term planning suffers. Teams lose the benefits that motivated adoption of Scrum in the first place.

Practical steps to fix scrumbut follow this short plan

  1. Admit current practice
  2. Choose one core ceremony to restore
  3. Give authority to the product owner role
  4. Enforce timeboxes
  5. Inspect adapt regularly

Admit current practice means a frank team conversation where reality gets named without blame. That clears confusion and opens the door to change.

Choosing one ceremony to restore keeps change manageable. Start with the most impactful meeting for the team and commit to trying for a sprint.

Giving authority to the product owner reduces scope creep and aligns priorities. A named decision maker beats a committee every time.

Enforcing timeboxes protects focus and forces trade offs. Short deadlines reveal blockers faster than gentle requests.

Inspect and adapt regularly through retrospectives that actually produce action items. Measure small improvements and celebrate wins that came from intentional change.

Tip

Run a single sprint with one restored practice and a clear metric. If metrics improve keep going. If no change then try a different practice. Small experiments beat grand declarations.

title: Top 5 Reasons Why You'll Love the Jakarta Servlet 6.0 API Re
description: A compact guide to why developers should care about Jakarta Servlet 6.0 API improvements for modern Java web apps and cloud deployments
heading: Top 5 Reasons Why You'll Love the Jakarta Servlet 6.0 API Release
body:
If you thought server side Java was frozen in a museum, meet Servlet 6.0. It trims the bloat, makes asynchronous work less spooky, and generally behaves like a modern API that actually wants developers to be happy. This is a pragmatic guide to what changed in the Jakarta Servlet API and why it matters for Jakarta EE web development, performance, cloud deployments, and developer productivity.

Key improvements you will actually use

Servlet 6.0 did not invent magic. It cleaned up names, removed legacy surprises, and added better hooks for non blocking processing. That means less brittle glue code, fewer hair pulling debugging sessions, and happier thread pools when traffic spikes.

API cleanup and clearer names

The package layout and method names are less archaeological and more straightforward. Less ceremony means your code reads like intent instead of a list of workarounds. This is a subtle win that pays off in maintenance and onboarding.

Improved asynchronous processing

Non blocking request handling is more predictable, which helps when you build reactive stacks or need high concurrency. You get finer control over callbacks and thread usage so throughput goes up and thread pools stop throwing tantrums.

Enhanced HTTP handling

Header parsing, multipart handling, and streaming responses are less fiddly. That translates to fewer custom parsers and less fragile code. In short, less boilerplate means fewer bugs and less time spent stabbing at malformed requests.

Cloud friendly performance and startup

Servlet 6.0 is kinder to containers with a smaller runtime footprint and faster startup. That matters for autoscaling, cold starts, and keeping infrastructure bills from becoming a horror story. If you run on containers or serverless platforms this matters a lot.

Developer ergonomics and diagnostics

Better error messages and convenience utilities cut down on guard code and detective work. You will spend more time building features and less time arguing with stack traces.

Upgrade checklist that will save your hair

  • Write tests around filters and session behavior before you change anything.
  • Run a quick performance smoke test on a realistic workload to spot regressions early.
  • Check multipart and header handling in code that parses raw requests.
  • Stage the rollout instead of flipping a global switch, unless you prefer panicked rollbacks.

When to care and when to be cautious

If your app is I O bound, or you plan to adopt reactive frameworks, the asynchronous improvements will feel like a gift. If you are upgrading a large legacy app, prioritize compatibility gates and tests first, then chase the performance wins in a measured way.

Final thoughts

Servlet 6.0 is not a flashy rewrite, it is a pragmatic cleanup that nudges Jakarta EE into the present. Expect fewer surprises, better throughput for concurrent loads, and slightly less agony during debugging. Upgrade with tests and a staged rollout, and your future self will send you a thank you note instead of a passive aggressive bug report.
seo_title: Why Servlet 6.0 Makes Jakarta EE Java Faster and Cleaner
seo_heading: Practical Servlet 6.0 changes for cloud ready Java apps and higher productivity

title: s3 bucket temp
description: Quick guide to create temporary S3 access using presigned URLs and short lived credentials for secure file sharing and testing
heading: s3 bucket temp quick guide
body:
This tutorial shows how to create temporary access to an S3 bucket using presigned URLs and temporary credentials for secure short lived file sharing.

  1. Prepare bucket and apply minimal policy
  2. Create a presigned URL for single file upload or download
  3. Use STS to generate temporary credentials for broader short lived access
  4. Test access with a real file transfer
  5. Revoke or let credentials expire then clean up

Step 1 set a bucket policy that allows only the required actions and only from known principals. Do not leave public read or write enabled unless the project aims for a data breach demo. Minimal permissions reduce blast radius.

Step 2 generate a presigned URL for one time upload or download. Presigned URLs grant a short lived signed link that clients can use without AWS credentials. Example pseudo command in case a quick copy helps

aws s3 presign bucket key --expires-in 3600

Step 3 for cases needing more than one object or programmatic access generate temporary credentials via STS and role assumption. This allows scoped policies and short lifetimes so long lived keys do not wander off.

Step 4 test access by using a curl or SDK call with the presigned URL or by configuring an AWS SDK with the temporary credentials and performing the desired operation. Testing prevents surprises when production runs.

Step 5 remove any test objects and revoke roles if manual revocation is supported. Otherwise wait for automatic expiration and then rotate any long lived keys used during testing. Cleaning up avoids noisy logs and accidental leaks.

Recap This guide covered preparing a secure bucket policy generating presigned URLs creating temporary credentials testing real file transfers and cleaning up to avoid exposure. The process lets developers share files without handing over permanent keys and keeps security teams mildly amused rather than furious.

Tip

Prefer short lifetimes for presigned URLs and roles. Shorter lifetimes mean less risk and fewer late night incident calls from monitoring teams.

title: install nginx ubuntu
description: Quick guide to install Nginx on Ubuntu with commands to start the web server and confirm a working default page
heading: Install Nginx on Ubuntu Step by Step
body:
This tutorial shows how to install Nginx on Ubuntu start the service adjust firewall rules and verify a default web page

  1. Update package index
  2. Install Nginx package
  3. Start and enable the Nginx service
  4. Allow HTTP traffic through the firewall
  5. Verify the web server is serving the default page

Update package index

Refresh the Ubuntu package index so the latest Nginx version is available.

sudo apt update

Install Nginx package

Install the web server using the package manager. This will pull in required dependencies.

sudo apt install nginx -y

Start and enable the Nginx service

Start service right away and enable automatic start on boot so the server survives a reboot.

sudo systemctl start nginx

sudo systemctl enable nginx

Allow HTTP traffic through the firewall

If the Ubuntu system uses UFW open the standard HTTP profile so visitors can reach the server.

sudo ufw allow "Nginx HTTP"

Verify the web server is serving the default page

Use a browser or a simple command line request to confirm the default Nginx page loads. Replace localhost with server IP when testing remotely.

curl -I http //localhost

This should return a 200 OK header and the classic Nginx welcome page will be available at the server root. If the header shows a different status check the service status and the Nginx configuration folder for errors.

Troubleshooting quick checks include viewing the service status

sudo systemctl status nginx

and scanning error logs in the Nginx log directory for clues. Adjusting firewall rules or correcting a malformed config file often resolves common failures.

The guide covered updating packages installing Nginx starting and enabling the service allowing HTTP traffic and verifying the default page so a working web server runs on Ubuntu

Tip

Use sudo nginx -t before reloading the service to check for configuration errors that would break the web server when reloaded

title: filezilla ftp nginx
description: Quick guide to connect FileZilla to an Nginx hosted site for FTP or SFTP transfers with permissions and security tips
heading: filezilla ftp nginx setup guide
body:
Quick summary for people who like less manual labor

This guide walks you through connecting FileZilla to an Nginx webserver for uploads and deployments, without inviting chaos. You will choose between SFTP and FTP, set up server packages on Linux, fix Nginx document root ownership and permissions, create a jailed deploy user, configure FileZilla Site Manager, and verify the upload in a browser. Use SFTP when possible, because encryption is nicer than regret.

Prepare the server

Decide whether you want SFTP or plain FTP. SFTP uses OpenSSH and avoids an extra FTP daemon, so it is the less ridiculous choice. On Debian or Ubuntu install OpenSSH with

sudo apt update
sudo apt install openssh-server

If you must use FTP for legacy reasons then use a maintained daemon such as vsftpd and disable anonymous logins. For example

sudo apt install vsftpd

Point Nginx to the right folder and set permissions

Edit your Nginx site config so root points to the folder you want users to upload into. Typical webroots are under /var/www. Ensure the webserver user such as www-data or nginx can read files, and avoid giving global write permissions to everything. A sensible setup might be

sudo chown -R root:root /var/www/example.com
sudo mkdir /var/www/example.com/uploads
sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/example.com/uploads
sudo chmod -R 755 /var/www/example.com

Note that if you use SFTP chroot later the chroot directory must be owned by root and not writable by others. That means the webroot itself should be root owned and the upload folder can be owned by the webserver user.

Create a deploy user and set up a jailed session

For SFTP you can create an SSH user that is jailed with internal-sftp. This keeps the user out of the rest of the system. Edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config and add a match block near the end of the file like this

Match Group sftpusers
    ChrootDirectory /var/www
    ForceCommand internal-sftp
    AllowTcpForwarding no
    X11Forwarding no

Then create the group and user

sudo groupadd sftpusers
sudo useradd -m -g sftpusers -d /uploads -s /usr/sbin/nologin deploy
sudo passwd deploy

Adjust paths to your site and make sure the ChrootDirectory is owned by root. Inside the chroot create a writable directory for uploads that is owned by the webserver user.

Key based authentication and SSH keys

Prefer key based auth. On your dev machine generate a key pair with ssh-keygen and copy the public key into /home/deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys. Make sure permissions are strict so SSH does not complain.

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "deploy key"
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub deploy@server.example.com

After testing you can harden SSH by disabling password authentication and allowing only the sftpusers group to SFTP if that matches your workflow.

Configure FileZilla Site Manager

Open FileZilla and create a new site in Site Manager. Choose protocol SFTP and set the host to your server IP or domain and port to 22. If you use keys choose the keyfile option and point FileZilla to your private key or use Pageant if you are on Windows. If you are forced to use FTP then configure the correct port and turn on explicit FTP over TLS if the server supports it.

Save the profile so deployments are a single click event. Set the transfer mode to default and test with a small file first.

Test upload and validate Nginx serves it

Upload a tiny HTML test file to the uploads folder. Then request the file in your browser. If you see the content you are golden. If not check file ownership and permissions and the Nginx error log at /var/log/nginx/error.log.

Security checklist to avoid future facepalms

  • Use SFTP with keys whenever possible.
  • Disable anonymous FTP and unnecessary services.
  • Keep the chroot directory owned by root and make writable subfolders for uploads.
  • Enforce strong passwords or disable password auth after adding keys.
  • Monitor logs and rotate them so they do not silently eat your disk.

Wrap up

Connecting FileZilla to an Nginx site for deployment is mostly about correct packages, sane permissions, and a jailed user that cannot wander off. Follow the steps above, test with a small file, and then enjoy painless uploads and fewer surprises at 2 AM. If you prefer FTP for compatibility test everything carefully and lock down the settings later. You will sleep better knowing your webserver is not an open invitation.
seo_title: FileZilla SFTP guide for deploying to Nginx on Linux servers
seo_heading: Securely upload and deploy files to Nginx with FileZilla and SSH keys

title: How to create and run a script in Ubuntu
description: Step by step guide to write and execute shell scripts on Ubuntu including permissions shebang and common pitfalls
heading: How to create and run a script in Ubuntu step by step
body:
Quick warning and promise

If you can type a few words into a file and press save you can make a script that actually runs on Ubuntu. It will feel magical for about five minutes and then you will forget how you did it. This guide keeps things short and accurate with a little sarcasm thrown in so you do not fall asleep before the terminal spits out Hello World.

Step 1 create the file

Open a terminal and make a new file with your favorite editor. Use a name that does not clash with system commands unless you enjoy subtle chaos.

nano hello.sh

Step 2 add a shebang and your commands

Put a shebang on the first line so the kernel knows which interpreter to use. A simple example is below. Then add the commands you want the script to run.

#!/bin/bash

echo "Hello World"

If you prefer portability use the env style shebang instead. That helps on systems where the interpreter lives in different places.

#!/usr/bin/env bash

Step 3 make the file executable

The kernel will not run your file unless the execute bit is set. This is an easy barrier to entry for scripts that try to be sneaky.

chmod +x hello.sh

Step 4 run the script

If the script is in your current directory run it with a relative path. Typing the file name alone will usually do nothing unless the folder is in PATH.

./hello.sh
# or run without changing permissions
bash hello.sh

Step 5 troubleshoot common problems

If the script refuses to run check file permissions and ownership. The ls command will show you the execute bit and who owns the file.

ls -l hello.sh

If the wrong interpreter runs or you suspect a different shell change the shebang or invoke the interpreter explicitly with a command like bash hello.sh. If you edited the file on Windows and it looks weird use a tool to fix CRLF line endings or recreate the file in the terminal based editor.

Make your script convenient to run

  • Create a bin folder in your home directory and put scripts there for personal tools
  • Add that folder to your shell startup file so it is in PATH across sessions
  • Pick names that do not shadow system utilities to avoid accidental chaos

Small but useful tips

  • Shebang decides which shell runs your script so set it intentionally
  • chmod +x sets execute permission and avoids mysterious permission errors
  • Use bash hello.sh when you do not want to change permissions or when testing

Follow these steps and you will have a usable Ubuntu shell script that runs from the terminal without drama. Add more commands as you learn and revel in the power of automation. Be careful though your future self will thank you or judge you depending on how tidy your scripts are.
seo_title: Turn a text file into a runnable Ubuntu script in 5 sane steps
seo_heading: Write a bash script add execute permission and run it from the terminal

title: Configure GitHub SSH Keys
description: Learn how to generate add and test SSH keys for GitHub so secure password free pushes happen from your machine.
heading: Configure GitHub SSH Keys for secure git access
body:
Want git to stop asking for passwords like a needy ex? Configure SSH keys for GitHub and enjoy password free pushes and pulls. This guide walks you through generating a modern key pair, loading it into the ssh agent, adding the public key to your GitHub account, and testing the connection so your developer life gets slightly less annoying.

Pick a modern key algorithm

RSA is that thing your grandpa still trusts. For everyone else pick ed25519 for better speed and security. Run this command and replace the email with yours so GitHub can label the key.

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"

The command will ask where to save the key and for a passphrase. Use a short memorable passphrase and let the agent do the heavy lifting for convenience and security.

Start the ssh agent and add the private key

The ssh agent holds your unlocked key so you do not type the passphrase every single time. On macOS and Linux run:

eval $(ssh-agent -s)
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

On Windows with Git Bash or WSL the same commands usually work. Windows native OpenSSH can be managed through the Services UI or the experimental agent integration in recent builds.

Copy your public key and add it to GitHub

Your public key is the file that ends with .pub. Copy it exactly and do not add extra newlines or stray spaces. Then paste it into GitHub under Settings then SSH and GPG keys and give it a descriptive title so you know what device this was for.

cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
  • Open GitHub settings
  • Go to SSH and GPG keys
  • Click New SSH key and paste the public key
  • Give it a name like "Work Laptop ed25519"

Test the connection and update your repo remote

Check that GitHub accepts your key with a quick test. If you see a friendly hello you are done. If you get permission denied go back and verify the public key you uploaded matches the local one.

ssh -T git@github.com

If your repository was cloned using HTTPS update the remote to the SSH URL so pushes skip password prompts. Replace username and repo with your actual values.

git remote set-url origin git@github.com:username/repo.git

Recap that does not require a PhD

Generate a key pair, start the agent, add the private key, copy the public key to GitHub, and test. After that git push and git pull will use SSH and your keyboard will sigh in relief.

Extra tips for developers

  • Use a passphrase and rely on the ssh agent for convenience and improved security
  • Keep private keys out of backups and shared drives
  • Create separate keys for personal and work accounts so revocation is less dramatic

If you run into trouble check file permissions on the .ssh folder and private key and confirm the right public key is uploaded to the right GitHub account. If you still have problems post the exact error and someone helpful will probably make a joke and then fix it for you.
seo_title: Secure GitHub access with SSH keys and zero password prompts
seo_heading: Create and manage SSH keys for GitHub on your local machine

title: Create and Configure GitLab SSH Keys
description: Learn how to generate SSH keys add a public key to GitLab and configure local SSH for secure passwordless Git access
heading: Create and Configure GitLab SSH Keys for secure Git access
body:
This tutorial shows how to generate an SSH key pair add the public key to a GitLab account configure local SSH and test passwordless Git access on clone push and fetch commands.

  1. Generate a key pair on the local machine
  2. Add the public key to GitLab
  3. Configure the local SSH client for GitLab
  4. Test the SSH connection and use the key

Generate a key pair on the local machine

Run a modern key generation command for better security. Example command is ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com" Follow the prompts to save the key to the default location or choose a custom path. Protect the private key with a passphrase or use an SSH agent for convenience.

Add the public key to GitLab

Open the GitLab profile settings and select SSH Keys. Copy the public key file usually found at ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub and paste the entire contents into the key field. Give a memorable title like the machine name and save the key. No black magic required just paste and save.

Configure the local SSH client for GitLab

Edit the SSH config file at ~/.ssh/config to add a host entry. Example lines are Host gitlab.com User git HostName gitlab.com IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 This avoids supplying a key path on every Git command and makes multiple accounts manageable.

Test the SSH connection and use the key

Confirm authentication with ssh -T git@gitlab.com A successful message from GitLab confirms the key is accepted. Then clone push and fetch using the SSH repo URL such as git@gitlab.com group/project.git Adjust file permissions if SSH complains by running chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

This guide covered generating a secure key pair adding the public key to a GitLab account configuring the local SSH client and verifying the connection for passwordless Git operations. Following these steps reduces friction and improves security for developers who use GitLab daily.

Tip

Prefer ed25519 keys for smaller size and better security. Use an SSH agent to avoid repeated passphrase prompts and add an expiry or named key per machine for easier key management.

title: Create and Configure BitBucket SSH keys for Git
description: Quick guide to generate add and test BitBucket SSH keys for seamless Git pushes and pulls without passwords
heading: Create and Configure BitBucket SSH keys for Git the easy way
body:
This tutorial shows how to create and configure BitBucket SSH keys for Git so secure password free pushes and pulls can happen.

  1. Generate an SSH key pair
  2. Start the SSH agent and add a private key
  3. Copy the public key into a Bitbucket account
  4. Test the SSH connection
  5. Configure Git to use the SSH clone link

Generate an SSH key pair Use a modern key type with a comment for identification. Run ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com" and follow prompts. Choose a passphrase unless the automation fairy showed up at the door.

Start the SSH agent and add a private key Start background agent with eval "$(ssh-agent -s)" then add a key with ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519. Agent keeps the private key unlocked for the session so repeated pushes do not demand a password.

Copy the public key into a Bitbucket account Display the public key with cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub then paste the full key into Bitbucket under Personal settings then SSH keys. That grants repository access without username and password drama.

Test the SSH connection Verify access using ssh -T git@bitbucket.org Expect a friendly welcome message that confirms authentication succeeded.

Configure Git to use the SSH clone link In a local repository update the remote using the SSH clone link from Bitbucket. For example run git remote set-url origin [SSH clone link from Bitbucket] Then perform a git fetch or git push to confirm the remote uses SSH.

Recap of the process Generate a secure key pair add the private key to an agent add the public key to Bitbucket test the connection and point local Git to the SSH clone link. That yields password free Git operations with proper authentication and fewer login nags.

Tip

Store multiple keys cleanly by adding a small config file at ~/.ssh/config with a Host entry for bitbucket.org that sets IdentityFile and IdentitiesOnly yes. Add a passphrase and rely on the agent for convenience and security at the same time.

title: Generate Git SSH Keys That Work Everywhere
description: Generate Git SSH keys that work across machines and services with secure steps agent setup and SSH config tips for cross machine use
heading: Generate Git SSH Keys That Work Everywhere
body:
Yes you can make a single SSH key behave itself across laptops, servers, CI runners and cloud boxes. You will still need to do a tiny bit of typing and remember a passphrase unless you enjoy living dangerously. This guide walks through secure ed25519 keys, loading them into an ssh agent, registering them with Git providers and keeping multiple keys from fighting each other.

Why ed25519 and not your grandpa key

ed25519 is fast small and secure. It gives better defaults than old RSA keys and reduces the chance that your future self has to explain why authentication broke. If you use hardware tokens like a YubiKey you can create a hardware backed key with the modern OpenSSH "-sk" algorithms if your system supports them.

Quick checklist

  • Create an ed25519 key pair
  • Protect the private key with a passphrase or hardware token
  • Load the key into ssh agent to avoid repeated prompts
  • Add the public key to GitHub GitLab or other providers
  • Use ssh config to map keys to hosts and enable safe forwarding

Step 1 Generate a key pair

Run this on each machine where you want the private key, or generate once and copy the key securely. Replace the email with something useful for later identification.

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

If you prefer a hardware backed key and your OpenSSH supports it try:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519-sk -C "you@example.com" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_sk

Step 2 Pick a passphrase that is annoyingly memorable

A long random passphrase stored in a password manager is ideal. If you use a YubiKey or other FIDO device you can skip a local passphrase because the token enforces physical presence. Either way do not leave the private key unprotected unless you enjoy giving strangers access to your repos.

Step 3 Load the key into ssh agent

ssh agent keeps your decrypted key in memory so Git operations do not keep asking for the passphrase. Start an agent per login session and add the key once.

eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

On macOS and many Linux desktops your key manager will integrate with the system keychain. If you have multiple keys add each one to the agent.

Step 4 Register the public key with Git providers

Copy the public key file and paste it into each provider account under the SSH keys section. The file is ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub or the hardware key public file. After adding a key push and fetch should authenticate without passwords for that account.

Step 5 Use ssh config to manage multiple identities

When you have more than one key you do not want Git to guess. Use an ssh config file to tie IdentityFile to hosts and to enable agent forwarding for jump hosts when needed. Keep the file simple and explicit.

~/.ssh/config

Host github.com
  HostName github.com
  User git
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
  IdentitiesOnly yes

Host gitlab.com
  HostName gitlab.com
  User git
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_work
  IdentitiesOnly yes

Host internal-jump
  HostName jump.example.com
  User youruser
  ForwardAgent yes

IdentitiesOnly yes prevents ssh from offering every key in your agent to a host which can avoid accidental auth failures or lockouts.

Agent forwarding and jump hosts

ForwardAgent yes is convenient when you need to hop through a bastion host to reach a Git server. It forwards authentication requests to your local agent so your private keys never leave your machine. That is convenient and reasonably safe unless the jump host is malicious. If you care about security avoid forwarding to untrusted boxes and prefer hardware tokens for critical keys.

Extra tips for a less broken life

  • Use meaningful comments when generating keys. It helps when you have many keys.
  • Rotate keys if a machine is lost or a key leaks and remove the public key from provider accounts immediately.
  • Consider separate keys for work and personal accounts to reduce blast radius.
  • Use YubiKey or another FIDO token for high value accounts and CI where supported.

Summary

Generate an ed25519 key protect it with a passphrase or a hardware token load it into an ssh agent add the public key to GitHub GitLab and other providers and use ~/.ssh/config to make keys behave. Do these and your Git SSH setup will be far less annoying and slightly more secure than your average developer rig.
seo_title: Create Portable SSH Keys for Git and Use Them on Any Machine
seo_heading: Set up ed25519 SSH keys and agents for GitHub and GitLab workflows

title: Fix Git's SSH Permission Denied (PublicKey) Error on GitHub
description: Quick guide to fix Git SSH Permission Denied PublicKey errors on GitHub by creating keys adding to agent uploading the public key and testing the connectio
heading: Fix Git's SSH Permission Denied (PublicKey) Error on GitHub
body:
So Git screamed Permission denied publickey What now

If you tried to push and Git replied with Permission denied publickey do not panic or throw your laptop out the window yet. This error usually means GitHub does not see a usable SSH key for your user or the SSH agent is asleep on the job. The fix is boring but predictable. Check for an existing key generate a modern one if needed add it to an agent upload the public key to GitHub and test the connection with SSH debug output.

Step 1 Check for existing SSH keys

Look in your home SSH folder for keys. Typical files are ~/.ssh/id_rsa or ~/.ssh/id_ed25519. If a key exists you do not need to generate another one unless you want to replace it with something newer.

ls -la ~/.ssh

Step 2 Generate a modern key if you need one

Use Ed25519 when possible because modern algorithms are less dramatic and more secure. Run this and type your email when asked.

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"

If you already have keys and are not sure which to use pick the ed25519 key or the one you expect Git to use.

Step 3 Add the private key to the SSH agent

The agent caches your unlocked private keys so Git can use them without asking for a password every time. Start the agent then add your key.

eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

On some systems you may need platform specific tweaks to store keys across reboots. That is soul crushing but solvable by reading platform docs.

Step 4 Upload the public key to GitHub

Copy the public key file and paste it into GitHub under Settings then SSH and GPG keys. Use a clear name so future you does not cry.

cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

Step 5 Verify your Git remote and file permissions

Make sure your repo remote uses the SSH URL and not HTTPS. An SSH remote looks like git@github.com:user/repo.git. Switch it if needed.

git remote -v
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:user/repo.git

Permissions on the SSH folder and keys must be strict or SSH will sulk. Set them like this.

chmod 700 ~/.ssh
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

Step 6 Test the SSH connection and debug

Run a verbose SSH test to see what GitHub sees. The debug output will tell you if keys are offered if the agent is working or if permissions are blocking access.

ssh -T -v git@github.com

Look for lines that mention offering public key and authenticate success or denial. If the wrong key is offered you can use an SSH config entry to force the right identity.

Optional Add a Host entry for GitHub

If you have multiple keys add a simple config entry so SSH stops guessing.

mkdir -p ~/.ssh
cat >> ~/.ssh/config <<'EOF'
Host github.com
  HostName github.com
  User git
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
EOF

Troubleshooting notes

  • If ssh-agent shows no identities run ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 again and check for errors.
  • If GitHub still denies access confirm the exact public key you uploaded matches ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub.
  • On Windows using Git Bash or an SSH client make sure the agent you start is the one your Git installation talks to.
  • If you see permission denied after all this double check file modes and that your account on GitHub has the key listed.

Recap and final sarcasm

Summary in plain terms. Check for keys, generate a modern key with ssh-keygen if needed, add it to an agent, upload the public key to GitHub, confirm the remote uses SSH and set strict file permissions, then test with verbose SSH to debug. If it still fails blame network gremlins then retrace these steps. You will win eventually.
seo_title: Get Git SSH PublicKey Access Working with GitHub Quickly
seo_heading: Troubleshoot SSH keys and Git remotes to stop Permission Denied errors

title: Find GitHub's SSH URL & Git Cloning!
description: Find the SSH URL on GitHub add SSH keys test the link and clone a repository using simple commands and clear steps.
heading: Find GitHub SSH URL and Git Cloning Guide
body:
This tutorial shows how to find a GitHub SSH URL and clone a repository using SSH keys and the command line in a few quick steps.

  1. Open the repository page on GitHub
  2. Click the Code button and pick SSH
  3. Copy the SSH link shown
  4. Generate or add a local SSH key pair
  5. Test the SSH connection to GitHub
  6. Run the clone command using the SSH link

Step 1 Navigate to the repository page on GitHub where source files live. No treasure hunt required. A repo home page holds the Code button near the top right area of the file list.
