title: GitHub URL Example | Learn how to use GitHub URLs & Git
description: Practical guide to reading and using GitHub URLs for cloning linking and pushing code with clear commands and common pitfalls
heading: GitHub URL Example Learn how to use GitHub URLs and Git
body:
This tutorial shows how to read and use GitHub URLs for cloning browsing and pushing code using HTTPS and SSH.

  1. Identify the URL type
  2. Clone with an HTTPS style URL
  3. Clone with an SSH style URL
  4. Add or change a remote
  5. Create permalinks for files and commits

Identify the URL type Recognize whether the provided address is a web friendly address or an SSH style address. A web friendly address usually contains the domain and path that a browser understands. An SSH style address uses a key based access method that requires a configured SSH key on the developer machine and an account on the hosting service.

Clone with an HTTPS style URL Use a clone command shown in a generic form to copy a repository locally. Example command format in a code friendly view git clone github.com user repo.git Replace placeholders with actual repository path as shown on the hosting site.

Clone with an SSH style URL Ensure an SSH key is added to the hosting account then use an SSH based clone command. The repository will transfer over secure shell and avoid password prompts after key setup.

Add or change a remote Use remote commands to point a local project at a different repository. Example flow in words is to run a remote add or remote set url command then push branches to the new destination.

Create permalinks for files and commits Use the file view on the hosting site to grab a stable link for a particular file version or an individual commit. That makes sharing a specific line of code less mysterious.

Summary recap of the tutorial topic The article covered how to tell different URL forms how to clone with web friendly and SSH approaches how to update a remote and how to create stable links for code references. Follow the steps and the next time a remote URL shows up the mystery will fade.

Tip

Keep both an HTTPS and an SSH workflow in mind. HTTPS is quick for occasional pulls while SSH saves time for regular contributors. Name remotes clearly so a push never goes to the wrong project.

title: Generate GitLab SSH Keys & setup SSH on GitLab
description: Generate SSH keys and add the public key to GitLab for password free git push and pull Learn keygen agent config and testing tips
heading: Generate GitLab SSH Keys and setup SSH on GitLab
body:
This guide teaches how to generate an SSH key pair and add the public key to GitLab so git push and pull work without typing a password.

  1. Generate the SSH key pair
  2. Copy the public key to GitLab profile
  3. Start the SSH agent and add the private key
  4. Test the SSH connection to GitLab

Generate the SSH key pair Use a modern algorithm and run the command below. Choose a passphrase for safety or leave empty for automation.

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"

Copy the public key to GitLab Display the public key with the following command and copy the output from the terminal. Then open GitLab profile settings and paste the public key into the SSH Keys section with a descriptive title.

cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

Start the SSH agent and add the private key Start the agent and add the key so repeated authentication does not require a passphrase every time. Use the commands below on Unix style systems.

eval "$(ssh-agent -s)" then ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

Optionally add a short host entry in ~/.ssh/config to simplify commands and force the correct key for gitlab.com

Test the SSH connection Verify that GitLab accepts the key by running the SSH test command. Expect a friendly greeting on success. If the test fails check that the public key was pasted correctly and that the agent has the private key loaded.

ssh -T git@gitlab.com

Recap of the process Generate a key pair add the public key to the GitLab account start the SSH agent add the private key and verify the connection This enables password free git operations over SSH

Tip

Prefer ed25519 keys for speed and security Use a passphrase for personal machines and a dedicated key without a passphrase for CI agents Keep a secure backup of private keys and revoke old keys in GitLab when no longer needed

title: How to Generate GitHub SSH Keys
description: Step by step guide to generate GitHub SSH keys add the public key to a GitHub account and test the SSH connection for secure passwordless Git access
heading: How to Generate GitHub SSH Keys Fast and Securely
body:
This tutorial shows how to generate a GitHub SSH key pair and add the public key to a GitHub account for secure passwordless pushes.

  1. Generate a new SSH key pair
  2. Start the SSH agent and add the private key
  3. Copy the public key to the clipboard
  4. Add the public key to the GitHub account
  5. Test the SSH connection

Generate a new SSH key pair

Run the following command to create an ed25519 key which is modern and fast

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"

When prompted choose a file name or accept the default and add a passphrase for better security. The private key must stay private and the public key is what gets shared.

Start the SSH agent and add the private key

Launch the agent and add the private key so the key can be used for authentication without retyping a passphrase constantly

eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"

ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

Copy the public key to the clipboard

Copy the content of the public key file and paste into GitHub key form

macOS use pbcopy < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub Linux use xclip -sel clip < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub Windows Git Bash use cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub then copy manually

Add the public key to the GitHub account

Open the GitHub web settings for SSH keys click new SSH key paste the public key and give a descriptive title like laptop or workstation. No magic here just paste and save.

Test the SSH connection

Verify the key is recognized by GitHub with a friendly authentication test

ssh -T git@github.com

A successful response will confirm authentication and may offer a warm welcome that proves the key works.

This tutorial covered generating an SSH key pair adding the private key to the agent copying the public key adding that public key to a GitHub account and testing the SSH connection so pushes and pulls can use SSH authentication without password prompts.

Tip

Prefer ed25519 keys for most users and protect the private key with a passphrase. Use an SSH config file to manage multiple keys per host and name keys clearly to avoid confusion when juggling machines.

title: How to Undo a Pushed Git Commit
description: Learn when to use git reset and git revert after a push and how to fix remote commits safely and without drama
heading: How to Undo a Pushed Git Commit Safely
body:
This tutorial gives a concise guide to undoing a pushed Git commit using git revert for safe history or git reset and a force push for private branches while advising on communication and recovery steps.

  1. Decide whether to revert or reset
  2. Run git revert to create a reversing commit
  3. Use git reset and force push for private branches only
  4. Push changes and notify collaborators
  5. Verify history and CI after the change

Decide between revert and reset

Choose git revert when the commit is already shared with others and preserving history is important. Choose git reset when the branch is private and rewriting history will not surprise teammates.

Run git revert

Use git revert HEAD to make a new commit that reverses the last change. For a specific commit use the commit hash like git revert abc123. This keeps history linear and avoids drama for collaborators.

Use git reset for private branches

To drop the last commit locally use git reset --hard HEAD~1. When the branch is private push the rewritten history with git push --force-with-lease origin branch-name. Force with lease reduces risk by checking for upstream changes first.

Push and tell the team

After a revert push normally with git push origin branch-name. After a reset push with force with lease and send a short message to teammates so no one spends an hour debugging a disappearing commit.

Verify history and CI

Check history with git log --oneline and confirm continuous integration passes. Use git reflog to recover a lost commit when needed because accidents happen and reflog is a time machine.

Recap choose revert for shared history and reset with caution for private branches. Use force with lease instead of blind force and always notify collaborators after rewriting history.

Tip

Prefer git revert for public branches and use git push --force-with-lease when rewriting history. Keep a branch backup before any destructive move and use git reflog to recover if necessary.

title: How to EDIT UNDO or CHANGE the last Git commit AMEND
description: Edit or undo the last Git commit message using git commit --amend and safe force push options for shared repositories and clean history.
heading: How to EDIT UNDO or CHANGE the last Git commit message with AMEND
body:
Quick fixes for the last commit

So you just committed something regrettable. Maybe a typo in the message, maybe you forgot to add a file, maybe you hit enter too soon while dreaming of coffee. Relax, Git has a tidy little tool for this kind of shame called amend. Use it when the bad commit has not yet wandered off to the remote.

Edit the last commit message locally

If the commit lives only on your machine then changing the message is painless. Run the command below to replace the most recent commit message without creating a new commit object.

git commit --amend -m 'New message here'

If you omit the -m argument Git will open your default editor so you can rewrite the message like a responsible adult.

Add staged changes into the previous snapshot

If you forgot to add a file just stage it and then amend the commit. Git will bundle the staged content into the previous snapshot and let you change the message too.

git add path/to/file
git commit --amend

This is great for small fixes and typos. It is not a magic spell that resurrects deleted files that never existed locally in the first place.

When the commit has already been pushed

Once you push a commit to a shared branch you are playing with other people's work. Rewriting that history is possible but you must be polite about it. After amending use a guarded forced push to update the remote while checking you did not stomp on anyone else.

git push --force-with-lease

Force with lease will refuse to overwrite the remote if someone else pushed in the meantime. It is the considerate version of nuclear option push.

Communicate with collaborators

If you rewrite history on a branch others use tell them. A quick message prevents surprise merges and future confusion. If you are the only person on the branch then go ahead and amend like a lone ranger.

Completely undo the last commit

Sometimes you need to uncommit entirely. Pick your weapon based on whether you want to keep your working tree changes.

  • Keep staged changes use reset soft which uncommits but preserves the index and working directory
    • git reset --soft HEAD~1
  • Discard the commit and working changes use reset hard which removes the commit and throws away local changes
    • git reset --hard HEAD~1

Warning do not use reset hard unless you are sure you do not need the work anymore. Git does not always forgive that level of commitment to deletion.

Best practices and safety tips

  • Use amend for small cosmetic fixes and missing files that you just staged
  • Avoid rewriting shared history unless you coordinate with teammates
  • Prefer git push --force-with-lease over git push --force when others may be working on the branch
  • When in doubt create a new commit instead of rewriting history to keep things simple and predictable

There you go. Amend when tidy fixes will do. Reset when you need to rewind. And when you must force push use the polite version so your team does not hate you. Now go commit responsibly or at least with slightly fewer regrets.
seo_title: Fix the Last Git Commit with Amend and Safe Force Push Today
seo_heading: Edit or undo your latest commit on the command line the safe way

title: Why Java Uses static & final for Constants
description: Learn why Java uses static and final for constants and how compile time inlining memory and immutability affect design and safety
heading: Why Java Uses static and final for Constants Explained
body:
What static and final actually do in Java

Static means there is one copy of the variable at the classloader level and not one per object instance. Final means the reference cannot be reassigned for primitives and for object references. Put them together and you get a shared constant that is meant to be stable and immutable in name and intent.

Quick example that looks familiar

public class C {
    public static final int MAX = 100
    public static final String NAME = "APP"
}

Why people reach for public static final

  • Memory efficiency since one copy lives in the class space rather than in every instance
  • Performance because the compiler may inline compile time values into callers
  • Clarity and convention because uppercase names signal intent to other humans

Hold your horses with compile time inlining and the constant pool

When a primitive or String literal qualifies as a compile time constant the compiler stores the actual value in the caller class file. That is called compile time inlining and the JVM constant pool ends up with that value baked into the dependent classes. The practical fallout is that changing a public static final value in a library will not change the value in code that was compiled against the old version until you rebuild those dependents. It is the source of many hair pulling moments in dependency management.

Mutable objects are not fixed just because the reference is final

Declaring an object reference final prevents rebinding the reference only. The object itself can still mutate via its methods. If you want true immutability use immutable classes or prefer enum types when you have a fixed set of values. Otherwise surprise state changes will haunt you at runtime.

Practical rules of thumb for Java constants

  • Use public static final for truly stable primitives and String literals that will not change across releases
  • Prefer enums for grouped constants and for type safety when you have a fixed set of values
  • Use accessor methods or package private constants for values that may evolve so you avoid the compile time inlining trap
  • For mutable data prefer immutable classes to prevent accidental state changes

Final thoughts and a tiny reality check

Public static final is fine when used for stable compile time constants. It is tiny, efficient and clear. However it creates brittle APIs when values are expected to change across versions. If you maintain a library imagine telling users to recompile every time you tweak a number. They will not be thrilled and neither will you.

If you want safety and clarity favor enums for fixed sets and prefer accessors for evolving values. Use public static final only when you are certain a value is forever or you enjoy fixing dependency bugs late at night.
seo_title: Stop Misusing Java constants Learn static final the smart way
seo_heading: When to use public static final in Java and when to pick enums instead

title: How to Unstage a File in Git
description: Remove a file from the Git staging index using git restore or git reset with clear commands and verification steps for safer commits.
heading: How to Unstage a File in Git
body:
This tutorial shows how to remove a file from the Git staging index using git restore or git reset and how to verify changes so commits stay clean.

  1. Check staged files
  2. Unstage a specific file
  3. Verify the staging index
  4. Discard working tree changes if desired

Check staged files with git status or use git status --short to get a compact view. This reveals which files are in the staging index and ready for commit. A quick peek avoids accidental commits of half finished work and preserves developer dignity.

Unstage a file by running git restore --staged path/to/file. That removes the file from the staging index while leaving the working tree changes intact. For older Git versions run git reset HEAD path/to/file which achieves the same effect using classic commands.

Verify the staging index again with git status. The file should now appear as modified rather than staged. If the goal was to prepare a cleaner commit use git add -p to stage only desired hunks before committing.

If the aim is to discard working tree changes as well run git restore path/to/file or use git checkout -- path/to/file on legacy setups. Be aware that discarding changes is destructive and cannot be undone without backups or reflog magic.

This guide covered checking staged files unstaging with git restore or git reset verifying results and optional discard of working tree changes so commits stay intentional.

Tip

Use git add -p to stage hunks rather than whole files when possible. That habit reduces the need to unstage files and keeps commit history meaningful and less embarrassing.

title: How to Convert a Java String to int or long Primitive Type
description: Fast guide to parse Java String to int and long using parseInt parseLong valueOf and safe parsing tips for real world code
heading: How to Convert a Java String to int or long Primitive Type
body:
This tutorial shows how to convert a Java String to primitive int and long types safely and clearly while avoiding common exceptions and surprises.

  1. Use Integer parseInt for int conversion
  2. Use Long parseLong for long conversion
  3. Handle NumberFormatException with try catch
  4. Use wrapper valueOf when a boxed type is needed
  5. Create a safe tryParse helper for graceful failures

Step 1 Use Integer parseInt to turn a decimal string into an int. Example usage int n = Integer.parseInt("123") This method will throw NumberFormatException when the string contains non digits or the value falls outside the int range.

Step 2 Use Long parseLong for larger integers. Example usage long l = Long.parseLong("1234567890123") This method behaves like Integer parseInt but covers the long range so choose the correct primitive based on expected magnitude.

Step 3 Handle NumberFormatException with try catch around parsing calls. Example pattern try { int n = Integer.parseInt(s) } catch (NumberFormatException e) { // handle bad input } Use targeted catch blocks to avoid surprising program termination and to provide a user friendly message or a fallback value.

Step 4 Use Integer valueOf or Long valueOf when a boxed type is required for collections or APIs that expect wrapper classes. Example Integer boxed = Integer.valueOf("123") This returns an Integer which may be cached for small values.

Step 5 Implement a safe try parse helper to avoid repeated try catch code. Example helper pattern static Integer tryParseInt(String s) { try { return Integer.parseInt(s) } catch (NumberFormatException e) { return null } } Use a null return or Optional to signal invalid input depending on coding style.

Recap The walkthrough covered parseInt parseLong try catch valueOf and a simple tryParse helper to handle bad strings. Follow these steps to reduce runtime surprises and make parsing logic readable and maintainable. A tiny bit of defensive coding prevents big debugging sessions later and keeps NumberFormatException from crashing production code.

Tip

Trim input and validate with a simple regex before parsing to avoid whitespace surprises. Check numeric range before converting to avoid overflow. When numbers may exceed long range consider BigInteger for safe handling.

title: My Video
description: Quick FFmpeg guide to extract a thumbnail from a short video in seconds with clear steps and useful tips
heading: My Video thumbnail extraction guide with FFmpeg
body:
When you need one thumbnail fast

Yes you can stare at the video and pick a frame by hand, or you can use FFmpeg and be marginally more efficient. This tiny tutorial explains how to pull a single thumbnail from a short clip using the command line. It is fast, repeatable, and perfectly suited for quick social previews or automated workflows in video editing and media tools.

Install FFmpeg

Get FFmpeg for your platform and make sure the binary is on the path. Common options include

  • Linux use your distro package manager such as apt install ffmpeg or similar
  • Mac use a package manager like brew install ffmpeg if you like typing commands
  • Windows download a build from the official site and add the exe to the system path

Pick a frame time and keep it simple

Give the seek time in plain seconds. That avoids weird time formats and keeps the command readable. Pick a moment that shows an important face or interesting motion. If you are automating choose a time a few seconds after a scene change to avoid black frames.

Run one clear command

Here is the minimal command that works for most cases and plays nicely in scripts

ffmpeg -ss 5 -i input.mp4 -vframes 1 -qscale 2 thumbnail.jpg

This seeks into the video at five seconds then saves one frame as a high quality JPEG. Replace the five with the second that best represents your video and rename input and thumbnail as needed.

Tune quality and file size without drama

Lower qscale values generally mean higher quality. If your goal is a small file size then resize or crop after extraction using a dedicated image tool or by adding FFmpeg filters. For bulk jobs sample frames every few seconds then pick the sharpest result programmatically.

Automation and batch tips

  • To generate many thumbnails script the command in a loop and save each sample with a timestamp in the file name
  • When automating choose a frame offset after scene cuts to avoid black or blank frames
  • For pipelines in video editing or media tools integrate this command into your preprocessing step to produce consistent previews

That is it. One tidy FFmpeg command, a little common sense about which second to pick, and you have a usable thumbnail for previews and production. If you want to get fancy later you can add filters or run a small image optimization step but for many projects this approach is fast and accurate.
seo_title: Grab a Perfect Thumbnail with FFmpeg in One Fast Command
seo_heading: Extract high quality thumbnails from videos with FFmpeg on Linux and Mac

title: Git Stash Tutorial
description: Learn how to save and restore uncommitted changes with Git stash for fast context switches and safe experiments
heading: Git Stash Tutorial for Developers
body:
What git stash actually does for you

Think of git stash as a short term memory for your repo when your brain and your branch are not aligned. It saves uncommitted changes so you can switch tasks without turning your working tree into a crime scene. This is essential for a clean developer workflow and solid version control discipline.

Quick stash cheats and commands

Yes you can wing it with one command. Here are the commands you will actually use while pretending you had a plan all along.

git stash push -m 'WIP message'   # save tracked changes with a note
git stash                         # quick save that omits a message
git stash push -u -m 'WIP with new files'   # include untracked files

Running any of those returns your working tree to HEAD so switching branches will not leave half finished experiments behind.

See what you stashed

List the stash stack and inspect entries before you resurrect anything. This helps avoid surprises when you reapply changes to a different base.

git stash list
git stash show -p stash@{0}   # view the patch for the top stash

Bring changes back using apply or pop

Two similar moves with different intents. Use stash apply when you want to keep the saved copy. Use stash pop when you are confident you will not need that backup again. Pop removes the stash after applying which is handy for cleanup when merges are tame.

git stash apply stash@{0}
git stash pop stash@{0}

Rescue work into a new branch

If your stash was born from a reckless experiment make a branch from it. This avoids polluting main branches and gives the work a proper home for testing and commits.

git stash branch new-branch stash@{0}

This command creates the branch and applies the stash in one polite motion. It is the civilized way to recover WIP without touching main.

When to stash untracked files

If you added new files that are not yet tracked use the -u flag when pushing the stash. Be careful with large generated files unless you enjoy slow disks and painful regret.

Cleaning up old stashes

Stash entries are helpful but lonely. Keep the list tidy so you do not accidentally resurrect something ancient and mysterious.

git stash drop stash@{0}   # remove a single stash
git stash clear            # remove all stashes

Quick stash tips for sane version control

  • Use messages with push so stash list is readable
  • Prefer apply for cautious restores and pop for cleanup
  • Create a stash branch for experimental work you want to keep
  • Include untracked files only when needed with -u

If you follow these steps you will be able to switch tasks without losing work and without dramatic regret. Git stash is a tiny rescue team for your developer workflow. Use it well and you will spend less time fixing your working tree and more time pretending the plan was always this clever.
seo_title: Save Your Work Fast With Git Stash and Smart Workflow Tips
seo_heading: Practical stash strategies for git apply pop and rescue branches

title: Rename a Git Branch
description: Quick guide to rename a Git branch locally and on a remote with safe commands and practical tips
heading: Rename a Git Branch Safely
body:
Why this exists and how not to wreck anything

Renaming a Git branch sounds cute until someone opens a pull request against the old name and the repo turns into a mystery novel. This guide shows how to rename a branch locally and on the remote while preserving commit history and keeping your teammates from mutiny. It is practical, safe, and mildly satisfying.

Rename the branch locally

If you are sitting on the branch you want to rename run the simpler command. If you are not on that branch run the variant that names both old and new. Both keep the commit history intact and do not rewrite anything scary.

git branch -m new-name
# or from another branch
git branch -m old-name new-name

Push the new branch and set upstream

Now send the newly named branch to the remote and tell Git to track it. This makes future pushes and pulls behave predictably and stops Git from acting like it has a secret agenda.

git push -u origin new-name

Remove the old branch from the remote

Once you confirm the new branch exists on the remote remove the old one so collaborators do not get confused by duplicate names. This is the polite way to avoid having two branches with the same ego.

git push origin --delete old-name

Update other clones and open pull requests

Tell your teammates to fetch and prune dead references so their local view matches the server. If a pull request targets the old branch update the PR target or recreate the PR with the new branch name. Yes this is mildly annoying. No it will not break history.

git fetch --prune
# then clean up local refs if needed
git branch -a

What to tell your team

  • Run git fetch --prune to remove the old remote ref from local listings.
  • If the PR target has to change edit the PR branch target or open a new PR from new-name.
  • If someone still complains remind them branches are cheap and names are free.

Verify and clean up

Check all branches and make sure the remote shows the new name. Remove any temporary local branches you made during the rename. A quick look with git branch -a gives a good status snapshot.

git branch -a

Common gotchas and reassurance

  • If CI or deployment references the old branch update the configuration to point to the new name.
  • If someone has unpushed work on the old branch they should either rebase onto the new-name or create a new branch from their work and push it.
  • Renaming does not change commits or history so blame and history remain intact.

Quick summary

Rename locally with git branch -m then push the new branch with git push -u origin new-name. Delete the old remote ref with git push origin --delete old-name. Ask teammates to git fetch --prune and update any open pull requests. You kept history, you kept the repo tidy, and you survived another day as a developer.

Tip If a branch backs an open pull request edit the target in the PR or create a new PR from the new branch name to avoid surprises for reviewers.
seo_title: Rename a Git branch without breaking history or open PRs
seo_heading: Safe steps to rename local and remote Git branches and notify teammates

title: How to download and install Git
description: Quick guide to download and install Git on Windows Mac and Linux with simple steps and verification commands
heading: How to download and install Git on Windows Mac and Linux
body:
Quick overview before you click anything

Want version control without a meltdown Welcome to the short path from zero to committed code. This guide shows how to download and install Git on Windows Mac and Linux and how to verify the setup so you can stop emailing files to yourself like it is 2003.

Pick the right installer

Identify your operating system and use the preferred installer for that platform. No need to flirt with sketchy sites unless you enjoy surprises.

  • Windows Choose 64 bit or 32 bit depending on your system architecture.
  • macOS Use the installer package or install with Homebrew if you like typing commands and feng shui.
  • Linux Use your distro package manager for the smoothest ride and fewer dependency arguments.

Download safely

Go to git-scm.com and grab the official installer. Save it somewhere obvious like the Downloads folder and avoid random downloads named stuff like setup_final_very_secure.exe.

Run the installer and pick sensible options

Run the installer on your platform and accept defaults for typical development unless you know exactly what you are doing. A few platform specific notes are below.

Windows tips

  • Select the option to add Git to your PATH so you can run git from Command Prompt or PowerShell.
  • Pick the credential manager option if you want fewer password prompts.

macOS tips

  • If you prefer GUI installers use the package. If you prefer the command line run brew install git.
  • Use the keychain helper to keep credentials safe and quiet.

Linux tips

  • Debian and Ubuntu sudo apt update && sudo apt install git
  • Fedora sudo dnf install git
  • Arch sudo pacman -S git
  • Consider the credential cache helper to avoid repeated prompts during a work session.

Set your identity so commits stop being anonymous

Open a terminal and run these commands to set your name and email. This is what shows up in commit history and in awkward blame moments.

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

Verify the installation

Make sure Git is installed and reachable from the command line. If this works you are officially in the club.

git --version

If the command prints a version number you are good to go. If not check your PATH or the package manager logs and then try not to panic.

Start using Git without drama

Create a repo or clone an existing project and make your first commit. Basic commands to begin are below.

git init
git clone https://example.com/yourrepo.git
git add .
git commit -m "First commit"

Troubleshooting and handy tips

  • If your terminal says command not found check that Git was added to PATH on Windows or that the package installed correctly on Unix like systems.
  • Enable credential caching on local machines to avoid repeated prompts. On macOS use the osxkeychain helper. On Windows use the credential manager option selected during setup. On Linux try the credential cache helper.
  • Use the package manager on Linux for cleaner upgrades and fewer mysterious breakages.

Parting advice

Git will not fix poor commit messages but it will save you from losing work. Install it, set your name and email, and then commit early and often. Welcome to version control with slightly less chaos.
seo_title: Install Git fast on Windows Mac and Linux without drama

title: Git Log Graph Tree Command
description: Quick guide to use git log graph tree command to visualize branches and commits with concise examples and a helpful tip.
heading: Git Log Graph Tree Command Guide
body:
If your git history looks like a bowl of tangled spaghetti this guide will help you make sense of it. You will learn how to use git log graph and tree style flags to map commits branches and merges. This is a pragmatic git tutorial for command line users who want readable git history and less guesswork when tracking git branches.

Quick visual log

When you want a fast overview of what happened use the classic combo that many developers swear by. It draws a simple ASCII tree on the left and keeps each commit short and labeled.

git log --graph --oneline --decorate --all

The graph shows merges and branch points. The oneline keeps messages compact while decorate adds branch and tag names. The all flag brings remote refs into view so nothing hides from you.

Add compact dates

If commit messages are cryptic or poetic adding short dates helps you scan history like a sane human being.

git log --graph --oneline --decorate --all --date=short

Focus on a single branch

Want to ignore the rest of the repo drama and track a feature branch only Use the branch name directly.

git log --graph --oneline --decorate branch-name

Show full metadata when you need it

For forensic level detail switch to a fuller format and include all refs. This reveals author and committer info plus timestamps.

git log --graph --pretty=fuller --all

Pipe into a pager for searching and scrolling

For long histories send output to a color aware pager to search without losing the decorate colors.

git log --graph --oneline --decorate --all | less -R

Handy tips for real projects

  • Set an alias to avoid repetitive typing. This saves keyboard wear and your patience.
  • Combine filtering flags like --since or --author for focused audits of git history and git branches.
  • Use --pretty formats to tailor how much metadata you see when debugging merges or build failures.
  • Remember that git graph is an ASCII interpretation not a diagram tool. It is excellent for quick mental models and terrible for making slides.
git config --global alias.lg "log --graph --oneline --decorate --all"
# then run
git lg

Wrap up If you want a readable git tree on the command line these flags are your best friends. They help visualize git graph relationships and reveal branch structure without requiring extra developer tools. Use aliases and pagers to make the workflow smooth and keep your repo history usable instead of dramatic evidence in a future code archaeology project.

title: Rename Master Branch to Main on GitHub
description: Quick guide to renaming the master branch to main on GitHub while preserving history and minimizing disruption
heading: Rename Master Branch to Main on GitHub step by step
body:
Why bother at all

If your repo still uses master as the default branch you are not doing anything wrong, you are just doing something old. Renaming master to main is mostly symbolic, but it avoids awkward naming in new forks and makes future contributors feel welcome. It also keeps your commit history intact, which is the important part unless you like chaos.

Before you touch anything

Do not be the person who renames a branch without checking local work. Make sure every clone has no uncommitted changes. Either commit, stash, or hide the evidence in a drawer. Then run:

git pull origin master

This gets the latest remote master so your local copy will match what you are about to rename.

Change the default branch on GitHub

On the repository page go to Settings and then Branches and set main as the new default branch. GitHub can offer to update open pull requests and will create redirects from the old default branch name for a while. Those redirects are helpful but not forever, so plan the switch properly.

Rename local branches and update remotes

On each machine run these commands. They are short and glorious.

git fetch origin
git branch -m master main
git push -u origin main
git branch -u origin/main main
git remote set-head origin -a

If you want to remove the old remote branch do this on a machine with push rights

git push origin --delete master

Or you can rely on GitHub redirects for a limited time while everyone updates.

Fix branch protection rules and CI

Branch protection does not magically move. Recreate or move protection rules to main so required checks, review requirements, and status checks keep working. Edit GitHub Actions workflows and any CI config that mentions master. Search the repo for the word master and update scripts, deployment references, and environment names.

Common places to check

  • .github workflows and action files
  • CI config files like .travis.yml or circleci config
  • deployment scripts and Kubernetes manifests
  • documentation, README files, and links in issue templates

Tell the team and external systems

Communication is the bridge between a smooth rename and a day of frantic Slack messages. Send the commands above and a short explanation. Remind integrators and external systems that reference the branch to update their settings. If you have deployment providers or bots that expect master update those too.

Verification and rollback

After the rename run your CI and a few quick deploy tests. Make sure protected branches behave as expected and that pull requests land on main. If something breaks you can restore the old branch name, but that is extra work. Test in a staging repo if you enjoy living dangerously but safely.

Quick checklist to avoid drama

  • Commit or stash local changes
  • Set main as default in repo settings
  • Rename local branches and push main to origin
  • Move branch protection rules to main
  • Update CI and workflow files that mention master
  • Notify collaborators and external systems
  • Search the repo for master and update references

Rename is a small set of coordinated steps and a little humility. Do the checks, update protections and CI, and tell everyone what you did. Your repo will keep its history, your pipelines will keep running, and your team will stop asking why build broke on a Monday morning.
seo_title: Switch your repo default from master to main on GitHub safely
seo_heading: Step by step branch rename guide for GitHub with CI and protection tips

title: GitHub Personal Access Token Create Use Fine Grained Access
description: Quick guide to create get and use GitHub personal access tokens with fine grained permissions for secure automation and CI
heading: GitHub Personal Access Token Create Use Fine Grained Access
body:
This tutorial teaches how to create and use GitHub personal access tokens with fine grained permissions for secure automation and workflows.

  1. Open GitHub and go to Settings then Developer settings then Personal access tokens then Fine grained tokens
  2. Choose name expiration repository access and permission scopes
  3. Generate token and copy the value once because GitHub shows the key only once
  4. Use token with git operations API calls or CI by storing the token as a secret in repository or environment
  5. Rotate revoke and limit token scope to follow least privilege practices

Step 1 Open the GitHub user interface and navigate to Developer settings then Personal access tokens and select Fine grained tokens. Pick the correct account or organization before making changes.

Step 2 Give the token a descriptive name and set an expiration period. Choose repository level access and then pick minimal permission scopes required for the task. No admin on everything unless chaos is the goal.

Step 3 Click Generate and copy the token value immediately. The token will not be shown again so paste the value into a secure vault or secret store right away.

Step 4 Use the token in place of a password for git over HTTPS or as an authorization header for API calls. For CI place the token in repository secrets or in a pipeline secret manager so credentials stay out of logs.

Step 5 Apply rotation and revocation rules. Revoke unused tokens and create new tokens on a schedule to reduce exposure. Limit scope often and test access with a narrow permission set before expanding.

This short guide covered how to create generate and use fine grained personal access tokens on GitHub along with practical storage and rotation advice. Following least privilege and secret management practices keeps automation functional without handing keys to the kingdom.

Tip

Store tokens in a vault or GitHub secrets and enable expirations. Test smallest permission set first and only expand when a feature truly requires extra access.

title: Git Set Remote Upstream URL
description: Quick guide to set or change Git remote upstream URL so the local repository points to the correct upstream for pushes and pulls.
heading: Git Set Remote Upstream URL Guide
body:
See and change the upstream remote URL then push with confidence

So your commits are ready to be shared but somehow they end up in the wrong place. Welcome to the small tragedy of modern version control. This guide shows how to inspect add or update an upstream remote and then push where you actually meant to. All with commands you can paste and a tiny amount of pride loss.

Check what your repo thinks is upstream

First step is to ask the repo what it thinks is the remote. Run this to list known remotes and their fetch and push targets.

git remote -v

The output lists remote names and their URLs. Look for a remote named upstream if the project expects one. If no upstream line appears then you will add one in the next step.

Add or update the upstream remote

If you need to add an upstream remote use this line. Replace REPO_URL with the address your hosting service gave you.

git remote add upstream REPO_URL

If the upstream already exists and points to some sad abandoned fork you can change it without touching any branches.

git remote set-url upstream REPO_URL

These commands only change the pointer the local repo uses for fetch and push. Your local branches remain intact and will not be rewritten by this.

Verify and push

Double check your work then push a branch to that upstream. Replace main with whatever branch name your project uses.

git remote -v
git push upstream main

If authentication fails check SSH keys or access tokens and verify your hosting permissions before blaming the terminal. Permissions are often the real villain in these stories.

Tips for sane remote names

When you have multiple remotes descriptive names save lives and debugging time. Use names like origin upstream fork or my-fork rather than cryptic one letter aliases.

  • If you fork and track the original project use upstream for the original and origin for your fork.
  • When collaborating make sure everyone agrees on which remote is authoritative to avoid surprise pushes.
  • Run git remote -v regularly so you do not accidentally push to an archived repo.

Quick recap

  • Run git remote -v to see current remotes
  • Use git remote add upstream REPO_URL to add a new upstream
  • Use git remote set-url upstream REPO_URL to change an existing upstream
  • Verify with git remote -v then git push upstream main

Follow these steps and your pushes will go where you expect. If not then at least you will know which command to scream at next.
seo_title: Fix your Git upstream remote so pushes hit the right repo
seo_heading: See and change the upstream remote URL then push with confidence

title: Change the Remote Git URL with Set Remote Origin
description: Quick guide to change a Git remote URL using git remote set-url and how to add origin if missing for local repos and pushes.
heading: Change the Remote Git URL with Set Remote Origin Guide
body:
This tutorial shows how to update a repository remote URL using git remote set-url and how to add origin when required.

  1. Inspect current remotes
  2. Replace the URL with git remote set-url
  3. Verify the new remote URL
  4. Add origin when no origin exists
  5. Push to the new remote and set upstream

Inspect current remotes Use a quick check to see remote names and URLs with git remote -v. That shows which remote name points where and avoids blind surgery on the wrong remote.

Replace the URL with git remote set-url Run git remote set-url origin https //new.example/repo.git to update the origin remote URL. This changes the stored URL for the remote name without touching branches or history.

Verify the new remote URL Running git remote -v again confirms the change. Verify fetch and push URLs match expectations before pushing any code to a new destination.

Add origin when no origin exists If git remote -v shows no origin use git remote add origin https //new.example/repo.git. That creates a named remote so standard push commands work as expected.

Push to the new remote and set upstream Use git push -u origin main or replace main with the branch name. The -u flag sets the upstream so future pushes can use the shorter git push form.

Summary of the tutorial content explains that this guide covered checking existing remotes updating a remote URL adding origin when missing and finally pushing a branch to the new remote with upstream configuration. These steps handle most remote URL changes without drama and avoid accidental pushes to the wrong place.

Tip

Use SSH URLs when possible for frequent pushes and configure a named remote for forks or mirrors to avoid overwriting central repositories by mistake.

title: How to Push an Existing Project to GitLab
description: Step by step guide to push an existing project to GitLab with remote setup add commit push and quick troubleshooting tips
heading: How to Push an Existing Project to GitLab Step by Step
body:
This tutorial teaches how to push an existing local project to GitLab using common Git commands and a GitLab remote.

  1. Create a new repository on GitLab
  2. Prepare the local project for version control
  3. Add the GitLab remote URL
  4. Stage and commit project files
  5. Push the branch to GitLab
  6. Verify the push and handle common errors

Create a new repository on GitLab

Sign in to GitLab and create a project. Choose a name and visibility level. Copy the HTTPS or SSH clone URL for later. Choosing SSH avoids typing credentials every push and looks slightly more professional.

Prepare the local project for version control

If the project lacks a Git database run git init in the project folder. If a Git database exists confirm branch name with git branch. Add a sensible .gitignore before staging to avoid committing generated files.

Add the GitLab remote URL

Link the local repository to the new GitLab project by running git remote add origin < URL> using the URL copied earlier. If a remote already exists replace or rename that remote using git remote set-url origin < URL> .

Stage and commit project files

Stage changes with git add . then commit with git commit -m "Initial commit" or a message that does not make maintainers cry.

Push the branch to GitLab

Push main branch with git push -u origin main or replace main with the correct branch name. The first push uses -u to set upstream so future pushes are shorter.

Verify the push and handle common errors

Open the GitLab project page and confirm files appeared. For authentication failures set up SSH keys or update personal access tokens. For non fast forward errors pull remote changes first then merge locally before pushing again.

This guide covered creating a GitLab repo linking a local project staging and committing files and pushing a branch so that the project lives on GitLab for collaboration and CI.

Tip

Use SSH keys for a smoother workflow and set a clear default branch name in GitLab to avoid repeated push flags.

title: Java Constructors Tutorial
description: Learn Java constructors and how to initialize objects with default and parameterized constructors plus best practices
heading: Java Constructors Tutorial Guide
body:
This tutorial teaches Java constructors and how to use constructors to initialize objects and enforce class invariants.

  1. Learn constructor basics
  2. Write default and parameterized constructors
  3. Apply constructor overloading
  4. Use this keyword and constructor chaining
  5. Follow practical best practices

1 Learn constructor basics

A constructor is a special method that runs when a new object of a class is created. The constructor name matches the class name and no return type appears. Constructors set initial field values and gatekeep proper state for the new object.

2 Write default and parameterized constructors

A default constructor takes no parameters and provides sane defaults. A parameterized constructor accepts values so the new object starts with meaningful state. Use parameter validation inside the constructor to avoid malformed objects.

public class Person { String name int age Person() { name = "Unknown" age = 0 } Person(String nameParam, int ageParam) { name = nameParam age = ageParam } }

3 Apply constructor overloading

Multiple constructors with different parameter lists provide flexible creation patterns. Overloading reduces boilerplate at call sites and offers clear defaults for common cases.

4 Use this keyword and constructor chaining

Use the this keyword to call another constructor from a constructor to avoid duplicated initialization code. Constructor chaining improves maintainability by centralizing setup logic.

public class Point { int x int y Point() { this(0, 0) } Point(int xParam, int yParam) { x = xParam y = yParam } }

5 Follow practical best practices

Keep constructors focused on initialization and avoid heavy logic or long running tasks. If complex setup is needed move that work to a factory method or builder. Prefer immutability when possible by declaring fields final and setting them once in the constructor.

Summary of the tutorial content Recap covers what a constructor is how to write default and parameterized constructors overloading and chaining and some guidelines for clean constructor design

Tip

Use constructor chaining to centralize validation and defaults and consider static factory methods when multiple construction pathways grow awkward or ambiguous

title: Complete Java Records Tutorial
description: Learn Java records for concise immutable data classes including declaration validation methods and migration from POJOs
heading: Complete Java Records Tutorial for concise immutable data classes
body:
This tutorial teaches how to use Java records to build concise immutable data carrier classes with validation and compatibility strategies for existing code bases.

  1. Declare a record
  2. Understand components and canonical constructor
  3. Add compact constructor for validation
  4. Add methods and customization
  5. Migrate from POJOs and handle serialization

Declare a record

A record is declared like a class but with less boilerplate. Example

record Person(String name, int age) { }

Understand components and canonical constructor

Components are the fields declared in the record header. The compiler generates a canonical constructor along with equals hashCode and toString so no more writing the same methods by hand like a medieval scribe.

Add compact constructor for validation

Use a compact constructor to validate values without repeating parameters. Example

record Person(String name, int age) { public Person { if(name == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("name null") if(age < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("age negative") } }

Add methods and customization

Records can include instance methods static methods and private members. Overriding toString or adding helper methods is allowed if generated behavior needs tuning.

Migrate from POJOs and handle serialization

Replace simple data holder classes with records to reduce code volume. For frameworks that rely on no arg constructors or mutable fields provide adapters or custom serializers. Records are final and immutable so some frameworks may need small adjustments.

Summary of the tutorial content The guide covered declaration component semantics canonical and compact constructors method additions and practical migration notes aimed at making code shorter and safer while keeping compatibility concerns in mind

Tip

Favor records for plain data carriers but avoid forcing records on types that require rich lifecycle control or mutable state. When a framework expects a no arg constructor write a thin adapter rather than sacrificing immutability.

title: Java Tic Tac Toe Game Tutorial
description: Build a playable Java Tic Tac Toe game with GUI game logic and a simple AI Step by step guide for beginners
heading: Java Tic Tac Toe Game Tutorial for Beginners Build a Playable Java Game
body:
This tutorial teaches how to build a playable Tic Tac Toe game in Java with a simple GUI game logic and a basic AI

  1. Set up project and user interface
  2. Model the game board and state
  3. Add win and draw detection
  4. Handle player input and turns
  5. Implement simple AI and polish

Set up project and user interface

Use a Java project with JFrame and JPanel and a GridLayout to create a 3 by 3 grid of buttons. Keep code organized by separating UI code from game logic to avoid a spaghetti disaster and to make debugging less painful.

Model the game board and state

Represent the board with a char[][] board = new char[3][3] and use constants for player marks like 'X' and 'O'. Implement methods to place a mark and to check available moves so the program stays predictable and testable.

Add win and draw detection

Scan rows columns and diagonals after each move to detect a win. If no moves remain declare a draw. Design detection functions to return clear results so unit tests remain happy.

Handle player input and turns

Attach listeners to buttons to map clicks to board coordinates. Alternate current player after a valid move and update the UI to reflect the new state. Disable buttons for taken squares to avoid double booking.

Implement simple AI and polish

Start with a random move for CPU then upgrade to a minimax algorithm for a serious challenge. Add score tracking and restart functionality so human competitors can complain and try again.

This tutorial covered project setup UI design board modeling win detection player turns and a basic AI approach for a Java Tic Tac Toe game that scales from console testing to a friendly GUI

Tip

Build a console version first to verify game logic then swap in a GUI layer for faster debugging and less hair loss

title: Spring Data with MySQL in 60 Seconds
description: Quick guide to integrate Spring Data JPA with MySQL using Spring Boot for fast CRUD setup and repository patterns
heading: Spring Data with MySQL in 60 Seconds Quick Guide

This quick tutorial shows how to wire Spring Data JPA to MySQL using Spring Boot for basic CRUD operations.

title: SOLID Liskov Substitution Principle
description: Clear and practical explanation of the Liskov Substitution Principle with rules and examples to keep subclasses safe and code maintainable
heading: SOLID Liskov Substitution Principle explained for developers
body:
What the Liskov Substitution Principle actually says

If you write object oriented code and then let inheritance run wild you will eventually debug behavior that lies to you. The Liskov Substitution Principle or LSP states that a subclass should be usable anywhere its superclass is expected without breaking the program or surprising the caller. In plain terms a subtype must behave like the type it replaces not just share method names.

Core rules that keep your code honest

  • Preserve expected behavior

    If the base class promises non negative results your subclass cannot start returning negatives for kicks. The contract is about what clients expect to happen not about method signatures alone.

  • Avoid stronger preconditions

    A subclass must not demand more from callers than the superclass required. If the base method accepts null then the subtype should not throw a tantrum when null shows up.

  • Avoid weaker postconditions

    The subtype must deliver at least what the parent promised. Do not hand back less useful or broken results and call it polymorphism.

  • Keep exceptions predictable

    Introducing new checked exceptions in a subclass forces client changes and creates maintenance paperwork. Runtime exceptions still sting but they do not change the method signature.

The classic rectangle and square trap

People love to show a square as a special rectangle and then wonder why setWidth and setHeight break everything. If a client sets width on a rectangle they expect height to stay independent. A square that changes both violates the original contract and turns a polite caller into a confused debugger. This example is a neat way to learn when inheritance is the wrong tool.

Practical advice for design and refactoring

Write a few client use cases first and then design interfaces to satisfy those use cases. If your subclasses need extra rules you will be safer using composition or refining the abstraction rather than forcing inheritance and hoping for the best.

  • Favor composition when state or behavior would constrain callers
  • Use tests to assert behavioral contracts not just API shape
  • Refactor hierarchies that leak expectations into subclasses
  • Document the expected behavior clearly to improve code quality and maintainability

Why this matters for SOLID and software design

LSP is one of the SOLID principles that keeps inheritance from turning into a liability. Applied well it improves substitutability polymorphism testability and overall code quality. Applied badly you get brittle hierarchies and surprising runtime behavior that makes refactoring a blood sport.

Keep Liskov in your design toolbox and treat it like a firewall between good object oriented intentions and messy runtime surprises. Your future self will high five you or at least stop cursing at the build logs.
seo_title: Make Inheritance Work Right with Liskov and Better Subtypes
seo_heading: Practical LSP rules for safer inheritance testing and refactoring tips

title: SOLID Liskov Substitution Principle What is it?
description: Clear explanation of the Liskov Substitution Principle from SOLID with examples pitfalls and practical design tips for safe subclassing.
heading: SOLID Liskov Substitution Principle What is it?
body:
The Liskov Substitution Principle states that derived types must be usable in place of their base types without altering desirable program behavior.

The principle demands that subclasses follow the base type contract. A classic violation occurs when a Square inherits from Rectangle and changes setter semantics so area or behavior that depends on rectangle assumptions becomes wrong. Surprising behavior in production is normally a symptom of broken substitutability.

A short pseudo code example that often causes trouble

class Rectangle { setWidth(w) {} setHeight(h) {} area() {} } class Square extends Rectangle { setWidth(s) { super.setWidth(s) super.setHeight(s) } setHeight(s) { super.setWidth(s) super.setHeight(s) } }

Design rules to follow for safe subclassing

  1. Define clear contracts for base types
  2. Avoid strengthening preconditions in subclasses
  3. Keep postconditions and invariants intact
  4. Prefer composition when behavior diverges
  5. Write tests that use subclasses through base type interfaces

Define clear contracts by documenting expected inputs outputs and side effects. That makes obligations explicit so subclass authors do not invent surprises.

Avoid stronger preconditions because client code will pass values allowed by the base type. Rejecting those values in a subclass breaks substitutability.

Preserve postconditions and invariants so callers can rely on returned results and object state after method execution. Changing guarantees breaks trust.

When behavior for a subtype differs substantially choose composition over inheritance. Delegation with a shared interface often leads to cleaner safe designs.

Testing helps catch violations early. Write tests that treat subclass instances as instances of the base type and verify that observable behavior remains consistent.

Tip

When unsure prefer a small interface with clear contract and use composition. That strategy reduces accidental contract changes and keeps substitutability honest.

title: Install Spring Tool Suite 2024
description: Step by step guide to install Spring Tool Suite 2024 for Spring Boot on Eclipse IntelliJ and VSCode with setup tips and troubleshooting
heading: Install Spring Tool Suite 2024 for Spring Boot developers
body:
So you want Spring Tool Suite and Spring Boot working in your favorite IDE without the usual misery. Good news you have options and none of them require sacrificing a rubber duck. This guide walks through getting STS 2024 running on Eclipse or using Spring tooling in IntelliJ or VSCode with the right Java setup and a few practical tips that actually save time.

Before you start check your Java JDK

Spring tooling needs a modern Java runtime. Aim for a supported LTS version like Java 17 or a newer stable release that matches your project. Confirm the runtime and architecture with a quick command in a terminal or command prompt.

java -version

If multiple JDKs live on your machine set JAVA_HOME to the one your projects expect and make sure your IDE points to that same JDK. Mismatched JDKs cause classpath chaos and mysterious build failures that feel personal.

Download and pick the right STS package

Decide whether you want the standalone STS distribution or the tooling package that you add to an existing IDE. The standalone gives you a ready made Eclipse experience. The plugin approach lets you keep the IDE you love while getting Spring features.

  • Standalone STS for a turnkey Eclipse based IDE experience
  • Tooling package for plugin install into an existing Eclipse
  • Or skip STS and install Spring tools in IntelliJ or VSCode from the marketplace

Install or extract STS on Windows macOS and Linux

On Windows run the installer from the downloaded archive and follow the wizard. On macOS drag the app into Applications or use the archive method. On Linux extract the tarball and move the folder to a sensible location. The important bit is that the app can see your chosen JDK.

Add Spring tooling to IntelliJ and VSCode

If you prefer IntelliJ or VSCode do not panic. Install Spring related extensions or plugins from the IDE marketplace. IntelliJ Ultimate has built in Spring Boot support while Community users can add plugins from the plugin repo. VSCode users should install the Spring tooling extension for help with starters and live bootstrapping.

  • Open the marketplace inside your IDE and search for Spring or Spring Boot
  • Install the pack that offers starter project generation and run support
  • Restart the IDE if the plugin asks like it means it

Configure workspace and set the default JDK

Create a dedicated workspace folder for Spring projects and set the default JDK in your IDE preferences. This avoids the classic scenario where different tools use different JDKs and your build behaves like it has trust issues.

  • Set JAVA_HOME system wide and confirm the IDE uses it
  • In Eclipse or STS update Installed JREs and set the default
  • In IntelliJ adjust Project SDK and Platform Settings

Launch and run a sample Spring Boot app

Create a new Spring Starter project in STS or generate one at start.spring.io and import it. Use the tooling run configuration or run the main application class. You should see Spring Boot log lines and the embedded server start in a few seconds depending on caffeine levels.

./mvnw spring-boot:run

Or run the main method for a quick local start. If your app fails to boot check the console for startup errors and the JDK version first. Most gremlins hide there.

Troubleshooting tips and quick checklist

  • Wrong JDK set in IDE is the most common mistake
  • Ports already in use will make the app less cheery on startup
  • Use the IDE log and boot logs to find startup stack traces
  • If plugins do not show features try restarting the IDE or reinstalling the extension
  • For Gradle projects use the wrapper so builds are predictable across machines

Follow these steps and your STS or Spring tooling in Eclipse IntelliJ or VSCode will behave better than the typical legacy setup. If something still breaks come back with the error output and we will make diagnostics slightly less painful.

title: Advanced Spring Boot Restful APIs Tutorial Build App
description: Advanced Spring Boot RESTful tutorial to build a full web app with controllers repositories services DTOs validation security and deployment tips
heading: Advanced Spring Boot Restful APIs Tutorial Build Full Web App
body:
Why bother with layered architecture

If you want a REST API that does not collapse into a pile of mysterious null pointer exceptions every time someone changes a field name then you want a layered Spring Boot app. Layered design separates controllers services repositories and DTOs so each part has one job and can be yelled at independently during debugging.

Project setup and dependencies you actually need

Start a Maven or Gradle project and add Spring Boot starters for web data and security. Configure application properties for your database and server port so the app behaves the same on your machine and in production where chaos reigns. Keep the build files tidy and avoid pulling in every starter just because it sounds useful.

Suggested starters

  • spring-boot-starter-web
  • spring-boot-starter-data-jpa
  • spring-boot-starter-security
  • H2 or a production grade database driver depending on your mood

Design data model and DTOs the sane way

Define your entity classes with clear relationships and map them using JPA annotations. Create DTOs for requests and responses so you never accidentally leak internal fields like passwords or experimental feature flags. DTOs also give you stable API contracts which your clients will appreciate more than they deserve.

Simple mapping pattern

Keep mapping logic in service layer methods or use a mapper library. Do not return raw entities from controllers. Raw entities bring lazy loading surprises and insecure fan mail.

@Entity
public class User {
  @Id
  @GeneratedValue
  private Long id;
  private String username;
  private String password;
}

public class UserDto {
  private Long id;
  private String username;
}

Persistence with Spring Data JPA

Use repository interfaces and let Spring implement basic CRUD methods for you. Derived query methods are great until they become Rube Goldberg machines. When that happens write a @Query or a custom repository method and move on with your life.

Service layer and business logic

The service layer orchestrates repository calls maps entities to DTOs and enforces business rules. This reduces duplication and gives controllers a simple API to call. Keep transactions at the service boundary so database state stays sane during multi step operations.

Controllers and REST endpoints

Controllers map routes validate input and return ResponseEntity objects with proper status codes. Use DTOs for request and response bodies and handle bad input gracefully so your API does not sound like it was written by a confused robot.

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {
  private final UserService userService;

  @GetMapping("/{id}")
  public ResponseEntity getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok(userService.findById(id));
  }
}

Validation and error handling

Use bean validation annotations to keep incoming data honest. Add a @ControllerAdvice class for consistent exception handling so clients get neat error objects instead of stack traces that lead to therapy sessions.

  • Use @Valid on DTOs
  • Return clear error responses with codes and messages
  • Log server side details but never expose them to clients

Security testing and deployment

Add Spring Security with JWT or basic auth depending on your threat model and patience. Test authentication flows with curl or Postman and lock down sensitive endpoints. Package the app in a container or a cloud friendly archive then test again because deployment is where assumptions go to die.

Final checklist before you push to production

  • DTOs separate public contract from internal model
  • Service layer handles transactions and business rules
  • Repositories use Spring Data JPA for persistence
  • Validation and controller advice provide consistent errors
  • Security is tested and sensitive endpoints are protected

Follow this pattern and your Spring Boot REST API will be predictable testable and slightly less likely to ruin someone's Monday. If it still breaks at least you will have good logs and a satisfying stack trace to rant about with your team.

title: Difference between Controller vs RestController in Spring
description: Clear comparison of Controller and RestController in Spring with examples response handling and use cases for web pages and REST APIs
heading: Difference between Controller vs RestController in Spring
body:
The key difference between Controller and RestController in Spring is that Controller returns view names while RestController returns serialized response bodies

Brief version for busy developers who like to move fast and later pretend mastery

  1. Controller behavior
  2. RestController behavior
  3. When to use each

Controller behavior

Controller stands for the traditional MVC approach. A Controller method usually returns a view name and relies on a view resolver to render HTML. Use a Controller when the goal is server side rendering with JSP Thymeleaf or another template engine.

RestController behavior

RestController is a convenience annotation that combines Controller with ResponseBody. Methods in a RestController return domain objects or collections that Spring converts to JSON XML or other formats using message converters. Use a RestController when building REST APIs consumed by SPAs mobile apps or other services.

Examples

Typical Controller example

@Controller public class PageController { @GetMapping('/home') public String home(Model model) { model.addAttribute('name', 'Guest') return 'home' } }

Typical RestController example

@RestController public class ApiController { @GetMapping('/users') public List list() { return userService.findAll() } }

Key practical differences

Controller favors view rendering and usually returns strings that match templates. RestController favors data exchange and returns objects that are serialized. Status codes headers and content type handling are handled in similar ways so mixing and matching is possible but clarity matters. Use a Controller for pages and a RestController for APIs to keep code intention obvious and reduce accidental HTML in JSON responses

Tip

When converting a Controller method to return JSON prefer adding ResponseBody on the method or switching to RestController for the whole class for brevity and to avoid unexpected view resolution mistakes

title: Spring Boot CommandLineRunner
description: Quick guide to using Spring Boot CommandLineRunner to run startup tasks in Java applications with practical steps and tips
heading: Spring Boot CommandLineRunner Guide for Running Startup Tasks
body:
A compact tutorial showing how to use CommandLineRunner to execute code at application startup in a Spring Boot app.

  1. Create or use a Spring Boot project
  2. Implement CommandLineRunner as a bean
  3. Register the runner in the application context
  4. Run the application and observe startup output

Create or use a Spring Boot project using Spring Initializr or preferred build tools. Choose the Spring Boot starter for web or the bare minimum for a CLI style application. A project skeleton saves time and avoids manual wiring drama.

Implement CommandLineRunner by creating a class that implements the CommandLineRunner interface. Use a bean annotation so Spring knows to manage that class. Keep the run method concise and focused on tasks like seeding a database or kicking off a background job.

Register the runner by annotating the class with @Component or by declaring a @Bean in a configuration class. Multiple runners are allowed so use ordering to control execution sequence when more than one task is present.

Run the application with your usual command for Maven or Gradle. Watch the logs during startup for the messages from the run method. Startup tasks run before the application fully accepts requests so there is a guaranteed early hook for setup chores.

Common uses include database seeding for development automation and quick health checks before the main service starts. Avoid heavy long running tasks inside the run method unless background threads are used. That keeps startup fast and predictable.

Summary of the tutorial This guide covered how to add a CommandLineRunner to a Spring Boot project how to register the runner and how to verify that startup tasks execute as expected

Tip

When multiple runners exist use the @Order annotation or implement Ordered to control sequence. For lengthy initialization move heavy work to async tasks to keep startup responsive.
