  4. Bind with ConfigurationProperties and validate
  5. Tune logging and actuator endpoints
  6. Configure datasource and connection pools
  7. Adjust Spring Data and repository behavior
  8. Speed up development with Devtools and IDE hints
  9. Protect secrets and use encrypted values
  10. Debug property resolution and precedence

1 Use application properties and YAML wisely Spring Boot accepts both property files and YAML. Prefer YAML for nested structures and properties for flat lists. Keep default values in application.yml and overrides in profile files.

2 Organize profile specific settings Use profile files named application dev.yml or application prod.yml. Activate the desired profile through environment variables or command line for predictable behavior across environments.

3 Externalize configuration with environment variables Environment variables win over packaged defaults. Map sensitive or deployment specific values to environment variables so the artifact stays portable.

4 Bind with ConfigurationProperties and validate Use @ConfigurationProperties to bind groups of properties to a typed class. Add JSR 380 validation annotations to fail fast when configuration is missing or malformed.

5 Tune logging and actuator endpoints Control log levels per package with logging.level package name equals debug. Expose actuator endpoints selectively and secure management endpoints in production deployments.

6 Configure datasource and connection pools Set spring.datasource.url username and driver. Tune pool size and timeouts on the pool implementation to avoid idle connections or resource starvation.

7 Adjust Spring Data and repository behavior Control repository settings like query lookup strategy and pagination defaults via properties to avoid surprising query generation at runtime.

8 Speed up development with Devtools and IDE hints Enable spring devtools for automatic restarts and use IDE support for YAML property completion to avoid typos that cause silent failures.

9 Protect secrets and use encrypted values Keep secrets out of VCS by using vault solutions or cloud key management. Use property placeholders with secure injection at deployment time.

10 Debug property resolution and precedence Use spring config import and the config tree to trace which file provided a value. Spring Boot follows a clear order so overrides behave predictably when understood.

This tutorial walked through practical steps to manage Spring Boot properties and configurations for development and production. Applying these patterns reduces surprises during deployment and improves maintainability while keeping developers slightly less grumpy.

Tip

Prefer typed configuration with validation and keep secrets out of files. Treat configuration as code and test profile switches in CI to avoid production surprises.

title: Spring Boot application.properties How it Works
description: Quick guide to Spring Boot application properties YAML profile precedence active property debugging for Kotlin Java and Graal
heading: Spring Boot application.properties How it Works
body:
If Spring Boot configuration behaved like a polite guest you would never read this. Sadly it does not. This guide explains where Spring Boot looks for application.properties and YAML, why one value wins over another, and what to do when spring.profiles.active seems to be playing hide and seek. Expect clarity, some sarcasm, and practical commands that do not require a ritual sacrifice.

Where Spring Boot looks for configuration files

The framework searches a few predictable spots in order. Think of it as a checklist that decides which file gets to be the boss. From highest priority to lowest when files are considered as external sources the usual search locations are

  • classpath root
  • classpath config directory
  • current working directory
  • config directory relative to where the jar runs
  • packaged files inside the jar

In practice external files usually override packaged defaults, so putting a file next to your jar will typically win over whatever lives inside the artifact.

Why precedence causes developer headaches

Spring Boot follows a documented order of precedence. If you ever wondered why that system property you set did not take effect the answer is probably that something with higher priority stomped it. Command line arguments and JVM system properties are near the top of the list. Application files and profile specific files live lower.

Quick debugging checklist

  • Check command line args first
  • Check system properties passed with -D when JVM starts
  • Look for an external application.properties or application.yml that may be overriding your change
  • Use logging at startup or spring boot startup diagnostics to see which file was loaded

How YAML merging and multi document files behave

YAML is convenient and also sneaky. A single YAML file can contain multiple documents and profile keyed sections. Spring Boot merges these documents by property path which can lead to accidental inheritance. In other words the map gets merged and key level values combine rather than one side wiping out the other.

To avoid surprising merges use explicit property paths or split profiles into their own files like application-dev.yml and application-prod.yml when you need clean overrides.

Activating profiles with spring.profiles.active

Flip a profile by setting spring.profiles.active=dev either in an env var or as a system property. Environment variables like SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE also bind automatically. Profile specific files such as application-dev.yml overlay the base application.yml according to the precedence rules, so those overlays rarely fail unless the file was not found at startup.

Practical examples

spring.profiles.active=dev
SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev
java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=dev
java -jar -Dspring.profiles.active=dev app.jar

Environment variables and property name mapping

When running in containers or cloud platforms set environment variables with uppercase and underscores. Spring will map them to kebab case or camel case property names. For example MY_APP_SERVER_PORT maps to my.app.server-port or my.app.serverPort depending on your property name style.

System properties passed to the JVM also bind and often outrank application files which is handy for quick testing without changing config files.

Graal native images and Kotlin runtime quirks

Building a Graal native image has a couple of surprises. Resources that look obvious to your IDE may not be visible to the native runtime unless you include them in resource configuration during the native build. That means profile files such as application-dev.yml need to be explicitly bundled if you expect them in production.

Kotlin brings nullability and reflection differences. Spring Boot property binding uses metadata and sometimes reflection. Kotlin classes that rely on default constructors or need reflection require the right metadata and possibly explicit configuration to bind correctly. If properties silently fail to bind check your generated metadata and any reflection settings used by the native image builder.

Debugging tips that actually help

  • Start with verbose startup logs to see which config file was loaded
  • Temporarily set a property via command line to ensure the precedence you expect
  • Split complicated YAML into profile files to stop accidental merging
  • For Graal builds verify resource inclusion and test property binding on the native binary early

Recap and final sarcasm

Spring Boot is predictable if you learn the rules and stop assuming the last file you edited is the one the runtime cares about. Remember the search locations, remember the precedence, and remember that YAML merging is friendly but sometimes too helpful. With a few checks you can stop guessing and start configuring like a responsible adult.
seo_title: Stop guessing Spring Boot config and master application.properties
seo_heading: Where Spring Boot picks up YAML and properties and how to tame precedence

title: How to Install Node JS on Windows 10/11 #React #ExpressJS
description: Step by step guide to install Node JS on Windows 10 and 11 including npm and npx setup PATH verification and quick troubleshooting
heading: How to Install Node JS on Windows 10/11 #React #ExpressJS
body:
If setting up NodeJS on Windows feels like assembling IKEA furniture blindfolded this guide will be your allen key. We will get Node.js and npm installed on Windows 10 or Windows 11 verify that npm and npx work and run a quick project scaffold to prove everything is actually working. This is useful for React ExpressJS Angular and general Node based development.

Download the LTS installer

Go to the official Node downloads page at nodejs.org and grab the LTS package for Windows. LTS is the version that will not panic in production. If you want to chase bleeding edge features you can pick the Current build but you asked for reliable setup so stick with LTS.

Run the installer

Double click the downloaded installer and follow the prompts. Leave the default options selected unless you have particular reasons to change them. The installer will add Node and the npm package manager to the system for you, which saves you the fun of manual copying.

Verify Node and npm

Open PowerShell or Command Prompt and run the following commands to confirm a successful install.

node -v
npm -v

Seeing version numbers means the runtime and package manager are present. If those commands return an error we fix PATH next.

Fix PATH if commands are not found

If your terminal says command not found do this without crying.

  • Open Start and search for "Edit the system environment variables"
  • Click Environment Variables and find Path under System variables or your user variables
  • Add the folder where Node was installed typically C\Program Files\nodejs and save changes
  • Close and reopen the terminal window and run node -v again

Test npm and npx with a sample app

Make a quick project folder and try scaffolding a simple app to confirm npm scripts and npx are functional. Two fast options.

  1. Quick scaffold with create react app via npx 
    npx create-react-app my-app
  2. Start a tiny Node project with npm init 
    mkdir test-node && cd test-node
npm init -y

If those commands install packages and create files you are golden. For ExpressJS or Angular projects use the framework specific CLI tools via npm or npx in the same way.

Do not forget Git

Git does not come with Node. Install Git separately if you want version control or to avoid mysterious hookup errors when creating projects that expect a repo.

Troubleshooting notes

  • If permissions errors appear run your terminal as administrator or check folder security settings
  • If a global package seems missing try reinstalling it with npm install -g package-name
  • When switching between Node versions consider a version manager for Windows like nvm for Windows to avoid friction

Recap in human terms: download the LTS from nodejs.org install with defaults verify node -v and npm -v fix PATH if needed and run a quick npx or npm init test. After that your Windows 10 or Windows 11 machine will be ready for React, ExpressJS, Angular and other Node based adventures. Now go build something and try not to break production on your first commit.
seo_title: Install Node.js on Windows 10 and 11 the easy and safe way
seo_heading: Prepare Windows 10 and 11 for Node npm npx and web frameworks

title: How to Install PostgreSQL on Windows 10 or 11 #postgres #jav
description: Step by step guide to install PostgreSQL on Windows 10 or 11 with tips for NodeJS Python and common setup checks
heading: How to Install PostgreSQL on Windows 10 or 11 Guide for NodeJS and Python
body:
This tutorial teaches how to install PostgreSQL on Windows 10 or 11 and configure a working developer environment for NodeJS and Python.

  1. Download the official Windows installer
  2. Run the installer with recommended defaults
  3. Set the postgres superuser password and port
  4. Install pgAdmin and optional tools with StackBuilder
  5. Verify the database service and test a local connection
  6. Connect from NodeJS or Python using client libraries

Download the official Windows installer Visit the official PostgreSQL site and grab the Windows installer for the stable release. Choose the correct architecture for the machine and save the file to a familiar folder.

Run the installer with recommended defaults Start the installer and accept the default components unless advanced requirements exist. The installer will create a data directory and register a Windows service for PostgreSQL.

Set the postgres superuser password and port During setup choose a strong password for the postgres superuser and accept the default port 5432 or change to a free port. Remember the password because the database will require credentials for administrative tasks.

Install pgAdmin and optional tools with StackBuilder Add pgAdmin for a GUI or use command line tools. StackBuilder offers drivers and extensions that may be useful for specific projects. Optional components are truly optional unless a project demands a feature.

Verify the database service and test a local connection Open Services and confirm the PostgreSQL service is running. Use psql -U postgres from the command prompt or open pgAdmin and connect using host localhost port 5432 user postgres and the chosen password to ensure the database accepts connections.

Connect from NodeJS or Python using client libraries For NodeJS install node postgresql client and configure host localhost port 5432 user postgres password as environment values. For Python install psycopg and use a connection object with host localhost port 5432 user postgres password for simple queries.

This process gets PostgreSQL installed and ready for development on Windows 10 or 11 along with basic verification and client setup for NodeJS and Python projects. Follow the steps and keep the superuser credentials secure while developing.

Tip

Create a non superuser role for application access and use that role for daily development. That reduces risk compared to running apps with the postgres superuser account.

title: Advanced Spring Data & JDBC Tutorial #SpringBoot #MySQL
description: Learn advanced Spring Data and JDBC practices for Spring Boot with MySQL and PostgreSQL using JDBCTemplate and JPA
heading: Advanced Spring Data and JDBC Tutorial SpringBoot MySQL Postgresql JDBCTemplate JPA
body:
If you want a Spring Boot app that actually behaves under load and does not surprise you at 2 AM with a flood of errors here is a compact guide to advanced Spring Data and JDBC techniques that work with MySQL and PostgreSQL. You will learn when to pick JDBCTemplate for raw SQL speed and when JPA makes your life easier for domain focused logic. No smoke and mirrors just practical choices and a few sarcastic comments to keep things human.

Project setup and dependencies

Start with the sensible Spring Boot starters for data and JDBC. Add Spring Data JPA when you need entity management and JDBCTemplate when you need precise SQL control. Keep JDBC driver versions aligned to your server and use Maven or Gradle as your build tool. If you do not like dependency conflicts you will learn to love the version matrix like a responsible grown up.

What to include

  • spring-boot-starter-data-jpa for repository patterns and entity mapping
  • spring-boot-starter-jdbc for JDBCTemplate and lightweight SQL work
  • mysql or postgresql driver matching your DB server
  • optionally NamedParameterJdbcTemplate when your queries get textual and messy

Datasource configuration and profiles

Declare multiple datasources when you talk to more than one database. Use Spring profiles to switch connections between environments so your dev machine does not surprise production. Use the Spring Boot property names that it expects and enjoy friction free startup unless you misname a property and then blame your IDE.

Using JDBCTemplate the right way

JDBCTemplate is great when you need control and low overhead. Prefer prepared statements and parameter binding to avoid SQL injection and to let the database cache query plans. Use RowMapper or BeanPropertyRowMapper for simple mapping and switch to manual mapping when performance matters.

Batch updates and bulk operations

When you need to write lots of rows avoid awkward for loops. Use jdbcTemplate.batchUpdate with a batch prepared statement to get proper performance. This reduces round trips and keeps the database from sighing in regret.

Integrating JPA for domain workflows

JPA is your friend when you want repositories, transactional boundaries, and entity relationships handled for you. Use projections and DTO mapping to avoid fetching entire graphs just because you asked for a single field. If you need complex SQL alongside JPA provide custom repository implementations that call JDBCTemplate for the hot paths.

Transactions and error handling

Use @Transactional for most cases and keep the transactional boundary small and purposeful. Reach for programmatic transactions only when you need fine grained control. Configure rollback rules for specific exceptions and do not mark everything as rollback always unless you enjoy debugging lost work.

Testing and profiling

Write integration tests against an embedded database or use Testcontainers for realistic behavior. Turn on SQL logging in development so you can see the queries you actually ran. Run explain plans for suspect queries and measure under realistic load. If performance is still a problem consider caching or targeted denormalization rather than premature micro optimization.

Quick checklist for performance

  • Prefer prepared statements and parameter binding for safety and speed
  • Use JDBCTemplate for performance critical raw SQL and JPA for domain operations
  • Profile SQL and use EXPLAIN to find slow queries
  • Batch inserts and updates to reduce round trips
  • Measure under realistic load and avoid guessing

Follow these patterns and you will have a codebase where JPA and JDBCTemplate coexist with minimal drama. You will avoid obvious pitfalls and keep performance predictable. When things do go wrong you will have logs and explain plans to shame the slow query into improving.
seo_title: Build Fast Spring Boot Services with Spring Data and JDBC
seo_heading: Practical JDBCTemplate and JPA patterns for MySQL and PostgreSQL

title: Git Uncommit Your Last Commit
description: Quick guide to uncommit the last Git commit with reset and revert options and safety notes for pushed commits
heading: Git Uncommit Your Last Commit Guide
body:
If you made a commit and immediately regretted it you are not alone and Git has several polite ways to help you pretend that never happened. This guide walks through uncommit techniques that keep your work safe or obliterate it if you are feeling dramatic. We will cover soft reset mixed reset hard reset git revert and how to handle pushed commits and force push when the apocalypse is necessary.

Quick decision map

Before typing anything ask yourself two questions

  • Was the commit pushed to a shared repo
  • Do you want to keep the edited files staged unstaged or gone forever

Your answers pick the method. If the commit is local and you want the changes back as staged use a soft reset. If you want the edits but not staged use the mixed reset. If you want those edits to vanish use the hard reset. If the commit is already public use git revert or a force push after getting verbal permission and possibly a bribe.

Soft reset keeps the changes staged

Soft reset is the polite undo. It moves your branch pointer back one commit while leaving the index and working tree alone. The previous commit becomes staged changes ready for a redo or an edit.

git reset --soft HEAD~1

Use this when you want to change the commit message combine changes or just pretend that you meant to do it that way in the first place.

Mixed reset unstages but keeps edits

This is the default mood for git reset. Run either of these

git reset HEAD~1
# or explicitly
git reset --mixed HEAD~1

The branch pointer moves back the index is cleared and your working tree still has the edits. This is useful when you want to selectively stage files or craft a cleaner commit history.

Hard reset is nuclear level cleanup

Hard reset moves the branch pointer and resets both index and working tree to match the target commit. In plain English your changes are deleted unless you have backups or superpowers.

git reset --hard HEAD~1

Use this only when you are sure you will never need those edits again or when you have saved them elsewhere. If nerves are fragile create a temporary branch first with

git branch backup-uncommit

What to do when the commit is already pushed

Do not rewrite public history without consulting teammates. If the commit is in a shared branch and you want a safe undo use

git revert HEAD

This creates a new commit that undoes the previous one. It is reversible and polite and the sort of thing HR likes.

If you absolutely must rewrite remote history for a good reason and you have team blessing do the reset locally and then force push

git reset --hard HEAD~1
git push --force

Expect angry messages and a ceremonial burning of a local branch if anything goes wrong. Always warn collaborators first and consider using git push --force-with-lease for slightly more civilized force pushing.

Summary and quick cheatsheet

  • Soft reset keeps the index and staged changes ready for recommit
  • Mixed reset leaves edits in your files but clears the index so you can restage
  • Hard reset removes the changes from index and working tree so they are gone locally
  • Revert creates a new commit that undoes a public commit without rewriting history
  • Force push rewrites remote history and should be used only with permission and grief counseling

Last minute tip

If you want an insurance policy before any reset run

git branch backup-uncommit

That gives you a recovery point and a small comfort that you may survive your own mistakes.

Now go forth and uncommit responsibly or at least with a dramatic flair that makes later apology emails worth it.
seo_title: Undo a Git commit and keep your changes safe every time
seo_heading: Practical ways to uncommit in Git and when to use reset or revert

title: How to add a new project to an existing Bitbucket repository
description: Quick guide to add a new project to an existing Bitbucket repository with clean commits branch push and pull request steps
heading: How to add a new project to an existing Bitbucket repository
body:
Prepare a branch and scaffold the new project

Want to drop a brand new project into a live Bitbucket repository without triggering a small office revolt This is the no-drama approach that keeps history clean and reviewers happy.

Start by creating a feature branch so the main branch stays usable for real work. Pick a descriptive name that tells future you what this was about.

git checkout -b feature/new-project

Put the code in a named folder

Keep the new project in its own subfolder so the repo does not look like a garage sale. This makes code management sane and avoids accidental breakage of unrelated files.

  • Make a folder like projects/new-project or services/new-project
  • Add a README in that folder that explains purpose setup and any pipeline quirks

Stage and commit with a clear message

Small commits that say what changed make reviews fast and rollbacks less dramatic. Commit messages are for humans and for future you who will be grumpy at 2 AM.

git add .
git commit -m 'Add new project scaffold'

Confirm remote then push

Double check the remote name so you do not push to the wrong place. Most teams use origin but confirm with a quick check.

git remote -v

If the remote is missing link the repo using Bitbucket instructions in the web interface then push the branch.

git push origin feature/new-project

Create a pull request and get it merged

Open the pull request in Bitbucket using the web UI Pick the target branch add a concise description and ask for reviewers. Use Bitbucket pipelines or checks if your repo has them so CI can do the boring testing for you.

Good PRs include a short summary of the changes a link to the new folder and any setup notes reviewers need to run the code locally.

Merge and clean up

Once approvals and pipeline checks pass merge the PR into main or whatever your team uses as the stable branch Then delete the feature branch both remotely and locally to avoid future confusion.

git checkout main
git pull origin main
git branch -d feature/new-project
git push origin --delete feature/new-project

Keep everyone in sync

Tell your teammates to pull the updated main on their machines so everyone is working from the same truth. A fresh pull avoids the classic mystery of missing files.

git pull origin main

Quick recap

  1. Create a branch with a meaningful name
  2. Add the project in its own folder and include a README
  3. Stage and commit with a clear message
  4. Push the branch and open a pull request in Bitbucket
  5. Run CI review and merge when ready then pull main on other machines

Follow this sequence and your repository history will stay tidy which makes audits easier and surprises rarer. If you must break something at least do it with a good commit message.
seo_title: Add a new project to a Bitbucket repo without breaking things
seo_heading: Branch push and pull request guide for Bitbucket project setup

title: Copy a file in a Docker container to your localhost machine
description: Quick guide to copy a file from a Docker container to a local machine using docker commands and a tar fallback method.
heading: Copy a file in a Docker container to your localhost machine
body:
If you ever need to extract a file from a Docker container and you are not in the mood for wild guesswork or dramatic coping rituals this guide has the practical steps. We cover the fast docker cp route and a reliable tar stream fallback that works even when the usual tools are being dramatic.

Find the container you actually need

First up, identify the container name or id. This is the handle for every command that follows so guessing is optional but not recommended.

docker ps
# or to include stopped containers
docker ps -a

Option 1 the simple path with docker cp

docker cp is the quick and obvious choice when the Docker engine is available. It copies a file from container to host using the familiar container path syntax. This works whether the container is running or stopped.

# copy a single file from container to host
docker cp my_container:/path/in/container/file.txt /path/on/host/file.txt

# copy a directory
docker cp my_container:/path/in/container/dir /path/on/host/dir

After you copy check the file exists and fix permissions if the file was created by root inside the container.

Option 2 the tar stream fallback when docker cp fails

Sometimes docker cp is not an option. Maybe the client tools are limited or the container has weird mount behavior. In that case you can stream the file out of the container with tar and unpack on the host. It is surprisingly reliable and only slightly cursed.

# stream a file or directory out of the container and extract it on the host
docker exec my_container tar cf - /path/in/container/file_or_dir | tar xf - -C /path/on/host

If permissions matter you can run the extract with sudo on the host or change ownership afterward.

Notes on the tar approach

  • Works with minimal tooling because it uses standard streams.
  • Preserves file names and directories when you stream a directory.
  • Can be adjusted to compress on the fly if you like smaller pipes and more CPU usage.

Verify file presence and fix permissions

Once the file is on the host run a quick check and sanity restore. Containers often write files as root so expect to change ownership.

ls -l /path/on/host/file.txt
# if needed make the file owned by your user
sudo chown $(id -u):$(id -g) /path/on/host/file.txt

Make future life easier with a bind mount

If file exchange is going to be recurring stop the pain and mount a host directory into the container at startup. Then files show up directly on localhost and you skip the copy step next time.

# example using a bind mount so /host/share maps to /container/share
docker run -v $(pwd)/host_share:/container/share image_name

Troubleshooting tips

  • If docker cp complains check container name and that Docker has the right permissions.
  • If tar extraction fails confirm there is enough disk space and that the host user can write to the destination.
  • When copying large data sets consider using a volume or a data container so you do not become the person who copies terabytes through pipes.

That is all. Use docker cp for the quick wins and keep the tar stream in your back pocket for when things get weird. You will save time and dignity in equal measure.
seo_title: Retrieve files from a Docker container to localhost fast
seo_heading: How to pull files from a running container to your host using tar and docker cp

title: How to run your Spring Boot JAR file from the command line
description: Quick guide to running a Spring Boot JAR from the command line with examples flags and troubleshooting tips
heading: How to run your Spring Boot JAR file from the command line
body:
This guide shows how to run a Spring Boot JAR from the command line and covers common flags and troubleshooting for a smooth start.

  1. Build the executable JAR
  2. Locate and verify the JAR file
  3. Run the application with java
  4. Pass profiles and properties
  5. Run as background process or service
  6. Monitor logs and health

Build the executable JAR

Use the Spring Boot Maven or Gradle plugin to produce an executable JAR. Example Maven goal is package and a proper spring-boot-maven-plugin configuration yields a single runnable artifact.

Locate and verify the JAR file

Confirm filename and permissions. A quick check with ls -l myapp.jar verifies presence and access rights. Ownership and execute bits matter on some systems.

Run the application with java

Start the application with a simple command like java -jar myapp.jar. For a specific JVM configuration prepend environment variables or use a wrapper script and call the JVM with desired memory settings.

Pass profiles and properties

Activate a Spring profile or override properties on the command line. Example java -jar myapp.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod --server.port=8081 changes runtime behavior without rebuilding.

Run as background process or service

For quick background runs use nohup java -jar myapp.jar &. For production use create a systemd service file and manage startup with systemctl.

Monitor logs and health

Tail logs with tail -f logs/spring.log or consult actuator endpoints for health and metrics. Proper logging configuration prevents ghost hunts at 3 AM.

Recap This walkthrough covered building the JAR running the Spring Boot application passing runtime options running as a background job and basic monitoring so deployments stop being mysteries.

Tip

Set a JAVA_OPTS environment variable for common JVM flags and keep a small wrapper script for start stop and status. That makes deployments less heroic and more repeatable.

title: Swagger Test Spring Boot REST APIs with SpringDoc
description: Add SpringDoc OpenAPI to a Spring Boot Maven project and use Swagger UI to test REST APIs quickly and visually
heading: Swagger Test Spring Boot REST APIs with SpringDoc OpenAPI Maven UI Example
body:
This tutorial shows how to add SpringDoc OpenAPI to a Spring Boot Maven project and use Swagger UI to test REST APIs in a browser.

  2. Configure package scanning or rely on auto configuration
  3. Run the Spring Boot application
  4. Open Swagger UI and try endpoints
  5. Harden documentation for production

Step 1 Add the SpringDoc dependency to the pom.xml file. Use the springdoc openapi ui dependency with the current version. Maven will download the required jars and the project will pick up the dependency.

Step 2 Configure package scanning if the controllers reside outside the main application package. Often no extra configuration is required because SpringDoc supports auto configuration. If controllers are in unusual locations add a springdoc.packagesToScan property or a configuration bean.

Step 3 Run the Spring Boot application as usual from the IDE or with mvn spring-boot run. The application will expose the OpenAPI JSON at /v3/api-docs and the Swagger UI pages at /swagger-ui.html or /swagger-ui/index.html depending on the version.

Step 4 Open a browser and visit the Swagger UI URL. The UI shows endpoints request schemas and example responses. Use the Try it button in the UI to send requests directly from the browser and inspect headers and payloads. Fill in example JSON and observe status codes and response bodies for quick debugging without writing curl commands.

Step 5 For production secure the documentation endpoints. Add actuator or security rules to restrict access to documentation. Expose documentation only for staging or on demand to avoid leaking API design to the whole world.

Summary This guide covered adding springdoc openapi to a Maven based Spring Boot project running the app and using Swagger UI to test endpoints quickly. The process is mostly dependency add run and browse which means fewer excuses for missing documentation.

Tip

If example responses look empty add @Schema examples on DTOs or use @OpenAPIDefinition for global examples. That gives the UI useful sample payloads and spares developers from guessing request shapes.

title: React Hello World App for Beginners #reactjs
description: Step by step guide to create a React Hello World app using Node and VS Code for absolute beginners. Fast and practical instructions.
heading: React Hello World App for Beginners with Node and VS Code
body:
If you are new to frontend web development and want to get a React app up and running without crying this is your guide. We will use Node and a friendly editor called VS Code so you can focus on JavaScript and not on mysterious build errors.

What you need before we start

Install Node and npm using the official installer or a version manager like nvm. Node provides the runtime and npm handles packages. A quick check to make sure everything is alive is to run

node -v
npm -v

If those print versions then congratulations you are slightly more qualified than a potato.

Create your React project the easy way

You have two good choices depending on how much magic you want. For a classic setup use Create React App. For a faster modern dev experience use Vite. Commands look like this

  • npx create-react-app hello-world for Create React App
  • npm create vite@latest hello-world for Vite

Either command scaffolds folders and installs dependencies so you can stop reading about setup and start making components instead.

Open the project in VS Code

Run code . inside the project folder to open VS Code. Install a React snippet pack and ESLint. Optionally add Prettier if you enjoy tidy chaos. These extensions make writing JSX and catching common problems less painful.

Edit the main component

The main component lives at src/App.js or src/App.jsx depending on the scaffold. Keep it functional for a modern feel. Replace the placeholder with this minimal example to prove the thing works

function App() {
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Hello World from React</h1>
    </div>
  );
}

export default App;

This uses JSX which looks like HTML but is really JavaScript pretending to be neat. No props yet just pure victory.

Run the development server and view your app

Start the server with the command generated by your scaffold. Typical commands are

  • npm start for Create React App
  • npm run dev for Vite

Open the URL shown in the terminal or try http //localhost 3000 for CRA. The server provides live reload so edit code and watch the browser update without baring your soul to the terminal.

Quick troubleshooting tips

  • If something fails check your Node version and reinstall nodejs if needed
  • Run npm install in the project folder if dependencies are missing
  • Check the browser console for runtime errors and the terminal for build errors

What to do next

Now that you have a minimal React hello world app you can expand into components props state and styling. Try creating a new component file and import it into App. Learn a state hook like useState to add interactivity. Each small step moves you from beginner to slightly scarier beginner.

Pro tip use the browser dev tools console when things go wrong. It will tell you what broke and sometimes insult you for good measure.

This short tutorial covered the essentials for getting a React hello world running with Node and VS Code. Have fun and try not to break production on your first day.

title: JDBC Tutorial for Beginners (Java Database Connectivity)
description: Learn JDBC basics for Java connecting to MySQL PostgreSQL SQL Server and H2 with examples on drivers connections statements transactions and pooling
heading: JDBC Tutorial for Beginners Java Database Connectivity
body:
This tutorial teaches JDBC basics for connecting Java applications to databases including MySQL PostgreSQL SQL Server and H2

  1. Add the JDBC driver or dependency
  2. Create a connection and manage credentials

Step 1 Add the JDBC driver by including the appropriate driver jar or Maven dependency for the target database. Many IDEs download the driver automatically when the correct dependency is declared

Step 2 Load the driver class when needed and obtain a Connection from DriverManager or a DataSource. Example pseudo call in Java

Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver")

Connection conn = DriverManager.getConnection("jdbc url","user","pass")

Step 3 Use PreparedStatement for parameterized queries and then iterate a ResultSet to map columns to Java types. PreparedStatement prevents SQL injection and often improves performance

Step 4 Wrap multiple statements in a transaction by disabling auto commit then commit or rollback based on success. Always close ResultSet Statement and Connection in a finally block or use try with resources for automatic cleanup

Step 5 Introduce a connection pool when the application serves concurrent requests. A pool reduces connection latency and improves throughput compared to opening a new connection per request

The tutorial covered how to add drivers create connections execute queries manage transactions and scale with pooling while highlighting best practices for resource management and security

Tip

Prefer PreparedStatement over simple Statement and adopt a connection pool early during testing to avoid surprises when the application hits production load

title: Spring Boot Actuator Full Tutorial
description: Learn Spring Boot Actuator basics and advanced tips for monitoring health metrics endpoints security and custom probes for production apps
heading: Spring Boot Actuator Full Tutorial for Monitoring and Management
body:
This tutorial shows how to add Spring Boot Actuator to a Spring application and use endpoints for health metrics monitoring and custom probes.

  1. Add the Actuator dependency
  2. Expose and configure endpoints
  3. Secure management endpoints
  4. Create custom health checks and metrics
  5. Export metrics to a monitoring system

Add the Actuator dependency Use the starter to get a sensible set of endpoints quickly. For Maven include the starter dependency in the project POM or add the Gradle equivalent. Spring will wire endpoint beans without excessive manual wiring.

Expose and configure endpoints Configure which endpoints are visible on the web and which are hidden by default. Use application properties to include health and info and to set endpoint base paths. Endpoint exposure keeps noise down and reveals meaningful telemetry.

Secure management endpoints Treat management endpoints as sensitive. Apply Spring Security rules to restrict access to roles or endpoints that require authorization. Exposed diagnostics without protection is a welcome sign for hackers and a bad day for developers.

Create custom health checks and metrics Implement HealthIndicator for domain checks like database connectivity and message queue status. Use Micrometer meters to record business metrics such as order processing time. Custom probes give observability some actual value.

title: Actuator Metrics in Spring Boot Examples
description: Enable and expose Spring Boot actuator metrics and view CPU memory and thread metrics with Micrometer and endpoints for quick monitoring.
heading: Actuator Metrics in Spring Boot Examples for CPU Memory and Threads
body:
So you want to stop guessing why production is melting down and actually know what your JVM is doing. Good call. This guide walks through enabling Actuator metrics in Spring Boot and exposing CPU memory and thread metrics for monitoring with Micrometer and Prometheus. Expect practical steps and a little sarcastic commentary to keep you awake.

Add Actuator and Micrometer to your project

If your build tool is tired of mystery, give it the dependencies that actually tell you what is wrong. Add the Spring Boot starter for Actuator and a Micrometer registry for Prometheus or whichever target you prefer. Micrometer is the facade and Prometheus is the recorder of sins.

Maven examples

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>

<dependency>
  <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
  <artifactId>micrometer-registry-prometheus</artifactId>
</dependency>

Gradle examples

implementation 'org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-actuator'
implementation 'io.micrometer:micrometer-registry-prometheus'

Expose actuator endpoints and secure them

By default Actuator endpoints may be limited or secured. Expose what you need in application.properties or application.yml and then lock things down with Spring Security or network rules before shipping to production. Monitoring is useful. Open endpoints to the internet is not.

# application.properties
management.endpoints.web.base-path=/actuator
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics,prometheus

With the Prometheus registry on the classpath the /actuator/prometheus endpoint will expose the Prometheus text format. The JSON metrics endpoint lives at /actuator/metrics and is great for quick debugging.

Query specific metrics for CPU memory and threads

Want the cliffs notes on CPU and memory usage? Use the metrics endpoint. Typical metric names to know are system.cpu.usage or system.cpu.count, jvm.memory.used, and various thread metrics such as jvm.threads.live.

# get all info for a metric
curl localhost:8080/actuator/metrics/jvm.memory.used

# get Prometheus scrape output
curl localhost:8080/actuator/prometheus

The JSON response from /actuator/metrics/{metricName} includes an array of measurements with timestamps and values and a list of available tags like pool or area. Those numbers are your friends when you are trying to spot trends and stop paging your teammate at 2am.

Integrate with Prometheus and long term storage

Add the Micrometer Prometheus registry and keep prometheus in the exposure list so the Prometheus server can scrape the application. Prometheus gives long term storage and query power so you can ask hard questions like why memory climbs only on Fridays.

# prometheus scrape config snippet
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'my-spring-app'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['host1:8080']
        labels:
          service: my-service
          environment: production

Then point Grafana or your alerting system at Prometheus. Make alerts sane. Do not fire an alert for a harmless percentile spike unless you enjoy being woken up without cause.

Monitoring tips and best practices

  • Prefer metric names over raw logs for trend detection. Metrics are built for math and slightly less drama.
  • Add tags like service and environment to make dashboards readable and alerts meaningful.
  • Watch JVM gc metrics such as jvm.gc.pause to correlate CPU and memory anomalies.
  • Alert on sustained CPU or thread count changes rather than single samples to reduce noise.
  • Secure actuator endpoints with network policies or Spring Security to avoid surprise pages and angry managers.

Summary

Enable Actuator and Micrometer, expose the metrics and prometheus endpoints, query jvm.memory.used, system.cpu.usage and thread metrics, and scrape with Prometheus for reliable long term monitoring. Add tags and sensible alerts and you will get fewer midnight messages and more time to enjoy coffee that is slightly above lukewarm.
seo_title: Monitor CPU memory and threads with Spring Boot Actuator
seo_heading: Expose JVM CPU memory and thread metrics for Prometheus monitoring

title: Spring Boot Actuator Endpoints
description: Learn how to enable and use Spring Boot Actuator endpoints for health env heapdump threaddump metrics and logging with clear steps and tips
heading: Spring Boot Actuator Endpoints Guide
body:
Quick overview

Spring Boot Actuator is the set of endpoints you call when your app is misbehaving and you need receipts for the crime scene. It gives you health checks, environment info, metrics, heapdump and threaddump access, and runtime logging control. Treat it like a surgeon tool and not a party trick on the public internet.

Install the Actuator dependency

Add the starter to your build and then decide which endpoints your app will actually need. Do not just enable everything and hope for the best.

org.springframework.boot spring-boot-starter-actuator

In application properties enable specific endpoints that you will use in production

management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,metrics,env,heapdump,threaddump,loggers

Expose and secure endpoints the smart way

By default many endpoints are not exposed and that is a feature. If you need remote access consider a separate management port or reverse proxy that lives on an internal network. Use Spring Security and role based authorization so only humans with badge access can call admin operations.

Key endpoints and why you will love or fear them

  • /actuator/health Check basic liveness and readiness for orchestration systems and probes.
  • /actuator/env See active configuration and profiles without rummaging through server folders.
  • /actuator/metrics Pull meter values for integration with monitoring tools. This is your telemetry source.
  • /actuator/heapdump Get a heap snapshot for analysis with tools like jvisualvm when memory is playing musical chairs.
  • /actuator/threaddump Collect thread stacks for deadlock or thread leak forensics.
  • /actuator/loggers View and change logging levels at runtime to quiet noisy classes or to turn up the heat on suspects.

Heap and thread dumps

Requesting a heapdump or threaddump is powerful and heavy. Heap snapshots can be large and can stall an instance. Prefer a maintenance window or an isolated debug host when you need them. Use jvisualvm or YourKit to open a heap file and look for retained sizes and leaking references.

Logging and metrics

Use the loggers endpoint to tame noisy packages without redeploying. Export metrics through Micrometer to a system like Prometheus. Then build Grafana dashboards to spot trends before they turn into incidents you have to explain to someone who does not code.

Best practices and safety rules

  • Keep actuator endpoints off public networks and behind internal firewalls or VPNs
  • Protect sensitive endpoints with role based auth and audit access
  • Limit exposure to only needed endpoints to reduce attack surface
  • Prefer maintenance windows for heavy operations like heapdump
  • Consider a dedicated management port or host for admin operations
  • Export metrics to Prometheus and build Grafana dashboards to avoid surprise incidents

Conclusion

Spring Boot Actuator is a practical toolkit for monitoring and debugging in production when used carefully. Add the starter, expose only what you need, secure access with Spring Security and role rules, and use Micrometer plus Prometheus for long term visibility. Do that and you will spend less time finger pointing and more time fixing real problems.
seo_title: Make Spring Boot Actuator Actually Useful for Monitoring
seo_heading: How to expose secure Spring Boot actuator endpoints for health metrics and dumps

title: Expose & Enable Spring Boot Actuator Endpoints
description: Quick guide to expose and enable Spring Boot Actuator endpoints for metrics info and health with secure configuration and testing tips
heading: Expose and Enable Spring Boot Actuator Endpoints for Metrics and Info
body:
If your app were a person you would want to know if it is breathing and not secretly eating memory like a raccoon in a dumpster. Spring Boot Actuator gives you that visibility with endpoints for metrics health and info. This guide walks through adding the starter configuring which endpoints are exposed and locking them down so your production secrets stay secret.

Add the actuator dependency

Actuator lives in the spring boot starter called spring boot starter actuator. For Maven add the dependency to your pom.xml and rebuild. This gives you the runtime endpoints that report everything from memory to custom metrics.

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>

Choose which endpoints to expose in application properties

By default only a handful of endpoints are exposed over HTTP. You should prefer explicit inclusion rather than wildcards unless you like drama. Edit application properties to select endpoints such as metrics health and info.

management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics
management.endpoint.metrics.enabled=true
management.endpoints.web.base-path=/actuator
management.server.port=8081

Why bind to a separate port

Putting management on its own port reduces the blast radius if something leaks. It also makes firewall rules and network policies less annoying to write.

Secure the endpoints with sensible rules

Do not throw actuator endpoints open to the public internet unless you enjoy stress testing by strangers. Use Spring Security to restrict access to roles or to internal networks. HTTP basic is fine for quick testing while OAuth or mutual TLS is the grown up choice for production.

  • Map actuator paths to roles so only operators can see metrics and sensitive info
  • Limit exposure to private networks or a bastion host
  • Enable audit logging so you can know who poked the health endpoint at 3 a m

Test endpoints locally and remotely

Verify the endpoints return the expected JSON payloads. Common checks include

  • /actuator/health for overall status
  • /actuator/info for build and metadata
  • /actuator/metrics for names you can query

Use curl or Postman for quick checks and add actuator probes to your deployment health checks so your orchestrator knows when to panic and when to chill.

Practical tips for less chaos

  • Expose only the endpoints you need for monitoring and debugging
  • Prefer explicit includes over all because less is safer
  • Automate checks so humans do not have to babysit status pages

Actuator gives you deep visibility into your Spring Boot app without requiring a crystal ball. Configure the management properties secure the endpoints and test them so your monitoring is useful and does not become an accidental data leak. If that sounds like extra work remember that knowing your app is alive beats finding out from angry users at 2 a m.

title: Spring Boot Configuration Properties #techtarget
description: Practical guide to Spring Boot Configuration Properties for type safe binding validation and best practices to manage application settings
heading: Spring Boot Configuration Properties Guide for Developers
body:
Spring Boot Configuration Properties are a binding mechanism that maps external settings from properties files or environment variables into Java objects

Use the feature to keep configuration type safe and centralized while avoiding scattering string keys across the code base. Typical usage involves a POJO annotated for binding and a properties file with matching names

  1. Define a properties class with a prefix
  2. Register the class for binding
  3. Validate values and prefer constructor binding for immutability
  4. Prefer externalized overrides for production

Example annotations look like

@ConfigurationProperties(prefix="app")

@Validated

Example properties entry looks like

app.name=myapp

Register the properties class using component scanning or explicit registration such as using configuration properties scan. Validation integrates with bean validation annotations such as @NotEmpty on fields to fail fast when required settings are missing. Constructor based binding combined with final fields yields immutable configuration objects which help avoid accidental changes at runtime

Avoid excessive use of single value injection via property expressions across many classes. Single value injection creates hidden coupling and makes testing harder. Prefer grouping related values into a dedicated properties class and inject that class where needed

Remember that Spring Boot supports relaxed binding of names so dots dashes and camel case commonly map without extra effort. Environment variables can override file values by using uppercase names with underscores such as APP_NAME The order of precedence favors environment variables then application properties then defaults so plan for that when deploying

Adopt validation and immutable classes to make configuration safer and easier to reason about and treat the properties class as a contract between deployment and code

Tip

Keep configuration classes small and focused and prefer constructor binding with final fields to get explicit contracts and easier testing

title: Spring Boot Soap Web Service Example
description: Step by step guide to build a SOAP web service with Spring Boot Maven XSD WSDL and a simple endpoint for testing
heading: Spring Boot Soap Web Service Example Guide
body:
This tutorial shows how to build a SOAP web service using Spring Boot and Maven.

  1. Project setup
  2. Define XSD contract
  3. Generate Java classes from XSD
  4. Create endpoint and service logic
  5. Configure WSDL exposure
  6. Test with a SOAP client

Project setup Use Spring Initializr or a preferred IDE to create a Maven project with Spring Boot and Spring Web Services dependencies. Add a dependency for JAXB or use the built in support for marshalling. Keep the packaging simple and avoid unnecessary frameworks for a clean example.

Define XSD contract Design a concise XML schema that describes request and response messages. Think of the schema as a contract that clients will follow. A clear schema prevents surprises when a consumer tries to call the service.

Generate Java classes from XSD Use a plugin such as jaxb2 or the Maven XJC goal to generate domain classes from the schema. Generated classes reduce manual parsing work and ensure message bindings match the contract.

Create endpoint and service logic Implement an endpoint class annotated for Spring Web Services mapping. Wire a service layer that performs business logic and returns the generated response objects. Keep endpoint methods focused on translation between XML messages and domain operations.

Configure WSDL exposure Configure a WSDL definition bean that references the XSD location and exposes a predictable URL. This makes the service discoverable for clients that require a formal WSDL for code generation.

Test with a SOAP client Use SoapUI or a simple curl call to post XML to the endpoint URL. Validate request and response against the XSD and iterate on message structure until schema validation passes without errors.

This tutorial covered creation of a SOAP web service from project creation to contract design to testing. Follow the numbered steps to produce a maintainable service that plays nice with strict clients and legacy systems.

Tip

Keep the XSD stable and versioned. Backwards compatible schema changes prevent breaking existing clients and make future enhancements far less painful.

title: SOAP Web Services in Spring #techtarget
description: Learn SOAP web services in Spring with WSDL generation endpoint mapping marshalling and testing tips for Java developers
heading: SOAP Web Services in Spring guide for developers
body:
Quick summary

If you are building SOAP services in Java and you like predictable contracts and fewer surprising production fires then Spring WS with a contract first approach will be your friend. This guide shows how to go from XSD to WSDL to a working endpoint using JAXB for marshalling and the Spring Web Services support built for Spring Boot.

What you will build and why it matters

You will design an XSD, generate domain classes with JAXB, wire up a Jaxb2Marshaller, implement an @Endpoint and publish a WSDL file that clients can consume. This keeps enterprise teams happy because the contract is explicit and versioning is straightforward. Also you will be spared late night calls that start with the words why is the XML different.

Project setup and dependencies

Create a Spring Boot project and add the Spring Web Services starter plus JAXB support. In plain English that means include spring boot starter web services and a marshaller library like Jaxb2Marshaller. No drama required just pick the right dependencies and move on with your life.

Notes on tools for schema to Java

  • Design the XSD first using a contract first approach so changes are deliberate.
  • Use the Maven jaxb2 plugin or xjc to generate Java classes from the XSD.
  • Keep your XSDs versioned so clients do not wake up to rude surprises.

Configure Spring Web Services and marshaller

Register a schema bean and a WSDL definition bean in your Spring configuration. Provide a Jaxb2Marshaller bean and wire it into the web service configuration so Spring can convert between SOAP XML and your Java objects. Think of the marshaller as a translator that does not tolerate slang.

What to register

  • Schema bean that loads the XSD from the classpath.
  • DefaultWsdl11Definition or equivalent to expose the WSDL built from the XSD.
  • Jaxb2Marshaller bean configured with the generated package names.

Implement the endpoint

Create endpoint classes annotated with @Endpoint. Use @PayloadRoot or a soap action mapping to route requests to handler methods. Accept the request payload as a generated JAXB object and return a response payload that will be marshalled back to XML. Keep methods focused and testable so the next developer does not cry.

Publish WSDL and test the service

Expose the WSDL with DefaultWsdl11Definition or similar and put your XSD on the classpath. Clients can fetch the WSDL and generate their own stubs if they must. Test the service with SOAP UI or a curl call that wraps the request in a SOAP envelope. Logging of SOAP messages helps a lot when servers act up and answers are needed fast.

Testing checklist

  • Confirm WSDL is reachable and lists the correct operations and types.
  • Validate request and response against the XSD to catch schema drift early.
  • Use SOAP UI to run sample requests and inspect raw XML when things break.

Tips and best practices

  • Favor contract first design and version XSDs early so clients do not suffer.
  • Use Jaxb2Marshaller for simple mapping and keep generated classes tidy.
  • Annotate endpoint methods with clear payload mappings for maintainability.
  • Enable logging for SOAP traces to speed up debugging when the network is in a mood.

If you follow these steps you will have a robust SOAP service stack built on Spring WS, backed by WSDL and XSD contracts, using JAXB for marshalling, and ready for Java clients and tools like SOAP UI. It is boring stability and yes it is worth it.
seo_title: Build reliable SOAP APIs with Spring WS and JAXB today
seo_heading: Contract first SOAP services in Spring with WSDL XSD endpoints

title: Spring Boot Logging Levels Configuration
description: Practical guide to Spring Boot logging levels configuration patterns and starter properties for effective debugging and file routing
heading: Spring Boot Logging Levels Configuration Guide
body:
If your Spring Boot logs look like a noisy karaoke night you did not attend then this guide will help you quiet the crowd. We will cover starter properties and logging levels while keeping things useful and slightly sarcastic. Keywords to enjoy include spring boot, logging levels, logback, log4j2, configuration, starter properties and log pattern.

Pick the right starter and logging framework

Spring Boot ships with Logback by default via spring boot starter logging. If you need features from Log4j2 then exclude the default starter and add spring boot starter log4j2 to your build. That swap is straightforward and keeps dependency chaos to a minimum.

Maven and Gradle notes

Exclude the default logging starter and add the log4j2 starter. No magic is involved. Just be careful not to leave multiple logging frameworks on the classpath or you will see duplicate messages and a headache.

Set logging levels and control the noise

Keep the root logger conservative and only open up DEBUG or TRACE for specific packages. This prevents production logs from becoming a firehose.

logging.level.root=INFO
logging.level.com.example=DEBUG

Levels follow the usual order from TRACE up to ERROR. Package scoped settings are your friend when you need to hunt a bug without drowning in unrelated chatter.

Configure log pattern and file paths

Use clear patterns that are easy to grep and monitor. The console and file pattern examples below avoid colon time separators to keep things filesystem friendly and boring in a good way.

logging.pattern.console=%d{yyyy-MM-dd HH-mm-ss} %-5level %logger{36} - %msg%n
logging.file.name=app.log
logging.file.path=/var/log/myapp

When both logging.file.name and logging.file.path are present the file name takes precedence. That saves you from accidental surprises when deployments try to be clever.

Use profiles and external configuration

Put environment specific rules in application-production.properties or other profile files. You can also override settings with environment variables or command line arguments on the JVM and container platforms. Profiles let you run verbose logging locally and stay sane in production.

Debugging and common pitfalls

  • If you see duplicate logs check for multiple logging frameworks on the classpath.
  • Increase framework specific packages to TRACE to diagnose filters and appenders.
  • For high throughput use an asynchronous appender to reduce logging latency under load.

Quick summary and a practical tip

Pick the right starter set, set a conservative root level, enable DEBUG for targeted packages, and use clear log patterns so your monitoring and alert rules do not weep. If you expect high volume then use async appenders and keep root at WARN in production while enabling DEBUG only where needed. That way logs help you instead of giving you stage fright.
seo_title: Tame Spring Boot logs with smart levels and patterns today
seo_heading: Practical Spring Boot logging tips for logback and log4j2 users

title: Java, JDBC & SQL Server Tutorial #driver #url #jar #download
description: Learn how to download and configure the Microsoft JDBC driver add a Maven dependency build a connection URL and run queries from Java
heading: Java JDBC and SQL Server Tutorial driver url jar download maven microsoft
body:
So you want Java to stop ghosting your SQL Server instance. Good news, it is not mystical. With the Microsoft JDBC driver and a sane connection URL you can be querying tables before your coffee gets cold. This guide covers the mssql-jdbc driver jar, the Maven dependency, building a connection URL, opening a connection with DriverManager, running a query, and closing things so your DBA does not light you on fire.

1 Download or add the JDBC driver

Grab the Microsoft JDBC driver jar from the official Microsoft site or declare the Maven artifact if you prefer a civilized build. The artifact coordinates are stable and boring in a good way.

Maven snippet

<dependency>
  <groupId>com.microsoft.sqlserver</groupId>
  <artifactId>mssql-jdbc</artifactId>
  <version>12.2.0.jre11</version>
</dependency>

If you use the jar directly, drop it on the classpath or into your app server lib folder. If you use Maven or Gradle, let the build tool handle the drama.

2 Construct the connection URL

The JDBC connection string is annoyingly simple and perfect for copy paste chaos. Here is the canonical form for SQL Server.

jdbc:sqlserver://localhost:1433;databaseName=MyDB

Replace localhost and 1433 with your host and port. The parameter separator is a semicolon so yes that punctuation matters. You can add authentication and other options as query like properties or URL parameters depending on taste and severity of life choices.

3 Open a connection and run a query

Modern Microsoft drivers usually auto register so you do not have to call Class.forName like it is 2003. Use DriverManager to get a Connection and then a PreparedStatement for safety and sanity.

String url = "jdbc:sqlserver://db.example.com:1433;databaseName=MyDB";
String user = "appuser";
String pass = "secret";

try (Connection conn = DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, pass);
     PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement("SELECT TOP 10 * FROM dbo.MyTable");
     ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {

  while (rs.next()) {
    // read columns by name or index
    System.out.println(rs.getString("SomeColumn"));
  }
}

Try with resources is your friend. It closes ResultSet, PreparedStatement and Connection even when exceptions try to ruin your day.

4 Close resources and handle exceptions

Always close things. If you are using try with resources you are done. If not, close ResultSet then PreparedStatement then Connection in a finally block. Log SQL state and error codes to make troubleshooting faster than a frantic stack overflow search.

5 Troubleshooting quick hits

  • Wrong port or host. Try ping, telnet or a modern replacement to see if the port is open.
  • Firewall or network rules blocking traffic between the app and the SQL Server.
  • Driver version mismatch with your JRE. The mssql-jdbc jar has variants for different Java versions so pick the right one.
  • Authentication issues. Double check credentials and whether SQL Server is using Windows integrated auth or SQL auth.
  • Connection pool exhaustion. Leaked connections lead to mysterious failures long after the original sin.

Final words

In short install the correct mssql-jdbc driver jar or add the Maven dependency, craft a valid connection URL, use DriverManager or a pool to open connections, run queries with PreparedStatement and always close resources. If something breaks log the SQL state and error code and blame the network first. The rest of the time blame yourself and then fix the driver version.
seo_title: Get Java talking to SQL Server with the right JDBC driver
seo_heading: Step by step guide to mssql jdbc, jar setup and connection URL tips

title: JDBC Connection Pooling with Hikari CP & MS SQL Server
description: Compact guide to set up Hikari CP for JDBC pooling with Microsoft SQL Server covering config best practices tuning and common pitfalls
heading: JDBC Connection Pooling with Hikari CP and MS SQL Server
body:
This tutorial shows how to set up Hikari CP for JDBC connection pooling with Microsoft SQL Server in a Java application in a few practical steps.

  1. Add driver and Hikari CP dependency
  2. Create and configure HikariDataSource

Add JDBC driver and Hikari CP to the build system so the runtime has the necessary classes. For Maven use group and artifact names in pom dependency entries. For Gradle use implementation lines in build script.

Create a HikariDataSource instance and set core properties. Example style without an actual URL to avoid copy paste danger

dataSourceClassName=com.microsoft.sqlserver.jdbc.SQLServerDataSource

username=yourUser

password=yourPassword

Bind the DataSource to application code so DAO classes request a connection from the pool rather than opening raw connections. Frameworks such as Spring Boot will accept a HikariDataSource bean and wire the pool automatically. Manual wiring is fine for small projects just be careful to close the DataSource on shutdown.

Tuning is where many developers pretend defaults are magical and then complain about performance. Start with small changes. Set maximumPoolSize to expected concurrent database threads plus a safety margin. Adjust connectionTimeout and idleTimeout based on observed latency and usage patterns. Too many connections will overwhelm the database rather than speed up the app.

Monitoring prevents surprises. Expose metrics using a metrics binder or JMX so the number of active connections idle connections and waiting threads are visible. Logs will reveal frequent connection acquisition failures which point to pool or database configuration issues rather than application bugs.

Summary recap of the flow Add dependencies Configure the pool Use the pool in code Tune parameters and keep an eye on runtime metrics. The goal is predictable latency and efficient database resource usage rather than heroic connection creation on demand.

Tip

If the database server is the bottleneck prefer lowering maximumPoolSize and focus on query optimization and indexing. A big pool will not hide slow queries and will only make the database sadder.

title: Statements, JDBC & SQL Server Database Delete Commands
description: Delete SQL Server rows safely using JDBC statements prepared statements transactions and resource cleanup to prevent injection and leaks
heading: Statements JDBC and SQL Server Database Delete Commands
body:
This tutorial shows how to perform DELETE operations on a SQL Server database from Java using JDBC statements and prepared statements while managing transactions and cleaning up resources.

  1. Open a JDBC connection
  2. Choose Statement or PreparedStatement
  3. Prepare and execute the DELETE
  4. Manage transactions and rollback when needed
  5. Close resources and verify results

Open a JDBC connection using a proper driver and a secure connection string. Authenticate using least privilege credentials so the database user can delete rows without full dbo permissions.

Choose between Statement and PreparedStatement based on use case. Statement is fine for one off ad hoc deletes. PreparedStatement prevents SQL injection and improves performance for repeated deletes.

Prepare and execute the DELETE using parameter binding to avoid injection. Example SQL

DELETE FROM Employees WHERE id = ?

Example Java style preparation without extra fluff

PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement("DELETE FROM Employees WHERE id = ?")

Bind parameters using the appropriate setter then call executeUpdate to remove rows. Check the returned update count to confirm how many rows were affected.

Manage transactions by disabling auto commit for multi row operations. Commit after successful batches and rollback on exceptions to maintain data integrity. Logging the reason for rollback helps with debugging later.

Close ResultSet when present and always close PreparedStatement and Connection in a finally block or use try with resources. Lack of cleanup leads to exhausted connection pools and sad developers.

Recap of the tutorial covers making a secure connection choosing the right JDBC API preparing the delete with parameters handling transactions and ensuring proper resource cleanup. Following these steps reduces risk of SQL injection and keeps the database healthy.

Tip

Use PreparedStatement for any user supplied value and test deletes on a staging environment before running on production to avoid accidental data loss

title: Java JDBC PreparedStatements Update Commands MS SQL Server
description: Quick guide to running JDBC PreparedStatement update commands from Java against MS SQL Server with safe parameter binding and resource handling
heading: Java JDBC PreparedStatements Update Commands for MS SQL Server
body:
This tutorial shows how to execute UPDATE commands with JDBC PreparedStatement from Java against MS SQL Server while avoiding SQL injection and resource leaks.

  1. Open a connection
  2. Create SQL with placeholders
  3. Bind parameters on the prepared statement
  4. Execute update and verify affected rows
  5. Close resources and handle exceptions

Open a connection using a DataSource or DriverManager. Prefer a connection pool for real world apps to avoid slow performance and drama when traffic spikes.

Create SQL with question mark placeholders to keep the database engine happy and the code safe. Example SQL in Java code

String sql = "UPDATE users SET name = ? WHERE id = ?"

Bind parameters by position on the prepared statement. Use typed setters to match column types so the database does not guess wrong. Example binding

preparedStatement.setString(1, name)
preparedStatement.setInt(2, id)

Execute the update with executeUpdate and check the returned row count to confirm success. A returned value of zero means no row matched the WHERE clause and may require investigation.

Close the prepared statement and connection to release resources. Use try with resources where possible to avoid manual closing code and reduce risk of leaks. Catch SQL exceptions and log useful details such as SQL state and error code for debugging.

Summary of the process is simple bind safe parameters execute the update and manage resources properly. Following these steps prevents SQL injection and makes update logic predictable and maintainable while keeping a clean code base.

Tip

Use a connection pool and prefer prepared statements over string concatenation. Check executeUpdate return value to confirm changes and wrap multiple related updates in a transaction to keep the database consistent.

title: SQL Server JDBC Connection String URL & Create Operations
description: How to build SQL Server JDBC connection URLs and perform create operations with clear examples and practical tips for robust connections
heading: SQL Server JDBC Connection String URL and Create Operations
body:
Prepare the driver and dependencies

Start like a normal responsible developer and add the Microsoft JDBC driver to your project. Use a recent driver for TLS support and modern authentication so you do not get surprised by a mysterious handshake error at 3 a m.

<dependency>
  <groupId>com.microsoft.sqlserver</groupId>
  <artifactId>mssql-jdbc</artifactId>
  <version>10.2.0.jre11</version>
</dependency>

If you are not on Maven pick the jar that matches your JRE and drop it on the classpath. If you are using a framework like Spring Boot it usually wires the driver for you and you can go back to arguing about tabs versus spaces.

Build a proper JDBC URL

The driver expects a URL in a format it understands. Here is the conventional form that actually works with SQL Server:

String url = "jdbc:sqlserver://localhost:1433;databaseName=TestDB;user=sa;password=Secret";

Notes and caveats

  • Replace localhost and credentials with real values or environment variables.
  • Prefer integrated authentication when possible to avoid embedding credentials.
  • You can add properties such as encrypt=true and trustServerCertificate=false for production security.

Open a connection and run create statements

For a demo you can use DriverManager directly. For anything that sees traffic use a connection pool and stop making the server cry. Try with resources keeps cleanup polite and predictable.

try (Connection conn = DriverManager.getConnection(url);
     Statement stmt = conn.createStatement()) {
    stmt.executeUpdate("CREATE TABLE Users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100))");
} catch (SQLException e) {
    System.err.println("SQL error code " + e.getErrorCode() + " state " + e.getSQLState());
    e.printStackTrace();
}

That example creates a simple Users table. Adjust data types and constraints to fit your schema and your desire to sleep well at night.

Use a connection pool for production

Connection pooling saves CPU and developer patience. HikariCP is a popular choice. Configure timeouts and max pool size based on your workload instead of guessing.

HikariConfig cfg = new HikariConfig();
cfg.setJdbcUrl("jdbc:sqlserver://db.example.com:1433;databaseName=ProdDB");
cfg.setUsername(System.getenv("DB_USER"));
cfg.setPassword(System.getenv("DB_PASS"));
cfg.setMaximumPoolSize(10);
HikariDataSource ds = new HikariDataSource(cfg);

Handle errors and close resources

Catch SQLException and log the error code and SQLState. Always close statements and connections or rely on a pool to do it for you. In other words do not leak resources unless you are collecting technical debt for the hobby section.

Test and tune for production

Do not promote a dev machine to production. Run the flow against a staging server and tune these things

  • Connection timeout and socket timeout
  • Max pool size and connection lifetime
  • Encryption and certificate handling
  • Authentication method such as integrated security or managed identity

Checklist and quick tips

  • Do not bake credentials into your code or URL. Use environment variables or a secrets store.
  • Use a modern driver release to get security fixes and better auth options.
  • Prefer connection pooling in any environment that gets more than one request per minute.
  • Validate your create statements in migrations or DDL scripts rather than ad hoc code.

This is a practical guide to forming SQL Server JDBC connection strings and running create operations from Java while staying less confused. Follow these steps and you will have a reproducible connection pattern that is easier to debug than a blob of string concatenation and regret.
