title: AWS Bedrock Pricing for Video Generation with Luma Labs AI
description: Compact guide to how AWS Bedrock pricing affects Luma Labs AI video generation costs and how to estimate total spend.
heading: AWS Bedrock Pricing for Video Generation with Luma Labs AI
body:
Quick reality check

If you are using AWS Bedrock with Luma Labs AI for video generation you will want to know where the bills actually come from. Spoiler alert, the model does most of the heavy lifting and your wallet notices. This guide walks through practical cost factors for Bedrock pricing and gives a tidy checklist for realistic cost estimation and optimisation.

Measure your input first

Start by measuring target video length and output resolution. Higher resolution and longer duration mean more frames and more compute per job. Before you guess wildly run short pilot renders to collect real world metrics for seconds of inference per frame at your chosen resolution and quality.

What to capture in the pilot

  • Seconds of model inference per frame at the target resolution
  • Number of refinement or denoising passes per frame
  • Average API request size and latency for your pipeline using the Amazon API

Understand model compute billing

Model compute is usually the dominant cost. Bedrock pricing often maps to inference time or compute units consumed per request. Take your measured compute seconds per frame and multiply by the model rate provided by the vendor to get a base cost per frame. If your workflow uses multiple passes for refinement or denoising include those passes in the calculation.

Quick formula that actually helps (pretend math is fun)

  • Compute per frame equals measured seconds per frame times passes
  • Base cost per frame equals compute per frame times model rate
  • Job cost equals base cost per frame times frame count

Storage and data transfer traps

Storage costs pile up as raw and rendered footage accumulates. Keep an archive strategy and delete intermediate files you no longer need. Also budget for data transfer, especially outbound delivery and cross region moves, since cloud providers love charging for leaving the party.

  • Use lifecycle rules to move archives to cheaper storage tiers
  • Keep heavy processing in a single region to cut cross region egress
  • Compress or delta encode intermediate assets where possible

Account for API request overhead and retries

When automation churns many short clips the per call overhead matters. Amazon API pricing and per request latency can add up when you have thousands of tiny calls. Batch requests where supported and add retry logic with exponential backoff to avoid repeated charges from transient failures. Logging and telemetry add minor cost but they give you the data needed to optimise, so do not skip them.

Put the budget together

Practical estimation is simple math plus a safety margin. Add up the model compute estimate, storage estimate, transfer estimate and API overhead, then tack on a contingency buffer for experimentation and early mistakes. Run a small pilot job to validate assumptions and adjust your numbers before you scale.

Simple checklist for a sane estimate

  • Measure seconds per frame at target resolution
  • Count passes and multiply compute accordingly
  • Estimate storage growth per project and apply lifecycle rules
  • Plan for outbound transfer and cross region traffic
  • Factor in API call pricing and retry safety margin
  • Run a pilot and update the model rates with measured data

Final tip

Short pilot runs will save you more than a few sleepless nights. Measure real world compute seconds per frame, multiply by expected volume and add a buffer for experimentation. Then you can scale without getting a bill that looks like a modern art experiment.

title: Java Spring Boot AWS Beanstalk Amazon Deployment JAR
description: Quick guide to package and deploy a Java Spring Boot JAR to AWS Elastic Beanstalk using Maven or the EB CLI. Steps and troubleshooting tips
heading: Deploy Java Spring Boot JAR to AWS Elastic Beanstalk
body:
If you want to package a Java Spring Boot app as a runnable JAR and throw it at AWS Elastic Beanstalk without crying later, this guide is for you. We cover building the artifact with Maven or Gradle, creating an Elastic Beanstalk application and environment, setting runtime variables, deploying with the EB CLI or console, and checking logs and health so you can blame a real error instead of the platform.

Build the runnable JAR

Use Maven or Gradle to produce a single runnable JAR that contains your Spring Boot main class and dependencies. The usual commands are:

mvn clean package
# or
./gradlew bootJar

Verify the produced JAR contains your Spring Boot main class. Make sure the spring boot plugin or spring boot gradle plugin is configured in your build file so the artifact is executable on the JVM you plan to use on AWS.

Create the Elastic Beanstalk application and environment

Open the AWS console and create a new Web server environment for Elastic Beanstalk. Pick a Java platform such as Amazon Corretto 11 or Corretto 17 that matches your build JVM. Name the application and environment with some dignity so your future self can find it.

Configure platform settings and environment variables

Set environment properties for things like database credentials and active profiles. You can do this in the console under configuration or with the EB CLI via configuration files. Ensure your application listens on the port the platform expects or set server.port in application.properties or environment variables.

Upload the JAR and deploy

There are two common workflows. Use the console to upload the JAR artifact, create a new application version, and deploy it. Or use the EB CLI to manage the lifecycle from your terminal.

eb init          # configure project and region for Beanstalk
eb create        # create environment for the first time
eb deploy        # upload and deploy a new version

The EB CLI will zip the artifact and push a version to Elastic Beanstalk for you if configured correctly. If you prefer CI CD, build a step that produces a predictable JAR name and push that artifact to the environment.

Monitor logs and environment health

After deployment, check the environment health panel in the console. Request logs from the platform when things go wrong and scan for stack traces. Common issues include wrong JVM version, missing environment variables, or the process listening on the wrong port.

Troubleshooting tips and common fixes

  • Use a predictable JAR name with a version number to avoid confusion during rollbacks or CI CD runs.
  • Match the Corretto or OpenJDK version on Beanstalk with the JVM used to build the JAR.
  • Confirm the Spring Boot main class is present and the manifest points to it.
  • Set server.port or rely on the platform provided port through an environment variable.
  • Store secrets in environment variables or use AWS Parameter Store instead of hard coding credentials.

Quick checklist before you click deploy

  • Artifact builds locally with mvn package or ./gradlew bootJar
  • Platform JVM version matches build JVM
  • Environment variables configured for DB and profiles
  • Port configuration is correct
  • EB CLI is initialized if you want command line deployment

If you follow these steps you will package a Spring Boot JAR, create an Elastic Beanstalk environment, configure runtime variables, deploy the artifact, and have a plan to check health and logs when the platform gets dramatic. Congratulations, you are now slightly less likely to be paged at 3 AM.

title: Route 53 AWS Beanstalk Domain Names DNS Alias CNAME
description: Practical guide to mapping Beanstalk apps to domains using Route 53 alias records and CNAME entries in Amazon hosted zones.
heading: Route 53 AWS Beanstalk Domain Names DNS Alias CNAME
body:
Why use Route 53 with Elastic Beanstalk

Because typing myapp.elasticbeanstalk.com into your browser is only funny for the first 30 seconds. If you want a professional looking site name and the joy of proper DNS management you map your Elastic Beanstalk environment to a custom domain with Route 53. This keeps traffic flowing to the load balancer while letting you control DNS from a single place.

Prerequisites

  • An AWS account with an Elastic Beanstalk environment running your app
  • A registered domain with a hosted zone in Route 53 or a registrar that lets you point name servers to Route 53
  • Basic comfort with the AWS console or the AWS CLI

Quick overview of what we will do

In plain human terms the plan is simple. Find the Beanstalk environment endpoint or the load balancer DNS name. Create or confirm the hosted zone in Route 53. For the root domain create an alias record that points to the load balancer or the environment target. For a subdomain use a CNAME that points to the environment endpoint. Then test and wait for DNS caches to behave.

Step 1 Create or find your Elastic Beanstalk environment

Open the Elastic Beanstalk console and either launch the environment or pick the one you already have. Note the environment name and look at the environment details for the endpoint. Typical endpoint looks like myapp.elasticbeanstalk.com and if you are using a load balancer you will also see the load balancer DNS name in the resources or environment configuration.

Step 2 Create or verify the Route 53 hosted zone

In Route 53 create a hosted zone for your domain if you do not already have one. Hosted zones are where DNS records live. If your registrar is not Route 53 make sure the domain uses the name servers Route 53 gave you. That is how queries reach the records you are about to create.

Step 3 Add the right record for the root domain or a subdomain

Rules of the DNS jungle you must remember

  • CNAME records cannot exist at the zone apex. In other words do not try to put a CNAME at example.com
  • For the naked domain create an alias record in Route 53 that points to the load balancer resource or to the Beanstalk environment target if the console offers it
  • For subdomains like www or app you can create a CNAME that points to the environment endpoint such as myapp.elasticbeanstalk.com

In the Route 53 console pick Create record and select Record type A alias for the apex or CNAME for subdomains. If using the CLI use the change resource record sets action to create the appropriate record set that points to the load balancer DNS name or the Beanstalk CNAME target.

Step 4 Test DNS and be slightly patient

DNS changes can be instant or move at the pace of a sleepy sloth. Use tools like dig or nslookup to verify the records resolve to your target. Example commands you can run from your terminal

dig example.com A +short
dig www.example.com CNAME +short
nslookup example.com

If the alias points to the load balancer you should see the load balancer DNS name in the resolution path or the IPs returned from the A record. For CNAMEs you should see the chain that ends at the environment endpoint.

Troubleshooting tips that actually help

  • If the record does not appear check that you are editing the correct hosted zone
  • If you see the old site clear local DNS cache or try from another network
  • If the console offers an alias to the Beanstalk environment but you prefer the load balancer target pick the load balancer for more predictable behavior
  • Remember health checks and HTTPS certificates are separate. Aliasing a domain does not magically attach an SSL certificate to your load balancer

Final sanity check

Once DNS resolves to the load balancer verify your application responds as expected. If you use HTTPS make sure you have an ACM certificate attached to the load balancer or use an alternate TLS termination solution. If everything works celebrate quietly and then do another deploy to remind yourself you did not actually fix anything forever.

Mapping domain names with Route 53 and Elastic Beanstalk is more paperwork than magic. Follow the steps and you get a friendly domain name that points to your app while keeping DNS management sane. And if it breaks later you can enjoy the sweet thrill of debugging DNS while the whole team watches.
seo_title: Point your domain to Elastic Beanstalk with Route 53 records
seo_heading: How to map an Elastic Beanstalk app to your custom domain in Route 53

title: Route 53, Sub Domains, S3 Buckets and Domain Name Mapping in
description: Compact guide to map subdomains to S3 static sites using Route 53 and optional CloudFront and ACM on AWS
heading: Route 53 Sub Domains S3 Buckets Domain Name Mapping Amazon AWS
body:
This tutorial shows how to map a subdomain to an S3 static website using Route 53 and optional CloudFront and ACM for HTTPS.

  1. Create an S3 bucket named after the subdomain and enable static website hosting
  2. Upload site files and configure public access or use CloudFront for security
  3. Create a hosted zone in Route 53 and add an alias record for the subdomain
  4. Optional provision an SSL certificate in ACM and attach to CloudFront
  5. Test DNS propagation and visit the mapped URL

Step 1 Create an S3 bucket with the exact name of the subdomain for example static.example.com. Turn on static website hosting in the bucket properties so the bucket can serve web content.

Step 2 Upload HTML CSS and assets to the bucket and set a bucket policy to allow public reads when using S3 website endpoints. If security matters and HTTPS is required choose CloudFront so the origin remains secure and public access can be locked down.

Step 3 In Route 53 open the hosted zone for the domain and add an A record alias that points at the S3 website endpoint for a simple setup or at the CloudFront distribution for a secure setup. Use alias records to avoid manual IP management and to support AWS targets.

Step 4 If HTTPS is desired request a public certificate in ACM in the us east 1 region for CloudFront. After validation attach the certificate to the CloudFront distribution so the browser shows a padlock and not a thrilling security warning.

Step 5 DNS changes take time so wait for propagation then load the subdomain URL. Check response headers and confirm the origin is the expected bucket or distribution. If redirect rules or index documents are misbehaving revisit bucket hosting settings and Route 53 records.

This tutorial covered creating a named S3 bucket for a subdomain enabling static hosting choosing between direct S3 hosting and CloudFront creating Route 53 alias records and adding an ACM certificate when HTTPS is needed. Follow these steps and the subdomain will point to the static site without mysterious DNS dark arts.

Tip

Use CloudFront when HTTPS performance or custom headers matter and request the ACM certificate in the region required by CloudFront to avoid headaches.

title: AWS EC2 User Data Script Sample Tutorial
description: Quick tutorial on using AWS EC2 user data to install packages run root scripts and log output at first boot
heading: AWS EC2 User Data Script Sample Tutorial
body:
Overview

This is a no nonsense guide to using AWS EC2 user data and cloud init for simple startup automation. You will learn how to run a root level bash script at first boot to install packages start services and write logs so you can prove the machine did something useful before it goes back to sleep.

Quick sample script

Drop this into the instance user data field or a launch template. It runs as root so no sudo is needed. It also uses a marker file to avoid doing the same work twice unless you want it to.

#!/bin/bash
set -e

# idempotent check
if [ -f /var/log/user-data-ran ]; then
  echo "User data already ran on $(hostname) at $(date)"
  exit 0
fi

apt-get update -y
apt-get install -y nginx

echo "Hello from root on $(hostname)" > /var/www/html/index.html
systemctl enable nginx
systemctl start nginx

echo "User data ran on $(date)" >> /var/log/user-data.log
touch /var/log/user-data-ran

Where to put the script

  • Paste the script into the EC2 launch wizard user data field when you create an instance
  • Or add it to a launch template so every new instance gets the same startup logic
  • You can also use Infrastructure as Code tools to inject the same user data into your templates for repeatable automation

What actually happens at boot

AWS and the cloud init system hand the user data script to the instance and run it as root during first boot. That means package installs systemd commands and file writes run with full permissions so be careful and test in a sandbox before you go nuclear in production.

Useful commands to verify behavior

  • Check cloud init output log at /var/log/cloud-init-output.log for script stdout and errors
  • Check your custom log at /var/log/user-data.log for script messages
  • Confirm nginx is running with systemctl status nginx
  • View the sample web page by curling the instance IP at port 80 if security groups allow it

Make startup scripts safe and idempotent

User data normally runs only once. If you want safe repeated behavior write a simple marker file check as shown in the example. That prevents duplicate package installs and confusing side effects during reboots.

  • Use a marker file like /var/log/user-data-ran to short circuit the script on subsequent boots
  • Log to a custom file so you do not lose your messages among generic cloud init output
  • Use systemctl enable to ensure services survive a reboot

Rerunning or debugging user data

If you need to rerun the script for testing you can SSH in and run the script manually or remove the marker file and reboot. For more advanced control use cloud init tooling to run specific modules but for most cases a manual rerun is good enough.

Tips and common pitfalls

  • Remember that the script runs as root so typos hurt more than usual
  • Keep network dependent commands after package updates so you fail fast if metadata or DNS is broken
  • Prefer small scripts in user data and heavier configuration from a configuration management system for long term maintenance
  • Include clear logging so the next human who inherits this can blame the right person

Follow these patterns and your EC2 startup automation will be predictable repeatable and slightly less likely to surprise you at 3 AM. If it still breaks you can always blame cloud init and then fix the bug.

seo_heading: Example bash user data that installs nginx and logs first boot actions on EC2

title: How to Install AWS CLI & Git on EC2 Instances
description: Quick guide to install AWS CLI and Git on EC2 using a user data script and a sample S3 get command for boot time automation
heading: How to Install AWS CLI and Git on EC2 Instances
body:
This tutorial teaches how to install AWS CLI and Git on an EC2 instance using a user data script and a sample S3 fetch for automated boot time setup.

  1. Prepare a user data script
  2. Launch EC2 with the script
  3. Verify installations on first boot
  4. Fetch sample file from S3 using AWS CLI
  5. Use an IAM role for secure access

Step 1 Prepare a user data script that runs as root on first boot. The script should update packages and install Git and AWS CLI so the instance is ready without manual SSH work.

Step 2 Launch the EC2 instance and paste the user data script into the user data field in the console or include the script in the CLI run instances call. Choose an Amazon Linux image for smoother commands.

Step 3 Verify that Git and AWS CLI installed by checking versions in the system logs or by connecting via SSH. Version commands provide quick confirmation.

Step 4 Use a sample S3 fetch command that avoids embedding credentials. The recommended pattern uses an instance role and a get object call to retrieve example files from the bucket.

Step 5 Apply an IAM role that grants read access to the target S3 bucket. This avoids credential handling on the host and keeps automation secure and auditable.

#!/bin/bash yum update -y yum install -y git aws-cli mkdir -p /home/ec2-user/app chown ec2-user ec2-user /home/ec2-user/app sudo -u ec2-user aws s3api get-object --bucket my-bucket --key sample.txt /home/ec2-user/app/sample.txt

The sample script shows a minimal practical setup. Package manager commands install Git and AWS CLI and the s3api get object command pulls a file into a user folder. Using sudo under ec2 user keeps permissions sane.

Testing during the first boot can be done by tailing cloud init logs or checking the target file presence. Apply a role with least privilege to allow the single get object action.

This guide covered preparing a user data script, launching an instance with that script, verifying installations, fetching a sample file from S3, and using an IAM role to avoid credential sprawl. Follow these steps to automate tool installation on new EC2 hosts and keep hands off the keyboard.

Tip

Attach an IAM role with scoped S3 read permissions rather than embedding credentials in the script. That keeps automation secure and makes rotation a non issue.

title: Amazon Machine Image Creation and Launch Custom AWS AMI

  4. Launch a new EC2 from the AMI

Prepare source EC2 Start from a clean Linux server with required packages installed. Configure applications users and security groups. Assign an IAM role when cloud resource access is required during launch.

Harden and clean the environment Remove SSH host keys and clear logs. Purge sensitive credentials and unnecessary packages. Update packages with sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y on Debian or use the equivalent command on other distributions. A tidy image reduces surprises later.

Create the AMI Use the AWS Console or use the AWS CLI with aws ec2 create-image to snapshot the instance volume and register a new AMI. Use a meaningful name and version tag so humans and automation can find the image.

Following these steps results in a reusable image that speeds provisioning and keeps systems consistent. Automation reduces human error and makes deployments predictable even when the caffeine level drops.

Tip

Include semantic version tags in AMI names and automate image creation with scripts or AWS Image Builder so pipelines can handle upgrades while humans enjoy fewer manual steps.

title: How to Create an AWS AMI for EC2
description: Step by step guide to create an AWS AMI from an EC2 instance for backups scaling and fast deployments
heading: How to Create an AWS AMI for EC2 step by step guide
body:
This tutorial shows how to create an AMI from an EC2 instance for backups scaling and fast deployments.

  1. Prepare the source EC2 instance
  2. Stop or finalize running services
  3. Create the AMI using the AWS console or CLI
  4. Adjust image and snapshot settings
  5. Test the new AMI by launching an instance

Prepare the source EC2 instance Keep the source instance updated and remove temporary files and logs. Clear any credentials that should not travel with the machine image. That step prevents surprises when cloning the environment.

Stop or finalize running services For consistent disk state pause databases or use application friendly backup modes. A stopped instance produces a cleaner snapshot for the image than a live capture with ongoing writes.

Create the AMI using the AWS console or CLI From the EC2 console choose create image from the instance or run the CLI command aws ec2 create-image with the instance id and a descriptive name. That command records EBS snapshots and registers the AMI for later launches.

Adjust image and snapshot settings Review snapshot encryption and storage options. Add tags for environment and owner to make future automation and cleanup less soul crushing. Confirm whether the root volume should be encrypted or left as legacy storage.

Test the new AMI by launching an instance Launch a fresh instance from the AMI and run basic health checks. Verify network settings key pairs and any user data scripts. Launch testing avoids propagating broken images into production.

Creating an AMI captures the OS configuration installed packages and disk layout so future instances boot from the same baseline. Use AMIs for scaling backups and consistent environment provisioning.

Tip

Tip Use automated tagging and a lifecycle rule that removes older AMIs and associated snapshots after validation. That avoids storage bloat and keeps snapshot costs under control while preserving trusted golden images.

title: Java, Spring, AWS & Amazon's Elastic Beanstalk Tutorial
description: Step by step guide to build and deploy a Spring Boot Java app to Amazon Elastic Beanstalk using EB CLI AWS CLI and practical tips
heading: Java Spring AWS Amazon Elastic Beanstalk Tutorial
body:
Why this guide exists and why you will need coffee

If you build Java microservices with Spring Boot and try to deploy them to AWS Elastic Beanstalk you want something that works and does not demand a ritual sacrifice. This walk through uses the EB CLI and AWS CLI to get a runnable jar up and healthy on Elastic Beanstalk. Expect commands, a few tiny surprises, and clear steps for Maven builds and environment setup.

Prepare the project

Start with a minimal Spring Boot service and a REST controller so you can prove the thing actually does anything other than compile. Make sure you have a pom.xml or Gradle build and a main class annotated with @SpringBootApplication. That annotation is your app saying please run me.

Checklist for local sanity

  • Use Maven or Gradle to define dependencies and packaging
  • Confirm your main class boots and exposes a health endpoint
  • Keep configuration lightweight while testing

Build the executable jar

Run the build command that matches your build tool and platform. With Maven run the familiar command below to produce a runnable jar in the target folder.

mvn clean package

Then verify locally with a command like

java -jar target/app.jar

Check the health endpoint or a simple REST call to confirm your app starts and does not immediately explode.

Configure AWS credentials and EB CLI

Store your AWS credentials and default region with the AWS CLI. It will prompt you for an access key and secret key. That is the only time you are going to say a prayer to IAM.

aws configure

Then initialize Elastic Beanstalk for your project with the EB CLI and select the Java platform and region when prompted.

eb init

Create an Elastic Beanstalk application and environment

Provision a test environment with a single instance and keep production on a load balanced environment if you expect real traffic. The create command will provision an application and environment resources for you.

eb create my-env
  • Single instance is fast and cheap for development
  • Load balanced environments are preferred for production traffic

Deploy and monitor

When the code is ready deploy it with the EB CLI. If things go sideways stream the logs and watch the health page in the AWS console like a hawk that cares.

eb deploy

Useful commands while debugging

  • eb logs to fetch logs
  • eb status to check environment state
  • eb setenv to update environment variables

Health checks and deployment strategy

Enable enhanced health checks for better insight and use immutable deployments for production to avoid half broken fleets. That reduces the chance of a deployment morning surprise.

Security and JVM tuning

Do not store secrets as plain environment variables if you can avoid it. Use AWS Parameter Store or Secrets Manager to keep secrets safer and easier to rotate.

If you need JVM tuning pass options with a custom Procfile so you control heap and garbage collector settings without editing the artifact.

Quick troubleshooting tips

  1. If the app does not start check the logs for exceptions and missing native libs
  2. Confirm the jar runs locally to rule out packaging problems
  3. Check environment variables and IAM permissions for any AWS calls your app makes
  4. Use enhanced health and EB event messages to find startup failures

CI and automation thoughts

In a DevOps friendly workflow build the jar in CI and run the EB CLI deploy step from a pipeline job. Keep credentials in secure pipeline storage and avoid committing keys into git. With Maven and the AWS CLI you can automate builds tests and deployments without manual intervention.

Tip Use immutable deployments for production and keep logs and health checks enabled. Store secrets in Parameter Store or Secrets Manager and tune JVM options through a Procfile for predictable performance.

That is the short path from a Spring Boot jar to a running service on AWS Elastic Beanstalk. No magic, just a few commands and a little patience. Now go break and fix things in production like a responsible engineer.

title: Deploy Docker Containers to Amazon EKS Clusters
description: Step by step guide to deploy Docker containers to Amazon EKS using eksctl kubeconfig YAML and ECR for images
heading: Deploy Docker Containers to Amazon EKS Clusters
body:
This tutorial shows how to deploy Docker images to an Amazon EKS cluster using eksctl kubeconfig YAML and Kubernetes manifests.

  1. Build and tag the Docker image
  2. Push the image to Amazon ECR
  3. Create the EKS cluster with eksctl using a YAML file
  4. Update kubeconfig so kubectl can talk to the cluster
  5. Apply deployment and service manifests
  6. Verify pods and services are running

Build the image Use a Dockerfile and create a compact image with a meaningful tag. Example command docker build -t my-app. Multi stage builds help keep the final image small and faster to pull on worker nodes.

Push to Amazon ECR Create an ECR repository and push the image to that registry. Example commands aws ecr create-repository --repository-name my-app and docker push 123456789012.dkr.ecr.region.amazonaws.com/my-app. The registry becomes the source for Kubernetes pod pulls.

Create the cluster Define cluster settings in a YAML file for eksctl and run the create command. Example eksctl create cluster -f cluster.yaml. The YAML can declare node groups networking and IAM roles so the cluster comes up consistent and repeatable.

Update kubeconfig Let AWS write kubeconfig so kubectl targets the new cluster. Example aws eks update-kubeconfig --name cluster-name --region region. After this the developer workstation can control the cluster with familiar kubectl commands.

Deploy manifests Create Deployment and Service YAML that reference the ECR image and apply with kubectl. Example kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml. The scheduler places pods on nodes and image pulls happen from the registry configured earlier.

Verify Check resource status with kubectl get pods and kubectl get svc. Logs help debug failing containers with kubectl logs. Expect some waiting during image pulls and node provisioning so coffee is allowed.

The tutorial covered building a Docker image pushing that image to Amazon ECR creating an EKS cluster with eksctl wiring kubeconfig and deploying Kubernetes manifests to run the container workload on the cluster.

Tip

Use minimal base images and multi stage builds to reduce image size. Smaller images mean faster pulls and happier autoscaling during deployments.

title: AWS Management Console Dark Mode How To Tutorial
description: Quick guide to enable dark mode in the AWS Management Console with practical tips for ECS EKS Bedrock and SageMaker.
heading: AWS Management Console Dark Mode How To Tutorial
body:
Ready to stop squinting at the AWS console like it is signaling a nuclear launch? This quick guide walks you through enabling the dark theme in the AWS Management Console and checking that key services such as ECS, EKS, Bedrock and SageMaker follow along. No drama, no magic commands, just the usual clicks and a little troubleshooting for when the internet throws a tantrum.

Sign in and set the console theme

First, sign in to the AWS Management Console with whatever credentials you normally use. Once you are on the console home screen, look to the top right for the account menu. Click the account menu, choose Preferences, then find Theme and select Dark theme. The console will switch to a darker palette that is easier on late night eyes and questionable lighting choices.

Verify the theme in key services

Changing the global console theme is satisfying, but some service pages are stubborn. Here is a short checklist for the usual suspects.

  • ECS â€” Open the ECS console and scan tasks and logs. Confirm lists and modal windows render in dark mode.
  • EKS â€” Visit the EKS cluster view and check cluster status, node groups and kubectl integrations. Some plugin screens may remain light, that is normal.
  • Bedrock â€” Open the Bedrock console and check model browsing and endpoints. Third party components inside pages may not inherit the global theme.
  • SageMaker â€” Look at studio and notebook interfaces. Notebook editors can follow the browser or require their own theme setting inside the notebook app.

Common visual hiccups and fixes

If a page refuses to go dark, start with the basics. Clear your browser cache and try a private window to rule out stale assets. Disable style forcing extensions because those can mess with AWS UI styling. If the problem persists, confirm the service uses a separate UI library that may override the global console setting.

Troubleshoot list

  • Clear cache and reload the console
  • Try a private or incognito window to isolate extensions
  • Temporarily disable extensions that inject CSS or manage themes
  • Check for service specific theme options inside the service console

Propagate preferences across devices

If you want the dark theme everywhere, use browser sync or set preferences through your AWS SSO profile where available. That helps keep your console settings consistent across machines, unless one machine is possessed by a stubborn extension.

Still a problem

If a particular page or embedded vendor UI refuses dark mode, capture a screenshot and file a support case or open a ticket with the service owner. Screenshots help the AWS console team and third party vendors spot which component is ignoring global settings.

There you go, dark mode in the AWS console with checks for ECS, EKS, Bedrock and SageMaker. Now go provision resources and look cool while doing it, or at least less like you were blinded by a thousand suns.

title: How to Set a Default AWS Region in the Amazon Management Con
description: Quick guide to set a default AWS Region in the Amazon Management Console using Login User Settings for ECS EKS and Bedrock
heading: How to Set a Default AWS Region in the Amazon Management Console Login User Settings ECS EKS Bedrock
body:
Stop accidentally creating servers in the wrong hemisphere and blaming DNS. This quick guide shows how to set a per user default AWS region in the Amazon Management Console using Login user settings so ECS, EKS, Bedrock and other services open in the region you actually meant to use.

Quick steps to set your default region

  • Sign in to the AWS Management Console with the account or SSO that reaches the console home page.
  • Click the top right avatar or account name to open the account menu.
  • Choose the Login user settings entry from the menu. The label may vary but look for words like login or user settings.
  • Pick your preferred default region from the dropdown. Look for region codes like us-west-2 or eu-central-1 that match your project needs.
  • Save the preference and verify the top right region selector now shows your chosen region.
  • Open a console page for ECS, EKS or Bedrock to confirm those pages default to the selected region.

Why this matters

Choosing a default region is not just about latency, although lower ping is nice. It prevents the delightful chaos of creating resources in the wrong geography, and it avoids the surprise that some managed services are not available everywhere. Setting a per user default saves time and reduces human error when switching between projects.

Detailed walkthrough

Sign in and find Login user settings

Sign in with a console account that has normal console access. If your org uses single sign on follow the usual steps to land on the console home page. Use the avatar or account name in the top right to open the account menu. The Login user settings link may be named slightly differently across accounts but it usually contains login or user settings. This is where the console stores per user preferences.

Pick and save a default region

From Login user settings pick a default region from the dropdown list. The selector uses standard region codes such as us-west-2, eu-central-1 and so on. Choose a region that matches your team or project to reduce latency and to keep resources together. Click save and then check the region selector in the console header to confirm it matches your choice.

Verify with a service page

Open a service like ECS or EKS to confirm the console is showing the selected region by default. If you use Bedrock or other managed services check their region availability before relying on them. Some services roll out region coverage slowly so the default will not help if the service is not offered in that region.

Best practices and sanity saving tips

  • Use a separate browser profile per project or role to keep default region preferences isolated. This avoids the classic mistake of building in the wrong geography.
  • Match the default region to your team or data residency requirements to avoid compliance headaches later.
  • Keep an eye on region codes like us-east-1 and us-west-2 when naming things. They look similar until you deploy a costly cluster to the wrong one.

Setting a default AWS region in the console is a tiny configuration that prevents a lot of future facepalms. Do it once, and enjoy fewer surprises when your cloud bill arrives.

title: How to Download and Install the AWS CLI
description: Quick guide to download and install AWS CLI for ECS EC2 EKS and S3 on Windows Mac and Linux
heading: How to Download and Install the AWS CLI
body:
If the cloud makes you feel nostalgic for operating systems that just worked this guide will help. You will download and install the AWS CLI then configure it so you can run commands for S3 EC2 ECS and EKS without crying into the console. Yes this is a tutorial for the command line and yes you will be more powerful afterwards.

Grab the installer

Pick the package that matches your system and stop hoping the web installer reads your mind. Windows users should use the MSI from the official AWS site. macOS fans can use Homebrew for a quick install. Linux users can choose the distro package manager or the bundled installer for more control.

Quick commands per platform

  • macOS with Homebrew run brew install awscli
  • Debian and Ubuntu try sudo apt update then sudo apt install awscli
  • RHEL or CentOS use sudo yum install awscli or your distro package tool
  • Windows use the MSI and follow the setup wizard

Install and make the shell happy

Most installers will drop the aws binary onto your PATH so the shell can find it. If your shell says command not found then either reopen the terminal or check your PATH like a detective who actually likes their job.

Verify the installation

Make sure the thing actually works by running the classic check.

aws --version

The output shows the AWS CLI version and runtime info if present. If you see nothing or a path error then the shell is not seeing the binary.

Configure credentials and default region

For basic access run the built in configuration helper. This writes credentials to the usual place and lets you stop typing them into every command.

aws configure

The prompts ask for an access key id secret access key default region and preferred output format. Heads up if this is for production use IAM roles or named profiles are the better choice than long lived keys on disk.

Test common commands

Now the part where you prove you deserve cloud powers. Try these to confirm you have access and the right permissions.

Troubleshooting and best practices

  • If aws is not found check PATH and reopen your terminal
  • Prefer IAM roles and instance profiles for production instead of static keys
  • Use named profiles for juggling multiple accounts with --profile
  • If a command fails check IAM policies and CloudTrail for clues
  • Consider installing AWS CLI v2 for the latest features and EKS helpers

Wrap up

You downloaded installed verified and configured the AWS CLI so you can now run commands across S3 EC2 ECS and EKS from the terminal. That is the core setup for a cloud focused command line workflow and it will save time once you get used to typing not clicking.

title: How to Create an AWS Access Key & Secret | AWS Console
description: Step by step guide to create an AWS access key and secret then configure the AWS CLI for S3 access without drama
heading: How to Create an AWS Access Key & Secret | AWS Console
body:
This tutorial shows how to create an AWS access key and secret using IAM and how to configure the AWS CLI for S3 access in a few practical steps.

  1. Open AWS Console and go to IAM
  2. Create or select a user and enable programmatic access
  3. Attach least privilege policies
  4. Create the access key and download the secret
  5. Configure the AWS CLI with the new credentials
  6. Test S3 access and adopt key rotation practices

Open the AWS Console and navigate to IAM from the services list. The goal here is to work inside the identity management area where credentials live.

Create a new user or pick an existing one and enable programmatic access for that account. Programmatic access grants the ability to use API and CLI calls which is required for S3 command line work.

Attach policies that match the required permissions. Try to avoid full administrator privileges like a plague. For S3 tasks attach a scoped S3 policy or AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess when possible to follow least privilege principles.

Create the access key and secret from the security credentials tab. The secret access key will be shown only once so either copy the credential to a secure vault or download the key file. Losing the secret means creating a new key pair rather than recovering the original secret.

Run aws configure and paste the access key id and secret access key when prompted then set preferred region and output format. The AWS CLI will store credentials in the user profile under the .aws folder so commands can authenticate.

Verify the credential by running aws s3 ls against a known bucket or the account buckets. If a permission error appears review attached policies and correct permissions rather than creating more keys.

Rotate keys regularly and delete unused credentials. Never commit keys to source repositories and avoid embedding the secret inside application code or public files.

This tutorial covered creating an access key and secret in IAM then configuring the AWS CLI for S3 use with basic testing and security advice to keep credentials tidy and safe.

Tip

Use an IAM role for EC2 or containers when possible so there is no long lived secret to manage and the cloud provider handles temporary credentials automatically.

title: How to Delete AWS Secret Access Keys in IAM
description: Quick guide to remove AWS secret access keys from IAM users using the Management Console and optional CLI steps for safe credential rotation
heading: How to Delete AWS Secret Access Keys in IAM
body:
So you found a rogue AWS secret access key and want it gone. Good call. This guide shows how to delete an AWS secret access key from an IAM user using the AWS Management Console and the AWS CLI while keeping your apps alive and your audit log satisfying. We will cover safe credential rotation and quick checks that the old key really stopped doing naughty things.

Who should do this

Sign in with an account that can manage IAM users. A root account can do it but do not make that a habit unless you enjoy panicking your team. Prefer an admin or an IAM user with appropriate permissions for IAM and for any resources the key touched like S3 or EC2.

Quick checklist before you act

  • Identify the Access Key ID to remove
  • Confirm no production job depends on it
  • Create a new access key if the user still needs programmatic access
  • Update apps or environment variables with the new key
  • Delete the old key and verify revocation

Delete the key using the AWS Management Console

Open the AWS Management Console and go to IAM. Click Users and pick the user who owns the secret access key. Open the Manage Security Credentials tab and scroll to Access Keys. Find the Access Key ID you want to remove and use the Delete action. AWS will tear it off like a bandage. Make sure you already rotated credentials if the user still needs programmatic access.

Delete the key with the AWS CLI

If you prefer a terminal and tasteful command line drama run this from an admin shell.

aws iam delete-access-key --user-name USERNAME --access-key-id ACCESSKEYID

This command permanently revokes the specified credential. No undo button exists. Plan accordingly.

Credential rotation best practices

Do not delete the old key before you create and test the new one. A safe rotation looks like this

  1. Create a new access key for the IAM user
  2. Update application configuration or environment variables that used the old key
  3. Deploy or restart the service that uses the new key
  4. Validate access to resources such as S3 buckets EC2 APIs or EKS clusters
  5. When validation succeeds remove the old key

Practical tip

Test against a noncritical resource first. If your app talks to S3 start with a read of a small object. If it talks to EC2 test a harmless describe call. This is the difference between a graceful rotation and a midnight pager party.

How to verify the key is truly gone

  • Run a simple API call using the deleted credentials and expect an authorization error
  • Search CloudTrail for requests that use the old Access Key ID and confirm they fail
  • Check application logs for authentication errors after you remove the key

Summary

Deleting an AWS secret access key in IAM is quick but do not be careless. Use the AWS Management Console or the AWS CLI to remove the key. Always rotate credentials by making a new key updating your applications validating access and then deleting the old key to avoid credential sprawl. Follow these steps and your S3 EC2 and EKS workloads will keep humming while that old key collects dust in a safer place which is not production.
seo_title: Remove old AWS IAM access keys and rotate credentials safely
seo_heading: Step by step guide to delete IAM secret keys and update your apps

title: AWS Parameter Store from Amazon's System Manager (SSM)
description: SSM Parameter Store SecureString with KMS and AWS CLI steps for encrypted parameters and minimal permissions
heading: AWS Parameter Store from Amazon's System Manager SSM
body:
This tutorial shows how to store encrypted values in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store using SecureString KMS encryption and the AWS CLI.

  1. Create or choose a KMS customer managed key
  2. Put a SecureString parameter via AWS CLI
  3. Grant KMS decrypt and SSM access via IAM and key policy
  4. Retrieve the parameter with decryption using AWS CLI
  5. Audit and rotate keys and monitor access

Step 1 Create or select a KMS key for encryption. A customer managed key allows control over rotation and access. Example command to create a key

aws kms create-key --description "SSM parameter key" and then create an alias for easier reference

aws kms create-alias --alias-name alias/ssm-params --target-key-id example-key-id

Step 2 Store a SecureString parameter using the AWS CLI. Use the KMS alias or key ARN to ensure encryption at rest. Example command

aws ssm put-parameter --name "/prod/db/password" --value "SuperSecret123" --type SecureString --key-id alias/ssm-params

Step 3 Grant permissions. Attach KMS decrypt permission to the application role and allow ssm service to use the key through a key policy. Keep permissions least privilege and avoid granting broad access to many principals.

Step 4 Retrieve the parameter decrypted via CLI when a running process needs the secret. Example command

aws ssm get-parameter --name "/prod/db/password" --with-decryption

Step 5 Audit and rotate. Use CloudTrail to log parameter calls and enable automatic KMS key rotation where appropriate. Regular rotation and audit reduce blast radius and make security teams slightly happier.

Following these steps yields encrypted parameters that are accessible only to roles with explicit permissions and a clear audit trail. This setup prevents casual secret leakage and saves explainers from awkward meetings.

Tip

Use a KMS alias for friendly commands and enable key rotation. Restrict key policy to the SSM service principal and only the specific IAM roles that require decrypt permission.

title: How to Create an IAM User in AWS Management Console
description: Quick guide to create an IAM user in the AWS Management Console with proper permissions MFA and role assignment for EC2 and EKS access
heading: How to Create an IAM User in AWS Management Console
body:
This tutorial shows how to create an IAM user in the AWS Management Console for EC2 and EKS access while assigning appropriate permissions and optional MFA.

Sign in to the AWS Management Console and open the IAM service Use administrator credentials to access the console then navigate to the Identity and Access Management page from the Services menu. No drama required just clicks.

Create a new user and choose programmatic or console access Pick a clear user name and select whether the new account needs access keys for APIs or a password for the web console. Choosing the wrong access type leads to confusion later.

Attach permissions using groups policies or role delegation Prefer adding the user to a group with managed policies for consistent permissions. For temporary elevated access use a role and avoid giving broad permissions directly to the user.

Add optional tags and review the user configuration Tags help with billing and auditing. Review the chosen policies and make sure the principle of least privilege is honored. Excessive permissions cause trouble faster than you can say sudo.

Save credentials and enable MFA for strong authentication Download the CSV with access keys or copy the console password. Immediately enable multi factor authentication for the account for additional protection.

Test access and adjust permissions as needed Use the intended workflow such as launching an EC2 instance or checking EKS cluster access to verify permissions. Tweak policies rather than escalating privileges to avoid surprises.

This tutorial covered creating an IAM user assigning the right type of access attaching safe permissions optionally enabling MFA and validating the setup so the new account can perform tasks without becoming a security risk.

Tip

Use groups and managed policies for repeatable permission control and enable MFA before sharing credentials to reduce risk and future headaches.

title: How to Create AWS IAM Admin Users in Management Console
description: Quick guide to create AWS IAM admin users using the AWS Management Console with secure permissions and MFA best practices.
heading: How to Create AWS IAM Admin Users in Management Console
body:
If you want to stop treating the AWS root account like a spare key hidden under the welcome mat this guide will help you create an IAM admin user in the Management Console and do it without causing a security incident. This version keeps things short and slightly snarky while covering permissions groups MFA and verification steps so you do not accidentally give everyone S3 access or leave the root account on daily duty.

Why you should not use the root account for daily work

The root account has full authority and a fragile ego. Use it once to bootstrap your environment then tuck it away in a password manager and forget it. Daily tasks belong to IAM admin users or scoped accounts with the correct permissions and MFA. That is better for security and for your future self.

Quick checklist before you start

  • Sign in with an existing administrator if you have one
  • Open the AWS Management Console and go to the IAM service
  • Decide if the new identity needs console access programmatic access or both
  • Plan permissions using AdministratorAccess only when absolutely necessary
  • Enable MFA and enforce a strong password policy

Step by step creation in the Management Console

  1. Step 1 Sign in as the right account

    If you are doing initial setup and there is no admin yet use the root account. Otherwise sign in with an existing administrator account that already has user creation permissions. This keeps the root account out of daily workflows and reduces risk.

  2. Step 2 Open IAM

    From the Management Console search for IAM and open the dashboard. This is where users groups roles and policies live. If it looks like a spreadsheet of permissions that is because it is.

  3. Step 3 Create the user

    Click Create user then choose console access for humans and programmatic access for CLI or SDK usage. Give the account a clear name that reflects its purpose for easier audits and less confusion later.

  4. Step 4 Assign permissions

    Attach the AWS managed policy named AdministratorAccess only when full admin rights are actually needed. Better practice is to use least privilege either by attaching custom policies or placing the user into a group with scoped permissions that limit access to services like S3 as required.

  5. Step 5 Enforce MFA and password policy

    Enable multifactor authentication for the new admin account and require a strong password. MFA turns credential theft into a minor inconvenience for attackers and a big relief for you.

  6. Step 6 Verify access and retire the root

    Log in with the new admin credentials and confirm you can access IAM S3 and any other needed services. After verification stop using the root account for daily tasks and store the root credentials securely in a password manager.

Best practices and final snarky advice

  • Use groups to manage permissions at scale and avoid editing the same policy a dozen times
  • Prefer least privilege over blanket AdministratorAccess whenever possible
  • Rotate keys and review access regularly to avoid surprises
  • Document who has admin rights and why so audits do not turn into mysteries

Follow these steps and you will have an AWS IAM admin user that is usable dependable and far less likely to start a chain reaction. Security is mostly boring repeated small choices done right. Do them and your cloud will be safer and your future self will thank you or at least not curse you.

title: AWS Batch Tutorial | How to Create Batch Jobs
description: Step by step guide to AWS Batch job setup including job definitions queues and Fargate EC2 and EKS options
heading: AWS Batch Tutorial How to Create Batch Jobs Job Definitions Queues and Fargate EC2 EKS
body:
How to set up job definitions job queues and mixed compute for AWS Batch

If you build Batch Jobs and want to stop guessing about compute choices this guide shows how to pick between AWS Fargate EC2 and EKS and get jobs running without unnecessary drama. Expect practical steps with a little sarcasm and no miracles.

What you need to know up front

AWS Batch coordinates containers for large scale workloads in cloud computing environments. You will create a job definition package a container image set vCPU and memory values and choose platform capabilities for Fargate or EC2. If you plan to run on Kubernetes use EKS to host batch pods.

Create a job definition and pick resources

Think of a job definition as the recipe that tells Batch how to cook your container. Include the container image command and resource settings. Match vCPU and memory to your workload and add sensible timeouts and retry behavior so a runaway job does not cost you a small fortune.

  • For Fargate set platformCapabilities to FARGATE and avoid host management.
  • For EC2 choose managed or unmanaged compute environment and pick the AMI and instance types that fit CPU memory and cost needs.
  • For EKS attach a Kubernetes cluster to run batch pods if you already use container orchestration.

Provision a compute environment

A compute environment defines resource type scaling policies and the IAM role Batch uses. Managed EC2 lets AWS handle instance lifecycle while unmanaged EC2 gives you more control. For cost savings mix spot instances with on demand fallback.

Job queue setup and routing

Create job queues and attach compute environments with priorities. Use higher priority for low latency environments and lower priority for spot based capacity. This routes workloads to the optimal resource type and keeps DevOps less grumpy.

Mixed workload tip

Put latency sensitive jobs on a priority queue that points to fast on demand capacity and send bulk parallel work to a queue that favors spot instances to save budget.

Submitting jobs and useful commands

Submit via the Console CLI or SDK. The CLI is quick and repeatable when you want to script things or when you are pretending to look busy.

aws batch submit-job --job-name myjob --job-queue myqueue --job-definition mydef

Monitoring and troubleshooting

Check the Console CloudWatch logs and use describe job CLI calls to inspect state. Capture container logs for debugging and add retries and timeout values in the job definition to prevent runaway costs. Job arrays are your friend for parallel tasks and reduce operational overhead.

Final checklist for sane Batch deployments

  • Define clear resource limits in job definitions
  • Use job queues to route to Fargate EC2 or EKS as appropriate
  • Combine spot capacity with on demand fallback for cost control
  • Monitor with CloudWatch and capture container logs
  • Add retries timeouts and job arrays for robustness

Follow these steps and you will have AWS Batch workflows that run predictably with fewer surprises. If that sounds like a miracle it is just good planning and a little sarcasm.

title: Create an AWS API Gateway & Mock Responses
description: Learn to set up AWS API Gateway mock responses using mapping templates for fast testing and predictable Lambda and ECS API development.
heading: Create an AWS API Gateway and Mock Responses with Mapping Templates
body:
This tutorial shows how to create an AWS API Gateway REST API with a mock integration and mapping templates to return controlled responses for development and testing.

  1. Create REST API resource and method
  2. Set method integration to Mock
  3. Add mapping templates for request and response
  4. Configure method response and integration response status codes
  5. Test using the API Gateway console and refine mapping templates

Create a new REST API in the API Gateway console. Add a resource path and choose an HTTP method such as GET or POST. This prepares the route that will serve mock responses instead of hitting a backend service.

For method integration choose Mock integration from the integration type picker. Mock integration returns a response from API Gateway so no Lambda or backend service is invoked while testing endpoints.

Add mapping templates under Integration Request for inbound shaping and under Integration Response for outbound shaping. Use Velocity Template Language to build a predictable JSON payload and to set headers that match client expectations.

Configure the Method Response status codes and match those to Integration Response mappings. Map the response body and set header mappings so the API Gateway response matches the contract the frontend or downstream service expects.

Test directly in the API Gateway console using the Method Test tool or send an HTTP request with curl or Postman. Adjust mapping templates to cover different status codes and error shapes so testing covers realistic scenarios.

Mock integration plus mapping templates offer a fast feedback loop for contract design and frontend integration. That saves time while building Lambda functions or ECS tasks by letting developers agree on response shapes before backend code lands.

Tip

When building mapping templates start small and add fields incrementally. Use a stable example response and map headers and status codes explicitly so automated tests can assert against a deterministic API behavior.

title: How to Create DynamoDB Database Tables to Store NoSQL for EC
description: Step by step guide to create DynamoDB tables for EC2 EKS API Gateway SNS and SQS with schema choices capacity and security best practices
heading: How to Create DynamoDB Database Tables to Store NoSQL for EC2 EKS API Gateway SNS and SQS
body:
If you need NoSQL storage that does not throw tantrums when traffic spikes then DynamoDB is the calm sibling in the AWS family. This guide walks through creating tables and wiring them into EC2 and EKS apps plus API Gateway driven APIs and event flows with SNS and SQS. You will get practical tips on keys indexes capacity IAM and monitoring with a side of sarcasm to keep it interesting.

Plan your primary key and indexing strategy

Stop picking keys like you pick passwords. Choose a partition key that spreads reads and writes across partitions. Add a sort key when you need ordered queries. Only add global secondary indexes if your query patterns cannot be satisfied with the main key. More indexes means more cost and more things to regret later.

  • Partition key examples userId productId tenantId
  • Sort key examples orderId createdAt
  • Use GSIs sparingly for alternate access patterns

Create the table with console or CLI and automate it

The Console is fine for exploration but automation is your friend when you have to do this again or for CI pipelines. Use CloudFormation or Terraform to store the table definition and keep it repeatable and versioned. If you use the AWS CLI do not forget to include attribute definitions and key schema if you intend to script creation.

Quick practical note

For test environments on demand capacity is great because it avoids surprise throttles while you figure out traffic patterns. For steady production workloads provisioned capacity with autoscaling gives predictable costs and performance. Pick what matches your traffic profile not what sounds trendy.

Pick capacity mode and configure autoscaling

Provisioned capacity is efficient for predictable workloads. On demand is safer for spiky traffic at the expense of unit cost. If you choose provisioned capacity enable autoscaling targets for reads and writes and tune threshold values with real load tests rather than guessing.

Set IAM roles and resource policies the least privilege way

Grant roles only the table actions they need. Avoid blanket DynamoDB permissions that are handy and dangerous. Use fine grained policies to restrict access to specific tables and to the specific actions like GetItem PutItem Query UpdateItem and so on. That keeps attackers and mischievous developers in check.

Integrate with EC2 EKS API Gateway SNS and SQS

Integration patterns are boring and vital. For EC2 and EKS call DynamoDB through official SDKs with signed requests. For API Gateway use a Lambda proxy or direct integration if you are brave and careful with mapping templates. For SNS and SQS let Lambdas consume messages and write durable state to DynamoDB so events do not evaporate into the void.

  • EC2 EKS use SDK clients with retries and exponential backoff
  • API Gateway use Lambda or direct write patterns when latency matters
  • SNS SQS typically pair with Lambda consumers to persist events

Test monitor and optimize

Run load tests to find hot keys instead of discovering them from a user angry ticket. Use CloudWatch metrics to watch consumed read and write capacity throttles and latency. If you see hot partitions enable adaptive capacity tune keys and consider sharding strategies or TTL for write heavy item types.

Keep an eye on trends not just spikes. Metrics tell the truth even when dashboards lie.

Quick checklist for post deploy

  • Verify table key schema matches query patterns
  • Confirm IAM roles are limited to required operations
  • Validate autoscaling policies under load
  • Watch CloudWatch for throttles and latency
  • Review cost impact of GSIs and large item sizes

Final thoughts

DynamoDB is great when you design to its strengths. Think in keys access patterns and capacity early. Automate creation and permissions and integrate with eventing systems so state is durable and recoverable. Do this and your app will behave better than most humans at a Monday standup.

title: How to Create an AWS S3 Bucket Amazon Web Services Practitio
description: Step by step guide to create an AWS S3 bucket with exam friendly options for AWS Practitioner Solution Architect and DevOps.
heading: How to Create an AWS S3 Bucket Amazon Web Services Practitioner Exam Solution Architect DevOps ECS
body:
So you need an Amazon S3 bucket and you want to avoid the face palm moments that make exam graders and production ops glare at you. This guide walks you through the AWS Management Console path while sneaking in best practices that please auditors and earn extra points on AWS Practitioner and Solution Architect style questions.

Quick summary

Open the AWS Management Console, go to S3, hit create bucket, pick a unique name and region, turn on sensible options like versioning and server side encryption, lock down public access unless absolutely required, and test permissions with a non admin user. That is the short version for people who skip tutorials and regret it later.

Who should follow this

  • AWS Practitioner and Solution Architect exam takers
  • DevOps and ECS teams provisioning cloud storage
  • Anyone who wants to avoid accidental public data leaks

Prerequisites

  • An AWS account and console access
  • An IAM principal that can create buckets and adjust S3 permissions
  • Basic knowledge of regions and compliance for your workload

Step by step in the console

  1. Sign in to the AWS Management Console with the principal that has S3 create permission so you do not get angry permission denied errors.
  2. Open the S3 service and click create bucket.
  3. Choose a bucket name and region. Name must be globally unique and lower case. Pick a region that matches latency and compliance needs for your project or exam scenario.
  4. Configure options. Consider enabling versioning to protect against accidental deletes. Turn on default server side encryption for data at rest. Add tags to label environment and owner to help with cost allocation.
  5. Set permissions. Keep block public access enabled unless you truly need a public site. Apply least privilege policies to IAM roles or users and avoid using root credentials for routine tasks.
  6. Review the summary, create the bucket, and verify that the console shows a successful creation message and the bucket appears in the list.
  7. Test access with a non admin principal to confirm your permission boundaries are correct and you are not leaking data to the internet.

Naming rules to remember

  • Must be globally unique and between 3 and 63 characters long
  • Use only lower case letters, numbers, dots and hyphens
  • No underscores and avoid dot sequences that look like IP addresses
  • Make names DNS compatible so features like virtual hosted style access work

Recommended configuration checklist

  • Enable versioning for accidental delete protection
  • Turn on server side encryption for data at rest as a default
  • Keep block public access enabled by default unless a public bucket is required
  • Use tags for environment owner and cost center to help with billing and audits
  • Apply least privilege to IAM users and roles and test with a limited principal
  • Consider MFA delete for extremely sensitive buckets and follow the documentation for setup

Permissions and testing

Do not assume paperwork rules work in practice. Create an IAM role or user with the minimal rights you intend to use and test common operations like put object list bucket and get object. That will reveal missing permissions before an app or exam scenario fails at 3am.

Exam friendly tips

  • Enable block public access and server side encryption for production buckets to reduce risk and score points
  • Use versioning to protect against accidental deletes in lab and real world questions
  • Pick a region that matches latency and compliance in exam scenarios
  • Tag buckets so exam or audit questions about ownership and cost allocation are easy to answer

Final thought. Creating an S3 bucket is not rocket science but small mistakes cause big headaches. Follow the checklist, test with a non admin principal, and keep your buckets locked down unless you intentionally want to host a public site. Now go make your bucket and try not to make it public by accident.

title: AWS S3 Static Website Hosting
description: Quick guide to host a static website on AWS S3 with configuration steps best practices and DNS options for production readiness
heading: AWS S3 Static Website Hosting Guide
body:
This tutorial shows how to host a static website on AWS S3 with minimal fuss and production awareness.

  1. Create an S3 bucket and set a public access policy
  2. Upload site files and set index and error documents
  3. Enable static website hosting in the bucket settings
  4. Optionally attach a CDN and configure DNS for custom domain
  5. Test the site and monitor for access problems

Step 1 Create a bucket

Pick a globally unique bucket name and choose a region near target users. The bucket name becomes part of the endpoint so pick something memorable. Disable block public access if the goal is a public site and apply a bucket policy that grants public read only to objects.

Step 2 Upload site files

Upload HTML CSS and assets with the correct content type metadata. Set the index document to index.html and the error document to a friendly 404 page. Use versioned filenames for assets to avoid cache headaches.

Step 3 Enable static website hosting

Turn on static website hosting from the bucket properties panel and copy the endpoint for quick testing. The console provides a simple endpoint for browsers to reach the site without extra proxies.

Step 4 Add CDN and DNS

For production scale use a CDN for TLS and global cache performance. Point a custom domain from the DNS provider to the CDN distribution or use an alias record if using Route 53. Configure HTTPS with a certificate to avoid mixed content warnings.

Step 5 Test and monitor

Open the endpoint and the custom domain if configured. Check console errors and verify asset caching behavior. Enable logging and alarms for unusual traffic patterns or access failures.

The tutorial covered creating a bucket uploading files enabling static hosting and adding DNS and CDN options for production. Follow the steps above and the static site will be live and ready for visitors with sensible defaults and room to scale.

Tip

Use cache busting via hashed filenames and set long cache lifetimes on static assets while keeping index html short lived to control deploy updates without user confusion.

title: Create AWS SSL Certificates in Amazon Certificate Manager
description: Short guide to request ACM certificates use Route53 DNS validation and enable TLS HTTPS for an S3 static website
heading: Create AWS SSL Certificates in Amazon Certificate Manager
body:
This tutorial teaches how to request an ACM SSL certificate validate with Route53 and attach TLS HTTPS to an S3 hosted website using CloudFront.

  1. Request a public certificate in ACM for the domain names
  2. Choose DNS validation and copy the validation record
  3. Confirm or create a Route53 hosted zone for the domain
  4. Add the validation record in Route53 or use the automatic option
  5. Wait for certificate issuance
  6. Create a CloudFront distribution using the ACM certificate and point the origin to the S3 bucket
  7. Update Route53 to point the domain to the CloudFront distribution

Step 1 request the certificate Request a public certificate in AWS Certificate Manager for the apex domain and any subdomains such as www. This reserves the certificate and prepares DNS validation records.

Step 2 pick DNS validation Choose DNS validation because Route53 can add records automatically. DNS validation avoids email hoops and is friendly to automation.

Step 3 prepare Route53 Confirm a hosted zone exists for the domain in Route53. If not present create a hosted zone and ensure name servers at the registrar match the hosted zone values.

Step 4 add validation records ACM provides CNAME entries for validation. Use the console button to have Route53 insert those records automatically or paste the records manually into the hosted zone. Certificate status will change to issued once DNS propagates.

Step 5 use CloudFront for HTTPS S3 website endpoints do not serve HTTPS directly. Create a CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket as origin and select the issued ACM certificate in the region required by CloudFront. Configure caching and behaviors as needed.

Step 6 update DNS Create an alias record in Route53 pointing the domain to the CloudFront distribution domain name. This provides TLS termination at CloudFront and secure HTTPS for the static site.

The guide covered requesting an ACM certificate validating through Route53 linking the certificate to a CloudFront distribution and updating DNS so the S3 hosted site is served over TLS.

Tip

Request certificates in the region required by the service that will use the certificate. For CloudFront request in the region that CloudFront accepts which avoids surprises during distribution setup.

title: GitHub Pages Free Website Hosting How-To Guide
description: Quick guide to host static HTML CSS and JavaScript on GitHub Pages with steps for repo setup deployment and optional custom domain.
heading: GitHub Pages Free Website Hosting How-To Guide for Static HTML CSS JavaScript
body:
If you want free hosting that does not require babysitting a server or pretending to love uptime alerts this is for you. GitHub Pages is a reliable way to host a static site made with HTML CSS and JavaScript. The rules are simple. Create a repo add your files push to the right branch and flip the Pages switch. Then enjoy your site and the extra time you get back for coffee or existential dread.

Quick overview of what you will do

High level steps so you know what to expect before you commit to commitment.

  • Create a public repository on GitHub
  • Add index.html and your CSS and JavaScript files
  • Commit and push to main or a gh-pages branch
  • Enable GitHub Pages in repository settings
  • Optionally add a custom domain and update DNS

Create the repository and add files

Use a new or existing public repository. Public repos get the free Pages hosting which means no hidden fees and no theatrics. Put your site entry point at the repository root as index.html or inside a docs folder if you prefer to keep multiple projects in one repo.

If you want to avoid Jekyll processing static assets add a file named .nojekyll to the root. This is handy when your build outputs files or when you use underscores in filenames.

Commit and push from your machine

From a local folder run these commands just like normal humans do. This will get your code into the repo.

git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"
git branch -M main
git remote add origin https://github.com/your-username/your-repo.git
git push -u origin main

If you use a static site generator or prefer the old school flow use a gh-pages branch instead. Many build tools or GitHub Actions can automate that push for you.

Enable GitHub Pages in settings

Open the repository settings then navigate to Pages. Choose the branch and folder where your site lives. Wait a short moment and GitHub will publish your static site at https://username.github.io/repository-name or at your custom domain when configured.

Make sure you enable HTTPS in settings once the domain is verified. That lock icon makes your site look trustworthy and prevents browsers from yelling at visitors.

Setup a custom domain if you want one

Want your site at a real domain instead of a GitHub subdomain Good choice. Add your domain to the Pages custom domain field or place a file named CNAME containing the domain in the repo root. Then update DNS at your registrar.

For apex domains set A records to GitHub Pages IPs 185.199.108.153 185.199.109.153 185.199.110.153 and 185.199.111.153. For subdomains use a CNAME to point to username.github.io. If your DNS provider supports ALIAS or ANAME that is fine too. Always check the official GitHub Pages docs for the latest recommended records.

Gotchas and tips

  • Public repo equals free hosting. Private repos have paid options so double check your privacy needs.
  • Use the docs folder when you host multiple small projects in one repository. Cleaner than chaos.
  • If files do not update clear your browser cache or append a version query to the asset URL while testing.
  • Enable the HTTPS toggle in Pages settings to get an automatic certificate from GitHub.
  • Need redirects or advanced routing Consider using a simple static router or deploy to a CDN that supports rules. For most static sites this is unnecessary over engineering.

Why this is a good idea for static sites

Low cost zero server maintenance and fast global delivery make GitHub Pages ideal for personal projects documentation portfolios and demos. You get to focus on HTML CSS and JavaScript and not on server logs or obscure package versions that break on Tuesdays.

Follow these steps and your static site will be live and forgotten in the best possible way. If you want automation consider adding a GitHub Action to build and deploy so every push becomes a tiny triumphant launch.
