title: Why carding never works - Illegal Detainment by York
description: A concise technical look at why carding fails and how illegal detainment by York officers undermines rights trust and evidence reliability
heading: Why carding never works Illegal Detainment by York Regional Police
body:
Quick summary for people who do not want a lecture

Carding is the practice of stopping people for paperwork and questions when officers do not have reasonable suspicion. The video involving York Regional Police and figures named Konstantin Orshansky and PC Wu reads like a public service announcement about what not to do. The short version is this. Random street checks erode community trust, create privacy and legal headaches, and often produce evidence that courts do not want to touch.

What went wrong in the video

The encounter shows how a routine stop becomes an illegal detainment when the legal threshold of reasonable suspicion is missing. That threshold is not a nice suggestion, it is a rule courts use to decide if a stop was lawful. When officers rely on bulk documentation rather than targeted investigation they trade short term activity for long term damage to investigations and community trust.

Key failures you can see on camera

  • No clear reasonable suspicion for the stop
  • Personal data collected and added to records with weak oversight
  • Trust eroded because people feel targeted and watched
  • Potential for evidence to be excluded in court

Why carding tends to fail

Courts and oversight panels have repeatedly criticized indiscriminate street checks. The legal fragility is the big one. If you stop someone without reasonable suspicion any evidence that follows can be thrown out. That turns an investigation into a pile of paperwork and a headline about illegal detainment.

Data misuse is another problem. Personal details collected during these checks often get stored in databases that do not have airtight controls. That creates privacy harms and biased targeting that stay around longer than the memory of the stop.

Operationally the practice is a waste of time. Officers spend hours on documentation that produces little actionable intelligence. Meanwhile real leads rot on the desk.

Community impact and civil rights

Repeated stops without clear cause make communities pull back. People stop talking to police, witnesses go silent, and community based intelligence dries up. That outcome is the opposite of what policing is supposed to accomplish. In the worst cases this also triggers complaints and litigation that cost agencies money and reputation.

Practical steps for people who are stopped

Here is what helps and it is not complicated. Keep calm. Ask if you are free to leave. State that you want to remain silent. If it is safe to do so record the exchange and note badge numbers and witnesses. Those little details make a big difference later when oversight bodies or courts review the encounter.

  • Ask if you are free to leave
  • Politely say you wish to remain silent
  • Record the interaction if safe and legal
  • Write down time stamps badge numbers and witness names
  • File official complaints and seek legal advice when detainment seems unlawful

What accountability looks like

Expect courts to treat evidence from arbitrary stops with skepticism and expect oversight bodies to push for change when patterns emerge. Public pressure and careful review by boards and ombudsmen can reduce misuse of stop and frisk style tactics and strengthen privacy protections.

Advice for police officers who want things to go better

If your unit wants real results focus on targeted investigations grounded in articulable facts. Use community engagement to build trust instead of bulk documentation. Training on legal standards and careful data governance will save you hours of paperwork and a lot of bad headlines.

Closing thought

Carding looks like efficient policing in a briefing room. In the real world it often backfires. The York Regional Police video with Konstantin Orshansky and PC Wu is an example of how an encounter can spiral into a civil rights issue and a public trust problem. Do better and the work gets easier. Keep doing carding and you end up with less cooperation, weaker evidence, and more oversight meetings to sit through.

heading: A Police Record Because You Asked for a Lawyer York Police Constable Orshansky
body:
This short clip shows York Police Constable Orshansky creating a formal police record after a citizen asked for a lawyer while being questioned. If that makes your eyebrows meet your hairline you are not alone. The video raises plain questions about the right to counsel and how police paperwork can suddenly appear when you do the sensible thing and say the words I want a lawyer.

What the video shows and why it matters

The officer writes up a formal police record after a request for legal counsel. A police record is simply the officer's official note of events, but when it appears right after you invoke the right to counsel you should pay attention. Requesting an attorney is a protected right in most jurisdictions and asking for one is not probable cause or suspicious conduct on its own.

That does not mean paperwork never follows a lawful request. It means the creation of that record should be documented and able to withstand review for fairness and accuracy. If it looks like the record is being used to punish or chill your rights you will want to do something about it.

Your rights in plain language

  • Right to counsel is protected. Say the words I want a lawyer and stop answering questions until counsel is present.
  • Right to identify officers. Ask for the officer name and badge number and write them down.
  • Right to record in many places. Use your phone or a bystander to record the interaction where local law allows it.
  • Right to a copy of formal records. Ask the officer for a copy of any police record they prepare.
  • Right to complain. If the record is wrong or your rights were ignored you can seek legal advice and file a complaint.

Step by step when you want a lawyer

  1. Say I want a lawyer and then stay quiet on substantive questions until counsel arrives. Clarity helps avoid accidental admissions and reduces escalation from misunderstandings.
  2. Ask the officer for their name and badge number right away. Those details matter if you later need to review or challenge the record.
  3. If it is lawful where you are record the exchange with your phone or ask a bystander to do it. A recording beats memory in most courtrooms and is much harder to misplace.
  4. Request a copy of the police record if one is made. A paper or digital copy lets your lawyer check for inaccuracies and omissions.
  5. Talk to an attorney if anything in the record is wrong or if you think misconduct occurred. Civilian oversight and internal affairs are official places to lodge complaints when behavior seems improper.

What to do if the record looks cooked

If the record contains mistakes or seems to restate your request for counsel as suspicious conduct take these steps. Keep calm and collect evidence. Get names, record dates and times, save any audio or video, and ask for the written record. Then contact a lawyer who handles police misconduct or citizen rights. They will help you decide whether to file a complaint with internal affairs or a civilian oversight board and whether a legal challenge is appropriate.

Short practical tips to remember

  • Speak clearly. I want a lawyer is a short phrase that reduces ambiguity.
  • Keep your hands visible and stay polite. Sarcasm wins hearts but not always police reports.
  • Do not resist. If you think your rights are being violated document it and complain later.

The clip with Constable Orshansky and the York Police is a compact example of how one routine request can lead to paperwork and why knowing your rights matters. You do not need to be suspicious to be careful. Being prepared and documenting what happens is the grown up version of carrying an umbrella. It is boring until you really need it.

Why each step matters

Step one prevents escalations that cost people their dignity and sometimes worse. Step two draws a line between a conversation and a detention. Step three creates a clear record of your non consent and your expectations. Step four builds the facts for any future complaint or legal action. Step five turns individual harm into institutional scrutiny so patterns can be fixed.

Recording video and handling evidence

Video forces transparency and often prompts policy review. It is best used responsibly and from a safe distance. If you decide to record keep the camera steady and start with a short narration of who you are and where you are. That simple timestamp can save a lot of headaches later. Never put yourself or others in danger for the sake of a shot.

Filing complaints and finding help

The trade off and the human cost

Public video and complaints have an upside. They bring transparency and can force change. The downside is the emotional toll of being treated as suspicious for no reason. That stress is real and it compounds when entire communities feel surveilled or targeted.

Why the surface numbers lie to you

What the deeper metrics say

Expected goals against and high danger save percentage are the bodyguards for pearls of truth in goaltending analysis. If Andersen's xGA is much better than actual goals allowed it points at defensive breakdowns or unlucky bounces. If both xGA and actual goals are bad then technique or positioning might be the real suspect. Video study is crucial here. Numbers point you to the scene and the tape shows you who was faking an alibi.

How to watch like a smart critic

  • Does his position leave predictable angles for high danger shots

Can Andersen bounce back

Yes. He has the technical tools. The complaints are fixable elements like rebound management and timing on recoveries. The bigger fix might be in front of him. If the Maple Leafs clean up slot coverage and limit odd man sequences his save percentage should follow. That is how goaltending and team defense tango.

Final thought for the doom merchants out there. Headlines love a villain. Real analysis loves trends and context. Track save percentage alongside expected goals and high danger save percentage over a larger sample and you will avoid crowing too soon. Frederik Andersen may have struggled, but calling him the worst ignores the messy reality of shots quality defensive support and small sample noise that haunt every goalie at some point.

What the camera and edit are doing to your brain

Editing is the secret puppeteer here. Short cuts between wide frames and close ups control rhythm and let viewers fill in missing time. Sound design then pulls the strings by suggesting impact. Final note for fans and creators

Yes it looks awful when edited the right way. No that does not always mean real harm occurred. And for crews who stage these angles remember that one bad cut or a misplaced camera can turn safety into scandal. What the crew actually did

The overhaul phase is when you trade flashy hose streams for method and elbow grease. Firefighters searched for hidden fuel, removed burned material, and saturated remaining pockets so embers could not restart the blaze. Hose lines and hand tools stayed front and center while teams checked every suspicious area.

Signs a hot spot is hiding in plain sight

  • Glowing embers inside walls or under floors
  • Localized steam when water hits a hot surface
  • Smoke pockets that linger after main suppression
  • Heat felt through materials even when flames are gone

Tools that made the job faster and safer

Thermal imaging cameras are the unsung heroes here. They show temperature contrast that our eyes cannot, letting crews map hot spots before they start tearing out structural elements. Probing tools and sensible technique round out the toolkit. No mystery gadgets were invented, just reliable technology used well.

Key equipment list

  • Thermal imaging camera for locating heat signatures
  • Probing poles and pike poles for inspection
  • Hand tools for overhaul and debris removal
  • Hose lines for final saturation

Scene safety and maintaining public safety

Command set up clear perimeters to keep curious onlookers and media where they belong. Establishing zones and egress routes for apparatus is routine but critical. Public safety and emergency response coordination reduce the chance of secondary injuries and make the overhaul process more efficient.

Why follow up matters

A smoldering pocket that is left alone can turn into a major problem overnight. Good overhaul reduces property loss and lowers risk to both crews and the public. The footage shows focused activity rather than dramatic flame shows, and that is exactly what keeps a fire dead for good.

Practical tip for firefighters

Use a thermal imaging camera to map hot spots before removing debris. That cuts down on guesswork and prevents dangerous rekindle events. It is not glamorous, but it works much better than hope.

If you live near Bloor and Simcoe and wondered what the fuss was about, now you know. It is firefighting, not pyrotechnics. The crew did the slow careful work that protects lives, property and the community.

seo_heading: Thermal imaging and overhaul tactics at the Bloor and Simcoe fire

title: Solve Jenkins unable to find valid certification path error
description: Quick fix for Jenkins unable to find valid certification path error with steps to export server certificate import into Java cacerts and restart Jenkins
heading: Solve Jenkins unable to find valid certification path error
body:
This tutorial shows how to resolve the Jenkins unable to find valid certification path error by importing the server certificate into the Java keystore and restarting the Jenkins service.

  1. Find the problematic certificate chain
  2. Export the server certificate
  3. Import the certificate into the Java cacerts keystore
  4. Restart Jenkins and verify the connection

Step one use a browser or openssl s client to inspect the server certificate chain. Look for missing or self signed entries that cause Java to refuse the connection.

Step two grab the server certificate from the TLS endpoint. A browser certificate export or openssl s client combined with redirection works fine for most setups.

Step three use the Java keytool that lives with the Java runtime. Example command for a typical Linux Java runtime is

keytool -importcert -file server.crt -keystore /usr/lib/jvm/java-8-openjdk/jre/lib/security/cacerts -alias myserver -storepass changeit -noprompt

Adjust the keystore path for the Java distribution used by the Jenkins process. Use a distinct alias per host to avoid stomping on other entries. The default keystore password often remains changeit but check organization policy before using defaults in production.

Step four restart the Jenkins service so the Java runtime loads the updated keystore. After restart run a job that triggered the original failure or curl the endpoint from the Jenkins host to confirm the TLS handshake succeeds.

If a corporate proxy or custom trust store sits in front of Jenkins then import the certificate into that trust store instead or configure Java runtime options to point Jenkins to the correct trust store path.

Recap the tutorial walked through discovering the bad certificate chain exporting the server certificate importing that certificate into the Java cacerts keystore and verifying that Jenkins can connect without the unable to find valid certification path error.

Tip

Keep a versioned backup of the original cacerts file before changes. That way rolling back after a keyboard adventure remains a one file copy and avoids a frantic search for the original trust store.

title: How to cherry-pick a commit with Git
description: Step by step guide to cherry pick a Git commit across branches with examples and tips for avoiding conflicts and keeping history tidy.
heading: How to cherry pick a commit with Git and keep history clean
body:
Quick summary for people who hate long reads

Want to lift a single fix from one branch into another without dragging the whole feature train with it? Welcome to cherry pick land. This git tutorial walks you through identifying the commit, switching branches, applying the commit with git cherry-pick, handling conflict resolution, and pushing the result while keeping your version control history readable and your coworkers only mildly annoyed.

Why use git cherry-pick

Sometimes you need only one commit from a branch. Maybe it is a tiny security patch or a fix that your release branch needs now. Cherry pick copies a commit onto your target branch without merging the full branch history. It is perfect for backporting or fast fixes in a developer workflow that values surgical precision.

Words of warning

  • Overuse creates duplicate commits across branches and future you will be grumpy.
  • If you cherry pick frequently you may prefer feature toggles or a cleaner branching strategy.

Step by step command line guide

Here is the usual safe recipe. Run these commands from your repo and breathe between steps.

1 Find the commit

Use the log to locate the commit hash. Anything that helps you identify the right change is fine, a GUI or the command line.

git log --oneline

2 Switch to the target branch

Make sure the cherry pick ends up where you expect. Old school people use checkout and the new folks use switch. Both work.

git switch target-branch
# or
git checkout target-branch

3 Apply the commit

Apply a single commit with this command. If you want to keep a trace of the original for future archaeology add -x.

git cherry-pick COMMIT_HASH
# or with a reference to the original
git cherry-pick -x COMMIT_HASH

To apply a range use the A..B notation or A^..B if you want to include A itself.

git cherry-pick A..B
# or
git cherry-pick A^..B

4 Handle conflict resolution like a calm detective

If git complains about conflicts do not panic. Check status, open the conflicted files, fix them, stage the fixes, and continue. If this whole thing was a bad idea you can abort and return the branch to the state it was in before the attempt.

git status
# edit files to resolve conflicts
git add path/to/file
git cherry-pick --continue
# if you want to give up
git cherry-pick --abort

5 Push and confirm

Push your target branch and glance at the log to make sure the commit landed. If you used -x you will see a line that points back to the original commit which saves hours of future detective work.

git push origin target-branch
git log --oneline

Common scenarios and tips

  • Backport a bug fix to release branches without merging the feature work.
  • If you need to apply multiple non consecutive commits consider cherry picking them one by one to keep messages clear.
  • Prefer rebasing or proper merges when you want to keep branches aligned instead of creating duplicates.

Closing note

Cherry pick is a useful git command for surgical fixes in your version control toolkit. Use it when appropriate and avoid letting it become the duct tape of your developer workflow. Your future self will thank you or at least stop sending passive aggressive comments in PRs.
seo_title: Grab one commit with git and avoid history chaos like a pro
seo_heading: Cherry pick a bug fix to another branch without duplicate commits

title: Example of How to Use the Git Reset Hard Command
description: Quick guide to using the git reset --hard command safely with steps for stashing selecting a commit executing reset and recovering with reflog
heading: Example of How to Use the Git Reset Hard Command
body:
Before you wreck anything

Run git status to see what is different in your working tree. If you have local edits you care about stash them with git stash push -m "wip" or commit to a throwaway branch. If you enjoy living dangerously skip the stash and accept the consequences.

Find the commit you actually want

Use a compact log view to pick the commit hash that matches the state you want to return to. For a quick list run

git log --oneline

Copy the 7 to 40 character hash that matches your target commit. Yes the hash looks like gibberish but it knows what it is doing.

Run git reset --hard and what it does to your files

When you run

git reset --hard <commit-hash>

Git moves the current branch pointer to that commit and replaces tracked files in your working tree with the versions from that commit. Staged changes and unstaged edits are discarded. This is a hard reset not a polite suggestion.

Quick checklist before you hit enter

  • Confirm you are on the intended branch with git branch
  • Save anything you might want with git stash push -m "save before reset" or make a temporary commit
  • Make sure the commit hash is the one you actually picked from the log

Pushing to a remote after a reset

If this branch is tracked remotely you will need to rewrite history on the remote to match your new local branch. That usually means a force push like

git push --force origin your-branch-name

Warning this rewrites history for everyone who shares the branch. Use force push only when you understand the social consequences and you are prepared to explain yourself to your team.

Recovering from a mistake with reflog

Made a mistake You are not the first and you will not be the last. The local reflog records where HEAD has been so you can often undo the undo. Run

git reflog

Find the entry that represents the state you want to get back to. It will look like HEAD@{3} or similar. Then run

git reset --hard HEAD@{3}

This jumps the branch back to that recorded position. Reflog is the safety net for moments when haste meets caffeine.

Tips to reduce future drama

  • Work on topic branches not on main or shared branches
  • Stash before any destructive command or make a small backup commit
  • Prefer force with lease if you must push altered history to a shared remote
  • Use git reflog as your first line of defense if something goes wrong

Summary

In short check your working tree stash or commit anything important pick the correct commit hash run git reset --hard and only push with force if you know what you are doing. If you accidentally delete something consult git reflog to find the previous HEAD and reset back. Follow these steps and you will trade panic for competence in fewer mistakes than you think.
seo_title: Fix messy commits with git reset --hard and reflog rescue
seo_heading: Step by step guide to git reset --hard stash and recover lost commits

title: Fix the jvm.dll missing or server JVM error in SonarQube
description: Quick guide to resolve jvm.dll missing or server JVM error when starting SonarQube by fixing Java installation and environment variables
heading: Fix jvm.dll missing or server JVM error in SonarQube
body:
This tutorial shows how to fix the jvm.dll missing or server JVM error when starting SonarQube by correcting Java installation and environment variables and making sure SonarQube uses the proper Java runtime.

  1. Install matching Java JDK 64 bit
  2. Set JAVA_HOME to the JDK folder
  3. Point SonarQube to the correct Java binary
  4. Fix PATH and remove conflicting JRE entries
  5. Restart SonarQube service or run startup script

Install matching Java JDK 64 bit

SonarQube requires a 64 bit Java JDK for server mode. Download a supported JDK version from Oracle OpenJDK or AdoptOpenJDK. Installing a 32 bit runtime is the most common reason for a missing jvm.dll error because the wrapper cannot load a 32 bit module into a 64 bit process.

Set JAVA_HOME to the JDK folder

Define the JAVA_HOME environment variable to point to the JDK root folder rather than a JRE. On Windows set a system variable and on Linux export the variable before starting SonarQube. The wrapper and launch scripts read JAVA_HOME first.

Point SonarQube to the correct Java binary

Edit bin/windows-x86-64/StartSonar.bat or conf/wrapper.conf and verify the path used for Java matches JAVA_HOME and targets the JDK bin folder. If a bundled or system JRE is referenced replace that path with the JDK path.

Fix PATH and remove conflicting JRE entries

Ensure PATH places the JDK bin before any older Java installations. Remove stray JRE paths that might supply a 32 bit jvm.dll. On Windows run where java to check which binary will be used on startup.

Restart SonarQube service or run startup script

After changes restart the SonarQube service or run the startup script from the SonarQube folder so new environment variables are picked up. Watch the logs for a successful JVM load message and for any remaining path mismatches.

This tutorial covered how to identify the root cause of a missing jvm.dll error for SonarQube and the practical steps to resolve the problem by installing a compatible JDK setting JAVA_HOME and ensuring startup scripts use the correct Java binary.

Tip

Check the SonarQube logs under logs and look for wrapper messages referencing jvm.dll. That log line often names the wrong Java folder which makes troubleshooting faster than guessing.

title: Jenkins vs. Maven - How Apache Maven and Jenkins CI Compare
description: Quick comparison of Jenkins and Maven to help choose the right tool for build management and continuous integration in Java projects.
heading: Jenkins vs. Maven How Apache Maven and Jenkins CI Compare
body:
The key difference between Jenkins and Maven is that Maven manages project build and dependency lifecycle while Jenkins orchestrates continuous integration and delivery pipelines.

Maven is a build automation and dependency management tool that uses a project object model in a pom.xml file. Maven enforces a standard layout and lifecycle so developers do not argue about where compiled classes belong. Common Maven commands include mvn clean install and a rich plugin eco system handles testing packaging and publishing.

Jenkins is a continuous integration server that runs jobs pipelines and coordinates agents across machines. Jenkins triggers builds on changes schedules or manual requests and captures console output test reports and artifacts. Jenkins Pipeline as code lets teams store pipeline logic alongside source code for reproducible automation.

When to use which tool is simple and slightly boring. Use Maven to declare dependencies compile sources run tests and produce artifacts. Use Jenkins to run those Maven goals on commit on a schedule or when a developer presses an overdramatic merge button. Maven does the building and dependency resolution. Jenkins does the automation scheduling and environment orchestration.

Integration notes for people who like harnessing chaos. Configure Jenkins jobs to call Maven goals or use a Jenkins Pipeline step that runs Maven inside a container. Cache the Maven local repository on build agents to speed up repeated builds. Attach test and coverage reports to Jenkins for quick feedback loops.

Choosing both together is not cheating. Maven keeps builds consistent while Jenkins provides the automation framework that scales across teams.

Tip

Use Maven to define reproducible builds and use Jenkins to execute those builds automatically. Add a declarative Jenkins Pipeline and cache the Maven repository on agents to reduce build time and network grief.

title: Getting started with the Nexus Maven repository manager - OS
description: Quick tutorial on setting up Nexus Repository Manager OSS version 2 for Maven repos Learn to install start configure and deploy artifacts
heading: Getting started with Nexus Maven repository manager OSS version 2
body:
This tutorial shows how to install configure and use Nexus Repository Manager OSS version 2 to host and proxy Maven repositories for local development and CI pipelines.

  1. Prepare system and download Nexus
  2. Start the Nexus server
  3. Access the web UI and login
  4. Create hosted and proxy Maven repos
  5. Configure Maven to use the Nexus server
  6. Deploy and retrieve artifacts

Prepare system and download Nexus by ensuring Java is present on the host and grabbing the Nexus OSS archive from Sonatype or a trusted mirror. Unpack the distribution into a chosen directory and set file permissions for the Nexus user.

Start the Nexus server by running the start script that came with the package. Watch the logs for a successful startup message and note the port used by the server so that clients can find the service.

Access the web UI and login using the default admin credentials then change the admin password. The web console is where repository creation user management and most configuration tasks happen with fewer surprises than a corporate meeting.

Create hosted and proxy Maven repos by adding a hosted repo for internal deployments and a proxy repo that points at the central Maven repository. Group repositories if a single endpoint for clients is preferred. Assign repository names that are stable and meaningful.

Configure Maven to use the Nexus server by editing the Maven settings file and adding a server element for credentials as well as a mirror element to point Maven requests to the Nexus endpoint. Use credential encryption if security policies require more than a sticky note on the monitor.

Deploy and retrieve artifacts using standard Maven goals such as mvn deploy after updating project POM coordinates. Use mvn dependency get for quick checks. Clean up snapshots and configure retention policies to avoid a hoarder style artifact store.

This tutorial covered end to end setup from download to deploying artifacts along with basic repository types and Maven client configuration so that developers and CI systems can rely on a controlled artifact source.

Tip

Enable scheduled cleanup and configure repository groups to reduce client configuration and keep storage under control. Use role based users for CI agents rather than sharing admin credentials.

title: Bottom Up SOAP Web Service in Eclipse Example
description: Step by step Bottom Up SOAP service tutorial using Eclipse JAX WS annotations WSDL generation and testing
heading: Bottom Up SOAP Web Service in Eclipse Example Guide
body:
If you like old school XML and telling the world what each method does with a verbose WSDL then welcome. This bottom up SOAP web service tutorial walks through creating a Java service in Eclipse annotating a POJO with JAX WS publishing a WSDL and testing with SOAP UI. It is practical and slightly smug about standards compliance.

What we are building

A simple bottom up SOAP web service written in Java. The service class is the source of truth and a WSDL is generated from it. You will package a WAR deploy it to Tomcat and exercise it from SOAP UI or a generated client. Keywords to whisper at developers are SOAP JAX WS Eclipse WSDL Tomcat and SOAP UI.

Step 1 Create project and service class

Create either a Dynamic Web Project or a Maven web project in Eclipse. Add a plain Java class and annotate it with @WebService. Add @WebMethod on public methods if you want to be explicit. This POJO is your contract and will drive WSDL generation so keep method names meaningful and parameter types JAXB friendly.

Example notes

  • Use simple JAXB compatible types or annotated JAXB classes for complex types.
  • Prefer explicit namespace values in @WebService and @WebMethod annotations to avoid surprise name mismatches later.
  • Keep business logic separate from JAX WS annotations when you can. Clean code helps during debugging.

Step 2 Add dependencies and prepare deployment

You need a JAX WS implementation at runtime. Pick Metro or Apache CXF or the implementation that matches your production environment. In a Maven project add the appropriate runtime dependency and scope it so the servlet container provides what it needs. For non Maven projects copy the runtime jars into WEB INF lib.

You can rely on servlet 3 annotations to publish endpoints or use web xml. The build must produce a WAR file that Tomcat or your servlet container can explode. If you already see servlet related errors during startup check for duplicate servlet API jars on the classpath.

Step 3 Publish and generate WSDL

Start Tomcat from Eclipse or deploy the WAR. JAX WS will expose a WSDL for the published endpoint. Typically the WSDL is available by adding ?wsdl to the service URL. Confirm the endpoint address service name and namespaces in the generated WSDL match what your clients expect before you hand it over.

Step 4 Deploy to Tomcat

Drop the WAR into Tomcat webapps or use Eclipse server publishing. Watch the server log for messages that the endpoint is published. If the endpoint does not appear check for classpath conflicts servlet version mismatches and missing runtime jars. These are the usual gremlins.

Step 5 Test with SOAP UI or wsimport

Import the generated WSDL into SOAP UI for quick manual testing. For a Java client use wsimport to generate client stubs and then call the service from a test app. Send sample SOAP requests and verify responses follow your Java method logic.

Common failure points

  • Namespace mismatch between WSDL and client bindings. Fix by specifying namespace values on annotations.
  • Parameter type incompatibilities when JAXB cannot marshal or unmarshal a type. Replace with JAXB friendly types.
  • Classpath collision between the container provided JAX WS and your bundled runtime. Remove duplicates and rely on container runtime where possible.

Quick troubleshooting checklist

  • Confirm the service class has public methods annotated or implicitly exposed
  • Check server logs for binding and publishing messages
  • Compare generated WSDL element and type names with what the client expects
  • Try a simple request from SOAP UI before blaming the network

This bottom up approach is great for learning or small services because you get a WSDL that reflects your code with minimal ceremony. If the WSDL does not match expectations add explicit annotation values then rebuild and redeploy. And if all else fails take a coffee break and stare at the XML until it makes sense.

title: Fix JFrog Artifactory 2097152KB object heap startup error
description: Short guide to fix Artifactory 2097152KB object heap startup error by increasing Java heap and updating startup options for a clean start
heading: Fix JFrog Artifactory 2097152KB object heap startup error
body:
This guide shows how to fix the JFrog Artifactory 2097152KB object heap startup error by increasing Java heap and adjusting startup options for a successful launch.

  1. Check Artifactory logs and current Java heap settings
  2. Edit the Artifactory startup configuration or default file
  3. Increase Java heap and object heap parameters
  4. Restart the Artifactory service and verify successful startup

Step 1 Check the log file under $ARTIFACTORY_HOME/var/log or use journalctl for system service logs. Search for the phrase object heap or OutOfMemoryError to confirm the 2097152KB requirement. Also run ps aux | grep java to see current Java options.

Step 2 Open the startup script or default file used by the installation. For RPM and DEB installs edit /etc/opt/jfrog/artifactory/default or edit $ARTIFACTORY_HOME/bin/artifactory.default for manual installs. Find the JAVA_OPTIONS or ARTIFACTORY_JAVA_OPTIONS line.

Step 3 Increase maximum heap and object heap values to exceed 2097152KB. A safe change is to set max heap to 3G or 4G depending on available memory. Example exports are below. Adjust values for the host hardware. export ARTIFACTORY_JAVA_OPTIONS=\"-Xms512m -Xmx3072m -XX MaxDirectMemorySize=512m\" Make sure the startup user has permission to allocate that memory.

Step 4 Restart the service with the standard command for the platform. For systemd use systemctl restart artifactory.service. Watch the log tail with tail -f $ARTIFACTORY_HOME/var/log/console.log and confirm that the JVM started with new heap values and that the object heap error no longer appears.

This tutorial covered how to identify the object heap constraint, where to change startup options, and how to set larger Java heap values so Artifactory can start cleanly. The process takes a minute and prevents a lot of angry console watching later.

Tip

When increasing heap provide a buffer above the required 2097152KB and monitor memory usage after startup. Use monitoring tools to catch memory growth before the next outage.

title: Not Git, but GitHub Interview Questions
description: Concise guide to common GitHub interview questions with clear answers that help prepare for technical interviews and real world workflows.
heading: Not Git but GitHub Interview Questions Explained
body:
If you are headed into a GitHub interview and you want answers that sound smart without turning into a lecture, welcome. This is a short practical guide to the common GitHub and Git questions you will see. Expect clear facts, useful examples, and the kind of sarcasm that keeps nerves in check but not morale.

Git and GitHub explained without the buzzwords

Git is the version control system that lives on your machine. It tracks commits and branches and lets you time travel when you break something, which you will. GitHub is a hosting platform for Git that adds collaboration features like issues, pull requests, a web interface, and CI integration. Know both. Interviewers love to make sure you do.

Branch versus fork

A branch is a new line of work inside the same repository. Use it for features and fixes when you can push to the repo. A fork is a full copy under another account. Forks are how outsiders contribute to open source without needing direct write access. Pick the right tool for the social setup, not just the code.

Pull request workflow that actually works

  1. Create a branch locally and name it clearly
  2. Make small commits with descriptive messages
  3. Push that branch to GitHub
  4. Open a pull request with a summary and linked issue if one exists
  5. Request reviews and respond to feedback promptly
  6. Merge when checks pass and reviewers approve

Reviews are the quality gates and the audit trail you can point to when something goes sideways. Treat them like the safety net you hope you never need.

Merge versus rebase

Merge preserves the true history and adds a merge commit. Rebase rewrites commits on top of a new base to produce a linear history. Use rebase for a tidy history when your commits are local and have not been shared publicly. Use merge when you want the record of how branches combined. Both are valid depending on policy and context.

Resolving conflicts like a human

Conflicts happen when two changes touch the same lines. Do this

  • Pull or fetch the target branch
  • Merge or rebase locally and inspect the conflict markers
  • Use diff tools or your editor to pick the correct changes
  • Run the tests or a quick manual check
  • Commit the resolution with a clear message

Explain your resolution when you create the follow up commit or PR comment. People like context when they review a compromise.

Protected branches and required reviews

Enable branch protection to require reviews, passing checks, and to prevent force pushes. This reduces accidental breakage and enforces quality. Know how to explain the trade offs between strict protection and developer ergonomics.

Authentication options you should know

SSH keys provide secure key based access. Personal access tokens replace passwords for command line and API usage when passwords are not allowed. OAuth apps and GitHub Apps are used for integrations with more granular permissions. Mention least privilege when asked about security.

GitHub Actions basics

Actions automate builds, tests, and deployments on events like push or pull request. Start simple with a workflow that runs tests and then expand with reusable actions and environment specific deployments. Know how to read a workflow YAML file and where to look for logs when things fail.

Security and best practices

  • Scan dependencies and automate alerts
  • Do not commit secrets and rotate keys if they leak
  • Use protected branches and required checks
  • Grant the smallest permissions needed to teams and tokens

Open source etiquette that wins hearts

Follow contribution guidelines, write helpful PR descriptions, link issues to changes, and respond professionally to feedback. Be patient and assume good intent.

Interview tips and a demo suggestion

Practice answering these questions out loud. If asked for a live demo show a short workflow on a private test repo. Create a branch, commit a small change, push, open a pull request, and explain your merge strategy. That sequence proves you know the tools and you can use them without panic.

If you want a cheat sheet or a small test repo to rehearse with, ask for one and I will not judge your commit messages. Much.
seo_title: Master GitHub Interview Questions With Practical Answers
seo_heading: Common GitHub topics to ace version control and pull request interviews

title: Jenkins Interview Questions
description: Top Jenkins interview questions with concise answers for DevOps roles Learn pipelines jobs agents plugins and best practices
heading: Jenkins Interview Questions for DevOps Engineers
body:
This article prepares candidates for common Jenkins interview questions with clear answers and practical concepts.

  1. What is Jenkins Jenkins is an open source automation server used for continuous integration and continuous delivery of software projects. It orchestrates build test and deploy workflows across teams.
  2. Master and agents The master schedules jobs and stores configuration while agents run build tasks. Use agents to scale workloads and isolate environments.
  3. Freestyle job versus Pipeline Freestyle jobs are simple GUI driven tasks. Pipeline provides code driven workflows defined in a Jenkinsfile that travel with source code and support complex logic.
  4. Declarative versus Scripted pipelines Declarative pipelines offer a structured simpler syntax with good defaults. Scripted pipelines provide full Groovy control for advanced use cases.
  5. Typical pipeline example Use a Jenkinsfile to define stages and steps. Example code snippet pipeline { agent any stages { stage('Build') { steps { echo 'Building' } } stage('Test') { steps { echo 'Testing' } } stage('Deploy') { steps { echo 'Deploying' } } } }
  6. Handling credentials Store secrets in the Credentials store and reference credentials by id in pipeline steps. Avoid printing sensitive values to logs.
  7. Common plugins to know Pipeline plugin credentials plugin Git plugin Blue Ocean and Kubernetes plugin often come up in interviews. Explain why each helps a delivery pipeline.
  8. Scaling and reliability Use distributed agents container based builds and pipeline as code. Configure backups of the Jenkins home directory and use role based access controls for security.

Practice explaining a full pipeline from commit to deployment and be ready to read a Jenkinsfile during an interview. Demonstrate knowledge of where logs live how to troubleshoot failed stages and how to secure secret data.

Tip

Bring a small concrete example such as a Jenkinsfile for a simple build and test flow. Showing a real snippet beats abstract talk and makes answers memorable.
